parentSessionTitle: Global Gateway Posters Day 1
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Personal financial literacy influences wellbeing, particularly during the transition from residency to independent practice when residents transform into small business owners. Despite growing emphasis on wellness, many residency programs provide little education on financial management. This study evaluated the financial literacy of graduating Canadian urology residents in comparison to staff urologists. It also examined perceptions of financial competence and the frequency of financial discussions between both groups. METHODS: We conducted a cross-sectional survey study at a national preparatory exam for graduating Canadian urology residents. The survey was administered to all residents and faculty attending the event and the response rate was 100% in both groups. We created a 40-item survey with demographic questions (11), Likert scale questions about comfort and perception of financial literacy (5), reimbursement-related questions to a urology practice (12), and validated financial literacy questions (9 true/false, 11 multiple choice). Descriptive statistics were generated and responses were analyzed using Welch’s t-test for group comparisons. RESULTS: A total of 38 residents and 13 staff completed the survey. Staff achieved higher objective financial literacy scores (77% vs. 63%; p=0.004). Staff also reported a greater perception in financial literacy skills (p<0.05). Both groups viewed financial literacy as highly important (p-0.765). Most respondents felt finances were discussed “not enough” during residency. Regarding reimbursement, both groups were equally likely to be wrong about true compensation with a delta varying from 0.4% to 44.1%. CONCLUSIONS: Staff urologists outperformed residents in both validated financial literacy questions and perceived self-competence in financial literacy. Despite these differences, both groups indicated a lack of adequate discussion of financial topics during residency. Discrepancies in perceived versus actual reimbursement underscores the importance of structured financial education within residency programs to ease the transition to practice.

title: GG01-37: To circ or not to circ — that is the question for patients with posterior urethral valves
parentSessionTitle: Global Gateway Posters Day 1
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Antibiotic prophylaxis (AP) and circumcision are commonly used to prevent urinary tract infections (UTIs) in children with posterior urethral valves (PUV), but there is insufficient research examining their efficacy when used together. This study compared the effectiveness of AP when used alone and in combination with circumcision in preventing UTIs in PUV patients. METHODS: We retrospectively reviewed PUV patients managed at our institution from 2000-2019 with a 2-year follow-up period after initial presentation. Patients were classified as ‘AP-only’ if they received AP but not circumcision, or if circumcision occurred after AP initiation due to breakthrough UTIs. Patients were classified as ‘combined treatment’ if they received both AP and circumcision without intervening UTIs. UTIs were defined based on patient symptoms, microbiological confirmation, and/or clinical documentation. An inverse probability-weighted multivariable Poisson regression model was used to compare UTI incidence rates between treatment groups, while accounting for informative censoring due to treatment change and adjusting for neonatal intensive care unit (NICU) admission status, distance to hospital, and socioeconomic deprivation. RESULTS: Out of 61 patients with PUV, 41 received AP only (67.2%), 12 received combined treatment (19.7%), 4 received circumcision only (6.6%), and 4 received none of the two interventions (6.6%). Median age at circumcision, AP initiation, and first UTI was 120 days (interquartile range (IQR) 32, 355), 11 days (IQR 2, 40), and 52 days (IQR 18, 132), respectively. The incidence rate of UTIs in the AP-only group was 0.17 per person-year (95% CI 0.14, 0.22), and 0.05 per-person year in the combined treatment group (95% CI 0.02, 0.11). Multivariable analysis showed that patients who received combined treatment had a 74% lower UTI incidence rate compared to those who received only AP (incidence rate ratio 0.26; 95% CI 0.10, 0.65; p=0.004). Greater patient distance from hospital (p=0.02) and greater socioeconomic deprivation (p=0.005) were each associated with higher UTI rates, whereas NICU admission was not significant (p=0.83). CONCLUSIONS: Combined treatment of circumcision with AP may be more effective than AP alone in preventing UTIs in PUV patients. In our cohort, geographical proximity to hospital and degree of socioeconomic deprivation were predictive of UTI occurrence. Further investigation through implementation of a national, multicenter PUV registry could inform future practices in the management of UTIs in PUV patients.

title: GG01-38: Leveraging Machine Learning Algorithms to Predict the Risk of Pathological Extraprostatic Extension After Robotic-Assisted Radical Prostatectomy
parentSessionTitle: Global Gateway Posters Day 1
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Pathological extraprostatic extension (pEPE) is an important prognostic indicator that is linked to increased risk of prostate cancer recurrence after robotic-assisted radical prostatectomy (RARP) and may influence decisions about adjuvant therapy. However, pEPE usually remains undiscovered until operative specimens are sent for pathology. While multi-parametric MRI has improved preoperative local staging, other preoperative variables may improve risk stratification for pEPE. Our study aimed to train machine learning models to use a comprehensive set of preoperative clinical, pathological, and MRI features to predict pathological pEPE after RARP. METHODS: Our database included 610 patients who underwent RARP. Preoperative variables that served as inputs to our models included age, BMI, PSA, clinical stage, PIRADS score, and biopsy features. Preoperative variables missing < 5% of their values were imputed with the mode or mean. The rest were imputed with multivariate imputation by chained equations (MICE). The database was split into training (80%, n=488) and testing (20%, n=122) sets. Multiple machine learning classifiers, including logistic regression, random forest (RF), xgboost, support vector machine, k-Nearest Neighbors, adaboost, and catboost were trained to predict pEPE status. Each model's hyperparameters were optimized using 5-fold cross validation on the training set. Final performance was evaluated on the test set using AUROC, sensitivity, specificity, positive predictive value (PPV), and negative predictive value (NPV). An error analysis was conducted on the best-performing model. RESULTS: 30% of patients in our database had positive pEPE status. The tuned random forest (RF) was the winning predictor of pEPE, with the highest AUROC (0.83). RF’s main strengths were its high specificity (0.89) and NPV (0.83). It achieved modest sensitivity (0.57) and moderate PPV (0.7). Fraction of cores that were positive and maximum percent positivity were the top contributors to the RF. Error analysis revealed that most of RF's false negatives (12/13) and false positives (6/7) occurred in patients with high-risk PIRADs of 4 or 5. This highlighted the unreliability of a high PIRADS score in the database: our best model was unable to find strong-enough patterns in the other pre-op variables to robustly stratify risk within this subgroup. CONCLUSIONS: Our study shows that considering the full preoperative picture can allow machine learning algorithms to predict postoperative pathologic EPE with high specificity and NPV. This can enable robust identification of low-risk patients, which can improve patient counseling before RARP.

title: GG01-39: The Value of Intraoperative point-of-care Urinalysis to Predict Positive Urine Cultures and Symptomatic Post-operative Infections During Cystoscopic procedures for Pediatric Patients
parentSessionTitle: Global Gateway Posters Day 1
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: To evaluate intraoperative point-of-care urinalysis (UA) for predicting positive urine cultures and postoperative UTIs in children undergoing cystoscopy, and to assess its potential to reduce unnecessary cultures and antibiotics. METHODS: In this retrospective cohort at a tertiary pediatric urology center (Aug 2023–Apr 2024), 62 cystoscopy cases with paired dipstick UA and quantitative culture were analyzed after excluding recent antibiotic use or incomplete data. Dipstick markers—leukocyte esterase and nitrite—were evaluated alone and combined (“either-positive” vs. “both-positive”). Positive culture was defined as≥105CFU/mL; postoperative UTI required fever, clinical signs, and a positive culture within 7 days. Diagnostic accuracy was assessed by ROC curves andχ2tests. A multivariable logistic regression adjusted for age, sex, procedure, laterality, and clinical condition. A retrospective QI model estimated reductions in culture orders and empiric antibiotics. RESULTS: Thirty-nine patients (62.9%) were dipstick-negative by the ‘either-positive’ rule; one had a positive culture (NPV 97.4%; 95% CI 86.5–99.9%). Of 23 dipstick-positive patients, 13 (56.5%) had positive cultures. In multivariable analysis, “either-positive” dipstick was the sole predictor of culture positivity (OR 330.2; 95% CI 30.5–3 574.1; p=0.003). QI modeling indicated that restricting cultures to the 23 dipstick-positive specimens would have averted 39 of 62 cultures (62.9%), at the expense of missing one infection (2.6% of un-cultured cases). CONCLUSIONS: Intraoperative dipstick UA reliably identifies pediatric cystoscopy patients at low risk for postoperative UTI, offering a rapid, cost-effective tool to enhance antimicrobial stewardship and reduce laboratory utilization. Prospective multicenter validation is recommended. | | | --- | | |

title: GG01-40: Phase 1/2 study of an anti-PD-L1/IL-15 variant fusion protein (SIM0237) in BCG-unresponsive high-risk non-muscle-invasive bladder cancer (NMIBC)
parentSessionTitle: Global Gateway Posters Day 1
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Treatment options for BCG-unresponsive (UR) NMIBC are limited. Anti-PD-1 monotherapy and IL-15 agonist in combination with BCG have shown clinical efficacy in BCG-UR carcinoma in situ (CIS) NMIBC. It remains unclear whether targeting both PD-(L)1 and IL-15 has synergistic effect in NMIBC. SIM0237 is an anti-PD-L1/IL-15 variant fusion protein. The single agent showed good safety profile and promising efficacy signal in patients with BCG-UR NMIBC in the dose escalation part. This abstract reported data from the dose escalation and expansion parts of SIM0237 monotherapy from the ongoing Phase 1/2 study (NCT06186414). METHODS: Patients with BCG-UR high-risk NMIBC received intravesical SIM0237 following the standard induction/maintenance treatment schedule. A re-induction course was allowed if the patients had persistent CIS or high-grade Ta at Month 3. Key study endpoints included DLT, safety, tolerability, PK and efficacy \[complete response (CR) rate and duration\ of CR for CIS NMIBC, disease-free survival (DFS) and DFS rate at specific time points\ for papillary-only NMIBC\]. RESULTS: From January 10, 2024 to the data cutoff date of August 8, 2025, a total of 43 patients (10 CIS with or without Ta/T1, 33 papillary-only) have received SIM0237 monotherapy, with 3, 10 and 30 patients at the dose levels of 75 mg, 150 mg and 300 mg, respectively. The median age was 62 years, with 81% male. The median number of prior BCG doses was 13\. Of the 7 CIS patients who had at least 1 post-baseline tumor assessment, 6 achieved a best response of CR and 5 were maintaining the CR status. In the 33 papillary-only patients, the median follow-up duration was 4.57 months. The median DFS was immature, with a 12-month DFS rate of 75.4% (95% CI, 48.9%-89.4%). TEAEs occurred in 38 (88.4%) patients and 23 (53.5%) patients had TRAEs. The majority of TRAEs were Grade 1/2 and limited in the urinary system. Nine (20.9%) patients had Grade 3 TEAEs and 1 (2.3%) had Grade 3 TRAEs. No Grade 4 or 5 TEAEs were reported. Four (9.3%) patients had SAEs and 1 had TRSAEs of urinary bladder haemorrhage and prostatic haemorrhage. Ten (23.3%) patients had dose interruptions due to TEAEs, and 4 (9.3%) had dose interruptions due to TRAEs. No DLT, immune-related AE or AE leading to SIM0237 discontinuation. PK data showed undetectable systemic exposure of SIM0237 in all 29 patients with serum samples analyzed. CONCLUSIONS: Intravesical SIM0237 was safe and well tolerated with promising clinical efficacy in patients with BCG-UR high-risk NMIBC. The Phase 3 study of SIM0237 monotherapy in this patient population is under plan.

title: GG01-41: Sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitors use in prostate cancer patients undergoing hormone therapy: a sequential target trial emulation study
parentSessionTitle: Global Gateway Posters Day 1
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Emerging evidence suggests that sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitors (SGLT2i) may be inversely associated with the risk of prostate cancer (PCa). This target trial emulation (TTE) study is designed to evaluate the impact of SGLT2i use on clinical outcomes in PCa patients undergoing hormone therapy (HT). METHODS: This TTE utilized electronic health records of the Hong Kong population between March 2000 and March 2025. A sequential TTE design was applied with monthly intervals. The study outcomes were: time to androgen deprivation therapy (ADT) failure, time to next-generation hormonal agent (NHA) failure, and overall survival (OS). Study outcomes were analyzed using marginal structural models fitted via weighted pooled logistic regression, with inverse probability weighting to address time-varying confounding and informative censoring. RESULTS: A total of 712 PCa patients who received both HT and SGLT2i for diabetes were identified, and 1167 non-diabetic PCa (non-SGLT2i) patients who underwent HT were included as the control group. SGLT2i use was significantly associated with improved time to ADT failure (hazard ratio, HR=0.65, 95% confidence interval, 95% CI: 0.43-0.97, p=0.036) and overall survival (HR=0.32, 95% CI: 0.21-0.50, p<0.001). However, a non-significant reduced risk was observed for NHA failure (HR=0.68, 95% CI: 0.38-1.21, p=0.188). Subgroup analysis comparing two SGLT2is (i. e., dapagliflozin and empagliflozin) indicated that dapagliflozin was associated with significantly greater protective effects on the overall survival compared to empagliflozin (HR=0.32, 95% CI: 0.12-0.85, p=0.022), whereas no significant differences were observed in terms of the other outcomes. CONCLUSIONS: The use of SGLT2i in PCa patients receiving HT was associated with a significantly reduced risk of disease progression and mortality.

title: GG01-42: Cardiologic and Oncologic Outcomes with GLP-1 Receptor Agonists in Men Receiving Androgen Deprivation Therapy for Prostate Cancer
parentSessionTitle: Global Gateway Posters Day 1
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Androgen deprivation therapy (ADT) is the backbone of treatment of advanced prostate cancer (PCa), however it is associated with adverse metabolic changes and cardiovascular toxicity. Accordingly, a significant proportion of PCa mortality is attributed to cardiovascular diseases. Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1RA) improve glycemic control and reduce cardiovascular events in diabetes, but evidence in men with PCa receiving ADT is limited. We aimed to assess survival and cardiovascular outcomes in men with type II diabetes (T2DM) on ADT who received GLP-1RA. METHODS: We performed a retrospective cohort study using the Hungarian National Health Insurance Fund (NEAK) database. Men with PCa initiating ADT between 2018-2024 were identified and classified to exposure groups: (1) T2DM with GLP-1RA use; (2) T2DM with metformin but no GLP-1RA use; (3) T2DM with no metformin and GLP-1RA therapy (4) no diabetes and no GLP-1RA therapy. The primary outcome was the incidence of major adverse cardiovascular events (non-fatal and fatal acute myocardial infarction and stroke); secondary outcomes included individual cardiovascular events, overall survival (OS), time to next treatment (TNT). RESULTS: A total of 13,944 men with prostate cancer initiating ADT (of which 2758 with T2DM) between 2018–2024 were included in the analysis. Of these, 135 had type 2 diabetes treated with iGLP-1RA, 1,582 were treated with metformin, 1,041 received other antidiabetic medications (non-incretin, non-metformin), and 10,708 had no diabetes. The median age (IQR) was 70 years (66–75) for incretin users, 73 (68–77) for metformin users, 74 (69–78) for non-incretin non-metformin users, and 73 (68–78) for non-diabetic men. Baseline cardioascular characteristics were balanced across biabetic study groups and markedly better for non-diabetic men. Median time to next treatment or death was 0.7 years (IQR 0.1–1.6) in incretin users, 0.8 years (0.2–1.8) in metformin, 0.9 years (0.2–1.9) in non-incretin non-metformin, and 1.1 years (0.5–2.1) years among non-diabetic men. Median overall survival was 1.7 years (IQR 0.9–2.7) among incretin users, 1.7 (0.8–2.6) in metformin, 1.4 (0.7–2.8) in non-incretin non-metformin, and 1.4 (0.6–2.5) years in non-diabetic men. The raw incidence of major adverse cardiovascular events was 32% in incretin users, compared with 52% in non-incretin non-metformin, 43% in metformin, and 35% in non-diabetic men. CONCLUSIONS: Patients with PCa and T2DM receiving ADT are at an elevated risk of cardiovascular morbidity and mortality. These preliminary results support consideration of GLP-1RAs for further prospective validation to mitigate the cardiovascular toxicity associated with ADT use.

title: GG01-43: Feasibility and Outcomes of Supine Mini-PCNL in Children Using a Digital Disposable Nephroscope with Vacuum-Assisted Suction Access Sheath: Early Clinical Experience
parentSessionTitle: Global Gateway Posters Day 1
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Supine percutaneous nephrolithotomy (S-PCNL) in children is technically challenging due to smaller renal anatomy, limited working space, and higher risks of bleeding or fluid overload. Safe access and effective instrument manoeuvrability require miniaturized equipment, precise technique, and considerable surgical expertise. Owing to its advantages of maintaining low intrarenal pressure, reducing operative time, and enhancing safety, we prospectively evaluated the feasibility and outcomes of using a vacuum-assisted suction sheath (VASS) in combination with a digital disposable nephroscope in paediatric patients. METHODS: Prospectively maintained records of 963 patients who underwent S-PCNL were analysed following institutional review board approval. Between January 2024 and September 2025, 23 paediatric patients who underwent S-PCNL using a VASS with a mini digital disposable nephroscope were identified. Baseline demographics, radiological findings, stone characteristics, urine cultures, 30-day non-contrast CT (NCCT) stone-free rates (SFR), postoperative infections, transfusion requirements, auxiliary procedures, and hospital stay were evaluated. Feasibility of achieving single puncture access per pelvicalyceal system (PCS), sheath manoeuvrability, and need for additional punctures were documented. Residual fragments (RF) were classified as follows: Grade A—stone-free (no RF), Grade B—single fragment≤4 mm, and Grade C—any fragment >4 mm or multiple fragments. RESULTS: Mean age of the patients was 10.6 years, including 17 males and 6 females. Most cases were Guy’s Stone Score (GSS) Grade II, with a mean stone size of 1.8 ± 0.3 cm; 25% had additional secondary stones. All procedures were performed under general anaesthesia using fluoroscopy-guided single-pass access with a 16/18 Fr sheath in the flank-oblique supine modified lithotomy (FOSML) position. Stone fragmentation was achieved using a digital disposable nephroscope with Holmium:YAG laser, and fragments were evacuated through the VASS. Mean operative time was 38.4 ± 14 minutes, with a mean VASS activation time of 16 ± 8 minutes. Complete clearance through a single tract was achieved in all patients, with no additional punctures required. Zero residual fragments (ZRF) were observed in 20 (87%) patients, and only one required an auxiliary procedure for residual calculi. Mean hospital stay was two days, and no perioperative mortality occurred. The VASS sheath demonstrated excellent manoeuvrability within the PCS, allowing complete access without increased bleeding. CONCLUSIONS: Supine mini-PCNL using a digital disposable nephroscope with a VASS is safe, feasible, and effective in children. It provides high stone-free rates, minimal morbidity, and short hospital stays. These encouraging outcomes support its potential as a preferred approach for paediatric renal stone management.

title: GG01-44: Deep Machine Learning Ensemble Model for Emphysematous Pyelonephritis Classification and Clinical Decision Intelligence
parentSessionTitle: Global Gateway Posters Day 1
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Emphysematous pyelonephritis (EPN) is a life-threatening necrotizing renal infection with mortality rates of 10–40%, requiring urgent intervention. The Huang–Tseng CT classification depends on subjective interpretation, often delaying decisions. EPN-CDI was developed as an AI-driven clinical decision support system integrating deep-learning segmentation and ensemble machine learning for automated EPN classification, severity assessment, and treatment recommendations. METHODS: EPN-CDI is an ensemble machine learning system combining automated CT segmentation (nnU-Net), radiomics feature extraction (PyRadiomics), and machine learning models (Random Forest, XGBoost, LightGBM) for outcome prediction. CT DICOM images underwent automated segmentation using nnU-Net v2. Radiomics features were extracted including first-order statistics, texture matrices (GLCM, GLRLM, GLSZM, GLDM, NGTDM), and morphological descriptors. Clinical parameters included demographics, vital signs, laboratory values (creatinine, eGFR, inflammatory markers, electrolytes), comorbidities, and microbiology. The system predicted: (1) Huang-Tseng classification, (2) ICU/HDU/Ward admission, (3) mortality probability, (4) dialysis requirement, and (5) treatment modality. Modified NEWS2, GREMP score (Gas, Renal impairment, Extended collection, Mental state, Platelets), and EPN-specific severity indices were integrated, generating automated PDF reports with therapeutic guidance. Internal validation included 194 patients with CT-confirmed EPN from a tertiary center. RESULTS: Automated segmentation achieved mean Dice coefficient 0.89 ± 0.03 for gas mapping. Ensemble model performance: classification AUC 0.91 (95% CI 0.87–0.95; accuracy 89.2%), mortality AUC 0.86, ICU need AUC 0.88—superior to NEWS2 (0.79) and radiologic grading (0.74; p0.05). Treatment recommendation concordance reached AUC 0.90 (sensitivity 89.8%, specificity 92.7%). Independent predictors included gas volume >30% of parenchyma (p=0.012), creatinine >3 mg/dL (p=0.021), and platelets 100×109/L (p=0.009). Full report generation was completed in mean 4.2 ± 1.3 minutes versus 45–60 minutes for traditional evaluation (p0.001), and inter-reader agreement improved (κ=0.84 vs 0.67). CONCLUSIONS: EPN-CDI enables rapid, objective, and accurate EPN classification, risk prediction, and treatment guidance, outperforming existing scores and radiologic grading. Its integration could standardize care, expedite critical decisions, and improve outcomes. Prospective multicenter validation is warranted.

title: GG01-45: Successful Non-Operative Salvage of Glans Ischemia Following Chordee Correction: A Two-Case Report
parentSessionTitle: Global Gateway Posters Day 1

speakers.organization: Kulkarni Uro Surgery Institue, Urokul Hospital

fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Glans ischemia is a rare urological emergency, and its occurrence following major penile reconstruction is exceptional. We report two cases of glans ischemia after chordee correction utilising a bovine pericardial graft. METHODS: Two patients developed dusky discoloration and cyanosis of the glans on postoperative day 3 and 6, respectively after undergoing chordee correction with bovine pericardium graft repair. Color Doppler ultrasound confirmed significantly reduced vascular flow, suggesting a delayed thrombotic or inflammatory etiology. A multimodal, non-operative management protocol was immediately initiated, consisting of antiplatelet therapy (Acetylsalicylic acid 75 mg), anticoagulation (Enoxaparin 60 mg), systemic vasodilators (Pentoxifylline 400 mg, Tadalafil 5 mg), and a course of five 90-minute Hyperbaric Oxygen Therapy (HBOT) sessions at 1.6–2.0 ATA. RESULTS: Clinical improvement was noted within 48 hours of initiating therapy. Substantial restoration of glans perfusion was observed after the third HBOT session, leading to complete resolution of ischemia in both patients. In total 5 sessions of HBOT were given for both. At 6-month follow-up, both individuals were asymptomatic, demonstrating normal glans appearance with no residual functional or cosmetic impairment. CONCLUSIONS: Glans ischemia is a rare but critical complication following complex penile surgery. These cases demonstrate that prompt recognition and aggressive, multimodal conservative management, integrating targeted pharmacotherapy with HBOT, can be highly effective in salvaging the glans penis, obviating the need for surgical intervention and yielding excellent long-term outcomes.

title: GG01-46: Urethral Diverticula Without Surgical Removal – Are We Lucky or Mistaken?
parentSessionTitle: Global Gateway Posters Day 1
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: The reported incidence of urethral diverticula ranges between 0.02% and 6%. The natural history of this condition remains poorly understood, and there is no consensus regarding which patients require surgical treatment or the optimal timing of intervention. Currently, most patients diagnosed with urethral diverticula are offered surgery, even if asymptomatic. This study aimed to evaluate the natural history of women with urethral diverticula who were managed without surgical intervention due to various reasons. METHODS: We conducted a retrospective analysis of patients diagnosed with urethral diverticula, with a minimum follow-up of 12 months. Demographic and clinical data, physical examination findings, imaging results, treatment type, and outcomes were analyzed. In addition, a telephone survey was performed. RESULTS: Of 125 women diagnosed with urethral diverticula, since 2006 31 women (aged 18–58 years; mean 35.8 years) did not undergo surgical treatment at diagnosis and met inclusion criteria. Sixteen symptomatic patients comprised Group 1, and 15 asymptomatic patients comprised Group 2.· In Group 1, four patients underwent puncture and drainage, and eight experienced spontaneous drainage. Six women (37.5%) eventually required surgery, between 1 and 20 years after diagnosis.· In Group 2, one patient had spontaneous drainage of the mass without recurrence, and only one patient (6.6%) underwent surgery. One patient was lost to follow-up. Overall, 22.6% of patients required surgery following an initial conservative approach: 37.5% of symptomatic women and 6.6% of asymptomatic women. CONCLUSIONS: Most asymptomatic patients with urethral diverticula can be safely managed with observation alone. Spontaneous drainage may lead to regression of the mass, further supporting conservative management as a reasonable option. Based on these findings, we suggest that the natural history of this condition more closely resembles that of paraurethral retention cysts rather than true diverticula.

title: GG01-47: Study on Functionalized Nanoparticle Drug Delivery System Modified by Sertoli Cell Membrane for Improving Cytoxan-Induced Testicular Injury
parentSessionTitle: Global Gateway Posters Day 1
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: With the younger age of cancer patients and the improvement of cancer treatment efficacy, fertility preservation in cancer patients has gradually become a new issue during cancer treatment. Cytoxan is a common used alkylating agent in cancer chemotherapy, but it has reproductive toxicity, which often leads to an increase in the level of reactive oxygen species in the tests and subsequent damage. Superoxide dismutase is the key to reducing ROS level; however, clinically, it is difficult to reduce testicular ROS levels through conventional drug delivery methods due to the low efficiency of testicular-targeted delivery and the presence of the blood-testis barrier. This study aims to design and synathesize a material that can be targeted to the tests, reduce testicular ROS levels, and thereby improve cytoxan-induced testicular injury, providing a new method for fertility protection in male cancer patients. METHODS: CAT-SchA@SCM was synthesized using techniques. The testicular accumulation of CAT-SchA@SCM was detected via immunofluorescence. To verify whether CAT-SchA@SCM could cross the blood-testis barrier (BTB), a BTB model was established in vitro using TM-4 cells. Testicular cell lines were treated with 4-hydroperoxycyclophosphamide (4-HC), a metabolite of cytoxan in vivo. A mouse model of cytoxan-induced testicular injury was established by intraperitoneal injection of cytoxan, followed by CAT-SchA@SCM injection for treatment. RESULTS: We designed and synthesized the CAT-SchA@SCM material using techniques including protein self-assembly and ultrasonic emulsification. Dynamic Light Scattering (DLS) and Transmission Electron Microscopy (TEM) analyses showed that the nanoparticles had a subspherical shape, along with good uniformity and stability. Probe labeling and immunofluorescence staining results demonstrated that CAT-SchA@SCM could accumulate in testicular tissue. Using an in vitro constructed BTB model, we found that CAT-SchA@SCM was capable of crossing the BTB. Cell line experiments indicated that CAT-SchA@SCM could significantly reduce the reactive oxygen species (ROS) levels in TM-4 cells and improve cell viability. Animal experiments showed that CAT-SchA@SCM could restore the testis weight, testis-to-body weight ratio, sperm motility and progressive motility, as well as the number of various testicular cell types in mice after cytoxan induction—suggesting that CAT-SchA@SCM could reverse cytoxan-induced testicular injury. Hematoxylin-eosin (H&E) staining of tissue sections from major organs revealed that CAT-SchA@SCM had no impact on the morphology of various tissues, indicating its biosafety at the therapeutic concentration. CONCLUSIONS: We designed and prepared CAT-SchA@SCM, a material encapsulated by Sertoli cell membranes and loaded with catalase (CAT) and schisandrin A (SchA). It was confirmed that this material could efficiently accumulate in testicular tissue and cross the BTB. Cell and animal experiments showed that CAT-SchA@SCM could significantly alleviate testicular tissue and cell damage induced by cytoxan and its metabolites. This study provides a new approach for fertility protection in male cancer patients.

title: GG01-48: Predictive and Prognostic Value of Biopsy Gleason Pattern 4 Proportion in Localized Prostate Cancer
parentSessionTitle: Global Gateway Posters Day 1
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Several policymakers have proposed that patients with intermediate-risk prostate cancer (PC) and a limited amount of Gleason pattern 4 (GP4) disease may be suitable candidates for active surveillance (AS). However, the supporting scientific evidence remains limited, and no consensus has yet been established on this issue. The aim of our study was to assess the predictive and prognostic value of the total extent of GP4 in prostate biopsies on the final pathologic findings after radical prostatectomy (RP) and oncologic outcomes during follow-up. METHODS: In this single-center retrospective cohort study, we included consecutive patients who underwent combined targeted and systematic prostate biopsies revealing international society of urological pathology (ISUP) grade group 1 to 3 prostate cancer, followed by RP between January 2015 and December 2024. All histologic samples were independently reviewed by a dedicated uropathologist. The amount of GP4 was quantified as the total length (mm) of pattern 4 carcinoma divided by the total length (mm) of carcinoma across all biopsy cores. GP4 thresholds were determined using the Youden and Liu indices. Logistic regression analyses were performed to assess associations with adverse pathological features, while Cox proportional hazards models were used to estimate biochemical recurrence-free survival (RFS) and metastasis-free survival (MFS). RESULTS: Among 247 patients included in the analysis, 78 (32%) had ISUP grade group 1, 126 (51%) had grade group 2, and 43 (17%) had grade group 3 disease on biopsy. The median age was 73 years (interquartile range \[IQR\] 68–77). A GP4 cut-off of 10% was identified as being associated with locally advanced disease (standard error 3.4, p=0.003), and a cut-off of 14% was associated with pathological upgrading at RP (standard error 2.7, p<0.001). Overall, 163 patients (66%) had a GP4 extent of less than 10%. In multivariable logistic regression analysis, a GP4 extent <10% was independently associated with lower likelihood of locally advanced disease (odds ratio \[OR\] 0.17, 95% confidence interval \[CI\] 0.08–0.33, p<0.001). During a median follow-up of 46 months, 51 patients (21%) experienced biochemical recurrence, and 9 patients (4%) developed metastases. In multivariable Cox regression analysis, a GP4 extent <10% was independently associated with improved RFS (hazard ratio \[HR\] 0.48, 95% CI 0.25– 0.93, p=0.03) and MFS (HR 0.08, 95% CI 0.02–0.45, p=0.004). CONCLUSIONS: In patients with localized PC, a GP4 extent below 10% on biopsy was strongly associated with more favorable pathological findings and improved oncologic outcomes. These results support the role of quantitative GP4 assessment in refining risk stratification and identifying candidates for AS among selected intermediate-risk patients.

GG02-21
                        The diagnostic accuracy of MRI for diagnosing intra-
                        prostatic cancer after previous radiotherapy: a
                        systematic-review and meta-analysis
                        Ali Abdul Hussein, Archana Gopalakrishnan, Nikhil Mayor, Hashim U. Ahmed, Taimur T. Shah, Alexander Light

INTRODUCTION
Approximately 25% of patients treated for
prostate cancer will develop biochemical
failure after radiotherapy within 10-15
years. Over a third of these patients
potentially have intra-prostatic recurrent
cancer and could be candidates for local
salvage treatment. MRI is first-line for

title: GG02-34: De Ritis ratio as a prognostic marker in patients with metastatic hormone-sensitive prostate cancer treated with upfront therapy

fulltext:
De Ritis ratio as a prognostic marker in patients with metastatic hormone-sensitive
 prostate cancer treated with upfront therapy                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                 GG02-34
N. Fujita1,*, T. Ichiyama1, D. Noro1, F. Yoneyama1, S. Tazawa1, H. Murasawa1, H. Horiguchi1, K. Ishimoto1, J. Narita1, W. Fukuokaya2, T. Yanagisawa2, S. Narita3, T. Kimura2, T. Habuchi3, and S. Hatakeyama1
1Department of Urology, Hirosaki University Graduate School of Medicine, Hirosaki, Japan; 2Department of Urology, The Jikei University, School of Medicine, Tokyo, Japan; 3Department of Urology, Akita

University School of Medicine, Akita, Japan
*Corresponding author’s E-mail address: naonao707012@hirosaki-u.ac.jp
Background
 The De Ritis ratio, defined as the serum aspartate aminotransferase to alanine aminotransferase ratio, has been reported as a prognostic biomarker in various malignancies, reflecting tumor metabolic activity
 and systemic inflammation.
   Despite its growing relevance in oncology, the prognostic significance of the De Ritis ratio in patients with metastatic hormone-sensitive prostate cancer (mHSPC) receiving upfront therapy remains poorly
   understood.

Methods
   This multicenter retrospective study included 1,204 patients with mHSPC who received upfront therapy between December 2015 and September 2025.
   The treatment regimens consisted of docetaxel, androgen receptor signaling inhibitors, or a combination of docetaxel and darolutamide.
   The De Ritis ratio was measured at the time of mHSPC diagnosis. The optimal cut-off value for predicting progression to castration-resistant prostate cancer (CRPC) was determined using receiver operating
   characteristic curve analysis. Patients were stratified into two groups based on the De Ritis ratio: lower and higher.
   Multivariable Cox proportional hazards regression analyses were performed to evaluate the impact of a higher De Ritis ratio on CRPC-free survival and overall survival (OS).

Results
   The median age and follow-up duration were 70 years and 55 months, respectively.
   The median De Ritis ratio was 1.3, and the optimal cut-off value was determined to be 1.8. Among the 1,204 patients, 231 (19%) had a De Ritis ratio above the cut-off (Fig. 1).
   Although the rate of PSA decline ≥90% was lower in the higher De Ritis ratio group, the difference was not statistically significant (Fig. 2).
   In contrast, the rate of PSA decline ≥99% was significantly lower in the higher ratio group compared to the lower ratio group (Fig. 3).
   Both CRPC-free survival (Fig. 4) and OS (Fig. 5) were significantly shorter in the higher De Ritis ratio group.
   After adjusting for age, performance status, Gleason score ≥8, CHHATED high-volume disease, initial PSA level, hemoglobin <12g/dL, and LDH ≥326 U/L, a higher De Ritis ratio remained independently
   associated with shorter CRPC-free survival and OS (Fig. 6).

  However, due to the limited sample size, definitive conclusions could not be drawn. Therefore, the present study aimed to externally validate this risk model in a larger, independent cohort.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                       Months

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   Sci Rep. 2025;15:10814.

Methods
  This multicenter retrospective study included 794 patients with mCRPC who received Ra-223 treatment.
  First, multivariable Cox proportional hazards regression analysis was performed to assess the association between OS from Ra-223 initiation and the three previously identified risk factors: EOD >1, incomplete
  Ra-223 treatment (<6 cycles), and PSA >10 ng/mL at the start of Ra-223.
  Patients were then stratified based on the number of these risk factors. OS was estimated using the Kaplan–Meier method and compared across groups using the log-rank test.
  Furthermore, the predictive performance of these factors for 2-year and 3-year OS was evaluated using receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve analysis.

Results
  The median age at Ra-223 initiation was 75 years. The median follow-up durations from CRPC diagnosis and Ra-223 initiation were 36 and 16 months, respectively.
  In multivariable analysis adjusted for age, Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group performance status ≥1, Gleason score ≥8, prior lines of mCRPC treatment, and time from CRPC diagnosis to Ra-223 initiation,
  all three risk factors were significantly associated with shorter OS (Fig. 2).
  Kaplan–Meier curves demonstrated clear separation according to the number of risk factors (Fig. 3).
  Patients with two or three risk factors had significantly shorter OS from both Ra-223 initiation and CRPC diagnosis compared to those with zero or one risk factor (Fig. 4 and 5).
  The area under the ROC curve (AUC) for predicting 2-year and 3-year OS was 0.811 (95% confidence interval [CI]: 0.781–0.841) and 0.778 (95% CI: 0.745–0.811), respectively (Fig. 6)
Fig. 2                                 Fig. 3                                         Fig. 4                                          Fig. 5                                       Fig. 6




Conclusion
   This external validation confirmed that EOD >1, PSA >10 ng/mL at Ra-223 initiation, and incomplete Ra-223 treatment
   are independent prognostic factors for poor OS in patients with mCRPC.

title: IP01-01: Benign cystectomy: The effect of socioeconomic status and discharge destination on patient outcomes
parentSessionTitle: IP01: Improving Access and Outcomes Across All Populations I
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: The impact of patient socioeconomic status (SES) on patient presentation, preoperative management, and surgical outcomes is often overlooked. Discharge destination (DD) after major surgery is also felt to play into emergency department (ED) and healthcare utilization. Benign cystectomy (BC) for non-oncologic bladder disease is a surgery felt to carry a high morbidity but remains understudied. The purpose of this study was to assess the effect of patient SES and DD after BC on surgical outcomes. METHODS: All BC performed from 2012-2025 at our institution were reviewed. SES was obtained using patient area deprivation index (ADI) scores, with a greater score corresponding to more socioeconomic deprivation (1 through 10). DD was classified as either home, home with nursing assistance (HNA), and skilled nursing facility (SNF). Patient demographics and surgical outcomes were reviewed. Outcomes were compared based on ADI score and DD using independent samples t-test, chi-squared test, and Kaplan-Meier survival analysis. RESULTS: 183 patients underwent BC. Median ADI score was 5 \Interquartile range (IQR) 4-8; [Table 1a\]. 90 ( Table 1b; 49%) patients were discharged to home, 78 (43%) patients were discharged to HNA, and 15 (8%) patients were discharged to a SNF. No association between ADI and DD was observed (p>0.05). Postoperative complication rate and 90-day readmission rates did not differ by ADI score (p>0.05), but a greater ADI score was associated with a higher mean number of ED visits after BC (p<0.05). Patients discharged to a SNF were more likely to experience a postoperative complication, visit the ED after BC, and have a greater length of stay (p<0.05). Preoperative bladder capacity had no relationship to ADI nor DD (p>0.05). Overall survival on Kaplan-Meier analysis was not different by ADI score (Figure 1a; p>0.05) but was lower in SNF patients (Figure 1b; p<0.05). CONCLUSIONS: Complication rate was equivalent by SES but patients with a greater ADI score (worse SES) appeared to utilize healthcare resources (ED) more frequently after BC. DD, specifically SNF patients, also were more likely to have a postoperative complication, utilize the ED, and have a longer postoperative stay. These results call for further study on the impact of SES and DD on BC outcomes. | | | --- | | |

title: IP01-02: Racial Disparities in Pre-operative Understanding of Erectile Dysfunction and Incontinence After Radical Prostatectomy
parentSessionTitle: IP01: Improving Access and Outcomes Across All Populations I
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Radical prostatectomy is a definitive treatment for prostate cancer but frequently leads to stress urinary incontinence (SUI) and erectile dysfunction (ED). Despite guidelines encouraging preoperative counseling, disparities in patient education may impact understanding and outcomes. We aimed to assess whether racial and age disparities exist in patients’ understanding of these complications and whether structured education influences recovery. METHODS: We conducted a retrospective study of 86 patients who underwent prostatectomy between 2016 and 2023 at a tertiary academic center. Patients completed a digital survey via Epic MyChart, assessing their understanding of ED and SUI, awareness of risks, and exposure to pelvic floor instruction. Outcomes were analyzed using descriptive statistics and ANOVA, stratified by race, age, and education exposure. RESULTS: Preoperative SUI education was associated with higher understanding (7.46 vs. 5.61, p=0.0015) and better improvement in leakage (7.97 vs. 6.11, p=0.0018). Pelvic floor instruction improved comprehension and recovery. Racial disparities were evident: Black patients reported lower understanding (5.44) than White (7.24) and Other (7.33) patients. Understanding declined with age, from 6.93 in patients <60 to 5.84 in those≥70. CONCLUSIONS: Structured education improves functional recovery after prostatectomy. However, significant disparities exist by race and age. These findings support the need for standardized and equitable preoperative counseling protocols in urologic oncology.

title: IP01-03: Postcode lottery and localised prostate cancer: Does address impact upon treatment offerings and patient choice?
parentSessionTitle: IP01: Improving Access and Outcomes Across All Populations I
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Once diagnosed with localised prostate cancer patients are faced with a variety of management options ranging from active surveillance to radical therapies including systemic treatment. Multi-disciplinary team meetings and clinics work to standardise decision making between clinicians and patients, by offering nuanced expert opinions upon appropriate management options. We determined if there were differences in MDT decision making, and patient selection of treatment option based upon indices of deprivation; a scoring system based on postcode. METHODS: A prospective review of patients diagnosed with prostate cancer (<rT4N0M0) between Oct 2024-Mar 2025. All patients received PSA, biparametric MRI and transperineal prostate biopsy+/-whole body imaging as appropriate. Primary outcome was to determine if differences in patient treatment choice, per D’Amico risk group, differed according to health and disability decile (HDD). Secondary outcomes included differences in incidence of each risk group per HDD and index of multiple deprivation (IDD), patient treatment choice and treatment offering according to HDD and IDD. RESULTS: 282 patients were diagnosed with localised prostate cancer and reviewed in MDT. 39, 171 and 72 patients were diagnosed with D’Amico low-, intermediate-and high-risk disease respectively. No statistically significant differences in D’Amico classification following diagnosis according to HDD or IDD were noted (p=0.404 and p=0.522 respectively). No statistically significant differences in patient choice, or treatment options offered were observed in this cohort according to HDD or IDD. CONCLUSIONS: Decision making within a multidisciplinary setting demonstrates standardisation of treatments offered and chosen by patients throughout a heterogenous cohort. | | | --- | | | | | | --- | | |

title: IP01-04: Do MDTs level treatment decision and patient choice for patients diagnosed with localised prostate cancer: an evaluation of ethnicity
parentSessionTitle: IP01: Improving Access and Outcomes Across All Populations I
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Patients of black descent have a higher incidence of prostate cancer and are often diagnosed with higher grade and later stage disease when compared to patients of Caucasian descent. Understanding of disease progression between the two ethnic groups once diagnosed with similar disease profiles is limited, thus patients should be offered similar treatment options. We evaluated if there were differences in treatment options offered to and chosen by patients with localised prostate cancer. METHODS: We evaluated patients reported in a prospective registry following diagnosis of localised prostate cancer (<rT4N0M0) between Oct 2024-Mar 2025. All patients received PSA, biparametric MRI and transperineal prostate biopsy+/-whole body imaging as appropriate. Primary outcome was to determine differences in treatment options chosen by patients of black and white descent per D’Amico risk group. Secondary outcomes included if treatment options offered per ethnic groups per D’Amico risk group differed. RESULTS: 116 patients of Caucasian and 110 of black descent were diagnosed with localised prostate cancer. 13, 76 & 27 Caucasian descent patients and 18, 63 & 29 Black descent patients had D’Amico low-, intermediate-and high-risk disease respectively (p=0.38). No significant differences in patient choice and treatment offering were noted between ethnicities. CONCLUSIONS: Despite differing incidence of prostate cancer reported in the literature, we did not demonstrate differences between ethnicities in risk stratification following diagnosis of localised prostate cancer. Further, no statistically significant differences were identified in the offering of treatment options and patient treatment choice after consideration of risk stratification. Standardisation may be a result of multidisciplinary review of treatment options and counselling of appropriate options with patients. | | | --- | | | | | | --- | | |

title: IP01-05: Impact of Socioeconomic Determinants of Health on Treatment Timelines in Bladder Cancer: An Analysis of the National Cancer Database
parentSessionTitle: IP01: Improving Access and Outcomes Across All Populations I

speakers.organization: Miami Cancer Institute, Baptist Health South Florida

fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: The impact of demographic and socioeconomic determinants on delays to cancer care for those with bladder cancer is not well studied. Our objective was to analyze the relationship between socioeconomic determinants of health and treatment delay in bladder cancer patients. METHODS: The National Cancer Database was queried for patients with bladder cancer from 2004 to 2021. Treatment delay was defined, based on the literature, as the initiation of neoadjuvant chemotherapy or radical cystectomy more than three months from the time of diagnosis. Demographic and socioeconomic variables were compared between patients with and without treatment delays, and multivariate logistic regression (LR) was done to assess the impact \[odds ratio (OR)\] of different variables on treatment delay. RESULTS: Of the 47,161 patients included in our study, 8,074 (17.12%) experienced treatment delay. Patients older than 70 years and males experienced a greater delay than younger patients and females (p<0.001). Similarly, black individuals \[7.3% (delay) vs 5.4%\ (no delay)\], patients with higher comorbid score (Charlson-Deyo Comorbid score≥3: 5.1% vs 3.9%), median income less than $46,277 (16.7% vs 14.1%), those in last two lower education level quartiles (16.7% vs 14.1% and 25.4% vs 24.2%) and patients utilizing government insurance (69.9% vs 66%) encountered more delays (all p<0.001). LR analysis revealed that older individuals (age > 80: OR 1.235, 95% Confidence Interval (CI) 1.115 – 1.368), black patients (OR: 1.346, CI 1.220 – 1.484), and a comorbid score≥3 (OR: 1.309, CI 1.168 – 1.467) had higher odds of treatment delay (all p<0.001). Higher education levels and female patients (OR: 0.799, CI 0.754–0.847) had a lower probability of delay (all p<0.001). CONCLUSIONS: Overall, 17.2% of bladder cancer patients experienced treatment delay. Patients older than 70 years, males, black individuals, individuals with a median income less than $46,277, patients in the lower two education quartiles, those claiming government insurance, and patients with greater comorbid scores were observed more in the treatment delay group. LR analysis revealed that older age (OR: 1.235), black individuals (OR:1.346), and higher comorbid score (OR: 1.309) had higher odds, and higher education level and female patients (0.799) had lower odds of delayed treatment.

title: IP01-06: Non-Metastatic Bladder Cancer Disparities among Hispanics in the United States Using the National Cancer Database
parentSessionTitle: IP01: Improving Access and Outcomes Across All Populations I

speakers.organization: University of Illinois College of Medicine

fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Bladder cancer (BC) features significant racial and ethnic disparities. Hispanic Americans, a diverse population with distinct genetic, socioeconomic, and cultural backgrounds, experience lower BC incidence than non-Hispanic Whites, while presenting with more advanced disease. Prior studies have treated Hispanics as a homogeneous group, potentially masking subgroup-specific disparities. This study evaluates differences in BC stage at diagnosis, treatments, and survival outcomes among Hispanics using the National Cancer Database (NCDB). METHODS: We conducted a retrospective analysis of 11,336 Hispanics (2004-2020) with urothelial BC. Patients were categorized into six groups based on country of origin: Mexican/Chicano, Puerto Rican, Cuban, South/Central American, Dominican, and Hispanic not otherwise specified. The subgroups were analyzed using Chi-square and Kruskal-Wallis tests. Kaplan-Meier survival analysis, log-rank test, and Cox proportional hazards models were used to assess survival differences. RESULTS: Stage at diagnosis varied significantly, with Cubans having the highest muscle-invasive BC (MIBC) rate (20.9%) and Dominicans the lowest (14.3%). Treatment patterns also differed across groups; among MIBC patients, Cubans had the lowest rate of radical cystectomy (24.2%) and the highest rate of local treatment (73.3%) (p=0.028). Differences in overall survival were seen among Hispanics with non-muscle-invasive bladder cancer (NMIBC), where Cubans had a 34% higher mortality risk (HR=1.34, p=0.002), while Dominicans and South/Central Americans had lower risks (HR=0.67, p=0.015; HR=0.68, p<0.001, respectively) compared to Mexicans. Among MIBC patients, survival was not significantly different (p=0.16) across groups. CONCLUSIONS: Hispanic subgroup disparities in BC stage at presentation, survival, and treatment highlight the need for targeted interventions. Aggregating Hispanics into a single category may obscure critical differences in BC care. Differences in healthcare access, immigration status, socioeconomic and structural determinants of health likely contribute to these disparities.

title: IP01-07: Cumulative Social Disadvantage and Risk of Overactive Bladder: A National Cross-Sectional Study with Machine Learning and Mediation Analysis
parentSessionTitle: IP01: Improving Access and Outcomes Across All Populations I
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Overactive bladder (OAB) is a prevalent urological disorder that impairs quality of life and disproportionately affects socially vulnerable populations. The influence of social determinants of health (SDoH) on OAB risk and severity remains underexplored. METHODS: This cross-sectional study analyzed data from 31,324 adults in the US National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey from 2005 to 2018. Eight SDoH indicators were examined, and a cumulative SDoH score was created. Survey-weighted logistic regression assessed associations between SDoH and OAB risk. Subgroup and sensitivity analyses explored demographic variation and robustness. Mediation analysis evaluated the indirect role of comorbidities. Multiple machine learning algorithms were applied for prediction, with SHAP analysis for feature interpretation. RESULTS: Six SDoH including unemployment, low income-to-poverty ratio, food insecurity, low education, non-private insurance, and lack of home ownership were independently associated with increased OAB risk. A clear dose-response relationship was observed, with risk rising as adverse SDoH accumulated (P for trend < 0.0001). Subgroups at heightened risk included men, middle-aged adults, and White individuals. Depression, obesity, cardiovascular disease, diabetes, and hypertension partially mediated these associations, with depression exerting the strongest effect. Among eight machine learning models, gradient boosting performed best with an AUC of 0.75. SHAP analysis identified age, BMI, and cumulative SDoH as the most influential predictors. A nomogram was developed for individualized risk estimation. CONCLUSIONS: Cumulative social disadvantage significantly contributes to OAB risk and severity, partly through mental and physical health pathways. Addressing SDoH may be vital for effective OAB prevention and management.

title: IP01-08: Social Determinants of Health and Elective Surgery Cancellations
parentSessionTitle: IP01: Improving Access and Outcomes Across All Populations I
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Elective surgery cancellations negatively affect the healthcare system leading to increased healthcare costs, adverse patient outcomes, and decreased scheduling efficiency. Social determinants of health (SDOH) are increasingly being recognized as dominant non-medical factors contributing to these effects. The goal of this study was to determine what demographic and SDOH factors are associated with elective surgery cancelations. METHODS: Patients scheduled for an elective surgery with a pediatric general surgeon or urologist between 10/2022 and 2/2024 were retrospectively reviewed. Patients admitted prior to surgery or whose surgery was cancelled >3 days before were excluded. Patient age, sex, race, ethnicity, primary language, insurance, area deprivation index, and SDOH questionnaire responses were compared between the surgery as scheduled and surgery cancelled cohorts with univariate and multivariate analyses. RESULTS: Of the 3,158 scheduled elective pediatric general or urological surgeries, 2,718 (86%) went as scheduled and 440 (14%) were cancelled. Cancellations disproportionately affected younger patients (4 vs 9 years, p<0.001), males (81% vs 57%, p<0.001), those with public insurance (65% vs 51%, p<0.001), and those of Hispanic/Latino ethnicity (11% vs 2%, p<0.001), Table 1. There was no significant difference in the day of week the surgery was scheduled or primary language spoken between the two cohorts. Cancellations were more likely among patients with positive SDOH screens (18% vs 12%, p=0.002), especially in those with transportation barriers and childcare needs, Table 1. On multivariable analysis, transportation barriers were associated with an almost threefold increased odds of cancellation (OR 2.9, p=0.002), and public insurance also significantly increased cancellation risk (OR 1.7, p=0.001). Interestingly, patients reporting difficulty "making ends meet" were less likely to cancel (OR 0.17, p=0.019). CONCLUSIONS: SDOH factors including public insurance and transportation barriers were associated with elective pediatric surgery cancellations. Younger, male, Hispanic/Latino children and those with positive SDOH screens are at highest risk. These factors may be used to systematically screen patients and create targeted presurgical outreach interventions to help mitigate cancellation rates. | | | --- | | |

title: IP01-09: The Impact of Community-Level Socioeconomic Distress on Stone Burden, Prevention, and Quality of Life in Patients with Nephrolithiasis
parentSessionTitle: IP01: Improving Access and Outcomes Across All Populations I
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Social determinants of health such as income and gender contribute to disparities in stone-related quality of life and timely management. The impact of community level socioeconomic disadvantage on nephrolithiasis-related quality of life and disease burden remains understudied. METHODS: We performed a nationwide cross-sectional survey of adult ResearchMatch registrants with kidney stones. Socioeconomic disadvantage was assessed using Distressed Community Index (DCI) with DCI≥75 defined as a disadvantaged community. Disease burden, preventative management, quality of life, and patient-reported barriers to care were compared between distressed and not distressed communities. Stepwise multivariable linear regression assessed the association between DCI and Wisconsin Stone Quality of Life (WISQOL). RESULTS: 126 of 938 respondents (13.4%) were from distressed communities. Individuals from distressed communities had lower WISQOL scores (83 vs. 87.5, P=0.005), were more likely to miss 5+days of work due to stones (17.5% vs. 8.4%; P=0.003) and were more likely to report barriers to making preventative dietary changes ( Table 1). Rates of completing of a 24-hour urine study (41.3% vs. 40.0%; P=0.77) and rates of seeing a dietician (15.9% vs. 12.1%; P=0.25) were similar between high and low DCI groups. On multivariable analysis ( Table 2), after controlling for demographics and emergency care utilization, DCI was inversely correlated with WISQOL score (β=-0.08,-0.13--0.03, P=0.003), however, addition of income to the model abolished the relationship between DCI and quality of life. CONCLUSIONS: In this study, stone-formers from socioeconomically distressed communities had greater work disruption, increased barriers to preventative management, and poorer stone-related quality of life. However, the relationship between DCI and WISQOL score was attenuated after controlling for income, highlighting a need for urologists to account for cost when recommending preventative regimens for nephrolithiasis. | | | --- | | | | | | --- | | |

title: IP01-10: Community-Based Knowledge-to-Action Translation to Improve Early Detection of Prostate Cancer Among Black Individuals
parentSessionTitle: IP01: Improving Access and Outcomes Across All Populations I
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Black prostate cancer (PCa) patients are 120% more likely to die compared to average US population, which is the largest racial disparity in cancer-related death in the US. In our previous work, Black men cited lack of awareness and knowledge to support shared decision making (SDM) with primary care providers (PCPs) as barriers to PCa screening and care. The objective of this study was to design a patient-centered, culturally relevant toolkit to improve the knowledge and awareness of PCa screening among Black Americans. METHODS: We convened a working group (WG) of Black PCa survivors and community advocates, clinicians, researchers, and health communications specialists. During monthly meetings, the WG followed Graham’s Knowledge-to-Action framework to synthesize information from: 1) peer-reviewed literature on the use of SDM aids; 2) interviews conducted by our research team with Black individuals regarding barriers and facilitators to access PSA testing; and 3) community input on PSA testing and PCa early detection. We then facilitated four iterative design sessions with the WG to develop recommendations for toolkit content, framing, and format. RESULTS: With the WG, we designed a framework with a comprehensive set of resources to increase knowledge and awareness of PSA testing for early detection of PCa among Black individuals, with detailed recommendations on the content, framing, and format. Recommendations encompass: 1) comprehensive interactive web-based information about PCa risk and screening; 2) printable SDM documents that present evidence-based information about the use of PSA testing to guide conversations between Black individuals and their PCPs; and 3) educational videos focused on PCa basics and dispelling common misconceptions about PCa risk and screening, with content delivered by Black PCa survivors and providers. CONCLUSIONS: This study addressed the need for a community-developed approach to increasing knowledge and awareness about PCa screening and early detection in an accessible, culturally relevant, and accurate manner. We used a collaborative process that centered the experiences of Black PCa survivors and advocates in the design of a toolkit that can facilitate SDM discussions between Black individuals and their PCPs for use of PSA testing for PCa screening. | | | --- | | |

title: IP01-11: Country Roads and Cancer Care: Comparing Measures of Travel Burden Among Patients with Bladder Cancer
parentSessionTitle: IP01: Improving Access and Outcomes Across All Populations I

speakers.organization: Charleston Area Medical Center Institute for Academic Medicine

fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Travel distance affects access, treatment, and outcomes, yet methods to measure burden vary. Comparing zip code centroid-based and network-based is essential to accurately assess geographic barriers to care. The aim of this study was to assess agreement on two measures of travel distance, zip code centroid-based network-based travel distance, and among patients with bladder cancer at a single tertiary medical center. METHODS: Patients diagnosed with bladder cancer by transurethral resection of bladder tumor between January 1, 2018, and December 31, 2022, were retrospectively identified from electronic health records. Demographic and clinical variables were abstracted by chart review. Travel distance was estimated using two approaches: centroid-based ZIP code calculations (ArcGIS) and network-based routing (Google Maps). Agreement and misclassification between approaches were analyzed, and association with patient demographics and survey-reported transportation concerns were evaluated. RESULTS: The average percent difference between network-and centroid-based travel distances was 38.8% (95% CI, 34.6–42.9%). Bland–Altman analysis demonstrated poor agreement with proportional systematic bias between the two methods of determining travel distance, showing a median bias of 5.7 (range, 2.39–87.7) between the two methods. Use of centroid-based distances led to 25.6% misclassification of patients based on travel bands. Misclassified patients were significantly more rural compared to appropriately classified patients (94.9% vs 84.3%, p<0.001). Patients who reported that transport was a high concern on the survey were more likely to be further away from the facility (33.4 vs. 17.0 miles, p=0.02) and located in travel bands 3 and 4 (64.9% vs 33.7%, p=0.03) as indicated in the network-based distance methods. CONCLUSIONS: Centroid-based travel distances underestimate the true travel distance and lead to patient misclassification, particularly among rural populations. Neither method was able to identify specific patient groups or treatment outcomes based on travel distance. Patient-reported survey responses indicated that patients with high concern regarding transportation did not include a specific patient demographic, but transport concern was reported higher in patients who were further away from the facility using network-based method of travel distance.

title: IP01-12: Socioeconomic vulnerability predicts mortality after radical cystectomy
parentSessionTitle: IP01: Improving Access and Outcomes Across All Populations I
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Radical cystectomy (RC) remains the cornerstone treatment for muscle-invasive bladder cancer (MIBC) but carries substantial morbidity and mortality. Traditional risk models emphasize clinical variables while overlooking community-level disadvantage. The Social Vulnerability Index (SVI) quantifies such vulnerability across four domains: socioeconomic status (RPL-1), household composition and disability (RPL-2), minority status and language (RPL-3), and housing and transportation (RPL-4). This study evaluated whether SVI or its component domains independently predict mortality after RC for MIBC. METHODS: A retrospective review of 144 patients who underwent RC for T2-stage MIBC was performed using an IRB-approved institutional database. Cox proportional hazards models assessed overall and cause-specific mortality, adjusting for age, sex, race, neoadjuvant chemotherapy (NAC), Charlson Comorbidity Index (CCI), travel time to UVA, and SVI (overall and domain-specific, derived from CDC 5-digit zip code data). Models were selected by Akaike Information Criterion (AIC). Cause-specific analyses distinguished bladder cancer–related mortality from non-cancer mortality. RESULTS: Median follow-up was 931 days (IQR 433–1,478). Mortality occurred in 31% of patients: 18% attributed tometastatic MIBC and 13% other causes. Median time to death was 307 days (IQR 147–602). The best-fit model included sex, travel time, and RPL-1; RPL-1 was significantly associated with higher mortality (HR 5.84, 95% CI 1.60–21.4, p=0.008). Cumulative incidence plots showed greater bladder cancer–related mortality overall. On subset analysis, RPL-1 predicted non-cancer mortality (HR 9.93, 95% CI 1.32–74.6, p=0.026) but not cancer-specific mortality (HR 3.99, 95% CI 0.73–21.9, p=0.110). CONCLUSIONS: The SES (RPL-1) domain—encompassing unemployment, lack of high school education, uninsured status, and poverty—emerged as an independent predictor of mortality after RC. Patients from socioeconomically vulnerable communities experienced excess overall and non–cancer mortality, suggesting deaths driven by structural inequities rather than tumor biology. Integrating SVI domains into perioperative risk models may enhance prognostication and guide targeted interventions to reduce disparities and improve survivorship.

title: IP01-13: County-Level Poverty as a Predictor for Prostate Cancer Mortality in Mississippi
parentSessionTitle: IP01: Improving Access and Outcomes Across All Populations I
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Mississippi has the second highest prostate cancer mortality rate of any state in the USA. Our state also faces significant socioeconomic challenges. Since poverty has been identified as a social determinant of health that may influence cancer outcomes, we explored how this relationship exists on the county level. Our county-level analysis underscores local-access disparities that the AUA seeks to address nationwide. METHODS: We conducted a cross-sectional using county-level data from Mississippi. Poverty rates (percentage of residents living below the federal poverty line) and age-adjusted prostate cancer mortality rates (2018–2022) were examined for 73 counties with complete data. Simple linear regression was used to evaluate the association between poverty and prostate cancer mortality. RESULTS: Regression analysis demonstrated that county-level poverty was a significant predictor of prostate cancer mortality (=99.92, 95% CI 53.00–146.84, p=0.000065). This result corresponds to an estimated increase of ~10 deaths per 100,000 for each 10% increase in poverty rate. The model explained 20.3% of the variation in prostate cancer mortality across counties (R2=0.2025). We found that Leflore, Bolivar, and Sunflower counties, all within the Mississippi Delta region, had the highest prostate cancer mortality rates. CONCLUSIONS: Counties with higher poverty rates generally experienced higher prostate cancer mortality. These findings highlight the role of socioeconomic determinants in cancer outcomes and suggest that targeted interventions in high-poverty areas may help reduce disparities in prostate cancer mortality across Mississippi, as well as the rest of the nation.

title: IP01-14: Building Sustainable Reconstructive Urology Capacity in the Underserved area of the Philippines: A Collaborative Global Surgery Mentorship Model
parentSessionTitle: IP01: Improving Access and Outcomes Across All Populations I
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Reconstructive urology restores function for patients with congenital, traumatic, infectious, and iatrogenic conditions, yet capacity-building in low-and middle-income settings often relies on brief visits that rarely shift local practice. We report a mentorship approach linking the University of Toronto, Eastern Virginia Medical School, and Queen’s University with two Philippine hospitals—St. Luke’s Medical Center (SLMC) and Philippine General Hospital (PGH). Objectives were to: (1) institute a year-round program anchored by a single, concentrated in-country teaching week; (2) deliberately move host teams toward higher-complexity reconstruction while preserving safety; and (3) evaluate feasibility, clinical outcomes, educational gains, and milestones for stepped autonomy. METHODS: From 2022–2024, monthly virtual boards standardized case selection, imaging, perioperative optimization, and resource readiness. This preparation led to one 6–7-day annual on-site session at SLMC/PGH where 2–3 visiting faculty and 1–2 trainees worked side-by-side with local surgeons. A prospective log captured case mix, operative duration, length of stay (LOS), and complications (Clavien–Dindo). Trainee learning was measured with 0–10 Likert scales (comfort; technical understanding) before and after the teaching week. The curriculum emphasized progressive complexity (e. g., redo hypospadias; long-segment/pan-urethral graft urethroplasty; augmentation cystoplasty; continent catheterizable channels; ileal ureter). Ethics approvals and temporary privileges were secured in advance; there was no industry or external funding, and outcomes were tracked prospectively. RESULTS: Thirty-three patients underwent surgery (median age 23 years; IQR 12.5–41.5); 33.3% were pediatric, and 84.8% had major reconstructive procedures. Median operative time was 240 minutes; median LOS was 2 days. Overall complications were 15.1%, including one major event (Clavien–Dindo≥III). Forty-five residents participated. Self-reported comfort increased from 2.51 to 6.93 and technical understanding from 5.18 to 8.84 (both p<0.001). The case portfolio advanced in complexity year-over-year while maintaining acceptable safety. Program success criteria include: each site independently performing predefined index reconstructions with≥2 credentialed local surgeons; outcomes approximating published benchmarks; rising independent volumes;≥80% clinic retention at 6–12 months; and emergence of a trainer-of-trainers. Sustained achievement for two consecutive years prompts tapering to remote support only. CONCLUSIONS: A continuous mentorship framework with a single, intensive annual on-site week can accelerate safe transfer of complex reconstructive skills while preserving local ownership. Early experience at SLMC/PGH demonstrates feasibility, meaningful educational improvement, and stable perioperative outcomes amid increasing complexity. The model is lean, scalable, and aligned with health-system priorities on workforce and quality, offering a practical route from joint cases to autonomous local expertise.

title: IP01-15: Perceived Barriers to LGBTQ+ Inclusivity for Urology Trainees
parentSessionTitle: IP01: Improving Access and Outcomes Across All Populations I
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Inclusive healthcare training environments are essential to equitable urological practice. This review synthesizes available evidence on barriers to LGBTQ+ (lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender, queer/questioning, and other sexual and gender minority) inclusivity perceived by trainees in urological surgical programs, identifying key educational and institutional gaps that limit preparedness to deliver competent LGBTQ+-affirming care. METHODS: A systematic search using Pubmed, Embase and Scopus examining LGBTQ+inclusivity among urology trainees and program directors. Study designs included seven cross-sectional surveys, two reviews, and one abstract encompassing residents, fellows, and applicants across U. S., Canadian, and international settings. Extracted data covered educational curricula, clinical exposure, institutional support, and geographic or demographic disparities. RESULTS: All ten studies reported measurable barriers. Educational: Six studies cited limited didactic exposure to transgender or LGBTQ+ care and five identified an absence of structured curricula. One national survey found 59.5% of applicants lacked any clinical or didactic exposure to genital gender-affirming surgery. Clinical: Eight studies documented insufficient hands-on experience; only 42% of programs had institutional transgender health initiatives. Trainees expressed low confidence counseling LGBTQ+ patients and reported uneven exposure across training levels. Institutional: Eight studies noted absent faculty expertise, limited administrative support, or fragmented interdepartmental collaboration. Program director attitudes and regional policies influenced inclusion of LGBTQ+ content. Geographic & Demographic: Barriers varied by American Urological Association region, gender, and training level; female residents and LGBTQIA+ applicants reported greater interest but less opportunity for transgender-care training. CONCLUSIONS: Educational, institutional, and structural barriers continue to impede LGBTQ+ inclusivity in urology training. Addressing these requires development of standardized curricula, expansion of clinical exposure through dedicated transgender health modules, and faculty development in culturally competent care. Reducing geographic and demographic inequities will help ensure future urologists deliver equitable, patient-centered care to LGBTQ+ populations.

title: IP01-16: DISPARITIES IN OUTCOMES FOR GENDER MINORITIES WITH ADVANCED PROSTATE CANCER
parentSessionTitle: IP01: Improving Access and Outcomes Across All Populations I

speakers.organization: Guy's and St Thomas' NHS Foundation Trust, London, UK

fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Advanced and metastatic prostate cancer (PCa) in sexual and gender minority (SGM) patients remains largely understudied. Current treatment frameworks focus on cisgender men, leaving insufficient guidance for treating those who have undergone (testosterone-suppressing) gender-affirming hormone therapy (GAHT). This literature review aimed to evaluate advanced/metastatic PCa therapy in gender minority (GM) patients, compare treatment outcomes with cisgender men and identify gaps in GM care. METHODS: Following PRISMA guidelines we searched PubMed, Embase, Medline and PsychInfo databases in October 2025, using MeSH terms for “sexual and gender minorities”, “advanced”, “metastatic” and “prostate cancer”. Studies met inclusion criteria if they assessed incidence of advanced/metastatic PCa in GM patients, prior gender affirmation and treatment outcomes. Quality assessment was performed using JBI checklists-studies included were either moderate or low-moderate in quality, with limitations frequently related to sample size and lack of comparison. Qualitative data extraction was conducted using NVivo. RESULTS: Of 62 articles screened, eight met the inclusion criteria. From these, excluding single case reports, two studies reported on a total of 57 GM patients combined and another (ongoing) plans to have ultimately enrolled 333 participants, although cisgender and GM participants are not separately tallied. Records suggest an increased proportion of metastatic PCa at diagnosis in GM patients, despite a much lower general incidence rate of PCa. One study suggested an association with GAHT and biochemical recurrences and bone metastases. These likely contribute to the reported higher mortality rate after PCa diagnosis in GM patients, compared to cisgender patients. However, treatment outcome data was generally indirect and incomplete.
