CONCLUSIONS: PCa appears more likely to be advanced or metastatic in a GM patient, with very limited report on treatment outcomes. Despite this, outcomes are well documented for cisgender men. Our findings highlight an inequity in available evidence and exemplify the need for further data collection, such as prospective case series with follow-ups on GM patients with advanced or metastatic PCa. A better understanding of reported disparities will help reduce outcome inequalities, improving care. | | | --- | | |

title: IP01-17: Impact of prostate cancer on partners: comparing evidence between sexual and gender minority populations and non-minority populations.
parentSessionTitle: IP01: Improving Access and Outcomes Across All Populations I

speakers.organization: Guy's and St Thomas' NHS Foundation Trust, London, UK

fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Prostate cancer (PCa) impacts not only the patient but their intimate partners, influencing sexual satisfaction and relationship quality. Research has largely focused on heterosexual and cisgender couples, leaving gaps in the understanding of how PCa affects sexual and gender minority (SGM) patients’ partners. This study aimed to compare current evidence on PCa’s impact on SGM patients’ partners’ sexual health versus non-SGM partners and identified key gaps in research. METHODS: A systematic search of PsycINFO, Medline and Embase databases was conducted in October 2025 for full-text articles published in English. Included studies focused on sex and relationships and partners’ experiences. Excluded studies included an intervention rather than focusing on the initial affect of PCa on patients and partners. Extracted data included patient characteristics, SGM status, relationship characteristics, partners’ sexual satisfaction and relationship impact. Findings were thematically synthesised to identify key factors affecting partners of SGM versus non-SGM patients. RESULTS: Of the 1969 records screened, five studies were included in the review. Three studies included non-SGM populations, and two included SGM populations. Non-SGM partners were assessed using validated tools such as SKIPPP-F. No validated assessment tools were reported by studies of partners of SGM patients. Five key factors impacting partners’ sexual health included: partner involvement, communication, sexual function and intimacy, emotional/relational adjustment, and partner wellbeing. SGM partners reported worse outcomes in all domains. Both SGM and non-SGM patients and partners reported that their sex life was worse post-treatment, along with loss of intimacy and lower satisfaction with sex and relationships. However, sex was perceived as more important in gay relationships compared to non-SGM relationships. CONCLUSIONS: PCa significantly affects partners’ sexual satisfaction and relationship quality in both SGM and non-SGM populations. However, partners of SGM patients experience more exclusion from care and higher relational strain. This highlights the need for inclusive clinical practice and validated assessment tools that specifically address the experiences of SGM patients and their partners to improve sexual and relational outcomes. | | | --- | | |

title: IP01-18: A Systematic Review of the Online Resources for Sexual and Gender Minorities Addressing Sexual Consequences of Treatment in Breast, Anal, Cervical and Penile Cancer
parentSessionTitle: IP01: Improving Access and Outcomes Across All Populations I
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Information on the sexual side effects of cancer treatments has been well researched within the heterosexual population. However, less is known about the sexual side effect burden on sexual and gender minority (SGM) groups. Limited understanding of SGM sexual practices among healthcare professionals, combined with patients’ fear of discrimination, drives many SGM patients to seek information online. After conducting previous research into SGM specific prostate cancer resources, we aimed to explore digital resources in breast (BCa), anal (ACa), penile (PCa), and cervical cancer (CCa). METHODS: We conducted this review according to PRISMA guidelines (PROSPERO CRD42024628689). A novel search was conducted of Google and YouTube in April 2025, with 21 key search terms. Online resources were included if they published sexual side effect information specific to SGM populations after BCa, ACa, PCa or CCa treatments. The AACODS checklist was used to assess resource quality. Data extracted from resources included: sexual side effect coverage, the inclusion of transgender (TG) information, ease of use, and quality of information. RESULTS: Eighteen websites and one YouTube channel met inclusion criteria. Eight resources for BCa, seven for ACa, two for CCa and two for PCa. Across all cancers, Cancer Council provided the highest-quality resources, offering inclusive, well-structured materials with comprehensive side-effect coverage and TG representation. Breast Cancer Network Australia and Young Survival Coalition (YSC) also performed strongly for BCa, with YSC uniquely highlighting identity and relationship challenges post-treatment. Macmillan scored well for accessibility and ease of use through its multilingual and audio features, but often lacked depth in side-effect detail. Overall, PCa materials were the weakest, showing minimal side-effect detail and poor inclusion of TG perspectives. CONCLUSIONS: There is a lack of SGM-specific online resources discussing sexual outcomes after BCa, ACa, CCa, and PCa treatment. This absence may impact SGM patients’ ability to make informed treatment decisions. Future research should examine the sexual effects of all cancer treatments in SGM patients to inform inclusive resources covering all sexual side effects and practices. Further work should also assess the accessibility and usability of online resources to ensure equitable patient access. | | | --- | | |

title: IP01-19: Invisible Barriers: Misgendering, Bias, and Care Avoidance in Urological Practice
parentSessionTitle: IP01: Improving Access and Outcomes Across All Populations I
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Transgender and gender-diverse patients frequently encounter discrimination in medical care, yet urology remains one of the least studied specialties regarding inclusivity. This systematic review analyzed the types, prevalence, and impact of discrimination experienced by transgender patients in urology care settings, aiming to identify actionable targets for improving equitable access and provider competency. METHODS: A semantic systematic search using Pubmed, Embase and Scopus. Twelve studies (2019–2025) met inclusion criteria: 6 qualitative, 5 cross-sectional, and 1 longitudinal cohort, encompassing over 31,000 transgender and nonbinary participants across urology, gynecologic, sexual health, and general clinical contexts. Data extraction followed PRISMA-adapted protocols emphasizing urology specific discrimination, care avoidance, and provider behavior. RESULTS: Prevalence of Discrimination: 23% avoided urologic care due to fear of mistreatment. 33% were asked to educate providers about transgender health. 15% experienced invasive or inappropriate questioning. 26% reported misgendering; 59% cited insufficient provider training; 18% noted absence of affirming imagery or language. 68% delayed or avoided healthcare following prior negative experiences. Patterns Identified: Interpersonal bias: Misgendering and assumptions about anatomy were common in both general and gender-affirming urology clinics. Structural discrimination: Administrative misclassification, lack of inclusive documentation, and insurance barriers were recurrent. Provider deficits: Only 27% of patients were asked their preferred terminology for anatomy. Intersectionality: Older, biracial, and disabled participants faced disproportionately higher denial rates (up to 8% for trans-specific care). Contextual factors: Hospital settings showed higher gender insensitivity than community-based or academic centers. Urology clinics reported more frequent discomfort during genital examinations than non-surgical specialties. CONCLUSIONS: Discrimination in urology care for transgender patients is prevalent, multifaceted, and driven by both interpersonal and structural factors. Fear of misgendering, inadequate provider training, and administrative barriers directly contribute to delayed presentation and reduced trust in urologists. These findings underscore the urgent need for trans-affirming training programs, inclusive documentation systems, and explicit EAU guidelines addressing gender diversity in urological care.

title: IP01-20: Redefining Prostate Cancer Care in Transgender Patients: Diagnostic Gaps, Screening Inequities, and Hormone Related Biases
parentSessionTitle: IP01: Improving Access and Outcomes Across All Populations I
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Prostate cancer risk persists in transgender women despite gender-affirming hormone therapy (GAHT). Hormonal suppression alters PSA levels and tissue morphology, complicating diagnosis. This review synthesized current evidence on prevalence, diagnostic accuracy, and oncologic outcomes in transgender patients receiving GAHT. METHODS: A semantic systematic review using the Pubmed, Embase and Scope databases was conducted and 12 studies (2006–2025) were selected including >140 000 transgender women and gender-diverse individuals. Extracted variables included PSA kinetics, histopathology, recurrence risk, and screening access disparities. RESULTS: Epidemiology & Risk: Prostate cancer incidence in transgender women on GAHT was 0.20 standardized incidence ratio (SIR) compared with cisgender men, equivalent to a 2.56-fold lower overall risk. Prevalence: 0.62 % (n = 589/95,460; _JAMA Oncol 2024_). Despite lower incidence, recurrence risk was higher among GAHT users (OR 1.83 for biochemical recurrence; OR 3.96 for bone metastasis). Diagnostic Challenges: PSA suppression: GAHT lowers PSA by 1.1–1.3 ng/mL (p < 0.001), making standard biopsy thresholds unreliable. Histopathology: Estrogen and antiandrogen therapy induce atrophic and metaplastic nuclear changes, leading to under-recognition or over-grading when hormone history is not considered. Access disparities: Only 23 % of transgender women aged ≥ 50 years ever underwent PSA screening; rates were lower in Black and non-binary individuals (OR 0.51, 95 % CI 0.25–1.01). Anatomical barriers: Post-vaginoplasty access limits digital rectal examination and biopsy feasibility. Healthcare Delivery & Awareness: Provider training deficits identified in 7/12 studies; only two national guidelines explicitly mention prostate screening for transgender patients. HIV-positive individuals were more likely to be screened (OR 3.61, 95 % CI 1.28–10.19). No standardized PSA cut-off or imaging protocol exists for transgender women. Oncologic Outcomes: PSA at diagnosis often underestimated disease burden; cases diagnosed at higher stage (T3+) were reported in long-term estrogen users. Survival data remain limited, but recurrence patterns suggest biologic differences driven by prolonged hormonal modulation. CONCLUSIONS: Prostate cancer in transgender women represents a diagnostic blind spot in modern urology. Hormone-induced PSA suppression and tissue remodeling obscure early detection, while inconsistent screening practices amplify health inequities. Despite lower incidence, evidence of increased recurrence risk warrants tailored PSA thresholds, modified biopsy algorithms, and multidisciplinary pathways integrating urology, endocrinology, and transgender health services. Development of EAU-endorsed guidelines is essential to ensure equitable, evidence-based care for all patients with prostates—regardless of gender identity.

title: IP01-21: Baseline reproductive and sexual health knowledge among undergraduate students
parentSessionTitle: IP01: Improving Access and Outcomes Across All Populations I
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Many undergraduate students are newly sexually active adults with unsafe sexual practices. We sought to assess undergraduate students' knowledge and attitudes on reproductive and sexual health. Our aim was to identify variables associated with knowledge deficiencies. METHODS: A novel, cross-sectional questionnaire was created with local expert input. The survey was distributed online from January to March 2021 at two universities in Manitoba, Canada, through student unions. Local ethics board approval was obtained, participation was voluntary, and data was anonymized. Chi-squared, Kruskal-Wallis, and univariable and multivariable-adjusted logistic regression analyses were used. P-value<0.05 was considered statistically significant. RESULTS: There were 309 respondents out of approximately 28,816 possible undergraduate students (n=309, response rate 1.1%). Of the respondents, 239 (77.3%) were females, 146 (47.2%) were≥22 years old, 49 (15.9%) were from a high socioeconomic status (SES), and 264 (85.4%) were from Manitoba. The overall mean knowledge score was 65.5%, with averages of 71.7% for STIs, 65.6% for infertility, and 59.2% for contraception/family planning. On multivariate analysis, higher knowledge scores were associated with identifying as female (male OR: 0.39, 95% CI: 0.18–0.87; p=0.021), older age (age 21 OR: 6.04, 95% CI: 1.78–20.49; p=0.004 and≥22 years OR: 4.07, 95% CI: 1.35–12.26; p=0.012), and university attended (University of Manitoba OR: 1.97, 95% CI: 1.11–3.49; p=0.021). On subgroup analysis, family SES was associated with higher STI knowledge scores (OR: 2.19, 95% CI: 1.07–4.48; p=0.032). Few felt that their post-secondary education on contraception/family planning (26.2%), STIs (34.6%), and infertility (4.5%) was adequate. CONCLUSIONS: Undergraduate students face unique barriers in obtaining adequate reproductive and sexual health knowledge. Younger males who attend smaller universities, and possibly those from lower SES, may be at greater risk of negative outcomes. We highlight the need for improved access to education and supports to assist students in making more informed decisions.

title: IP01-22: Improved Access to Peri-Operative Education for Patients Undergoing Radical Prostatectomy
parentSessionTitle: IP01: Improving Access and Outcomes Across All Populations I
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Radical prostatectomy is associated with well-documented adverse effects on urinary and sexual function, often accompanied by anxiety, depression, and reduced quality of life. Patient adherence with post-operative exercises and self-management of symptoms is critical for optimal recovery. We created the Prostatectomy Care Companion Application (PCCA), a digital education program embedded in the electronic health record, to provide a standardized pathway that included instructional videos and handouts accessed through EPIC’s MyChart application. Our objective was to evaluate patient engagement with the application. METHODS: Patients enrolled from November 2022 to July 2025 were evaluated for initial and continued engagement with the PCCA program. Educational video topics included PCCA introduction, prostatectomy procedure, pelvic rehabilitation, sexual health, and pre-and post-operative expectations. Primary outcomes included patient enrollment in the PCCA and ongoing engagement with app content over time. Retrospective review of app usage logs was performed to evaluate patterns of enrollment and interaction across months of prostatectomy. RESULTS: 349 patients were identified: Engagement with the application has increased over time (see (https://www.auajournals.org/doi/abs/10.1097/01.JU.0001191272.33670.20.22#F1)) with a >1.5-fold increase (approximately 15% to 30% engagement) after the onboarding of a Pathway Coordinator in Fall 2024. As of July 2025, engagement was almost 50% of all patients offered this resource. Initial engagement appeared to promote continued use, as 97.6% of patients who activated the PCCA remained active at their last appointment. CONCLUSIONS: Through this initiative, we developed a library of standardized, evidence-based educational materials for prostatectomy patients, underwent iterative review by our clinical team, and were integrated into our preoperative application pathway. These findings highlight the PCCA’s value in enhancing patient engagement and facilitating access to comprehensive post-surgical care.

title: IP01-23: Social Predictors of No Shows at an Urban, Safety-Net Urology Clinic: A Mixed Effects Model Study
parentSessionTitle: IP01: Improving Access and Outcomes Across All Populations I
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Clinic non-attendance negatively affects patient outcomes and disrupts clinic workflow. This study aims to identify predictors of patient no-shows at an urban, safety-net urology clinic. METHODS: A retrospective cohort study including all scheduled patients and appointments from April 2024 to April 2025 was conducted. Patient sociodemographic factors (SDOH; including education, employment, insurance, social support, etc.) were abstracted from EPIC reports. The primary outcome was clinic attendance. Continuous and categorical variables were analyzed using student’s T-test and chi-square, respectively. A multivariate mixed-effects logistic regression model was performed to adjust for covariates. RESULTS: Among 6,945 scheduled appointments, 1,752 (25.2%) were no-shows. On univariate analysis, select significant factors associated with no-shows included women gender (odds ratio \[OR\] 0.84, 95% confidence interval \[CI\] 0.73-0.98), non-Hispanic Black race (OR 1.57, CI 1.33-1.89), Asian/Pacific Islander race (OR 0.50, CI 0.42-0.61), inactive patient portal (OR 2.06, CI 1.84-2.30), divorced (OR 1.59, CI 1.31-1.92), single (OR 1.64, CI 1.44-1.86), non-English language (OR 0.67, CI 0.59-0.74), interpreter needed (OR 0.67, CI 0.60-0.76), assigned primary care provider (OR 0.56, CI 0.48-0.67), unemployment (OR 1.50, CI 1.33-1.77), new visits (OR 2.23, CI 1.99-2.51), procedural visits (OR 0.77, CI 0.63-0.92), history of being unhoused (OR 2.43, CI 2.10-2.82), lead days (OR 1.00, CI 1.00-1.003), historical no show rate (OR 1.09, CI 1.08-1.10), and social vulnerability index (OR 1.18, CI 1.11-1.25). On multivariable analysis, history of being unhoused (OR 2.29, CI 1.53-3.42), patient portal inactivation (OR 1.84, CI 1.37-2.47), social worker on file (OR 1.33, CI 1.02-1.72), new visits (OR 1.47, CI 1.26-1.72), procedural visits (OR 0.64, CI 0.49-0.83), historical no show rate (OR 1.11, CI 1.09-1.13), and lead days (OR 1.00, CI 1.00-1.01) remained significant. CONCLUSIONS: Predictors of urologic clinic no shows were history of being unhoused, historical no-show rate, new visits, assigned social worker, inactive patient portal, and increased time from appointment scheduling, of which the latter two are intervenable. This study offers upstream solutions for improving attendance for a safety-net clinic and healthcare access for urologic patients. | | | --- | | |

title: IP01-24: National Trends and Disparities in Surgical Management of Neurogenic Bladder
parentSessionTitle: IP01: Improving Access and Outcomes Across All Populations I
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Neurogenic bladder (NGB) includes a heterogeneous group of patients with impaired bladder control. Surgical management ranges from continent procedures that preserve urinary control to incontinent diversions. Prior studies report NGB treatment disparities but are limited to single institutions or specific NGB etiologies. We examined national trends and disparities in continent versus incontinent urinary diversions among NGB patients. METHODS: We conducted a retrospective cross-sectional analysis using the National Inpatient Sample from 2016 to 2022. ICD-10 codes were used to classify NGB patients by congenital or acquired etiologies (e. g. cerebral palsy, spina bifida, multiple sclerosis, paraplegia). Outcomes included continent (bladder augmentation, neobladder, continent catheterizable channels, artificial urinary sphincter) or incontinent procedures (ileal conduit, vesicostomy, cutaneous ureterostomy, colon conduit, sphincterotomy). Patient demographics, comorbidities, and hospital characteristics were compared by diversion type. Multivariable analyses identified predictors of incontinent diversions. RESULTS: A total of 312,486 patients with NGB were identified, including 19,539 with congenital and 133,700 with acquired etiologies. Among these, 1,564 admissions involved a continent or incontinent urinary diversion, with 60% receiving incontinent procedures. Patients undergoing incontinent diversions were older and more likely to have public insurance. Hospital characteristics did not differ by diversion type. On adjusted analysis, NGB etiology was not associated with diversion type. Independent predictors of incontinent diversion included older age, male sex, public insurance, lower household income, and pre-existing colostomy. CONCLUSIONS: Our findings highlight the influence of demographic and socioeconomic factors on surgical management of NGB. As the first national study covering a wide range of NGB etiologies and inpatient treatments, these results underscore disparities in access to continent urinary diversions and the need for strategies to ensure equitable care for all NGB patients. | | | --- | | | | | | --- | | |

title: IP01-25: Barriers to Electronic Health Record M-ISI Questionnaire Completion in Urology Patients: The Impact of Age and Social Vulnerability
parentSessionTitle: IP01: Improving Access and Outcomes Across All Populations I

speakers.organization: University of Rochester School of Medicine and Dentistry

fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Collecting patient-reported outcomes (PROs) through electronic health record (EHR) patient portals (ePP) helps clinicians better understand patients’ experiences while streamlining workflows. However, these digital tools can unintentionally amplify disparities in participation. We evaluated demographic and social factors associated with M-ISI completion. METHODS: This was a single-center retrospective study of all adults with diagnoses of incontinence, LUTS, BPH, elevated PSA, or prostate cancer who were distributed M-ISI via ePP at an outpatient urology clinic from June 2019 to June 2025. M-ISI was sent 7 days before the visit. Completion rates were analyzed at patient and encounter levels. The CDC Social Vulnerability Index (SVI) by ZIP code served as a neighborhood-level socioeconomic measure. Statistical comparisons were performed using Wilcoxon rank sum, chi-square, and multivariable logistic regression tests. RESULTS: EHR record data identified 24,746 unique patients and 166,028 encounters when M-ISI was distributed. Completion rate was 22.1% by encounter and 44% by patient. Completers were younger (71.3 ± 10.8 vs 72.9 ± 13.7 yr, p<0.001) and lived in less vulnerable areas (median SVI 32.5 vs 46.2). Non-completers were more likely non-White (7.7% vs 16.4%) and Latinx (1.1% vs 2.6%, both p<0.001). In multivariable analysis, older age (OR 0.99, 95% CI 0.986–0.988), female sex (0.85, 0.82–0.87), non-White race (0.49, 0.47–0.51), Latinx ethnicity (0.61, 0.54–0.68), and high social vulnerability (SVI≥75: 0.67, 0.64–0.70) independently predicted lower completion (all p<0.001). CONCLUSIONS: Despite automated EHR ePP distribution, M-ISI was completed in one in five encounters. Older age and higher social vulnerability were major barriers to completion, highlighting the need for alternative delivery methods and interventions to promote inclusive patient evaluation. | | | --- | | | | | | --- | | |

title: IP01-26: PELVIC FLOOR DISORDERS ARE COMMON AND BURDENSOME AMONG WOMEN WITH BLADDER CANCER
parentSessionTitle: IP01: Improving Access and Outcomes Across All Populations I

speakers.organization: Desai Sethi Urology Institute - University of Miami

fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Pelvic floor disorders (PFDs) disproportionately affect women with bladder cancer (BC), yet they are underassessed and undertreated, despite a significant impact on quality of life (QOL). The Survivorship and Pelvic floor InterventioNs (SPIN) study was created for women with BC (newly diagnosed, undergoing treatment, or previously treated) to receive PFD care from a urogynecologist. This study aimed to describe the prevalence and severity of PFDs among women enrolled in SPIN. METHODS: Women were recruited to SPIN during urologic oncologist visits. Participants completed validated questionnaires prior to their initial visit, including the Pelvic Floor Distress Inventory (PFDI-20), Female Sexual Function Index (FSFI), Perceived Stress Scale (PSS), and a series of questions assessing the relationship between PFDs and BC treatments. Descriptive statistics summarized patient characteristics and scores. Group comparisons used Wilcoxon rank-sum, with significance set at p<0.05. RESULTS: Of 33 women enrolled, 25 completed their baseline surveys (median age 68 years, IQR 63–73; 93.9% White, 54.5% Hispanic). Baseline PFD burden was substantial: UDI-6 scores (subset of PFDI-20 examining urinary bother) had a median score of 41.7 (IQR 25, 45.8) and PFDI-20 score 70.8 (IQR 52.1, 97.9). 54.5% reported overactive bladder (OAB) symptoms and 48.5% stress urinary incontinence (SUI). Women with SUI had higher urinary distress than those without (UDI-6: 41.7 vs 0, p>0.01). Sexual dysfunction was prevalent (80%) with median FSFI 5.0 (IQR 3.6, 19.6). Perceived stress was moderate to high (median PSS 20.5, IQR 18.5–23). 29.2% reported oncologist discussion of sexual health impacts, 41.7% reported discussions of bladder symptom impacts, while 50% of participants reported no discussion of treatment effects. CONCLUSIONS: Baseline findings reveal a significant burden of PFDs among women with BC, with 50% of patients reporting these symptoms were not assessed during oncologic visits. This highlights the need for multidisciplinary care to improve QOL and outcomes for female BC patients. | | | --- | | |

title: IP01-27: A DEDICATED UROGYNECOLOGIC PROGRAM FOR WOMEN WITH BLADDER CANCER ALLOWS FOR MARKED IMPROVEMENT IN PELVIC FLOOR DISORDERS AT 3 MONTHS
parentSessionTitle: IP01: Improving Access and Outcomes Across All Populations I

speakers.organization: Desai Sethi Urology Institute - University of Miami

fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Women with bladder cancer (BC) often experience pelvic floor disorders (PFDs) that are overshadowed by their cancer treatment priorities, however they can severely impact patient quality of life (QOL). The Survivorship and Pelvic floor InterventioNs (SPIN) study was created for women with BC (newly diagnosed, undergoing treatment, or previously treated) to receive PFD care from a urogynecologist. This study assesses if participants demonstrate improvement in PFDs symptoms between baseline and three-month follow-up by participating in SPIN. METHODS: Women with BC were recruited during their urologic oncologist visits. Participants completed validated questionnaires prior to their initial visit, including the Pelvic Floor Distress Inventory (PFDI-20), Female Sexual Function Index (FSFI), Perceived Stress Scale (PSS), and a series of questions assessing the relationship between PFDs and BC treatments. Descriptive statistics summarized participant characteristics and questionnaire scores. Paired Wilcoxon signed-rank compared baseline and 3-month results, with significance defined as p<0.05. RESULTS: 13 women completed both baseline and 3-month assessments. At baseline, participants demonstrated significant symptom burden with a median UDI-6 (subset of PFDI-20 examining urinary bother) score of 37.5 (IQR 29.2, 45.8), PFDI-20 score of 81.3 (IQR 66.7, 103.1), FSFI score of 5.0 (IQR 4.2, 25.5), and PSS of 18 (IQR 11, 21). After three months, urinary distress decreased substantially (UDI-6 20.8, IQR 0, 37.5; p=0.0137), overall pelvic floor distress improved (PFDI-20 37.5, IQR 18.8, 87.5; p=0.0105), and sexual function increased (FSFI 13.4, IQR 5.2, 29.6; p=0.0034). Perceived stress decreased from baseline to 3-months \[PSS 10 (6.5, 15), p=0.0020\]. CONCLUSIONS: Enrollment of women with BC in a structured urogynecologic program addressing PFDs (SPIN) significantly improves PFD symptom bother. We propose that all women with BC be offered automatic referral to urogynecologic care to help improve PFD symptom burden and QOL.

title: IP01-28: Bridging the Gap in Rural Urinary Incontinence Care: Provider Perspectives and the Development of an Educational Urinary Incontinence Care Initiative
parentSessionTitle: IP01: Improving Access and Outcomes Across All Populations I

speakers.organization: A.T. Still University Kirksville College of Osteopathic Medicine

fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Urinary Incontinence (UI) is an extremely prevalent condition across all demographics that can significantly affect a patient’s quality of life. However, the proportion of those with UI who seek care remains low, indicating the existence of barriers to care. Currently, there is a gap in research evaluating rural UI care. This study explored provider-identified barriers to rural UI care, aiming to reduce disparities through the creation of an educational packet — the Urinary Incontinence Care Initiative. METHODS: This cross-sectional study surveyed rural medical providers in Northeast Missouri. Rurality was established by county using the Health Resource & Service Administration’s definition of ‘fully rural.’ The survey assessed providers’ views and practices in UI management and evaluated perceived barriers to care. Based on the results, an educational packet was created and distributed to 57 rural medical practices. RESULTS: Among 38 respondents, 21 providers met criteria for further analyses. The majority were physicians (17, 81.0%). Most providers agreed or strongly agreed they feel comfortable diagnosing (20, 95.2%) and treating UI (17, 81.0%). Around half always screen UI patients for depression (12, 57.1%). One-third reported never sharing online resources with UI patients (7, 33.3%). Physicians were more likely to inform patients of community resources than nurse practitioners (P=.012). Lack of support and care resources, low patient health literacy, and limited access to secondary care providers were the top-tanked barriers to UI care. The majority of providers expressed interest in educational materials on community resources (11, 68.6%), online resources (11, 68.6%), and a UI screening tool (10, 62.5%). CONCLUSIONS: Rural providers feel comfortable managing UI; however, many believe patients lack necessary support and care resources. The UI Care Initiative was created to increase awareness of available resources and reduce educational barriers. This packet included evidence-based materials for providers (UI screening tool, treatment algorithm, referral list) and for patients (UI education, pelvic floor exercises, community and online resource guide). Overall, the packet aimed to address the identified disparities in rural UI care.

title: IP01-29: Bridging the Gap at Cutler Center for Men: Early Outcomes from a Comprehensive, Navigation-Based Model of Preventive Care
parentSessionTitle: IP01: Improving Access and Outcomes Across All Populations I
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Men experience shorter life expectancy and higher rates of preventable illness, in part due to lower healthcare engagement. To address this gap, University Hospitals (UH) launched the Cutler Center for Men (CCM) – a free, multidisciplinary, male-focused program offering personalized navigation, preventive alerts, and community engagement. This received media attention and was featured in the New York Times. We evaluated the program’s impact on healthcare utilization, clinical outcomes, and community engagement among enrolled men versus non-members within the same health system. METHODS: We conducted a propensity-matched observational study comparing 1,270 CCM members to 3,810 non-member men matched by age, comorbidities, race, income, insurance, and prior healthcare use. Primary outcomes included annual primary care visits, prostate cancer screening, diabetes control (A1c <8%), influenza vaccination, and outpatient visit frequency. Program-level metrics included enrollment growth, care coordination, and community outreach. RESULTS: Between September 2023–2024, 3,300 men enrolled in CCM (30% annual growth), accounting for 15% of all new UH Urology Institute encounters. Members demonstrated a 55% increase in overall encounters post-enrollment, 82% PCP assignment, and a Net Promoter Score of 84—nearly double national healthcare benchmarks. After adjustment, members were 70% more likely to receive prostate cancer screening (95% CI 1.47–1.96, p<0.05), 37% more likely to complete an annual primary care visit (95% CI 1.16–1.63, p<0.05), and 36% more likely to achieve diabetes control (A1c <8%) (95% CI 1.18–1.57, p<0.05). No difference was found in influenza vaccination. Community events and social engagement more than doubled compared with baseline. CONCLUSIONS: Enrollment in a dedicated men’s health center significantly improved preventive care utilization, chronic disease control, and healthcare engagement. These data demonstrate that a free, system-integrated, gender-specific model can effectively close gaps in men’s health outcomes. The CCM’s navigation-based framework represents a replicable, outcomes-driven blueprint for health systems seeking to promote male population health improvement.

title: IP01-30: Surgical Glove Sizing Disparities Among Operating Room Staff: A Multi-Institutional Analysis
parentSessionTitle: IP01: Improving Access and Outcomes Across All Populations I
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Use of commercialized surgical instruments tailored to male subjects has been shown to impact both ease of instrument use and result in more injuries in the operating room (OR) for female users. Furthermore, improper glove sizing can impair dexterity and safety in surgery. We investigated whether female surgical staff were more likely to wear incorrectly sized sterile gloves and identified predictors of mismatch. METHODS: We conducted a cross-sectional survey study of surgical personnel at Phoenix Children’s and Mayo Clinic Arizona. Participant demographics, usual glove size worn, and hand dimensions were collected. Correct sterile glove size was determined using the ProtexisTM PI manufacturer’s guide based on hand width. Mismatch was defined reported glove size differing from the recommended size. Independent-samples t-tests and chi-square tests were used for univariate analysis. Binary logistic regression was used to identify independent predictors of incorrect sizing. Statistical significance was set at p<0.05. RESULTS: Among 124 surgical staff, 36 (29%) wore an incorrect sterile glove size. There were no differences in mean age, sex, or ethnicity between those who wore correct vs incorrect gloves (p=0.61-0.73). Staff with mismatched gloves had greater mean hand width (9.25 ± 0.75 cm vs 8.67 ± 0.74 cm; p<0.001), and circumference (20.74 ± 2.08 cm vs 19.66 ± 2.68 cm; p=0.04). On multivariable analysis, male sex strongly predicted correct glove fit (OR 11.6, p=0.002), while greater hand width predicted mismatch (OR 0.08, p<0.001). Among those with mismatched gloves, Hispanic participants were more likely to wear gloves that were too small (37.5% vs 7.1%; p=0.03). CONCLUSIONS: Nearly one-third of surgical staff wore incorrectly sized sterile gloves. Female staff remained disproportionately affected even after adjusting for hand dimensions, suggesting current glove designs better accommodate male hand proportions. Most mismatches resulted from oversizing. These findings highlight ergonomic and equity gaps in glove design. Expanding glove size ranges and refining fit standards could enhance comfort, dexterity, and safety in the OR. | | | --- | | | | | | --- | | |

title: IP02-01: Metabolomics analysis identifies serum biomarkers predicting risk of intravesical tumorrecurrence after intravesical Bacillus Calmette–Guérin therapy (BCG) in patients withnon-muscle invasive bladder cancer
parentSessionTitle: IP02: Bladder Cancer: Non-invasive I
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Evidence on metabolomics research and metabolomics-based biomarkers predicting treatment outcomes is still limited in bladder cancer. Here, weexplored serum metabolites which were potentially associated with risk of intravesicalrecurrence after intravesical BCG therapy. METHODS: Two independent cohorts, discovery cohort (n=23) and validation cohort (n=40),were included in this study. Blood was taken before induction BCG therapy (pre-BCG blood;both discovery cohort and validation cohort) and after 6 doses of BCG (post-BCG blood; onlydiscovery cohort). Metabolome analysis of serum samples was conducted using capillaryelectrophoresis time-of-flight mass spectrometry. The endpoint was intravesical recurrence-freesurvival, which was analyzed with the Kaplan–Meier estimates, the log-rank test, and Coxproportional hazard model. RESULTS: Of 353 metabolites quantified, nine (2.5%) including four amino acids and four (1.1%) werefound to be upregulated and downregulated, respectively. Heatmap of hierarchical clusteringanalysis for the fold-changes of serum metabolites differentiating 10 recurrent cases and 13non-recurrent cases in the discovery cohort. The higher number of metabolites showing highfold-change were observed in the non-recurrent cases as compared to the recurrent cases( (https://www.auajournals.org/doi/abs/10.1097/01.JU.0001191276.85430.b0.01#F1)). A metabolome response-based score model using 16 metabolites including threonine and N6,N6,N6-trimethyl-lysine well stratified the risk of post-BCG recurrence. In addition, pre-BCG metabolome-based score models using six metabolites, octanoylcarnitine, S-Methylcysteine-S-oxide, theobromine, carnitine, indole-3-acetic acid, and valeric acid weredeveloped from the discovery cohort. Univariate and multivariate analysis confirmed highpredictive accuracy in the validation cohort and combination cohort ( (https://www.auajournals.org/doi/abs/10.1097/01.JU.0001191276.85430.b0.01#F2)). CONCLUSIONS: We demonstrated that numerous types of serum metabolites were altered inresponse to intravesical BCG therapy and developed high performance and non-invasive scoremodels which well differentiates risk of post-BCG recurrence.

title: IP02-02: Dynamic Prediction of Recurrence and Progression Risk in Non-Muscle Invasive Bladder Cancer Using Conditional Survival: A SEER-Medicare Analysis
parentSessionTitle: IP02: Bladder Cancer: Non-invasive I
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Predicting recurrence and progression risk in non-muscle invasive bladder cancer (NMIBC) is essential for counseling and risk-adapted management. However, conventional models do not account for the change in baseline risk over the time. We therefore examined the conditional survival free of recurrence and progression among older adults with NMIBC to develop a dynamic risk prediction model. METHODS: We identified patients aged 66-89 years with a diagnosis of Ta/Tis/T1 cN0 cM0 bladder cancer treated with TURBT from 2000-2017 in the SEER-Medicare linked database. The conditional recurrence-free (RFS) and progression-free (PFS) survival were estimated using the Kaplan-Meier method. Associations of baseline characteristics with RFS and PFS at pre-specified landmark times were evaluated using Cox proportional hazards models. RESULTS: A total of 39,862 patients were included. Of these, 26,339 (66%) had Ta, 11,758 (29%) had T1, and 1765 (4%) had Tis disease. Median follow-up was 65 months. Baseline 60-month RFS and PFS were 0.39 and 0.85 respectively. Given a 6-, 12-, 24-, 36-, 48-, and 60-months event-free survivorship, the 60-month RFS and PFS were 0.52, 0.62, 0.73, 0.78, 0.82, 0.85 and 0.86, 0.87, 0.89, 0.90, 0.90, and 0.91 respectively ( (https://www.auajournals.org/doi/abs/10.1097/01.JU.0001191276.85430.b0.02#F1)). Conditional RFS rapidly improved within the first 24 months, then plateaued. When stratified by T stage, patients with T1 disease demonstrated the greatest improvement in conditional RFS. On multivariable analyses, T stage and tumor grade were less predictive of RFS with longer landmark times. CONCLUSIONS: Among patients with NMIBC, the risks of disease recurrence and progression decrease with longer event-free intervals. These observations are most pronounced among those at highest risk, as evidenced by tumor stage and grade. Dynamic risk prediction can improve patient counseling and risk-adapted management during follow-up.

title: IP02-03: Prospective Open-Label Study to Evaluate the Safety and Efficacy of Intravesical Sustained-Release Gemcitabine Docetaxel combination (NDV-01) in High-Risk NMIBC: Update with 9-month Complete Response Data
parentSessionTitle: IP02: Bladder Cancer: Non-invasive I

speakers.jobTitle: Chairman, The Department of Urology& Pediatric Urology

fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Sequential intravesical gemcitabine and docetaxel (Gem/Doce) represents a promising option to treat patients with high-risk NMIBC – including those who are BCG-naïve, -exposed and -unresponsive. Gem/Doce is not available in a sustained-release formulation, limiting intravesical exposure. NDV-01 an investigational intravesical agent designed for sustained release of Gem/Doce continuously over a 10-day period. NDV-01 does not require a specialized pharmacy or hood. NDV-01 may also help overcome the burdens to patient and to provider of traditional Gem/Doce. METHODS: The study is a phase 2, single-arm, open-label trial of NDV-01 in subjects with HG NMIBC. Subjects were given 6 bi-weekly instillations followed by monthly maintenance instillations through month 12. Complete response (CR) was defined as a negative cystoscopy, cytology, and biopsy (if indicated). The first assessment for CR was evaluated at 3 months. Subjects with a non-CR at 3 or 6 months were eligible to be reinduced with an additional 6 bi-weekly course of therapy. Disease assessments for CR were also performed at 6, 9, and 12 months. Twenty-five patients have reached the first disease assessment (3-months follow-up) and are included in the per-protocol efficacy analysis. Twelve patients are pending their first response assessment.) All 36 patients who have received >=1 treatment are included in the safety analysis. RESULTS: Baseline characteristics of the 36 enrolled subjects (of a planned 70 patients) are shown in Table 1. All patients were ECOG 0-1. Of the 36 patients who received >=1 dose of NDV-01, 22 (61%) had a TRAE (62% dysuria, 9% asymptomatic positive urine culture, 7% hematuria). No patient had >=Grade 3 TRAE and no patients discontinued treatment due to AEs. Response rates in the 25 patients who received >=3-month disease assessment are shown in Table 2. Two subjects have reached 12-month assessment, and both have a CR. No patient had progression to muscle invasive disease, and no patient has undergone a cystectomy. Of patients with BCG-UR disease, the CR for the 11 participants who had >=3 -month assessment were: CR anytime (10/11 (91%)); 3-month (9/11(82%), 6-month (7/9(78%)), and 9-month (7/8(88%)). CONCLUSIONS: NDV-01 is a novel sustained formulation of Gem/Doce for intravesical use. NDV-01 provides excellent 9-month safety and efficacy in patients with high-risk NMIBC -- including those who are BCG-naïve, -exposed and -unresponsive. The study remains ongoing to provide longer term follow-up and a larger sample size. | | | --- | | | | | | --- | | |

title: IP02-04: ADVANCED-2 (Cohort A): Preliminary Efficacy and Safety Data in BCG-Naïve Participants With High-Grade Non-Muscle Invasive Bladder Cancer
parentSessionTitle: IP02: Bladder Cancer: Non-invasive I
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: There continues to be a significant unmet need for safe, effective, and bladder-sparing treatment options for patients with non-muscle invasive bladder cancer (NMIBC), and this need is more pronounced in patients who are unable to receive Bacillus Calmette-Guérin (BCG). TARA-002 is a lyophilized biological preparation for intravesical instillation containing inactivated cells of Streptococcus pyogenes (Group A, type 3) Su strain. TARA-002 rapidly enters cancer cells, activating TLR2 and NOD2 to trigger innate immunity, inflammation, and potential immunogenic cell death. This abstract presents interim efficacy and safety data of TARA-002 from the BCG-naïve cohort of the ADVANCED-2 study. METHODS: ADVANCED-2 (Cohort A) is an ongoing Phase 2, open-label study to evaluate the safety and efficacy of intravesical TARA‑002 in adults ≥ 18 years with high-grade (HG)-NMIBC CIS (±Ta/T1) who are BCG-naïve. Key exclusion criteria include penicillin allergy; history of ≥ T2 bladder cancer, nodal, or metastatic disease; and concomitant prostatic or upper tract urothelial involvement. Each participant is treated with intravesical TARA-002 induction (6 weekly doses), reinduction (if disease persists at 3 months) and maintenance (through 24 months). Response is assessed every 3 months for 2 years. Long-term follow-up is conducted up to 60 months. Safety is monitored throughout the study. The primary endpoint is HG complete response (CR) at any time. The key secondary endpoint is duration of response at 12 months. RESULTS: As of October 24, 2025, 31 BCG-naïve participants (median age: 71.0; range: 45 to 89) have been enrolled. The majority of BCG-naïve participants are White (93.5%, 29 of 31), male (80.6%, 25 of 31), and non-Hispanic (90.3%, 28 of 31). The majority of participants had a baseline ECOG score of 0 (83.9%, 26 of 31) and baseline diagnoses of CIS only (58.1%, 18 of 31). TARA-002 demonstrated 72.4% (21 of 29) HG CR at any time in evaluable participants. The 6-month CR was 66.7% (18 of 27), the 9-month CR was 61.1% (11 of 18), and the 12-month CR was 42.9% (6 of 14). Most treatment-emergent adverse events (TEAEs) were mild and transient. No participants experienced drug-related serious AEs (SAEs) or drug-related TEAEs leading to withdrawal or death. CONCLUSIONS: Preliminary data suggest that TARA-002 monotherapy is well-tolerated and produces clinically meaningful rates of initial CR coupled with durability of response in BCG-naïve HG NMIBC with CIS (±Ta/T1) through twelve months of treatment. Updated efficacy and safety data will be provided based on evaluable time points at the time of the presentation.

title: IP02-05: Cost-Effectiveness Analysis of Sasanlimab plus BCG for High-Risk Non-muscle Invasive Bladder Cancer (NMIBC): Analysis From CREST
parentSessionTitle: IP02: Bladder Cancer: Non-invasive I
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: The phase 3 CREST trial demonstrated that combining sasanlimab, a subcutaneous checkpoint inhibitor, with BCG (s+BCG) improved event-free survival compared to BCG alone for patients with BCG-naïve high-risk NMIBC. However, patients treated with s+BCG experienced higher rates of ≥ grade 3 treatment-related adverse events (AE), including 15.7% with ≥ grade 3 immune AE, and the cost of checkpoint inhibitors is substantial. We used a Markov model to weigh the costs, toxicities, and efficacy of s+BCG to further investigate its utility. METHODS: We used a decision-analytic Markov model to compare s+BCG to BCG alone for BCG-naïve high-risk NMIBC. Efficacy and toxicity model probabilities were extracted from the CREST trial. Cost data for sasanlimab were extrapolated from subcutaneous nivolumab pricing ($24,225/dose), as sasanlimab is not currently FDA approved. The model used a U. S. Medicare payer perspective with a lifetime time horizon. One-way and probabilistic sensitivity analyses were performed to vary all model inputs across biologically plausible ranges. Incremental cost-effectiveness ratios (ICERs) were compared using a willingness to pay threshold of $100,000/quality-adjusted life year (QALY). RESULTS: Over a patient’s lifetime, the combination of s+BCG resulted in 0.03 additional QALYs (6.11 vs 6.08) at an additional cost of $191,666 relative to BCG alone. Combination therapy was found not to be cost effective over a lifetime horizon (ICER=$6,440,594). On one-way sensitivity analysis ( Figure), the combination of s+BCG became cost-effective only if the per dosing price of sasanlimab was reduced by > 90% (to $1244/dose) from the existing pricing of a currently available subcutaneous checkpoint inhibitor. The combination therapy was cost effective in 0% of 100,000 Monte Carlo simulations in probabilistic sensitivity analyses at $100,000/QALY. CONCLUSIONS: At anticipated pricing consistent with currently available immunotherapy, sasanlimab is not cost effective as a combination therapy with BCG relative to BCG alone for patients with high-risk NMIBC. Further efforts are needed to improve the efficacy/toxicity profile of novel therapies in this disease space, while continued scrutiny of the healthsystem cost implications of new agents remains warranted.

title: IP02-06: Prognostic Outcomes Comparing Upfront Radical Cystectomy and Primary BCG Therapy in Very-High Risk Non-Muscle Invasive Bladder Cancer: An Updated Analysis in the Modern BCG Era
parentSessionTitle: IP02: Bladder Cancer: Non-invasive I
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: The European Association of Urology (EAU) has defined very-high risk (VHR) non–muscle invasive bladder cancer (NMIBC) as a subgroup of NIMBC with very high rates of local recurrence, progression to muscle-invasive disease, and metastasis for whom upfront radical cystectomy (RC) is recommended. This study aimed to compare survival and progression outcomes among VHR patients treated with primary Bacillus Calmette-Guérin (BCG) therapy versus upfront RC in the modern era of bladder sparing approaches. METHODS: We performed an IRB-approved retrospective review of consecutive patients diagnosed with NMIBC from 2000 to 2023 to identify patients meeting 2021 EAU VHR criteria: high-grade T1 with or without carcinoma in situ (CIS), high-grade Ta with CIS, lymphovascular invasion (LVI), prostatic urethral involvement, or variant histology. Additional risk factors (tumor volume, multifocality, and age at diagnosis) were incorporated into the EAU classification. Overall survival (OS) and cancer-specific survival (CSS) was defined from diagnosis to death; progression-free survival (PFS) was defined as the interval from diagnosis to disease progression, or death. Survival outcomes were estimated using the Kaplan-Meier method and compared via the log-rank test. RESULTS: Among 285 patients with VHR NMIBC, 166 underwent primary BCG therapy and 119 underwent upfront RC, with a median follow-up of 51 months (IQR 28–83). Variant histology was more prevalent in the RC group (43% vs 17%, p<0.001) while T1 (P=0.202), CIS (P=0.125), LVI (P=0.169), and prostatic urethral involvement (P=0.535) were similar across both groups ( Table 1). 5-year OS (82% vs 76%, P=0.71), CSS (96% vs 95%, P=0.67), and PFS (71% vs 70%, P=0.59) did not differ significantly between BCG and RC cohorts, respectively ( (https://www.auajournals.org/doi/abs/10.1097/01.JU.0001191276.85430.b0.06#F1)). Outcomes remained comparable across all EAU-defined VHR subgroups and were unaffected by the number or type of VHR risk factors (p>0.05). CONCLUSIONS: In the modern BCG era, patients with VHR NMIBC experience comparable survival and progression outcomes with primary BCG therapy versus upfront radical cystectomy. Bladder-sparing management with intravesical BCG should be offered as an option even for patients meeting EAU VHR criteria.

title: IP02-07: Holmium Laser En Bloc Resection vs Monopolar TURBT for Bladder Tumors >3 cm: A Prospective Randomized Trial—Interim Analysis
parentSessionTitle: IP02: Bladder Cancer: Non-invasive I
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Monopolar TURBT fragments the specimen, complicates pathological assessment and may increase the risk of understaging. Prior RCTs largely enrolled tumours ≤3 cm, limiting applicability to larger lesions. We aimed to compare safety and specimen quality between holmium laser en bloc resection (HoLEBT) and monopolar TURBT (RTUb) for tumours larger than 3 cm. We previously conducted a pilot study (2018–2019) of HoLEBT with morcellation for bladder tumours >3 cm. In that cohort, detrusor muscle was present in all specimens and no intra- or peri-operative complications were recorded. These findings provided the rationale for a definitive randomised trial comparing HoLEBT with monopolar TURBT to clarify the optimal endoscopic approach for large bladder tumours. Objectives: To compare HoLEBT with monopolar TURBT regarding presence of detrusor muscle in the specimen assessment, intra- and peri-operative complications, and oncological outcomes. METHODS: Prospective, single-centre, single-blind, randomised (1:1) trial (planned n=100): HoLEBT (n=50) versus monopolar TURBT (n=50). The protocol received Institutional Review Board approval and was registered in ReBEC (RBR-67npwrk) and on ClinicalTrials. gov (NCT05833997). Key inclusion criteria: bladder tumours >3 cm confirmed by CT/MRI within 3 months before randomisation. Exclusion criteria: prior bladder cancer; radiological suspicion of ≥pT2 disease, N+ or M+; urethral stricture; previous chemotherapy or radiotherapy. Central pathology review was pre-specified; patients with pT1 undergo re-TURBT at 30–60 days. Primary endpoints: detrusor muscle representativeness in the specimen. Secondary endpoints: intra- and postoperative complications, length of stay (LOS), residual tumour at re-TURBT, and 24-month oncologic outcomes (recurrence, progression, overall and cancer-specific survival). RESULTS: These are interim analyses after randomization of 82 patients (HoLEBT n=40; RTUb n=42). Final results may be available at the time of presentation, as the last cases are expected to complete in December 2025. Baseline age and tumor size were comparable between arms. Operative time (median \[IQR\]) was 38.4 min \[31.9–45.1\] for HoLEBT vs 42.6 min \[32.3–53.0\] for RTUb (p=0.495). Detrusor muscle was present in 80.0% vs 71.4% of specimens (p=0.44). Bladder perforation occurred in 0/40 vs 8/42 cases (p=0.003), and obturator reflex in 0/40 vs 8/42 (p=0.003). Length of stay was 1.68 vs 1.97 days (p=0.48). Hematuria requiring >2 days of irrigation or readmission occurred in 4/40 vs 9/42 (p=0.132). CONCLUSIONS: In tumors >3 cm, HoLEBT appears feasible and demonstrates a markedly lower rate of perforation and obturator reflex compared with monopolar TURBT, with similar operative time, LOS, and detrusor muscle presence in this interim. This RCT directly addresses the evidence gap for larger bladder tumors and may influence endoscopic management in this subset. Final results, including oncologic endpoints, are anticipated to provide additional guidance on technique selection.

title: IP02-08: Efficacy of Nadofaragene firadenovec in Doubly Resistant Patients: A Real World Case Series
parentSessionTitle: IP02: Bladder Cancer: Non-invasive I
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: BCG-unresponsive (BCG-U) non-muscle-invasive bladder cancer (NMIBC) remains a formidable clinical challenge, with high recurrence and progression risk. Treatment strategies vary significantly, and many patients receive multiple therapies in hopes of avoiding radical cystectomy. Nadofaragene firadenovec (NF), a non-replicating adenoviral vector delivering IFN-α2b, was recently approved for BCG-U NMIBC. This study reports outcomes of NF use in highly pre-treated BCG-U NMIBC following treatment with both BCG and gemcitabine + docetaxel (gem/doc). METHODS: We retrospectively reviewed patients with high-risk NMIBC treated with NF who met FDA BCG-U criteria and had prior gem/doc. All declined or were ineligible for cystectomy. Demographic, clinical, and treatment data were collected. Outcomes included complete response (CR) (absence of high-grade recurrence on cystoscopy, urine cytology, or biopsy), cystectomy, and adverse events (AEs). Kaplan-Meier analysis censored patients at recurrence or last follow-up. RESULTS: 18 patients received NF following BCG and gem/doc failure. Median age was 77.4 years (IQR 73.2–81.5); 83% male, 94% White. Patients received a median of 16.5 BCG, 14 gem/doc and 2 (IQR 1-3) NF instillations. 94% of patients declined cystectomy, 11% were deemed medically ineligible. Median time from NMIBC diagnosis to NF was 6.4 years (IQR 4.3-11.1). Of 10 patients (55.6%) with ≥3 months of CR, 7 recurred and 3 maintained CR at last follow-up of 3, 6, and 9 months. On Kaplan–Meier analysis of CR patients, median response was 4.9 months (IQR 3.1–6.5). Two (11%) underwent cystectomy, one had pT2 disease (both N0). AEs occurred in 33%: grade 1–2 in 22%, grade 3 in 6%, and grade 4 in 6%. Events included fever, UTI, unsteadiness, hypertension, and one febrile illness with altered mental status requiring hospitalization. No deaths occurred. CONCLUSIONS: While NF achieved CR in a portion of BCG and gem/doc-refractory NMIBC patients (55.6%), 72% of all patients recurred within 6 months and none achieved 12-month CR. Nearly all declined cystectomy despite surgical candidacy, reflecting real-world patient preference for bladder sparing therapies. These findings suggest that patients who failed both BCG and gem/doc could represent a biologically resistant cohort compared with BCG-U alone, less likely to benefit from NF. Studies elucidating the optimal sequencing of BCG-U agents are needed.

title: IP02-09: Development and Validation of a Urinary Extracellular Vesicle miRNA-Pair Model for the Non-Invasive Diagnosis of Urothelial Carcinoma
parentSessionTitle: IP02: Bladder Cancer: Non-invasive I
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Urothelial carcinoma (UC) is the most common malignancy of the urinary tract. Current diagnostic methods, such as cystoscopy and urine cytology, are either invasive or have limited sensitivity. Urinary extracellular vesicles (EVs) contain stable microRNAs (miRNAs) that may serve as promising non-invasive biomarkers. This study aimed to develop and validate a miRNA-pair-based diagnostic model for UC using EV-derived miRNAs. METHODS: Urine samples were collected from 43 UC patients and 34 patients with non-malignant urinary diseases as the NGS discovery cohort. EVs were isolated using a ZrO2 magnetic bead adsorption method, followed by characterization through transmission electron microscopy (TEM), nanoparticle tracking analysis (NTA), and Western blotting. Feature selection was performed using univariate analysis combined with a genetic algorithm. For PCR validation, an independent cohort comprising 71 UC patients, 42 with non-malignant urinary diseases, and 57 healthy controls was analyzed. A logistic regression model was constructed using the qPCR cohort as a training set. An independent external validation set (51 UC, 72 benign urinary diseases, and 51 other cancers) was used to assess diagnostic performance. RESULTS: 34 discriminative miRNA pairs that showed distinct clustering between cancer and benign samples. Recursive feature elimination with logistic regression identified three optimal miRNA pairs (hsa-miR-21-5p/hsa-miR-27a-3p, hsa-miR-96-5p/hsa-miR-152-3p, hsa-let-7c-5p/hsa-miR-29c-5p) that showed significant differences between UC and control groups (p<0.05). The three-pair miRNA model achieved an AUC of 0.90 in the training cohort and 0.88 in the external validation cohort. The model score significantly differentiated UC patients from benign and healthy controls, as well as from other cancer types. The diagnostic sensitivity and specificity were 93.0% and 74.7% in the training cohort, and 86.3% and 78.0% in the validation cohort, respectively. CONCLUSIONS: This study developed a novel urinary EV-based miRNA-pair model with high accuracy for non-invasive diagnosis of urothelial carcinoma. The three-pair miRNA signature demonstrated robust performance across multiple cohorts and holds promise for clinical application as a simple, reproducible liquid biopsy tool.

title: IP02-10: Macrophage-encapsulated Engineered EcN Expressing IL-15&IL-15Ra Fusion Protein Enhances Therapeutic efficacy in Intravesical Therapy
parentSessionTitle: IP02: Bladder Cancer: Non-invasive I
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: The efficacy of Bacillus Calmette-Guérin (BCG) in bladder cancer is limited by adverse reactions and a high rate of treatment failure. We propose an innovative approach: a recombinant Escherichia coli Nissle 1917 (EcN) strain engineered to express an IL-15&IL-15Rα fusion protein (EcNIL-15), encapsulated within macrophages endowed with tumor-specific tropism and adhesion capabilities (Macs@EcNIL-15). This system enables targeted intratumoral delivery and sustained release of the IL-15/IL-15Rα complex, promoting specific tumor cell killing. METHODS: The recombinant EcNIL-15 strain expressing the IL-15&IL-15Rα fusion protein was constructed. Bone marrow-derived macrophages (BMDMs) were used to encapsulate EcNIL-15. The release of EcNIL-15 and IL-15&IL-15Rα expression were validated using bladder cancer organoids and an orthotopic bladder cancer model. The therapeutic efficacy and safety of Macs@EcNIL-15 instillation were assessed in orthotopic bladder tumor models. RESULTS: We generated the recombinant EcNIL-15 strain, and confirmed the expression and secretion of the IL-15&IL-15Rα in vitro. The supernatant from EcNIL-15 cultures significantly promoted T-cell proliferation in co-culture with splenocytes. Immunofluorescence assays verified the intratumoral colonization and IL-15&IL-15Rα expression by EcNIL-15. Encapsulation within macrophages significantly enhanced the intratumoral colonization and expansion efficiency of EcNIL-15 in vivo (Tropism). The released EcNIL-15 specifically colonized and proliferated within tumors, effectively preventing bacterial entry into the bloodstream or infection of other organs (Safety). The sustained secretion of IL-15&IL-15Rα induced potent activation and proliferation of T cells and NK cells (Efficacy). The intratumoral colonization of EcNIL-15 persisted for several weeks before gradual immune clearance, allowing for sustained local IL-15&IL-15Rα production and enabling long-term tumor suppression with a single administration. Intravesical Macs@EcNIL-15 resulted in significant tumor regression in the orthotopic model and a marked prolongation of mouse survival. CONCLUSIONS: We have developed a novel intravesical therapy for bladder cancer. Macs@EcNIL-15 enables specific adhesion and infiltration into bladder tumors, and a single instillation facilitates rapid intratumoral colonization by EcNIL-15 and the sustained release of the IL-15&IL-15Rα fusion protein, leading to continuous immune cell activation and direct tumor killing, thereby achieving potent and durable antitumor effects.

title: IP02-11: Predicting Cancer-Specific Mortality in Non-Muscle-Invasive Bladder Cancer: Comparative Performance of AUA vs EAU Risk Classifications
parentSessionTitle: IP02: Bladder Cancer: Non-invasive I
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Risk stratification in non-muscle-invasive bladder cancer (NMIBC) traditionally focuses on recurrence and progression, as in the European Association of Urology (EAU) and American Urological Association (AUA) classifications. Since these events ultimately drive cancer-specific mortality (CSM), assessing their ability to predict CSM may refine patient counseling and follow-up. We compared the accuracy of these models in predicting CSM. METHODS: We relied on 2192 consecutive patients with non-muscle-invasive bladder cancer (NMIBC) treated with transurethral resection of bladder tumor (TURBT) at seven tertiary-referral European centers (2015-2022). Patients were categorized according to: (1) the 2021 EAU classification into low- (LR), intermediate- (IR), high- (HR), and very high-risk (VHR) groups, based on T stage, WHO 1978/2004 grade, presence of carcinoma in situ (CIS), and additional factors (age >70 years, multifocality, and tumor size ≥3 cm); and (2) the AUA classification, which lacks a VHR group but expands HR category. Kaplan-Meier estimates were used to assess CSM. Time-dependent receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curves and area under the curve (AUC) values at 2 and 5 years were calculated to test model discrimination. RESULTS: Median age was 70 years (IQR: 63-77). Overall, 1364 (62%) harbored Ta, 702 (32%) T1, and 118 (5.3%) Tis stage; 328 (15%) had CIS, 1254 (57%) HG disease, and 135 (6.2%) VH. Multifocality was reported in 989 (45%) patients, with median tumor size of 2 cm (IQR: 1-3). According to EAU criteria, 501 (23%) were LR, 989 (45%) IR, 599 (27%) HR, and 126 (5.6%) VHR; according to AUA criteria, 370 (17%) were LR, 1,005 (45%) IR, and 840 (38%) HR. Median follow-up was 49 months (IQR: 30-68). The 2- and 5-year CSM rates were 0.0% and 1.3% for EAU LR vs. 2.3% and 4.5% for IR vs. 7.1% and 14% for HR vs. 6% and 15% for VHR patients; corresponding values for AUA were 0.0%, 4.7%, and 4.8% at 2 years and 0.0%, 9.3%, and 10% at 5 years. The EAU classification demonstrated superior discrimination for CSM (AUC 0.70 vs. 0.58 at 2 years, p=0.028; 0.75 vs. 0.61 at 5 years, p=0.001). CONCLUSIONS: Although developed to predict recurrence and progression, both models provide prognostic insight into CSM. The EAU classification showed superior accuracy compared with the AUA system, supporting its broader prognostic utility in NMIBC.

title: IP02-12: Risk Stratification of Ta High-Grade Non–Muscle Invasive Bladder Cancer: Insights from a Multicenter Cohort Study
parentSessionTitle: IP02: Bladder Cancer: Non-invasive I

speakers.organization: IRCSS San Raffaele Hospital, Milan, Italy

fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: The oncological risk of Ta high-grade (TaHG) non–muscle invasive bladder cancer (NMIBC) patients remains uncertain. We aimed to evaluate the oncological outcomes of TaHG patients treated with Bacillus Calmette-Guérin (BCG) by applying the 2021 European Association of Urology (EAU) risk stratification and assessing the prognostic value of individual risk factors. METHODS: We identified 529 TaHG patients without carcinoma in situ (CIS) treated with BCG from 16 tertiary centers between 2003 and 2024. As a comparator arm, a total of 151 ‘pure’ intermediate risk (IR) NMIBC patients (with recurrent TaLG and T1LG tumors) treated with BCG were also included. BCG failure was defined as the development of BCG-unresponsive status, BCG relapsing status or identification of muscle invasive bladder cancer during follow-up. TaHG patients were stratified in three groups based on the number of EAU risk factors (i. e. age >70 year, multifocality and tumor size >3 cm; 0, 1, 2-3 risk factors). Cumulative incidence analyses and Cox regression models analyzed the 5-yr risk of HG-recurrence, progression and BCG failure among TaHG patients stratified according to the number of EAU risk factors and compared their risk with those of ‘pure’ IR-NMIBC patients. RESULTS: At a median follow-up of 40 months (IQR: 37-42), 114 (22%) TaHG patients experienced a HG-recurrence, 49 (9%) patients had progression and 107 (20%) had BCG failure. No differences in rates of HG-recurrence, progression and BCG failure were detected among TaHG patients within risk groups based on the number of EAU risk factors. Patients with IR-NMIBC (recurrent TaLG and T1LG) had a significant lower risk of 5-yr HG-recurrence (14%) compared to IR-TaHG (25%, p=0.038) and high-risk (HR)-TaHG (31%, p=0.003) ( (https://www.auajournals.org/doi/abs/10.1097/01.JU.0001191276.85430.b0.12#F1)). Similarly, IR-NMIBC patients had a significant lower risk of 5-yr progression (6%) compared to IR-TaHG (13%) and HR-TaHG (15%) (all p<0.05). Patients with IR-TaHG (adjusted OR: 2.07) and HR-TaHG (adjusted OR: 2.45) had a significant higher risk of BCG failure compared to IR-NMIBC (all p<0.05). CONCLUSIONS: Patients with TaHG NMIBC represent a homogenous population associated with higher risk of HG-recurrence, progression and BCG failure compared to ‘pure’ IR-NMIBC. These findings may support the consideration of all TaHG tumors as high-risk in clinical practice, regardless of individual risk factors.

title: IP02-14: Therapy-Induced Tertiary Lymphoid Structures in the Tumor Microenvironment Reflect Immune Reprogramming After Intravesical Bacillus Calmette-Guerin for non-muscle invasive bladder cancer
parentSessionTitle: IP02: Bladder Cancer: Non-invasive I
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Intravesical Bacillus Calmette-Guerin (BCG) is standard of care for intermediate- and high-risk non-muscle invasive bladder cancer (NMIBC). Recently, immune checkpoint inhibitor (ICI) was indicated for BCG-unresponsible NMIBC. Recent evidence suggests that tertiary lymphoid structures (TLSs) within the tumor microenvironment (TME) may play a critical role in orchestrating antitumor immune responses. However, the change in the TME including forming TLS before and after BCG remains unclear. In this study, we assessed the association of TME and BCG treatment for NMIBC. METHODS: Our retrospective study included 18 BCG-unresponsible patients with intermediate- and high-risk NMIBC. Tissue samples were obtained through transurethral biopsy or resection before and after the administration of BCG in all patients. Post-BCG samples were collected when intravesical recurrence as BCG-unresponsible. Additionally, tissues from patients with acute bacterial cystitis were analyzed as controls. We assessed the density of several immune cell types (CD4, CD8, Foxp3, Bcl6, CD204, CD20, CD21, CD38) in intra-tumoral and peri-tumoral areas between pre-BCG and post-BCG tissues via multiplex fluorescence immunohistochemical analysis. RESULTS: BCG-unresponsible was classified as BCG-refractory in 3 cases, BCG-resistance in 5 cases and BCG-relapsing in 10 cases. The formation of TLS was observed in 11 cases (61%) in post-BCG tissues, while TLS was not observed in all cases in the pre-BCG tissues and acute bacterial cystitis tissues. Seven cases of TLS non-formation were all BCG relapsing cases. Comparison according to TLS formation revealed a difference in the timing of recurrence. In peri-tumoral areas, the densities of TLS-associated cells, including CD20+ and CD38+ cells, were significantly higher (p=0.029 and p=0.013, respectively), while the densities of CD21+ and Bcl6+ cells also tended to be higher in the TME of post-BCG tissue compared with pre-BCG tissue. In the intra-tumoral area, there was no difference in the change in immune cells between pre-BCG and post-BCG tissues. CONCLUSIONS: This study suggests that TLS formation in the TME may be associated with early recurrence following BCG treatment, which may benefit from ICIs for BCG-unresponsible NMIBC.

title: IP02-15: BCG therapy reshapes the urinary microbiome and immune cell landscape in non–muscle-invasive bladder cancer
parentSessionTitle: IP02: Bladder Cancer: Non-invasive I
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Intravesical BCG is the standard treatment for intermediate- and high-risk NMIBC; however, 30–40% of patients experience recurrence or progression. The bladder immune milieu and urinary microbiota may be associated with its efficacy; however, their longitudinal interplay remains unclear. Here, we aimed to define these temporal interactions and their clinical relevance. METHODS: This single-center prospective study included 23 patients with NMIBC who completed six BCG instillations. Urine was collected at four time points: pre-TURBT, pre-induction BCG, post-induction BCG, and 3 months later. Urinary sediment transcripts (PD-L1, PD-L2, CD33, MSR1/CD204) were quantified using qRT-PCR, and the microbiota was profiled using 16S rRNA V3–V4 sequencing. Alpha and beta diversity and microbe–immune associations were tested using linear mixed-effects models, and progression risk was analyzed using a Cox proportional hazard model. RESULTS: PD-L1 and PD-L2 expression levels increased significantly after BCG induction (P=0.003), and CD33 and MSR1 showed similar upward trends. Alpha and beta -diversity did not change over time. Lower Actinobacteria and enrichment of Enterobacteriaceae were associated with lower PD-L1 and higher MSR1 expression, respectively. These findings align with reduced IFN-γ/STAT1–IRF1-dependent PD-L1 induction and activation of the IL-10–PPARγ/LXR–MSR1 axis under heightened LPS tone. The Firmicutes/Bacteroidetes ratio and relative abundance of Enterobacteriaceae correlated with PD-L1 dynamics. Post-BCG immune and microbiota indices were significantly associated with longer progression-free survival. CONCLUSIONS: BCG induces coordinated temporal remodeling of urinary immune gene expression and the urinary microbiome. Increased PD-L1/PD-L2 and myeloid markers indicate immune reprogramming, whereas changes in the Firmicutes/Bacteroidetes ratio reflect mucosal ecology. Urine-based immune–microbiota profiling may serve as a predictor of response to BCG in patients with NMIBC.

title: IP02-16: Single-Center Prospective Study of Transurethral Gas-Bladder Ultrasonic Scalpel Bladder Tumor Resection: A Report on Technical Feasibility and Preliminary Efficacy
parentSessionTitle: IP02: Bladder Cancer: Non-invasive I
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Muscle-invasive bladder cancer (MIBC) requires radical cystectomy (RC). A proportion of non-muscle-invasive bladder cancer (NMIBC) also needs partial cystectomy or RC. However, RC causes numerous postoperative complications that severely reduce quality of life. For patients strongly willing to preserve the bladder, or young patients demanding high quality of life, exploring safe and effective bladder-sparing strategies is critical. This study evaluated the technical feasibility, safety, and preliminary efficacy of a novel surgery—transurethral gas-bladder ultrasonic scalpel bladder tumor resection (STURBT)—based on the self-developed S-scope (a visualized, large-channel, multi-functional platform). METHODS: This single-center, single-arm prospective trial was approved by the No. S2022-303-01 and ChiCTR2200062202. Conducted from 2022 to Dec 2024, it enrolled patients undergoing STURBT. Surgical steps: 1) Transurethral insertion of S-scope under direct vision to establish CO2 gas bladder (pressure: 6-14 mmHg); 2) Inserting ultrasonic scalpel via S-scope’s main channel, circularly incising bladder wall 1 cm from tumor edge to resect tumor and basal tissue en bloc; 3) Bipolar electrocoagulation for hemostasis; 4) Removing specimens en bloc or in pieces with a basket; 5) Irrigating the field with distilled water. Baseline data, surgical parameters, perioperative complications, postoperative pathology (muscle layer acquisition rate), and follow-up recurrence were recorded. RESULTS: 26 patients were enrolled (24 males, 2 females), with median age 61 years (range: 44-77). Median tumor size was 4.5 cm (range: 2-7). Median surgical time was 116 min (range: 25-210), median hemoglobin decrease 8 g/dL (range: 1-28). Median postoperative bladder irrigation duration was 2 days (range: 1-3). Pathological staging: 23 T1 cases, 3 T2 cases; 21 specimens (80.8%) contained muscle layer. Intraoperative/postoperative advantages: multi-instrument/energy platform collaboration, minimal blood loss, no urinary extravasation, no obturator nerve reflex. Median follow-up was 18 months (7-35); 2 patients had recurrence and underwent RC. Complications occurred in 2 cases (7.7%): 1 urethral stricture, 1 subcutaneous emphysema (both Clavien-Dindo I). CONCLUSIONS: STURBT based on S-scope was preliminarily confirmed safe, feasible, and effective in this single-center trial. It solves key limitations of traditional TURBT: en bloc resection (no fragmentation), no fluid irrigation (reduced seeding risk), clear resection margins (facilitating pathological assessment), sufficient resection depth (high muscle layer rate), no obturator nerve reflex.

title: IP02-17: A Randomized Multicenter Crossover Study to Evaluate Patient Preference and Satisfaction with Urine-Based Molecular Testing versus Cystoscopy for Surveillance of Non-Muscle-Invasive Bladder Cancer (NMIBC)
parentSessionTitle: IP02: Bladder Cancer: Non-invasive I
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Cystoscopy remains the standard for non-muscle-invasive bladder cancer (NMIBC) surveillance, but is invasive, costly, and burdensome. The Cxbladder Monitor (CxbM), a urine-based mRNA assay, offers a noninvasive alternative with validated diagnostic accuracy. We conducted a randomized, multicenter, crossover clinical trial to evaluate patient preference, satisfaction, and quality of life comparing CxbM versus cystoscopy during NMIBC surveillance. METHODS: In this trial conducted at Mayo Clinic between November 2023 and September 2025, adults with NMIBC and a minimum of 9 months of recurrence-free survival were randomized 1:1 to two distinct surveillance regimens: Arm A (CxbM at 3 months, cystoscopy at 6 months) or Arm B (reverse order). This cross-over design enabled within-subject comparisons and minimized interindividual variability. The primary endpoint was overall patient preference (Patient Preference Questionnaire, PQ). Secondary endpoints included satisfaction, convenience, time burden, health-related quality of life (EORTC QLQ-NMIBC24), fear of recurrence (FCRI-SF), and test performance. Comparisons were with Wilcoxon rank sum test for continuous variables and Chi-squared test for categorical variables between the two arms. RESULTS: Of the 107 patients randomized, 97 completed the study protocol; their mean age was 74 years, and 77.4% were male. CxbM was preferred by 74.2% of participants, cystoscopy by 19.4%, and 6.5% had no preference (p<0.001). CxbM was associated with markedly less pain (p<0.001), greater convenience (p<0.001), and no instances of missed work compared to cystoscopy. Five recurrences (5.2%) were detected, all noninvasive with no missed high-grade events. Discordant error rates were comparable between arms (13 (44.8%) vs 11(45.8%), p>0.99). CONCLUSIONS: Patients strongly preferred CxbM over cystoscopy, providing less pain, more convenience, and improved satisfaction while maintaining comparable diagnostic performance, quality of life, and fear of cancer recurrence. Incorporating CxbM into NMIBC surveillance may enhance patient adherence and experience without compromising oncologic safety. Guideline organizations should consider this data when refining evidence-based surveillance recommendations to optimize patient-centered care in NMIBC. | | | --- | | |

title: IP02-18: Impact of chronic kidney disease on prognosis in patients with high-risk non-muscle-invasive bladder cancer who underwent adjuvant bacillus Calmette-Guérin therapy
parentSessionTitle: IP02: Bladder Cancer: Non-invasive I

speakers.organization: Hirosaki University Graduate School of Medicine

fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Immune dysfunction is a well-recognized complication in patients with chronic kidney disease (CKD), potentially impairing host defense mechanisms against malignancy. Bacillus Calmette-Guérin (BCG) therapy is a cornerstone of adjuvant treatment for high-risk non-muscle invasive bladder cancer (NMIBC), relying on robust local immune activation to prevent tumor recurrence and progression. However, the efficacy of BCG may be compromised in individuals with CKD due to impaired immunological responses. We hypothesized that patients with CKD may exhibit suboptimal antitumor immunity following adjuvant BCG therapy, resulting in inferior oncological outcomes.
