METHODS: We conducted a multi-institutional retrospective study assessing 209 patients with high-risk NMIBC who underwent transurethral resection of bladder tumor (TURBT) and subsequent adjuvant induction BCG therapy from December 1998 to April 2019. Patients were divided into two groups: those with preoperative estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) ≥ 60 ml/min/1.73 m2 (non-CKD group), and those with eGFR < 60 ml/min/1.73 m2 (CKD group). Multivariable analyses were performed to assess the impact of CKD on intravesical recurrence and muscle-invasive bladder cancer (MIBC) progression, adjusting for the competing risk of death using the Fine-Gray competing risk regression model. RESULTS: Median age and follow-up period after TURBT were 72 years and 45 months, respectively. Of 209 patients, 71 (34%) were diagnosed with CKD before TURBT. In the Fine-Gray competing risk regression model, CKD showed significantly higher probabilities of intravesical recurrence and MIBC progression, with an adjusted subdistribution hazard ratio of 1.886 (95% confidence interval \[CI\] 1.069–3.330, P=0.028) and 3.740 (95% CI 1.060–13.20, P=0.040), respectively ( Fig. A and B). Moreover, metastasis-free survival, cancer-specific survival, and overall survival in the CKD group were significantly shorter than those in the non-CKD group (Fig. C-E). CONCLUSIONS: CKD presents a risk factor of poor oncological outcomes in patients with high-risk NMIBC who underwent adjuvant induction BCG therapy after TURBT. These findings suggest that impaired renal function may compromise the efficacy of BCG-mediated antitumor immunity, underscoring the need for tailored surveillance and therapeutic strategies in this vulnerable population.

title: IP02-19: Prognostic significance of symptom-driven recurrence in high-risk non-muscle-invasive bladder cancer
parentSessionTitle: IP02: Bladder Cancer: Non-invasive I

speakers.organization: Hirosaki University Graduate School of Medicine

fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Because patients with high-risk non-muscle invasive bladder cancer (NMIBC) have high recurrence and progression rates, it is recommended that they undergo intensive surveillance after transurethral resection of bladder tumor (TURBT). However, no study has demonstrated that such an intensive surveillance contributes to improving oncological outcomes. Moreover, no study has investigated an association between symptomatic recurrence and poor prognosis in patients with high-risk NMIBC. METHODS: We retrospectively evaluated 428 patients with primary high-risk NMIBC who underwent TURBT from November 1993 to April 2019. Of the 428 patients, 140 had experienced recurrence at any site and were divided into two groups: patients who had experienced recurrence detected by the surveillance (asymptomatic group) and patients who experienced recurrence detected by a symptom-driven investigation (symptomatic group). Background-adjusted multivariable analyses with the inverse probability of treatment weighting (IPTW) method were performed to evaluate the impact of symptomatic recurrence on cancer-specific survival (CSS) and overall survival (OS) after first recurrence in patients who experienced recurrence. Moreover, multivariable analysis was performed to identify predictive factors of symptomatic recurrence in the entire cohort. RESULTS: Median age and follow-up periods were 72 years and 55 months, respectively. Of the 140 patients who experienced recurrence, 106 (76%) were diagnosed by a symptom-driven investigation (symptomatic group). Muscle invasive bladder cancer progression rate in the symptomatic group was significantly higher than that in the asymptomatic group (23.5% vs. 6.5%, P=0.005). CSS and OS after the first recurrence in the symptomatic group were significantly shorter than those in the asymptomatic group ( Fig. A and B). In the background-adjusted multivariable analyses with the IPTW model, symptomatic recurrence was significantly associated with shorter CSS along with shorter OS after the first recurrence ( Fig. C). In the multivariable analysis, only tumor grade was selected as a significant predictive factor of symptomatic recurrence after TURBT ( Table). CONCLUSIONS: Symptomatic recurrence was significantly associated with poor oncological outcomes in patients with primary high-risk NMIBC. Patients with grade 3 tumors may require more intensive surveillance after TURBT.

title: IP02-20: Immune Microenvironment Signatures of Response to Cretostimogene Grenadenorepvec in BCG-Unresponsive Non–Muscle Invasive Bladder Cancer
parentSessionTitle: IP02: Bladder Cancer: Non-invasive I
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: A novel agent under investigation for BCG-unresponsive NMIBC is cretostimogene grenadenorepvec (creto), an adenoviral dual-mechanistic oncolytic gene therapy. The BOND-003 phase 3 clinical trial demonstrated a 75% CR rate at any time. Our tertiary care academic medical center investigated a cohort of creto-treated patients with variable responses for whom tissue is available to perform multiplex immunofluorescence (MIF), to better understand the tumor microenvironment associated with treatment response. METHODS: Patients who provided informed consent and received creto for whom at least one pre- and one post-treatment FFPE tissue sample were available were included. MIF staining was performed with the Opal Polaris 7-color fluorescence immunohistochemistry kit. Antibodies used were CD8, FoxP3, TCF1, PD1, MHC-II, and CD4. Vectra Polaris Automated Quantitative Pathology Imaging System was used for multispectral imaging. QuPath-0.2.3 was used to quantify whole slide fluorescence intensity within each cell and calculate cellular density. Patients were classified as Responder \[R\] if they had no recurrence during follow-up, Early Non-Responder \[ENR\] if they developed high-grade recurrence < 1 year after starting creto, Late Non-Responder \[LNR\] if they recurred > 1 year after starting treatment, and Progressor \[P\] if they were upstaged to > T1 at any point during follow-up. RESULTS: A total of 15 specimens from six patients were included (1 R, 3 ENRs, 1 LNR, 1 P). There was no difference in post-treatment recruitment of CD8+ or CD4+ cells between responders (R + LNR) vs non-responders (ENR + P). An increased post-treatment ratio of CD8+ to FOXP3+ cells was seen with responders compared to non-responders ( (https://www.auajournals.org/doi/abs/10.1097/01.JU.0001191276.85430.b0.20#F1)). An increased ratio of CD4+/FOXP3+ and CD4+/PD1+ was also seen with responders compared to non-responders. CONCLUSIONS: In this analysis of MIF performed in patients who received creto, pre- and post-treated tissue demonstrates immunologic hallmarks of response vs non-response that is similar to what has been shown in other studies in bladder cancer. These data indicate that effective anti-tumor immunity in this context depends less on total immune infiltration and more on the equilibrium between effector and regulatory immune subsets.

title: IP02-21: Longitudinal Quality of Life After Radical Cystectomy: A Comparative Analysis of Overall Trends between muscle-invasive versus non-muscle-invasive bladder cancer.
parentSessionTitle: IP02: Bladder Cancer: Non-invasive I
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: To compare Quality of life (QoL) trajectory between patients with muscle-invasive (MI) versus non-muscle-invasive (NMI) bladder cancer (BC) treated with radical cystectomy (RC). METHODS: Within our institutional database we identified all patients treated with RC for non-metastatic bladder cancer for whom QoL was assessed using the EORTC QLQ-C30 questionnaire at baseline and at multiple follow-up points up to 36 months. The overall cohort was stratified between “true” NMIBC (as confirmed by RC pathology, NMIBC-yes) vs those exhibiting MIBC either prior or at RC pathology (NMIBC-No). Spaghetti plots, linear mixed-effects models and interaction tests were used to analyze the overall trajectories and to test for differences between MIBC and NMIBC groups over time. Multivariable adjustments for age-adjusted Charlson comorbidity index, robot-assisted approach and urinary diversion were performed. RESULTS: Descriptive characteristics were reported in Table 1. At baseline, NMIBC patients exhibited lower Fatigue (FA; estimate -6.44, p=0.016) and Constipation (CO; estimate -7.63, p=0.017). However, both MIBC and NMIBC patients demonstrated significant QoL deterioration over time across multiple functional (PF, RF, SF) and symptom (FA, DY, AP, CO) domains compared to their baseline ( (https://www.auajournals.org/doi/abs/10.1097/01.JU.0001191276.85430.b0.21#F1)). Trajectories were largely parallel between groups, although significant interactions indicated less favorable symptom progression for NMIBC for Constipation (CO, estimate +9.80 at 3 mos, p=0.032), Insomnia (SL, Estimate +10.40 at 3 mos, p=0.021) and Diarrhoea (DY, Estimate +11.20 at 36 mos, p<0.001). Conversely, NMIBC patients showed a trajectory advantage only in Social Functioning (SF; Est. +10.45 at 12 mos, p=0.034). CONCLUSIONS: In this study, patients undergoing RC for both MIBC and NMIBC experienced a significant and sustained deterioration in several QoL domains. Contrary to potential expectations, the long-term QoL trajectories were largely parallel between the two groups. These findings suggest that the impact of RC on QoL is substantial, irrespective of the disease stage, and patient counseling should emphasize that long-term QoL changes are common for both cohorts.

title: IP02-22: Survival Outcomes of BCG only, BCG plus EMDA-MMC, or Upfront Radical Cystectomy in High-Risk Non-Muscle Invasive Bladder Cancers (NMIBCs): A Multicentre Collaborative Study from Two Independent Tertiary Referral Institutions
parentSessionTitle: IP02: Bladder Cancer: Non-invasive I
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: High-risk categories of Non-Muscle Invasive Bladder Cancer (NMIBC) remain a therapeutic challenge due to the substantial risk of recurrence and progression despite guideline-based intravesical therapy. The choice between conservative bladder preservation and early radical surgery is still debated, especially in those with adverse pathological features. This study compared survival outcomes among alternative treatment strategies within this high-risk setting. METHODS: High- or Very High-risk NMIBCs treated at two tertiary referral centers between 2009 and 2024 were reviewed. All patients underwent TURBT followed by one of three treatment approaches: Bacillus Calmette–Guérin (BCG) alone (I), sequential BCG plus electromotive administration of mitomycin C (EMDA-MMC) (II), or upfront radical cystectomy (RC) (III). Demographic, clinical, and pathological data were assessed. Recurrence-free survival (RFS), Progression-free Survival (PFS), and Overall Survival (OS) were estimated using Kaplan–Meier methods. Multivariable Cox regression modeling was applied to identify predictors independently associated with survival imbalances. RESULTS: A total of n=1178 patients were included, n=852 BCG only, n=249 BCG/EMDA-MMC, and n=77 upfront RC. Kaplan–Meier analysis revealed no significant differences in RFS or PFS between the BCG and BCG/EMDA-MMC groups, nor in OS among the three treatment strategies. On multivariable analysis, both recurrence and disease were not influenced by the type on intravesical treatment (HR: 0.95, 95%CI 0.732-1.238, p=0.71 for RFS and HR: 0.80, 95%CI 0.557-1.155, p=0.24 for PFS, respectively for BCG/EMDA-MMC vs. BCG only). Similarly, none of the evaluated therapeutic approaches (BCG/EMDA-MMC vs. BCG only vs. upfront RC) was independently impacting OS (HR: 1.00, 95%CI 0.701-1.424, p=1.00 for BCG/EMDA-MMC vs. BCG only: HR: 1.13, 95%CI 0.591-2.143, p=0.72 for upfront RC vs. BCG only; HR: 0.89, 95%CI 0.47-1.7, p=0.73 for BCG/EMDA-MMC vs. upfront RC). CONCLUSIONS: Survival outcomes were primarily influenced by age, tumor stage, presence of concomitant CIS, and Re-TURBT. Of note, type of treatment modality (i. e., BCG only, sequential BCG/EMDA-MMC, or upfront RC) did not significantly affect RFS, PFS, or OS. These findings suggest that patient and tumor characteristics, rather than treatment modality, may preferably guide individualized management decisions in high-risk NMIBCs.

title: IP02-23: Duration of response to UGN-102 by age at baseline across 3 clinical trials in patients with low-grade intermediate-risk bladder cancer
parentSessionTitle: IP02: Bladder Cancer: Non-invasive I
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: UGN-102, a reverse thermal hydrogel formulation of mitomycin (75 mg), is FDA-approved for the treatment of adult patients with recurrent low-grade intermediate-risk non-muscle invasive bladder cancer (LG-IR-NMIBC). Emerging data suggest that while bladder cancer is mostly diagnosed in older adults (≥70 years), young onset bladder cancer (YOBC) has a distinct profile with higher percentage of LG disease. Here we assessed the therapeutic efficacy of UGN-102 in different age groups, across three prospective clinical trials. METHODS: Data were pooled from three studies. OPTIMA II (NCT03558503)1 and ENVISION (NCT05243550)2 were single arm studies and in ATLAS (NCT04688931)3, patients were randomized to receive UGN-102 or transurethral resection. Only the UGN-102 treated patients are included in this analysis. All patients were randomized to receive six once-weekly intravesical instillations of UGN-102. Eligible patients had LG-IR-NMIBC with ≥1 prior episode of NMIBC. Outcomes included complete response (CR) at 3-months, and Kaplan-Meier (KM) estimates of duration of response (DoR) up to 12 months (pooled) and up to 24 months (ENVISION). RESULTS: In total, 338 patients treated with UGN-102 were included in this analysis. The CR rates at 3 months in the pooled data were 78.4% (29/37) and 75.7% (228/301) in patients <55 and ≥55 years, respectively. The CR rates were 73.5% (86/117) and 77.4% (171/221) in patients <65 and ≥65 years, respectively. The KM estimate of DoR was ≥ 75.9% in all pooled age subgroups at 12 months after CR, and ≥70.0% across ENVISION subgroups at 24 months after CR. In ENVISION, the median KM DoR was 29.63 months (95% CI: NE,NE) in patients <65 years; this was not estimable in the other age subgroups due to the low event rate. CONCLUSIONS: UGN-102 demonstrated robust CR rates across all age groups. Most patients remained event-free 12 months after CR in pooled data, and 24 months after CR in ENVISION. These findings support UGN-102 as an effective, durable, and age-independent treatment option for recurrent LG-IR-NMIBC. Limitations include the small size of some subgroups. 1\. Chevli KK, et al. J Urol. 2022;207(1):61–9. 2\. Prasad SM, et al. J Urol. 2025;213(2):205–16. 3\. Prasad SM, et al. J Urol. 2023;210(4):619–29. | | | --- | | |

title: IP02-24: Patient Experiences and Preferences for Chemoablation and Intravesical Drug-Releasing Systems in Non-Muscle-Invasive Bladder Cancer — A Mixed-Methods Study
parentSessionTitle: IP02: Bladder Cancer: Non-invasive I
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Transurethral resection of bladder tumor (TURBT) remains the gold standard for non-muscle-invasive bladder cancer (NMIBC), yet emerging office-based intravesical therapies offer less invasive alternatives. Patient perspectives on the procedural burden of TURBT and preferences for novel therapies remain poorly characterized. This study examines patient experiences with TURBT and their preferences when presented with alternative intravesical approaches. METHODS: We conducted a cross-sectional, mixed-methods study of 80 NMIBC patients aged >18 years who had undergone at least one TURBT within the past two years. Patients were stratified by tumor grade (low vs high). Quantitative surveys assessed demographics, treatment history, and preferences among repeat TURBT, chemoablation (UGN-102), and an intravesical drug-releasing system (TAR-200). Semi-structured interviews were conducted via a secure virtual platform using a standardized questionnaire covering TURBT experiences and hypothetical treatment scenarios informed by published efficacy and side-effect data. Descriptive statistics and thematic analysis identified key patient perspectives. RESULTS: Of the 80 eligible patients, 40 completed semi-structured phone interviews (21 low-grade, 19 high-grade; 50% response rate). The mean age was 70 years (range, 46–89), and 75% of the participants were male. Most (70%) described their TURBT experience as positive but cited emotional stress (32%), anesthesia burden (19%), and recovery time (13%) as notable challenges. When presented with alternatives, 50% preferred chemoablation to avoid anesthesia and frequent procedures, while 50% favored TURBT for reassurance of complete removal. In contrast, 94% preferred TURBT over TAR-200, citing doubts about efficacy. Nearly half (48%) stated that information about clinical trials would have influenced their treatment choices. Thematic analysis identified three domains: (1) procedural fatigue, (2) desire for shared decision-making, and (3) openness to less-invasive therapy. CONCLUSIONS: While most patients reported positive TURBT experiences, nearly half would have considered a clinical trial. Patients expressed interest in novel delivery systems for chemoablation, but only half preferred this approach over TURBT when efficacy was equal, underscoring that outcome efficacy outweighs procedural burden.

title: IP02-25: Predictors of Disease Recurrence and Progression of Non-Muscle-Invasive Bladder Cancer Following En Bloc Resection of Bladder Tumour
parentSessionTitle: IP02: Bladder Cancer: Non-invasive I

speakers.organization: urology and nephrology center, Mansoura University, Egypt

fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: To investigate the predictors of oncological outcomes of non-muscle-invasive bladder cancer (NMIBC) following en bloc resection of bladder tumour (ERBT). METHODS: The Global ERBT Registry (NCT04934540) is a prospective multinational database contributed by 74 institutes from 27 countries. Baseline patient and disease characteristics were recorded. Only patients with histologically confirmed NMIBC were included in this analysis. Primary outcomes were 1-year recurrence rate and 1-year progression rate. Multivariable Cox regression analyses were also performed. RESULTS: A total of 2216 NMIBC patients who received ERBT were included in this analysis. The median age was 69 years. The median tumour size was 1.7 cm, and the median number of tumour was 1. 80% were primary tumours, and 64% had single tumour. 68% of the patients had Ta disease, and the rest (32%) had T1 disease. 46% of them had high-grade disease, 52% had low-grade disease, and 2% had papillary urothelial neoplasm of low malignancy potential. 7.1% of the patients had concomitant carcinoma-in-situ (CIS). Detrusor muscle sampling rate was 77%, and clear resection margin was achieved in 85% of them. Overall, the 1-year recurrence rate was 16% and the 1-year progression rate was 1.3%. Upon multivariable analyses, recurrent (HR 2.12, 95% 1.52-2.94), multiple (HR 1.39, 95% 1.03-1.89), and high-grade tumours (HR 1.44, 95% 1.03-2.02) were associated with disease recurrence; T1 disease (HR 11.1, 95% 1.35-90.3), and presence of CIS (HR 3.99, 95% 1.31-12.1) were associated with disease progression. CONCLUSIONS: In NMIBC patients who received ERBT, recurrent, multiple and high-grade tumours were associated with disease recurrence; T1 disease and presence of CIS were associated with disease progression.

title: IP02-26: Development of a Non-Muscle Invasive Bladder Cancer (NMIBC) Genomic Score (NGS) that Outperforms Clinical Parameters to Predict Early BCG Failure
parentSessionTitle: IP02: Bladder Cancer: Non-invasive I
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Although BCG is the standard of care for high-grade (HG)-NMIBC, half of patients recur and 25% progress. Given emerging intravesical therapies, better biomarkers are needed to identify patients at risk for BCG failure. METHODS: We included HG-NMIBC patients treated at Memorial Sloan Kettering (MSKCC) who developed early BCG failure \[HG recurrence within 6 months of complete induction (n=24)\] or long-term response \[no recurrence 5+ years after complete induction (n=40)\]. All underwent targeted exome sequencing with MSK-IMPACT. Three machine learning algorithms (logistic regression, random forest, and support vector machine) were employed for genomic feature selection using a stratified 60:40 train-test split and 5-fold cross validation. Random forest achieved the highest test AUC and was selected for feature identification. A normalized NMIBC Genomic Score (NGS) from 0 to 100 was developed using variable importance weights, with patients stratified into risk groups. Kaplan-Meier analysis and multivariable Cox regression adjusting for AUA risk, demographics, and CIS were performed. Time-dependent ROC analysis at 12 months evaluated discriminatory performance. RESULTS: The groups had similar clinicopathologic characteristics. Random forest variable importance weights were: Mutation Count (100.0), TP53 (38.6), PIK3CA (28.7), TERT (23.2), KDM6A (17.9), FAT1 (17.4), and ERCC2 (15.1). Only TP53 was associated with early failure. Patients were stratified into intermediate/high NGS (n=42) and low NGS (n=22) groups. Those with low NGS demonstrated superior HG recurrence-free survival (HG-RFS) compared to intermediate/high NGS (median not reached, p=0.025). On multivariable Cox regression, low NGS remained protective (HR 0.32, 95% CI 0.11–0.96, p=0.04). ROC analysis at 12 months showed that adding genomic variables to AUA risk resulted in a 22% relative improvement in AUC (AUA Risk AUC: 0.545, Combined: 0.666). CONCLUSIONS: This preliminary evaluation of the novel NGS, derived from the clinically implemented MSK-IMPACT assay, demonstrates independent association with early BCG failure in HG-NMIBC, suggesting utility for risk stratification beyond clinical parameters. Prospective validation in a larger cohort will determine whether this biomarker could identify patients who will benefit from alternative therapies or early cystectomy.

title: IP02-27: Safety and Technical Feasibility Outcomes of En Bloc Resection of Bladder Tumour: First Analysis from The Global ERBT Registry
parentSessionTitle: IP02: Bladder Cancer: Non-invasive I

speakers.organization: The Chinese University of Hong Kong

fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: To report the safety and technical feasibility outcomes of en bloc resection of bladder tumour (ERBT) utilising data from the Global ERBT Registry. METHODS: The Global ERBT Registry (NCT04934540) is a prospective multinational database contributed by 74 institutes from 27 countries. Baseline patient and disease characteristics were recorded. Peri-operative outcomes including the technical success rate of ERBT, operative time, single-dose intravesical chemotherapy instillation rate, hospital stay, and 30-day complications were recorded. Final pathology results including presence of detrusor muscle and resection margin status were recorded. RESULTS: A total of 2630 patients were included in this analysis. The median age was 69 years. The median tumour size was 1.7 cm and the median number of tumour was 1. 80% were primary tumours, and 65% had single tumour. The majority of the patients had right lateral wall (31%), left lateral wall (31%) and posterior wall (19%) tumours. The technical success rate of ERBT was 97%, and the median operative time was 30 min. Single-dose intravesical chemotherapy was instilled in 40% of the patients; mitomycin C was the commonest instillation agent (74%). The median hospital stay was 2 days. All-grade 30-day complications occurred in 7.6% patients. Among them, 1.5% were Clavien-Dindo grade 3 or above complications, and the most common were haematuria (0.8%) and bladder perforation (0.4%). 91% of the patients had urothelial carcinoma, and among them, 96% were non-muscle-invasive bladder cancer (NMIBC). Among those with NMIBC, clear resection margin was achieved in 85% of them. The detrusor muscle sampling rate was 77%. CONCLUSIONS: The Global ERBT registry demonstrated that ERBT was safe, technically feasible and highly generalisable in the real-world setting. | | | --- | | | | | | --- | | |

title: IP02-28: AI-informed Quantitative Mitosis Index Predicts BCG Maintenance Therapy benefit in High-Risk Non–Muscle-Invasive Bladder Cancer
parentSessionTitle: IP02: Bladder Cancer: Non-invasive I
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Bacillus Calmette–Guérin (BCG) maintenance therapy is a standard of care for high-risk non–muscle-invasive bladder cancer (HR-NMIBC), yet patient benefit varies widely. A practical biomarker identifying patients most likely to benefit could optimize treatment selection. This study evaluated whether AI-informed quantitative mitosis Index, a key histologic indicator of tumor proliferation, predicts BCG maintenance therapy benefit from routine H&E images. METHODS: Transurethral resection specimens from 341 BCG-naïve NMIBC cases were collected from two independent institutions (University Hospitals Cleveland Medical Center \[UHCMC\], n=185; Emory University \[EU\], n=156). Mitotic figures were automatically detected using a YOLO-based deep learning model trained on multi-institutional, multi-cancer datasets. The upper tertile of mitotic activity in the UHCMC cohort was used to define the high-risk group, and the same threshold was applied to the EU cohort. All patients in the EU cohort received BCG induction therapy, and the additive benefit of BCG maintenance was assessed using Cox proportional hazards models with interaction terms. The primary endpoint was 24-month high-grade recurrence-free survival (hgRFS). RESULTS: The validation cohort included only HR-NMIBC patients. Of 156 validation cases, 108 (69%) received BCG maintenance, and 22.4% experienced high-grade recurrence (hgR) within 2 years (median hgRFS: 7.7 months). In a multivariable Cox analysis, a significant interaction was observed between mitotic risk classification and maintenance therapy (interaction p=0.039). Stratification by mitotic activity revealed differential BCG maintenance therapy benefits, with mitosis-low patients showing modest but not statistically significant risk reduction (HR=0.54, 95% CI 0.25-1.16, p=0.115), while mitosis-high patients experienced substantial benefit (HR=0.115, 95% CI 0.03-0.41, p=0.0009). CONCLUSIONS: Quantitative mitotic assessment on routine H&E slides could serve as an objective biomarker to stratify patients and identify those who benefit from BCG maintenance therapy over induction in high-risk NMIBC, warranting further validation in larger, independent cohorts, particularly in the era of current BCG shortage.

title: IP02-29: Reduced versus full dose BCG maintenance in NMIBC patients treated with full dose induction: A matched analysis
parentSessionTitle: IP02: Bladder Cancer: Non-invasive I
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Due to the ongoing shortage of bacillus Calmette- Guérin (BCG) and considering its immunological mechanism, a reduced BCG dose during maintenance—while administering a full dose at induction—has been proposed for managing non-muscle invasive bladder cancer (NMIBC). METHODS: This multicenter retrospective cohort study included 989 patients from four academic institutions between 2004 and 2023. Among these, 625 patients received full dose BCG during both induction and maintenance, whereas 364 received a full induction dose followed by a reduced maintenance dose (one-third or less). The primary outcome was time to progression (muscle-invasive, nodal, or metastatic disease). Secondary outcomes included overall survival (OS), cancer-specific survival (CSS), and recurrence-free survival (RFS). Survival probabilities were estimated using the Kaplan-Meier method. Differences based on treatment were analyzed using propensity score matching (PSM) with logistic regression and 1:1 matching with replacement. Cox regression models evaluated covariates' association with outcomes. RESULTS: After matching, 606 intermediate and high-risk NMIBC patients were included: 303 in the full-dose group and 303 in the reduced-dose group. The median (IQR) age was 70. 7 (63.3-77.1) years; 77% were male, 38% had T1HG NMIBC, and 79% had high-grade disease. Baseline clinical and pathological features were similar between groups. The median (IQR) follow-up was 5.9 (3. 2-10. 0) years for the full dose maintenance group and 5.6 (3.0-8.2) years for the reduced dose group. The estimated five-year cumulative incidence of tumor progression was 14% (95% CI 10%-19%) for the full dose group versus 10% (95% CI 7%-14%) for the reduced dose group (p=0.144). Multivariable Cox regression, adjusting for age, sex, treatment year, and carcinoma in situ, showed no significant difference in the primary outcome between the full and reduced BCG maintenance doses (hazard ratio, 0.69; 95% CI, 0.44-1.11; P=0.13). No significant differences were found for CSS and OS; however, RFS was improved with the reduced dose (hazard ratio, 0.53; 95% CI, 0.43-0.67; p<0. 001). CONCLUSIONS: This cohort-matched study found no difference in progression, CSS, or OS between reduced and full BCG doses for maintenance in NMIBC patients who completed full BCG induction. These results support the need for a randomized clinical trial comparing full versus reduced maintenance BCG in patients after full BCG induction, especially given the shortage of BCG.

title: IP02-30: Development of a Machine Learning-Driven, Nanoscale Imaging Platform for Non-invasive Bladder Cancer Diagnosis in a Prospective, Cross-sectional, Case-Controlled Study
parentSessionTitle: IP02: Bladder Cancer: Non-invasive I
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Bladder cancer (BC) has a high recurrence rate, driving frequent surveillance cystoscopies with increasing cost, discomfort, and procedural risk. A reliable noninvasive rule-out test could reduce negative cystoscopy. We assessed whether a clinic-to-central-lab nanoscale urine imaging pipeline ( (https://www.auajournals.org/doi/abs/10.1097/01.JU.0001191276.85430.b0.30#F1)) can run reproducibly in routine practice, and we defined operational metrics, specimen adequacy criteria, and technical issues to guide multicenter validation. METHODS: In a prospective, cross-sectional, case-controlled study, we enrolled 95 surveillance patients with prior BC; 38 had recurrence confirmed by histology, 54 had no recurrence confirmed by negative cystoscopy, and 3 lacked a final diagnosis. Urothelial cell surfaces were scanned with a nanoscale cantilever to quantify biophysical properties (e. g., adhesion). Surface features underwent a standardized data cleaning pipeline. A finalized gradient-boosting model produced a binary patient-level output (“cancer signature detected” vs “not detected”) with thresholds prespecified for a highly sensitive use case. Performance was compared against cystoscopy/histology. RESULTS: Clinic collection with same-day courier to a central Cellens laboratory yielded an end-to-end turnaround of 2–3 days for evaluable specimens. Of 95 enrolled, 76 patients (80%) were evaluable (27 recurrence, 49 non-recurrence); 19 were non-evaluable due to inadequate urothelial cellularity (n=8), insufficient medical records (n=5), or covered with other particles (n=6). Preliminary patient-level performance on the 76-patient analysis set showed an AUC of 88.1 (95% CI: 79.1-97.0). All of the 27 positive recurrence on both low grade and high-grade patients were detected, which means that patients with negative results can be safely managed without cystoscopy. CONCLUSIONS: We demonstrated that a nanoscale urothelial cell imaging method using Atomic Force Microscopy with Machine Learning is operationally feasible with a predictable 2–3 day turnaround and 80% evaluability in routine urology practice. As samples can be collected from home, this test potentially offers patients a surveillance option outside of the clinic. By identifying those who truly need cystoscopy, this test will help provide greater access to care to patients and improve their quality of lives.

title: IP03-01: Incidental prostate cancer detection following robot-assisted simple prostatectomy versus holmium laser enucleation of the prostate in men with large benign prostatic hyperplasia: results from a high-volume European referral centre
parentSessionTitle: IP03: Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia: Surgical Therapy & New Technology I

speakers.organization: Division of Urology, IRCCS Azienda Ospedaliero-Universitaria di Bologna, Bologna, Italy

fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Robot-assisted simple prostatectomy (RASP) and holmium laser enucleation of the prostate (HoLEP) are established surgical options for men with large-volume benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH). An often underestimated endpoint in this setting is the detection of incidental prostate cancer (iPCa), which may be influenced by differences in specimen retrieval and pathological assessment. METHODS: We analysed data of 468 patients with symptomatic BPH due to large (>100 ml) prostate glands who underwent RASP (n=206, 44%) and HoLEP (n=262, 56%) at tertiary referral centre. Preoperative characteristics included age, body mass index (BMI), prostate volume, prostate-specific antigen (PSA), and PSA density (PSAD). Patients with elevated PSA or abnormal digital rectal examination underwent preoperative multiparametric magnetic resonance imaging and targeted and/or systematic biopsy to exclude clinically significant prostate cancer prior to surgery. Postoperative parameters included PSA, specimen weight, and pathological evaluation. The primary endpoint was the rate of incidental prostate cancer (iPCa) on final pathology. RESULTS: Median age and BMI were comparable between the two groups (all p>0.5), as shown in Table 1. Median prostate volume was larger in RASP (180 ml, IQR 130–220) compared with HoLEP (120 ml, IQR 110–140; p0.001). Median preoperative PSA was 6.9 ng/mL (IQR 4.8–9.2) in RASP and 6.8 ng/mL (IQR 4.7–9.0) in HoLEP (p=0.7), resulting in lower PSAD for RASP (0.038 ng/mL2, IQR 0.028–0.052) compared with HoLEP (0.057 ng/mL2, IQR 0.041–0.071; p0.001). Median postoperative PSA was 1.35 ng/mL (IQR 0.9–1.9) in RASP and 1.28 ng/mL (IQR 0.8–1.7) in HoLEP (p=0.4). Median specimen weight was 115 g (IQR 90–145) for RASP and 105 g (IQR 85–130) for HoLEP (p=0.6). iPCa was identified in 9.0% of RASP and 3.4% of HoLEP specimens (p=0.018). All tumours were ISUP Grade Group 1. CONCLUSIONS: RASP was associated with a significantly higher rate of iPCa detection compared with HoLEP, despite comparable baseline characteristics, lower PSAD, and similar specimen weight. This difference likely reflects intact specimen retrieval in RASP, providing a potential diagnostic advantage in men with large BPH. | | | --- | | |

title: IP03-02: Quality of Life and Early Outcomes Following External Beam Radiotherapy After Holmium Laser Enucleation (HoLEP): A Propensity-Matched Cohort Study
parentSessionTitle: IP03: Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia: Surgical Therapy & New Technology I

speakers.organization: University of Wisconsin School of Medicine and Public Health

fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Prostate cancer is incidentally identified (IPCA) in 5–12% of men after holmium laser enucleation of the prostate (HoLEP) for benign prostatic hyperplasia. The optimal management of these patients remains uncertain. While most are monitored with active surveillance, those with higher-grade disease or evidence of progression may require definitive treatment with external beam radiotherapy (EBRT). Limited data describe the safety, toxicity, and urinary quality-of-life outcomes of EBRT delivered after HoLEP. Therefore, we aim to directly compare patient reported urinary quality of life (QOL), surgical complications, and functional outcomes in patients receiving EBRT after HoLEP compared with propensity score matched non-EBRT HoLEP patients. METHODS: We included men who underwent HoLEP between 2020-2024 with IPCA. Radiation oncology databases were used to identify patients who received EBRT after HoLEP. Propensity score based on age and grade group was used to generate a matched cohort of patients who did not receive EBRT. Comprehensive clinical data were collected and groups compared with respect to preoperative characteristics, perioperative complications, radiation toxicity, and International Prostate Symptom Score (IPSS) responses. RESULTS: There were 38 patients in the EBRT group and 98 in the non-EBRT group. Patients receiving EBRT had higher preoperative PSA (27.6 vs 7.3 ng/mL, p=0.04), lower IPSS QOL (3.63 vs 4.44, p=0.03), and were more likely to have an indwelling catheter (37.0% vs 5.1%, p<0.001) compared to non-EBRT patients ( Table). Average postoperative IPSS QOL (2.34 vs 2.37, p=0.92) and total IPSS (6.92 vs 8.16, p=0.36) scores were similar between groups at a median follow-up of 27 months. In the EBRT group, mean IPSS QOL improved from 3.63 pre-HoLEP to 2.34 post-HoLEP and remained stable post-EBRT (2.20). RTOG acute GU toxicity was mild to moderate in most EBRT patients (grade 0–2 in 97.2%), with a single grade 3 event and no grade 4 toxicity. Perioperative surgical complications and patient reported pad use for incontinence were similar in the EBRT and non-EBRT cohorts ( Table). CONCLUSIONS: Patients receiving EBRT after HoLEP experienced low rates of high-grade toxicity and sustained urinary QOL improvement comparable to HoLEP-only patients. Further study is warranted to define optimal timing, fractionation, and long-term outcomes of post-HoLEP radiotherapy. | | | --- | | |

title: IP03-03: Comparing Short Term Perioperative Outcomes for Transurethral Resection of the Prostate, Photoselective Vaporization, and Holmium Laser Enucleation treatments of Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia
parentSessionTitle: IP03: Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia: Surgical Therapy & New Technology I

speakers.organization: Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai

fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: To compare 30-day perioperative outcomes among patients undergoing transurethral resection of the prostate (TURP), photoselective vaporization (PVP), or holmium laser enucleation (HoLEP) for benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH). METHODS: ACS-NSQIP data from 2015–2020 were reviewed to identify patients who underwent TURP, PVP, or HoLEP. The primary outcome was a composite “suboptimal” 30-day outcome (any major complication or reoperation); the secondary outcome was 30-day hospital readmission. Multivariable logistic regression compared outcomes by procedure type, adjusting for age group (<65, 65–74, ≥75 years), race, ASA class, case urgency, inpatient status, and comorbidities available in the ACS-NSQIP database. Interaction terms assessed whether procedure effects differed by age group. RESULTS: We identified 63,643 patients (mean age 70; 67.8% TURP, 25.8% PVP, 6.4% HoLEP). Overall, 11.7% experienced a 30-day suboptimal outcome and 16% were readmitted within 30 days. On adjusted analysis, HoLEP was associated with significantly lower odds of a suboptimal outcome compared to TURP (odds ratio ~0.7–0.8 in patients ≥65, p<0.01), indicating ~20–30% fewer complications, whereas PVP had no significant difference versus TURP. This improvement became more significant for older age groups. PVP was associated with higher odds of 30-day readmission versus TURP (OR ~1.2, p<0.001), while HoLEP’s readmission risk was similar to TURP. As expected, higher-risk clinical factors (urgent case, inpatient admission, elevated ASA, serious comorbidities) were independently associated with increased complications (all p<0.001). CONCLUSIONS: In this national cohort, HoLEP demonstrated the lowest perioperative morbidity among BPH surgeries, especially in older patients, without increasing readmissions. PVP and TURP had comparable complication profiles, but PVP patients were more likely to be readmitted. These data support the safety and favorable outcomes of HoLEP for BPH and may guide patient counseling and surgical selection, while highlighting the need to reduce readmissions after PVP.

title: IP03-04: Risk of Climacturia After Laser Enucleation of the Prostate for Benign Prostatic Obstruction
parentSessionTitle: IP03: Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia: Surgical Therapy & New Technology I

speakers.organization: ASST Settelaghi - University of Insubria, Varese - Italy

fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Anatomical endoscopic laser enucleation of the prostate (AEEP) is considered a first-line surgical treatment for benign prostatic obstruction (BPO) and is associated with a high rate of retrograde ejaculation, with possible negative impact on orgasmic function and transitory urinary incontinence (UI). Climacturia is defined as orgasm-associated UI, extensively reported after radical prostatectomy in association with UI. We aimed to investigate the prevalence and risk of climacturia in patients treated with AEEP for BPO. METHODS: We analyzed data recorded prospectively from 202 consecutive patients treated at a single center with holmium or thulium laser AEEP for BPO. Preoperative and perioperative clinical and functional data, including International Prostate Symptom Score (IPSS) and Sexual Encounter Profile (SEP) 2-3 questionnaire were collected. All patients were reassessed at regular follow-up visits after surgery. The prevalence of postoperative climacturia was assessed with a dedicated questionnaire. Kaplan-Meier analysis was used to estimate the risk of UI. A landmark analysis was used to assess preoperative predictors of climacturia within 3 months after surgery. RESULTS: Overall, 75 (37%) and 127 (63%) patients were treated with HoLEP and ThuLEP, respectively. Median (IQR) age was 71 (65, 75) years with a body mass index of 22.4 (20.6, 25.8). Patients had a high median prostate volume \[94 (65, 113) ml\] with a median PSA of 3.3 (1.4, 6.9) ng/mL and an IPSS of 20 (11, 25). A total of 118 (58%) patients were sexually active with normal erection according to SEP 2-3 questions. At 3 months after surgery, estimated urinary continence recovery was 93% (95% CI: 80%, 99%). Climacturia was reported by 16% (N=33) of cases, with 46% (N=92) of patients reporting being sexually active after surgery. At logistic regression analysis, prostate volume (PV) emerged as the only preoperative predictor of climacturia (OR: 1.01; 95% CI: 1.00, 1.02; p=0.01). The adjusted risk of climacturia for a patient with a PV of 40 cc was 9% (95% CI: 2–15%) compared to 22% (95% CI: 14– 30%) for one with a PV of 100 cc ( (https://www.auajournals.org/doi/abs/10.1097/01.JU.0001191280.81177.3f.04#F1)). Of note, all patients recovered from climacturia at 12 months post-treatment. CONCLUSIONS: This is the first study reporting the risk of climacturia after AEEP. Patients should be counseled regarding the risk of transient climacturia after surgery, which appears higher for patients with larger prostate volumes.

title: IP03-05: Prostatic Urethral Lift in Young Men Seeking Ejaculatory and Fertility Preservation: Semen Parameters up to 18 Months follow-up
parentSessionTitle: IP03: Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia: Surgical Therapy & New Technology I
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Minimally invasive surgical therapies (MIST) aim to relieve LUTS due to BPH while preserving sexual and ejaculatory function. We prospectively assessed semen parameters up to 18 months after prostatic urethral lift (PUL/UroLift) in men under 50 prioritizing fertility and contextualized these findings against other MIST. METHODS: In this single-center cohort (n=20), semen analyses (WHO 6th edition) were performed at baseline, 6, and 18 months after UroLift. Functional outcomes were prospectively collected through uroflowmetry with post-void residual (PVR) measurement, and subjective outcomes through the International Prostate Symptom Score (IPSS) questionnaire. Ethical Committee at the University Hospital ‘Ospedali Riuniti’, Foggia, Italy—Protocol 155/CE/2017 authorization number 618 of 18 December 2017. RESULTS: Semen parameters remained stable (median total sperm count 29.5→31.0→30.5 million/mL; p=0.88). Ejaculate volume and pH were unchanged. Motility, vitality, and morphology remained within reference thresholds. LUTS improved durably (Qmax +67%, PVR −50%, IPSS −60%). Complications occurred in 15% (1 had prostatitis treated with antibiotic therapy, 1 patient required a bladder catheter for 7 days due to acute urinary retention), re‑treatment in 10% (1 for LUTS e 1 for calcification of device). This series provides the first evidence in the literature of paternity achieved after PUL, observed in two patients. Baseline, peri-operative, and safety data are summarized in Table 1. Semen parameters at baseline, 6, and 18 months are reported in Table 2. Functional outcomes are presented in Table 3. Ejaculation preservation and semen-analysis evidence across contemporary MIST are outlined in Table 4. CONCLUSIONS: In carefully selected young men, PUL preserved semen quality and ejaculation through 18 months while providing durable symptom relief. Ejaculation‑sparing MIST should be central to counseling of fertility‑conscious patients.

title: IP03-06: Sexual function outcomes of the 5-year treatment with Rezum compared to doxazosin, finasteride and combination drug therapy for men with benign prostatic hyperplasia: cohort data from the Medical Therapy of Prostatic Symptoms (MTOPS) Trial
parentSessionTitle: IP03: Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia: Surgical Therapy & New Technology I
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Alpha blockers and 5-ARIs are a mainstay of LUTS/BPH treatment; however, there can be associated sexual function deterioration with these agents. Water vapor thermal therapy (WVTT, Rezum), a minimally invasive procedure for LUTS/BPH, serves as an efficacious treatment while preserving sexual function. We compared sexual function over 5 years after continuous daily treatment with pharmaceutical agents in the NIH-Medical Therapy of Prostatic Symptoms (MTOPS) study versus a single WVTT procedure (Rezum RCT) in subjects with matched criteria for LUTS severity and prostate size. METHODS: We used baseline sexual function data from cohorts of the MTOPS study (n=1157) randomized to doxazosin, finasteride, combination therapy, and placebo, and sexually active men at baseline (n=86) who received WVTT. MTOPS participants completed the Brief Male Sexual Function Inventory, while Rezum RCT participants completed the IIEF-15 and Male Sexual Health Questionnaire. Average percentage changes from baseline were compared using a linear mixed repeated measures model with fixed effects for treatment and follow-up visits ( (https://www.auajournals.org/doi/abs/10.1097/01.JU.0001191280.81177.3f.06#F1)). RESULTS: Men experienced significant worsening of sexual desire, erectile and ejaculatory function, and overall sexual satisfaction with finasteride and combination drug therapy. Men on doxazosin similarly had a significant decline in sexual desire, erectile and ejaculatory function, but overall sexual satisfaction was preserved. WVTT patients experienced a significant increase in sexual desire and erectile function at 1-year follow-up and a significant increase in overall sexual satisfaction over 5 years. There was a significant decrease in ejaculatory function of approximately -10% (vs. -20% combination therapy) from baseline levels from 3-5 years of follow-up with WVTT. CONCLUSIONS: WVTT may offer more favorable outcomes for sexual function compared to pharmacologic treatments, which are consistently associated with declines across multiple domains.

title: IP03-07: Comparative Risk of Erectile and Ejaculatory Dysfunction Following UroLift vs. Optilume in Men Undergoing Minimally Invasive BPH Therapy: A Propensity-Matched Cohort Study of 12-Month Outcomes
parentSessionTitle: IP03: Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia: Surgical Therapy & New Technology I

speakers.organization: UC San Diego School of Medicine

fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Minimally invasive surgical therapies (MISTs) have become increasingly popular for management of benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH). Two popular therapies include Optilume, a urethral dilation balloon coated with paclitaxel, and UroLift, an implant that mechanically widens the lumen of the prostatic urethra. However, data on sexual side effects and outcomes of these treatments is scarce. This study aimed to compare the 12-month outcomes of erectile dysfunction (ED) and ejaculatory dysfunction (EJD) following these procedures. METHODS: We conducted a retrospective cohort study using the TriNetX research network. Men with BPH undergoing UroLift or Optilume were identified, while those with prior ED or EJD were excluded using CPT and ICD codes. The UroLift and Optilume cohorts included 8630 and 1214 patients, respectively. Propensity score matching based on age, race, BMI, hypertension, diabetes, hyperlipidemia, testicular hypofunction yielded 1169 matched patients per group. Median follow-up was 365 days for UroLift and 127 days for Optilume. Primary outcomes were new-onset ED and EJD within one year post-procedure. Risk differences, relative and odds ratios, and Kaplan-Meier survival analyses were used. RESULTS: After excluding those with baseline ED, new-onset ED occurred in 6.76% of UroLift patients and 2.78% of Optilume patients, with Optilume associated with significantly lower risk (RR 0.412, 95% CI 0.259–0.655; ARR 3.97%; p=0.0001). Twelve-month ED-free survival was 92.25% for UroLift vs. 93.46% for Optilume (log-rank p=0.2730, HR 0.764, 95% CI 0.472-1.238; p=0.3487). Among patients without baseline EJD, new-onset EJD occurred in ≤10 patients per group with no significant difference in risk (RR 0.979, 95% CI 0.409–2.344) or one-year EJD-free survival (UroLift 99.22% vs Optilume 99.86%; log-rank p=0.0848; HR 0.194, 95% CI 0.024–1.553). CONCLUSIONS: Both UroLift and Optilume demonstrate low rates of new-onset ED and EJD at 12 months. Although UroLift had a higher absolute ED incidence, survival analysis showed no significant difference. EJD was rare across both procedures. Both Optilume and UroLift are viable options for men prioritizing sexual preservation with Optilume potentially preferred in those who are at an elevated baseline risk for ED.

title: IP03-08: Preservation of Sexual Function with Urocross Expander - A Novel Non-Permanent Prostatic Expander for LUTS/BPH
parentSessionTitle: IP03: Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia: Surgical Therapy & New Technology I

speakers.jobTitle: Professor and Director Center for Male Health
speakers.organization: Stritch School of Medicine Loyola University Medical Center

fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Many treatments for LUTS/BPH have negative effects on sexual function. Data from a prospective, randomized, double-blind, sham controlled study evaluating the Urocross Expander was evaluated to determine the impact of treatment with this novel technology on sexual function. The Urocross Expander is a novel MIST that combines mechanical urethral dilation with urethral reshaping using a non-permanent nitinol device removed after 6 months. METHODS: 240 subjects were randomized in a 2:1 fashion to receive the Urocross or Sham (160:80). Baseline measures included assessments via the International Index of Erectile Function (IIEF) and Men’s Sexual Health Questionnaire – Ejaculatory Dysfunction (MSHQ-EjD). Men were queried regarding history of ErectileDysfunction (ED) at the baseline (BL). RESULTS: Baseline IIEF and MSHQ-EjD were similar between the Urocross and Sham arms for sexually active subjects (IIEF 16.0±6.3 vs 16.5±5.9, MSHQ-EjD 8.2±3.3 vs 8.9±3.2). A total of 132 men randomized in the Urocross Arm claimed they are sexually active at BL. Men with active sexual activity reported overall better score of IIEF from BL, with the average IIEF score improved from 16.0 (n=132) at baseline to 17.7 (n=67) at 1yr post treatment, indicating a categorical change from “Mild to Moderate ED” to “Mild ED” ( Figure 1A). At 7mo post-treatment (1mo post-retrieval), men with severe ED improved the most and men with no ED before surgery are maintained at the BL level ( Figure 1B). Men with active sexual activity also report overall better score of MSHQ from BL through 12 months. MSHQ score has an average of 2.0 improvement at 12mo (6mo post-retrieval), regardless of their history of ED or not. CONCLUSIONS: Treatment with Urocross resulted in significant symptom relief while preserving erectile and ejaculatory function. These results offer support for the use of Urocross in men seeking treatment for LUTS/BPH who are concerned with preserving sexual function.

title: IP03-10: Morcellation Safety Checklist Significantly Reduces Errors and Enhances Team Communication During HOLEP
parentSessionTitle: IP03: Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia: Surgical Therapy & New Technology I
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Holmium Laser Enucleation of the Prostate (HoLEP) requires a critical multi-step transition from enucleation to morcellation. Despite high surgical volume, we experience preventable errors with morcellation device assembly, fluid management, and suction setup. Surgical checklists can improve consistency, reduce omissions, and facilitate communication among surgical teams. This study evaluates the impact of a novel safety checklist on morcellation errors, troubleshooting, efficiency, and complications. METHODS: We perform HOLEP using the Piranha morcellator in three distinct operating room (OR) settings, each with unique staffing pool and no dedicated teams for HOLEP. A team of physicians and staff developed a ten-item Morcellation Safety Checklist (MSC) as a “read-do” checklist (Fig.1) designed to be used before the start of morcellation. Baseline outcomes data were recorded with post-HOLEP REDCap surveys measuring morcellator efficiency, assembly or irrigation errors, pauses for troubleshooting, and complications. Prior to MSC implementation, OR staff at all three sites were engaged to ensure readiness and compliance. The MSC was attached to each morcellator and added to surgeon preference cards. Post-implementation surveys assessed impact of MSC on performance and safety outcomes. RESULTS: From September to October 2025, morcellator performance data were collected for 88 consecutive HOLEPs (43 pre-MSC and 45 post-MSC) performed by five surgeons at three facilities. Morcellator errors were reported in 44% of HOLEPs (19/43) pre-MSC compared to 17% (8/45) post-MSC implementation. Use of MSC corrected 12 morcellator setup errors in six cases prior to beginning morcellation. Irrigation fluid out errors occurred in 6.97% (3/43) pre-MSC and were eliminated (0/45) post-MSC. Pauses for troubleshooting were reduced from 21 pre-MSC to 13 post-MSC. Morcellator efficiency was not impacted by MSC: 7.7g/min pre-MSC vs. 6.4g/min post-MSC (p=0.18). No morcellator complications were reported in either group. CONCLUSIONS: Adoption of an MSC provides a standardized framework for the complex, team-based transition from enucleation to morcellation, independent of surgeon or site. The MSC reduces morcellator errors, reduces troubleshooting, and promotes safety and team engagement without sacrificing efficiency. This low-cost intervention may be implemented to improve morcellation safety.

title: IP03-11: Effect of Local Anesthetic-Eluting Foley Catheter(Free-Foley) on Urethral Pain and Discomfort After HoLEP: A Randomized Controlled Trial
parentSessionTitle: IP03: Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia: Surgical Therapy & New Technology I
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH) is common in middle-aged and older men and often requires surgical treatment. Following surgery, a large-bore (18–20 Fr) Foley catheter must be maintained to ensure adequate drainage, which invariably causes severe urethral pain and catheter-related bladder discomfort (CRBD). Systemic analgesics alone may be insufficient to relieve this localized discomfort, and their use is limited in elderly patients due to systemic side-effect risks. This study evaluated whether a Free-Foley catheter that continuously elutes 2% lidocaine can effectively reduce post-operative urethral pain and discomfort and decrease systemic analgesic use. METHODS: In a prospective, multicenter, randomized, double-blind trial, 108 male patients aged 50–79 undergoing HoLEP were allocated to either the experimental group (FreeFoley with 2% lidocaine solution, 1 ml/hr infusion) or the control group (FreeFoley with normal saline, 1 ml/hr). Pain and discomfort were assessed using the Visual Analog Scale (VAS) at postoperative recovery and at catheter removal. Primary outcomes included differences in VAS scores and systemic analgesic use. Secondary outcomes included catheter-related complications and patient satisfaction. RESULTS: 108 patients were analyzed. VAS scores were significantly lower in the experimental group compared to control group along the perioperative course (the day of surgery: 3.01 ± 1.60 \[experimental group\] vs 4.07 ± 1.65 \[control\], p<0.001; the day of catheter removal 2.35 ± 1.26 \[experimental group\] vs 3.03 ± 1.25 \[controls\], p<0.001). Analgesic requirement was also markedly reduced (5.6% vs 27.8%, p<0.001). No significant differences were observed in catheter-related complications or satisfaction. CONCLUSIONS: The anesthetic-eluting Foley catheter effectively reduces postoperative urethral pain and discomfort, as well as analgesic requirements, without increasing catheter-related complications. | | | --- | | |

title: IP03-12: A Randomized, Placebo-Controlled Trial Evaluating Tadalafil 5 mg for Management of Early Storage Symptoms and Erectile Dysfunction After HoLEP
parentSessionTitle: IP03: Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia: Surgical Therapy & New Technology I

speakers.organization: urology and nephrology center, Mansoura University, Egypt

fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: To test whether short-term tadalafil (5 mg daily) started on the day of HoLEP improves early postoperative sexual function deterioration and storage urinary symptoms versus placebo. METHODS: Prospective, parallel-group, randomized, placebo-controlled trial at a tertiary center (NCT05955001). Men≥40 y with BPH/LUTS scheduled for HoLEP were randomized 1:1 to tadalafil or placebo for 3 months starting from the day of surgery. Primary outcome was IIEF-15 orgasmic function at 3 months. Secondary outcomes included IIEF-15 total with its domains,MSHQ-ejaculatory (1, 3, 6 months), urinary outcomes including IPSS total, storage subscore, and IPSS-QoL (2 weeks, 1, 3, 6 months). Analyses were available-case, baseline-adjusted ANCOVA (adjusted mean difference, AMD; two-sided α=0.05) with supportive longitudinal models. RESULTS: A total of 160 screened; 144 randomized (tadalafil 73; placebo 71). At 3 months, 130 (90.3%) contributed primary data. During treatment, sexual outcomes favored tadalafil. At 1 month, IIEF-15 total was higher (AMD +22.7, 95% CI +15.1 to +30.3; p<0.001); domains also favored tadalafil, including erectile function (AMD +8.15; p<0.001). For the primary endpoint, orgasmic function showed superiority at 1 month (AMD +2.7, 95% CI +1.6 to +3.8; p<0.001) and 3 months (AMD +2.3, 95% CI +1.4 to +3.2; p<0.001), with convergence by 6 months after discontinuation. Urinary outcomes improved in both groups after HoLEP; baseline-adjusted differences already favored tadalafil at 2 weeks for IPSS total (AMD−5.67; p<0.001), storage (AMD−2.98; p<0.001) and IPSS-QoL (AMD−0.71; p<0.001), persisted at 1 and 3 months (e. g., IPSS total AMD−4.97 and−2.62, both p≤0.002), and were no longer evident at 6 months. By 6 months, both arms remained significantly better than baseline for IPSS total, storage, and QoL. Adverse events with tadalafil were infrequent (headache 6.4%, musculoskeletal pain 6.5%, dyspepsia 5.1%); three patients discontinued. Thirty-day complication rates were similar between groups. CONCLUSIONS: Tadalafil 5 mg daily, begun on the day of HoLEP and continued for 3 months, provides a transient, clinically meaningful early benefit in sexual function (including the preregistered orgasmic domain) and in storage-predominant LUTS, with group differences dissipating after therapy stops. These data support short-term PDE5I therapy to bridge the vulnerable early postoperative period.

title: IP03-13: Examining the Effects of Preoperative Bowel Function on Holmium Laser Enucleation of Prostate (HoLEP) Outcomes
parentSessionTitle: IP03: Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia: Surgical Therapy & New Technology I
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: The relationship between bowel and bladder function is well-described, however the association between bowel function and outcomes from benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH) surgery is not well characterized. We sought to investigate the association of preoperative bowel function on urinary recovery after holmium laser enucleation of prostate (HoLEP). METHODS: We performed a prospective cohort study and recruited patients undergoing HoLEP by a single surgeon at a high-volume center between Dec 2023 and Sep 2024. Preoperative bowel function was evaluated using the validated Constipation Scoring System (CSS) and Vaizey Incontinence Score (VIS) patient questionnaires. Primary outcomes include change in International Prostate Symptom Score (IPSS) and Michigan Incontinence Severity Index (MISI) scores at 3 months. Statistical analysis was performed using Pearson correlations and linear regression as appropriate. RESULTS: We enrolled 120 patients, with 93 patients completing 3-month follow-up included in the analysis. Mean age was 71.1 and mean preoperative prostate size was 102.2g. Forty-four (47%) patients had history of prior urinary retention. Mean preoperative CSS and VIS were 2.9 and 1.2, respectively. Mean preoperative IPSS total and quality of life (QoL) scores were 18.0 and 4.3. Mean preoperative MISI severity and bother were 5.2 and 1.7. Postoperative IPSS total, QOL, and MISI bother scores improved by 12.0, 2., and 0.6 respectively, while MISI severity worsened by 0.3. Higher CSS scores were correlated with higher VIS scores (r=0.452, p<0.001) and less improvement in postoperative IPSS total scores (r=-0.211, p=0.043). Higher VIS was associated with less improvement in MISI severity (r=-0.261, p=0.012). On linear regression controlling for age, BMI, prostate size, and history of urinary retention, higher VIS continued to be predictive of less improvement in MISI severity (β=-0.308, p=0.013). Higher CSS was associated with decreased change in IPSS total scores however did not reach statistical significance (β=-200, p=0.083). CONCLUSIONS: Patients with higher degree of self-reported preoperative constipation and bowel incontinence appear to have less improvement in urinary symptoms after HoLEP, suggesting that optimization of bowel function may help maximize BPH surgery outcomes. | | | --- | | |

title: IP03-14: Comparative Efficacy and Outcomes of Holmium and its Moses 1.0 and Moses 2.0 Pulse Modulation Laser Modes in Patients Undergoing HoLEP for Treating LUTS in BPH Patients with Trainee Involvement
parentSessionTitle: IP03: Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia: Surgical Therapy & New Technology I
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Moses™ pulse modulation was developed to enhance the efficiency of Holmium laser enucleation of the prostate (HoLEP) by optimizing energy delivery to tissue. While studies have compared either Moses 1.0 (M1) or Moses 2.0 (M2) with standard Holmium (SH), direct comparisons across all three platforms remain limited. This study aimed to evaluate perioperative and functional outcomes among SH, M1, and M2 HoLEP performed in an academic setting with trainee involvement. METHODS: We retrospectively reviewed all men who underwent HoLEP between June 2022 and May 2024 at a single academic institution. Patients were categorized by laser platform: SH, M1, or M2 based on OR where case was performed. All patients were kept overnight for observation and planned to be discharged next day after voiding trial. Baseline demographics, perioperative parameters, complications, and functional outcomes up to 6 months were analyzed using ANOVA or Kruskal–Wallis tests, with p<0.05 considered significant. RESULTS: A total of 389 patients were included (SH n=206; M1 n=126; M2 n=57). Baseline characteristics were comparable among groups ( Table 1). Median operative times were 105 (80–157) for M1, 100 (37–163) for M2, and 95 (73–115) minutes for SH (p=0.25), and median resected prostate weights were similar (85 g vs 79 g vs 84 g respectively, p=0.44). Median hospital stay was slightly longer with Moses lasers (1.6 days each) than with SH (1.4 days, p<0.001). Hemoglobin drop and transfusion rates were low and did not differ significantly among groups, and rates of acute urinary retention and urethral stricture were similarly infrequent. Continence recovery at 4–6 weeks was comparable among groups (73.2% M1 vs 81.0% M2 vs 73.8% SH, p=0.60). At 6 months, IPSS, Qmax, and PVR improvements were significant within each group but comparable across modalities. CONCLUSIONS: HoLEP was safe and effective across all laser platforms. Perioperative and functional outcomes were comparable, with similar continence recovery, hemoglobin drop, and transfusion rates. No clinically meaningful differences were observed among technologies. Thus, laser selection should be guided by institutional availability and surgeon preference rather than expected outcome differences. | | | --- | | |

title: IP03-15: Early Apical Release in Holmium Laser Enucleation of the Prostate. Is It Worth it? A Meta-Analysis and Meta-Regression on Perioperative and Postoperative Outcomes.
parentSessionTitle: IP03: Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia: Surgical Therapy & New Technology I
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Holmium Laser Enucleation of the Prostate (HoLEP) is a standard surgery for benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH), but early continence issues persist. Early Apical Release (EAR), often with en-bloc enucleation, aims to release apical mucosa early, reducing sphincter strain and functional risks. Evidence for its benefits is limited, with varying techniques among urologists. This meta-analysis compares EAR to standard HoLEP on efficacy, safety, operative times, and complications. METHODS: We searched PubMed, Embase, Cochrane through April 2025 for studies comparing EAR vs standard HoLEP. Followed PRISMA; extracted data from reports; assessed quality per Cochrane. Outcomes: operative time, American Urological Association Symptom Score (AUASS) at 3 months, Clavien-Dindo (≤2 and≥3a), overall complications, postoperative incontinence (<30 days and 1–3 months). RESULTS: Six studies were included, comprising 3,538 patients (1,440 EAR and 2,098 standard). There was no significant difference in AUASS at 3 months (MD-0.10; 95% CI-1.42 to 1.22; p=0.88; I2=75%) or operative time (MD-0.09 minutes; 95% CI-11.51 to 11.33 minutes; p=0.99; I2=93%). No statistically significant difference was observed in early postoperative incontinence, both within 30 days (OR 0.33; 95% CI 0.10–1.03; p=0.06; I2=90%;) and at 1–3 months (OR 0.38; 95% CI 0.13–1.14; p=0.09; I2=67%). However, EAR was associated with significantly higher rates of complications: Clavien-Dindo≤2 (OR 1.44; 95% CI 1.11 to 1.87; p=0.006; I2=0%), Clavien-Dindo≥3 (OR 2.53; 95% CI 1.24 to 5.17; p=0.01; I2=0%), and overall complications (OR 1.46; 95% CI 1.18 to 1.79; p=0.0004; I2=0%). Meta-regression showed that prostate size (=-0.0891, p=0.015) and incontinence definition varying from 0-2 pads (=-3.2059, p=0.001) significantly moderates the treatment effect on incontinence risk, explaining part of heterogeneity. CONCLUSIONS: EAR was not superior to non-EAR standard techniques. Moreover, EAR was associated with a significantly higher overall complication rate, including both Clavien-Dindo grade≤2 and≥3 complications. No significant differences were observed between the techniques regarding symptom relief or operative time. These findings suggest that familiarity with both approaches may be beneficial to optimize patient outcomes and tailor the surgical strategy to individual clinical scenarios.

title: IP03-16: HoLEP for Large and Mega Glands: Real-World Outcomes and Evidence of Size-Enhanced Efficiency
parentSessionTitle: IP03: Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia: Surgical Therapy & New Technology I
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: While not formally standardized, the term “mega gland” is most applied to prostates larger than 200cc on preoperative imaging. Mega gland prostates are traditionally perceived as technically challenging for holmium laser enucleation of the prostate (HoLEP) due to increased vascularity, difficult planes, and instrument length limitations. This study evaluates perioperative and postoperative outcomes of HoLEP for mega glands compared with large glands (120–200cc) in a contemporary real-world cohort. METHODS: We conducted a single-center, retrospective analysis of patients who underwent HoLEP for glands≥120cc between January 2021 and June 2025. Patients were categorized into large (120-200cc) and mega (>200cc) gland groups. Baseline characteristics, intraoperative parameters, and postoperative outcomes were compared using Wilcoxon rank-sum, Pearson’s chi-square, and Fisher’s exact tests on R (v4.4.3). RESULTS: Out of 602 HoLEPs performed during the study period, there were 208 patients with large gland prostates and 35 with mega gland prostates. Baseline characteristics were broadly similar between groups, though mega glands demonstrated higher baseline PSA (9.9 vs 5.6 ng/mL, p=0.001). Operative time was longer for mega glands (114 vs 96 min, p=0.003), as expected. However, enucleation speed (2.8 vs 1.6 g/min, p<0.001) and energy efficiency (0.8 vs 0.5 g/kJ, p<0.001) were significantly higher in mega glands, despite similar enucleation times. Postoperatively, length of stay was slightly longer (1.0 \[1.0–1.0\] vs 1.0 \[1.0–2.0\] days, p=0.011) for mega group. No significant differences were observed in catheter duration, failed void trial, ED visits, readmission, or 3-month PROM evaluation (MISI, p=0.248; IPSS, p=0.533). CONCLUSIONS: Although large prostates have traditionally been viewed as technically challenging, our data suggests a volume threshold beyond which HoLEP becomes more efficient, with higher enucleation speed and energy efficiency in glands >200 ml. This highlights HoLEP as a size-enhanced procedure—not merely size-independent—achieving excellent perioperative and functional outcomes. Further work is needed to define this efficiency threshold more precisely and explore its clinical implications. | | | --- | | |

title: IP03-17: Perioperative outcomes and prevalence of urethral strictures during surgery for benign prostatic hyperplasia: results from the GRAND study
parentSessionTitle: IP03: Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia: Surgical Therapy & New Technology I
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Limited data exist on the prevalence of urethral strictures during surgery for benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH). We aimed to analyze their perioperative outcomes and trends. METHODS: The German Nationwide Inpatient Data (GRAND) registry was used to identify male patients diagnosed with urethral stricture who underwent surgery for BPH between 2005 and 2022. Multivariable regression analyses were performed to compare perioperative morbidity. RESULTS: A total of 1,367,065 BPH surgeries were performed in Germany. Of them, 150,356 had a relevant concomitant urethral stricture (11%). Their median age was 72 years (interquartile range: 66-78). Patients with urethral stricture during BPH surgery underwent an internal urethrotomy in 113,501 (75%) cases, a dilation of the urethral stricture in 29,848 (20%) cases, or a meatoplasty in 7,007 (5%) cases. The annual prevalence of relevant urethral strictures during BPH surgery has decreased from 11,329 (7.5%) cases in 2005 to 5,900 (3.9%) in 2022. Compared to patients with no urethral stricture, those with urethral strictures during BPH surgery displayed higher rates of postoperative incontinence (4.5% versus 3.6%) and reoperations (1.2% versus 0.8%). On the contrary, they were associated with lower rates of perioperative acute urinary retention (9.3% versus 9.8%). CONCLUSIONS: Urethral strictures during surgery for BPH display a high prevalence and may affect perioperative outcomes.

title: IP03-18: Plasma-Kinetic Enucleation of the Prostate (PKEP): Safety and Efficacy in Patients on Antiplatelet and Anticoagulant Therapy
parentSessionTitle: IP03: Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia: Surgical Therapy & New Technology I
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Discontinuation of anticoagulant or antiplatelet therapy prior to surgery carries an increased risk of thromboembolic events, while continuation raises concerns about perioperative bleeding. Plasma-kinetic enucleation of the prostate (PKEP) is a minimally invasive and effective technique for the treatment of benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH). The aim of this study was to evaluate the safety and efficacy of PKEP in patients receiving antiplatelet (AP) or anticoagulant (AC) therapy. METHODS: Data were retrospectively reviewed for patients who underwent PKEP between March 2023 and July 2025. All patients underwent preoperative transrectal ultrasound (TRUS) evaluation to assess prostate size. Demographic characteristics, intraoperative parameters, and postoperative outcomes were analyzed. RESULTS: Among 116 operated patients, 64 (Group A) were on anticoagulant or antiplatelet therapy, and 52 (Group B) were not. Patients in Group A were older. No significant differences were found in prostate size, resected tissue weight, or operative time ( Table 1). Most patients were catheterized preoperatively, and all were catheter-free within a median of 0.5 days postoperatively in both groups (p=0.39). The mean IPSS decreased from 24 to 9.2, with an average improvement of 14.8 points, showing no intergroup difference (p=0.7). Postoperatively, 4 patients in Group A and 3 in Group B required blood transfusions (6.2% vs. 5.7%, p=0.91). One patient in each group required endoscopic coagulation for hemostasis. The overall complication rate did not differ significantly between groups (20.3% vs. 19.2%, p=0.88), despite the higher mean age in Group A ( Table 2). CONCLUSIONS: PKEP is a safe and effective procedure even in patients maintained on anticoagulant or antiplatelet therapy. The surgery can be performed without discontinuation of blood thinners, achieving significant symptomatic improvement without an increased risk of bleeding or major complications. | | | --- | | | | | | --- | | |

title: IP03-19: Single Lateral Lobe Sparing Hemi-Holmium Laser Enucleation of the Prostate (Hemi-HoLEP) Outcomes Compared to Standard Whole-Gland HoLEP
parentSessionTitle: IP03: Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia: Surgical Therapy & New Technology I
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: There is limited data on outcomes of holmium laser enucleation of the prostate (HoLEP) in patients with prior pelvic XRT given potential risks of poor wound healing and incontinence. The objective of this study was to investigate post-operative outcomes of a novel approach, hemi-HoLEP, in which we spare the smaller of the two lateral lobes to avoid a circumferential epithelial defect. METHODS: We retrospectively identified 11 hemi-HoLEP patients and propensity-score matched with a 3:1 ratio to 33 whole-gland HoLEP controls based on age and prostate specimen weight. All HoLEP patients had at least 3 months of follow up. Statistical analysis was performed using t-tests, Fisher’s exact test, and Chi-squared tests (p<0.05). RESULTS: Hemi-HoLEP patients were more likely to be actively in urinary retention prior to surgery (64% vs 24%, p=0.043). Average specimen weight was 13g in the control cohort and 17g in the hemi-HoLEP cohort (p=0.5). Enucleation time was significantly shorter in the hemi-HoLEP cohort (13.3 vs 16.9 minutes, p=0.031). All hemi-HoLEP patients planned for same-day trial of void (TOV) passed their same-day TOV (8/8, 100%). There were no incidences of urethral stricture or bladder neck contracture in either group. Complications and medical visits at 90 days post-operatively were similar amongst both groups (p>0.05). Hemi-HoLEP patients had increases in their Michigan Incontinence Symptom Index (M-ISI) bother scores post-op compared to pre whereas control patients showed slight decreases (0.27 vs-0.39, p=0.04). Post-operative outcomes are summarized in Table 1, and differences in AUA Symptom Score and M-ISI scores are listed in Table 2. CONCLUSIONS: We describe outcomes of a novel approach to treatment of benign prostatic hyperplasia after pelvic XRT using hemi-HoLEP. Although our series is limited, hemi-HoLEP patients had similar post-operative outcomes to standard healthy controls. Based on these results, we noted that hemi-HoLEP is a viable treatment option for post-XRT benign prostatic hyperplasia patients. Larger, prospective studies are needed to better understand these findings. | | | --- | | | | | | --- | | |

title: IP03-20: Cost-Effectiveness of Contemporary BPH Surgical Options for Glands 30-80cc: Insights from a Microsimulation Model
parentSessionTitle: IP03: Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia: Surgical Therapy & New Technology I
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: BPH surgical options vary significantly in regards to costs and outcomes, as do individual patient priorities. Herein, we performed a comprehensive cost-effectiveness analysis (CEA) for BPH procedures, assessing sensitivity to variations in weighting of different outcomes. METHODS: Using a microsimulation model, a CEA was performed comparing HoLEP, TURP, WVTT, PUL, RWT, iTIND, and Optilume. Model probabilities were based on published values, and effectiveness was calculated using post-operative complication severity, sexual function, and urinary symptom scores (IPSS). The model was performed from a U. S. Medicare payer perspective, with quality-adjusted life years (QALYs) and incremental cost-effectiveness ratios (ICERs) used to assess cost-effectiveness at a willingness-to-pay threshold of $100,000/QALY. Univariate and probabilistic sensitivity analyses were performed. RESULTS: Over a patient’s lifetime, HoLEP resulted in the highest QALYs (12.25), followed by iTIND (12.02) and WVTT (11.98). Lifetime BPH costs per patient ranged from $6,557 (WVTT) and $8,431 (HoLEP) to $13,327 (PUL). HoLEP was most cost-effective (ICER $6,931). However, the probability and utility value (effectiveness) of post-operative ejaculatory dysfunction significantly impacted model outputs. In addition, the cost-effectiveness of HoLEP was dependent upon relatively high post-HoLEP urinary symptom utility values as well as longer life expectancy ( Figure 1-2). CONCLUSIONS: Using currently published data, HoLEP is the most cost-effective option for patients with a gland size 30-80cc. However, ejaculatory-preserving therapies (e. g. WVTT, PUL, iTIND) become favored if higher patient priority is given to antegrade ejaculation. Similarly, HoLEP is only cost-effective at longer life expectancy (>10 years), and with high symptom improvement. Such findings highlight the benefit of HoLEP on a systems-level, while also emphasizing the imperative of surgical selection driven by individual patient priorities.

title: IP03-21: Three-Year Reintervention Outcomes After Rezum vs UroLift: A TriNetX Comparative Analysis
parentSessionTitle: IP03: Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia: Surgical Therapy & New Technology I
