speakers.organization: Shin Kong Wu Ho-Su Memorial Hospital

fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Rezum and UroLift are minimally invasive options for benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH), yet head-to-head long-term data are sparse. We examined three-year reintervention rates for both treatments in a large real-world cohort. METHODS: From the TriNetX US Collaborative Network, we identified men ≥40 years who underwent Rezum or UroLift between January 2018 and December 2020 via CPT codes. Patients were followed for three years for subsequent urologic procedures. Propensity score matching balanced baseline factors, and Cox proportional hazards models compared reintervention risk overall and by age strata. RESULTS: We included 3,231 patients (Rezum 792; UroLift 2,439). After matching, overall reintervention risk was similar (HR 1.19; 95% CI 0.82–1.73). Among patients ≥65 years, Rezum showed a significantly lower reintervention rate than UroLift (HR 0.60; 95% CI 0.37–0.97). In those aged 40–64 years, rates were similar (HR 1.49; 95% CI 0.87–2.55) ( (https://www.auajournals.org/doi/abs/10.1097/01.JU.0001191280.81177.3f.21#F1)). Within the Rezum cohort, younger patients (40–64 years) had higher risk than those ≥65 years (HR 2.12; 95% CI 1.15–3.93), whereas no age-related difference was observed after UroLift (HR 0.85; 95% CI 0.62–1.17) ( (https://www.auajournals.org/doi/abs/10.1097/01.JU.0001191280.81177.3f.21#F2)). CONCLUSIONS: Rezum was associated with fewer three-year reinterventions than UroLift in adults ≥65 years, while outcomes were comparable in those aged 40–64 years. These findings suggest patient age may influence the durability of minimally invasive BPH therapies and should be considered during treatment selection.

title: IP03-22: Matched Comparative Analysis of Robot-assisted Simple Prostatectomy (RASP) versus Holmium Laser Enucleation (HoLEP) for Large (>100 ml) Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia (BPH): Experience from a High-volume Center
parentSessionTitle: IP03: Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia: Surgical Therapy & New Technology I

speakers.organization: Division of Urology, IRCCS Azienda Ospedaliero-Universitaria di Bologna, Bologna, Italy

fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: In men with large benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH; >100 ml), both robot-assisted simple prostatectomy (RASP) and holmium laser enucleation of the prostate (HoLEP) represent established treatment options. Comparative data remain scarce and often limited by baseline imbalances. We aimed to provide a matched comparative analysis of peri-operative and functional outcomes between RASP and HoLEP in a high-volume centre. METHODS: We analysed data of 468 patients with symptomatic BPH due to large (>100 ml) prostate glands who underwent RASP (n=206, 44%) and HoLEP (n=262, 56%) at OLV Hospital, Aalst (Belgium) between 2011 and 2024. A 1:1 propensity-score matched (PSM) cohort was generated to reduce baseline imbalances. Pre-, intra-, and post-operative data were collected, with complications graded according to Clavien–Dindo (CD). Functional outcomes were assessed by International Prostate Symptom Score (IPSS), maximum urinary flow rate (Qmax), and post-void residual volume (PVR) at immediate, 6-, and 12-month follow-up. RESULTS: At baseline, age, BMI, IPSS, Qmax and PVR were comparable (all p>0.05), whereas RASP patients presented with larger prostate volume, higher PSA, and higher Charlson Comorbidity Index (CCI) (all p<0.05). Median operative time was longer for RASP (130 vs. 110 min; p<0.001), while length of stay (LOS) was shorter after HoLEP (2 vs. 3 days; p<0.001). Intra-operative complication rates were similar (14% vs. 15%), but major Clavien–Dindo (CD) grade III–V events occurred only in HoLEP (0% vs. 8.3%; p=0.016). At 6 months, both groups showed an improvement of maximum flow rate (Qmax +14 vs. +14 ml/s; p=0.8), a reduction of PVR (−73 vs. −53 ml; p=0.3), and a decrease of IPSS (−17 vs. −17; p=0.9). At 12 months, Qmax was +11 vs. +13 ml/s (p=0.2), PVR −74 vs. −55 ml (p=0.2), and IPSS −18 vs. −18 (p=0.8) for RASP and HoLEP, respectively. Functional outcomes and complication rates are shown in (https://www.auajournals.org/doi/abs/10.1097/01.JU.0001191280.81177.3f.22#F1). After PSM, a balanced cohort of 144 patients (72 vs. 72) was obtained. In this analysis, functional outcomes remained equivalent and peri-operative differences were confirmed. CONCLUSIONS: Both RASP and HoLEP provided equivalent functional improvements in large BPH. HoLEP was associated with shorter length of stay, whereas RASP showed longer operative time. After PSM, results were confirmed, supporting both as effective options depending on patient profile and expertise.

title: IP03-23: Multi-Institutional Outcomes of Robot-Assisted Simple Prostatectomy: A Retrospective Study by the ERUS Scientific Reconstructive Working Group
parentSessionTitle: IP03: Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia: Surgical Therapy & New Technology I
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Management of large-volume prostate adenomas remains challenging in benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH). This study evaluated surgical techniques, perioperative outcomes, functional results, and complication rates of robot-assisted simple prostatectomy (RASP) in a multi-institutional cohort. METHODS: a retrospective analysis included patients who underwent RASP between January 2013 and July 2024 at 17 centers in Europe and the United States. Functional outcomes including uroflowmetry, post-void residual volume (PVR), International Prostate Symptom Score (IPSS), and Quality of Life (QoL), were evaluated at 6 weeks and 1 year postoperatively. Statistical significance was set at p<0.05 (paired t-test). Postoperative complications were assessed at 30 and 90 days. Surgical techniques were systematically analyzed and video-validated. RESULTS: a total of 1345 patients underwent RASP. Median age was 70 years (IQR 65–76), median prostate volume 140 ml (IQR 110–180). Median operative time was 144 min (IQR 116–180) with median blood loss of 300 ml (IQR 150–440). Functional outcomes are shown in Table 1. Clavien–Dindo ≥ III complications occurred in 41/1344 (3%) at 30 days and 6/1218 (0.5%) at 90 days. Regarding surgical technique, 1196/1345 (89%) were treated with the DaVinci multiport system, 94/1345 (7%) with the SinglePort, and 55/1345 (4%) with the Hugo-RAS system. A transperitoneal approach was used in 1023/1345 (76%) and an extraperitoneal in 321/1345 (24%). Transvesical access was applied in 719/1344 (54%) and transcapsular in 625/1344 (46%). Standard enucleation was performed in 1151/1345 (86%), urethra-sparing in 186/1345 (14%). After standard enucleation, no closure of the prostatic fossa was performed in 363/1151 (32%), posterior vesico-urethral reconstruction (180°) in 297/1151 (26%), and full vesico-urethral reconstruction (360°) in 441/1151 (38%). CONCLUSIONS: Robot-assisted simple prostatectomy provides significant improvements in urinary function and quality of life for patients with large-volume prostatic adenoma, with low perioperative morbidity and stable outcomes at 1 year. Despite variations in surgical techniques across centers, postoperative outcomes were consistent throughout this large multi-institutional cohort. | | | --- | | |

title: IP03-24: Resident Surgical Learning Curve for Robotic-Assisted Simple Prostatectomy
parentSessionTitle: IP03: Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia: Surgical Therapy & New Technology I

speakers.organization: The University of Texas Medical Branch

fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Learning curves for fully trained urologists performing robotic-assisted simple prostatectomy (RASP) are well described, but data on trainees are limited. We aimed to characterize the learning curve of multiport RASP among urology residents. METHODS: Consecutive RASP cases performed by three urology senior residents (2021–2024) were retrospectively reviewed. Metrics included operative time, percent prostate enucleated, IPSS improvement, and Clavien–Dindo ≥2 complications. Moving average curves and best-fit trendlines were used to assess performance over time. RESULTS: Eighty-seven cases were analyzed (Resident A=25; B=27; C=35). Median patient age was 68 years (IQR 62–72), prostate volume 108 cc (90–131), and preoperative IPSS 25 (18–27); 62% were catheter-dependent. Median operative time was 136 min (116–159), decreasing from >160 min to ~120 min after 15 cases before plateauing. Percent prostate enucleated increased from ~50% to 70% after 15 cases. Median IPSS improvement was 80% (66–85) with stable grade ≥2 complication rates (9 events, 10%). (https://www.auajournals.org/doi/abs/10.1097/01.JU.0001191280.81177.3f.24#F1) depicts aggregated moving-average curves. CONCLUSIONS: Residents achieved proficiency in multiport RASP after approximately 15 cases, as reflected by improved operative time and extent of enucleation. Functional outcomes and complication rates remained stable across experience levels, suggesting early attainment of safety and efficacy.

title: IP03-25: Efficacy of Robot-Assisted Simple Prostatectomy in Prostatic Enlargements: A Comparative Study Above and Below 150 grams
parentSessionTitle: IP03: Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia: Surgical Therapy & New Technology I

speakers.organization: Koc University, School of Medicine, Istanbul, Turkey

fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Robot-assisted simple prostatectomy (RASP) is a minimally invasive alternative to open surgery for large benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH). We compared perioperative and functional outcomes of RASP in patients with large (<150 g) versus very large (≥150 g) prostates. METHODS: A retrospective single-center analysis was performed. Fifty-eight patients underwent RASP, stratified by prostate weight into Group 1 (≥150 g, n=39) and Group 2 (<150 g, n=19). RESULTS: All cases were completed robotically with no conversion to open surgery. Group 1 had higher PSA (9.7 vs 5.6 ng/mL, p=0.037) and longer operative time (148.5 vs 121.8 min, p=0.019) than Group 2, while estimated blood loss, length of stay, and catheterization time did not differ significantly. Pre- and postoperative IPSS, Qmax, and PVR were comparable between groups (all p>0.05). All patients showed significant improvements in symptoms and voiding parameters: mean IPSS decreased from 22.8 to 7.4, Qmax increased from 9.0 to 20.5 ml/s, and PVR decreased from 136.3 to 37.1 ml (all p<0.001). Improvements in IPSS, Qmax, and PVR were similar in Group 1 vs Group 2 (ΔIPSS 16.3 vs 14.1, p=0.361; ΔQmax +11.6 vs +11.1 ml/s, p=0.912; ΔPVR −120.2 vs −75.1 ml, p=0.076, respectively). Continence and erectile function outcomes were similar between groups; one patient (<150 g) developed new-onset mild stress incontinence managed conservatively, and no new erectile dysfunction occurred. Antegrade ejaculation was preserved in 10/51 sexually active patients (19.6%), without a group difference (p=0.982). Complications were infrequent and two Group 1 patients developed urethral strictures; all other complications were Clavien grade I–II. CONCLUSIONS: RASP is a safe and effective treatment for large prostate adenomas (≥150 g), providing symptom relief and urinary function improvement comparable to outcomes in smaller glands. While operative time was longer for larger prostates, perioperative morbidity and overall outcomes did not differ between groups. These findings support the use of RASP as a viable minimally invasive alternative to open surgery even for prostates above 150 g. | | | --- | | | | | | --- | | |

title: IP03-26: Comparing Outcomes of Single-Port vs Multi-Port Robot-Assisted Simple Prostatectomy: A Prospective Single-Center Experience
parentSessionTitle: IP03: Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia: Surgical Therapy & New Technology I
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Robot-assisted simple prostatectomy (RASP) is an established option for the surgical management of large benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH). The recent introduction of single-port (SP) robotic platforms aims to further minimize surgical invasiveness. However, comparative data between SP and conventional multi-port (MP) RASP are still limited. This study aimed to compare perioperative and functional outcomes between SP and MP RASP performed at a single high-volume referral center. METHODS: A prospective cohort of men undergoing RASP for symptomatic BPH with prostate volume >80 ml was analyzed. All procedures were performed according to either a transvesical or transcapsular approaches, without retrigonization. Baseline, perioperative, and functional variables, including age, BMI, ASA score, indwelling catheter, prostate volume, surgical approach (transvesical vs transcapsular), BPH6 achievement and OAB recovery (defined as: an OABq-SF improvement ≥11 points, absence of postoperative pharmacologic treatment for urgency and a postoperative ICIQ-SF score <6) were compared between SP and MP procedures. Continuous data were compared using the Mann–Whitney U test, and categorical variables using the Fisher exact test. Statistical significance was set at p<0.05. RESULTS: A total of 93 patients were included: 89 (96%) underwent MP-RASP and 4 (4%) SP-RASP. SP patients were slightly younger and had smaller prostates (median 93 vs 116 g, p=0.08) ( Table 1). No significant differences were observed in operative time (110 vs 100 min, p=0.59), length of stay (3 vs 3 days, p=0.24), or BPH6 achievement (25% vs 54%, p=0.34). OAB recovery was achieved in 100% of SP and 73% of MP cases (p=0.57) ( Table 2). CONCLUSIONS: Single-port RASP achieved perioperative and functional results comparable to those of multi-port surgery in this prospective cohort. Despite the limited sample size, these findings suggest that the introduction of the single-port platform does not jeopardize outcomes of RASP. Larger multicenter studies are needed to confirm these early results and to better define the role of the Single port surgery in the management of large BPH. | | | --- | | | | | | --- | | |

title: IP03-27: A longitudinal analysis of PSA following robotic-assisted simple prostatectomy
parentSessionTitle: IP03: Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia: Surgical Therapy & New Technology I
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Aging men are at risk for prostate cancer (PCa) and benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH). Men undergoing robotic assisted simple prostatectomy (RASP) for BPH may be on active surveillance for low grade PCa, have PCa identified incidentally on RASP pathology, or have a delayed PCa diagnosis post-operatively. Unlike radical prostatectomy, RASP preserves the peripheral zone, leading to detectable but poorly defined normative PSA values. This leads to difficulty distinguishing PSA reflecting benign remnant tissue from clinically significant (cs) PCa. We evaluated PSA trends in patients following RASP to inform post-RASP PCa screening and surveillance. METHODS: We identified all patients who underwent RASP at our institution from 5/1/2015 to 9/30/2023. Patients having (1) no PCa; (2) non-csPCa (GG1); or (3) csPCa (≥GG2) were compared for post-operative PSA metrics using Kruskal Wallis and Fisher Freeman Halton tests. RESULTS: PSA data were available for 214/288 patients who underwent RASP. 171 had no diagnosis of PCa, 29 had non-csPCa, and 14 had csPCa. Significant differences in PSA and PSA change emerged over time. PSA values among groups did not differ significantly within the first 12 months, but did at 12-24 months (p=0.048) and >24 months post-RASP (p=0.012). Highest median post-RASP PSAs were observed in the csPCa group (p=0.001). The median time to reach post-RASP PSA nadir was shortest for the csPCa group (189 days), followed by non-csPCa (293 days) and benign groups (430 days) (p=0.015). Data are summarized in Table 1. CONCLUSIONS: We present the first detailed analysis of longitudinal PSA trends after RASP in men with and without PCa. While pre-RASP PSA and the initial post-RASP PSA nadir did not differ significantly among groups, the time to nadir did. Patients with clinically significant prostate cancer (csPCa) reached their PSA nadir faster, likely due to earlier PSA rise from recurrence, whereas the benign group reached nadir later as PSA declined with natural fluctuations and resolution of postoperative inflammation. Among groups, those with csPCa demonstrated the highest PSA at 12-24 months of follow-up, a trend which continued when PSA was assessed beyond 24 months. Our findings suggest that a single early post-RASP PSA value is insufficient for men who would benefit from continued PSA monitoring. Instead, serial PSA monitoring beyond one year may be necessary to effectively identify patients with underlying csPCa who warrant further investigation. Furthermore, these data can provide a reference for urologists and patients when interpreting post-RASP PSA values. | | | --- | | |

title: IP03-28: Predictors of Same-Day Discharge Trifecta Following Single Port Transvesical Robotic Simple Prostatectomy: A Report from the Single Port Advanced Research Consortium (SPARC)
parentSessionTitle: IP03: Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia: Surgical Therapy & New Technology I
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: To evaluate the incidence and predictors of same-day discharge trifecta following Single Port (SP) Transvesical Robotic Simple Prostatectomy (RASP), defined as outpatient surgery without postoperative complications or readmission. METHODS: A retrospective review of the prospectively maintained, IRB-approved SP Advanced Research Consortium (SPARC) database identified 503 patients who underwent SP-RASP. Only Transvesical procedures with ≥3 months follow-up were included. Baseline clinicodemographic, perioperative, and postoperative variables were collected, with inferential statistics as presented. Postoperative complications within 90 days were classified according to Clavien-Dindo, with major complications defined as grade ≥3a. Multivariate logistic regression was used to identify independent predictors of trifecta achievement. RESULTS: Of 220 eligible patients, outpatient surgery was achieved in 54.6%. Postoperative complications occurred in 23.9%, and readmission in 4.6%, yielding a trifecta outcome in 59.5%. Trifecta and non-trifecta groups were similar in age, body habitus, prostate volume, LUTS severity, and uroflowmetry results. Patients achieving trifecta had lower comorbidity burden (median CCI 3 vs. 4, p=0.003), shorter operative time (median 165 vs. 191 min, p<0.001), lower intraoperative blood loss (median 75 vs. 100 ml, p<0.001), and were less likely to require continuous bladder irrigation (0.8% vs. 14.3%, p<0.001). On multivariate analysis, lower comorbidity burden (OR 0.767, 95% CI 0.590–0.990, p=0.043) and shorter operative time (OR 0.992, 95% CI 0.987–0.999, p=0.002) independently predicted trifecta success. CONCLUSIONS: The same-day discharge trifecta after SP Transvesical RASP can be achieved in over half of patients. Nevertheless, while lower comorbidity burden and shorter operative time were identified as independent predictors of success, larger cohort data remain necessary to further enhance our best-practice patient selection and to guide perioperative planning. | | | --- | | | | | | --- | | |

title: IP03-29: Development of a High-Fidelity Surgical Training Model for Single-Port Robot-Assisted Transvesical Simple Prostatectomy (SP-RASP)
parentSessionTitle: IP03: Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia: Surgical Therapy & New Technology I
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: SP-RASP has emerged as a unique regionalized robotic approach for the treatment of benign prostatic hyperplasia. Due to the unique anatomical orientation of this procedure, surgeons encounter steep learning challenges such as limited triangulation and single-port instrument articulation. To address the need for realistic training modalities, this project was aimed to develop and validate a high-fidelity model that can replicate the tactile and visual properties of the key procedural steps in SP-RARP. METHODS: A 120-gm prostate adenoma, prostate capsule, bladder, and surrounding pelvic anatomy were reconstructed from patient imaging data. Polyvinyl alcohol hydrogel was molded into 3D printed casts to create each structure separately. Hydrogels of varying formulations were made to mimic the texture of each organ and crosslinked using a freezing process to recreate realistic dissection planes. 5 experts and 5 novices defined by caseload performed key procedural steps under standard robotic visualization: bladder entry, prostate dissection, and vesicourethral anastomosis. The realism of the model was then evaluated by experts with a post-surgery questionnaire that assessed the anatomical realism, tissue handling, and educational value. Performance metrics (adenoma resected, resection efficiency, and errors) were compared between both groups. RESULTS: Ten total surgeons, 5 novices and 5 experts, rated the model via a survey. The survey responses were rated on a five-point scale: 5=Strongly Agree, 4=Agree, 3=Neutral, 2=Disagree, and 1=Strongly Disagree. On average, novices rated the model’s replication of human anatomy at 4.5, while experts rated it at 4.2. Similarly, novices gave the model’s educational value an average rating of 4.9, compared to 4.7 from experts. Further breakdown of these results is depicted in Figure 1A. Figure 1B displays the anatomical model during the main steps of the procedure. Feedback revealed that participants wanted the surgical planes to be more difficult to distinguish and separate. CONCLUSIONS: The custom hydrogel-based model for SP-RASP provides a reproducible and realistic platform for skill enhancement and surgical practice in SP-RARP. Its high fidelity, reproducibility, and ability to differentiate in performance make it a promising addition to SP robotic surgical education.

title: IP03-30: Implementation of mini-HoLEP (MiLEP) in Very Large Prostates: A Propensity Score–Matched Study
parentSessionTitle: IP03: Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia: Surgical Therapy & New Technology I
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Mini-HoLEP (MiLEP) using a 22-Fr resectoscope has been shown to have several advantages over the conventional 26-Fr system. However, its implementation in treating very large prostates (≥150 cm3) has been scarcely reported. We aimed to characterize the feasibility, safety, and perioperative outcomes of MiLEP in patients with prostates ≥150 cm3. METHODS: A retrospective review of all 635 HoLEP procedures performed in our institution after MiLEP introduction (September 2022–August 2025) revealed a cohort of 135 (21%) procedures performed in prostates ≥150 cm3. Of these, 96 were done with a 26-Fr instrument and 39 with MiLEP. Propensity score matching (1:1) on age, ASA class, prostate volume, and presence of an indwelling catheter yielded two matched comparison groups of 29 patients each. Statistical analyses were performed using univariable and multivariable models. RESULTS: Post-matching baseline characteristics are shown in Table 1; univariable comparisons appear in Table 2. Compared with standard HoLEP, MiLEP was associated with a significantly lower need for meatal dilation (p=0.001), better intraoperative preservation of body temperature (p=0.009), and higher tissue-removal efficiency (p=0.013). Multivariable models confirmed and strengthened these findings. No case required conversion from MiLEP to standard HoLEP; conversely, two procedures were converted from HoLEP to MiLEP—one for an anterior urethral stricture and one due to a penile prosthesis. Complication rates were similar between groups. CONCLUSIONS: We report, for the first time, expanding MiLEP use to prostates ≥150 cm3, demonstrating feasibility, safety and effectivity. MiLEP's previously documented advantages were reproduced in the ≥150 cm3 population. | | | --- | | | | | | --- | | |

title: IP04-01: Assistance of Large Language Model-based AI Agent in Preoperative Communication Reduces Anxiety of Prostate Cancer Patients and Workload of Clinicians: A Prospective, Randomized, Phase II Trial
parentSessionTitle: IP04: Surgical Technology & Simulation: Artificial Intelligence
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Preoperative communication is crucial in reducing patients' anxiety but demands considerable effort from clinicians. This study aims to evaluate whether AI agent-assisted preoperative communication reduces patient anxiety, and decreases clinician workload compared to standard communication. METHODS: We developed an AI agent using DeepSeek-R1 for preoperative communication, based on clinical guidelines and our institute's experience. Patients with newly diagnosed prostate cancer scheduled for radical surgery at our center were enrolled, excluding those with severe mental illness or cognitive dysfunction. Upon admission, patients were randomized at the ward level into control and AI agent-assisted groups. Both groups immediately received baseline emotional and cognitive assessments such as GAD-7 and B-IPQ. Specific questions of the two groups were collected via our AI agent. The AI agent-assisted group then received personalized responses from our AI agent, validated for scientific accuracy before delivery. Both groups then received preoperative communication from clinicians blinded to group assignments and underwent emotional and cognitive assessments again. Clinicians' workload was assessed using NASA-TLX. Primary endpoints were GAD-7 scores and NASA-TLX results. Secondary endpoints included other emotional (VAS-A, I-PANAS-SF), disease cognition scales (APAIS, B-IPQ), patient satisfaction, and communication time for clinicians. This study is registered with ClinicalTrials. gov (NCT07082049). RESULTS: From Feb to Aug 2025, a total of 245 patients were randomized into control (n=124) and AI agent-assisted (n=121) groups. The two groups of patients totally asked 3,294 questions, averaging 13.94 questions per patient. These questions covered various aspects of surgery, including anesthesia, perioperative care, and management. Patients in the AI agent-assisted group experienced notably lower anxiety levels compared with the control group, with decrease in GAD-7 scores (median (IQR): 3.5 (2.0-5.0) vs. 7.5 (6.5-9.0), p<0.001). Clinician workload was notably reduced in the AI agent-assisted group, with lower NASA-TLX scores (median (IQR): 38.0 (24.5-52.5) vs. 57.0 (37.0-77.5), p<0.001) and remarkable nearly half the communication time compared to the control group (11.7 mins vs. 20.9 mins, p<0.001). CONCLUSIONS: AI-assisted preoperative communication significantly reduces patient anxiety, enhances disease perception, and decreases clinician workload, identifying previously unaddressed patient concerns.

title: IP04-02: Predicting 1-year Erectile Function Recovery after Robotic-Assisted Radical Prostatectomy from Raw Surgical Video via an Automated, Artificial Intelligence-Based System
parentSessionTitle: IP04: Surgical Technology & Simulation: Artificial Intelligence
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Surgical outcomes vary widely as a function of surgeon performance, but the specific aspects of surgical performance that define outcomes are not well understood. We implement “Frame-to-Outcome” (F2O), an end-to-end artificial intelligence (AI) system, to identify metrics that predict erectile function (EF) outcomes after robotic-assisted radical prostatectomy (RARP) from raw surgical video. METHODS: We analyzed 130 videos of RARPs by 30 surgeons from 4 international hospitals. Patients with clinically localized prostate cancer and EF sufficient for intercourse prior to surgery were included. F2O uses frame-level classification and spatiotemporal modeling to convert video of the nerve-sparing step into a sequence of standardized surgical gestures, where each gesture represents the smallest meaningful interaction between instrument and tissue. F2O-predicted gestures were then evaluated with effect size analysis to discern the features (e. g. gesture frequency, duration) associated with EF recovery at 12 months (defined as Sexual Health Inventory for Men score >17), where a positive effect size denotes higher value in the EF recovery group. Results were compared with features derived from human-annotated data. For overlapping features, we report mean absolute difference in effect sizes and Pearson correlation coefficients with corresponding p-values. RESULTS: In our data, 44/130 patients (33.8%) recovered EF at 12 months while 86/130 (66.2%) did not. F2O correctly predicted EF recovery with mean accuracy of 0.75 (95% CI 0.70-0.81). EF recovery was positively associated with higher frequency (d=0.26, p=0.13) and duration (d=0.31, p=0.06) of spread gestures and negatively associated with frequent energy cut gestures (d=-0.26, p=0.16). When comparing gesture features against those derived from our prior work using human annotated data, effect size directions were concordant with small mean absolute difference (0.13) and strong correlation (r=0.97, p<0.001). CONCLUSIONS: F2O generates gesture features from surgical video to accurately predict 12-month EF outcomes after RARP, without need for human effort. While prior effort to quantify surgical performance using gestures has been limited by scalability due to reliance on human annotators, F2O enables fully automated processing of surgical video to correctly predict outcomes.

title: IP04-03: A Non-invasive MRI-based Multimodal Fusion Deep Learning Model (MF-DLM) for Predicting Overall Survival in Bladder Cancer: A Multicenter Retrospective Study
parentSessionTitle: IP04: Surgical Technology & Simulation: Artificial Intelligence
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Accurate prognosis prediction in bladder cancer (BCa) is crucial for personalized treatment. This study aimed to develop and validate a non-invasive model using MRI for predicting the overall survival (OS) in BCa patients. METHODS: This retrospective multicenter study included 1131 BCa patients from eight institutions. We developed a multimodal fusion deep learning model (MF-DLM), leveraging a cross-attention mechanism to integrate four key preoperative data modalities: 3D deep learning features using a modified 3D ResNet50 network, 3D radiomics features, morphological MRI features, and clinical features. Patients were stratified into low- and high-risk prognostic groups based on MF-DLM scores, and model interpretability was evaluated using SHAP and Grad-CAM. RESULTS: The MF-DLM demonstrated excellent performance in predicting overall survival (OS), achieving higher C-index values than pT stage (training: 0.902 vs. 0.793, p<0.001; validation: 0.864 vs. 0.757, p=0.014; external test: 0.841 vs. 0.760, p=0.047). In addition, MF-DLM-based low-risk group demonstrated significantly longer OS in the training, validation, and external test sets (p<0.001). In the adjuvant therapy (AT) cohort, high-risk patients had significantly worse prognosis compared with low-risk patients (p<0.0001). Additionally, high-risk pT3/4 patients exhibited no statistically significant OS difference between those who received AT and those who did not (p=0.18), whereas low-risk pT3/4 patients experienced significantly improved OS with AT (p=0.0059). Besides, the low-risk group had better OS than the high-risk group in neoadjuvant therapy cohort (p=0.0032). CONCLUSIONS: The MF-DLM can reliably predict OS in BCa patients and provide additional prognostic stratification beyond pT and pN stages. Furthermore, MF-DLM-based risk groups can identify patients most likely to benefit from perioperative therapy.

title: IP04-04: Development and validation of a deep learning tool for automated reading of fluorescence confocal microscopy images in radical prostatectomy
parentSessionTitle: IP04: Surgical Technology & Simulation: Artificial Intelligence
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Fluorescence confocal microscopy (FCM) is a more feasible alternative to the NeuroSAFE procedure for intraoperative margin assessment in radical prostatectomy (RP) with reasonable diagnostic accuracy. However, FCM images still require interpretation by a pathologist in a time of increasing workforce pressure. We aimed to develop and validate an AI model capable of distinguishing benign from malignant tissue on FCM images in RP, enabling real-time intraoperative decision-making without reliance on a pathologist. METHODS: FCM images from 153 patients were obtained from the IP8-FLUORESCE study using the Histolog Scanner. Pathologist-annotated regions containing cancer/benign tissue were used to create a dataset of 275 images reflecting real-world class imbalance (tumour 13%, benign 87%). A modified deep learning architecture was developed using the established ResNet50 convolutional neural network. To optimise performance on minority (tumour) classes, we applied modified focal loss, balanced data sampling, and classier head with dropout. A supervised learning approach was used. The model was trained on 80% of the data and tested on the remaining 20%. External validation was performed using 46 annotated margins (23 tumour, 23 benign) from an independent dataset. To improve explainability, gradient-weighted class activation maps (Grad-CAMs) were applied to highlight areas the model had identified as suspicious for cancer. RESULTS: On internal testing, our model achieved 87.5% (47.4-99.7) sensitivity, 97.9% (89.2-100.0) specificity, and AUC of 0.98 (93.1-100.0) for cancer detection. The model performed well on external validation: 91.3% (73.2-97.6) sensitivity, 73.9% (53.5-87.5) specificity, and AUC 0.83 (0.74-91.4). Grad-CAM heatmaps accurately localised malignant glands, highlighting features consistent with pathology assessment (Fig1). CONCLUSIONS: Our AI-driven deep learning model demonstrated high accuracy for classifying RP surgical margin status in a realistic, imbalanced dataset. Grad-CAMs provide interpretable visual outputs for clinicians. This approach has the potential to streamline the use of FCM for intraoperative margin assessment and limit reliance on pathologists. The study was limited by the small number of positive cases. Prospective clinical evaluation on larger datasets is required.

title: IP04-05: Generating Natural-Language Surgical Feedback Directly from Video by Extracting Essential Components: Instrument, Action, Target Tissue
parentSessionTitle: IP04: Surgical Technology & Simulation: Artificial Intelligence
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Surgeons-in-training need consistent feedback, but expert coaches are not always available. We built a machine-learning pipeline able to watch surgical videos and automatically generate relevant, coaching-style comments. The key to our approach is representing the variability of trainer feedback in a standardized format: instrument, action, and target tissue (IAT triplet). METHODS: We use a dataset of 33 robot-assisted urology surgeries with ~4.2k video-to-text pairs of trainer-trainee dialogue and employ a large language model (LLM) to extract IAT triplets from human feedback transcripts, grouping similar terms and normalizing inconsistent delivery. We then train a surgery-specific video-based model (PeskaVLP) to predict triplets by combining visual content, estimated motion of instruments, and provided procedure/task context ( Fig. 1.1a). Using the IATs predicted from the video to guide an LLM (1.1b), we generate coaching-style natural language feedback. We evaluate our approach in a 5-fold cross-validation setup, reporting AUCs for predicting IAT components from video. We further assess how well generated feedback matches actual trainer delivery by using a published 1-5 content alignment rubric (higher is better) ( Fig. 1.3) and estimating ratio of important words captured (ROUGE) and word-level mistakes (WER). RESULTS: When predicting IATs, adding instrument motion and procedure/task context improved performance over baseline model for each component ( Figure 1.2a), raising AUCs for Instrument (0.65→0.73); Action (0.58→0.61); Tissue (0.70→0.79) compared to video alone. For feedback, using the extracted IAT triplets to condition LLM generation produced trainer-style feedback that scored better on the alignment rubric 2.17→2.44 (+12%) due to better preservation of core actionable guidance (examples in 1.3). Crucially, the proportion of acceptable outputs (score ≥ 3) increased from 21% to 42%, and word-level metrics improved as well (WER ↓~31%, ROUGE ↑~64%), see 1.2b. CONCLUSIONS: By anchoring our model’s interpretation of surgical video around explicitly defined IAT triplets and using those to guide language generation, we produce feedback whose content and complexity is more aligned with real-world trainer delivery. Future work will improve the triplet abstraction and control delivery style, such as urgency or encouragement.

title: IP04-06: The UROFLOW Trial:  First-in-Class Real-World Comparative Analysis of a Smartphone-Based AI Uroflowmetry App Versus Standard Clinic Uroflowmetry
parentSessionTitle: IP04: Surgical Technology & Simulation: Artificial Intelligence

speakers.organization: San Lucas Urology Residency Ponce PR

fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Uroflowmetry remains the cornerstone of objective lower urinary tract evaluation, yet its clinical utility is limited by access, repeatability, and clinic follow up adherence. Artificial Intelligence Enhanced digital home uroflowmetry offers scalable, patient-centered remote monitoring of physiologic voiding in a more natural environment. We compared its performance against gold-standard clinic uroflowmetry, in a real world setting where reproducibility and clinic–home uroflowmetry concordance remain unexplored. METHODS: A total of 170 patients from five centers were enrolled to be part of a prospective cohort trial. All (100%) completed baseline clinic uroflowmetry; 140 (82.4%) also performed at least one remote AI uroflowmetry “MenHealth App”. At 4 week follow-up, only 50 (29.4%) returned for repeat clinic testing, whereas 82.4% engaged with remote AI monitoring (3,586 total remote uroflow tests).For comparative analysis, clinic uroflowmetry (n=50 with follow-up) was compared against MenHealth remote uroflowmetry (n=141 flows). Median Qmax, Qavg, voided volume, and flow time were assessed with Mann–Whitney U tests, while Spearman correlations were performed between objective measures, symptom scores, and quality-of-life (QoL) domains. RESULTS: AI Uroflowmetry “MenHealth” demonstrated reduced variability across repeated measures, with tighter clustering and greater internal consistency compared to clinic uroflowmetry. In paired data (n=50), clinic parameter reproducibility was strong (r=0.79 for flow time), but “MenHealth” achieved greater stability in repeated recordings, supporting the value of frequent at-home sampling. The MenHealth App captured physiologic voiding patterns through mobile uroflowmetry across the day, in contrast to conventional single-timepoint clinic testing, demonstrating lower values for Qmax (16.6 vs 33.9 ml/s), Qavg (9.4 vs 11.6 ml/s), and voided volume (212 vs 312 ml; all p<0.001). MenHealth App demonstrated that Voided volume correlated strongly with Qavg (ρ=0.778, p<0.001) and flow time (ρ=0.796, p<0.001). Symptom scores correlated with QoL (ρ=0.551, p<0.001). QoL differed significantly by age group (p=0.004), peaking in middle-aged/early elderly participants. CONCLUSIONS: AI-driven home uroflowmetry achieved higher compliance than clinic uroflowmetry and captured physiologic voiding patterns through mobile uroflowmetry across the day, in contrast to conventional single-timepoint clinic testing. These findings support AI-based home uroflowmetry as a novel urological tool to expand access, adherence, and equity in urologic care.

title: IP04-07: Developing an Artificial Intelligence Model for Intraoperative Identification of Urinary Stone Composition
parentSessionTitle: IP04: Surgical Technology & Simulation: Artificial Intelligence

speakers.organization: University of Florida College of Medicine

fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Determination of urinary stone composition guides diagnosis and management. To date, there is no study exploring artificial intelligence (AI) for endoscopic urinary stone identification or how deep neural networks can identify and predict stone patterns. We aimed to evaluate the efficacy of an AI model to identify stone composition based on intraoperative endoscopic imaging and use heatmaps to visualize stone patterns indicative of composition. METHODS: We conducted a cross-sectional analysis of intraoperative images of patients undergoing ureteroscopy or percutaneous nephrolithotomy from 03/2023 to 10/2025. In- and ex-vivo images of stones were catalogued. Stone type was classified by dominant composition (>70%). Our model included a deep neural network utilizing a Vision Transformer and Pubmedbert model to process image and metadata text. Domain-adversarial training was utilized with a gradient reversal layer to learn endoscope invariant image features representing stone composition. Heatmaps were generated to visualize maximal image feature activation during prediction. Model performance was evaluated through precision, recall, and F1 score (harmonic mean of recall and precision). RESULTS: A total of 229 patients were included, comprising 2,324 images. Pure stone compositions accounted for 87% (n=200) of data. Table 1 depicts model performance across pure compositions. The model demonstrated strong performance in identifying calcium oxalate stones (F1 score: 0.88) and moderate performance in identifying infectious stones (F1 score: 0.59) and calcium phosphate stones (F1 score: 0.53). Lower performance for other compositions was demonstrated, likely attributable to small sample size. Heatmaps of calcium oxalate and uric acid stones are depicted in (https://www.auajournals.org/doi/abs/10.1097/01.JU.0001191284.35857.1d.07#F1). CONCLUSIONS: We developed a novel AI model to identify stone composition based on intraoperative endoscopic imaging, illustrated visually via heatmapping. Our model demonstrates strong performance among well-represented compositions and underscores the need for rare stone type representation, with heatmaps highlighting stone patterns for future studies. | | | --- | | |

title: IP04-08: Real-Time Image-Guided Robot-Assisted Partial Nephrectomy: Design and Methodology of the BISTOURY-CLINICAL Prospective Trial
parentSessionTitle: IP04: Surgical Technology & Simulation: Artificial Intelligence

speakers.organization: Fondazione Policlinico Universitario Campus Bio-Medico, Rome, Italy

fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: The BISTOURY-CLINICAL trial was conceived as the translational phase of a multi-step research programme focused on AI-driven 3D navigation. This prospective clinical protocol aims to evaluate the feasibility, safety, and workflow integration of real-time image-guided robot-assisted partial nephrectomy (RAPN) performed with the Hugo™ RAS platform. The study also establishes a standardized methodological framework for multimodal data acquisition, synchronization, and validation, forming the technological basis for future autonomous and adaptive robotic systems. METHODS: This is a prospective, single-centre, observational trial enrolling 30 consecutive patients scheduled for RAPN. Eligibility criteria are displayed as follows: patients aged ≥18 years with solitary, localized renal masses eligible for partial nephrectomy, adequate renal function, and no prior ipsilateral surgery. The methodological design consists of four sequential phases: (1) Preoperative phase: acquisition of contrast-enhanced CT scans, automated segmentation and 3D patient-specific model generation; (2) Intraoperative phase: synchronized acquisition of endoscopic video and optical tracking data, enabling dynamic registration and augmented-reality visualization within the surgical field; The intraoperative technological framework integrates intraoperative 3D reconstruction based on monocular videos (BodySLAM), and a deformable registration pipeline (CPD+OpVD) for dynamic alignment between preoperative and intraoperative models (3) Postoperative phase: anonymised integration of all data streams for quantitative evaluation of spatial alignment accuracy, temporal stability and workflow feasibility, as well as qualitative assessment of surgeon orientation and usability via structured questionnaires; (4) Simulation and cross-validation phase: replication of selected procedures in a controlled robotic simulation environment to benchmark system performance and refine algorithmic components. Primary endpoints are system feasibility (no procedural delay >5 min), registration accuracy (<5 mm RMS error), and real-time performance stability (≥20 fps). RESULTS: The clinical phase has begun, and the first two RAPN procedures have been successfully performed using the Hugo™ RAS platform. In these cases, the CPD+OpVD pipeline achieved an average RMSE reduction of 51.03 ± 10.78% relative to rigid registration, with a mean computational time of 1.22 ± 1.16 s per endoscopic frame. CONCLUSIONS: These promising preliminary results demonstrate the potential of real-time deformable registration for image-guided robotic surgery and encourage the continuation of clinical experimentation toward an integrated AI-assisted surgical workflow.

title: IP04-09: Convolutional Neural Network for CT-Guided Kidney Stone Identification and Needle Path Planning in Percutaneous Nephrolithotomy
parentSessionTitle: IP04: Surgical Technology & Simulation: Artificial Intelligence

speakers.organization: American University of Beirut Medical Center

fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Percutaneous nephrolithotomy (PCNL) is the standard treatment for renal stones larger than 2 cm but demands accurate access tract planning to prevent injury to surrounding organs. Although preoperative CT scans offer crucial anatomical information, their interpretation remains manual. This study aimed to create an artificial intelligence (AI)–driven application employing convolutional neural networks (CNNs) to automatically detect kidney stones and generate safe needle trajectories for PCNL planning. METHODS: A dataset of 1,942 de-identified CT images was collected and segmented using 3DSlicer and TotalSegmentator to delineate the kidneys, collecting systems, vasculature, bowel, and musculoskeletal structures. A convolutional neural network (CNN) utilizing the YOLOv8 architecture was trained to detect kidney stones, determine spatial coordinates, calculate stone size and distance from the skin, and produce optimized percutaneous access trajectories. The generated outputs were integrated into an interactive interface that displayed annotated CT slices, visualized trajectories, and provided quantitative data such as puncture angle, needle length, and confidence scores. RESULTS: The AI application was successfully developed, enabling seamless integration between non-contrast CT imaging and automated segmentation. It consistently processed all CT datasets, automatically detecting kidneys, collecting systems, renal stones, and surrounding organs. The algorithm produced quantitative stone measurements with associated confidence scores and generated a virtual percutaneous access path connecting the skin to the stone’s center, calculating both puncture angle and needle length. Additionally, an alert feature identified cases where critical structures such as the pleura or colon were in close proximity. CONCLUSIONS: The proposed AI system shows the potential for automated kidney stone detection and trajectory planning in PCNL. Further validation will evaluate its accuracy, user performance, and relationship with intraoperative results.

title: IP04-10: Deep Learning–Based Prediction of Surgical Necessity in Gray-Zone Bladder Outlet Obstruction Using Urodynamic Pressure–Flow Signals: A Prospective Multicentre Study
parentSessionTitle: IP04: Surgical Technology & Simulation: Artificial Intelligence

speakers.organization: Istanbul Medeniyet University School of Medicine

fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: To prospectively evaluate a deep learning model for predicting the need for surgical intervention in men with persistent lower urinary tract symptoms (LUTS) and equivocal bladder outlet obstruction (BOOI 20–40), a group in which standard urodynamic parameters are often inconclusive for guiding management decisions. METHODS: This multicentre prospective study enrolled 265 men with persistent LUTS despite medical therapy across two tertiary centres (2024–2025). Patients underwent pressure–flow urodynamics with detrusor pressure and flow signals sampled at 100 Hz and converted to time–frequency spectrograms. The reference standard for surgical indication was determined by blinded consensus of three senior urologists (κ=0.86) integrating cystoscopy and 6-month outcomes, independent of model outputs. A 104-layer stacked residual network (SR-Net) was trained and validated using 10-fold cross-validation. Model performance was assessed using a confusion matrix, reporting accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, and predictive values. Comparisons with expert interpretation of conventional urodynamic parameters (Qmax, BOOI, PdetQmax) used the McNemar test, and spectral energy differences were evaluated by Mann–Whitney U (p<0.05). RESULTS: Baseline characteristics are shown in Table 1. The cohort (mean age 67 ± 8 years) exhibited severe LUTS (mean IPSS 26.9 ± 3.4), reduced Qmax (9.7 ± 8.2 ml/s), and elevated PVR (173 ± 158 ml). Spectrograms showed higher spectral energy density among surgery-indicated patients (p<0.05). The SR-Net achieved 74.7% accuracy (95% CI 69.2–80.2), sensitivity 73.3%, specificity 76.1%, PPV 75.4%, and NPV 74.2% ( Table 2). The confusion matrix ( (https://www.auajournals.org/doi/abs/10.1097/01.JU.0001191284.35857.1d.10#F1)) demonstrated 102 true positives, 96 true negatives, 35 false positives, and 32 false negatives. Expert prediction reached 73.1% accuracy (95% CI 67.5–78.7) with no significant difference (p=0.58). At 6 months, 89% of conservatively managed patients improved without surgery. CONCLUSIONS: The SR-Net model analyzing urodynamic spectrograms achieved moderate accuracy (74.7%) for predicting surgical benefit in men with equivocal BOO, comparable to expert interpretation. While feasible, its modest gain and reliance on invasive testing limit clinical adoption. External validation and integration with non-invasive parameters are warranted before clinical use. | | | --- | | | | | | --- | | |

title: IP04-11: A Tiered AI-Enhanced Curriculum for Urology Residents: Integrating ChatGPT to Improve Guideline Adherence and Clinical Reasoning
parentSessionTitle: IP04: Surgical Technology & Simulation: Artificial Intelligence
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Traditional urology training often provides fragmented exposure to guideline-based management, leading to variable progression from diagnostic reasoning to advanced clinical decision-making. The expansion of the EAU Guidelines further increases the challenge of ensuring consistent, evidence-based education. AI tools may help bridge this gap by providing adaptive, interactive, and structured learning experiences tailored to different residency stages. This study aimed to evaluate the impact of a tiered AI-assisted curriculum on knowledge improvement, guideline adherence, and clinical reasoning among urology residents. METHODS: A single-center study was conducted over an 8-week period, involving 14 urology residents participating in a structured program. The curriculum was organized into 3 progressive learning levels. The initial stage focused on the fundamentals of diagnostic criteria, risk stratification, LUTS/BPH management, urolithiasis, and urinary infections. Intermediate modules were based on oncological guidelines. The final stage emphasized the management of multimodal and refractory cases, perioperative strategies, and complication handling. Residents used ChatGPT through interactive case discussions simulating clinical reasoning and required justification of diagnostic and therapeutic choices. Pre- and post-intervention assessments evaluated guideline-based knowledge and decision accuracy. Self-reported confidence was measured using a Likert scale. All AI responses were reviewed by faculty for clinical accuracy and Guideline adherence. RESULTS: Completion of the program led to a significant overall improvement in knowledge, with mean scores increasing from 66.9% to 86.7% (p<0.01). The most pronounced gain was observed among senior residents, who demonstrated a 27.1% increase in performance for complex case management. Confidence rose from 3.0 to 4.5 (p<0.01). Improved clarity in diagnostic reasoning (85.7%), stronger understanding of algorithms (78.6%), and greater time efficiency in clinical decision-making (71.4%) was reported. Faculty confirmed high guideline consistency (94.8%) across ChatGPT outputs, with minor inaccuracies in 7.2% of responses, involving risk stratification nuances and therapeutic sequencing in advanced disease. CONCLUSIONS: The tiered ChatGPT-enhanced curriculum effectively improved residents' knowledge, guideline adherence, and confidence across all levels of training, highlighting the potential of AI-assisted education to standardize learning in urology. Limitations were observed, including occasional oversimplification and dependence on the user's ability to formulate precise clinical prompts. While AI cannot replace expert supervision, its integration into structured residency programs may serve as a valuable adjunct to traditional mentorship.

title: IP04-12: Feasibility of AI-synchronized robotic respiratory compensation independent of activation timing in lithotripsy
parentSessionTitle: IP04: Surgical Technology & Simulation: Artificial Intelligence
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Compensating for respiratory motion can substantially improve the precision of robot-assisted intrarenal laser lithotripsy. In Zamenix, using this function requires the operator to manually press a dedicated action button at the precisely defined target instant shown on the flexible ureteroscope display during respiration-driven renal motion. Because timing is influenced by user experience, scope position, and dynamic intrarenal conditions, the button is not always pressed at the optimal moment. In this study, we assessed how precisely operators could identify and click the target instant and compared this with the start-time detection performance of an AI-assisted respiratory-synchronization model. METHODS: We assembled a validation set of 20 ureteroscopic videos recorded at multiple intrarenal sites and environments in eight pigs, each containing 5–6 respiration cycles. These videos were evaluated by eight urologists familiar with intrarenal procedures. Participants independently viewed the randomized videos and pressed a timing-logging button to mark the target moment for respiratory-motion compensation. To obtain each participant’s near-optimal click per video, the task was repeated in two rounds. For the AI-assisted synchronization model, we prepared a training set—distinct from the validation set—of respiration-induced renal-motion videos and trained the model to detect the same target timing. RESULTS: Timing error was defined as the time difference (ms) between the target timing and the click. Across 1,909 total clicks from eight participants on 20 videos, the mean error relative to the target timing was 453.98 ± 194.86 ms. We generated just over 100 image-sequence samples (short clips) per video as inputs to the AI-assisted synchronization model, enabling it to locate the target timing. Across 2,478 samples, the overall mean error was 70.22 ± 141.72 ms, with erroneous detections observed in 0.44% (11 samples). CONCLUSIONS: These findings support the operational feasibility of integrating AI-assisted synchronization into robotic respiratory-motion compensation to improve urologists’ working conditions. We confirm the potential for AI assistance to enable more effective and consistent use of the compensation feature, reducing inter-user variability, which is expected to help improve outcomes in robot-assisted RIRS.

title: IP04-13: Leveraging Deep Learning for Optical Biopsy: Malignancy Prediction from Fluorescence Confocal Microscopy of Prostate Biopsies
parentSessionTitle: IP04: Surgical Technology & Simulation: Artificial Intelligence
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Conventional histopathology requires fixation, embedding, and staining, delaying diagnosis and limiting same-day decision-making. Fluorescence confocal microscopy (FCM) enables rapid, label-free imaging of fresh, unfixed tissue with near-histologic resolution. However, interpretation remains expert-dependent and subject to variability. We developed a weakly supervised deep learning framework to predict malignancy directly from FCM images of prostate biopsies, aiming to assess the feasibility of automated diagnostic support during tissue acquisition. METHODS: Fresh prostate biopsy cores were scanned using an FDA-cleared FCM system. Final histopathology served as the reference standard. Each slide was divided into overlapping tiles, and a multiple-instance learning (MIL) architecture was trained using weak (core-level) labels without manual region annotation. A Top-K pooling strategy focused learning on the most informative tiles within each biopsy core. Model performance was evaluated using 5-fold cross-validation with patient-level grouping to prevent data leakage. Primary metrics were the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) and average precision (AP). RESULTS: A total of 62 FCM slides from 52 patients, comprising 198 prostate biopsy cores (98 malignant, 96 benign), were analyzed. Each slide corresponded to a biopsy location containing an average of 3.25 cores. The deep learning model achieved a mean AUC of 0.81 ± 0.08 and AP of 0.85 ± 0.09 across folds. Heatmap visualizations localized high-probability regions consistent with malignant glandular morphology on FCM images when reviewed by an expert genitourinary histopathologist. CONCLUSIONS: Weakly supervised deep learning can distinguish malignant from benign prostate biopsy cores using fluorescence confocal microscopy of fresh tissue. This proof-of-concept study demonstrates the potential of AI-driven optical biopsy to accelerate prostate cancer diagnostics and support same-session clinical workflows.

title: IP04-14: Bringing Depth Perception Back to Robotic Surgery: AI Diffusion-Based Stereo Reconstruction from Monoscopic Surgical Video
parentSessionTitle: IP04: Surgical Technology & Simulation: Artificial Intelligence
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Surgical video recordings are conventionally monoscopic (mono), limiting depth perception for postoperative review and surgical training. In contrast, intraoperative robotic console view provides stereoscopic cues critical for spatial understanding. We adapted a stereo video generation framework that converts standard mono surgical videos into stereoscopic format for immersive visualization on 3D/VR displays. METHODS: The AI-based framework comprises two stages: depth-based video splatting and stereo video inpainting ( Fig. 1a). First, per-frame scene geometry is estimated using a mono video depth model. The left-eye video is then warped into a right-eye viewpoint through depth-based splatting, yielding an occlusion mask to identify regions that need to be filled in. Next, a diffusion-based video inpainting model fills occluded areas conditioned on the warped frames and masks, producing a photometrically coherent right-eye sequence. Since we have true stereo videos (both right and left eye recordings) in this dataset, quantitative image fidelity was assessed against ground-truth right-eye videos using peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR), structural similarity index (SSIM), and learned perceptual image patch similarity (LPIPS). RESULTS: From 12 robotic cases with stereo video (median duration 38.9 min at 30 fps), we utilized one eye’s video (left) to generate the other eye (right), resulting in 12,912 stereo pair frames. Generated right-eye views achieved a mean PSNR of 14.95 ± 0.91 dB, SSIM 0.26 ± 0.03, and LPIPS 0.48 ± 0.03 . While the PSNR and LPIPS meets the standard for perceptual quality (PSNR > 13, LPIPS < 0.5) and confirms the visual realism of the output, the lower SSIM (where SSIM > 0.7 is generally considered robust) reflects the difficulty of applying generative stereo synthesis to the surgical domain. CONCLUSIONS: A depth-guided splatting and diffusion-based inpainting framework can reconstruct realistic stereo video from mono endoscopic recordings, enabling immersive visualization for retrospective review and surgical education. While quantitative metrics reflect the inherent difficulty of dynamic surgical scenes, this work establishes a reproducible foundation for applying generative stereo synthesis in clinical video workflows and novel VR-based surgical training.

title: IP04-15: From Cystoscopy to Cystectomy: Enhancing Urologic Surgical Training with ChatGPT Across the Full Spectrum of  Procedures
parentSessionTitle: IP04: Surgical Technology & Simulation: Artificial Intelligence
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Contemporary urologic surgical training faces increasing challenges due to reduced operative exposure, complex surgical techniques, and time-limited learning environments. ChatGPT, an advanced large language model developed by OpenAI, offers an innovative, real-time educational tool that enhances preparedness, procedural understanding, and clinical decision-making. This study aimed to assess the impact of ChatGPT on knowledge acquisition and confidence among urology residents across a comprehensive range of urologic interventions. METHODS: A prospective study was conducted involving urology residents in high-volume academic training programs. Over a 6-week period, participants engaged with ChatGPT modules tailored to core urologic procedures: cystoscopy, rigid and flexible URS, nephrostomy placement, ureteral stenting, TURP, TURBT, RIRS, HoLEP, PCNL, ECIRS, prostate biopsy, orchiectomy, laparoscopic nephrectomy, laparoscopic pyeloplasty, laparoscopic cystectomy and prostatectomy, RARP, RAPN, and RARC. Each module included step-by-step walkthroughs, simulated intraoperative challenges, complication management, and guideline-based decision-making. Participants completed pre- and post-module multiple-choice knowledge assessments and self-reported confidence evaluations (5- point Likert scale), followed by a satisfaction and feedback survey. RESULTS: A total of 27 Residents participated in the study. Post-intervention analysis revealed improvement in procedural knowledge, with mean test scores increasing from 62.1 to 81.5% (p<0.01). Confidence in performing or assisting procedures improved from a baseline mean of 2.8 to 4.2 (p<0.01). ChatGPT was rated “useful” or “very useful” by 77.7% of participants; 85.18% expressed willingness to integrate it into their study routine. The most appreciated features were the model's clarity in procedural sequencing, adaptability to different training levels, and its utility in reinforcing intraoperative decision-making. The most common limitation was the lack of anatomical visuals (70.37%) and oversimplification of complex cases (33.3%). The faculty review confirmed high content relevance and clinical coherence, with minor factual inaccuracies found in 10.1% of AI responses. CONCLUSIONS: ChatGPT proved to be an effective cognitive training tool across a wide range of urologic procedures, significantly improving both procedural knowledge and trainee confidence. Its flexibility and accessibility make it a promising supplement to traditional surgical education, particularly in resource-limited or high-volume training environments. While it cannot replace hands-on experience or expert mentorship, its integration into structured curricula could enhance the standardization and scalability of urologic education. Future studies should evaluate long-term retention, clinical applicability, and outcomes in multi-institutional settings.

title: IP04-16: AI-SKALPEL: AI-Segmentation of Kidney Anatomy and Lithiasis for Precision and Enhanced Learning
parentSessionTitle: IP04: Surgical Technology & Simulation: Artificial Intelligence
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: 3D visualization of surgical anatomy using virtual reality or 3D printed models has been shown to improve surgical outcomes, trainee performance, and reduce the rate of complications. However, creation of 3D models requires significant effort to manually annotate the relevant anatomy for each individual patient. While artificial intelligence (AI)-based methods can dramatically improve annotation efficiency, existing segmentation models for kidney stones and the collecting system are either proprietary, not publicly available, and/or require contrast enhanced CT scans. We thus aimed to develop an open source AI segmentation tool capable of delineating kidney stones and the collecting system on non-contrast CT scans. METHODS: 2,000 publicly available CT scans and radiology reports (AMOS-MM dataset) were evaluated for kidney and ureteral stones. Stone size, volume, and Hounsfield units were calculated, and the presence of hydronephrosis was noted. Manual segmentation was performed to delineate all stones, and a subset of scans with hydronephrosis had bilateral collecting systems annotated in an iterative fashion. Segmentations were used to train Residual Unet models to automatically delineate the stones and collecting systems. Pseudomasks were generated for surrounding organs (colon, spleen, liver, lungs, bony structures) based on previously published work. RESULTS: A total of 174 non-contrast CT scans with 537 kidney/ureteral stones were identified in the AMOS-MM training cohort. Of these, 106 scans had at least one ureteral stone. Mean stone size and volumes were 4.6 mm and 255 mm3. There were 42 stones over 1 cm and 11 stones over 2 cm in size. Hydronephrosis was present in at least one collecting unit in 46 scans. AI segmentation was robust with an average Dice score of 0.97 for the collecting system and median normalized surface distance (NSD) of 0.93 for kidney stones on a held-out test set. Average manual segmentation times per scan were 4.8 minutes for stones and 30.4 minutes for the collecting systems, compared to average AI inference times of 3 seconds for stones and 26 seconds for the collecting systems. CONCLUSIONS: We describe AI-SKALPEL, a freely available AI-segmentation tool for kidney stones and the collecting system. Work is ongoing to validate the model on private, retrospective clinical cohorts.

title: IP04-17: First Fully Automated, Multi-Modal, Large-Language-Model–Driven Prostate Cancer Registry Integrating Biopsy, MRI, Operative, and Pathology Reports
parentSessionTitle: IP04: Surgical Technology & Simulation: Artificial Intelligence
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Manual registry development in prostate cancer remains limited by fragmented diagnostic, imaging, operative, and pathology data. Prior automation efforts targeted single report types or relied on rule-based systems. We developed and validated a locally deployed large language model (LLM) framework that unifies these four domains into a structured, patient-centric registry. METHODS: Reports from 1,179 prostate cancer patients were retrieved from Epic Clarity, including biopsy pathology, prostate MRI, robotic radical prostatectomy operative notes, and surgical pathology. All reports were processed on institutional GPU servers using the locally deployed Qwen3-8B model. Domain-specific prompts were designed for each report type to mirror reporting conventions and output structured JSON. Twenty-seven key variables were extracted across diagnostic, imaging, intraoperative, and pathologic domains. Records were linked by MRN and procedure episode to form a longitudinal dataset. Concordance with manually curated references was evaluated using Cohen’s κ, intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC), percent agreement, and mean absolute deviation (MAD). RESULTS: A total of 3,426 reports were processed. Complete linkage across all four domains was achieved in 1,157 of 1,179 patients (98.1%), verified through one-to-one MRN alignment with no mismatches. Median performance across 27 variables was κ=0.93, ICC=0.95, and 97.5 percent agreement. According to interobserver reliability benchmarks, these values correspond to “almost perfect” and “excellent” agreement ranges typical of expert human raters. CONCLUSIONS: This study establishes the first fully automated cross-domain large-language-model prostate cancer registry integrating biopsy, MRI, operative, and pathology data within institutional infrastructure. Using domain-specific prompts and structured JSON outputs, it achieved near-complete longitudinal linkage and expert-level concordance while preserving institutional governance. This provides a scalable blueprint for real-time outcome tracking and next-generation AI-assisted prostate cancer research. | | | --- | | |

title: IP04-18: From Data to Decisions: Development of Machine Learning Models and an Artificial Intelligence Application to Personalize Care in Inflatable Penile Prosthesis Surgery
parentSessionTitle: IP04: Surgical Technology & Simulation: Artificial Intelligence

speakers.organization: Department of Urology, University of California, Irvine

fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: We developed and deployed a web-based, real-time risk calculator for predicting intraoperative, postoperative non-infectious, and infection-related complications following inflatable penile prosthesis (IPP) surgery. The platform enables transparent, multi-center validation and comparative endpoint assessment of machine-learning based risk models. METHODS: Using a multicenter dataset of 5,815 IPP procedures, machine learning models were developed in Python 3.13. Two feature sets were engineered: a Gamma set (pre-operative variables) and a Sigma set (combined pre- and intra-operative variables). Data preprocessing utilized Scikit-Learn pipelines with ten classifiers tested, including Logistic Regression, Random Forest, Gradient Boosting, and Bernoulli NB. Given low complication rate (<7%), class imbalance was addressed using weighting and resampling techniques with 240 configurations evaluated (80 per target). Final models included Logistic Regression for intraoperative events, Random Forest for non-infectious complications, and Gradient Boosting for infection prediction. Trained models were serialized and deployed through Next. js frontend and FastAPI backend to allow real-time web access. RESULTS: The calculator generates individualized risk estimates in 0.62 ± 0.03 seconds across all endpoints. Model recall for intraoperative, non-infectious, and infectious complications was 74%, 75%, and 79%, respectively. Output visualization displays predicted complication probabilities derived from model distributions, allowing users to explore differences between high- and low-risk patient profiles. Stratification demonstrated stepwise increases in infection probability among patients with multiple comorbid risk factors. Technical performance, data privacy, and security were verified; multi-center prospective validation is ongoing. CONCLUSIONS: This open-access IPP complication risk calculator provides a transparent, real-time platform for individualized complication prediction. The tool’s risk estimates align with published multi-institutional complication rates and facilitate external validation across institutions without compromising data privacy. Broader adoption will allow refinement of predictive performance and integration into future clinical decision-support systems for prosthetic urology.

title: IP04-19: AI-Assisted Stone Prevention: A Patient-Centric Assessment of LLM Performance on Urine Study Interpretations
parentSessionTitle: IP04: Surgical Technology & Simulation: Artificial Intelligence
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Use of large-language models (LLMs) has increased exponentially in recent years. While much study is currently focused on adoption of artificial intelligence technologies for providers, there remains a paucity of data on the state of current commercially available platforms available to the public. As there is not currently a consensus on how patients should be counseled on use of these platforms, there remains a need to assess real-world performance of these technologies from a patient perspective. This study intends to assess the accuracy and readability of common AI platforms on interpretation of 24-hour urine studies and their provided dietary recommendations. METHODS: A series of 4 hypothetical 24-hour urine study results were created to personify 4 classic patient archetypes for recurrent kidney stone formers (low fluid intake, high urinary calcium oxalate, hypocitraturia, high uricosuria). Each table was uploaded to 3 commercially available AI models (Gemini, Perplexity, ChatGPT) with the same prompt requesting interpretation of the uploaded results and dietary recommendations to prevent kidney stone formation. Each generated response was then compared to AUA Nephrolithiasis Medical Management Guidelines for accuracy (with inaccuracies classified as major or minor) of interpretation and dietary recommendation. Reading comprehension of each response was then calculated using both the Flesch-Kincaid Reading Level (FKRL) and Simple Measure of Gobbledygook (SMOG) indices to assess readability. RESULTS: Of the 4 archetypes, all 3 AI models accurately interpreted the 24-hour urine studies in diagnosis of the underlying metabolic risk factors associated with recurrent nephrolithiasis. ChatGPT had 2 minor inaccuracies when providing dietary recommendations for the high uric acid and hypocitraturia patients, while the remaining AI models did not have any inaccuracies in dietary recommendations. Mean FKRL (9.58 Gemini vs 11.26 Perplexity vs 7.86 ChatGPT, p<0.001) and SMOG indices (12.03 Gemini vs 12.08 Perplexity vs 10.01 ChatGPT, p<0.001) were significantly different between the 3 AI models, with ChatGPT having the easiest level of comprehension and Perplexity having the most difficult. CONCLUSIONS: Current commercially available AI platforms are able to accurately assess 24-hour urine study results and overall provided appropriate dietary recommendations. ChatGPT did provide the easiest/lowest required reading comprehension for responses for each prompt while Perplexity had the most difficult. Further studies are needed to better inform urologists on how to counsel patients on using these technologies.

title: IP04-20: Pathological Characteristics and Cause-specific Diagnostic Accuracy of a Deep Learning Model for False-positive Photodynamic Diagnosis of Bladder Cancer
parentSessionTitle: IP04: Surgical Technology & Simulation: Artificial Intelligence

speakers.organization: Department of Urology, Kochi Medical School, Kochi University

fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: False-positive (FP) findings in photodynamic diagnosis (PDD) arise from biological and optical factors, including tangent illumination, inflammation, non-neoplastic epithelial alterations, and chromosomal instability in premalignant mucosa. These FP mechanisms complicate intraoperative decision-making and may result in unnecessary resection. Building on our previous study demonstrating the feasibility of a deep learning (DL) model for distinguishing true and false positives, we analyzed its cause-specific diagnostic performance according to pathological background and compared its accuracy with that of expert urologists. METHODS: A total of 1,192 intraoperative PDD-positive cystoscopy images (486 true positives, 706 false positives) from Kochi Medical School Hospital were used to train a ResNet-50–based DL model fine-tuned with PDD data. Performance for distinguishing true and false positives was previously reported at AUA2024 (accuracy 64.3%, sensitivity 60.9%, specificity 66.7%). An independent test dataset of 153 images (104 false positives) was used for pathological differentiation. FP lesions were categorized as: (1) inflammation, (2) non-neoplastic epithelial alterations (reactive atypia, squamous metaplasia, or mild dysplasia), or (3) no pathological findings. The diagnostic accuracy of the DL model was compared with that of 17 expert urologists. RESULTS: Among 104 false-positive images, the DL model correctly identified FP lesions with accuracies of 60.0% for inflammation, 75.0% for non-neoplastic alteration, and 67.9% for no pathological findings, all comparable to or exceeding expert urologists (52.9%, 61.8%, and 57.3%, respectively). The DL model effectively identified false-positive lesions across different pathological backgrounds. CONCLUSIONS: The DL model showed reliable accuracy in distinguishing pathological causes of PDD false positives and performed at an expert level across all categories. This pathological stratification highlights the biological heterogeneity of PDD false fluorescence and represents a step toward AI-assisted fluorescence imaging for optimized bladder cancer surgery and early lesion detection.

title: IP04-21: Comparative validation of AI-assisted MRI screening pathways in the IP1-PROSTAGRAM study
parentSessionTitle: IP04: Surgical Technology & Simulation: Artificial Intelligence
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Several studies have evaluated MRI as an upfront or sequential screening tool for prostate cancer, with variable PSA thresholds and biopsy criteria assessed. However, screening MRI can be challenging to interpret consistently. AI decision support systems (AI-DSS) may have a role in standardising assessment which could improve the balance of harms and benefits of screening with MRI. We retrospectively validated the Lucida Pi AI-DSS on the IP1-PROSTAGRAM cohort, comparing its performance with 3 MRI-based screening pathways. METHODS: 371 men with complete records from IP1-PROSTAGRAM were included. Men underwent Prostagram™ MRI, ultrasound and PSA, with systematic biopsy for any positive test and targeted biopsy if positive imaging. 159 (42.9%) underwent biopsy, detecting 15 (4.0%) GG ≥2 and 19 (5.1%) GG1 cancers. Alternative pathways were modelled using (P1) MRI for all; (P2) MRI if PSA ≥1; and (P3) MRI if PSA ≥3. In each pathway, a radiologist PI-RADS score of ≥3 and ≥4 was compared with AI-DSS. Outcomes: biopsy recommendation rate, GG ≥2 and GG1 detection, benign biopsy rate (GG0), and 3 derived utility metrics: selectivity (GG ≥2/GG1), efficiency (GG ≥2/\[GG1+GG0\]), and selective biopsy avoidance (GGx \[no biopsy\]/GG0). RESULTS: AI-DSS maintained or improved GG ≥2 detection whilst reducing biopsy rates in most scenarios. In P1, AI-DSS achieved similar GG ≥2 yield (11/371, 3.0%) to PI-RADS ≥3 (3.5 %) and ≥4 (3.0 %), with fewer biopsies (9.2% vs 16.7% and 9.7%), GG1 cases (1.1% vs 1.9% and 1.3%), and benign biopsies (5.1% vs 11.3% and 5.4%), improving almost all utility metrics. In P2, AI-DSS maintained GG ≥2 detection (11/371, 3.0%) relative to PI-RADS ≥3 (3.0 %) and ≥4 (2.7%), reducing biopsy rates compared with PI-RADS ≥3 (8.4% vs 11.1%), with a modest increase compared with PI-RADS ≥4 (7.0%), and the lowest GG1 yield (0.5%). In P3, only 9% of men progressed to MRI, yielding 6/371 (1.6%) GG ≥2 cancers and missing half of all GG ≥2 cases; here, AI-DSS offered no additional benefit.
