speakers.organization: American University of Beirut Medical Center

fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Failure-to-rescue (FTR) is a common quality metric used in general surgery, but its exploration in the urology field is not well studied. It is defined as death following one or more major post-operative complications. In patients undergoing partial nephrectomy, associated with slightly more acute complications versus radical nephrectomy, assessing FTR via ACS-NSQIP database may prove to be crucial. METHODS: Using the appropriate CPT codes, patients that underwent partial nephrectomy between the years of 2019-2022 were selected. We decided to assess changes in the FTR rate based on age group percentiles of the patient population, <52 years (25th percentile, 52-69 (25th-75th percentile), and >69 years (75th percentile). FTR was measured as death following development of any Clavien Dindo Grade 3+ complication 30 days post-operatively. Univariate logistic regression followed by adjustment for baseline characteristics was done by multivariate binary logistic regression. RESULTS: 13,301 patients were found that underwent partial nephrectomy on the NSQIP database. The mortality rate in this population was 0.2% while FTR overall in this population was 5.96%, with it steadily increasing with age: 2.50% (<52 years), 3.64% (52-69 years), and 11.29% (>69 years). The most common complication Grade that occurred in patients that survived partial nephrectomy was Clavien Dindo Grade 2 (76.3%) while patients that died mainly developed Clavien Dindo Grade 4 (95.7%). After adjustment with multivariate binary logistic regression, older age groups were associated with higher odds of FTR in comparison to the young age group (<52): 1.501 (52-69, p-value=0.630) and 7.140 (>69, p-value=0.014). CONCLUSIONS: Partial nephrectomy is a surgery known to have acute post-operative complications that require their own immediate attention. Monitoring proves crucial in these patients, especially the older age groups, as they could lead to significantly higher mortality rates. Moreover, evaluating failure-to-rescue rates these patients at an institutional level may further provide a quality assessment metric to provide the best care for their patients. | | | --- | | | | | | --- | | |

title: IP05-24: Surgery on the Edge: Real-World Outcomes of Partial and Radical Nephrectomy in Patients with Stage 4 Chronic Kidney Disease
parentSessionTitle: IP05: Kidney Cancer: Localized: Surgical Therapy I
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Patients with stage 4 chronic kidney disease (CKD4) have a substantial risk of end-stage renal disease (ESRD). Management of localized renal tumors is controversial, as both radical (RN) and partial nephrectomy (PN) may precipitate renal decline, yet evidence on postoperative functional and oncological outcomes in this high-risk group is limited. We aimed to characterize renal function trajectories, ESRD risk, and perioperative morbidity among CKD4 patients undergoing renal surgery. METHODS: We retrospectively analyzed 4,019 consecutive patients who underwent PN or RN (1987-2023) at a tertiary center. CKD4 was defined as baseline eGFR 15-29 ml/min/1.73m2. Outcomes included postoperative renal function decline (ΔeGFR=pre - postoperative eGFR) and progression to ESRD (eGFR15 ml/min/1.73m2) at last follow-up. ESRD was modelled as a competing-risk event with death as competing endpoint. 90-day postop complications were recorded. Multivariable linear regression (MVA) assessed predictors of ΔeGFR. Fine–Gray competing-risk regression identified predictors of ESRD. Logistic regression compared complication rates between PN and RN. RESULTS: 67 CKD4 patients met inclusion criteria; 37 (55%) underwent RN. RN patients had larger tumours (7 vs 4.7 cm, p=0.002), with otherwise comparable baseline characteristics. At a median follow-up of 20 months, 15% progressed to ESRD. Median postoperative ΔeGFR was 1 ml/min/1.73m2 (IQR –2.3, 6.2), with no difference between PN and RN (p>0.9). On MVA, RN predicted greater short-term functional decline (p=0.007). The 60-month cumulative incidence of ESRD was similar in PN and RN (22% vs 20%, HR 0.65, p=0.4). Younger age was associated with lower ESRD risk (HR 0.94, p0.001). Overall, 57% had postop complications, with no difference between PN and RN (60% vs 54%, OR 0.78, p=0.6). Bleeding/hematoma occurred more often after PN (40% vs 16%), whereas acute kidney injury was more frequent after RN (30% vs 17%). CONCLUSIONS: In patients with CKD4 undergoing renal surgery, RN led to greater short-term renal function decline but did not increase long-term ESRD risk compared with PN. Overall complication rates were high but comparable between approaches. These data provide contemporary real-world benchmarks for counselling CKD4 patients with localized renal tumours and call for individualized surgical strategies in this rare, high-risk population.

title: IP05-25: From Glycemic Control to Renal Outcomes: Do GLP-1 Agonists Slow Kidney Function Decline After Radical Nephrectomy?
parentSessionTitle: IP05: Kidney Cancer: Localized: Surgical Therapy I
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Radical nephrectomy (RN) results in immediate reduction in renal function and accelerates age-related decline. While glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1 RAs) have shown reno-protective effects in patients with diabetes, their impact on renal function after RN remains unexplored. The present study aims to evaluate the association between GLP-1 RA use and renal function outcomes following RN using a multi-institutional dataset. METHODS: A retrospective cohort analysis was conducted using the TriNetX US Collaborative Network (2005–2024). Adult patients (≥18 years) undergoing RN were stratified by GLP-1 RA use. Outcomes included change in eGFR, acute kidney injury (AKI), chronic kidney disease (CKD), and dialysis dependence defined by ICD-10 codes at 1, 2, and 5 years. Kaplan-Meier survival analysis and Cox proportional hazards models were used to assess event-free survival and risk. RESULTS: After matching, 3,840 patients per cohort were analyzed. Mean eGFR was consistently higher in the GLP-1 RA group at 1 year (49.5 vs. 44.4 ml/min/1.73m2, p=0.01), 2 years (49.2 vs. 43.9, p=0.005), and 5 years (49.2 vs. 43.4, p=0.001). GLP-1 RA exposure was associated with significantly lower AKI rates at 1 year (6.3% vs. 12.3%, RR 1.95), 2 years (8.8% vs. 16%, RR 1.82), and 5 years (12.6% vs. 20.8%, RR 1.65; p for all 0.001). CKD incidence was lower in GLP-1 RA cohort at 1 year (15.8% vs. 26.2%, RR 1.66), 2 years (20.3% vs. 30.1%, RR 1.49), and 5 years (24.1% vs. 37%, RR 1.53; p for all 0.001). Dialysis dependence was markedly lower in GLP-1 RA cohort at 2 years (0.8% vs. 5.7%, RR 7.07) and 5 years (1.7% vs. 8.1%, RR 4.86; p0.001). Kaplan-Meier analysis confirmed improved event-free survival for AKI and dialysis dependence (p0.05), but not for CKD (p=0.11) ( Figures 1 and 2). Cox modeling revealed GLP-1 RA use was independently associated with reduced risk of AKI (HR 0.58, p0.0001) and dialysis dependence (HR 0.37, p0.0001), but not CKD (HR 0.92, p=0.51). CONCLUSIONS: GLP-1 RA use was associated with significantly better preservation of renal function and fewer renal complications and after radical nephrectomy for RCC. These findings highlight the reno-protective potential of GLP-1 RAs post-nephrectomy and support prospective evaluation.

title: IP05-26: Long-Term Renal Function After Radical Nephrectomy and IVC Thrombectomy: A Multicenter Analysis
parentSessionTitle: IP05: Kidney Cancer: Localized: Surgical Therapy I

speakers.organization: University of Alabama at Birmingham Heersink School of Medicine

fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Radial nephrectomy with inferior vena cava (IVC) tumor thrombectomy is a complex operation presumably associated with surgically induced acute kidney injury (AKI). However, specific risk factors associated with AKI and long-term renal insufficiency (LTRI) for IVC tumor thrombectomy patients are not well described. We evaluated incidence of and clinicopathological factors associated with LTRI in surgically treated patients after radical nephrectomy and IVC tumor thrombus. METHODS: We conducted a multicenter review of patients undergoing radical nephrectomy with IVC tumor thrombectomy between 2015 and 2025. Patient demographics, preoperative, and postoperative variables were collected. LTRI was defined as a ≥1 chronic kidney disease stage decline from baseline at most recent follow-up. Temporary AKI was defined as a 1.5x increase in baseline creatinine at discharge after surgery. Univariate logistic regressions were performed. Variables with clinical relevance were included in a multivariable logistic regression model to identify independent predictors of LTRI. Rates of AKI and LTRI were compared between tumor thrombi levels 0-2 vs. 3-4, and the eGFR change for each patient was plotted. RESULTS: Among 117 patients with complete follow-up data, the AKI rate was 15.5% and the LTRI rate was 50.4% ( Table). Median follow-up length was 530 days. On both univariate and multivariate analyses, older age and pre-existing hypertension were significantly associated with LTRI. Neither AKI nor LTRI rates differed by tumor thrombus level, but eGFR decline long-term was lower in patients with level 3-4 IVC thrombus compared to those with level 0-2 (p=0.03). Many patients who did not develop LTRI experienced an improvement in renal function long-term ( Figure). CONCLUSIONS: Age and hypertension at the time of surgery are independently associated with LTRI. Tumor thrombus level does not predict temporary adverse renal function outcomes, though patients with higher level thrombi appear to have less eGFR decline long-term. Presumably, this may be related to removing bulky tumor thrombus from the IVC and improving contra-lateral kidney outflow. | | | --- | | |

title: IP05-27: When the Thrombus Rises: Inferior Vena Cava Involvement Impairs Preoperative Renal Function in Renal Cell Carcinoma
parentSessionTitle: IP05: Kidney Cancer: Localized: Surgical Therapy I
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: In renal cell carcinoma (RCC), a venous tumor thrombus (VTT) extending into the inferior vena cava (IVC) may impair both ipsi-and contralateral renal venous outflow, predisposing to renal dysfunction. We compared survival outcomes between renal vein (RV) and IVC VTT and assessed whether caval extension is independently associated with preoperative chronic kidney disease (preopCKD). METHODS: From a prospectively maintained database, we retrospectively analyzed patients undergoing nephrectomy with VTT, dichotomized as RV or IVC (T3b/T3c) involvement. Overall (OS) and cancer-specific survival (CSS) were analyzed using restricted mean survival time (RMST) up to =60 months. Multivariable logistic regression assessed the association between VTT extension and preopCKD (eGFR 60 ml/min/1.73 m2), adjusting for renal-function confounders (diabetes, Charlson Comorbidity Index \[CCI\], smoking, ECOG, age, sex, BMI, tumor size). RESULTS: Among 389 patients, 238 (61%) had RV VTT and 151 (39%) IVC VTT (111 T3b, 40 T3c). Median follow-up was 75 months (IQR 67–84). For OS (τ=60), RMST was 44 months (95% CI 41–47) for RV VTT vs 33 months (95% CI 28–37) for IVC VTT, a ΔRMST of +11months (95% CI +6 to +18; p<0.001). The RMST ratio (RV/IVC)=1.35 (95% CI 1.16–1.57; p<0.001) indicated 35% more event-free survival time for RV VTT. For CSS, RMST was 46 months (95% CI 43–49) vs 38 months (95% CI 34–43), ΔRMST +8 months (95%CI +2 to +13; p=0.006) and RMST ratio 1.21 (95% CI 1.05–1.38; p=0.009). PreopCKD occurred in 59 (25%) RV VTT and 56 (37%) IVC VTT (p=0.01). At multivariable analysis, IVC VTT was independently associated with higher odds of preopCKD (OR 2.15, 95% CI 1.23–3.79; p=0.025), together with higher CCI (OR 1.50; p=0.006), increasing age (OR 1.10; p<0.001), higher BMI (OR 1.09; p=0.041), and larger tumor size (OR 1.10; 95% CI 1.01–1.19; p=0.048). CONCLUSIONS: IVC involvement by VTT is associated with significantly shorter 5-year event-free survival for both OS and CSS and with increased risk of preoperative CKD, reflecting the hemodynamic burden of caval obstruction on bilateral renal drainage. These findings underscore the importance of proactive renoprotective strategies in patients with IVC thrombus extension and warrant validation in larger multicentric cohorts.

title: IP05-28: Long-term outcomes of surgical and endovascular interventions for sporadic renal angiomyolipoma
parentSessionTitle: IP05: Kidney Cancer: Localized: Surgical Therapy I
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Renal angiomyolipomas (AMLs) are the most common benign renal tumors, composed of varying proportions of dysmorphic blood vessels, smooth muscle, and fat tissue. Approximately 80% of AMLs occur sporadically, most often in middle-aged women, and are frequently discovered incidentally. Larger tumors (>4 cm) or symptomatic lesions carry increased risks of hemorrhage and renal function decline. Treatment options include partial or total nephrectomy and selective arterial embolization, each with distinct implications for renal preservation and retreatment. However, long-term outcomes, particularly renal function preservation and retreatment rates, remain limited. This study evaluates renal function preservation and retreatment rates after intervention for sporadic AMLs using a large clinical database. METHODS: Adult patients (18–90 years) with sporadic renal AML who underwent nephrectomy (n=2,987) or arterial embolization (n=1,293) were identified from the TriNetX US Collaborative Network. Patients with tuberous sclerosis or who were deceased were excluded. Outcomes included need for secondary treatment and renal function (serum creatinine and estimated glomerular filtration rate \[eGFR\] were assessed from the most recent available measurements prior to initial intervention, within 5 years, and within 10 years). Kaplan-Meier analysis and comparative risk estimates, including risk difference, risk ratio, odds ratio, hazard ratio were used to compare retreatment rates between groups. RESULTS: After exclusions, nephrectomy patients were 58% female (mean age 66), and embolization patients were 81% female (mean age 63). Patients undergoing embolization had significantly higher rates of repeat intervention compared to those receiving nephrectomy (13.8% vs. 2.1%, p<0.001). When comparing the embolization and nephrectomy cohorts, the nephrectomy group had a significantly lower GFR compared to the embolization group within 5 and 10 years and no significant difference in creatinine levels. CONCLUSIONS: Selective arterial embolization is associated with better renal function but a higher likelihood of repeat intervention, whereas nephrectomy provides more durable tumor control at the cost of reduced renal reserve. These findings highlight the clinical trade-off between renal preservation and definitive disease control when selecting therapy for sporadic AML. Embolization may be preferred for patients for whom renal preservation is a priority, particularly younger individuals, those with bilateral disease, or pre-existing renal impairment, while nephrectomy is best reserved for large symptomatic tumors, failed embolization, or suspected malignancy. Prospective studies incorporating tumor characteristics and symptom burden are needed to guide long-term management strategies.

title: IP05-29: Single Port Robotic Nephroureterectomy: A Multi-Institutional Experience from the Single Port Advanced Research Consortium (SPARC)
parentSessionTitle: IP05: Kidney Cancer: Localized: Surgical Therapy I
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: To investigate the safety and efficacy of robotic nephroureterectomy (RNU) performed using the purpose-built Single Port (SP) robotic platform. METHODS: A retrospective review was completed on the IRB-approved multi-institutional database of the Single Port Advanced Research Consortium (SPARC) to identify all consecutive patients who underwent SP-RNU between 2018 and 2025. Baseline clinicodemographic, intraoperative, and postoperative outcomes were collected, with descriptive statistics as presented. RESULTS: A total of 125 patients were included, with a median age of 70 years (IQR 62 – 77) and a median BMI of 26.8 kg/m2 (IQR 23.2 – 30.8). All cases were completed successfully within a median operative time of 223 minutes (IQR 185 – 271) and a median intraoperative blood loss of 80 ml (IQR 50 – 150). Supine position was preferred in 51.6% and most cases were completed via a retroperitoneal approach (80.5%). An additional port was utilized in 48% of the procedures. On histopathology, urothelial carcinoma was identified in 83.1%, with positive surgical margins reported in 7.1%. Postoperatively, the median length of stay was 2 days (IQR 1 – 3), with major complications observed in 12.8%. At a median follow-up of 6 months (IQR 2 – 11), 25.4% of the cohort received neoadjuvant therapy, and recurrence was observed in 21.9%. CONCLUSIONS: RNU can be safely and effectively completed using the SP robotic platform, featuring satisfactory perioperative and oncological outcomes. Nevertheless, longer follow-up data remain necessary to ensure the adequacy of the technique and optimal patient selection amidst the growing repertoire of minimally invasive surgical modalities. | | | --- | | |

title: IP05-30: Robotic partial nephrectomy for complex versus non-complex renal tumors: a single-surgeon decade-long experience analyzing functional and oncologic outcomes, recurrence, predictors of complications, and trifecta/pentafecta achievement.
parentSessionTitle: IP05: Kidney Cancer: Localized: Surgical Therapy I
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Robot-assisted partial nephrectomy (RAPN) is increasingly used to treat complex renal tumors. This study compared functional and oncological outcomes of RAPN in complex (RENAL score ≥7) versus non-complex tumors (RENAL score <7). Secondary aim was to identify predictors of postoperative complications in both groups. METHODS: A prospectively maintained uro-oncology database was reviewed for all RAPN procedures performed between January 2012 and July 2024 at Kokilaben Dhirubhai Ambani Hospital, Mumbai. A total of 635 patients were categorized into complex (n=358) and non-complex tumors (n=277) using the RENAL Nephrometry Score (radius, exophytic/endophytic, nearness to sinus/collecting system, anterior/posterior, polar location). Demographics, tumor complexity, perioperative and pathological data were analyzed. Trifecta was defined as negative margins, no postoperative complications, and warm ischemia time (WIT) <25 min. Pentafecta additionally required >90% estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) preservation and no chronic kidney disease (CKD) stage up-migration at 1 year. Predictors of outcomes and complications were evaluated by logistic regression. RESULTS: Median follow-up was 67 months. Complex tumors showed higher clinical T stage (p=0.007), RENAL scores (p=0.002), and longer WIT (p<0.0001). Trifecta and pentafecta were significantly more frequently achieved in non-complex tumors. However, recurrence rates were similar (p=0.999). No perioperative mortality occurred. One-year eGFR preservation did not differ (p=0.706). Complex tumors demonstrated marginally higher Clavien-Dindo ≥3 complications, but without statistical significance (p=0.511). On multivariate analysis, multifocality predicted major complications in complex tumors, while prolonged WIT was the major predictor in non-complex tumors. Higher pre-operative eGFR and shorter WIT predicted better trifecta and pentafecta outcomes in both groups. CONCLUSIONS: RAPN is safe and effective for complex renal tumors with comparable functional preservation, major complication rates, and recurrence to non-complex tumors. Though trifecta/pentafecta achievement is lower in complex cases due to tumor anatomy and longer ischemia, modern robotic platforms facilitate precise excision and reconstruction, enabling successful management of challenging renal masses.

title: IP06-01: Robotic-Assisted Ultrasound-Guided Percutaneous Nephrolithotomy: Initial Clinical Experience from a Consecutive Series of Ten Cases
parentSessionTitle: IP06: Stone Disease: Surgical Therapy (including ESWL) I
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Safe and precise renal access remains the most critical and technically demanding step of percutaneous nephrolithotomy (PCNL). Fluoroscopy-guided access emits ionizing radiation and offers limited soft-tissue discrimination, whereas ultrasound guidance eliminates radiation but requires advanced hand-eye coordination. The Focalist system (Mendeara Inc.) is a robotic-assisted handheld ultrasound platform that orients the needle and provides real-time needle-tip tracking and on-screen trajectory planning. We present the first consecutive clinical series worldwide evaluating feasibility, workflow integration, and perioperative outcomes using this system for PCNL access. METHODS: A prospective observational study included ten consecutive renal units undergoing ultrasound-guided PCNL with the Focalist system between August and September 2025. Procedures were performed by an endourologist or trainee. Primary endpoints were successful collecting-system access and first-attempt success. Secondary outcomes included time metrics, radiation exposure, papillary targeting, complications, and surgeon-reported usability (5-point Likert scale). RESULTS: Robot-assisted ultrasound-guided access was successful in 8/10 renal units (80%) with first-attempt success in 6/10 (60%) and papillary access in 7/8 (87.5%) successful cases. Mean time from target acquisition to needle at target was 270 ± 324 s; needle insertion time averaged 14 ± 19 s. Mean fluoroscopy time was 15.5 ± 23.7 s (mean air kerma 5.5 ± 11.3 mGy). No device-related complications occurred. Usability scores were high (ease of setup 5.0, ease of use 4.1, confidence in placement 4.6), with smooth workflow integration across attending, fellow, and resident operators. CONCLUSIONS: Robot-assisted ultrasound-guided renal access using the Focalist system was feasible, safe, and rapidly adoptable across experience levels, achieving high access success with minimal fluoroscopy and no complications. Real-time needle tracking and ergonomic probe stabilization supported efficient targeting, while limited ultrasound field of view contributed to two failures. This low-capital, bedside robotic adjunct may lower barriers to urologist-performed ultrasound-guided PCNL. Larger comparative studies are warranted to validate performance, learning curves, and cost-effectiveness. | | | --- | | |

title: IP06-02: Solving challenges of flexible ureteroscopes toward the social implementation of ureteroscope-assisted robots-AI-based Software as Medical Device development research
parentSessionTitle: IP06: Stone Disease: Surgical Therapy (including ESWL) I
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Robotic ureteroscopy (rURS) is emerging in Western countries as a potential paradigm shift from flexible ureteroscopy (fURS). Despite its utility, fURS imposes ergonomic strain on surgeons due to structural limitations. This study aimed to quantitatively compare the motion characteristics between expert and novice surgeons during flexible ureteroscopy (fURS) using an AI-based pose estimation application. By analyzing joint trajectories, speeds, and angular variations, ergonomic stability and surgical proficiency were evaluated. METHODS: Five participants (experts: n=3, novices: n=2) performed standardized fURS tasks on a 3D-printed kidney phantom. The AI-based system (MediaPipe Pose) estimated three-dimensional joint coordinates and calculated movement distances (cm), velocities (cm/s), and angular variations. Statistical comparisons between groups were performed using t-tests and Wilcoxon tests. RESULTS: Experts demonstrated significantly smaller joint movements than novices, as shown in (https://www.auajournals.org/doi/abs/10.1097/01.JU.0001191292.44613.d7.02#F1). The right wrist movement distance was markedly shorter in experts (471 cm) than in novices (3558 cm, p=0.0227), as were right elbow movements (277 cm vs. 2653 cm, p=0.0355). Angular variation of the shoulder was also significantly smaller in experts (32 cm vs. 90 cm, p=0.0102). In terms of motion velocity, novices showed higher speeds at the elbow (14.0 cm/s vs. 4.8 cm/s, p=0.0323) and wrist (19.2 cm/s vs. 8.0 cm/s, p=0.0488). Operation time was shorter in experts (65 s vs. 186 s, p=0.0603). CONCLUSIONS: The AI-based Pose Estimation Application successfully distinguished between expert and novice operators. Experts maintained stable postures with limited and controlled joint movements, whereas novices exhibited greater motion variability and longer procedure times. These findings demonstrate the potential of AI-driven motion analysis as a reliable tool for evaluating surgical proficiency and providing real-time feedback during robotic or endoscopic training.

title: IP06-03: Artificial Intelligence-Based Prediction of Postoperative Sepsis in Patients Undergoing Suction Mini-Percutaneous Nephrolithotomy: A Multicenter Analysis from the Global STUMPS Registry
parentSessionTitle: IP06: Stone Disease: Surgical Therapy (including ESWL) I

speakers.organization: Istanbul University, Istanbul Faculty of Medicine, Department of Urology

fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Suction mini-PCNL has advanced stone removal with lower infection rates. This study leveraged an artificial intelligence model to accurately predict postoperative sepsis following suction mini-PCNL. METHODS: We analyzed data from the STUMPS registry, a prospective, multicenter cohort of adult patients undergoing suction mini-PCNL across 30 centers between March-November 2024. Baseline patient characteristics, stone features, operative details and perioperative labs were recorded. Postoperative sepsis within 30 days was defined using qSOFA criteria. A supervised machine learning model (XGBoost) was developed to predict sepsis using patient, stone, and procedural variables. Data were split into training (80%) and test (20%) sets, with categorical variables one-hot encoded. Model performance was evaluated using AUC, sensitivity, specificity, and confusion matrices. Feature importance was assessed using SHAP values to identify key predictors of postoperative sepsis. RESULTS: A total of 2,172 patients were included, with 87 developing postoperative sepsis. Age and preoperative GFR were similar between groups, while patients with sepsis had higher BMI and preoperative hemoglobin. Stones were slightly larger in the sepsis group. Operative factors differed markedly: lithotripsy time, number of tracts, and total operative time were higher in sepsis patients. Sheath size and peri-/postoperative labs did not differ significantly. The XGBoost model predicted postoperative sepsis with excellent accuracy (AUC 0.946). At the optimal cutoff, sensitivity was 0.88, specificity 0.99, overall accuracy 98.4%, and Cohen's κ=0.802. Positive and negative predictive values were 0.75 and 0.995, respectively. SHAP analysis identified lithotripsy time, high Guy's stone score, stitch-based tract closure, sheath size, and exit type (exit tubeles with stent) as the strongest contributors to sepsis risk. Prolonged procedures, complex stones, and certain closure techniques increased risk, while pre-operative WBC/HGB, GFR and procedural nuances also contributed. CONCLUSIONS: Operative complexity, stone burden, and patient physiological status are key predictors of postoperative sepsis after suction mini- PCNL. Machine learning models can reliably identify high-risk patients, supporting early risk stratification and targeted preventive strategies. | | | --- | | |

title: IP06-04: Comparing Extracorporeal shock wave lithotripsy and Ureteroscopic lithotripsy for the managemengt of  Lower Ureteric Stones: A Randomized Trial
parentSessionTitle: IP06: Stone Disease: Surgical Therapy (including ESWL) I
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Acute colic due to lower ureteric calculi is a significant cause of morbidity, necessitating prompt and effective management. Extracorporeal Shock Wave Lithotripsy (ESWL) and Ureteroscopic Lithotripsy (URSL) are widely employed treatment modalities. Comparative data on their outcomes, particularly in acute settings, remain sparse. This study aim to evaluate and compare the efficacy, patient satisfaction, and cost-effectiveness of ESWL and URSL in managing lower ureteric stones presenting with acute colic. METHODS: A randomized controlled trial was conducted at AIIMS, Jodhpur, involving 164 patients presenting with acute colic due to lower ureteric stones. Patients were randomized equally into two groups: ESWL (Group A, n=82) and URSL (Group B, n=82). Primary outcomes included stone-free rates (SFR) at 1 week, 8 weeks, and 3 months. Secondary outcomes encompassed pain intensity, analgesic requirements, complications, quality of life (EQ-5D-5L), loss of working days, and treatment costs. RESULTS: URSL demonstrated significantly higher SFR at all time points compared to ESWL (95% vs. 55.83% at 3 months, p<0.0001). Group A exhibited fewer complications (43.33% vs. 25%, p=0.006) and shorter recovery times, reflected in fewer working days lost (5.08 ± 1.08 vs. 8 ± 0.64 days, p<0.0001). While ESWL was less expensive (mean: Rs 4386.67 ± 1827.76 vs. Rs 5049.17 ± 2067.26, p=0.009), URSL yielded higher patient satisfaction scores (4.07 ± 0.66 vs. 3.78 ± 0.71, p=0.002). CONCLUSIONS: For lower ureteric calculi, URSL offers superior stone clearance and patient satisfaction, particularly for larger or more complex stones, while ESWL remains a viable, less invasive, and cost-effective option for smaller stones. These findings highlight the importance of tailoring treatment decisions based on patient and stone-specific factors.

title: IP06-05: Reduced likelihood of post-operative urinary tract infection with single-use ureteroscope with real-time infrarenal pressure monitoring vs. all other single-use ureteroscopes for patients with kidney stones
parentSessionTitle: IP06: Stone Disease: Surgical Therapy (including ESWL) I
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Ureteroscopy (URS) carries inherent risks including intrarenal pressure (IRP) elevation and can lead to complications such as urinary tract infection (UTI). This study compared post-operative UTI associated with the LithoVue™ Elite Single-Use Digital Flexible Ureteroscope (LVE) with pressure monitoring vs. all other single-use ureteroscopes as comparative effectiveness evidence for LVE with pressure monitoring is needed. METHODS: This retrospective cohort study used electronic health record (EHR) data from Truveta. Patients undergoing URS with laser lithotripsy between January 1, 2023-June 1, 2025 and with ≥30 days follow-up after the index URS procedure were included. The prevalence of post-operative UTI 30 days from the index URS encounter was evaluated and compared for patients treated with LVE with pressure monitoring vs. all other single-use ureteroscopes. Propensity score matching was used to control for differences in baseline characteristics. RESULTS: 208 patients treated with LVE with pressure monitoring (mean age 61.4; 48.1% female; 85.1% White) were matched to 416 patients treated with other single-use ureteroscopes without pressure monitoring (mean age 61.8; 48.4% female; 85.1% White). Compared to patients treated with other single-use ureteroscopes, lower proportions of patients treated with LVE with pressure monitoring had post-operative UTI 30-days post-index (5.2% vs. 10.8%; p=0.033). Multivariable analyses confirmed significantly higher likelihood of 30-day UTI with other single-use ureteroscopes (odds ratio 2.41 \[95% confidence\ interval 1.21-5.27\]; p=0.020). Given the prevalence of URS and the high incidence of post-operative UTI with URS, use of LVE with pressure monitoring could have a transformative impact on URS patient care. CONCLUSIONS: LVE with pressure monitoring was associated with reduced 30-day post-URS UTI. These findings support clinical improvement associated with LVE and suggest that IRP monitoring may contribute to better patient outcomes. Use of LVE with pressure monitoring may be a strategy to improve patient quality of care and to help healthcare decision makers manage the expanding burden of patients with kidney stones.

title: IP06-06: Robotic Flexible Ureterorenoscopic lithotripsy with the Zamenix™ System: A Preliminary Clinical Study
parentSessionTitle: IP06: Stone Disease: Surgical Therapy (including ESWL) I
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: This study presents our initial clinical experience with robotic flexible ureterorenoscopic stone removal using the Zamenix™ robotic system, a newly developed platform designed to enhance precision and ergonomics in endourological stone surgery. METHODS: We retrospectively reviewed 18 consecutive patients who underwent robotic flexible ureterorenoscopic stone removal with the Zamenix™ system between August and December 2024\. Demographic data (age, sex, and body mass index \[BMI\]) and stone characteristics (size, location, and composition) were collected. Operative parameters, perioperative complications, and stone-free rates were analyzed. RESULTS: The cohort included 18 patients with a mean age of 52.3 ± 15.2 years (range 25–78), and 55.6% (n=10) were male. The mean BMI was 27.3 ± 5.1 kg/m2 (range 17.0–43.0). The mean stone volume was 1450.2 ± 1093.1 mm3 (range 93.2–4046.8). Stone laterality was right in 38.9%, left in 22.2%, and bilateral in 38.9% of cases. The mean operative time was 107.2 ± 26.3 minutes (range 65–175). The overall stone-free rate was 88.9%, with complete stone clearance in 38.9% of patients. Subclinical residual fragments were identified in 50.0%, and stone-free failure occurred in 11.1%. Stone composition was predominantly calcium oxalate (66.7%), followed by struvite (22.2%), cystine (5.6%), and uric acid (5.6%). Postoperative complications were limited to one case of fever and one case of steinstrasse, both managed conservatively. CONCLUSIONS: Robotic flexible ureterorenoscopic lithotripsy using the Zamenix™ system appears to be a safe and effective option for renal stone management. The system offers ergonomic and technical advantages; however, its relatively long setup time compared with conventional ureteroscopy remains a limitation to be improved in future iterations. | | | --- | | |

title: IP06-07: Surgeon-Reported Performance Outcomes of a Novel 6.3-French Single-Use Flexible Ureteroscope
parentSessionTitle: IP06: Stone Disease: Surgical Therapy (including ESWL) I
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Single-use flexible ureteroscopy (fURS) devices often involve tradeoffs between scope diameter, optical quality, and mechanical durability. The HugeMed HU30M is a novel single-use, 6.3-French flexible ureteroscope. Its smaller diameter may reduce trauma and the need for ureteral pre-stenting but has a potentially greater risk of mechanical breakdown. We aim to evaluate the performance outcomes of this device for primary and complex fURS. METHODS: Consecutive fURS cases using the HU30M were analyzed from 4/2025 to 10/2025. Selection criteria for use were either 1) primary fURS without pre-stenting or dilation, or 2) complex cases with increased risk of mechanical device damage (>15 mm total, >10 mm inferior pole stone burden, or bilateral fURS). Surgeons rated device performance after each case on a 1-5 Likert scale for optical quality (5=similar to Karl Storz FLEX-XC), maneuverability (5=able to perform complete renoscopy), and mechanical durability (5=no visible or functional breakdown). Up and down maximum deflection was assessed before and after use. RESULTS: We performed 59 fURS cases using 62 HU30M devices on 75 renal units. Of the 59 cases, 43 (73%) were primary fURS, 27 (46%) for large stone burden, and 16 (27%) were bilateral. Primary fURS was achieved in all cases. In 58 (98%) cases, surgeons reported that the HU30M would acceptably replace their default fURS device (Boston Scientific LithoVue in 66% cases, FLEX-XC in 32% cases). Average performance ratings of the HU30M were 4.0 (SD 0) for optical quality, 4.9 (SD 0.5) for maneuverability, and 4.7 (SD 1.0) for durability (Figure). There were no significant differences in surgeon ratings based on indication for use (all p>0.05). Complete 270° up and down deflection was observed before use for all 62 scopes. After use, up and down deflection was 270° for 60 (97%) and 56 (90%) scopes, respectively. Of the 7 devices with deflection loss, all cases involved large stone burden requiring prolonged deflection. Of these, 2 were critical breakdowns causing case interruption and device replacement. CONCLUSIONS: A novel 6.3-French single-use flexible ureteroscope was successfully deployed for both primary and complex fURS in 100% of cases with a critical breakdown incidence of only 3%. Based on performance outcomes comparable to reusable digital devices, surgeons reported that the HU30M could replace their default fURS device in 98% of cases.

title: IP06-08: Comparison Between Ureterorenoscopy With Lithotripsy Alone Versus Combination With Hydrogel for Kidney Stone Removal: INTERIM Results
parentSessionTitle: IP06: Stone Disease: Surgical Therapy (including ESWL) I

speakers.organization: University Clinic of the Technical University of Munich

fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Residual fragments after flexible ureteroscopy (fURS) remain a relevant issue in endourological stone management. Even small clinically insignificant residual fragments can serve as a nidus for recurrence, making the achievement of zero residual fragments a key therapeutic goal. The MediNiK® hydrogel method was developed to enhance fragment retrieval and improve the stone-free rate (SFR). METHODS: This single-center, comparative study reports the interim results of an ongoing investigation including patients undergoing fURS for renal calculi. Patients were divided into two groups: URS alone (Group 1, n=30) and URS + MediNiK® (Group 2, n=30). All procedures were performed using disposable flexible ureteroscopes and a thulium fiber laser (TFL) for lithotripsy. A standard ureteral access sheath (UAS) without suction was used in all cases. In the MediNiK® group, a biocompatible hydrogel was applied intrarenally after laser fragmentation to encapsulate and facilitate retrieval of residual stone fragments. ( (https://www.auajournals.org/doi/abs/10.1097/01.JU.0001191292.44613.d7.08#F1) illustrates the application of the hydrogel methode). Postoperative non-contrast CT was performed in all patients to assess the SFR, graded as A (complete clearance), B (≤ 2 mm fragments), or C (2.1–4 mm fragments). Demographic and operative data, SFR, need for second-look URS, and perioperative complications (Clavien-Dindo) were analyzed. RESULTS: Baseline characteristics were comparable between groups (median age 57 vs 59 years; BMI 25.5 vs 26 kg/m2). Median stone size was 11 mm in the URS group and 12 mm in the MediNiK® group (stone volume 402 vs 625 mm3). A higher proportion of patients in the MediNiK® group achieved complete clearance (Grade A=94%) compared to URS alone (66%). Including Grade B fragments, total clearance reached 97% vs 69.5%. The second-look URS rate was lower with MediNiK® (3% vs 13.5%). Operative time was slightly longer (87 vs 76 min), while readmissions and complications were comparable. CONCLUSIONS: These interim findings suggest that the MediNiK® hydrogel method may improve stone-free outcomes and reduce the need for secondary procedures, without increasing perioperative morbidity. Further data from the ongoing study will clarify its long-term safety and efficacy in achieving zero residual fragments.

title: IP06-09: Are SGLT2 inhibitors a new risk factor for urinary tract infections after ureteroscopy in diabetic patients?
parentSessionTitle: IP06: Stone Disease: Surgical Therapy (including ESWL) I

speakers.organization: Rambam Health Care Campus, Haifa, Israel

fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Urinary tract infection (UTI) following ureteroscopy (URS) is a frequent complication, particularly among diabetic patients. Sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 inhibitors (SGLT2i), increasingly used for diabetes and heart failure, induce glucosuria that may predispose to infection. We aimed to determine whether SGLT2i use increases the risk of postoperative UTI after URS. METHODS: We conducted a retrospective study of diabetic patients who underwent URS between 2018 and 2024 at a tertiary medical center. Patients were included if SGLT2i was used prior to surgery. The primary endpoint was postoperative UTI or fever >37.8°C within 30 days. Multivariate logistic regression and propensity score matching were performed to identify independent predictors. RESULTS: Among 1,220 diabetic patients, 213 (17.5%) were treated with SGLT2i. Post-URS UTI occurred more often in SGLT2i users (21.1% vs 12.1%, p<0.001). On univariate analysis, SGLT2i use was associated with higher UTI risk (odds ratio \[OR\] 2.36). A positive preoperative urine culture was the strongest predictor of postoperative UTI across both groups (OR 4.05). Propensity-matched analysis confirmed the independent link between SGLT2i use and postoperative UTI (OR 2.18). ICU admission was rare but twice as common among SGLT2i users (0.02% vs 0.01%). CONCLUSIONS: SGLT2i therapy independently increases the risk of postoperative UTI in diabetic patients undergoing URS, particularly among those with preoperative bacteriuria. Awareness of this risk may support more tailored perioperative infection prevention strategies or, temporarily placing the patient on alternative medications.

title: IP06-11: Reassessing American Urological Association Guidelines: Impact of a 72-Hour Antibiotic Prophylaxis Regimen Following Ureteroscopy
parentSessionTitle: IP06: Stone Disease: Surgical Therapy (including ESWL) I

speakers.organization: University of Rochester School of Medicine & Dentistry

fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Current AUA Guidelines recommend single-dose perioperative antibiotic prophylaxis (ABX PPX) only for uncomplicated, non-infected ureteroscopy (URS) for urolithiasis. However, clinical observation suggests higher rates of post-stent removal UTI than current literature estimates of 3%. We instituted a novel prophylactic ABX course for 72 hours at the time of stent removal at home. This study aimed to (1) determine the post-stent removal UTI rate and (2) evaluate whether a 72-hour ABX PPX regimen reduces infection risk compared to single-dose perioperative ABX. METHODS: We retrospectively studied adults undergoing ureteral stent removal via string following URS by one urologist from 2/1/2022 to 2/29/2024 (STUDY00010773). The NO-ABX cohort received standard single-dose perioperative ABX, while the 72HR-ABX cohort received a novel 72-hour regimen starting 24 hours before removal. Subjects were identified via CPT code. Exclusion criteria included positive preop urine culture, infection-related stones, history of recurrent UTI, or PPX ABX given immediately postoperatively for any reason. The primary endpoint was UTI within 7 days post-stent removal. Fisher’s exact test was used to compare infection rates between cohorts (p<0.05). RESULTS: Of 669 subjects screened, 171 met inclusion criteria for uncomplicated, non-infected URS (NO-ABX: n=145; 72HR-ABX: n=26). There were no differences in demographics, BMI or Diabetes prevalence between groups ( Table 1). Post-stent removal UTI occurred in 15.2% (22/145) of patients in the NO-ABX group and 0% (0/26) in the 72HR-ABX group. Fisher’s exact test demonstrated a statistically significant difference between groups (p=0.028; odds ratio=0, 95% CI 0.00–0.94). CONCLUSIONS: At our institution, post-stent removal UTI rates were lower among patients who received prolonged antibiotic prophylaxis. These preliminary findings suggest a possible benefit of extended antibiotic duration in reducing post-stent infection risk and may help inform evidence-based post–stent removal antibiotic stewardship. | | | --- | | |

title: IP06-13: Stratification and Management of Persistently Positive Urine Cultures in Urological Stone Surgery
parentSessionTitle: IP06: Stone Disease: Surgical Therapy (including ESWL) I
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Standard practice for urological stone surgery involves a single preoperative urine culture with antibiotic treatment if positive. Our enhanced protocol includes re-culturing after treatment. This study evaluates whether this approach is justified by examining the prevalence of persistent positive cultures despite antibiotics, identifying risk factors for persistence, and determining if our protocol improves outcomes or could be optimized through patient risk stratification. METHODS: A retrospective review analyzed 224 patients with positive preoperative urine cultures who underwent urological stone surgery under a single surgeon. All patients received antibiotic treatment with re-culture prior to intervention. Persistent positivity was defined as any growth >10K on subsequent urine culture. Risk factors were assessed using univariate and multivariate logistic regression. Secondary outcomes included immediate and 30-day postoperative sepsis rates. The study findings informed the development of a risk scoring tool to identify patients most likely to benefit from this targeted management approach. RESULTS: Despite antibiotic therapy, 28.6% of patients demonstrated persistent positive cultures. Notably, 65.6% of persistent cases showed an organism shift between initial and re-culture. Significant risk factors in univariate analysis included history of urosepsis (OR=5.01, p=0.0011), multi-drug resistant organisms (MDRO) (OR=4.38, p=0.0029), recurrent urinary tract infections (UTIs) (OR=3.07, p=0.0003), and presence of indwelling devices (OR=2.51, p=0.0028). Multivariate analysis revealed that history of UTIs (OR=2.47) and presence of indwelling devices (OR=1.81) were the only independent predictors that remained significant. The persistent positive and the treated groups demonstrated similar sepsis within 24 hours of surgery (3.13% vs 2.50%) and after 30 days (4.69% vs 3.13%). CONCLUSIONS: The frequent shift in organisms among persistently positive cultures underscores the limited reliability in single preoperative culture to guide therapy. Notably, our stratified management approach maintained comparable sepsis rates despite treating a high-risk cohort, suggesting that risk-based stratification with tailored interventions can effectively mitigate infectious complications in urological stone patients. Further prospective validation of our risk-stratification tool is warranted to confirm the efficacy and to optimize resource utilization across diverse practices settings.

title: IP06-14: Intrarenal antibiotic irrigation during PCNL reduces postoperative infections and eliminates sepsis in high-risk patients: A matched cohort study
parentSessionTitle: IP06: Stone Disease: Surgical Therapy (including ESWL) I
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Despite use of oral and parenteral antibiotics, percutaneous nephrolithotomy (PCNL) may still be complicated by a host of infectious complications: urinary tract infections (UTIs), systemic inflammatory response syndrome (SIRS), and urosepsis. Patients with diabetes mellitus, history of recurrent UTIs, positive preoperative urine cultures, or indwelling urinary devices are especially at risk. We evaluated the impact of intraoperative intrarenal antibiotic augmented irrigation on postoperative infection rates in this high-risk population. METHODS: A retrospective matched cohort study was conducted using a prospectively maintained PCNL database (2020-2024) of over 600 patients. Fifty high-risk cases receiving genitourinary (GU) irrigant (40 mg neomycin base, 200,000 units polymyxin B sulfate per 3 L saline) were matched 1:1 to saline controls ( Table 1). The primary endpoint was 30-day symptomatic UTI; secondary endpoints included SIRS, sepsis, infection-related readmission, infection-related prolonged hospital stay, and emergency department (ED) visits due to UTI. Multivariable logistic regression was performed. RESULTS: At < 30 days postoperative, the fifty patients receiving GU irrigant had fewer postoperative symptomatic UTI events than the control group (6% vs. 34%, p=0.001). Secondary outcomes were almost all more sanguine among the GU irrigant patients: • SIRS criteria: 16% vs. 48% (p=0.001) • Sepsis: 0% vs. 16% (p=0.006) • Infection-related readmission: 6% vs 16% (p=0.200) • Infection related prolonged length of stay: 0% vs. 20% (p=0.001) • ED visits for UTI: 6% vs 16% (p=0.200) In the adjusted complete case model (n=99), GU irrigant remained independently protective against UTI within 30 days (adjusted OR 0.11; 95% CI 0.03–0.44; p=0.002). CONCLUSIONS: Among high-risk PCNL patients, intrarenal neomycin/polymyxin-B irrigation was associated with significantly fewer infectious complications. | | | --- | | | | | | --- | | |

title: IP06-15: Does Doppler Ultrasound Reduce Perioperative Bleeding Compared to B-Mode Ultrasound in Ultrasound-Guided Percutaneous Nephrolithotomy? A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
parentSessionTitle: IP06: Stone Disease: Surgical Therapy (including ESWL) I
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Percutaneous nephrolithotomy (PCNL) remains the gold standard treatment for large renal stones and can be safely guided by ultrasound (US). However, it is associated with significant perioperative bleeding, with transfusion rates ranging from 5-15% in contemporary series. We aimed to conduct a systematic review and meta-analysis to evaluate if the use of Doppler US can reduce bleeding during PCNL compared to B-mode US. METHODS: A systematic review was conducted following Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines, searching Medline, Embase, Scopus, Cochrane Library and Web of Science from inception to September,27 2025, for comparative studies evaluating PCNL guided by B-mode versus Doppler US. Study risk of bias was assessed using the ROBINS-I and RoB-2 ( (https://www.auajournals.org/doi/abs/10.1097/01.JU.0001191292.44613.d7.15#F1)). Primary endpoint was blood transfusion rate (BTR). The protocol was registered on PROSPERO (CRD420251147765). Statistical analysis was performed using Review Manager 5.4.1 (Cochrane Collaboration). RESULTS: Of 3821 studies, 7 met the inclusion criteria comprising 1,993 patients were included, with 49.6% receiving Doppler US PCNL. There was no difference in age, sex and body mass index (BMI) between groups. The mean stone size was 28.9 mm vs 28.5 mm (p=0.55) for Doppler US and B-mode US, respectively. Doppler US significantly reduced BTR (OR 0.24, 95% CI 0.12–0.48, p<0.0001, (https://www.auajournals.org/doi/abs/10.1097/01.JU.0001191292.44613.d7.15#F2)) and hemoglobin decrease (MD -5.01 g/L; 95% CI -8.22, -1.81; p=0.002). Subgroup analyses showed consistent BTR reduction with Doppler US in both randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and non-RCTs ( (https://www.auajournals.org/doi/abs/10.1097/01.JU.0001191292.44613.d7.15#F2)), with similar effect sizes regardless of study design. Furthermore, there was no statistically significant difference in operative time (MD -1.0 min; 95% CI -3.04, 1.04; p=0.34). CONCLUSIONS: In conclusion, Doppler US PCNL has a lower BTR and lower hemoglobin decrease than B-Mode US PCNL with no increased operative time. Therefore, Doppler US PCNL may be a viable strategy to reduce perioperative bleeding in selected patients.

title: IP06-16: Clinical Predictors of Effective Renal Angioembolization After PCNL Procedures
parentSessionTitle: IP06: Stone Disease: Surgical Therapy (including ESWL) I

speakers.organization: Carol Davila University of Medicine and Pharmacy

fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Percutaneous nephrolithotomy (PCNL) is the standard first-line treatment for large renal calculi. Although instrument miniaturization and technical improvements have been achieved, postoperative bleeding remains a significant complication. This study aims to identify predictive factors associated with the success or failure of selective angioembolization following PCNL. METHODS: This prospective study enrolled 51 patients who underwent selective angioembolization for post-PCNL hemorrhage between January 2020 and January 2025. Demographic, clinical, and procedural variables were documented, including age, BMI, stone size and location, puncture site, number of access tracts, comorbidities, and preoperative use of anticoagulant or antiplatelet therapy. Hematologic parameters, such as pre- and postoperative hemoglobin levels, hemoglobin drop, and transfusion requirements, were evaluated. Statistical analysis was performed using IBM SPSS Statistics. The study received institutional ethics committee approval and was conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki. RESULTS: Among the 51 patients included, 13 experienced primary angioembolization failure, stratifying the cohort into two groups: Group I, with successful embolization, and Group II, with recurrent or persistent bleeding requiring reintervention (procedural failure). Patient characteristics, including BMI and comorbidities, showed significant differences only for ischemic heart disease (18.42% in Group I vs. 53.84% in Group II, p=0.034) and preoperative anticoagulant/antiplatelet therapy (21.05% vs. 69.23%). Although stone size did not correlate with outcome, higher failure rates were observed in patients with multiple stones and staghorn calculi (p=0.019). One of the most relevant predictive factors was the number of punctures and dilation tracts created during PCNL, with multiple tracts present in 46.15% of Group II (p=0.006). Intraoperative transfusion did not influence success; however, lower postoperative day 1 hemoglobin levels and increased postoperative transfusion requirements were strong predictors of embolization failure (p=0.0012 and p=0.0009, respectively). Variability in embolic agents used may also have contributed to outcome differences. CONCLUSIONS: Angioembolization is the most effective method for postoperative hemorrhage following PCNL. Medical history, procedural complexity, and postoperative monitoring are critical factors in the prompt detection of embolization failure.

title: IP06-17: Ureteroscopy in Patients Receiving Systemic Anticoagulants: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Safety, Efficacy, and Peri-operative Management
parentSessionTitle: IP06: Stone Disease: Surgical Therapy (including ESWL) I
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: To evaluate the safety and efficacy of ureteroscopy (URS) in patients receiving systemic anticoagulant (AC) therapy, including vitamin K antagonists and direct oral anticoagulants (DOACs), and to compare outcomes with non-AC controls. The PICO framework was used to formulate the research question: In adults undergoing URS for stone disease, does continuation, interruption, or bridging of AC compared with non-anticoagulated or interrupted therapy influence peri-operative bleeding, thromboembolic events, and stone-free rates (SFR)? METHODS: A systematic review of PubMed, Embase, and Scopus identified studies reporting URS outcomes in patients on AC. The review adhered to PRISMA standards and was registered with PROSPERO (CRD420251154766). Data were extracted for peri-operative management strategy, bleeding and thromboembolic events, transfusion requirements, and SFR. Antiplatelet-only cohorts were excluded. Quantitative results were pooled, and comparative data were summarised where available. Risk of bias for non-randomised studies was evaluated independently by two reviewers using the Newcastle–Ottawa Scale (NOS). RESULTS: Eleven studies were included published between 1998 and 2024 with a total of 770 AC patients and 10,099 controls. The pooled rate of clinically significant bleeding ranged from 3% to 15%, with the lowest rates when AC was withheld and the highest when continued through surgery. In comparison, non-AC control groups demonstrated bleeding rates of 1–3% (OR 5.67 (95% CI 1.48-21.7, p=0.011). Transfusion requirements were < 1% overall, and no study reported mortality. Thromboembolic complications were extremely rare—only one deep-vein thrombosis (0.1 %) was identified after temporary interruption. Stone-free rates averaged 88–94%, comparable to non-anticoagulated cohorts. Registry data indicated a modest rise in hospitalisation (4.3% vs 3.2%, p=0.02) among anticoagulated patients but no excess emergency visits (10.1% vs 9.4%, p=0.42) or re-operations. Across studies, outcomes were most favourable when AC was paused pre-operatively without bridging, and when contemporary holmium:YAG laser lithotripsy and controlled irrigation techniques were employed. On NOS assessment, seven studies were of moderate and four of low quality, with primary risks arising from retrospective design and variable bleeding definitions. CONCLUSIONS: URS can be performed safely in patients on AC therapy, though continuation during the peri-operative period increases bleeding risk compared with both interrupted therapy and non-AC controls. Temporary cessation without bridging minimises haemorrhagic and thromboembolic complications while maintaining high SFR. Current evidence supports an individualised, guideline-based approach to peri-operative AC, but larger prospective studies are needed to define optimal management across specific drug classes.

title: IP06-18: POST-OPERATIVE TRAJECTORIES OF PAIN INTERFERENCE AND INTENSITY AFTER URETEROSCOPY FOR NEPHROLITHIASIS IN YOUTH: A PKIDS STUDY
parentSessionTitle: IP06: Stone Disease: Surgical Therapy (including ESWL) I
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Youth with nephrolithiasis frequently undergo ureteroscopy to treat their stones, yet post-operative recovery courses are variable. We assessed the trajectories of pain interference and pain intensity following ureteroscopy and examined clinical predictors of trajectory group membership, hypothesizing that stone size would be significantly associated with trajectory group. METHODS: Participants aged 8-21 years from 31 centers in North America who underwent ureteroscopy between 2020 and 2023 as part of a prospective observational study were included. Outcomes of post-operative pain interference and pain intensity were evaluated at baseline and at weeks 1, 3, and 6 using Patient-Reported Outcomes Measurement Information System questionnaires. Group-based trajectory models were used to identify distinct recovery patterns. Classification trees identified predictors of trajectory group membership. RESULTS: Among 823 participants undergoing ureteroscopy (median age 15.6 years; 65% female), 667 had stents which were removed a median of 5 days post-surgery. Four distinct trajectory groups were identified for each outcome (see Figure). The groups included: High Stable Pain, Gradual Improvement, Rapid Rise and Recovery, and Early Pain with Recovery. For pain interference, the four groups were equally divided among the cohort. For pain intensity, nearly a third of the cohort were in each of the High Stable Pain and Early Pain with Recovery groups. For both pain interference and intensity, significant clinical predictors of group membership were age, baseline pain interference/intensity scores, baseline anxiety, and largest stone size. CONCLUSIONS: We identified distinct recovery trajectories for pain intereference and intensity after ureteroscopy with variable prevalences in our cohort. We also found significant clinical factors associated with group membership for pain interference and intensity. These findings highlight the heterogeneity in recovery and underscore the need for personalized pain management strategies.

title: IP06-19: Widespread pain at non-urologic pain sites is associated with greater stent-associated symptoms after ureteroscopy
parentSessionTitle: IP06: Stone Disease: Surgical Therapy (including ESWL) I
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Most patients undergoing ureteroscopy (URS) for urinary stones receive ureteral stents, which can result in pain and urinary symptoms. Presence of pre-operative chronic pain conditions is associated with worse symptoms. Here we evaluated the association between pre-op pain at non-urologic body sites and post-op stent-associated symptoms (SAS). METHODS: The STENTS cohort is the largest multi-center prospective cohort study evaluating SAS to date. Participants completed a body map marking pain locations pre-operatively. We divided participants into 4 pain location categories: no pain sites, only expected urological pain sites (e. g., left flank pain for left stones), 1-2 non-urologic sites, 3+ non-urologic sites. ANOVA models were used to compare SAS across baseline, post-operative day (POD) 1-9, and 30 days post stent removal. SAS measures of interest included PROMIS pain intensity, pain interference, and urinary symptoms assessed by LURN SI-10. For POD 1-9, repeated measures mixed effects models with clinical site as random effect were used to evaluate the association of pre-operative pain distribution category on each SAS. Covariates included age, sex, depression, chronic pain, and baseline pain intensity. RESULTS: 462 participants were included in the analysis with a mean age of 50 years (SD 17) and 47% females. At baseline, 46% did not report any pain sites, 19% had pain at expected urologic sites only, 22% at 1-2 non-urologic sites, and 13% at 3+ non-urologic sites. SAS varied between baseline pain distribution categories at multiple time points, particularly for the outcomes of pain intensity and pain interference (Fig). Multivariable mixed effects models demonstrated higher SAS with 3+ pain sites at baseline (Table). CONCLUSIONS: Pain at multiple, non-urologic body sites is associated with higher SAS, particularly pain intensity and pain interference. These findings highlight an association between pre-operative complex chronic pain at surgically unrelated sites and post-op SAS.

title: IP06-20: Outcomes of Immediate Versus Delayed Endoscopic Treatment for Pregnancy-Associated Urolithiasis: Prospective Controlled Trial
parentSessionTitle: IP06: Stone Disease: Surgical Therapy (including ESWL) I
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Symptomatic upper urinary tract obstruction during pregnancy often requires urgent intervention. While ureteral stents may bridge patients to postpartum care, definitive ureteroscopy during gestation is increasingly feasible. Evidence comparing these approaches remains limited. METHODS: Single-center randomized prospective trial, 2018–2022; n=119. Patients were assigned to primary antepartum ureteroscopy or serial stenting with postpartum ureteroscopy. Outcomes included stone-free rate, operative parameters, and stent-associated morbidity. RESULTS: Stone-free rates were comparable (96.6% vs 96.7%). Antepartum ureteroscopy demonstrated significantly shorter operative time (median 60 vs 97 minutes, p=0.002). Stent-related morbidity was substantially higher in the delayed-treatment cohort, including encrustation, migration, and reflux pyelonephritis (63% incidence, p<0.001). Overall Clavien-Dindo complication profiles were similar. CONCLUSIONS: Primary ureteroscopy during pregnancy is safe, effective, and minimizes cumulative stent-related morbidity. When feasible, definitive treatment during gestation may optimize clinical outcomes and reduce infectious and mechanical stent complications.

title: IP06-21: The Rate of Repeat Surgical Intervention among Brushite Stone Formers at a Single Institution
parentSessionTitle: IP06: Stone Disease: Surgical Therapy (including ESWL) I
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Brushite (calcium monohydrogen phosphate) stone formers are notorious for requiring high rates of surgical intervention for large stone burdens and stone recurrence even after removal. The actual rate and timing of repeat surgeries has not been reported. We sought to assess the rates of repeat surgical therapy among brushite stone formers at our institution. METHODS: We conducted a retrospective, IRB-approved, single-institution review of all patients with any amount of brushite on stone analysis from January 2014 to June 2024. Patient demographics, medical histories, procedures, lab results, medications, and 24-hour urine chemistries were collected. All percutaneous nephrolithotomy (PCNL) procedures were done in prone split leg position. Ureteroscopy (URS) procedures were performed without the assistance of a suction (sheath or scope). Repeat surgery was defined as a procedure on the same side as the initial surgery >=3 months after the index surgery (or either side in the case of bilateral). Descriptive statistics were generated and Chai squared analysis was used to assess differences in rates of repeat surgery (p<0.05). RESULTS: We identified 119 brushite stone formers (40% male) with a median age of 37 years (IQR 27-53). Median follow-up was 3.9 years (IQR 0.7-8.5). 61 (51.3%) patients reported prior stone removal at another institution. 98 patients (82%) underwent initial stone surgery at our institution: 36 PCNL, 61 URS, and 1 SWL. 40 (41%) patients required a repeat surgery at a median of 22.8 months after the index procedure. After initial PCNL, 12 patients (33%) required 3 PCNL and 9 URS; after initial URS, 28 (46%) patients required 24 URS, and 4 PCNL. There was no difference in repeat surgery rates based on the index procedure (p=0.22). CONCLUSIONS: In light of aggressive initial stone removal, brushite stone formers have high rates (41%) of repeat surgery, with over half occurring within 2 years of the index case. URS was the most utilized salvage procedure. This data provides discrete data for patient counseling on the risk of recurrent surgery and underscores the importance of aggressive stone prevention.

title: IP06-22: Assessing Stone Volume is Valuable for Surgical Planning in Pediatric Urolithiasis
parentSessionTitle: IP06: Stone Disease: Surgical Therapy (including ESWL) I
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Pediatric urolithiasis requires a meticulous approach to selecting the optimal treatment strategy. While guideline-based treatment selection utilizes maximum stone diameter, this linear measurement inadequately reflects the true volume. Volume may more accurately determine stone burden in pediatric patients. This study aims to evaluate the effectiveness of treatment methods for pediatric urolithiasis based on stone volume and to determine its prognostic value on stone-free rate (SFR). METHODS: A retrospective cohort study was conducted on patients aged 1 to 17 years treated for single urinary tract stones at a single center January 2023 to June 2025. Stone volume was calculated using data from non-contrast computed tomography using 3D Slicer software \[Panthier F, et al. World J Urol. 2021\]. Ultrasound-guided Extracorporeal shock wave lithotripsy (ESWL) was used as the first-line treatment for all patients, followed by semirigid or flexible ureteroscopy (URS) for those requiring subsequent intervention. Patients were divided into three volumetric groups: Group I 100 mm3, Group II 101-200 mm3, and Group III 201-370 mm3. The maximum linear size of the stones did not exceed 20 mm. Treatment efficacy was assessed by the SFR 3 months post-procedure on ultrasound. Statistical analysis was performed using SPSS, using Kruskal-Wallis tests to identify group differences, and Spearman's correlation analysis for relationships between variables. RESULTS: The study included 72 patients, 39 (54.2%) boys and 33 (45.8%) girls. There were 37 patients in group I (51.4%), 21 in group II (29.2%), and 14 in group III (19.4%). The overall SFR was 93.1%. Group I achieved a 100% SFR, Group II achieved 90.5%, and Group III achieved 78.6%. Re-interventions (URS) were required for 10 (47.6%) patients in Group II and 8 (57.1%) patients in Group III. We identified a positive correlation between stone volume and the number of repeat surgical interventions (ρ=0.489, p<0.001), as well as between patient age and stone volume (ρ=0.243, p=0.04). The Kruskal-Wallis test showed a statistically highly significant difference in treatment outcomes (single intervention, re-intervention, residual fragments) depending on stone volume across the three groups (H=14.738, p=0.001). CONCLUSIONS: Stone volume is a key predictor of treatment success for pediatric urolithiasis and directly correlates with the need for re-interventions. For stones with a volume up to 100 mm3, ESWL as a first-line treatment demonstrates maximum efficacy. With an increase in stone volume, the likelihood of requiring additional procedures to achieve a stone-free status significantly increases.

title: IP06-23: Predictors of Failure after Endoscopic Management of Iatrogenic Ureteral Strictures
parentSessionTitle: IP06: Stone Disease: Surgical Therapy (including ESWL) I
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Iatrogenic ureteral strictures (IUS) represent a challenging complication of endourological stone treatment, often requiring complex reinterventions with high failure rates. This study aimed to identify risk factors associated with treatment failure after endoscopic management of IUS. METHODS: This retrospective multicenter study included adult patients who underwent endoscopic treatment for IUS following prior ureteroscopic management of urolithiasis. Failure was defined as the need or reintervention after primary IUS treatment. Potential predictors were grouped into: baseline patient characteristics, features of the initial stone procedure, and stricture and treatment-related characteristics. Univariate logistic regression was performed to identify variables associated with failure(p<0.15). Statistically and clinically relevant variables were included in a multivariate Firth logistic regression model to adjust for small-sample bias. Effect sizes were reported as odds ratios (OR) with 95% confidence intervals (CI); p<0.05 was considered statistically significant. RESULTS: Of 101 patients, 63 (62%) had successful outcomes and 38 (38%) required reintervention. Descriptive characteristics are summarized in Table 1. Treatment approaches included balloon dilation alone (n=43), laser endoureterotomy alone (n=31),combined laser + balloon (n=21), and ureteral dilators (n=6). At univariate analysis, only three variables met criteria for multivariate modeling: residual stone fragments at the stricture site, proximal IUS location, and the use of balloon dilation alone (compared to combined laser and balloon treatment).In the multivariate model, residual fragments (OR 7.41; 95% CI 2.25–26.3; p=0.001) and balloon dilation alone (OR 3.70; 95% CI 1.10–13.9; p=0.041) were independently associated with failure. Proximal IUS location showed a trend toward significance (OR2.50; 95% CI 0.90–7.10; p=0.074). CONCLUSIONS: Endoscopic treatment of IUS results in a considerable failure rate (38%). The presence of residual fragments from previous lithotripsy and the exclusive use of balloon dilation, when compared to combined laser and balloon approaches, emerged as independent predictors of recurrence. Proximal IUS may also carry a higher risk of failure. Prospective studies are warranted to refine risk stratification and treatment strategies. | | | --- | | |

title: IP06-25: Postoperative Complications Following Flexible Ureteroscopy. An Institutional Series of 1,389 Cases
parentSessionTitle: IP06: Stone Disease: Surgical Therapy (including ESWL) I
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: This study aimed to evaluate the incidence of postoperative complications (PCs) following flexible ureteroscopy (RIRS) for stone treatment in an unselected Institutional series. METHODS: We analyzed data from our prospectively maintained RIRS for stone treatment institutional database (June 2014 to December 2024). The primary outcome was the overall incidence of PCs, classified according to the modified Clavien-Dindo system for RIRS, within 90 days from the intervention. The secondary outcome was the identification of factors associated with PCs. Descriptive statistics were performed to assess associations between clinical variables and PCs. RESULTS: A total of 1,389 RIRS procedures were included. Most patients were male (61%, 847/1,389), with a mean age of 56 ± 14 years and a mean BMI of 26 ± 5. The mean stone size was 11.9 ± 5.5 mm. Almost half of the patients had multiple stones (42.7%, 593/1,389). Preoperative urine culture was positive in 18.3% (254/1,389), and a preoperative stent was present in 38.3% (532/1,389). The mean operative time was 69.4 ± 30 minutes. Overall, PCs occurred in 11.5% of cases (160/1,389). Minor complications (Clavien grade I–II, mainly fever and urinary tract infection) occurred in 6.7% (93/1,389), while Clavien grade III complications occurred in 4.0% (56/1,389), mainly due to urgent stent placement (for stent dislodgment or renal colic). Clavien grade IVb complications (urosepsis) were rare, occurring in 0.6% (8/1,389). Three patients (0.2%) died within 90 days after the procedure (Clavien grade V). One of these patients died due to septic shock, while two patients died of myocardial infarction after being discharged. When comparing patients with and without complications, the rate of PCs was significantly higher in patients with stones >10 mm (16.9% vs. 11.3%, p=0.01) and was associated with a lower stone-free rate (62.5% vs. 72.7%, p=0.02). Other characteristics — such as sex, diabetes mellitus, ASA score, positive preoperative urine culture, and multiple stones — did not reach statistical significance when comparing patients with and without complications. CONCLUSIONS: In this large Institutional cohort, postoperative complications following RIRS occurred in about 1 in 10 patients, with the majority being minor and self-limiting. Patients with postoperative complications had significantly larger stone size and worse SFR. These data underline the importance of proper patient selection and preoperative risk assessment.

title: IP06-26: Construction and Validation of an Omics-Guided Drug-Coated Ureteral Stent for Targeted Therapy of Ureteral Stricture
parentSessionTitle: IP06: Stone Disease: Surgical Therapy (including ESWL) I
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Ureteral stricture represents a challenging urological condition that often leads to hydronephrosis and renal function impairment. While drug-eluting stents have been proposed as a solution, existing approaches often rely on empiric selection of antiproliferative agents, lacking precision tailored to the specific molecular signature of ureteral strictures. This strategy may pose risks of off-target effects. Consequently, there is a pressing need to develop a novel, targeted therapeutic strategy grounded in a deep understanding of the disease's molecular mechanisms. METHODS: RNA sequencing was performed on stricture tissue samples from 5 patients with ureteral strictures and 5 normal tissues. The LINCS L1000 database was queried with the disease-specific gene signature to identify potential therapeutic compounds. KEGG pathway enrichment analysis confirmed the critical role of the JAK-STAT pathway. A novel dual-layer coaxial stent was developed. The core therapeutic layer was fabricated by conjugating the identified small-molecule drug, thalidomide, to form a stable PLGA-TK-PEI matrix. The outer layer was coated with pDNA encoding STAT3-specific shRNA via classical adsorption. A rabbit model of ureteral stricture was employed for in vivo validation. Hydronephrosis was monitored by ultrasound, and harvested ureteral tissues were analyzed by histology and RNA-seq to evaluate fibrotic progression and pathway modulation. RESULTS: Transcriptomic analysis revealed significant activation of the JAK-STAT signaling pathway. LINCS database screening thalidomide as a candidate capable of reversing the disease signature. Given STAT3's pivotal role, we supplemented the approach with STAT3 shRNA for targeted inhibition. Histological assessments demonstrated that the stent exhibited a reduction in ureteral fibrosis. RNA-seq analysis of rabbit tissues confirmed the therapeutic mechanism, which was consistent with the initial findings from human patient samples. CONCLUSIONS: In conclusion, this study successfully demonstrates a translational "omics-to-therapy" pipeline. By integrating patient-derived transcriptomic data with bioinformatic drug discovery, we rationally developed a novel coaxial stent for the synergistic delivery of thalidomide and STAT3 shRNA. This targeted strategy effectively mitigated ureteral fibrosis and hydronephrosis in preclinical models by specifically inhibiting the JAK-STAT pathway, offering a promising and precise therapeutic approach for preventing ureteral stricture recurrence.

title: IP06-27: Association of stent-associated symptoms with acceptability of future stent placement: Results from STENTS
parentSessionTitle: IP06: Stone Disease: Surgical Therapy (including ESWL) I

speakers.organization: University of Washington Department of Urology

fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: The STudy to Enhance uNderstanding of sTent associated Symptoms sought to better understand stent associated symptoms (SAS) in patients who had ureteral stents placed after ureteroscopy (URS) for urinary stones. This study analyzes the association between postoperative pain intensity, pain interference, and urinary symptoms with patient acceptability of future stent placement. METHODS: This prospective, observational cohort study included those undergoing URS with stent placement for stone treatment across 4 centers. Participants completed SAS surveys on post-op day 1 and 3, and at time of stent removal they completed the ureteral stent symptom questionnaire which included a “global question” assessing their attitude towards future stent placement. Multivariable ordinal logistic regression including patient characteristics and SAS was used to examine the association of post-op pain intensity, pain interference and urinary symptoms with patient acceptability of future stent placement. RESULTS: 424 participants (mean age 49.5 ± 16.9 years, 46% female) were included. Global question scores are shown in the Figure. Greater pain intensity, pain interference, and urinary symptoms were all associated with decreased acceptability of future stent placement ( Table). Younger age was associated with decreased acceptability in all models. When urinary symptoms were adjusted for, female sex was associated with decreased acceptability of future stent. CONCLUSIONS: In patients with ureteral stent placement after URS for urinary stone disease, greater pain intensity, pain interference and urinary symptoms during the immediate post-operative period were all associated with decreased acceptability of future stent placement.

title: IP06-28: PIGTAIL SUTURE STENT VS CONVENTIONAL DOUBLE J STENT – A RANDOMIZED, SINGLE-BLIND, PROSPECTIVE CLINICAL TRIAL
parentSessionTitle: IP06: Stone Disease: Surgical Therapy (including ESWL) I

speakers.organization: Hospital das Clinicas da Faculdade de Medicina da Universidade de São Paulo (HC-FMUSP)

fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Double J (DJ) stents are a valuable tool after ureteroscopy. However, they are associated with significant morbidity, symptoms and decline in quality-of-life (QoL). Despite advancements in design and materials, these issues remain.
