fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Male urethral sling failure is commonly managed with salvage artificial urinary sphincter (AUS). Our objectives were to characterize sling-to-AUS transitions, define patient- and institutional-level contributors, and compare outcomes of primary versus salvage AUS. METHODS: We analyzed longitudinal ambulatory surgery records from California’s Department of Health Care Access and Information (2007–2016). Adult male California residents who underwent index AUS or sling placement were identified. Annual AUS and sling caseloads were aggregated per facility and dichotomized at the median: low (1–8) vs high (≥9). AUS-to-sling caseload ratio was to characterize centers: sling-dominant (≤0.5) or none (>0.5). A multivariable Cox proportional hazards model was used to identify factors associated with salvage AUS placement among sling patients. Another univariable model compared the long-term AUS failure risk in salvage versus primary AUS recipients. RESULTS: The 1,400 sling patients had a median follow-up of 2.9 years (IQR 1.3–5.2). 17% of sling surgeries were performed at centers with high sling volume. Sling recipients traveled a median of 17 km (IQR 8.2–34) for surgery, and 22% underwent insertion at their closest facility. By eight years, 20% (95% CI 17%–25%) of sling recipients required salvage AUS. In the multivariable model, a facility’s higher AUS-to-sling ratio (aHR 1.57, 95% CI 1.11–2.23) and greater patient travel distance (aHR 1.14 per 50 km, 95% CI 1.02–1.27) were associated with increased likelihood of salvage AUS placement. Conversely, high sling volume at the index center was linked to reduced risk (aHR 0.59, 95% CI 0.36–0.94). Salvage AUS showed durability comparable to that of primary AUS (HR 0.79, 95% CI 0.55–1.13). CONCLUSIONS: One in five sling recipients ultimately required salvage AUS. Salvage AUS had a similar success rate to that of primary AUS. Institutional experience and geographic access influence reoperation trajectories, underscoring the importance of careful patient selection and counseling.

title: IP09-04: SUSTeR study : Sub-Urethral Sling Treatment Removal, a retrospective multicentric cohort about mid and long term midurethral sling complications between 2010-2024 : Symptomatic recovery is it possible ?
parentSessionTitle: IP09: Urodynamics/Lower Urinary Tract Dysfunction/Female Pelvic Medicine: Male Incontinence

speakers.organization: Service de transplantation d'organes et d'urologie, Centre Hospitaler universitaire de Toulouse

fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Patients who a synthetic mid-urethral sling (MUS) may develop complications. Symptoms may include pain, bladder emptying problems, exposure, bladder overactivity (OAB) and even recurrence of stress urinary incontinence (SUI). These complications may necessitate a removal, a challenging surgery. The SUSTER study is a French multicentric study of synthetic MUS removals in women for medium and long term complications, focusing on the post-operative symptomatic evolution. METHODS: A retrospective study named was conducted in 11 specialised centers. Recent ICS 2024 terminology about MUS removal was used. Adult women which underwent MUS removal between 2010 and 2024 were included. Were excluded patients with neuro-baldder damage, pelvic radiotherapy, vaginal mesh implantation for prolapse. Statistical analysis was performed using R version 4.5. RESULTS: 551 patients were included for 705 screened. The average age at removal was 59,9 years. MUS were implanted for pure SUI in 64,3 %. Removals were total in 18,6 %, 63,2 % partial. TOT removed were for 63,1 %. Main symptoms leading to removal are presented in (https://www.auajournals.org/doi/abs/10.1097/01.JU.0001191316.72449.22.04#F1). Removals were made for exposure in 51,5 % and for functionnal causes in 49,5 %. It exists different causes for removal distinguising MUS type. Before removal pain was found in 49,3 %. At early postoperative visit only 20,7 % had pain (p<0,05 vs before) with 62,3 % of painful paintents cured. Different pain locations weren't even cured at the same rate. Total removal significativly improved pain cure rate in TOT. 36,1 % and 7,4 % had dysuria befrore and after removal. OAB or urge urinary incontinence were improved only if it was symptom leading to removal. Symptoms were stable at late visit. Finaly leading to removal symptom were persistant in 36,4 % at early visit and 39,5 % at late. Only 23,4 % were totaly asymptomatic (no pain/dysuria/SUI or OAB/UUI) at early and 27,4 % at late visit. TVT were less symptomatic than TOT (68,8% vs 79,4% p<0,05). Post removal SUI rate was 60,5 %, treated in 45,8 %, efficacy in 68,8 %. CONCLUSIONS: Removal in MUS complications shows significant improvement in pain and dysuria. However, some patients remain symptomatic after MUS removal and require follow-up. SUI is the main symptom after MUS removal but surgical treatments seems to be effective.

title: IP09-05: Evolving Trends and Perioperative Outcomes of Surgical Treatment for Male Stress Urinary Incontinence: Results from the GRAND study register
parentSessionTitle: IP09: Urodynamics/Lower Urinary Tract Dysfunction/Female Pelvic Medicine: Male Incontinence
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: We aimed to assess the perioperative outcomes and trends of artificial urinary sphincter (AUS), and adjustable or non-adjustable slings for male stress urinary incontinence (SUI). METHODS: We used the GeRmAn Nationwide inpatient Data (GRAND), provided by the Research Data Center of the Federal Bureau of Statistics (2005-2023). We assessed, through multiple patient-level analyses, the perioperative morbidity and mortality, as well as the length of hospital stay of surgical management for SUI during the last years in Germany. RESULTS: Overall, 24,234 men underwent surgery for SUI in Germany: 15,271 (63%) received an AUS, 7,819 (32%) a non-adjustable sling, and 1,144 (5%) an adjustable sling. Among AUS patients, 77% received a one-cuff device. While AUS remained the most common option, implantation rates for AUS and non-adjustable slings declined, whereas adjustable sling use increased. Procedures decreased substantially during the COVID-19 pandemic. Perioperative mortality was <0.1% across groups. Compared to AUS, non-adjustable slings had higher urinary retention risk (12% vs. 11%, OR 1.1, 95% CI 1.02–1.21, p=0.02) but lower wound infection risk (0.7% vs. 1.4%, OR 0.5, 95% CI 0.4–0.7, p<0.001). Median hospital stay was 6 days (AUS) versus 5 days (slings). The multivariate analyses showed shorter hospital stay with non-adjustable (–2.1 days, p<0.001) and adjustable slings (–0.98 days, p<0.001). Two-cuff AUS carried higher retention rates (12% vs. 10%, OR 1.13, p=0.04) and longer hospitalization (+0.6 days, p<0.001). In total, 5,700 AUS and 1,435 sling explanations were performed, mainly due to infection or mechanical failure. CONCLUSIONS: Male SUI surgery is safe, with AUS remaining the gold standard in Germany. Adjustable slings represent an expanding option for selected patients.

title: IP09-06: Barriers to Post-Prostatectomy Stress Incontinence Care: Knowledge Gaps, Patient Concerns, and Urologist Communication
parentSessionTitle: IP09: Urodynamics/Lower Urinary Tract Dysfunction/Female Pelvic Medicine: Male Incontinence
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Stress urinary incontinence following radical prostatectomy (RP) significantly impairs quality of life. Studies indicate a gap in care. The aim of this study was to assess the level of knowledge regarding available aids and treatment options. METHODS: We analysed follow-up data from the multicentre prospective HAROW study and a single-centre cross-sectional study conducted in Dresden. Patients who underwent RP with the daily use of ≥ 2 pads were included. The survey asked patients about their knowledge of incontinence surgery, aids, information behaviour and barriers to treatment. RESULTS: In total, 99 patients were surveyed (HAROW: 62; Dresden: 37). The median age at the time of RP was 67 years (47–85), with a median postoperative interval of 11 years (0–15). Continuous urinary leakage was reported by 70% (68/97) of the patients. 53% (51/96) used more than three pads per day. The mean quality of life score was 4.7 ± 1.4 (EORTC-C30 QoL). Pads were the primary aid used by 91% (86/96) of the patients. Condom catheters (5%, 4/85) or penile clamps (1%, 1/84) were rarely used; 86% (32/37) were unaware of these options. 62% (55/89) had no knowledge of surgical treatment options (Tab.1). Younger age (p=0.002) and fewer pads used (p=0.04) were associated with better awareness of surgical treatment options. Information about incontinence was most frequently provided by urologists (88%, 85/96), followed by partners (59%, 52/88) and hospital staff (53%, 46/86). The three most common reasons for not pursuing further treatment were adequate coping with continence aids (69%, 62/90), doubts about the effectiveness of surgery (55%, 49/90) and fear of health-related risks (44%, 46/91) (Fig.1). CONCLUSIONS: These findings reveal substantial knowledge gaps regarding continence aids and surgical treatment options among men with stress urinary incontinence after receiving prostatectomy. In addition to limited knowledge, fear-related concerns hinder treatment uptake. More targeted patient education may improve therapy utilization and enhance quality of life.

title: IP09-07: Adjustable-Transobturator-Male-System (ATOMS) After Radiotherapy and Prostatectomy: Success Rates and Challenges in Postoperative Incontinence Treatment
parentSessionTitle: IP09: Urodynamics/Lower Urinary Tract Dysfunction/Female Pelvic Medicine: Male Incontinence
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Postoperative male stress urinary incontinence is a major adverse effect following radical prostatectomy, leading to a significant reduction in quality of life. Adjustable male slings, such as the ATOMS sling, provide a potential solution to address this issue. Previous studies have shown a reduction in incontinence rates with sling use; however, data are limited regarding outcomes in patients who have undergone both radical prostatectomy and radiotherapy. This study seeks to investigate the impact of radiotherapy on postoperative outcomes following ATOMS implantation. METHODS: Patients who underwent ATOMS implantation between November 2018 and May 2024 were included in this study. Eligibility was restricted to patients post-radical prostatectomy, excluding those with prior desobstructive surgery. Clinical parameters, including preoperative pad usage and results from a 24-hour pad test, were assessed both pre- and postoperatively. Additional details regarding the ATOMS implantation procedure were collected, including initial fill volume, time to first adjustment, and the frequency and volume of adjustments. Statistical analysis was performed using Chi-squared and Mann-Whitney U tests. RESULTS: A total of 117 patients who received ATOMS implantation were included. Among them, 63% underwent conventional radical prostatectomy, while 37% underwent robotic-assisted radical prostatectomy; 42% of patients received radiotherapy either before or after their prostatectomy. Notably, patients without a history of radiotherapy used significantly more pads preoperatively (5 vs. 4, p=0.015). Radiotherapy-experienced patients had a significantly higher incidence of urinary retention (0 vs. 4 cases, p=0.029) and need for explantation of the ATOMS (1 vs. 3 cases, p=0.043). Complete continence (defined as 0 pads/day) was achieved significantly less often in radiotherapy patients compared to those without radiotherapy (24.5% vs. 52.9%, p=0.002). Adjustments were more frequently required in patients who had not undergone radiotherapy (51.5% vs. 59.2%, p=0.032). No significant differences were observed between the two groups for postoperative voiding symptoms or wound healing complications. CONCLUSIONS: This study indicates that patients receiving ATOMS implantation after both radical prostatectomy and radiotherapy may have a reduced likelihood of achieving full continence postoperatively and an increased risk of urinary retention. However, ATOMS implantation appears to be a viable and safe option in terms of postoperative voiding function and wound healing. Therefore, ATOMS implantation can be recommended to post-radiotherapy patients with appropriate preoperative counseling.

title: IP09-08: Paraurethral Balloon Placement is an Effective Salvage Technique For Male Stress Incontinence After Sling Failure
parentSessionTitle: IP09: Urodynamics/Lower Urinary Tract Dysfunction/Female Pelvic Medicine: Male Incontinence

speakers.organization: Division of Urology, University of Colorado Anschutz Medical Campus

fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Male stress urinary incontinence (SUI) affects up to 60% of men after prostate surgery. Adjustable paraurethral balloons (PUBs), specifically the ProACT™ system, are a minimally invasive, adjustable option for SUI. However, outcomes following a failed male sling, particularly in patients with a history of pelvic radiation, are limited. Here, we describe our institutional experience with ProACT™ following sling failure to assess continence outcomes, complications, and predictors of success. METHODS: A retrospective review was conducted on 34 men with prior male sling failure who underwent PUB placement between 2021-25 at a single institution. Demographic data, previous interventions (e. g., prior AUS, urethroplasty, radiation), perioperative details, and complications were collected. Treatment success was defined as either "cured" (0-1 pads per day \[PPD\] or <50 g pad weight) or "improved" (≥50% reduction in PPD or 24-hour pad weights). Fisher's exact test was used to identify predictors of outcomes. RESULTS: The median preoperative pad usage was 4 PPD (range 1-10). Of the 34 patients, 41% (n=14) had prior pelvic radiation, 12% (n=4) had prior AUS (3 explanted), and 6% (n=2) had prior urethroplasty. Among 25 patients with > 3 months of follow-up (median 6.4 months), the overall treatment success rate was 72% (n=18): 15 were cured and 3 were improved. Patients without prior radiation were significantly more likely to be cured (93% vs 10%, p<0.001) and achieve treatment success (93% vs 40%, p<0.01). The overall complication rate was 12% (4/34). There was only one Clavien-Dindo grade IIIa or greater complication: a urethral erosion requiring device explant. Notably, 36% (n=9) of patients required device revision after initial placement. CONCLUSIONS: To our knowledge, this is the largest reported series of patients undergoing ProACT™ after male sling. Despite a complex cohort with a high prevalence of prior radiation, AUS, and urethroplasty, the achieved treatment success rate of 72% is comparable to published outcomes for patients without prior continence interventions. These findings support ProACT™ PUB as a safe and effective option for men with SUI following sling failure, although success is significantly reduced in the setting of prior pelvic radiation. | | | --- | | |

title: IP09-10: Closing the Gap in Post-Prostatectomy Incontinence Care: A Single-Center Analysis of Patient-Reported Outcomes
parentSessionTitle: IP09: Urodynamics/Lower Urinary Tract Dysfunction/Female Pelvic Medicine: Male Incontinence

speakers.organization: Corewell Health William Beaumont University Hospital

fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Stress urinary incontinence (SUI) is a common and distressing condition affecting men after prostatectomy, with reported rates of 10–22% at one year after surgery. AUA Guidelines recommend pelvic floor physical therapy (PFPT) and permit surgical intervention as early as six months post-prostatectomy if bothersome SUI persists. Despite this, only 3–5% of patients undergo surgery. This study evaluated the prevalence and severity of post-prostatectomy urinary leakage using patient-reported surveys and examined the relationship between urinary incontinence severity and treatment received. METHODS: A retrospective review was conducted of post-prostatectomy patients enrolled in the Michigan Urological Surgery Improvement Collaborative (MUSIC) database at a single institution from June 2015–May 2024. Inclusion criteria were men ≥18 years with prostate cancer who underwent radical prostatectomy and completed at least one post-operative MUSIC/EPIC-26 survey. Demographics, comorbidities, PFPT completion, and surgical interventions for SUI were extracted from the EMR. Patients were classified as continent or incontinent based on EPIC-26 urinary domain scores. Statistical analyses compared outcomes between these groups. RESULTS: We reviewed 325 patients (mean age at prostatectomy 64.3, mean BMI 31.4) with a median follow-up survey at 23 months postop. Overall, 244 patients (75%) reported some degree of urinary leakage: 121 (37%) had worsening or de novo leakage, 78 (24%) transient, resolving leakage, and 45 (14%) pre-existing leakage that persisted postoperatively. Fifty-five (17%) reported no leakage. The EPIC-26 urinary continence score averaged 49 in patients with persistent/worsening leakage versus 91 in those with resolved/no leakage (p<0.001). PFPT was performed by 30% of patients with persistent/worsening leakage compared to 13% with resolved/no leakage (p<0.001). Only eight patients (2.5%) underwent surgical management (5 artificial urinary sphincters, 2 male slings, 1 both), with a median interval of 712 days from prostatectomy to surgery (range 230-1650 days). CONCLUSIONS: Post-prostatectomy incontinence remains under-recognized and undertreated. Patient-reported EPIC-26 survey data reveal higher rates of persistent or worsening urinary leakage than previously reported. Despite guideline-supported options, few patients pursue surgical intervention. Greater patient and provider education is needed to promote timely and proactive management of post-prostatectomy stress and urge incontinence.

title: IP09-11: Artificial Urinary Sphincter in Men Aged 75 Years and Older: Is It Worth Implanting? A Single-Center Experience
parentSessionTitle: IP09: Urodynamics/Lower Urinary Tract Dysfunction/Female Pelvic Medicine: Male Incontinence
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Stress urinary incontinence (SUI) following prostate surgery significantly impairs quality of life in elderly men. While the artificial urinary sphincter (AUS) remains the gold standard for treatment, its safety and efficacy in older patients, particularly those aged 75 and older, remains questionable due to potential age-related surgical risks and comorbidities. METHODS: A retrospective review was conducted on 50 male patients aged ≥75 years who underwent AUS implantationbetween March 2012 and October 2023 at a high-volume tertiary center, with follow-up data collected through February 2024. Collected variables included demographic characteristics, history of pelvic radiotherapy, continence outcomes, perioperative complications, and the need for revision or explantation. Continence status was categorized as dry, social continence (≤1 pad/day) or significant incontinence (≥2 pads/day).Patients were stratified by age group and history of radiotherapy, and outcomes were compared accordingly. Statistical analyses were performed using chi-square tests, with significance defined as p<0.05. RESULTS: The study cohort included patients aged 75–79 years (n=39) and patients aged ≥80 years (n=11). At a mean follow-up of 3.1 years, continence outcomes were excellent, with 88% of patients achieving complete continence or requiring ≤1 pad per day. Only one patient had a perioperative complication with a cuff erosion and removal one month postoperatively. Repeat surgery was required in a further 7 patients after the perioperative period. Four revisions were performed for cuff erosion, two for device infection, and one for revision of the cuff due to persistent leakage. Patients with a history of pelvic radiotherapy had higher rates of revision surgery (17.8%) compared with non-radiated patients (13.6%), although this difference was not statistically significant (OR 1.43, 95% CI 0.30–6.38; p=0.647). Similarly, older age was not associated with a higher risk of complications (OR 1.18, 95% CI 0.20–6.90; p=0.85). Continence outcomes were comparable between patients with and without prior radiotherapy (13.6% vs 10.7%; OR 0.79, 95% CI 0.14–4.37; p=0.789). Age also had no significant effect on continence outcomes, with rates of significant incontinence of 12.8% among patients <80 years and 9% among those ≥80 years (OR 0.66, 95% CI 0.06–6.32; p=0.719). CONCLUSIONS: Artificial urinary sphincter (AUS) implantation in men aged ≥75 years is safe and effective, yielding favorable continence outcomes and a low rate of reoperation. Among this elderly cohort, neither advanced age nor a history of pelvic radiotherapy meaningfully increased the risk of AUS-related complications, revision surgery, or poorer continence results. AUS remains a reliable and effective treatment option for appropriately selected older patients.

title: IP09-12: Efficacy and Patient Satisfaction with Combined Inflatable Penile Prosthesis and Mini-Jupette Sling in Men with Erectile Dysfunction and Climacturia Following Pelvic Surgery: Institutional Experience
parentSessionTitle: IP09: Urodynamics/Lower Urinary Tract Dysfunction/Female Pelvic Medicine: Male Incontinence
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Climacturia and arousal incontinence are bothersome sequelae of pelvic surgery that significantly impact quality of life. The Mini-Jupette sling, originally developed to address climacturia in men undergoing inflatable penile prosthesis (IPP) placement, has also been observed to improve stress urinary incontinence (SUI) in select cases. This study evaluates functional outcomes, continence improvement, and patient satisfaction following simultaneous IPP and Mini-Jupette sling placement in men with erectile dysfunction (ED) after pelvic procedures. METHODS: We retrospectively reviewed men with ED and climacturia who underwent concurrent IPP and Mini-Jupette sling placement between December 2023 and May 2025 at a tertiary center. Data collected included demographics, baseline pre- and postoperative continence status, characterized by pad use per day (drops, moist, or soaking), climacturia resolution, residual leakage pattern, complications, need for secondary continence surgery, and patient-reported satisfaction. RESULTS: Twenty-nine men met inclusion criteria. Preoperatively, all had climacturia; 11 reported arousal incontinence, and 24 had coexisting SUI. At a mean follow-up of 9 months, 26 men (90%) reported resolution of climacturia, and 14 (48%) achieved complete continence. In men with SUI, mean pad use decreased from 2.2 to 0.9 pads per day. Among patients with persistent SUI, 53% experienced improvement in severity (e. g., soaking to moist or moist to drops), and only one continued to report soaking-level incontinence. Three men (10%) required additional continence procedures. Overall, 72% of patients were satisfied or highly satisfied with their outcomes. No device-related or sling complications were observed. CONCLUSIONS: Simultaneous IPP and Mini-Jupette sling placement is a safe and efficient approach for men with ED and climacturia following pelvic surgery. Although not designed for SUI, the Mini-Jupette demonstrated meaningful improvement in mild-to-moderate SUI severity and high patient satisfaction. Further prospective studies are warranted to refine patient selection and quantify objective continence outcomes.

title: IP09-13: Challenges and Outcomes of Artificial Urinary Sphincter Management in the Setting of Bladder Cancer
parentSessionTitle: IP09: Urodynamics/Lower Urinary Tract Dysfunction/Female Pelvic Medicine: Male Incontinence
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: The artificial urinary sphincter (AUS) is the gold standard for the treatment of severe stress urinary incontinence. However, the long-term durability of AUS in patients with bladder cancer has not been well characterized. Surveillance and treatment modalities for bladder cancer—including cystoscopies, biopsies, resections, and intravesical therapies—may adversely affect device longevity and complication risk. Characterizing AUS outcomes in this population is critical to guide patient counseling and surgical decision-making. METHODS: We conducted a retrospective review of our institutional AUS database to identify patients with a history of bladder cancer who underwent AUS implantation from 1986 to the present. Clinical records were reviewed to capture demographics, oncologic treatments, and device-related outcomes. RESULTS: A total of 2,215 patients underwent AUS implantation at our institution during the study period. A total of 32 patients had a history of bladder cancer. Thirteen (41%) were diagnosed prior to AUS placement, and nineteen (59%) were diagnosed after implantation, with a median interval of 3.7 years (IQR 2.7–9.2). Median follow-up was 4.9 years (IQR 0.1 to 8.2). Fourteen patients (44%) required AUS revision, and five (36%) underwent multiple re-interventions. Among the 20 revision procedures, indications included urethral atrophy (n=8, 40%), erosion (n=8, 40%), and mechanical failure (n=4, 20%). Patients requiring revision had undergone significantly more prior transurethral procedures than those without revision (median 14 vs. 8, p=0.03). Two patients (11%) ultimately underwent cystectomy. CONCLUSIONS: Bladder cancer patients with AUS represent a high-risk population for device revision, particularly in the setting of frequent transurethral instrumentation. In this single-institution series, revision was most commonly performed for urethral atrophy and erosion. The number of transurethral procedures was significantly associated with re-intervention risk. These findings suggest that bladder cancer surveillance and treatment may adversely affect AUS outcomes. Larger studies are warranted to further define this relationship.

title: IP09-14: Changing the Paradigm of Artificial Urinary Sphincter Revision
parentSessionTitle: IP09: Urodynamics/Lower Urinary Tract Dysfunction/Female Pelvic Medicine: Male Incontinence
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: The artificial urinary sphincter (AUS) remains the gold standard for managing stress urinary incontinence in men. While AUS devices show high efficacy and patient satisfaction, reoperation for mechanical or non-mechanical failure remains a long-term issue, affecting nearly 50% of patients by ten years. Traditionally, AUS revision surgery requires complete device explantation and replacement—including the urethral cuff, pressure-regulating balloon (PRB), and pump. Our institution previously reported that most mechanical failures involve the cuff (46.1%) or PRB (22.6%), while the pump failed in only two cases. Pump removal increases pain and the risk of scrotal complications such as hematoma or infection. We therefore evaluated AUS revision outcomes when the original pump was preserved. METHODS: This prospective analysis includes AUS revisions for mechanical or non-mechanical failure performed at a single institution from 2023 to present. Following IRB approval, data on demographics and intraoperative findings were collected. RESULTS: Forty-nine AUS revisions were analyzed. Median time from primary surgery to revision was 8.1 years (IQR 4.1–13). Most failures (66.7%) were due to cuff leak. The existing AUS pump was preserved in all cases. Median operative time was 42 minutes (IQR 33–48). All procedures were outpatient. Devices were reactivated after 2 weeks (vs. 6 weeks for total replacement). Since no pump replacement was performed, no pump-related complications (hematoma, pain, malposition) occurred. To date, no device failures or reoperations have been noted due to pump malfunction. CONCLUSIONS: Most AUS revisions replace the entire device, yet our findings confirm failures mainly originate from the cuff or PRB, not the pump. Review of our institutional database (>3,500 AUS procedures) revealed only two true pump failures. While longer-term follow-up is needed, this “preserve the pump” approach may reduce recovery time, minimize morbidity from scrotal exploration, and decrease costs by avoiding unnecessary pump replacement.

title: IP09-15: Decisional Regret and Quality of Life After Artificial Urinary Sphincter Implantation Following Radical Prostatectomy
parentSessionTitle: IP09: Urodynamics/Lower Urinary Tract Dysfunction/Female Pelvic Medicine: Male Incontinence

speakers.organization: HelseBergen Urological Department Haukeland University Hospital

fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: The artificial urinary sphincter (AUS) remains the gold-standard treatment for stress urinary incontinence (SUI) following radical prostatectomy (RP). While long-term continence outcomes are well established, decisional regret has been less well studied. The aim of this study was to evaluate decisional regret, quality of life, and symptom burden in men with an AUS METHODS: In this ethically approved study, all men who underwent AUS implantation after RP at a tertiary center between 2012–2023 were identified and contacted by post. Participants completed the EPIC-26, Decisional Regret Scale (DRS), and Hospital Anxiety and Depression Scale (HADS). The overall response rate was 87.5% (n=91), with a median follow-up of 82 months (IQR 49–100). RESULTS: The median age at surgery was 69 years (IQR 65–72). Prior radiotherapy was reported in 34% and reoperation in 25% of patients. Severe baseline incontinence (>400 g/24 hr) was present in 63.7% of men, with a median pad count of 5/day. Pad use improved significantly postoperatively (93.8% using ≥3 pads/day preoperatively vs. 60.8% pad-free postoperatively; p<0.001), but deteriorated over time (pad-free 16.5% at follow-up; p<0.001), though remained better than baseline. Overall, 35% of respondents reported no regret, 34% mild regret, 30% moderate regret, and 1.3% severe regret. Reoperation was the only independent predictor of higher decisional regret (+18 DRS points; 95% CI 7.2–28.8; p=0.001). Better urinary continence correlated with lower anxiety (ρ=–0.259, p=0.019) and depression (ρ=–0.359, p<0.001), while greater pad use was associated with higher depression (ρ=+0.289, p=0.007). Bowel and hormonal EPIC-26 domains were also negatively correlated with anxiety and depression (all p<0.001). CONCLUSIONS: AUS implantation provides durable improvement in continence and psychological wellbeing for men with post-RP SUI, though function may decline over time. Reoperation is the principal driver of decisional regret, underscoring the need for long-term counselling and follow-up.

title: IP09-16: Impact of Prior Urethral Surgery on Long-Term Outcomes and Reoperation Risk After Artificial Urinary Sphincter Implantation: A Real-World Analysis
parentSessionTitle: IP09: Urodynamics/Lower Urinary Tract Dysfunction/Female Pelvic Medicine: Male Incontinence
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: The artificial urinary sphincter (AUS) is the established standard for managing moderate-to-severe stress urinary incontinence (SUI) after radical prostatectomy (RP). Erosion remains a significant complication, with limited data on modifiable risk factors. This study assesses long-term outcomes and identifies predictors of AUS failure, with a focus on prior urethral interventions. METHODS: This study retrospectively reviewed a prospectively collected database of patients who received primary AUS (AMS 800) implantation for male severe incontinence between 2014 and 2018. Baseline data, including age, BMI, and comorbidities, were recorded. Outcomes encompassed pad usage (social continence: 0–1 pad/day) at 3–36 months, reoperation/explantation rates and Kaplan-Meier device survival. Univariate logistic regression evaluated predictors of reoperation, emphasizing prior urethral surgery (urethrotomy/urethroplasty). RESULTS: Forty-eight patients were included in the study, accounting 85 surgeries between AUS implantation, revision, substitution and explantation. In total, 62 AUS were implanted. Radical prostatectomy was the main SUI etiology (open n=38; laparoscopic n=5; robotic n=3; TURP n=2). After AUS implantation, social continence (0–1 pad/day) was achieved in 93.5% (n=58) within 6 months. Four patients failed due to hematoma (n=3) or early malfunction (n=1). Overall, 50% (n=31) required reoperation: 32.3% explantation and 17.7% revision, mainly for infection (14/62), erosion (14/62), or malfunction (11/62). For implants from 2014–2018, 1-, 3-, and 5-year revision-free survival rates were 88.6%, 71.4%, and 68.6%, with mean lifetime 68 months. Prior urethral surgery (urethrotomy/urethroplasty) was a strong predictor of re-intervention (OR 6.8, 95% CI 2.1–21.7, p<0.001), with ~50% due to erosion. Pelvic radiotherapy (OR 1.4, p=0.18) and open radical prostatectomy etiology (OR 2.7, p=0.06) were not significant. Re-intervention was also higher in patients with diabetes, obesity, or peripheral arterial disease (p<0.001), but not with dyslipidemia or hypertension. Older age (>70 y) increased re-intervention risk vs <60 y (p=0.034). Second and third AUS implantations had higher rates (62.5%), with mean device lifetimes of 48.1 and 23 months, respectively. CONCLUSIONS: These results demonstrate sustained AUS efficacy, with 80% social continence at 3 years. Prior urethral surgery remains a strong predictor of failure and should prompt careful patient selection and tailored perioperative management. Further prospective studies are needed to confirm these findings and refine clinical guidelines.

title: IP09-17: Early Outcomes of the SAFER Study: In Situ Urethroplasty vs. Conservative Management at Artificial Urinary Sphincter Explantation for Erosion
parentSessionTitle: IP09: Urodynamics/Lower Urinary Tract Dysfunction/Female Pelvic Medicine: Male Incontinence

speakers.organization: Department of Urology, Medical University of Gdańsk

fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Urethral erosion of the artificial urinary sphincter (AUS) remains a challenging complication in male incontinence surgery, occurring in up to 5% of patients. Despite its clinical relevance, no standardized approach exists for management at the time of AUS explantation. The Systematic assessment of Artificial urinary sphincter Failure and Erosion Recovery (SAFER) study reports early outcomes of different erosion management strategies. METHODS: SAFER is a multi-institutional study including patients from eight international centers who underwent AUS explantation due to urethral erosion. Baseline parameters, previous treatments, and AUS characteristics were systematically collected and analyzed descriptively. Erosion management at explantation was categorized as in situ urethroplasty (urethrorrhaphy, excision and primary anastomosis \[EPA\], or augmented repair) versus conservative management (catheter drainage only, by Foley ± suprapubic tube). The primary endpoint was stricture-free survival (SFS), assessed by Kaplan–Meier analysis and log-rank testing between treatment groups. Only patients with ≥3 months of follow-up were included. RESULTS: A total of 170 patients were analyzed. Median age was 75 yr (IQR 68–79) and BMI 27 (IQR 24–29). In 53 patients (31%), the explanted device was not the first AUS. Cuff locations were membranous (9.0%), bulbar (54%), transcorporal (11%), and distal double cuff (26%), with a median cuff size of 4.5 cm (IQR 4–4.5). Among 147 patients with prior prostate cancer treatment, 49% had prostatectomy alone, 42% prostatectomy plus irradiation, 8.8% irradiation ± ADT, and 0.7% cystoprostatectomy. In situ urethroplasty was performed in 57 patients (34%), comprising urethrorrhaphy in 82%, EPA in 11%, and augmented repair in 1.8%. At a median follow-up of 18 mo (IQR 10–42), no statistically significant difference in SFS was observed between in situ urethroplasty and conservative management (p=0.3). CONCLUSIONS: Preliminary SAFER data show that immediate in situ urethroplasty at AUS explantation yields SFS comparable to conservative management. Primary urethral repair appears safe and feasible in selected patients. Ongoing analyses will identify predictors of stricture formation and inform individualized risk stratification for AUS erosion management.

title: IP09-18: Post-Operative Antibiotic Use Does Not Impact Device Infection Rates after Artificial Urinary Sphincter Placement
parentSessionTitle: IP09: Urodynamics/Lower Urinary Tract Dysfunction/Female Pelvic Medicine: Male Incontinence
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Clinical practice regarding postoperative antibiotics after artificial urinary sphincter (AUS) placement varies among urologists, and there is not robust literature to support or dispute their role in preventing device infection. The objective of this study is to evaluate the impact of postoperative antibiotic use on AUS device infection. METHODS: A retrospective cohort study of all patients undergoing AUS placement or revision at a single institution between January 2016 and March 2025 was performed. We compared rate of AUS infection between two cohorts of patients: those treated with prophylactic oral antibiotics after AUS surgery vs. those who were untreated. Patients how had erosions were excluded from analysis. Demographic, preoperative laboratory testing, and postoperative infection data were reviewed. The two cohorts were compared using Chi-square/Fischer Exact test, t-test, and multivariate analysis. RESULTS: A total of 742 AUS cases were performed by three fellowship-trained surgeons during the study period. The overall AUS infection rate was 1.6% (12/742). Median age was 71, median BMI was 28.6, 50.7% of patients had a history of radiation, 33.5% of cases were revisions, and 27.5% patients had diabetes. Of these 742, 151 (20.4%) did not receive postoperative antibiotics (20.4%), while 591 (79.6%) patients did receive postoperative antibiotics. Demographics were statistically similar between these two groups. None of the patients in the no postoperative antibiotic cohort developed device infection. Furthermore, there was no statistically significant difference in the rate of infection between the two cohorts (0% vs. 2.03%, respectively, p=0.16). There was no statistically significant risk factor demonstrated to be a predictor of infection. On bivariate analysis, patients who had preoperative urinalysis (UA), positive preoperative urine culture, and revision cases were more likely to receive post operative antibiotics (p=0.02, p=0.003, p=0.001, respectively). However, none of these had an increased risk of infection (p=1 for all). CONCLUSIONS: The use of postoperative antibiotics was not associated with lower rates of AUS infection, calling into question the utility of routine postoperative antibiotics after device placement.

title: IP09-19: Post-prostatectomy urinary incontinence recovery with Elitone® for Men: Preliminary findings from first clinical series
parentSessionTitle: IP09: Urodynamics/Lower Urinary Tract Dysfunction/Female Pelvic Medicine: Male Incontinence

speakers.jobTitle: Chief of Urology, Hartford Hospital and Director of Robotic Surgery, Hartford HealthCare

fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Urinary incontinence after prostate surgery is nearly universal, with men often told to expect recovery over 6–12 months. This prolonged period affects quality of life, emotional health, and return to work. Accelerating recovery could improve outcomes and reduce healthcare burden. Neuromuscular stimulation can aid continence recovery, but traditional delivery via anal probe is intrusive and poorly tolerated. Elitone, an FDA-cleared perineal-applied device for women with stress and urge incontinence, has treated 30,000+ patients and is Medicare-covered. The new Elitone for Men incorporates a male-specific electrode to deliver the same stimulation externally, avoiding internal probes. This study evaluated its safety, usability, and efficacy following prostate surgery. METHODS: A prospective, IRB-approved case series enrolled men before or shortly after radical prostatectomy. Baseline evaluation occurred one week after catheter removal; treatment began 4–5 weeks post-surgery. • 20-minute home sessions, 5×/week for 12 weeks. • Pre-modulated 50Hz/10Hz stimulation cycles with rest, inducing strong but comfortable pelvic contractions. • Daily logs recorded treatment, leaks, pad use, and bathroom visits. • Outcome measures: 24-hour pad weight, leaks, pad use, and Incontinence Quality of Life (I-QoL) scores at 12 weeks. • Compliance verified by onboard memory. RESULTS: Of 20 men enrolled, 16 completed treatment with verified use. • 24-Hour Pad Weight: Leakage fell 61% at Week 6 and 78% at Week 12. • Stress Leaks: Reduced 61% at Week 6 and 82% at Week 12. • Quality of Life: I-QoL improved 20.9 ±18.5 points at Week 6\. • Satisfaction: 100% reported satisfaction and willingness to recommend. • Usability: Confirmed suitable for unsupervised home use. • Safety: No adverse events reported. CONCLUSIONS: Outcomes of Elitone for Men parallel the original Elitone for women, which achieved a 72% reduction in leaks/day in its pivotal trial. Prior studies showed that internal stimulation accelerates post-prostatectomy recovery. Elitone for Men delivers equivalent parameters through an external perineal electrode, eliminating the invasiveness barrier and improving acceptance. These results highlight Elitone for Men as a convenient, at-home therapy that promotes rapid continence recovery, meaningful quality-of-life gains, and greater post-surgical confidence.

title: IP09-20: Effect of Post Operative 4-Aminopyradine on Urinary Continence After Robot Assisted Radical Prostatectomy: Results From a Double Blinded Randomized Clinical Trial
parentSessionTitle: IP09: Urodynamics/Lower Urinary Tract Dysfunction/Female Pelvic Medicine: Male Incontinence
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Urinary incontinence (UI) remains a significant long-term complication of robot assisted radical prostatectomy (RARP). 4-Aminopyradine (4AP) has been reported to improve functional recovery from neuropraxia related trauma. Herein, we investigated if a course of 4 AP post-RARP reduces the severity of UI. METHODS: This double blinded randomized clinical trial (IRB STUDY00003721) was conducted at the University of Rochester. 36 subjects with clinically localized prostate cancer scheduled to undergo RARP were enrolled. Randomized patients needed to have a bilateral nerve sparing with at least 25% of the nerves spared on each side and 50% of the total nerves spared which was determined by the surgeon performing RARP. Patients were randomized 1:1 (18 in the 4AP group and 18 in the placebo group) to either 2 months of oral 4AP, 10 mg twice a day, or oral placebo, twice a day, starting the morning after surgery. Urinary continence and bother were measured using the Michigan Incontinence Symptom Index (M-ISI) for 1 year from surgery. Generalized estimation equation was used to study the effects of treatment and time on M-ISI scores. RESULTS: (https://www.auajournals.org/doi/abs/10.1097/01.JU.0001191316.72449.22.20#F1) shows longitudinal plots of M-ISI incontinence severity and bother sub scores. Men in both groups had no significant difference in M-ISI scores pre-operatively. There was significant improvement over time for UI severity (p<0.0001), and marginally significant in UI bother (p=0.07). While there was a trend for 4AP to reduce UI severity (p=0.55) and UI bother (0.69), this was not statistically significant. CONCLUSIONS: A 2-month course of twice daily 4AP did not lead to significant change the severity or bother from UI following RARP. Larger studies are warranted to assess if altering the dose, duration and timing of 4AP can help improve reduce UI after RARP.

title: IP09-21: ContiPants: A Reusable, Selectively Compressive Urinary Incontinence Brief for Patients Post-Radical Prostatectomy
parentSessionTitle: IP09: Urodynamics/Lower Urinary Tract Dysfunction/Female Pelvic Medicine: Male Incontinence
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Male stress urinary incontinence (SUI) affects up to 75% of men after radical prostatectomy (RP). Penile clamps offer temporary continence through indiscriminate circumferential compression that constricts dorsal vasculature, inflicts pain, and often slips. We developed ContiPants, a washable brief that provides selective ventral urethral compression via a drawstring mechanism. This study evaluates its occlusive function, comfort, reusability, and stability in comparison with existing devices. METHODS: A bench-top urethral leak model (500 ml reservoir, 3 mm urethral lumen) was constructed to simulate post-RP SUI. ContiPants was assessed against four commercial penile clamps (Cunningham, Wiesner, Dribblestop, PaceyCuff) on the bench-top model at the manufacturer-indicated tension for each device. Additional testing assessed ContiPants’ (1) material durability across 0-50 wash/dry cycles (2) odor retention after three wash cycles evaluated by eight independent raters (1-5 odor scale), (3) discretion by phantom side-profile assessment, and (4) motion stability via simulated sit-stand and hip-rotation maneuvers. RESULTS: ContiPants limited leakage to 26 ± 4 ml from a 500 ml baseline (≈ 95% occlusion), approaching Cunningham clamp performance (9 ± 3 ml; ≈ 98%). ContiPants’ synthetic polyester-spandex blend showed < 3 mm dimensional change and < 5% variance in light transmittance after 50 wash/dry cycles. Odor testing deemed mean scores < 1.3 (1-5 scale). Side-profile visualization demonstrated a 15% protrusion when compared to baseline garments. Simulated motion maintained the compressive element on the ventral aspect of the penis with < 5 mm displacement. CONCLUSIONS: ContiPants achieved comparable occlusive performance on a simulated leakage model while prioritizing comfort, discretion, and reusability. Testing confirmed mechanical durability, hygienic. Simulated motion demonstrated stability, addressing slippage, a major limitation of penile clamps. Minor bulk and discretion remain areas for future optimization. These findings establish ContiPants as a proof of concept for a new class of wearable incontinence management beyond SUI: selectively compressive, reusable, and dorsal-vasculature-sparing garments that integrate seamlessly into daily life.

title: IP09-22: Urodynamics and Cystoscopy Prior to Artificial Urinary Sphincter (AUS) Implantation: Essential Tools or Merely Recommendations?
parentSessionTitle: IP09: Urodynamics/Lower Urinary Tract Dysfunction/Female Pelvic Medicine: Male Incontinence
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Prior to artificial urinary sphincter (AUS) implantation, it is common practice to perform a urological evaluation that includes urodynamics and cystoscopy, in order to identify bladder and urethral characteristics that may compromise surgical outcomes or patient safety. However, it remains debated whether these assessments are essential for all candidates or should be reserved for selected cases. METHODS: A retrospective, questionnaire-based study was conducted among men who underwent AUS implantation between 2021 and 2025 at our institution. For each patient, demographic data, oncologic background, urodynamic and cystoscopic findings, surgical outcomes, and quality-of-life parameters, based on the ICIQ-UI-SF questionnaire, were collected before and after surgery. RESULTS: Fifty-five patients aged 56-86 years (median 71, IQR 67-75) underwent AUS implantation during the study period. Forty-three patients (78%) participated in the questionnaire study, and all underwent preoperative urodynamic and cystoscopic evaluations. Thirty-nine patients (91%) were operated on for stress urinary incontinence (SUI), while the rest had mixed urinary incontinence (MUI). Twenty-four patients (56%) received anticholinergic or 3-receptor agonist therapy prior to surgery. Urodynamic studies revealed detrusor overactivity (DO) in 9 men (21%), decreased bladder compliance (10-15 ml/cmH2O) in 7 (16%), and a positive abdominal leak point pressure (ALPP) in 28 (65%) with a mean of 42.8 cmH2O. Cystoscopy demonstrated bladder neck or urethral narrowing not requiring intervention in 10 patients (23%), and weak contraction of the external sphincter in 12 patients (28%). In multivariate analysis - BMI, diabetes, prior radiation, hormonal therapy, or time interval between prostate surgery and AUS implantation were not associated with urodynamic abnormalities (DO, low compliance, reduced bladder capacity) or bladder neck/urethral strictures. At a median follow-up of 23 months (IQR 14.5-36.5), pathological findings on urodynamics or cystoscopy were not correlated with preoperative incontinence severity nor predictive of postoperative outcomes in terms of leakage, quality of life, or pad usage. CONCLUSIONS: According to our findings, urodynamic and cystoscopic findings do not necessarily predict the success of AUS implantation. Although further prospective studies are required to examine this question, we conclude that these evaluations should be reserved for selected cases, such as patients at high risk of surgical failure or those presenting with clinically complex SUI.

title: IP09-23: Evaluating ChatGPT-5 and Gemini-2.5 for Urodynamic Study Interpretation: Agreement With Expert Urologists
parentSessionTitle: IP09: Urodynamics/Lower Urinary Tract Dysfunction/Female Pelvic Medicine: Male Incontinence

speakers.jobTitle: Chairman of the Department of Urology at Fundación Santa Fe de Bogotá and Full Professor of Urology at Universidad de los Andes School of Medicine

fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Urodynamic studies (UDS) are key for assessing lower urinary tract dysfunction, yet interpretation remains subjective and operator dependent. Variability limits standardization and accuracy, underscoring the need for reproducible methods. Artificial intelligence (AI) and large language models (LLMs) may assist in this process. However, it is necessary to compare interrater performance between AI and clinicians. We aimed to evaluate the agreement between UDS interpretations generated by ChatGPT-5 Plus and Gemini 2.5 Pro (paid versions) and those of expert urologists at our institution. METHODS: A random sample of 160 UDS (80 men, 80 women) conducted at our hospital between April to October 2025 was selected. Each report included values and urodynamic traces. Three expert urologists (>10 years of experience) independently reviewed all studies using standardized diagnostic criteria. Anonymized reports were submitted to ChatGPT-5 and Gemini 2.5. In the unlabeled version (UL), the model received a general prompt with urodynamic parameters without predefined diagnostic labels, whereas in the labeled version (L), prompts included expert-defined diagnostic criteria. The primary outcome was inter-rater agreement (Cohen’s kappa). RESULTS: Overall, Cohen’s kappa values showed poor to slight agreement across most parameters, with consistently higher concordance for ChatGPT-5+ compared to Gemini 2.5 Pro. The strongest agreement was seen for urine leakage (κ=0.39 for ChatGPT-5+ no-std; κ=0.16 for Gemini no-std) and bladder outlet obstruction (κ=0.24 and κ=0.04, respectively), reaching slight to fair levels (see Figure 1). Negative kappa values for uroflowmetry curve, bladder sensation, and type of urinary incontinence (UI) indicated disagreement beyond chance. CONCLUSIONS: AI LLMs showed poor to slight agreement with expert urologists for most urodynamic parameters; ChatGPT-5+ (no-std) performed best but remained below clinically acceptable agreement. These findings align with previous reports indicating that earlier ChatGPT versions were not suitable for the analysis or diagnosis of urodynamic traces. AI may help standardize UDS interpretation, but routine clinical use is premature. Progress will require standardized criteria, multicenter external validation, and experts' supervision to ensure the accuracy and safety of its outputs.

title: IP09-24: Moderate Concordance Between UroCuff and Urodynamics: Results from a High-Volume Academic Practice
parentSessionTitle: IP09: Urodynamics/Lower Urinary Tract Dysfunction/Female Pelvic Medicine: Male Incontinence
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: The Penile Cuff Test (PCT), or “UroCuff”, is a promising and non-invasive technique to assess men with lower urinary tract symptoms (LUTS) for bladder outlet obstruction (BOO). Urodynamic studies (UDS), despite their invasiveness, remain the gold standard for comprehensively assessing storage and voiding dysfunction. We evaluated the accuracy of PCT compared to UDS in the diagnosis of BOO. METHODS: We performed a retrospective study of men with LUTS who underwent both PCT and pressure-flow UDS at an academic tertiary care-center between January 2024 and June 2025. Only men who voided at least 50cc on PCT were included; a sensitivity analysis of those voiding ≥150cc was performed. PCT results were compared to UDS findings as the gold standard, with BOO defined on UDS as a BOO index ≥40. PCT was considered accurate if it correctly predicted BOO as measured by UDS. Sensitivity, specificity, positive predictive value (PPV), negative predictive value (NPV), and overall accuracy were calculated. RESULTS: 81 men were included with a median age of 73 years (interquartile range \[IQR\] 67.75-78.0). 27 men (33.3%) were classified as having BOO by UDS. Patients were predominantly White (51.9%), with median baseline International Prostate Symptom Score of 19 (IQR 10-26) and Quality of Life score of 4 (IQR 3-5). Mean PSA was 1.8±1.9 ng/mL. Common comorbidities included hypertension (42%), hyperlipidemia (33%), and prostate cancer (13.6%) (Table). Median Pcuff, int was 107.20 (IQR 75.30-155.10). PCT demonstrated 67.9% overall accuracy in classification of BOO compared to UDS. Sensitivity was 44.4%; specificity was 79.6%; PPV was 52.2%; and NPV was 74.1%. When only analyzing men who voided at least 150cc on PCT (N=33), accuracy was 63.6%; sensitivity was 33.3%; specificity was 81.0%; PPV was 50.0%; NPV was 68.0%. CONCLUSIONS: In a large, contemporary cohort, PCT had lower concordance with pressure-flow UDS than previously reported, demonstrating moderate accuracy (67.9%), high specificity (79.6%), but limited sensitivity (44.4%) for identifying BOO in men with LUTS. This brings forth the importance of shared decision making in deciding to undergo PCT or UDS for evaluation of LUTS. | | | --- | | |

title: IP09-25: Can Clinical or Urodynamic Parameters Predict Early Urinary Incontinence Outcomes After Radical Retropubic Prostatectomy?
parentSessionTitle: IP09: Urodynamics/Lower Urinary Tract Dysfunction/Female Pelvic Medicine: Male Incontinence
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Urinary incontinence (UI) is a distressing complication following radical retropubic prostatectomy (RRP), significantly affecting quality of life (QoL). Identifying predictors of UI is crucial, as they may assist in guiding treatment decisions. METHODS: Eighty-four patients undergoing radical retropubic prostatectomy (RRP) were prospectively evaluated. The following parameters were assessed preoperatively and at 1 month postoperatively: urinary incontinence symptoms and quality of life (QoL), measured by the Portuguese-validated ICIQ-SF; International Prostate Symptom Score, IPSS; erectile function (International Index of Erectile Function–5, IIEF-5); and the 60-minute Pad Test. Preoperative urodynamic parameters included maximum urinary flow rate (Qmax), maximum detrusor pressure (Pdet. max), and cystometric capacity. Pelvic floor muscle (PFM) strength was evaluated using a transrectal sensor (PerinaStim perineometer). Prostate weight was recorded immediately after surgery. RESULTS: The mean age and body mass index (BMI) were 57 years and 26.8 kg/m2, respectively. The tumor was organ-confined in 81% of patients, and 25% were classified as high risk. Urinary incontinence (UI) was identified in 5% of patients prior to radical prostatectomy (RP); however, 80% experienced a significant worsening of urinary leakage after surgery (p0.001), according to the ICIQ-SF. Preoperatively, the IIEF-5 revealed that 44% of patients had erectile dysfunction (36% mild, 8% moderate), with a significant postoperative worsening observed in 90% of cases (p0.001). The mean 60-minute Pad Test value increased significantly after surgery compared to pre-prostatectomy (5.0 g vs. 1.0 g, respectively; p0.001). Pelvic floor muscle (PFM) strength was significantly lower after RRP (46.2 cmH2O vs. 53.4 cmH2O, p=0.037). However, PFM strength did not correlate with either UI (p=0.73) or sexual dysfunction (p=0.39). Urodynamic parameters are presented in Table 1. No significant correlations were found between any urodynamic variables and UI, or between PFM strength and worsening of UI or sexual function. CONCLUSIONS: Preoperative erectile dysfunction did not correlate with one-month postoperative outcomes. Pelvic floor muscle (PFM) strength was not a predictor of urinary incontinence or sexual dysfunction. No preoperative urodynamic parameter correlated with urinary incontinence at one month after surgery. | | | --- | | |

title: IP09-26: Incidence and Management of Overactive Bladder after Stress Incontinence Surgeries
parentSessionTitle: IP09: Urodynamics/Lower Urinary Tract Dysfunction/Female Pelvic Medicine: Male Incontinence

speakers.organization: Southern Illinois University School of Medicine

fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: While stress urinary incontinence (SUI) surgeries such as artificial urinary sphincters (AUS) and sling procedures have proven highly effective at improving symptoms of stress incontinence, patients may develop symptoms of Overactive Bladder (OAB) post-operatively. This study investigated the incidence of OAB following male stress-incontinence procedures, as well as treatment methods used and their efficacy. METHODS: This is a retrospective review of male patients who underwent artificial urinary sphincter or male sling placement at a single institution by a single surgeon from 2020-2025. Demographics and clinical outcomes were collected via chart review. Descriptive statistics were performed. Fisher’s exact and chi-2 tests were used for categorical variables. T-test was used for continuous variables. Logistic regression was used to evaluate factors associated with developing post-op OAB with variables included based on univariate and clinic significance. RESULTS: Of 56 patients identified to have undergone SUI surgery, 41.0% (n=23/56) reported OAB symptoms post-operatively, but only 19.6% (n=11/56) of patients developed de novo OAB, or symptoms not already present pre-operatively. Regarding OAB management, 73.9% (n=17/23) had resolution of symptoms with treatment. 87.0% (n=20/23) were first treated with oral medications, and 65.2% (n=15/23) had symptomatic resolution after their first treatment method. Table 1 compares patients who developed OAB to those who did not. On multiple logistic regression, adjusting for history of radiation and presence of pre-operative OAB symptoms, patients undergoing sling were at 8.6 times increased odds of developing OAB compared to AUS patients (p=0.016). CONCLUSIONS: Patients who undergo SUI surgery may develop OAB due to new outlet obstruction. There is a higher chance of experiencing these symptoms if patients also had pre-operative symptoms of OAB. The majority of patients with OAB had symptomatic improvement with medications. | | | --- | | |

title: IP09-27: Comparative Outcomes in Postoperative Medical Therapy Use Across Common BPH Procedures
parentSessionTitle: IP09: Urodynamics/Lower Urinary Tract Dysfunction/Female Pelvic Medicine: Male Incontinence

speakers.organization: University of Vermont Larner College of Medicine

fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Many patients continue to require medication for lower urinary tract symptoms (LUTS) after surgery for benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH). Understanding differences in postoperative medication use among different BPH surgeries may guide patient counseling on surgical options and expectations. This study compared medication discontinuation rates across common BPH procedures, using transurethral resection of the prostate (TURP) as the reference. METHODS: We conducted a retrospective cohort analysis using the TriNetX Diamond Network (2006–September 2025). Adult males (≥18 years) undergoing primary BPH surgery on preoperative medications were included, and five medication classes were evaluated postoperatively: alpha-blockers, 5-alpha-reductase inhibitors (5ARIs), phosphodiesterase type-5 inhibitors (PDE5is), antimuscarinics, and B3 agonists. The primary outcome was proportion of patients off all BPH-related medications at 2 years. Odds ratios (ORs) were calculated relative to TURP. RESULTS: Among 40,125 men worldwide (mean age 70.4 ± 5.69) treated with BPH surgery on preoperative medications, 20.5% remained medication-free at 2 years, while 79.5% required at least one BPH-related medication. Discontinuation rates varied across procedures: Holmium laser enucleation of the prostate (HoLEP) (25.7%), photoselective vaporization of the prostate (PVP) (24.7%), and UroLift (20.3%) showed higher rates compared with TURP. Conversely, robotic waterjet therapy (RWT) had a lower medication-free rate (8.2%). Alpha-blocker monotherapy was the most common regimen among those requiring postoperative treatment. CONCLUSIONS: While postoperative medication use remains common after BPH surgery, the likelihood of remaining medication-free differs across procedures. HoLEP, PVP, and UroLift are associated with significantly higher odds of discontinuing medication compared with TURP, whereas patients undergoing RWT are more likely to continue medical therapy. These findings support individualized preoperative counseling and highlight the need for further work to optimize management of persistent LUTS after BPH surgery. | | | --- | | |

title: IP09-28: Is Surgery for Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia an Offramp for Medical Therapy in Men with Lower Urinary Tract Symptoms? A Retrospective Review
parentSessionTitle: IP09: Urodynamics/Lower Urinary Tract Dysfunction/Female Pelvic Medicine: Male Incontinence

speakers.organization: University of Vermont Larner College of Medicine

fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH) procedures are often performed to improve lower urinary tract symptoms. However, postoperative pharmacologic therapy remains common despite the desire for stopping medical therapy being a significant motivator for many patients pursuing surgical management. Therefore, understanding patterns of medication use after surgery is important for counseling and setting postoperative expectations. This study reports medication use after BPH surgery across major medication classes. METHODS: We conducted a retrospective cohort study using the TriNetX Diamond Network (2006–September 2025). Adult males (≥18 years) undergoing primary BPH surgery while on preoperative medications were included. Five medication classes were evaluated: alpha-blockers, 5-alpha-reductase inhibitors \[5ARIs\], phosphodiesterase type-5 inhibitors \[PDE5is\], antimuscarinics, or B3 agonists. Postoperative medication use was assessed at 1 year. RESULTS: Among 50,273 men worldwide (mean age 70.4 ± 9.27 years) treated with BPH surgery on preop BPH medications, 77.5% of patients (38,983) were prescribed at least one BPH-related medication by 1 year following their index surgery, while 22.5% (11,290) required no pharmacologic therapy. Among postoperative users, monotherapy predominates (74.7%), with alpha blocker monotherapy being the most common (36.2%). Combination therapy was less common, accounting for 25.3% of postoperative medical regimens: the most common combination therapy was alpha blocker + 5ARI (13.5%). CONCLUSIONS: Our study suggests that for most men, BPH surgery does not present an offramp for medical therapy in men with LUTS with a majority of patients being on 1 or more medications at 1 year post-outlet procedure. These findings can assist medical providers in counseling patients on realistic expectations regarding postoperative medication use after surgical management of BPH. In addition, it highlights the need for further research on LUTS in men during the post-BPH surgery state.

title: IP09-29: Preoperative Objective Parameters as Predictors of TURP Efficacy: A Retrospective Cohort Study of 200 Patients
parentSessionTitle: IP09: Urodynamics/Lower Urinary Tract Dysfunction/Female Pelvic Medicine: Male Incontinence
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: To investigate the efficacy of transurethral resection of the prostate (TURP) for benign prostatic hyperplasia and identify preoperative objective urodynamic and imaging parameters significantly associated with substantial postoperative symptomatic improvement. The aim is to provide an objective basis for the accurate clinical assessment of surgical benefit and optimal timing for intervention. METHODS: This retrospective cohort study included 200 patients who underwent TURP between 2023 and 2024. Preoperative data collected included Quality of Life (QoL) score, urodynamic parameters \[maximum flow rate (Qmax), voided volume (VV), post-void residual urine\ (PVR), bladder contractility index (BCI), bladder outlet obstruction index (BOOI)\], and imaging parameters \[prostate volume (PV), intravesical prostatic protrusion (IPP),\ membranous urethral length (MUL), and prostatic transitional zone thickness (PZT)\]. A postoperative-to-preoperative International Prostate Symptom Score (IPSS) ratio (Post/pre IPSS ratio) of ≤0.5 was defined as the primary indicator of good surgical outcome. Univariate and multivariate regression analyses were performed to assess the correlation between preoperative parameters and treatment efficacy RESULTS: Univariate and multivariate regression analyses identified Qmax, BCI, BOOI, and PZT as having statistically significant correlations with postoperative outcome. ROC curve analysis demonstrated considerable area under the curve (AUC) values for these parameters: 0.722, 0.914, 0.780, and 0.827, respectively. Patients with preoperative Qmax <10.48 ml/s, BCI >118.9, BOOI >45.49, and PZT <8.6 mm experienced significantly greater improvement in lower urinary tract symptoms following TURP. In contrast, QoL score, PVR, VV, PV, MUL, and IPP showed no significant association with surgical outcome in this study. CONCLUSIONS: Preoperative Qmax, BCI, BOOI, and PZT are effective predictors of the degree of symptomatic improvement after TURP. Combined assessment of these parameters, particularly BOOI (confirming obstruction) and BCI (evaluating bladder compensatory function), can assist urologists in more accurately identifying patients most likely to derive significant benefit from surgery. This facilitates optimized clinical decision-making, helps determine the optimal timing for surgery, and may avoid overtreatment in patients with low potential benefit. These findings provide an important reference for the individualized and precise application of TURP.

title: IP09-30: Urodynamic findings and outcomes in men undergoing artificial urinary sphincter (AUS) placement for post-prostatectomy stress urinary incontinence with and without prior radiation therapy
parentSessionTitle: IP09: Urodynamics/Lower Urinary Tract Dysfunction/Female Pelvic Medicine: Male Incontinence
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: The impact of radiation therapy (XRT) on urodynamic (UDS) parameters and outcomes of artificial urinary sphincter (AUS) implantation in post-radical prostatectomy (RP) patients remains controversial. Some studies have reported no adverse radiation effects, while others noted changes in preoperative UDS and continence outcomes. We reviewed our AUS implants to compare the UDS parameters and continence outcomes between post-RP patients with and without a history of XRT. METHODS: We reviewed the charts of patients undergoing AUS implant for post-RP incontinence and divided patients into two groups: those with (Group 1) and those without (Group 2) a history of pelvic XRT. The groups were compared with respect to demographic (age, comorbidities, prior urethral procedures), clinical (symptom scores, voiding diaries, pad usage), and UDS (cystometrogram with leak point testing and pressure-flow studies) variables as well as postoperative outcomes. RESULTS: Of 96 patients reviewed, 50 (52%) had a history of XRT. The mean age at the time of AUS placement was 67.8 years (SD 7.82). Mean follow-up for Group 1 and Group 2 patients was 2.8 years (SD 4.0) and 3.1 years (SD 3.2), respectively. There were no significant differences between groups with respect to demographics, prior urethral procedures, preoperative AUA symptom scores, voiding frequency, and pads per day (ppd) usage (6.0 in Group 1, 5.4 in Group 2). However, maximum voided volume per void was significantly lower in Group 1 (mean 282 ml vs 479 ml, p=0.008). UDS characteristics were not significantly different between groups. Following AUS implant, there was no significant difference in pad usage between groups (1.6 ppd in Group 1, 1.3 ppd in Group 2, p=0.64) with social continence (0-1 ppd) achieved in 69% of Group 1 and 70% of Group 2 patients. CONCLUSIONS: In a cohort of post-RP patients who underwent AUS implant, we did not find any major differences between patients with and without pelvic XRT with regard to demographic, clinical, and UDS parameters. In addition, AUS outcomes were similar between groups. As a result, the necessity of UDS prior to AUS implantation in post-RP patients is questionable. These results suggest that UDS may offer limited prognostic value, warranting further studies on its clinical utility in this population. | | | --- | | |

title: IP10-01: Quality of Images Needed for Accurate Artificial Intelligence Interpretation of Nephrolithiasis- Considerations for Data Collection
parentSessionTitle: IP10: Surgical Technology & Simulation: Instrumentation & Technology I

speakers.organization: University of Florida, Department of Urology

fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Advancements in artificial intelligence (AI) technology bring new opportunities for intraoperative endoscopic analysis of stones. Whereas fiberoptic technology of rod lens endoscopes has been used historically, digital platforms provide improved pixelation and superior image quality. Limited study exists regarding the impact of image quality on AI model efficacy. We performed a real-time endoscopic analysis of stone images using AI to predict stone composition across various endoscopes. METHODS: We performed a cross-sectional analysis of patients undergoing ureteroscopy or percutaneous nephrolithotomy from March, 2023 to August, 2025. Endoscope type included a digital non-disposable and disposable flexible ureteroscopes, a rigid rod lens cystoscope, a semirigid rod lens ureteroscope, a rigid rod lens nephroscope and isolated digital camera head. Images were captured in both in-vivo and ex-vivo. Stone morphology included whole, cross-sectional and fragmented stones to represent a real-world experience. Deep learning artificial neural network AI model was used. Stone compositions included calcium oxalate monohydrate (CaOxM), calcium oxalate dihydrate (CaOxD), calcium phosphate carbonate (CaPCO3), calcium phosphate hydroxyl (CaPOH), uric acid, cystine and struvite. AI efficacy was quantified using precision, recall, and F1 scores- a harmonic mean of recall and precision. RESULTS: A total of 324 stone images were captured and utilized by the AI model. Table 1 demonstrates the AI model’s efficacy, as determined by F1, stratified by endoscope type. F1 scores were highest for flexible digital endoscopes (F1- 0.784), followed by non-disposable rigid rod lens (F1- 0.696) and lastly flexible non-disposable fiberoptic endoscopes (F1- 0.602). Predictive accuracy was highest for calcium oxalate monohydrate. Prediction efficacy varied significantly depending on endoscope type and stone composition. CONCLUSIONS: We describe the first known study of an AI model developed to predict stone composition using real-time endoscopic images. Digital flexible endoscopes demonstrated the highest predictive accuracy to classify stone composition. While increased data is important for machine learning algorithms, consideration for endoscope type in data collection should be considered in how they will impact the algorithm and its efficacy. | | | --- | | |

title: IP10-02: A Validated Custom Pipeline for Three-Dimensional Kidney Stone Renderings to Create an Open Access Repository
parentSessionTitle: IP10: Surgical Technology & Simulation: Instrumentation & Technology I
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Three-dimensional (3D) rendering of urologic anatomy and pathology plays a crucial role in simulation and surgical training. However, no standardized library of accurate and reproducible 3D kidney stone models classified by composition currently exists. Our objective was to develop and validate a repository of high-fidelity 3D renderings of commonly encountered kidney stones. METHODS: We received kidney stones classified by the Louis C. Herring Laboratory including: calcium oxalate monohydrate (COM), cystine (Cyst), magnesium ammonium phosphate hexahydrate/carbonate apatite (MAPH/CA), and calcium hydrogen phosphate dihydrate (CHPD). Except for the fragmented MAPH/CA stone (80% MAPH, 20% CA) and the fragmented CHPD stone (which contained 1% hydroxyl apatite), all others were unfragmented and composed of a single material. Each stone was photographed on a custom rotating stage positioned between two fixed 4K UHD webcams, placed 7.5 cm apart and approximately 10 cm from the stone ( Figure 1A). The stage was rotated in 18° increments and 360° images were captured. The images were imported into Adobe Substance 3D Sampler for 3D renderings. To validate the renderings, five endourologists completed a Likert-scale survey evaluating model fidelity in terms of geometry and surface texture (1=Strongly Disagree, 5=Strongly Agree). RESULTS: 3D models were successfully generated for all uric acid (UA) stones (5/5), most COM stones (8/11), the MAPH/CA stone fragments (2/2), and the CHPD fragments (3/3), but not for any cystine stones (0/4) ( Figure 1B). Regarding the accuracy of the simulated stone morphology and texture, endourologists highly agreed for COM and UA stones (mean 4.4-4.6, median 5), moderately agreed for CHPD (mean 4.2-4.25, median 4), and were neutral regarding struvite stones (mean 3.2-3.4, median 3). CONCLUSIONS: This method produced accurate 3D kidney stone renderings for COM, UA and CHPD stones. Rendering failure or poor resolution in other stones was likely due to excessive surface reflectivity. Expanding this workflow with additional stone types and validation metrics could facilitate the creation of a robust, reproducible 3D kidney stone library for educational and research applications. All models are freely available at:https://github. com/Uro-GLiDER.

title: IP10-03: Quantifying Image Quality During Flexible Ureteroscopy for Kidney Stone Treatment
parentSessionTitle: IP10: Surgical Technology & Simulation: Instrumentation & Technology I
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Poor image quality during endoscopic stone surgery due to bleeding, debris, or technical factors can impact adequate visualization of the collecting system during kidney stone treatment. The aim of this work is to describe and quantify image quality during various parts of endoscopic stone surgery using standard image quality metrics. METHODS: We obtained 140 videos of flexible ureteroscopy (41 fiberoptic, 99 digital) for kidney stone treatment. We manually identified surgical tasks within each video which included: stone localization, laser ablation, basket retrieval, and residual dust assessment. We evaluated intraoperative image quality using standard image quality metrics throughout each video: a) noise variance (i. e., image blur), b) high-frequency variance (i. e., image contrast variation), c) image sharpness, and d) estimated signal-to-noise ratio (SNR, i. e., image clarity). We compared the means for these metrics for each surgical task to identify how image quality changes during fURS using an analysis of variance (ANOVA). RESULTS: Stone localization, laser ablation, basket retrieval, and dust assessment were seen in 71, 98, 52, and 40 of the videos, respectively. Significant between-group differences were seen across surgical tasks in noise variance (p=0.007), high-frequency variance (p=0.019), sharpness (p=0.018), and SNR (p=0.004). Image quality metrics demonstrated the poorest image quality during laser ablation (high noise variance and sharpness) and best image quality during dust assessment (low noise variance and high SNR) ( Table 1). For digital scope video, there was a significant difference in image quality between surgical tasks as measured by noise variance (p=0.02), sharpness (p=0.0005), and SNR (p=0.02). For fiberoptic scope video, there was only a difference in image quality between surgical tasks as measured by SNR (p=0.03). CONCLUSIONS: Image quality varies significantly across surgical tasks during ureteroscopy with the poorest image quality noted during stone lasering as measured by four different metrics. Future work will evaluate how these metrics associate with clinical outcomes. | | | --- | | |

title: IP10-04: Automation of a Real-Time Digital Software for Kidney Stone Measurement during Ureteroscopic Lithotripsy
parentSessionTitle: IP10: Surgical Technology & Simulation: Instrumentation & Technology I
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Accurate stone size estimation is an important aspect of ureteroscopic lithotripsy to ensure safe extraction or spontaneous passage of fragments and reduce the risk of ureteral injury. We have developed and validated a novel software that can provide accurate measurements of stone fragments visualized during ureteroscopy. However, the software requires additional personnel to operate, and it functions on paused video frames, which can add time and cost. We aimed to develop an automated software tool that can detect the outline of stones in endoscopic video frames to enable unassisted, real-time digital stone measurement. METHODS: The software tool was developed using Visual Studio Code and computer vision libraries (OpenCV). Several image processing techniques were used to analyze the endoscopic video frames before automating the stone outline. Frame operations such as CLAHE filters, gaussian blur, and morphology operations were applied to increase contrast, enhance edge preservation of the stone, and remove background noise that may be present. An OpenCV convex hull function was used to determine the smallest convex polygon that encloses the entirety of the stone boundary. The maximum ferret diameter was calculated using a “rotating calipers” algorithm. For the calibration, ureteroscopic images of black squares of known sizes (1-10.5 mm) were placed at defined distances (3-15 mm) from the ureteroscope. Pixel sizes of the checkerboard and x coordinates of the guidewire were measured using ImageJ. These two sets of measurement were fit into a multivariate linear model using Excel Solver and an evolutionary optimization algorithm RESULTS: The prototype software tool showed consistency automatically capturing the outline and ferret diameter of mock kidney stones during in vitro testing ( Figure).
