fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Robot-assisted kidney transplantation (RAKT) is being increasingly utilized for more complex organs and recipients. Consequently, postoperative ICU admissions may rise as higher-risk recipients undergo RAKT. In this study, we evaluated the incidence and predictors of ICU admission after RAKT and compared graft and patient outcomes between ICU and non-ICU cohorts. METHODS: Patients in our prospectively maintained robotic kidney transplant database (RoKiT) transplanted from 10/2019 to 10/2025 were categorized based on postoperative ICU admission. Demographic, donor, intraoperative, and post-transplant variables were compared between groups. Multivariable logistic regression was performed to identify factors associated with ICU admission. RESULTS: Of 209 RAKT recipients, 32 (15.3%) required postoperative ICU admission, with a median ICU stay of 1 day. The most common indications were hemodynamic instability (12/32, 38%) and respiratory distress (7/32, 22%). Baseline demographics were comparable between groups. On univariate analysis, ICU admission was more common after deceased donor transplants (87.5% vs. 49.8%, p<0.001), transplants with kidneys with multiple arteries (31% vs. 12%, p=0.019), surgery with the multiport vs. the single port robot (88% vs. 66%, p=0.01), and the presence of delayed graft function (DGF, 44% vs. 10%, p=0.002). On multivariable analysis, multiport robotic surgery (OR 3.64, p=0.05), deceased donor transplantation (OR 4.36, p=0.02) and DGF (OR 3.09, p=0.035) were associated with increased odds of ICU admission. CONCLUSIONS: In our diverse series of RAKT recipients, use of the multiport robot, deceased donor transplantation, and DGF were associated with three-fourfold odds of ICU admission. These data may help inform future interventions to mitigate intraoperative cardiopulmonary stress and in organ-recipient matching. | | | --- | | |

title: IP11-07: Single-Port Robotic-Assisted Kidney Transplantation: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis on the da Vinci Platform
parentSessionTitle: IP11: Transplantation & Vascular Surgery

speakers.organization: Case Western Reserve University School of Medicine

fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Single-port (SP) robotic platforms have emerged as a next-generation minimally invasive option for complex procedures, yet outcomes in robotic-assisted kidney transplantation (RAKT) remain poorly characterized. This systematic review and single-arm meta-analysis summarize perioperative and early graft outcomes from published SP-RAKT series. METHODS: Our protocol was registered on PROSPERO (CRD420251086071) and followed PRISMA. PubMed, Embase, Scopus, and Web of Science were queried on September 1, 2025. Only studies reporting outcomes with SP-RAKT in adult patients were included. Studies with SP robotic nephrectomy were excluded. Data were extracted on patient characteristics, complications, and outcomes. Weighted or simple pooled averages were calculated across studies. Study quality was assessed descriptively using the Joanna Briggs Institute and MINORS criteria. RESULTS: 17 studies published since September 20, 2019 encompassing 278 SP-RAKT procedures were identified. Mean recipient age was 49.3±5.7 years, and BMI 31.3±0.99 kg/m2, with living donors in 69% of cases. Mean operative time was 257.6±103.8 minutes, estimated blood loss 67.1 ml, vascular anastomosis time 53.2 minutes, and hospital stay 2.4 days. Delayed graft function occurred in 5% of patients, and no case required conversion to open surgery reported. Overall postoperative complication rate was 11%. Renal outcomes were favorable, with mean serum creatinine of 2.91 mg/dL at discharge and 1.75 mg/dL at last follow-up. No graft losses reported through 6 and 12 months in cohorts with available follow-up. Recovery-related outcomes included mean postoperative pain score 3.51, opioid consumption 61.2 morphine milligram equivalents, and readmission rate 27% within 90 days. Across studies, outcomes were comparable to conventional or multiport RAKT benchmarks, with reduced incision morbidity and acceptable warm ischemia times. CONCLUSIONS: Early experience with SP-RAKT suggests the approach is feasible and safe, with low rates of delayed graft function and complications. Operative times remain longer in initial cases but improve with surgeon experience. Current evidence is limited by small single-arm series and heterogeneity in reporting; prospective multi-center studies and standardized outcome reporting are needed. | | | --- | | |

title: IP11-08: Single-Port Robotic Autotransplantation: A Minimally Invasive Novel Solution for Nutcracker Syndrome
parentSessionTitle: IP11: Transplantation & Vascular Surgery
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Nutcracker syndrome (NCS) can present with left flank pain, pelvic congestion syndrome (PCS) and hematuria. Kidney autotransplantation (KAT) remains uncommon but can be definitive in a subset of patients. KAT is traditionally performed via open surgery with associated morbidity. We present the first institutional series of single-port (SP) robotic KAT for NCS, demonstrating the feasibility and outcomes of this minimally invasive approach. METHODS: Between August 2022 and October 2025, 22 consecutive patients with symptomatic Nutcracker syndrome underwent SP KAT through a peri-umbilical incision. A retrospective review was performed to collect demographic, clinical, operative, and postoperative data. Outcomes were summarized using descriptive statistics and reported as median \[IQR\] or number (%). RESULTS: Median age was 28 (23–34) years; 90% were female, and median BMI was 21.9 (20.5–24.2). Previous abdominal surgery occurred in 55%, and 41% had concomitant May–Thurner syndrome. Preoperative creatinine was 0.86 (0.69–0.96) mg/dL and hemoglobin 12.9 (11.7–13.6) g/dL. Two patients (9%) had prior renal vein transposition and two (9%) had gonadal vein transposition. Median operative time was 6 hr 14 min (IQR: 5 h14 min – 6 h 44 min), vascular anastomosis time 40 (35.5–48.5) minutes, estimated blood loss 62.5 (50–100) mL, and Δ hemoglobin 1.7 (0.72–2.17) g/dL. Most grafts had a single renal artery (74%), with two in 21% and three in 5%; implantation into the opposite iliac fossa occurred in 45%. No intraoperative complications or ICU admissions occurred. Postoperative creatinine was 0.81 (0.70–0.94) mg/dL, and median hospital stay was 3 (2–4) days. Postoperative day-1 pain score was 7 (6–8), and 30-day readmission occurred in three patients (13.6%). At last follow-up, 82% of patients reported complete or improved pain resolution, with stable renal function in all cases. CONCLUSIONS: Single-port robotic kidney autotransplantation is a safe and effective surgical option for Nutcracker syndrome. We report a high rate of pain relief, preserved renal function, and minimal morbidity. This represents a novel tool for treating this vascular disorder. | | | --- | | |

title: IP11-09: Robotic Single-Port Extraperitoneal versus Multi-Port Living Donor Kidney Transplantation
parentSessionTitle: IP11: Transplantation & Vascular Surgery
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Kidney transplantation has evolved from an open approach to minimally invasive techniques with the introduction of multi-port (MP) robotic platforms. The emergence of single-port (SP) allows extraperitoneal graft placement without Trendelenburg positioning. We compared perioperative and early postoperative outcomes in recipients of living donor (LD) SP and MP robotic kidney transplants (RAKT). METHODS: We queried our prospectively maintained robotic kidney transplant database (RoKIT) for LD RAKT performed from October 2019 to October 2025. Baseline, transplant, and post-transplant characteristics were compared. Temporal trends of operative and anastomosis times were plotted to visualize our learning curves. RESULTS: A total of 46 SP and 47 MP RAKT were performed. Our first SP case was performed in 2019 and the first MP case in 2023. Baseline characteristics were similar. In the SP group, operative times (4:21 vs 3:58, hr:min, p=0.01) and anastomosis times (47 vs 36 min, p<0.001) were longer. Warm ischemia time was slightly longer in the MP group (4 vs 3 min, p=0.045). Multiple arteries were more frequent in MP (25.5% vs 0%, p<0.001). Postoperative pain was lower in SP (median 5 vs 7, p=0.005). Other postoperative outcomes were comparable. CONCLUSIONS: Single-port and multi-port robotic-assisted kidney transplantation (RAKT) demonstrated comparable outcomes in living donor recipients. The longer operative times observed with the SP approach likely reflect its adoption earlier in our learning curve rather than procedural limitations. With lower postoperative pain and comparable outcomes, SP appears to be a safe and viable alternative to the conventional multi-port approach.

title: IP11-10: From Innovation to Expertise: Learning Curve and Outcomes in the Largest Series of Single-Port Robotic Kidney Transplantation
parentSessionTitle: IP11: Transplantation & Vascular Surgery
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Single-port robotic extraperitoneal kidney transplantation (SP-RAKT) is a novel, minimally invasive transplant approach, offering a single incision that enhances cosmesis and potentially accelerates recovery. Yet, data on its learning curve and clinical outcomes remain scarce. In this study, we present the world’s largest single-center experience with SP-RAKT, highlighting the procedural learning curve, perioperative safety, and early clinical outcomes. METHODS: We queried our prospectively maintained transplant database (RoKiT) and retrospectively analyzed the data. CUSUM analysis was used to assess learning curves for operative and anastomosis times. Descriptive statistics were used to summarize perioperative and graft outcomes. RESULTS: From October 2019 to October 2025, 65 SP-RAKT were performed by a single surgeon. Median age was 50.4 years, the median BMI was 31.5 kg/m2, and 40 (61%) were male. 46 (71%) were living-donor recipients. Two cases involved dual artery anastomosis, one was a simultaneous kidney–pancreas, and one was a dual kidney transplant. 28 (43.1%) patients were preemptive. Median operative time was 4 hours and 18 minutes, and anastomosis time was 48 minutes. CUSUM analysis demonstrated proficiency after 19 cases. Eight patients (12%) developed delayed graft function (6 deceased, 2 living), 4 (6%) required ICU admission, and 21 (32%) were readmitted within 30 days. Length of hospital stay was 2 days. Median creatinine improved from 2.58 mg/dL at discharge to 1.47 mg/dL at 3 months. One case was converted to open, and 2 patients developed lymphoceles. No graft loss or patient death was observed. CONCLUSIONS: Our experience demonstrates that SP-RAKT is technically feasible and associated with safe, reproducible outcomes. A learning curve of 19 cases was identified, beyond which operative efficiency plateaued. As the largest series reported to date, this study reinforces the potential for broader implementation of SP-robotic platforms in kidney transplantation. | | | --- | | |

title: IP11-11: Pushing Boundaries: Single Center Comparison of Robotic and Open Dual Kidney Transplantation
parentSessionTitle: IP11: Transplantation & Vascular Surgery
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Dual kidney transplantation (DKT) allows the utilization of marginal donor kidneys, expanding the donor pool and decreasing organ discard. Traditionally performed through an open approach, it remains technically demanding and carries greater morbidity than standard kidney transplantation. Robotic kidney transplantation reduces surgical morbidity and offers a minimally invasive alternative. We present our early institutional experience comparing robotic and open DKT, demonstrating its feasibility and safety. METHODS: A retrospective review was performed of all DKT procedures conducted between January 2024 and July 2025. Donor and recipient demographics, operative details, perioperative outcomes, and graft function at discharge and follow-up were analyzed. A descriptive comparison between robotic and open cases was performed to assess feasibility and early outcomes. RESULTS: Ten DKTs were performed, 5 robotic and 5 open. Baseline characteristics were comparable, including recipient age (73 vs 67 years), BMI (26.8 vs 25.2 kg/m2), and KDPI (81 vs 96). Four robotic cases used a multi-port approach (two Pfannenstiel, two transvaginal insertions) and one single-port with a midline incision. Among robotic cases, two kidneys were transplanted bilaterally and three transplants ipsilateral, while in the open group, four cases were ipsilateral and one bilateral. In the open group, four used an extended right Gibson and one a bilateral anterior rectus sheath incision. Median operative time was longer in robotic cases (5 hr 18 min vs 3 hr 45 min), while blood loss (100 vs 200 ml) and hospital stay (4 vs 5 days) were lower. Median pain scores at day 1 were 6 in robotic vs 7 in open cases. Among open recipients, three required transfusions and one developed a lymphocele. One robotic recipient required readmission due to primary graft failure. CONCLUSIONS: Robotic dual kidney transplantation is a feasible alternative to the open approach, utilizing minimally invasive techniques that avoid extended or bilateral incisions. Ipsilateral graft placement is feasible, preserving the contralateral side for future use or when unsuitable due to calcification, prior grafts, or arterial disease. Our experience across varied incisions and robotic platforms highlights the versatility and expanding potential of robotics in kidney transplantation. | | | --- | | |

title: IP11-12: Robot assisted kidney transplantation with double artery allografts: perioperative and graft survival outcome comparison of different anastomotic techniques from a tertiary centre
parentSessionTitle: IP11: Transplantation & Vascular Surgery

speakers.jobTitle: Vattikuti Fellow of Robotic Urologic Surgery

fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: The early concerns of multiple vessel grafts as a contraindication for robot assisted kidney transplantation (RAKT) have been largely dispelled by many evidences in recent literature. In this article, we described our experience with the different perioperative parameters and outcomes of RAKT with double artery allograft kidney. METHODS: This is a retrospective analysis of the patients who underwent RAKT with double artery reconstruction over six years. The patients with deceased renal transplantation, ABO incompatibilities, more than two arteries, and less than one-year follow-up were excluded. Three techniques were used: end-to-side anastomosis, double anastomosis to external iliac arteries and pantaloons anastomosis. RESULTS: Out of total 80 patients included in the study, end-to-side, trousering, and double anastomosis were done in 45, 11, and 24 patients. The mean age, body-mass-index (BMI), Charlson Comorbidity Index were similar in both groups. The cold ischemia time, arterial anastomosis time, and console time were significantly more in the patients with double anastomosis (32.11 ± 6.97, 35.64 ± 4.50, and 38.17 ± 5.36 minutes; 12.80 ± 4.34, 14.45 ± 3.21, and 19.38 ± 4.77 minutes; 156.09 ± 49.13, 169.91 ± 32.04, and 185.21 ± 57.78 minutes, respectively, p<0.05). The warm ischemia time, setting up time, total surgical time, blood loss, blood transfusion rate, postoperative hemodialysis, hospital stay, pain Score (Visual Analogue Score at postoperative day1,2, and 3), re-exploration, complication as per Clavien Dindo classification were comparable among all the three groups. Graft function in terms of serum creatinine, eGFR (Glomerular filtration Rate) for one, three months and one-year, delayed graft function, graft loss rates were similar (Table). 80 patients with double-arterial-anastomosis were compared with 194 patients who underwent single-arterial-anastomosis during the period. The console time, total surgical time, and arterial anastomosis time were significantly less (p<0.05). However, the other parameters like hospital stay, pain score, re-exploration, complication rate, graft function, graft loss were similar in both groups. CONCLUSIONS: Robot assisted kidney transplantation can be performed safely and effectively in recipients with double renal arteries with good results without increasing complications. | | | --- | | |

title: IP11-13: Trends in Robotic Kidney Transplantation: A Single-Center Experience of Increasing Volume and Expanding Complexity
parentSessionTitle: IP11: Transplantation & Vascular Surgery
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Once considered experimental, robotic kidney transplantation (RAKT) is becoming more widely adopted. We describe the evolution of our RKT program since 2019, from our first case to one of the largest global experiences, highlighting both growth trajectory and expanding case complexity. METHODS: All RAKT performed from October 2019 to October 2025 were retrospectively analyzed. Annual data were categorized as open vs. robotic, and within robotic cases, by single-port (SP) vs. multi-port (MP) platforms. Complex robotic cases included deceased–donor (DDT), multiple renal arteries (MRA), recipient iliac vessel calcification, dual kidney transplant (DKT), or simultaneous kidney–pancreas (SKP) transplant. Temporal trends were visualized using time-series regression and cumulative trend plots to model robotic adoption. RESULTS: Between 2019 and 2025, 209 robotic kidney transplants (RKT) were performed (65 SP, 144 MP), including 115 deceased-donor (55%) cases. The median recipient age was 55.2 years (IQR, 44.6–62.9) and BMI was 31.8 (IQR, 28.1–36.9). The median operative time was 3 hours 52 min (IQR, 198–275) and anastomosis time was 44 minutes (IQR, 35–53). One case (0.4%) was converted to open surgery. The median hospital stay was 3 days (IQR, 2–4), and delayed graft function occurred in 41 patients (21.5%). The annual volume of RAKT increased from a single case in 2019 to 96 cases by October 2025. Progressive expansion in case complexity was observed over time; in 2025, DDT accounted for 52 cases, MRA grafts for 30 cases, and recipients with calcified vessels for 21 cases. Also, 5 DKT (3 in 2024 and 2 in 2025) and 4 SKP transplants (all in 2025) were performed robotically. Institutional transplant activity demonstrated a consistent annual increase, accompanied by a declining trend in open transplant procedures beginning in 2024. CONCLUSIONS: This study demonstrates the evolution of a new robotic kidney transplant program into a high volume, complex practice within six years. Our findings support the feasibility and reproducibility of RAKT even in challenging scenarios.

title: IP11-14: Age-Stratified Length of Stay Benefit of Robotic Versus Open Approach in Deceased-Donor Kidney Transplantation: Evidence from a European Multicenter Registry
parentSessionTitle: IP11: Transplantation & Vascular Surgery
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Prolonged hospitalization after kidney transplantation increases the risk of infection, deconditioning, and healthcare costs—particularly in older recipients. Robotic-assisted kidney transplantation (RAKT) may mitigate these risks by reducing wound burden and enhancing early mobilization, yet robotic access remains limited. Identifying which recipients derive the greatest benefit is therefore essential for case selection and resource allocation. This study evaluated whether increasing recipient age modifies the postoperative length-of-stay (LOS) advantage of RAKT compared with open deceased-donor kidney transplantation (DDKT). METHODS: All adult DDKT recipients (2018–2025) from a prospective European registry were analyzed. Living donors and conversions were excluded. LOS (days) was modeled as a function of surgical approach, age, BMI, and metabolic comorbidities. An interaction term tested whether age modified the LOS difference between techniques. Propensity weighting (age, BMI, comorbidity count) estimated confirmatory average treatment effects (ATEs) within age strata. RESULTS: Among 342 deceased-donor recipients, RAKT was associated with shorter hospitalization across all ages, with increasing benefit in older patients. Overall: RAKT reduced mean LOS by 2.2 days (p=0.04). Age effect: Each additional year prolonged LOS by 0.1 days (p=0.02). Interaction: The robotic advantage increased by ~0.25 days per year (p=0.09), yielding a 2–3-day gain per decade. Predicted LOS was similar below age 40 but diverged thereafter, reaching an 8–10-day shorter stay with RAKT by age 70. Propensity-weighted analyses confirmed this gradient (no difference <50 years; ~5 days shorter ≥60 years; (https://www.auajournals.org/doi/abs/10.1097/01.JU.0001191324.44573.90.14#F1)). CONCLUSIONS: In deceased-donor kidney transplantation, RAKT shortens hospitalization for all recipients, with a progressively greater advantage in older or comorbid patients. Because extended LOS increases exposure to nosocomial infection and mobility decline, minimizing hospitalization is particularly valuable in this group. Robotic access appears to offset the effect of aging on LOS, supporting its prioritization for elderly or frail recipients most likely to benefit from enhanced recovery and lower inpatient complication risk. Conducted on behalf of the ERUS-RAKT Working Group, European Association of Urology Robotic Urology Section (ERUS).

title: IP11-15: Does Iliac Vessel Calcification Preclude Candidacy for Robotic Kidney Transplantation?
parentSessionTitle: IP11: Transplantation & Vascular Surgery
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Aorto-iliac vascular calcification is increasingly common among kidney transplant candidates and often considered a contraindication to robotic-assisted kidney transplantation (RAKT). Extensive vascular calcification poses technical challenges during recipient vessel dissection and anastomosis, often prolonging operative time and increasing the risk of complications. Data on the feasibility and outcomes of RAKT in this high-risk cohort are limited. METHODS: We retrospectively reviewed all robotic deceased donor kidney transplants performed between July 2024 and June 2025. Preoperative recipient CT scans were manually reviewed to assess iliac vessel calcification, which was graded based on morphology and thickness (PMID: 40455172): grade 0=no calcification, grade 1=<1 mm, grade 2=1–2 mm, and grade 3=>3 mm. For this study, we included recipients with grade ≥1 (any measurable calcification). Demographic, intraoperative, and postoperative outcomes were analyzed. RESULTS: Among 205 RAKT recipients, 45 (22%) had CT-defined iliac vessel calcification. Compared with non-calcified recipients, those with calcification were older (64 vs 53.5 years, p<.001), received kidneys with higher Kidney Donor Profile Index scores (67% vs 44%, p=.002), and more frequently received deceased-donor kidneys (78% vs 49%, p<.001). Single-port RAKT was less common in the calcified group (64% vs 84%, p=.03). Median hospital stay was longer (4 vs 3 days, p<.001), and delayed graft function (DGF) occurred more in the calcified group (49% vs 12%, p<.001). In the setting of deceased donor recipients, logistic regression showed that DGF was independently associated with BMI, iliac calcification, and multiple arteries. Anastomosis times were similar between the groups. Rates of ICU admission, postoperative complications, readmission, and graft function at 3 months and 1 year were also comparable. CONCLUSIONS: RAKT in recipients with iliac vessel calcification is feasible and safe in carefully selected patients. Although the calcified group demonstrated higher rates of delayed graft function, perioperative parameters and graft outcomes at 3 months and 1 year were comparable to those of non-calcified recipients. The presence of iliac calcification should not be considered an absolute contraindication to RAKT but rather a factor warranting individualized preoperative evaluation and surgical planning. | | | --- | | |

title: IP11-16: Robotic Kidney-Pancreas Transplantation – The Cleveland Clinic Experience with Ipsilateral Allograft Placement and Single Port Approach
parentSessionTitle: IP11: Transplantation & Vascular Surgery
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Simultaneous kidney/pancreas transplantation (SPK) is the most definitive treatment for Type 1 diabetes with end-stage renal manifestations. Robot-assisted SPK may mitigate the morbidity of open SPK, however it has not yet been widely adopted. Reports of robotic SPK describe surgery with the multiport system and placement of the allografts on the bilateral iliac vessels, rendering a future second transplant more challenging. Here we present outcomes of our robotic SPK recipients. METHODS: Retrospective review of patients who underwent robotic SPK at our institution from 1/2025 – 10/2025. Donor/recipient variables, intraoperative data and postoperative outcomes were collected. RESULTS: Four patients underwent robotic SPK during the study period. Three had surgery using the multiport system, with four 8 mm robotic ports, 12 mm assistant port and Pfannenstiel incision to introduce the allografts. One was transplanted with the single port system, with graft introduction and implantation performed through a 5 cm periumbilical incision. Pancreata were prepared with iliac artery Y-graft anastomoses to the superior mesenteric and splenic arteries similar to the open approach. Our first patient had placement of the kidney on the left and pancreas on the right. The subsequent three had anastomosis of the kidney to the left external iliac vessels, kidney reperfusion, re-clamping distal to the kidney and pancreas implantation while maintaining kidney perfusion. Enzymatic drainage was enteric in all cases with robotic hand-sewn anastomosis of donor duodenum to recipient small bowel. Mean operative time was 5h 57 mins, with mean kidney and pancreas vascular anastomotic times of 30 and 41 minutes. Our first patient was admitted to the ICU intubated and extubated POD1. All four had otherwise unremarkable postoperative courses and were discharged after a median of four hospital days. None had major complications or needed reintervention. At most recent follow-up, all had good allograft function. CONCLUSIONS: Robot-assisted SPK is safe and feasible. We demonstrate excellent outcomes and short hospital length of stay, with operative and anastomotic times comparable to the open approach. We believe this to be the first description of ipsilateral graft placement, saving the contralateral iliac vessels for a future transplant, and the first report of SPK through a single micro-incision using the single-port robot.

title: IP11-17: Prediction and explanation of kidney transplant outcomes with multimodal anesthesia timeseries deep learning
parentSessionTitle: IP11: Transplantation & Vascular Surgery
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: An increasing proportion of kidney transplants are sourced from deceased donors. However, deceased donor transplants have a higher risk of delayed graft function (DGF). We hypothesize that the complex interaction between operative parameters such as hemodynamics, fluid strategies, and medication use can impact perfusion to the newly transplanted kidney and influence DGF. Clinicians' limited capacity to analyze these intricate data poses a challenge in identifying subtle factors contributing to DGF, and in choosing optimal management strategies to mitigate these factors. METHODS: We have used time-series focused machine learning strategies to explain and predict DGF with multimodal inputs, incorporating tabular pre-transplant donor and recipient characteristics, with granular intraoperative anesthesia time-series from deceased-donor kidney transplant surgeries (n=424), both donation after cardiac death and neurologically-determined death (DCD and NDD). Two models were constructed: DGFpredict-time, based on a multimodal convolutional neural network, and DGFpredict-explain based on gradient-boosted trees. RESULTS: 121 DGF events were captured in our cohort derived from a single academic medical center (57/276 NDDs, 64/148 DCDs). DGFpredict-time predicts 80.07\\% (CI: 77.4-82.7\\% in 10-fold bootstrap) of DGF events in test splits, resulting in an AUROC of 0.87 (0.85-0.88). For DGFpredict-time, timeseries salience maps identified post-vascular anastomosis BP as the most influential feature of intraoperative management for DGF incidence in DCD kidneys, with normalized salience post anastomosis being 84.0\\% versus 37.8\\% pre-anastomosis (in DCDs). DGFpredict-explain was found to be 74.79\\% (CI 72.2-77.4\\%) accurate for DGF, AUROC 0.71 (0.69-0.72). In SHAP explanatory analyses, pre and post-anastomosis MAP was found to be within the top-5 predictors of DGF incidence. Dependency analysis indicated a MAP of 76.0 mmHg (or below) was identified as an optimal target at which to start pressors, and 37.3 cc/kg cumulative intraoperative crystalloid as an optimum for DGF prevention. Lastly, our gradient-boosted tree models were run in reverse with grid search to determine optimal recommendations for selected patient vignettes, showcasing personalized model recommendations for anesthesia targets, fluids, and pressor use based on donor or recipient preoperative characteristics. CONCLUSIONS: Our explanatory ML models help identify patients at risk of DGF, point to modifiable components of intraoperative management to prevent DGF, and demonstrate new methods to analyze complex timeseries data from the operating room.

title: IP11-18: Artificial Intelligence–Based Integrative Model for Predicting Kidney Graft Loss: Comparison with the Estimated Post-Transplant Survival (EPTS) Score
parentSessionTitle: IP11: Transplantation & Vascular Surgery
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Traditional risk indices such as the Estimated Post-Transplant Survival (EPTS) score rely primarily on pre-transplant recipient characteristics and exclude dynamic post-operative and surgical variables. We developed and validated an artificial intelligence (AI)–based integrative model that incorporates early renal function, immunosuppressive intensity, and surgical parameters to predict kidney graft loss, and compared its performance with an EPTS-based logistic regression model. METHODS: A retrospective cohort of 207 kidney-transplant recipients (2010–2024) from a single tertiary center was analyzed. Variables included recipient age, BMI, diabetes status, donor type, ischemia time, and renal function (eGFR at 1 month and 1 year). Feature engineering added ΔeGFR (1-year – 1-month) and an immunosuppressive regimen-intensity score. A HistGradientBoostingClassifier (XGBoost-like) algorithm was trained using balanced bootstrap sampling (1:1), five-fold cross-validation, and a 70/30 hold-out validation split. Performance was compared against a logistic regression model based on EPTS variables. RESULTS: A total of 207 kidney transplant recipients were analyzed. Baseline characteristics are summarized in Table 1. Mean age was 49.4 ± 12.6 years, and 58.9 % were male. Diabetes was present in 66.6 % of recipients, and 12 % received a kidney from a living donor. 32 (15.5%) experienced graft loss. Patients with graft loss tended to be older (52.3 ± 11.8 years) and more frequently diabetic (78.1 %) compared to those with functioning grafts (48.8 ± 12.7 years; 64.6 %). The predominant immunosuppressive regimen was tacrolimus + mycophenolate \+ steroids (77.8 %) across all groups. The AI model achieved a cross-validated AUC=0.79 ± 0.04, outperforming the EPTS-based logistic regression model (AUC=0.60). CONCLUSIONS: This integrative AI model combines surgical, functional, and pharmacologic data to predict graft loss more accurately than EPTS alone. The model demonstrates robust discrimination and interpretability, supporting its potential for personalized risk stratification and clinical decision support in kidney transplantation.

title: IP11-19: AI-based Quantification of Collagen Microarchitecture on 3-Month Protocol Biopsy Predicts Early Renal Function Decline After Kidney Transplantation
parentSessionTitle: IP11: Transplantation & Vascular Surgery
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Early interstitial fibrosis is a key determinant of long-term graft function after kidney transplantation. However, at 3 months post-transplant, fibrotic changes are often subtle, and conventional histologic scores provide limited prognostic value. We evaluated whether AI-based quantification of collagen microarchitecture on 3-month protocol biopsies could predict early post-transplant renal function decline. METHODS: We analyzed 151 living-donor kidney transplant recipients at Kagawa University. Three-month protocol biopsies stained with Masson trichrome were processed using a computer vision–based pipeline for automated collagen segmentation and extraction of features including collagen area, thickness, fiber density, tortuosity, curvature, branching points, and orientation. Patients were divided into training and validation cohorts (2:1). Cox proportional hazards models were developed in the training cohort with five-fold cross-validation. Multivariate models combined features significant in univariate analysis with additional features improving model performance. The final model was validated in the hold-out validation cohort (N=52). The endpoint was ≥20% eGFR decline within 24 months from baseline. Survival curves were generated using the Kaplan-Meier method with log-rank testing. RESULTS: Among 151 recipients, 57 (37.7%) experienced ≥20% eGFR decline within 2 years. Disordered collagen orientation (HR=2.38, 95% CI 1.37 – 4.13, p<0.05) and increased branching (HR=1.71, 95% CI 1.01 – 2.90, p<0.05) were significantly associated with early eGFR decline. A multivariable Cox model integrating the significant features with fiber curvature (not independently significant) improved predictive performance in the validation cohort (HR=2.49, 95% CI 1.01–6.18, p<0.05). CONCLUSIONS: AI-based quantification of collagen microarchitecture on 3-month protocol biopsies predicts early renal function decline after kidney transplantation, providing objective morphologic biomarkers for risk stratification and post-transplant surveillance.

title: IP11-20: More than KDPI: Failure to Achieve an estimated GFR>30 mL/min Within Three Months Post-Kidney Transplant
parentSessionTitle: IP11: Transplantation & Vascular Surgery
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: The Kidney Donor Profile Index (KDPI) is widely used to predict post-transplant graft survival. Although higher values are associated with delayed graft function (DGF), there are significant limitations in predicting early graft function. In our study, we investigated donor and recipient factors associated with the inability to achieve an estimated GFR (eGFR) of 30 ml/min within 3 months post-transplant, and the subsequent impact on one-year outcomes. METHODS: We retrospectively reviewed 364 adult kidney transplant recipients at a single center. Recipients were divided into two groups: those who achieved an eGFR >30 ml/min (n=325) and those who did not (n=36). Continuous and categorical variables were compared using Student's t-test and chi-square analysis. RESULTS: Failure to achieve an eGFR >30 ml/min by 3 months was associated with increased donor age (51.4 years vs 41.3), increased recipient age (62.6 years vs 58.7 years), donor/recipient gender discrepancy (13.4% vs 7%), female donor, open-offer kidney, longer warm ischemia time (WIT) (30.2 vs 16.5 minutes), higher KDPI (62% vs 50%), donation after circulatory death (DCD), and a non-tacrolimus based regimen, all with statistical significance. This was also associated with a subsequently higher readmission rate (69% vs 40%) and an eGFR persistently <30 ml/min at 1 year. Multivariable regression analysis remained significant for older donor age (OR 0.889, p=0.002) and longer warm ischemia time (OR 0.979, p=0.008) as independent factors with decreased ability to achieve eGFR>30 ml/min by 3 months post-transplant, as well subsequent readmission within 90 days (OR 0.372, p=0.025). There was no statistically significant difference in achieving an eGFR>30 ml/min associated with donor/recipient age discrepancy (>10 years), blood loss, cold ischemia time, or recipient gender, BMI, race, operative time, or dialysis vintage. CONCLUSIONS: Failure to achieve an eGFR>30 ml/min within three months post-transplant can be predictive of diminished graft function at 1-year and is associated with higher readmission rates. Our study supports the relationship of high KDPI with worse early graft function; however, warm ischemia time can also be carefully considered when evaluating deceased donor kidneys in addition to KDPI. | | | --- | | |

title: IP11-21: Maybe two is better than none: Evaluating the benefit of expanded criteria donor dual kidney transplants
parentSessionTitle: IP11: Transplantation & Vascular Surgery
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Marginal kidneys such as expanded criteria donor (ECD) kidneys and kidneys from donors with diabetes have been utilised increasingly to address the shortage of deceased donor kidneys. Although they present a higher risk of allograft failure, they may offer survival benefit over remaining on the waitlist. Dual kidney transplantation (DKT) is one way of utilising marginal ECD kidneys that would otherwise have been discarded. In this study, we present outcomes from our 16-year experience of performing dual kidney transplantation at our centre. Objective: to evaluate if ECD DKT provided any survival benefit to patients compared to remaining on the waitlist. METHODS: A retrospective analysis of dual kidney transplants performed at our centre between 2009-2024 was carried out to evaluate various surgical, graft and patient outcomes. ECD kidneys were considered for DKT if the Remuzzi score was between 4-6. Based on the waitlist in 2009, survival data of patients who received ECD DKT was compared to those of patients who remained waitlisted. Graft and patient outcomes were also specifically compared between diabetic and non-diabetic donor kidneys utilised for dual kidney transplantation. Additionally, target trial emulation was conducted to assess the effect of duration from waitlist to transplant on overall survival, taking into consideration patients' age, gender, and dialysis vintage. RESULTS: 241 patients were included, of which 38 (15.8%) were ECD DKT recipients and 203 (84.2%) received no transplant. 1-year and 5-year graft survival of dual kidney transplants were 87% and 71% respectively. ECD DKT recipients had 29% lower risk of mortality than waitlist patients, although this was not statistically significant (95% CI 0.32-1.64; p=0.38). This effect was persistent when overall survival was adjusted for gender, age and dialysis vintage (HR 0.84; 95% CI 0.38-1.86; p=0.68). On subgroup analysis among ECD DKT recipients, graft survival and overall survival was similar between donors with and without diabetes (HR 1.69; 95% CI 0.38-.86; p=0.46). Finally, on trial emulation, ECD DKT within 6 years of initial waitlisting was found to yield the greatest survival benefit compared to longer wait times. ECD DKT recipients who received a transplant within 6 years of waitlist had a 23% risk reduction in mortality (95% CI 0.11-0.38, p<0.05), and increased restricted mean survival time of 0.84 years (95%9 CI 0.25-1.46, p<0.05) compared to waitlist patients who did not receive a transplant. CONCLUSIONS: ECD DKT at our centre confer survival benefit, particularly with a 23% reduction in mortality if transplant is done within 6 years from date of waitlist. Donor diabetes was not a significant factor on survival post-transplant. This study supports the use of DKT in marginal ECD kidneys, which can also help to address the shortage of deceased donor kidneys.

title: IP11-23: Outcomes for localized renal cell carcinoma in solid organ transplant recipients is comparable to non-transplant recipients
parentSessionTitle: IP11: Transplantation & Vascular Surgery

speakers.organization: University of Wisconsin Hospitals and Clinics

fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Solid organ transplant recipients (SOTRs) on chronic immunosuppression who develop localized renal cell carcinoma (RCC) present management challenges due to possible increased oncologic risk and comorbidity. Few data are available for RCC standard therapies (surgery, ablation, or surveillance) to demonstrate whether outcomes are comparable to non-SOTRs. This matched cohort study evaluated outcomes of SOTRs on chronic immunosuppressive therapy with localized RCC to a non-SOTR cohort. METHODS: Patients were identified with tissue diagnosis of localized RCC after transplantation between 2000-2020. Transplant patients were matched 1:2 as able to non-transplant patients based on treatment type (surgery, ablation, or surveillance), age, tumor size, and grade. Clinical variables and survival outcomes were compared. Cox models evaluated if transplant status was associated with survival across different treatment strategies adjusting for confounders. RESULTS: 81 SOTRs with localized RCC were matched to 161 non-SOTRs. Age, tumor size, stage and grade were similar between SOTR and non-SOTR cohorts (p>0.5 for all). Among SOTRs, median age was 57 years and initial treatments included surgery (65%), ablation (23%), and active surveillance (10%). Most common histologies were clear cell (43%) and papillary (41%) RCC. Median tumor size was 3.0 cm, and median follow-up was 68 months. Among all SOTRs, 3-year MFS and OS were 97% and 88%, respectively. In the surgical cohort (SOTR n=53; non-SOTR n=104), SOTRs had greater comorbidity and underwent radical nephrectomy more often (p<0.05 for both). Postsurgical complications were higher (11% vs 3%, P=0.04). Metastasis-free (MFS) and overall survival (OS) were similar to non-SOTR ( Fig A).In the ablation cohort (SOTR n=19; non-SOTR n=43), local recurrence free survival was higher in SOTRs compared to non-SOTRs (log-rank P=0.01). MFS and OS did not differ ( Fig B).In the active surveillance (SOTR n=9; non-SOTR n=14), SOTRs had comparable MFS and OS. Among SOTR, no metastasis occurred over a median follow-up of 89 months. CONCLUSIONS: SOTRs with localized RCC have similar oncologic outcomes compared to non-SOTR regardless of management strategy for localized RCC. Carefully selected SOTRs with localized RCC may be offered percutaneous ablation or active surveillance. Larger, prospective studies are warranted.

title: IP11-24: Comprehensive management strategies and clinical outcomes in ABO-incompatible living donor kidney transplantation: A single-center cohort study of high-titer (=1:256) versus low-titer recipients
parentSessionTitle: IP11: Transplantation & Vascular Surgery
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: ABO-incompatible living donor kidney transplantation (ABOi-LDKT) is a critical pathway to expand the donor pool. However, recipients with high preformed ABO antibody titers (IgM/IgG ≥1:256) present significant perioperative challenges, including difficulties in antibody depletion, and increased risks of bleeding, antibody rebound, rejection, thrombotic microangiopathy (TMA), and infection. This study aimed to systematically evaluate the comprehensive management strategy and clinical efficacy of our center's desensitization protocol—the "Friendship Protocol" in ABOi-LDKT recipients. METHODS: A retrospective analysis was conducted on 29 ABOi-LDKT recipients between 2023 and 2025\. Patients were divided into a high-titer group (≥1:256, n=8) and a low-titer group (1:256, n=21) based on preoperative ABO antibody titers. Baseline characteristics included gender, age, BMI, PRA status, and plasma exchange (PE) strategies. Both groups received the "Friendship Protocol" for intensified desensitization: CD20 inhibitor (200 mg for weight ≥50kg; 100 mg for 50kg) combined with sequential PE (target titer ≤1:16), with conversion to or supplementation with AB plasma if needed. The preoperative immunosuppressive regimen consisted of Tacrolimus + MPA, followed by sequential administration of rATG and a single dose of Complement C5 inhibitor (900 mg) to prevent ABMR and TMA. Primary endpoints included renal function recovery, incidence of rejection, and complications. RESULTS: No significant differences were observed between the high-titer and low-titer groups in the baseline data. The high-titer group required significantly more PE sessions (median 6 vs. 2, P=0.002) and more frequently received combined compatible and AB PE (4 vs. 0 cases, P=0.003). All high-titer recipients achieved the target preoperative titer through flexible PE, including the use of AB plasma in 5 cases. Postoperatively, antibody rebound occurred in 5 cases (71.4%), with a peak titer of 1:128, but none developed clinical symptoms or rejection. Serum creatinine levels decreased significantly in both groups postoperatively, with a 100% dialysis discontinuation rate and no instances of DGF. Four cases of TCMR occurred (no intergroup difference), all of which were reversed after immunosuppressive adjustment. No ABMR or TMA events were recorded. In the high-titer group, 2 patients (28.6%) experienced hemoglobin decline related to bleeding, managed successfully with transfusion and coagulation correction. Two patients (28.6%) developed BK viruria, which subsided after adjustment of immunosuppression. No significant differences were found between groups regarding severe complications (bleeding, infection) or drug adverse events. CONCLUSIONS: The "Friendship Protocol," incorporating individualized antibody depletion (including AB plasma augmentation) and intensified immunosuppression (sequential Rituximab, rATG, and Eculizumab), successfully enabled safe transplantation in high-titer ABOi-LDKT recipients. Despite requiring more intensive plasma exchange, the high-titer group demonstrated comparable renal function recovery, rejection control, and overall safety to the low-titer group. This strategy provides a replicable perioperative management pathway for challenging ABOi-LDKT cases.

title: IP11-25: Novel Use of a Breast Tissue Expander in Kidney Retransplantation: A Case Report
parentSessionTitle: IP11: Transplantation & Vascular Surgery
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Kidney transplantation remains the gold standard for treating patients with end-stage renal disease (ESRD), offering superior survival and quality of life compared to dialysis. Despite a 5-year allograft survival rate of 77–88%, an increasing number of patients require repeat transplantation, now accounting for approximately 15% of kidney transplants in the United States. Allograft nephrectomy of a previous transplant is often leveraged to create room for a new graft in the original iliac fossa. Total resection of the allograft are major operative procedures which require dissection through dense scar, which then results in further scar deposition in the retransplant site. This case report describes a novel surgical approach using a tissue expander to maintain a potential space and minimize scar formation following kidney allograft nephrectomy. METHODS: A 37-year-old male with diabetes mellitus and ESRD had previously undergone simultaneous kidney-pancreas transplantation. The kidney graft later failed due to chronic rejection. During the left iliac fossa allograft nephrectomy, a tissue expander was placed within the resected fossa to preserve the surgical space and prevent scar formation before the anticipated living donor retransplantation. The expander remained in place for two months. RESULTS: At the time of the planned living donor kidney retransplantation, the tissue expander was removed, and the new graft was successfully implanted into the preserved iliac fossa. The procedure was uncomplicated, and the patient demonstrated immediate graft function postoperatively. Although the preserved space facilitated reoperation, a significant pseudocapsule was noted both around the fossa and enveloping the target recipient vessels, necessitating meticulous dissection. This intraoperative finding had not been previously described in similar contexts. CONCLUSIONS: This case represents the first documented use of a tissue expander to maintain an iliac fossa following kidney allograft nephrectomy prior to retransplantation. The technique effectively preserved surgical space and supported an uncomplicated graft implantation. However, the formation of a pseudocapsule indicates the need for further study to refine this approach and evaluate its long-term outcomes.

title: IP11-26: An isochoric supercooled porcine kidney sustains life upon autotransplantation and contralateral nephrectomy
parentSessionTitle: IP11: Transplantation & Vascular Surgery
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: There is a critical need to enhance preservation strategies for donor organs for transplantation. Isochoric supercooling – a cryoprotectant-free method by which graft temperature is lowered beneath 0 °C without ice formation – has shown promise for organ preservation in ex vivo models of multiple organs. However, it has not been demonstrated in large animal transplantation with long-term functional outcomes. Here we report a case study of a successful autotransplantation of a porcine kidney following multi-day supercooling with sustained long-term in vivo function. METHODS: The right kidney of a juvenile Yorkshire pig was surgically removed and flushed with clinical cold storage solution. The kidney was then placed in an isochoric chamber for controlled multi-day supercooling to -4 °C. On the day of autotransplantation, the kidney was rewarmed and kept on ice before implantation. Vascular anastomoses were performed to the aorta and inferior vena cava. A ureteral stent was placed across the ureterocystostomy. The animal was recovered for 5 days, simulating the clinical practice of providing dialysis to transplant recipients in the first days after transplantation, after which the left kidney was removed through a flank incision. The animal was then recovered and followed until 30 days after autotransplantation. Urine output was assessed semi-quantitatively using absorbent pads underneath the cage. Kidney functional panels were drawn at regular intervals through a jugular central venous catheter. RESULTS: Multi-day supercooling to -4 °C and autotransplantation with delayed contralateral nephrectomy were successfully performed. The animal survived for 30 days after autotransplantation, during which it continued to urinate and exhibited stabilization of blood urea nitrogen, creatinine, and potassium. CONCLUSIONS: This case study demonstrates that isochoric supercooling can preserve porcine kidneys for multi-day durations with sustained post-transplant function, supporting its promise as a clinically translatable organ preservation strategy.

title: IP11-27: Silicon (Si)-Based Agent Suppresses Oxidative Stress and Antibody-Mediated Rejection, Promoting Long-Term Graft Survival after Kidney Transplantation
parentSessionTitle: IP11: Transplantation & Vascular Surgery

speakers.organization: The University of Osaka Graduate School of Medicine

fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Antibody-mediated rejection (ABMR) is a major determinant of long-term graft survival after kidney transplantation. Ischemia–reperfusion injury (IRI) amplifies both innate and adaptive immune responses through the excessive production of reactive oxygen species (ROS), leading to oxidative tissue damage and contributing to the development of ABMR. We focused on molecular hydrogen, which possesses antioxidant properties and can suppress ROS production, and developed a novel orally administered silicon (Si)–based agent that continuously generates molecular hydrogen in the intestinal tract. In this study, we evaluated the efficacy of this Si-based hydrogen-generating agent as a novel therapeutic strategy to reduce oxidative stress and immune activation after kidney transplantation. METHODS: Male Lewis rats received kidney grafts from Fischer-344 (allogeneic) or Lewis (syngeneic) donors (F344→Lewis model). The Si-based agent was administered orally starting one week before transplantation and continued thereafter. Short-term (1 week) and long-term (3 months) models were used to evaluate early immune responses and chronic graft outcomes, respectively. Endpoints included oxidative stress markers, histopathology, immunostaining, graft gene expression, donor-specific antibody (DSA) levels, renal function, and safety. RESULTS: At 1 week, Si treatment significantly reduced serum malondialdehyde (MDA) levels and tended to lower urinary 8-OHdG, indicating attenuation of oxidative stress. CD3+ T-cell and peritubular inflammatory cell infiltration were decreased, and DSA binding to donor B cells was significantly reduced. At 3 months, graft survival improved (62% vs. 31%), accompanied by stable serum creatinine and lower urinary protein in the Si-treated group. Chronic graft injury was alleviated: serum MDA levels decreased, PPAR was upregulated, IL-6 and CCL2 were downregulated, macrophage infiltration was reduced, cg scores improved, and C4d deposition was suppressed. DSA levels remained lower at 3 months. No hepatotoxicity or electrolyte abnormalities were observed, and Si administration showed no adverse interaction with cyclosporine. CONCLUSIONS: The orally administered Si-based hydrogen-generating agent suppressed IRI-associated oxidative stress, attenuated both innate and adaptive immune activation, mitigated ABMR, and improved graft survival and function. Given its established safety profile and convenient oral administration, this approach represents a promising therapeutic strategy to prevent or ameliorate chronic ABMR and improve long-term kidney transplant outcomes.

title: IP11-28: Neutrophil Suppression in Xenotransplantation Using Genetically Modified Swine Endothelial Cells in a Novel Xenotransplantation Model
parentSessionTitle: IP11: Transplantation & Vascular Surgery

speakers.organization: The University of Osaka Graduate School of Medicine

fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Recent clinical attempts of xenogeneic kidney transplantation from genetically engineered pigs to humans have drawn worldwide attention, demonstrating the potential feasibility of pig-to-human organ transplantation. However, early xenograft injury remains a major challenge, mainly driven by innate immune mechanisms such as neutrophil-mediated cytotoxicity. Although existing genetically modified pigs express human CD47 (hCD47), its effect on neutrophils is insufficient. PlexinB2, which suppresses neutrophil activity via SEMA4D, has been suggested to provide superior protective effects. In this study, we evaluated the role of human PlexinB2 (hPlexinB2) in xenotransplantation. METHODS: Human neutrophils were co-cultured with swine endothelial cells (SECs) expressing human CD47 (hCD47), human PlexinB2 (hPlexinB2), or wild type controls. Neutrophil-mediated cytotoxicity, reactive oxygen species (ROS) production, and neutrophil extracellular trap (NET) formation were quantified using flow cytometry and WST-8 viability assays. For in vivo analysis, SECs were transplanted subcutaneously into humanized NOG mice (hG-CSF knock-in) reconstituted with human hematopoietic stem cells. Neutrophil infiltration into SEC grafts was assessed by flow cytometry and immunohistochemical staining for human markers, including CD66b and myeloperoxidase. RESULTS: Compared with wild-type SECs, both hCD47- and hPlexinB2-expressing SECs significantly suppressed neutrophil-mediated cytotoxicity (P=0.005 and P=0.002, respectively). Among them, hPlexinB2 induced greater reductions in ROS production (p<0.01) and NET formation (P=0.002). In vivo, SEC grafts were infiltrated by human neutrophils; however, in hPlexinB2 grafts, flow cytometry demonstrated a decreased number of CD66b-positive neutrophils (p<0.001), and myeloperoxidase staining revealed significantly fewer human neutrophils compared with WT (p<0.01). CONCLUSIONS: We established the first in vivo murine xenotransplantation model of human neutrophil responses to pigs. Using this model, we showed that hPlexinB2 markedly suppressed neutrophil activity in xenotransplantation, suggesting that hPlexinB2 expression in pigs may be a strategy to enhance xenograft survival.

title: IP11-29: Creatinine Trajectories, A Dynamic Predictor Of Post Kidney Transplant Recovery And Delayed Graft Function
parentSessionTitle: IP11: Transplantation & Vascular Surgery
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Delayed Graft Function (DGF) remains a widely used outcome metric after kidney transplantation, yet binary definitions fail to capture the dynamic nature of early graft recovery. Creatinine trajectories offer a quantitative alternative, potentially improving prediction and guiding clinical decision-making METHODS: We analyzed 211 kidney transplant recipients (2024-2025) at Cleveland Clinic Weston: living donors (n=22), DBD (n=98), DCD with NRP (n=29), DCD without NRP (n=56). Creatinine slopes were derived via least-squares regression across three recovery phases (Day 1-7, 7-30, 30-90). Multivariable logistic regression assessed DGF predictors, adjusting for KDPI, ischemia time, and BMI. RESULTS: Phase 1 slopes demonstrated the fastest decline for DBD grafts (-0.71), intermediate for DCD-NRP (-0.57), and negligible for DCD non-NRP (+0.02). Phase 2 showed convergence of DCD-NRP with DBD (-0.035), while DCD non-NRP lagged (-0.087). Phase 3 demonstrated stabilization for DBD and DCD-NRP, but persistent variability for DCD non-NRP. Trajectory 2 (Days 7-30) showed the highest predictive performance for DGF (AUC=0.83; Pseudo R2=0.25), exceeding Phase 1 and 3 slopes. Living donors maintained favorable recovery across all phases. CONCLUSIONS: Dynamic creatinine trajectories provide a nuanced, phase-specific assessment of renal recovery and outperform traditional binary DGF definitions. The intermediate recovery phase (Day 7-30) is the most informative predictor, facilitating early risk stratification and clinical interventions. DCD-NRP grafts exhibit recovery kinetics comparable to DBD kidneys, supporting safe expansion of the donor pool. Integrating trajectory-based metrics into transplant practice may improve outcome prediction, reduce unnecessary organ discard, and optimize patient management.

title: IP11-30: Usefulness of Screening for Urological Malignancies After Kidney Transplantation
parentSessionTitle: IP11: Transplantation & Vascular Surgery
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Advances in immunosuppressive therapy have prolonged the survival of kidney transplant recipients; however, they have also led to an increased risk of developing de novo malignancies. Under immunosuppression, the incidence of malignancies is higher than in the general population, and oncological outcomes tend to be poorer. The effectiveness of post-transplant cancer screening remains uncertain, largely due to the limited number of available studies. This study aimed to evaluate the usefulness of regular screening for urological malignancies after kidney transplantation, focusing on its impact on early detection, clinical course, and long-term survival. METHODS: We retrospectively analyzed 2,760 patients who underwent kidney transplantation within the Osaka University Kidney Transplant Group, identifying those with newly diagnosed urological malignancies. Clinical and pathological data at diagnosis, follow-up findings, and details of screening practices were collected. Overall survival (OS) and cancer-specific survival (CSS) were estimated using the Kaplan–Meier method. RESULTS: Among the 2,760 recipients, 321 developed malignancies, corresponding to a cumulative incidence of approximately 40% at 40 years post-transplant. There was no significant difference in cumulative cancer incidence between urological malignancies and other malignancies ( Figure a). Urological malignancies included 47 cases of renal cell carcinoma, 20 of prostate cancer, and 15 of urothelial carcinoma. Recipients who underwent regular cancer screening had significantly better OS and CSS compared with those who did not undergo screening. The 20-year survival rates for patients with urological malignancies were 76.6% for renal cell carcinoma, 84.6% for urothelial carcinoma, and 92.9% for prostate cancer. Notably, patients with urological malignancies had better survival than those with other types of malignancies, and their survival did not differ significantly from recipients without malignancies ( Figure b). CONCLUSIONS: These findings suggest that regular screening for urological malignancies in kidney transplant recipients facilitates earlier diagnosis and contributes to improved long-term survival. Implementing individualized screening strategies tailored to each patient’s risk profile is essential for optimizing clinical outcomes in this population.

title: IP12-01: More than just size: the search for accurate stone volume assessment
parentSessionTitle: IP12: Stone Disease: Epidemiology & Evaluation I
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Maximum linear measurement (MLM) and ellipsoid formulae (EF) poorly reflect true stone burden, prompting greater interest in direct volumetric analysis. Recent CT-based tools such as 3D Slicer®, Enterprise Imaging, and Visage Imaging® offer alternative approaches for determining stone volume. Herein for the first time, we compare prolate EF (stones <1.5 cm), scalene EF (stones >1.5 cm), 3D Slicer, Enterprise Imaging, and four Visage Imaging methods: Balloon Contour, 3D Segmentation, Balloon Contour + 3D Segmentation \[Multi\], and 3D Segmentation + Eraser tool against gas pycnometry, the gold standard for volume assessment. METHODS: A total of 64 air-dried human stones (Group 1: <1.5 cm; 0.415–1.288 cm) and 54 fabricated Bego stones (Group 2: >1.5 cm; 1.544–6.131 cm) were CT-scanned in air and within a phantom. Stone volumes were measured using all of the aforementioned methods, each of which was then compared to gas pycnometry using ANOVA with Dunnett’s post hoc analysis, stratified by stone MLM. RESULTS: When measured in air, Group 1 stone volumes measured with Enterprise Imaging and Visage Balloon Contour were not significantly different from gas pycnometry, overestimating volumes by 12% and 7%, respectively. In contrast, for the larger Group 2 stones, only the ellipsoid formulae differed significantly from gas pycnometry, overestimating volumes by 57% ( (https://www.auajournals.org/doi/abs/10.1097/01.JU.0001191328.95269.a6.01#F1)).When measured in the phantom, Group 1 volumes obtained using Enterprise Imaging, Visage Multi, and Visage Balloon Contour were not significantly different from gas pycnometry, with overestimations of 12%, 9%, and 9%, respectively. For the larger stones in Group 2, ellipsoid formulae overestimated volume by 75%. Notably, Visage 3D Segmentation in the phantom significantly overestimated Group 1 and Group 2 volumes by 189% and 933%, respectively; however, incorporation of the Eraser tool reduced these overestimations to 130% and 27% ( (https://www.auajournals.org/doi/abs/10.1097/01.JU.0001191328.95269.a6.01#F1)). CONCLUSIONS: Across all stone sizes and imaging conditions, only Enterprise Imaging and Visage with the Balloon Contour tool produced volume measurements equivalent to gas pycnometry.

title: IP12-02: From Length to True Burden: Making Sense of Linear Stone Measurements
parentSessionTitle: IP12: Stone Disease: Epidemiology & Evaluation I

speakers.organization: University of Rochester School of Medicine and Dentistry

fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Advances in software have enabled broader use of three-dimensional (3D) volumetric measurements in surgical planning for urolithiasis. However, stone volume remains less familiar to clinicians who have developed intuition around traditional linear measurements. We aimed to develop a reference tool that clarifies the relationship between commonly used linear benchmarks and 3D volume measurements. METHODS: We retrospectively analyzed preoperative CTs for patients undergoing surgery for urolithiasis between 6/10-12/31/24. Using Spectra IDS7, we measured maximal stone length in any plane and calculated 3D volumes, summing them to obtain total length and volume. Number of stones and staghorn status were recorded. Volume distributions for common linear benchmarks were analyzed (5, 10, 15, 20 mm ± 2.5 mm). Stone length and volume were log-transformed to normalize their distributions and regression models were used to predict log(total stone volume) from log(total stone length), stone number, and binary staghorn status. RESULTS: A total of 653 stone procedures were analyzed. Figure 1a illustrates the distribution of 3D stone volumes among cumulative stone lengths at clinically relevant cutoffs. The interquartile range of stone volumes was narrow for small stones (5 mm: 77.7 mm3) but increased substantially and non-linearly as length increased (10 mm: 267.8 mm3; 15 mm: 571.9 mm3; 20 mm: 815.2 mm3), reflecting greater variability in stone number and morphology at higher stone burdens. In regression, stone volume was strongly predicted by stone length and was significantly influenced by stone number and the presence of staghorn morphology ( Figure 1b). Stones with greater length contributed disproportionately more to total volume, staghorn stones were roughly three times larger than non-staghorn stones, and cases with multiple smaller stones tended to have lower total volumes at similar cumulative lengths. CONCLUSIONS: We provide a reference tool for estimating stone volume from cumulative stone length. Variability in 3D volume increases nonlinearly with stone length and is significantly modulated by stone number and complex stone morphology. Incorporating these reference relationships into clinical workflows could improve preoperative planning.

title: IP12-03: Multimodal integration of CT-derived 3D morphology, radiomics, and deep learning features for predicting urine culture positivity and clinical stratification in ureteral stone patients
parentSessionTitle: IP12: Stone Disease: Epidemiology & Evaluation I
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: It is important to assess the risk of urinary tract infection and the need for intervention in patients with ureteral stones based on imaging. Although CT attenuation has been associated with urine culture positivity, it is unclear whether features of the segmented renal pelvis and bladder on CT can predict culture positivity. The aim of this study was to evaluate whether image features from multimodal imaging could predict urine culture positivity and stratify patients into risk groups. METHODS: We retrospectively analyzed 71 hospitalized patients with ureteral stones and hydronephrosis (2020–2024). Renal pelvis and bladder were manually segmented and morphology, radiomics, and deep learning features were extracted. LASSO regression selected predictors, and risk scores were calculated as weighted sums of coefficients. The ROC curve determined the optimal cut-off for predicting culture positive. Patients were stratified into risk groups by cut off value for clinical comparison. RESULTS: Among 71 patients, 28 had positive urine cultures. Coefficient contribution was 33.9% from morphology, 0.7% from radiomics, and 65.5% from deep learning. The risk score demonstrated high discrimination for culture positivity (AUC 0.986), with an optimal cut-off of 0.489. High-risk groups were older (p<0.001), had higher CRP (p<0.001), longer hospitalization (p<0.001), and more frequent stenting (p=0.036). CONCLUSIONS: This study demonstrated that a multimodal risk score integrating CT-derived 3D morphology, radiomics, and deep learning features could predict voided urine culture positivity in patients with ureteral stones. The score enabled stratification into clinically distinct groups that differed in systemic inflammation, length of hospitalization, and need for ureteral stenting, thereby providing prognostic information beyond infection risk alone. This approach offers a non-invasive tool to support early risk assessment and guide personalized management strategies. | | | --- | | |

title: IP12-04: CT-Derived Skeletal Muscle Mass and Visceral Adiposity Metrics Influence 24-hour Urine Lithogenic Parameters in Stone-forming Patients
parentSessionTitle: IP12: Stone Disease: Epidemiology & Evaluation I
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Urine composition is influenced by systemic and phenotypic factors, many of which are implicated in nephrolithiasis. While several urine constituents are known to promote or inhibit stone formation, the relationship between body composition and urinary lithogenic profiles remains poorly defined. The aim of this study is to evaluate associations between CT-derived body composition metrics and 24-hour urine parameters in a diverse stone-forming population. METHODS: A retrospective review of 443 stone-forming patients from the Emory Nephrolithiasis Database was conducted. All patients underwent 24-hour urine analysis via LithoLink and CT imaging within 120 days. Skeletal Muscle Index (SMI) and Visceral Adipose Tissue Index (VATI) values were calculated from axial CT images at the L3 vertebral level. Spearman correlations and multivariable logistic regression analyses were conducted to analyze associations between body composition quartiles and urine abnormalities. RESULTS: Patients in the highest SMI quartile had significantly greater odds of elevated urinary volume defined as greater than 1.5 liters (OR 2.71, 95%CI 1.38-5.34), oxalate (OR 2.11, 95%CI 1.07-4.16), uric acid (OR 2.60, 95%CI 1.08-6.26), and sodium (OR 2.70, 95%CI 1.35-5.41) levels compared to the lowest quartile (all p<0.05). Patients in the 4th quartile of VATI values had significantly lower odds of urine volume (OR 0.44, 95%CI 0.20-0.98, p<0.05). Increasing age and black race were independently associated with lower odds of select stone-promoting abnormalities. Increasing age was associated with reduced risk of supersaturation of calcium phosphate (OR 0.97, 95%CI 0.95-0.99) and 24-hour uric acid (OR 0.96, 95%CI 0.94-0.98) (all p<0.05). Black race was associated with reduced odds of raised urinary volume (OR 0.44, 95%CI 0.25-0.77) and hypercalciuria (OR 0.50, 95% 0.26-0.96) on 24-hour measurements (all p<0.05). CONCLUSIONS: CT-derived body composition metrics are associated with urinary lithogenic profiles in stone-forming patients. These findings support the integration of body composition assessment into routine stone risk evaluation and management.

title: IP12-05: Artificial Intelligence Derived Body Composition is Associated with 24-hour Urine Markers Using Routine CT Imaging
parentSessionTitle: IP12: Stone Disease: Epidemiology & Evaluation I
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: While 24-hour urine collections remain the gold standard for metabolic risk assessment in stone formers, their utility is limited by inaccuracy and poor completion rates. Body composition determined using routine imaging may offer a practical surrogate, but existing data is limited and segmentation times prolonged. We investigated whether artificial intelligence (AI) based CT segmentations predict skeletal muscle index (SMI. cm2/m2) accurately and whether this correlates with 24-hour urine markers and associated abnormalities. METHODS: Following IRB approval, our nephrolithiasis database was reviewed for patients ≥18 years who underwent 24-hour urine collections between 2010-2022 with pre-collection CT imaging. Patients on alkalinizing agents or inaccurate collections were excluded. SMI was calculated at L3 using human segmentation (ground truth) subsequently used to train a UNet deep learning (DL) model. Correlations between DL-based SMI and urine markers were assessed using Spearman analysis and multivariable logistic regression identified independent predictors of lithogenic abnormalities. RESULTS: A total of 195 patients were included (median age 58 years, 44.6% female, 16.4% Black). DL segmentation achieved high concordance with human segmentation (DSC 0.90 ± 0.11) while reducing time-to-segment from 7.5 minutes to <1 second per scan. DL-based SMI correlated with nearly all 24-hour urine parameters. On multivariable analysis, higher SMI independently predicted hyperuricosuria (OR 11.49, 95%CI 2.00-65.89), lower risk of hypocitraturia (OR 0.22, 95%CI 0.07-0.71), and reduced odds of elevated urine pH (OR 0.33, 95%CI 0.12-0.89). CONCLUSIONS: AI-based CT body composition analysis strongly correlates with 24-hour urine abnormalities and may serve as a practical surrogate for metabolic evaluation in stone formers, offering a rapid, cost-effective alternative to urine collections. Further research is warranted to validate this study’s findings. | | | --- | | | | | | --- | | |

title: IP12-06: Artificial intelligence deep learning combined with radiomics in preoperative imaging diagnosis of medullary sponge kidney stones
parentSessionTitle: IP12: Stone Disease: Epidemiology & Evaluation I
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Medullary sponge kidney (MSK) is a rare congenital anomaly frequently associated with nephrolithiasis. Accurate preoperative differentiation between MSK stones and non-MSK multiple kidney stones remains challenging, yet it is essential for effective clinical decision-making. This study aims to develop a novel diagnostic model that integrates radiomics and deep learning features to improve the differentiation of MSK stones using CT imaging. METHODS: This single-center, retrospective study included patients who underwent surgical treatment for multiple kidney stones at Beijing Tsinghua Changgung Hospital between 2022 and 2024\. All MSK and non-MSK cases were confirmed via endoscopic surgery. Radiomics features were extracted from manually delineated regions of interest (ROI) on nephrographic-phase CT images, while deep learning features were derived from a ResNet101-based model. Three diagnostic signatures—Radiomics (Rad), Deep Transfer Learning (DTL), and Deep Learning Radiomics (DLR)—were developed. A Combined model was constructed by integrating clinical variables with DLR features to further enhance diagnostic accuracy. Model performance was evaluated using AUC, calibration curves, Net Reclassification Index (NRI), and Integrated Discrimination Improvement (IDI) analyses. Additionally, Gradient-weighted Class Activation Mapping (Grad-CAM) visualization was employed to identify imaging regions critical to classification, improving interpretability. RESULTS: A total of 73 patients with multiple kidney stones were analyzed, comprising 34 MSK cases and 39 non-MSK cases, encompassing 110 kidneys in total. The DLR signature demonstrated high diagnostic accuracy, with AUCs of 0.96 in both the training and test cohorts. The Combined model further enhanced diagnostic performance, achieving AUCs of 0.98 in the training cohort and 0.95 in the test cohort. Calibration curves indicated strong agreement between predicted probabilities and observed outcomes. Furthermore, NRI and IDI analyses highlighted the superior predictive power of both the DLR and Combined models compared to other approaches. CONCLUSIONS: This study introduces an innovative approach for MSK stone diagnosis by integrating radiomics and deep learning features. The proposed model offers high diagnostic accuracy and promising clinical utility

title: IP12-07: Nephrocalcinosis – a radiological finding worthy of genetic testing
parentSessionTitle: IP12: Stone Disease: Epidemiology & Evaluation I
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Although nephrocalcinosis (NC) is traditionally considered an acquired condition, recent evidence suggests that monogenic causes account for a substantial proportion of cases. Despite that, there is poor evidence on the true impact of genetic mutations in NC prevalence and phenotype. This study aimed to analyze the results of genetic testing in patients with NC to understand how the testing may influence our comprehension of this clinical presentation. METHODS: NC patients were selected from our kidney stone disease (KSD) genetics database at a tertiary academic institution between May 2019 and May 2025. The genetic testing was done through Invitae® or PreventionGenetics® panels. NC diagnosis was made according to CT scan findings. Mild NC was defined as increased pyramidal density, while severe NC was defined as pyramids calcification. Demographic and laboratory parameters were also collected. Statistical analysis was performed via t-test and Chi-Square testing as appropriate. RESULTS: Out of 360 KSD patients with imaging data, NC was identified in 50 (13.9%) patients, out of which 29 (58%) had genetic mutations. The prevalence of NC was higher among patients with genetic abnormalities relative to those with negative tests (19.4% vs. 10%, p=0.01). NC patients were further categorized into mild (n=25) or severe (n=25) groups. There was no association between CKD and NC severity (p=0.31), although 5 out of the 6 patients with CKD stages 3b or higher were in the severe group. The rate of pathologic mutations was higher in the NC severe group, although marginally significant (32% vs. 12%, p=0.09). In the severe NC group, the most common mutated genes were SLC4A1 (n=5), CYP24A1 (n=3), SLC12A1 (n=3), while in the mild group were SLC26A1, ATP7B, and SLC22A12 with 2 mutations each ( Table 1, (https://www.auajournals.org/doi/abs/10.1097/01.JU.0001191328.95269.a6.07#T1)). CONCLUSIONS: Genetic testing demonstrates a high diagnostic yield in NC patients and improves our understanding of the NC phenotype. Distinct gene mutations were observed in patients with different severity of NC, suggesting that specific genetic mutations may lead to varying disease severity.

title: IP12-08: Using non-destructive 3D micro-CT imaging to predict relative calcium oxalate and uric acid compositions in kidney stones
parentSessionTitle: IP12: Stone Disease: Epidemiology & Evaluation I
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Urologists try to predict kidney stone composition using indicators like Hounsfield units and urine pH. Definitive analysis relies on Fourier Transform Infrared Spectroscopy (FTIR), a destructive technique that requires stone pulverization. However, the 3D spatial distribution of different materials may be relevant to the management of certain mixed composition stones. One example is a core of calcium oxalate (CaO) encased in a shell of uric acid (UA). Such information is completely lost in FTIR. In contrast, volumetric micro-CT (mCT) is a non-destructive modality with sufficient resolution to enable the separation of different stone materials, making it a promising tool for 3D, non-destructive compositional analysis of stones. Our study aimed to evaluate the ability of mCT to predict CaO:UA ratios in PCNL-derived stones and to validate predictions against FTIR analysis. METHODS: Kidney stone fragments were retrieved from 29 patients who underwent PCNL at St. Michael's Hospital in Toronto. A representative fraction of each stone was sent for FTIR, and the rest was scanned with mCT. On FTIR, 19/29 patients had pure CaO, 6/29 had pure UA, and 4/29 had both CaO/UA. Stones from 2 patients with pure CaO and UA (on both FTIR and mCT) were used for calibration. Pure CaO/UA intensity distributions were plotted and analyzed.
