Fisher's d' metric was used to assess histogram separability, and a ROC analysis was performed to determine the optimal intensity threshold for material classification. The threshold was then used to classify voxels in the remaining (test) stones as CaO or UA. Each material's relative composition was computed as the ratio of its voxel count to the total count. mCT-derived compositions of CaO and UA were compared to FTIR for each patient, and a visual inspection of incorrectly classified voxels was performed to investigate errors. RESULTS: Calibration histograms for CaO and UA demonstrated excellent separability, with Fisher's d'=4.2. ROC analysis yielded an intensity threshold with high discriminatory power (AUC=99%). The threshold achieved a 100% accuracy on test stones that were pure CaO on FTIR (n=18). When applied to test stones that were pure UA on FTIR (n=5), the threshold resulted in a mean error of 11±13% (i. e. on average, 11% of voxels in each pure UA stone were classified as CaO). On the mixed 4 mixed stones, the mean error was 24±22%. Visual inspection revealed that our classification separated CaO and UA well in all mixed test stones. This suggests that errors can be attributed to FTIR and mCT analyzing different fragments from each patient. CONCLUSIONS: Our study suggests that mCT can nondestructively compete with FTIR in kidney stone composition analysis.

title: IP12-09: Validation of the Diminished Nephrogram as an Indicator of Renal Obstruction in Patients with Acute Ureteral Stones
parentSessionTitle: IP12: Stone Disease: Epidemiology & Evaluation I
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: The quantified diminished nephrogram has shown promise in distinguishing clinically significant obstruction from benign hydronephrosis without obstruction. We sought to validate the diminished nephrogram as an objective imaging marker of upper urinary tract obstruction by characterizing it in patients presenting with acutely obstructing ureteral calculi. METHODS: We reviewed records of patients who presented to our institution’s emergency department between January 2020 and July 2023 with an ICD-10 diagnosis indicative of nephrolithiasis and who underwent contrast-enhanced computed tomography (CT) of the abdomen and pelvis. Diminished nephrogram was quantified separately in the renal cortex and medulla as the difference in renal attenuation (DRA) between the obstructed and unobstructed kidneys. Hydronephrosis was assessed using anterior-posterior renal pelvis diameter (APRPD) and maximal ureteral diameter. RESULTS: A total of 281 patients met inclusion criteria: 206 with obstructing ureteral stones (study group) and 75 with non-obstructing renal stones (control group). Differences in attenuation between kidneys in patients with obstructing stones were significantly greater than differences in patients with non-obstructing stones (cortical differences: -7 vs 1 HU p<0.001, medullary differences: -47 vs 1 HU p<0.0001). The previously reported very high specificity and modest sensitivity of a difference of -15 HU for identifying obstructed kidneys was confirmed in this cohort (Medullary: Specificity 97%, Sensitivity 75%; Cortical: Specificity 100%, Sensitivity 25%). CONCLUSIONS: We confirmed that a medullary DRA of 15 HU on contrast-enhanced CT as a highly specific indicator of renal obstruction. The diminished nephrogram is a reliable, objective marker of obstructive uropathy and may be useful in the evaluation of suspected ureteral obstruction. | | | --- | | |

title: IP12-10: Very-Low-Dose CT with Automated Assessment: An Ex Vivo Study Quantifying Residual Small Stones
parentSessionTitle: IP12: Stone Disease: Epidemiology & Evaluation I
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: We have reported CT characteristics that distinguish residual tiny fragments from dust on standard-dose CT (SDCT) (World Journal of Urology, 2025), also with 1 mSv low-dose CT (LDCT). Although radiation exposure is a major concern, postoperative CT is increasingly used as it can accurately detect and quantify very small residual stones after laser lithotripsy. Urinary stones exhibit inherently high contrast relative to the surrounding soft tissues, suggesting that radiation dose can be further reduced without compromising clinically meaningful information. To comply with the ALARA (as low as reasonably achievable) principle, this study aims to evaluate an even lower-dose protocol (effective dose ~0.2 mSv), hereafter referred to as very-low-dose CT (VLDCT), for accurately evaluating small-sized stones. METHODS: Calcium oxalate stone were sieved into three categories: small fragments (2.00-2.36 mm), tiny fragments (1.00-1.40 mm) or dust (< 250 µm). A uniform 0.25 g sample from each category was implanted into ex vivo porcine kidneys (n=24). CT images were acquired at three dose settings equivalent to SDCT, LDCT, and VLDCT (tube current: 250/50/10 mA, respectively; tube voltage: 120 kVp). Volumetric and attenuation values (maximum, mean and standard deviation \[SD\]) were calculated automatically using software. Intragroup comparison was performed. RESULTS: For dust, VLDCT produced volumetric and attenuation values that did not differ significantly from SDCT or LDCT. For tiny fragments, VLDCT slightly overestimated the volume compared with SDCT or LDCT (p<0.05), whereas all types of attenuation metrics remained comparable. For small fragments, VLDCT showed higher measured volume and mildly lower mean attenuation values (p<0.05), however, maximum and SD values were similar. CONCLUSIONS: VLDCT approaches the diagnostic performance of SDCT or LDCT for assessing residual small stones. However, as stone size increases, VLDCT tends to overestimate volume and to yield lower mean CT values. These findings suggest that effective postoperative surveillance can be achieved at radiation doses far below 1 mSv when using automated assessment.

title: IP12-11: GLP-1 Receptor Agonists Reduce Kidney Stone Events in Obese Patients: Evidence from a Real-World Cohort
parentSessionTitle: IP12: Stone Disease: Epidemiology & Evaluation I

speakers.organization: Case Western Reserve University School of Medicine

fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: The use of glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1A) has surged in recent years. Originally intended for blood sugar control, they have been increasingly utilized for weight loss. The implications of this on urological health is poorly researched. There is an association between obesity and nephrolithiasis, and recent evidence suggests changes in urine chemistry (e. g. decreased urinary oxalate) associated with GLP-1A use may impact stone recurrence. We queried a real-world population dataset to assess the impact of GLP-1A on stone formation in nondiabetic obese patients. METHODS: In this retrospective cohort study, we included nondiabetic adults >18 years old in the TriNetX US Collaborative Research Network (~ 130 million patients) diagnosed as obese/overweight within the last 20 years. Patients prescribed GLP-1A were identified. The primary outcome was the subsequent rate of stone events among patients with a history of nephrolithiasis, comparing those treated with GLP-1A versus non-users. Secondary analysis compared stone event rates in those without a history of stone disease. One-to-one propensity matching for demographics, comorbidities, insulin use, and sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 inhibitors was performed to standardize cohorts. RESULTS: Among non-diabetic, obese patients with a history of nephrolithiasis, GLP-1A use was associated with significantly lower rates of stone events compared with non-users (27.1% vs 43.1%, p<0.001); This association remained after propensity matching (27.2% vs 30.8%, p<0.001). In patients without a prior history of nephrolithiasis, GLP-1A use was likewise associated with lower rates of new stone formation (0.59% vs 1.4%, respectively, p<0.001); persisting after propensity matching (0.60 vs 0.80%, p<0.001). CONCLUSIONS: In non-diabetic, obese patients, GLP-1A therapy was associated with a significantly lower incidence of kidney stone events, independent of prior stone history. While a definitive lithoprotective mechanism cannot be confirmed in the current study, these findings suggest that GLP-1A use may reduce the risk of nephrolithiasis. Given the widespread adoption of GLP-1A agents for weight management, further research is warranted to elucidate the biological and metabolic factors underlying this association. | | | --- | | |

title: IP12-12: Distinct urinary microbial profiles in calcium oxalate urolithiasis: A 16S rRNA-based comparative study
parentSessionTitle: IP12: Stone Disease: Epidemiology & Evaluation I
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: While urinary tract infections are well-established contributors to struvite stones, the role of the urinary microbiome in non-infectious stones such as calcium oxalate (CaOx) remains poorly defined. This study aimed to characterize the urinary microbiome in CaOx stone-forming patients using 16S rRNA sequencing and to compare it with that of healthy individuals. METHODS: Urine samples were collected prior to surgical intervention from 39 patients with confirmed CaOx urolithiasis and 37 age-matched healthy controls. Microbial DNA was extracted and analyzed using 16S rRNA gene sequencing. Alpha diversity (Chao1, Shannon, Simpson, OTUs) and beta diversity (PCoA) were assessed. Differential taxonomic abundance was evaluated at the genus level. This study was approved by the Institutional Review Board of the Korea University Hospital. RESULTS: CaOx patients exhibited significantly increased richness (Chao1 and OTU indices), but significantly reduced diversity and evenness (Shannon and Simpson indices), suggesting microbial overgrowth with reduced ecological balance. Beta diversity analysis revealed distinct microbial clustering between the two groups. Uniquely, CaOx patients had a significant enrichment of environmental and biofilm-associated genera such as Ralstonia, Pelomonas, Sphingomonas, and Paracoccus, which are not commonly reported in previous stone microbiome studies ( (https://www.auajournals.org/doi/abs/10.1097/01.JU.0001191328.95269.a6.12#F1)). In contrast, beneficial genera with anti-inflammatory or barrier-protective roles—including Faecalibacterium, Bacteroides, and Bifidobacterium—were significantly depleted ( (https://www.auajournals.org/doi/abs/10.1097/01.JU.0001191328.95269.a6.12#F1)). CONCLUSIONS: This study identifies a dysbiotic urinary microbiome profile in CaOx stone patients prior to treatment. Unlike infection-related stones, the CaOx-associated microbiome is characterized by non-traditional, biofilm-capable genera and a loss of protective commensals. These findings suggest that even in non-infectious stones, the urinary microbiome may play a mechanistic role, potentially offering new diagnostic and therapeutic targets.

title: IP12-13: Development and Validation of a Predictive Model for Kidney Stone Recurrence: Integrating Gut Multi-Omics and Clinical Profiles
parentSessionTitle: IP12: Stone Disease: Epidemiology & Evaluation I

speakers.organization: Department of Urology, Beijing Friendship Hospital, Capital Medical University

fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Kidney stone recurrence remains a pervasive clinical challenge, yet prognostic tools leveraging integrated multi-omics approaches are still lacking. This study aimed to develop and validate an integrated model predicting kidney stone recurrence by combining gut multi-omics and clinical features. METHODS: We conducted a prospective study including patients undergoing surgical treatment for kidney stones at Beijing Friendship Hospital between July 2022 and April 2024. A comprehensive analytical approach was employed, combining 16S rDNA sequencing and liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry (LC-MS) of fecal samples with detailed clinical profiling. Variable selection was performed using univariate and multivariate logistic regression, followed by development of a clinically applicable nomogram. Model performance was rigorously assessed through receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analysis and calibration curves, with all statistical analyses executed in R software version 4.2.2 (release date: 31 October 2022). RESULTS: Among 203 enrolled patients, 100 (49.26%) experienced stone recurrence during follow-up. Gut microbiome analysis revealed significantly reduced alpha diversity in recurrent cases (Kruskal-Wallis test, p<0.05). LEfSe analysis identified distinct microbial signatures characterized by enriched _Proteobacteria_ and depleted _Firmicutes_ (LDA > 2.0, p<0.05). Multivariate analysis established Proteobacteria (OR=0.003, p=0.030) and Firmicutes (OR=36.003, p=0.025) as independent predictors of recurrence. The resulting nomogram demonstrated strong predictive performance, with AUCs of 0.883 (training) and 0.817 (validation). Calibration curves showed excellent agreement between predicted and observed outcomes (Hosmer-Lemeshow test: p=0.968 training, p=0.672 validation). CONCLUSIONS: _Firmicutes_ and _Proteobacteria_ serve as independent risk and protective factors for kidney stone recurrence. We developed and validated a novel predictive model that integrates gut multi-omics signatures with clinical parameters to accurately stratify recurrence risk in kidney stone patients.

title: IP12-14: Gut Microbiome and Metabolome Signatures in Renal Stone Recurrence: A Multi-Omics Study
parentSessionTitle: IP12: Stone Disease: Epidemiology & Evaluation I
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: This study explores the differential characteristics between single episode kidney stone patients and recurrent kidney stone patients from the perspective of differences in gut microbiota structure and metabolites, and identifies microbial markers that predict the occurrence and recurrence of kidney stones. METHODS: This study collected fecal samples from patients with recurrent stones (n=37), patients with initial stones (n=38), and healthy controls (n=39) for 16S rDNA sequencing, untargeted metabolomics sequencing and metagenomic sequencing to obtain differential microbial communities and metabolites, and analyzed their correlation. RESULTS: Compared to incident cases, recurrent stone patients exhibited further reduced gut microbial richness and diversity, with enrichment of Enterobacterales, Proteobacteria, Gammaproteobacteria, Enterobacteriaceae, Escherichia-Shigella, and Bacilli. In the recurrent kidney stone group, 27 metabolites were upregulated and 164 downregulated, primarily enriched in purine metabolism, phenylalanine/tyrosine/tryptophan biosynthesis, and caffeine metabolism pathways. We identified 10 metabolites as recurrence biomarkers and found significant correlations between Escherichia-Shigella and Asn-Tyr, Leu-Ala-Ile, Tyrosyl-Alanine, or 3'-hydroxyhexobarbital. Additionally, gender-specific gut microbiota signatures were observed. Oxalate decarboxylase and short-chain fatty acid-related enzymes decreased during stone formation but rebounded with recurrence. Caffeine and its metabolites were significantly downregulated in recurrent patients, supporting their potential role in inhibiting stone formation and recurrence. CONCLUSIONS: Recurrent kidney stone patients exhibit reduced gut microbiota diversity, evenness, and overall gut metabolism. We identified 10 biomarkers distinguishing initial from recurrent cases, and propose that caffeine metabolism and aromatic amino acid metabolism influence stone recurrence—potentially serving as clinical biomarkers for recurrence.

title: IP12-15: Optimal Preoperative Culture Timing: Within 14-days Associated with Reduced Early Sepsis Risk in Urolithiasis Surgery
parentSessionTitle: IP12: Stone Disease: Epidemiology & Evaluation I
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Despite positive cultures being linked to increased sepsis risk, the optimal latency between urine culture and surgery for urolithiasis remains unclear. We evaluated whether the timing of urine culture is associated with early sepsis, defined as ≤24 hours after surgery. METHODS: We performed a retrospective analysis of 4639 patients from a single institutional database who underwent ureteroscopy or percutaneous nephrolithotomy (PCNL) for urolithiasis between 2000-2025. We excluded patients who received IV antibiotics within 1 week before surgery and those without a urine culture 45 days before surgery. Comorbidity data was extracted from ICD codes and stone size was extracted from preoperative radiology reports using a HIPAA compliant large language model. Outliers were manually reviewed. We conducted four separate binary logistic regression and chi-squared analyses, stratifying patients by preoperative urine culture submission timing using cutoffs of ≤7 vs. >7 days, ≤14 vs. >14 days, ≤ 21 vs. >21 days, and ≤28 vs. >28 days prior to surgery. RESULTS: There were 2845 patients who met inclusion criteria of which 101 patients (3.6%) experienced sepsis within 30 days postoperatively and 31 (1.1%) experienced sepsis within 24 hours postoperatively. Only the 14-day cutoff showed a statistically significant association with early postoperative sepsis, conferring a protective effect. This remained consistent across subgroup analyses for stone-size, ureteroscopy procedures, UTI history and Charlson Comorbidity Index (CCI). Multivariate and propensity score analysis showed similar protective effects when adjusting for demographics, CCI, prior urologic history, preoperative culture results, and procedure characteristics (adjusted OR=0.18-0.53 across models). There was additionally a non-significant trend towards increased likelihood of sepsis and longer culture-to-surgery latency, with the exclusion of the 7 day cutoff group. CONCLUSIONS: Lower rates of early sepsis was associated with obtaining cultures within 14 days prior to surgery. This effect was robust on subgroup, multivariate and propensity score analyses and offers evidence for optimal preoperative culture submission timing.

title: IP12-16: A Novel Nomogram with an External Validation to Stratify Risk of Sepsis in Patients Undergoing Ureteral Stent Placement for Obstructing Stones and Presumed Urinary Tract Infection
parentSessionTitle: IP12: Stone Disease: Epidemiology & Evaluation I
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Patients with obstructing ureteral stones and concomitant infection are at risk of developing urosepsis, even if adequately treated with emergent decompression. This study aimed to develop and externally validate a nomogram for predicting the risk of urosepsis after ureteral stent placement in this population. METHODS: A retrospective chart review was conducted on 187 patients from two centers (2016–2020) with obstructing ureteral stones, suspected UTI, and urgent stent placement. Septic shock was defined as qSOFA positivity plus vasopressor need >1 hour post-stenting. A training model was generated using multiple logistic regression based on previously identified risk factors. The model utilized a 76/24 partition, where age, purulent urine, UTI history, WBC, and lactate levels on presentation, along with a qSOFA score, were used to generate a nomogram. A validation of the nomogram was performed in a third center (2018–2023). RESULTS: In the nomogram cohort, 18 (9.6%) patients developed septic shock. The risk factors had the following point accrual potential: age (0-100), purulent urine (0,45), UTI history (0,35), WBC (0-50), lactate (0-100), qSOFA (0,50), with the total score ranging from 0-350. The lowest point accrual is 100 points, which correlates to an estimated risk of 10%. In the external validation cohort, 22 (9.7%) patients developed septic shock, with a receiver operating characteristic analysis revealing an area under the curve of 90.5% (p=0.001). CONCLUSIONS: Our nomogram offers a potentially useful clinical tool for predicting septic shock and guiding hospital resource allocation. Its strong performance suggests excellent generalizability. A prospective study is needed to determine whether the use of a nomogram may help identify patients most likely to benefit from ICU admission.

title: IP12-17: Stone Treatment for Patients with Recurrent UTIs and Concurrent Non-obstructing Kidney Stones: Does It Matter?
parentSessionTitle: IP12: Stone Disease: Epidemiology & Evaluation I
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Recurrent urinary tract infections (rUTIs) have a profound impact on the healthcare system, accounting for nearly 7 million medical visits per year and $3.5 billion in medical spending. Patients with coexisting rUTIs and kidney stone disease (KSD) may benefit from definitive stone treatment, although the cure rate is not well-established. Our objectives were to assess and predict treatment response to stone clearance in patients with concurrent rUTIs and asymptomatic kidney stones. METHODS: Between 2019 to 2023, patients with rUTIs (defined as ≥3 culture proven UTIs in 12 months) and KSD who underwent surgical stone removal at a single tertiary center from were identified. Patient demographics, urine cultures, stone composition, stone and infection-free rates during a 12-month follow up period were reviewed. RESULTS: 112 patients met inclusion criteria with a mean age of 57 ± 16 years. The mean stone size was 12 ± 10 mm. Stone composition consisted of calcium oxalate monohydrate (45%), calcium oxalate dihydrate (27%), calcium phosphate (54%), struvite (21%), and uric acid (6%). During the one-year follow up period, 101 patients (91%) were free from rUTIs, 73 of which (61%) had no symptomatic UTI recurrence. Initial stone burden ≤ 5 mm, pre-op culture pattern inconsistent with bacterial persistence, and presence of Enterococcus or multiple organisms were less likely to experience complete resolution of rUTIs (p<0.05) ( Table 1). The presence of residual stones and multiple organisms on urine culture were independently predictive of unresolved recurrent UTI during follow up. CONCLUSIONS: Treatment of asymptomatic non-obstructive kidney stones in patients with rUTIs leads to significant reduction in symptomatic UTIs, with 91% of patients free from recurrent UTIs, 61% of which were completely infection-free at a one-year follow-up. Those with initial stone burden <5 mm, presence of residual stones, Enterococcus, and multi-organism preoperative urine cultures were less likely to experience cure after definitive stone surgery. These factors could aid in the counseling of patients with rUTIs being considered for stone surgeries with the primary goal of UTI prevention. | | | --- | | |

title: IP12-18: From 28 to 6: External Validation of the WISQOL Short Form in a Large Tertiary Stone Cohort
parentSessionTitle: IP12: Stone Disease: Epidemiology & Evaluation I
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: The Wisconsin Stone Quality of Life questionnaire (WISQOL) is the first validated stone-specific health-related quality of life (HRQOL) instrument. A short form (WISQOL-SF, 6 items) was previously developed and internally validated, but external validation has not been performed. We aimed to externally validate the WISQOL-SF against the full 28-item WISQOL full form (FF) in a large real-world stone patient cohort. METHODS: We retrospectively identified 2,199 patients completing WISQOL-FF for the first time at the University of Rochester Medical Center from February 2020 to November 2023. All patients with suspected urolithiasis in our clinic were offered WISQOL at every clinic encounter. In addition to the 28 items in WISQOL, information about patients’ current stone status, symptoms, and recent ER and hospital encounters are gathered simultaneously. Standardized scores (0–100) were calculated separately for both WISQOL-FF and WISQOL-SF. Comparative analyses included paired t-tests, two one-sided tests (TOST) for equivalence (±3 points), Cronbach’s α for reliability, Pearson/Spearman correlations, subgroup discriminant validity (stone status, symptoms, ER visits, recent trauma, hospitalization, gender, age), and multivariable logistic regression (high vs low score by median split). RESULTS: Patients were 49.3% female with a mean age of 58.2 ± 15.8 years. The mean WISQOL-SF score was 77.9 vs 76.2 for the WISQOL-FF (mean diff +1.8, 95% CI 1.4–2.2, p<0.001). Despite statistical difference, equivalence testing confirmed scores were interchangeable within ±3 points. Internal consistency was high (Cronbach’s α: FF=0.965, SF=0.880). Agreement was excellent (Pearson r=0.94, Spearman ρ=0.90, ICC=0.94). Both WISQOL-FF and WISQOL-SF discriminated expected subgroups: lower HRQOL in patients with stones and/or symptoms, recent ER visits, trauma, and hospitalization, and higher HRQOL in men and older patients (all p<0.01). Multivariable regression demonstrated consistent independent predictors across WISQOL-FF and WISQOL-SF. CONCLUSIONS: The WISQOL-SF demonstrates equivalent psychometric performance to the full form in a large cross sectional external validation cohort. By reducing completion time from 5–6 minutes to ~1 minutes, the WISQOL-SF offers a practical, patient-friendly instrument for routine clinical and research use in stone disease. | | | --- | | |

title: IP12-19: Longitudinal Validation of the WISQOL-Short Form: Equivalent Responsiveness to the Full Instrument in a High-Volume Stone Center
parentSessionTitle: IP12: Stone Disease: Epidemiology & Evaluation I
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: The Wisconsin Stone Quality of Life (WISQOL) questionnaire is the most widely used stone-specific patient-reported outcome measure (PROM). A short form (WISQOL-SF, 6 items) has recently shown strong cross-sectional performance in our prior external validation study, but its longitudinal responsiveness is unknown. We evaluated the ability of WISQOL-SF to capture temporal change relative to the full 28-item form (FF) in a large real-world stone cohort. METHODS: Adult patients with ≥2 WISQOL submissions from routine follow-up clinic encounters between Nov 2020-Jun 2025 were included. Standardized scores were calculated separately for both WISQOL-FF and WISQOL-SF. Rate of change in scores between consecutive submissions was calculated and correlated (Pearson and Spearman coefficients). A scatter plot was generated to demonstrate the strength and linearity of longitudinal relationship. Bland–Altman analysis assessed agreement in absolute scores across short, medium, and long intervals. A generalized estimating equation model evaluated if the SF–FF relationship remained robust after adjusting for clinical factors (stone status, symptoms, ER visit, traumatic event, hospitalization, sex, age) and time since baseline. RESULTS: Patients (n=1,203, 48.2% female) completed 4,152 WISQOL questionnaires (3.5 ± 2.1 per patient, range 2-16). SF and FF rate of change for total standardized score were strongly correlated (r=0.886; ρ=0.779; p<0.001). Tight clustering of data points around the identity line (Figure) confirmed strong alignment between SF and FF across follow-up intervals. Bland–Altman analysis showed a mean bias of 2.31 (95% LoA −14.40 to 19.02) with no systematic drift over time. In the GEE model, FF remained the dominant predictor of SF (β=1.132; 95% CI 1.105–1.159; p<0.001), with no significant effect of time since baseline (p=0.659). Female sex was associated with slightly higher SF scores (β=1.49; 95% CI 0.60–2.37; p=0.001), and the presence of stones at the time of WISQOL completion was associated with slightly lower scores (β=−0.79; 95% CI −1.49 to −0.08; p=0.029). All other covariates were non-significant. CONCLUSIONS: WISQOL-SF demonstrated excellent longitudinal validity, high agreement, and robust performance across time and clinical subgroups. These findings support the use of WISQOL-SF as a reliable and efficient PROM for longitudinal assessment in kidney stone patients.

title: IP12-20: Association of Social Determinants of Health with Postoperative Complications and Acute Care Utilization after Stone Surgery: Insights from Epic COSMOS
parentSessionTitle: IP12: Stone Disease: Epidemiology & Evaluation I
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Social determinants of health (SDOH)—including insurance type, socioeconomic status, and access to care—may affect surgical outcomes. However, evidence assessing their relationship with stone surgery outcomes remains limited. We aimed to evaluate the association between adverse SDOH and postoperative complications and acute care utilization following definitive stone surgery using the multi-institutional COSMOS database. METHODS: We performed a retrospective cohort study of adult patients undergoing ureteroscopy (URS), percutaneous nephrolithotomy (PCNL), or extracorporeal shockwave lithotripsy (ESWL) between 2015–2025 captured within Epic COSMOS. Surgery episodes were separated by 90 days. Patients were defined as SDOH-positive if, within 365 days before surgery, they had Medicaid, were uninsured/self-pay, or carried ICD-10 Z59 codes for adverse SDOH; SDOH-negative included those with commercial or Medicare coverage and no adverse SDOH codes. The primary outcome was any 30-day event (emergency department \[ED\] visit, readmission, or infectious complication). Secondary outcomes included each component and 90-day repeat stone intervention. RESULTS: Among 951,563 stone surgery episodes (859,470 SDOH-negative; 73,312 SDOH-positive), SDOH-positive patients were younger (median 44 vs 61 years), and more often female and Black or Hispanic. At 30 days, SDOH-positive patients showed higher risks of ED visits (18.7 % vs 10.3 %, p<0.001), readmissions (5.5 % vs 4.8 %, p<0.001), and infectious complications (12.2 % vs 9.7 %, p<0.001). Overall, 26.6 % of SDOH-positive vs 18.5 % of SDOH-negative patients experienced a composite 30-day event (p<0.001). Ninety-day repeat interventions were similar (13.6 % vs 13.8 %, p=0.2). Findings were consistent when restricted to first surgeries (25.8 % vs 18.3 %, p<0.001). CONCLUSIONS: Across a large national cohort, adverse SDOH were associated with increased short-term postoperative morbidity and acute care use after stone surgery, despite comparable 90-day reintervention rates. Integrating social risk factors into perioperative assessment may improve risk stratification and post-discharge follow-up in endourology.

title: IP12-21: Incidence and Predictors of Opioid Prescriptions 1–2 Years After Ureteroscopy
parentSessionTitle: IP12: Stone Disease: Epidemiology & Evaluation I
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Although opioid-sparing approaches are increasingly common, practice patterns for postoperative pain management following ureteroscopy (URS) for urolithiasis remain highly variable. The extent to which perioperative exposure contributes to prolonged opioid use among otherwise opioid naive patients remains uncertain. This study aimed to characterize the incidence and determinants of opioid prescriptions 1–2 years after URS. METHODS: Using the TriNetX Research Network, we conducted a retrospective cohort study of adults undergoing URS between 2015 and 2024 with at least one outpatient encounter prior to the index procedure and documentation of continued follow-up beyond the defined 2-year observation period. Opioid prescriptions (codeine, hydrocodone, hydromorphone, morphine, oxycodone, and tramadol) occurring 1–2 years after URS were analyzed using two-proportion z-tests (Wald method), Kaplan–Meier estimation, and Cox proportional hazards modeling. Baseline confounders were balanced using 1:1 propensity score matching (greedy nearest-neighbor algorithm; caliper=0.1 SD). RESULTS: In a cohort of 17,256 opioid naive patients, opioid prescriptions occurring 1–2 years after URS were identified in 2,767 individuals (16.0%), of whom 1,092 (6.3%) had ≥2 encounters where an opioid was prescribed. Patients with perioperative opioid exposure had a higher adjusted incidence of subsequent prescriptions compared to those without exposure (17.73% vs 15.08%; weighted absolute risk difference 2.65%, 95% CI 0.78–4.52%; NNH=38, 95% CI 22–128). In the Cox proportional hazards model adjusting for the same covariates, perioperative exposure remained associated with a higher hazard of later opioid prescription (HR 1.12, 95% CI 1.01–1.24). Preoperative history of chronic ischemic heart disease, chronic kidney disease, affective mood disorders, and nicotine dependence were independently associated with increased hazard. CONCLUSIONS: Nearly one in five opioid naive patients undergoing URS received opioid prescriptions 1–2 years later. Perioperative exposure significantly increased the incidence of later opioid use. Further prospective studies are needed to clarify causal pathways and address this study’s limitations.

title: IP12-22: Association Between Low Bone Density, Bisphosphonate Therapy, and Urinary Stone Disease: An International Retrospective Review
parentSessionTitle: IP12: Stone Disease: Epidemiology & Evaluation I
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: The relationship between low bone density (LBD) and urinary stone disease has been described in prior studies, with evidence suggesting shared metabolic mechanisms involving calcium and phosphate homeostasis. Bisphosphonates (BPs) may mitigate stone risk by reducing bone resorption and urinary calcium excretion. However, existing data are limited by small sample sizes and single-center designs. Using a large multicenter database, we aimed to (1) compare urinary tract stone incidence between patients with and without LBD, (2) evaluate the effect of BP use on stone formation among patients with LBD, and (3) assess rates of stone-related procedures, including ureteroscopy (URS), percutaneous nephrolithotomy (PCNL), and extracorporeal shock wave lithotripsy (ESWL). METHODS: A retrospective cohort study was performed using the TriNetX database (2005–2025). Adults ≥18 years were included. LBD was defined using ICD-10 codes. Patients on oral bisphosphonate therapy for over one year were identified. Patients with urinary stones or BP initiation prior to LBD diagnosis were excluded. Subsequent analyses used 1:1 age- and sex-matched cohorts. Outcomes included urinary stone incidence and stone procedure rates and were identified based on ICD-10 and CPT codes. Risk ratios (RR) with 95% confidence intervals (CI) were calculated. RESULTS: The initial comparison of LBD vs non-LBD patients included 145,949,059 individuals. Patients with LBD had higher stone incidence than controls (3.805% vs 1.643%; RR=2.316, 95% CI 2.305–2.327; p<0.0001). The LBD not using BPs cohort was 82.55% female, while the LBD with BP use cohort was 90.21% female. Among patients with LBD, BP users had lower stone incidence than non-users (2.028% vs 4.48%; RR=0.453, ARR=2.452%, 95% CI 0.441–0.465; p<0.0001). BP use was also associated with fewer stone procedures overall (0.46% vs 0.722%; RR=0.637, 95% CI 0.600–0.677; p<0.0001) in patients with LBD. By procedure type, BP users had lower rates of URS (0.439% vs 0.652%; RR=0.673, 95% CI 0.632–0.716), PCNL (0.016% vs 0.047%; RR=0.339, 95% CI 0.253–0.454), and ESWL (0.026% vs 0.09%; RR=0.287, 95% CI 0.229–0.360; all p<0.0001). CONCLUSIONS: LBD is associated with more than double the risk of urinary stone formation compared to patients without LBD. Among patients with LBD, bisphosphonate use is linked to significantly reduced stone incidence and lower rates of stone-related procedures. These findings suggest a potential protective role of bisphosphonates in urinary stone disease prevention. Limitations include a female-predominant cohort due to hormonal predisposition to low bone density.

title: IP12-24: Urinary pH Fluctuation Triggers Rapid Growth and Phase Transition of Calcium Phosphate Stones
parentSessionTitle: IP12: Stone Disease: Epidemiology & Evaluation I
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Calcium phosphate (CaP) kidney stones often grow rapidly and are clinically serious. Although high urinary pH due to bacterial infection is known to promote growth, the underlying mechanisms remain unclear. We obtained a CaP stone that had rapidly developed around a ureteral stent after surgery. The patient’s urinary pH fluctuated from 8 and 5.2 over 90 days. To elucidate the rapid growth process, we conducted in vitro experiments to evaluate the pH dependence of Brushite crystal growth and its phase transition to Apatite. Correlating experimental results with clinical data, including stone growth period and urinary pH profile, we revealed key factors driving rapid CaP stone formation. METHODS: Three experiments were performed:(1) Thin sections of the CaP stone were analyzed by polarized light microscopy and Raman spectroscopy to map crystal phases.(2) Synthesized Brushite powder was dispersed in a solution containing 2 mm phosphate and calcium ions (pH 5–6) and maintained under stirring. The time-dependent phase change was monitored by powder X-ray diffraction and Raman spectroscopy, and the duration of the phase transition from Brushite to Apatite at 37 °C was determined.(3) Urine containing Brushite crystals obtained from a patient and about 1 ml of urine was placed into a vial. The pH was varied from 5 to 8 to estimate nucleation and growth rates under urinary conditions. RESULTS: (1) The CaP stone consisted mainly of metastable Brushite, while Apatite was deposited around the stent surface; partial transformation from Brushite to octacalcium phosphate (OCP) was observed.(2) At pH 6, Brushite transformed into Apatite via OCP, whereas at pH 5 it was estimated to be stable for several months at physiological temperature.(3) When urine pH was 6.5, Brushite size remained almost unchanged. At pH 5, it dissolved completely within 50 minutes, while at pH 8, Brushite nucleated and grew at approximately 60 μm/h. CONCLUSIONS: These findings demonstrate that urinary pH fluctuations strongly influence both growth and phase transition of CaP. Under alkaline conditions, Brushite grows rapidly, accelerating stone formation. Once formed, Brushite transforms around pH 6 into Apatite—a denser, harder, and more stable phase. These results suggest that proper urinary pH control could prevent rapid CaP stone formation, particularly after surgery when alkaline urine can accelerate growth around ureteral stents.

title: IP12-25: EQUIL Supersaturation: A Practical Web-based Stone Risk Tool
parentSessionTitle: IP12: Stone Disease: Epidemiology & Evaluation I
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: In 1970, FORTRAN EQUIL2 was created to calculate groundwater mineral supersaturation (SS). Over a decade later, Dr. Birdwell Finlayson engineered the EQUIL algorithm to predict SS ratios for important urinary mineral components. Today, many commercial labs including Quest, ARUP, and Litholink use proprietary versions of EQUIL2 to calculate SS, and although useful in counseling, there has never been an accessible tool for physicians and patients to use to help visualize how altering 24-hour urine variables could affect future stone SS risk. Our goal was to develop an online EQUIL-based tool to fulfill this need. METHODS: Using older BASIC and R versions, EQUIL2 was ported into JavaScript™. Using the classic EQUIL equation, analytes from three different laboratory providers were input into our calculator. The Site presents SS values and normal ranges for CaOx, CaP, and UA computed by EQUIL2. After calculating, crystal SS are placed into stone risk categories of normal (green), moderate (brown), or high (red) risk depending on published ranges \[ (https://www.auajournals.org/doi/abs/10.1097/01.JU.0001191328.95269.a6.25#F1)\]. RESULTS: We found that means calculated using EQUIL, particularly for CaP, differed from those of commercial labs as much as 175%. We used a training set to modify the existing EQUIL program with a separate validation dataset to evaluate model performance. Once validated, we created parameters that can be adjusted to assess for corresponding SS changes. For example, a user can increase the volume parameter to immediately see how increasing urine output could reduce overall SS for stone types. CONCLUSIONS: We have developed an online version of EQUIL that is accessible to the public, allowing patients with physician guidance to better understand how to reduce future stone risk by varying their own laboratory results. Further work is needed to assess user interface, the impact of this tool on patient care and stone recurrence rates, and how this tool can be used in addition to dietary counseling to lower stone risk.

title: IP12-26: 24 hour urine collection: predicting stone formers vs. non-stone formers based on a composite score
parentSessionTitle: IP12: Stone Disease: Epidemiology & Evaluation I
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: While 24-hour urine collection (24-hr-UA) has long guided clinical management of stone formers (SF), there still remains a controversy as to how to best alter its parameters to successfully reduce recurrence rates. We propose guidance with a new composite score to better differentiate SF from non-stone formers (NSF) clinically. METHODS: The Registry for Stones of the Kidney and Ureter (ReSKU), a prospective observational registry at UCSF, was queried to obtain the initial 24-hour urine collection (24-hr-UA) data following referral for stone diagnosis to define our stone-forming (SF) cohort. This data was augmented with non-stone-forming (NSF) data, utilizing 24-hr-UA from kidney donor registry participants within transplant clinics at UCSF who were confirmed to be stone-free as part of their donor evaluation. Individual parameters of the 24-hr-UA were first transformed into their respective normal curve equivalents to standardize all parameters. Orthogonal vectors were subsequently generated for each parameter using principal component analysis (PCA) to reduce overall noise in the dataset, given the known heterogeneity in the SF population. A linear discriminant analysis (LDA) was then performed on the outcomes of SF versus donors, and the resulting linear combination was designated as our composite score. RESULTS: The study population comprised a total of 183 donors and 414 stone formers (SF). The median age at urine collection was 47 for donors and 55 for SF. PCA revealed a heterogeneous population for both SF and donors, with significant overlap between the groups. Correlation analysis demonstrated expected patterns among individual 24-hour urine collection elements. LDA showed a clear separation of donors and SF ( (https://www.auajournals.org/doi/abs/10.1097/01.JU.0001191328.95269.a6.26#F1)) around a mean of 0. The urinary elements most positively contributing to the composite score were supersaturation of uric acid, calcium, oxalate, and pH. Conversely, the urinary elements most negatively contributing to the composite score were citrate, uric acid, sodium, and ammonium. CONCLUSIONS: Our proposed usage of 24-hr-UA composite score better distinguishes between SF and NSF than individual parameters alone. The next step is to determine the practical implication of using this method to predict for stone risk/recurrence in a population of exclusive stone formers. Nevertheless, this is an innovative adoption of a classic tool in the clinical management of stone disease.

title: IP12-28: Association Between LHRH Agonist Therapy and Urinary Stone Disease in Men with Prostate Cancer: A Live Database Analysis
parentSessionTitle: IP12: Stone Disease: Epidemiology & Evaluation I

speakers.organization: University of Vermont Larner College of Medicine

fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Androgen deprivation therapy (ADT) with luteinizing hormone–releasing hormone (LHRH) agonists is a cornerstone of prostate cancer treatment but may impact calcium metabolism and thus urinary stone risk. This study explored the association between LHRH agonist use and urinary stone incidence in men with prostate cancer, and whether concomitant antiresorptive therapy modifies this risk. METHODS: A retrospective cohort study was performed using the TriNetX US Network (2005–2025). Adult males (≥18 years) with prostate cancer were included; those with prior urinary stones were excluded. Exposure groups were defined by receipt of LHRH agonists (leuprolide, goserelin, or triptorelin) versus no LHRH therapy. A secondary analysis examined LHRH users receiving antiresorptive agents (bisphosphonates or denosumab) versus those not receiving them. All cohorts were propensity-score matched for age. Outcomes included urinary stone incidence and stone-related procedures identified by CPT codes. RESULTS: Among 86,799 matched patients per group, stone incidence was higher in those receiving LHRH agonists versus non-users (3.24% vs 1.64%; risk ratio \[RR\] 1.98, 95% CI 1.86–2.11, p<0.0001). When limited to stones ≥1 year after therapy initiation, the association remained significant (RR 2.23, p<0.0001). Stone-related procedures were 2.72 times more frequent in men receiving LHRH agonists (1.12% vs 0.41%, p<0.0001). Among LHRH users, antiresorptive therapy was associated with a lower stone incidence (1.75% vs 2.93%; RR 0.60, 95% CI 0.53-0.68, p<0.0001, n=22,567 per group). CONCLUSIONS: LHRH agonist therapy was associated with nearly double the risk of urinary stone disease and a greater need for stone-related procedures in men with prostate cancer. The risk attenuation observed with concomitant bisphosphonate or denosumab use suggests that preservation of bone mineral balance may mitigate ADT-related lithogenic changes. These findings highlight a potential lithogenic consequence of ADT and raise the possibility that antiresorptive therapy may confer protective effects against nephrolithiasis in this population.

title: IP12-29: Androgen-Deprivation Therapy and Nephrolithiasis: Divergent Stone Risk by Prior Stone History in Prostate Cancer
parentSessionTitle: IP12: Stone Disease: Epidemiology & Evaluation I
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Androgen-deprivation therapy (ADT) is standard for prostate cancer, but its impact on kidney-stone risk is uncertain and may differ by prior nephrolithiasis. We assessed associations between ADT duration and nephrolithiasis, and secondarily osteoporosis, stratified by stone history. METHODS: We conducted a retrospective cohort study in the multi-institution TriNetX network including 512,489 men with prostate cancer (ICD-10 C61). To reduce immortal-time bias, follow-up began 6 months after diagnosis. ADT within 6 months was classified as long term (continuing ≥12 months), short term (no records after month 6), or ADT-naïve (no ADT); patients first exposed after month 6 were excluded. The primary outcome was first post–time-zero nephrolithiasis (N20–N23); the secondary outcome was incident osteoporosis (M80–M81). Within strata defined by prior nephrolithiasis, we performed 1:1 propensity-score–matched comparisons between exposure groups and estimated risks at 12, 24, and 36 months. RESULTS: In men with a stone history, long-term ADT showed the highest recurrence risk, with short-term ADT generally between long-term and naïve ( (https://www.auajournals.org/doi/abs/10.1097/01.JU.0001191328.95269.a6.29#F1)). In men without prior nephrolithiasis, long-term ADT was associated with the lowest cumulative stone risk, short-term ADT intermediate, and ADT-naïve the highest ( (https://www.auajournals.org/doi/abs/10.1097/01.JU.0001191328.95269.a6.29#F2)). Across strata, osteoporosis risk rose in a duration-related pattern (long > short \> naïve). CONCLUSIONS: In this large cohort, ADT was linked to heterogeneous kidney-stone risk—lower incident stones in men without prior nephrolithiasis but higher recurrence among stone-formers—while consistently increasing osteoporosis with longer exposure. These findings support proactive bone-health care for all patients on ADT and intensified stone-prevention strategies in those with a stone history.

title: IP12-30: Which neurogenic bladder patients are at higher risk of sepsis after percutaneous nephrolithotomy?
parentSessionTitle: IP12: Stone Disease: Epidemiology & Evaluation I

speakers.organization: Faculdade de Medicina da Universidade de Sao Paulo, Brazil

fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Patients with neurogenic bladder are at increased risk of kidney stone formation, particularly infection stones, which puts them at risk for sepsis during stone manipulation. Our objective was to identify predictors of sepsis following percutaneous nephrolithotomy in this population, without investigating causal pathways. METHODS: We retrospectively analyzed a consecutive sample of patients with neurogenic bladder who underwent percutaneous nephrolithotomy at our referral center between 2009 and 2020\. We also systematically searched PubMed until February 2025 for studies that investigated neurogenic patients undergoing this procedure. We then performed a single-arm meta-analysis of postoperative sepsis, including our own cohort, and meta-regressions to search for predictors. RESULTS: In our cohort, sepsis rate was 6% \[1%; 19%\], 2/36 patients. The Charlson Comorbidity Index was the only predictor (p=0.02). In the meta-cohort (13 cohorts, 2,369 patients), the combined sepsis rate was 12% \[7%; 17%\], despite high heterogeneity (I2=75%), with no evidence of publication bias (p=0.09). We identified younger age (p=0.04), non-urethral urinary diversions (p=0.04)—particularly ileal conduits (p0.001)—and non-traumatic etiologies (p=0.02), especially spina bifida (p=0.009), as predictors of sepsis. CONCLUSIONS: We recommend the development of a targeted antibiotic prophylaxis protocol, tailored to these predictors, for patients with neurogenic bladder undergoing percutaneous nephrolithotomy. We motivate further research on causal pathways.

title: IP13-01: Liquid Biopsy Using Next-Generation Sequencing to Predict Lymph Node Metastases in Penile Squamous Cell Carcinoma
parentSessionTitle: IP13: Penile & Testicular Cancer I

speakers.organization: Faculdade de Medicina, Universidade de São Paulo

fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Lymph node status is the most important prognostic factor in penile squamous cell carcinoma (SCC). Inguinal lymphadenectomy remains the gold standard for staging but is associated with significant morbidity. Current non-invasive methods show poor sensitivity for micro metastases. Liquid biopsy through circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) analysis and next-generation sequencing (NGS) offers a minimally invasive alternative for molecular risk stratification. This study aimed to evaluate whether ctDNA levels and mutational profiles correlate with pathological lymph node involvement (pN). METHODS: A single-center observational study included 21 patients with penile SCC who underwent partial or total penectomy and inguinal lymphadenectomy between 2015–2023. Preoperative plasma samples were collected for ctDNA extraction (Qiagen QIAamp). Sequencing was performed on the DNBSEQ™ platform using a 40-gene hybrid-capture panel including _TP53, NF1, TJP2, ALK_, and _FGFR_ family genes. Variant calling was conducted using the DRAGEN pipeline (hg38). Variables analyzed included ctDNA concentration, number of variants, histopathologic features, and HPV status. Associations with pN were evaluated using Mann-Whitney and Fisher’s exact tests. RESULTS: Median age was 63 years (range 32–82); 13 patients (61.9%) were pN+. Mean ctDNA concentration was higher in pN+ versus pN− (1.10 vs 0.72 ng/µL; p=0.328). The mean number of variants was significantly greater in pN+ than in pN− (20.6 vs 17.0; p=0.045). Microvascular invasion correlated with nodal metastasis (p=0.024), whereas perineural invasion, histologic grade, and HPV status showed no significant association. The most frequent variants were _NF1_, _TJP2_, _TP_ 53, and _ALK_ (95–100% of cases). CONCLUSIONS: Liquid biopsy with NGS demonstrated that higher ctDNA mutational burden correlates with lymph node metastases in penile SCC. Although ctDNA concentration alone was not discriminatory, molecular profiling may serve as a biomarker for nodal involvement and help avoid unnecessary lymphadenectomies. This is a pioneering study in penile cancer, supporting further validation in multicenter cohorts and the development of disease-specific genetic panels.

title: IP13-02: Single-Cell Transcriptomic Characterization of the Tumor Immune Microenvironment and Heterogeneity Landscape in Penile Cancer
parentSessionTitle: IP13: Penile & Testicular Cancer I
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Penile cancer is a rare but aggressive malignancy of the male genitourinary system, where lymph node metastasis predicts poor prognosis. The tumor immune microenvironment (TME) plays a critical role in tumor progression and treatment response. This study applied single-cell RNA sequencing to systematically delineate the TME of penile cancer at different disease stages, aiming to uncover molecular mechanisms of tumor progression and immune evasion, and to identify potential immunotherapeutic targets. METHODS: Fresh tumor and adjacent tissues from four penile cancer patients were analyzed, including one non-metastatic and three lymph node–metastatic cases. High-risk human papillomavirus (HPV) status was confirmed by in situ hybridization and p16 immunohistochemistry. A total of 36,601 cells were processed using Cell Ranger and Seurat pipelines. Integrated analyses, including bulk RNA sequencing, cell–cell communication, pseudotime trajectory, and functional enrichment, were performed to characterize TME heterogeneity. RESULTS: Nine transcriptionally f cellular clusters were identified, highlighting marked heterogeneity within the tumor immune microenvironment. Interactions among epithelial, fibroblast, and endothelial cells promoted epithelial–mesenchymal transition, angiogenesis, and invasion. Lymph node–metastatic tumors showed increased cell cycle activity and proliferative potential. Non-metastatic tumors exhibited active innate immune responses with dendritic cell activation but also early immunosuppression through regulatory T-cell enrichment. Metastatic tumors were dominated by M2-like macrophages, exhausted and naïve T cells, indicating an immunosuppressive milieu. During progression, the TME shifted from immune activation to suppression, reflecting gradual immune escape and T-cell exhaustion as a hallmark of advanced disease. CONCLUSIONS: This study constructs the first single-cell immune atlas of penile cancer, revealing marked heterogeneity and dynamic remodeling of the TME during disease progression. The findings provide potential biomarkers and therapeutic targets for immunotherapy and offer a molecular basis for individualized treatment strategies. Validation in larger patient cohorts is warranted.

title: IP13-03: Survival of the fittest: Outcomes in node positive penile cancer patients where non-surgical management is utilised in place of RILND.
parentSessionTitle: IP13: Penile & Testicular Cancer I
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Approximately one-third of penile squamous cell carcinoma (pSCC) cases present with nodal disease at presentation. Radical inguinal lymph node dissection (RILND) is the standard of care for nodal-positive disease but carries substantial morbidity, with many patients unfit for surgery. This study evaluates outcomes in node positive disease managed non-surgically. METHODS: We conducted a retrospective cohort study of 287 adults with newly diagnosed pSCC from January 2017 to December 2024, across four regional referral centres. Data was obtained from multidisciplinary team (MDT), pathology, and electronic health records. Patient demographics, treatment modalities, and survival outcomes were analysed. RESULTS: 85 patients (29.6%) had nodal disease at presentation (N1=31, N2=13, N3=41). Mean age was 65.6 (range 31–92), with 41.2% presenting with palpable nodes. Nodal status was determined at MDT based on radiological and pathological assessment (core node sampling or sentinel node biopsy). Twelve patients with distant metastases were excluded. Median follow-up was 19.5 months. 56.5% were fit for RILND; of these 18.75% received neoadjuvant systemic anti-cancer therapy (SACT), and 20.8% received adjuvant radiotherapy. 43.5% of patients were unfit for RILND and received SACT plus radiotherapy (10.8%), radiotherapy alone (56.8%), SACT alone (10.8%), or supportive care (21.6%). The Kaplan-Meier curve below demonstrates that the best survival was in patients undergoing surgical node management. Among non-surgical patients, SACT plus radiotherapy offered the most favourable outcomes, followed by radiotherapy alone, while supportive care yielded the poorest survival. Recurrence rates were 31.7% in the surgical cohort and 30% in the non-surgical cohort, though recurrence in the latter is likely underestimated, as 72.2% died from their primary disease before recurrence could be assessed. CONCLUSIONS: RILND remains the optimal treatment for node-positive pSCC, but a significant proportion of patients (43.5%) are unfit for surgery. Although SACT in combination with radiotherapy appears to offer the best survival for these patients, prognosis in this group remains poor. Further research is needed to optimize systemic therapies and improve prognosis in patients unfit for surgical nodal management.

title: IP13-04: Real-World Patterns and Predictors of Surgical Lymph-Node Management in Penile Cancer: Insights from the Epic COSMOS Database
parentSessionTitle: IP13: Penile & Testicular Cancer I
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Accurate management of regional lymph nodes, through sentinel node biopsy or inguinal lymph-node dissection (ILND) — either for staging or therapeutic purposes — is essential for disease control and survival in penile cancer. Current international guidelines recommend surgical nodal evaluation for all patients with ≥ T1b disease; however, adherence in real-world practice remains uncertain. We aimed to assess national patterns of surgical lymph-node management, including both staging and therapeutic dissections, and to identify factors associated with their use in patients with penile cancer. METHODS: Epic COSMOS, an aggregated electronic health record dataset encompassing over 300 million patients from >1,700 hospitals and 40,000 clinics across North America and abroad, was queried for men diagnosed with penile cancer stage ≥ T1b between 2015 and 2025. Patients with distant metastases or 1 year of follow-up were excluded. Surgical lymph-node management included any node biopsy or inguinal lymph-node dissection (ILND) performed within six months of diagnosis, in both clinically node-negative (N0) and node-positive (N+) cases. Demographic, clinical, and socioeconomic characteristics were compared by lymph-node surgical status, and multivariable models were used to assess factors independently associated with surgical management. RESULTS: Among 679 eligible patients, 240 (35%) underwent surgical lymph-node management. Patients who received lymph nodes surgery were younger (median 66 vs 69 years, p=0.011) and more frequently diagnosed in recent years (p<0.001). In multivariable analysis, higher T stage (T2 vs T1b: OR 1.60, 95% CI 1.01–2.57, p=0.047) and later year of diagnosis (OR 1.14 per year, p<0.001) were independently associated with undergoing lymph node surgery, whereas older age predicted lower odds (OR 0.99 per year, p=0.042). BMI, comorbidity, and insurance type were not significant predictors. Geographic variation persisted, with patients from the Southern part of United States less likely to undergo nodes surgery (OR 0.60, 95% CI 0.37–0.95, p=0.029). CONCLUSIONS: Despite established guidelines, only one in three men with ≥ T1b penile cancer underwent surgical lymph-node management, whether for staging or therapeutic intent. Utilization increased modestly over time but remained suboptimal even in most recent years, underscoring significant undertreatment of potentially curable regional disease and the need for broader adherence to evidence-based surgical practice.

title: IP13-05: Comparative real-world outcomes of multimodal treatment strategies in patients with locally advanced N3-stage penile cancer: a retrospective cohort study
parentSessionTitle: IP13: Penile & Testicular Cancer I
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Penile cancer is a rare malignancy, with a global incidence of approximately 0.8 cases per 100,000 men. N3-stage locally advanced disease typically presents with fixed inguinal lymph node metastases and poor prognosis. Chemotherapy is commonly used in this setting, and there has been a growing number of studies investigating immunotherapy and targeted therapy for the treatment. However, comparative data on the outcomes of different multimodal regimens remain limited. Our study aims to evaluate the outcomes of different multimodal treatments in patients with locally advanced N3-stage penile squamous cell carcinoma (PSCC). METHODS: We retrospectively analyzed 107 patients with locally advanced N3-stage PSCC treated at our center between 2008 and 2024. Patients either received multimodal therapy or surgery alone. Clinical responses were assessed using RECIST 1.1. Treatment-related adverse events (TrAEs) and postoperative complications were graded by CTCAE v5.0 and Clavien-Dindo classification. Progression-free survival (PFS) and overall survival (OS) were estimated using the Kaplan-Meier method and compared by log-rank test. The approval of study was obtained from the Institutional Review Board of West China Hospital. RESULTS: Among 107 patients that all received surgery, 16 received chemotherapy, 19 received chemotherapy and targeted therapy, 2 received chemotherapy and immunotherapy, 16 received chemotherapy, targeted therapy and immunotherapy. 54 underwent surgery alone. Median OS was 14.8 months (95% CI, 12.1-18.1) in the multimodal group, compared with 5.8 months (95% CI, 4.7-7.5) after surgery alone (HR 0.26; 95% CI, 0.17-0.40; p<0.001). Median PFS for patients receiving multimodal therapy was 4.4 months (95% CI, 3.5-6.0), with no statistical significance between different multimodal groups. The overall disease control rate (DCR) and objective response rate (ORR) were 79.2% and 62.3% respectively, with different DCR and ORR in each group. Treatment-related toxicities and postoperative complications were acceptable. CONCLUSIONS: Multimodal treatment significantly improved OS compared with surgery alone in patients with locally advanced N3-stage PSCC. Although no statistical significance in OS was observed among different multimodal treatment groups, the combination of chemotherapy, targeted therapy and immunotherapy appeared to yield the most favorable outcomes.

title: IP13-06: Penile Cancer Treatments and Their Psychiatric Sequelae: A National Analysis
parentSessionTitle: IP13: Penile & Testicular Cancer I
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Penile cancer patients may be particularly vulnerable to depression, anxiety, and social isolation, yet population-level data on mental health outcomes are lacking. We investigated the incidence and predictors of mental health disease (MHD) following penile cancer diagnosis and treatment using nationally representative datasets. METHODS: We conducted a retrospective analysis of the de-identified MarketScan® Commercial Claims (MCCD) and Medicare Supplemental (MSD) databases (2009–2023). Eligible patients were ≥18 years with a confirmed penile cancer (required of disease-specific treatment within three years of initial diagnosis). Those with pre-existing MHD were excluded. Treatments were categorized as radical (radical penectomy/perineal urethrostomy), partial (partial penectomy), topical (imiquimod/5-FU), or local excision. The primary outcome was new-onset MHD (major depressive disorder or generalized anxiety disorder requiring pharmacologic therapy) within 36 months. Multivariable Cox models identified predictors. RESULTS: Among 1,633 patients (1,044 MCCD; 589 MSD), 151 (14.5%) and 83 (14.1%) developed MHD, respectively. In MCCD, radical penectomy (HR 3.33, 95% CI 1.72-6.47, p<0.001), CCI 2 (HR 1.74, 95% CI 1.03-2.96, p=0.040), and CCI 3+ (HR 2.45, 95% CI 1.54-3.91, p<0.001) predicted increased MHD risk, while age in the 3rd quartile was protective (HR 0.47, 95% CI 0.30-0.75, p=0.001). These variables did not significantly correlate with MHD in the MSD cohort. CONCLUSIONS: Penile cancer patients face high rates of MHD, particularly after radical surgery, in the presence of comorbidities. This relationship appeared to differ between MSD and MCCD cohorts. Survivorship models should integrate timely mental health support and address access disparities.

title: IP13-08: Age-Stratified Association Between Inflammatory Penile Disorders and Penile Cancer: A Tenfold Increased Risk Across All Age Groups
parentSessionTitle: IP13: Penile & Testicular Cancer I

speakers.organization: State University of New York, Downstate, College of Medicine

fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Inflammatory disorders of the prepuce and glans (IDPG), including phimosis, paraphimosis, balanitis, and balanoposthitis, are proposed risk factors for malignant penile cancer (MPC), a rare but aggressive disease. Additional established risks include human papillomavirus infection, smoking, low socioeconomic status, and lack of circumcision. Chronic inflammation is thought to promote carcinogenesis; however, large-scale studies directly linking IDPG to oncologic outcomes remain limited. To address this gap, we conducted a retrospective cohort study evaluating the association between IDPG and adverse outcomes, including MPC, amputation, nodal metastasis, and mortality. METHODS: The TriNetX Research Network (TNX) contains the aggregated and de-identified healthcare records of over 150 million patients from 107 healthcare institutions. We queried TNX for patients diagnosed with IDPG. Inclusion criteria included at least 1 year of follow up after IDPG diagnosis, and no prior history of MPC. Patients were split into those diagnosed with IDPG (n=81,163) at 35-55, 55-75, and 75+ years old. We identified control patients without IDPG (n=3,842,747) who met inclusion criteria, and performed 1:1 nearest-neighbor propensity score matching (PSM) on demographics, comorbidities, and measures of healthcare use. We analyzed 20 year incidence of MPC, penile amputation, radiation, chemotherapy, metastasis, and all-cause mortality. Risk ratios (RR) were calculated within TriNetX on Aug 8th, 2025. RESULTS: IDPG patients showed higher rates of mortality, MPC, amputation, and nodal metastasis. Radiation use was increased only in the 35–55 IDPG- group, while chemotherapy exposure was not significant between groups. Of note, patients who are IDPG+ had a 10-12X higher risk of MPC than the IDPG- group. Median follow-up (days, IQR) was shorter in IDPG patients than controls across all age groups: 35–55 (1648, 1901 vs. 1726, 2017), 55–75 (1606, 1769 vs. 1823, 1986), and 75+ (1145, 1200 vs. 1266, 1320). CONCLUSIONS: IDPGs were linked to higher risks of MPC, mortality, amputation, and nodal metastasis across all age groups, suggesting an independent and clinically significant effect beyond age related comorbidity. These results underscore the importance of early hygiene, timely diagnosis, and targeted management in this high-risk population. | | | --- | | |

title: IP13-09: Prognostic Impact of Recurrence on Survival in Surgically Treated Penile Cancer: A 12-Year Retrospective Cohort (2013–2025)
parentSessionTitle: IP13: Penile & Testicular Cancer I
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Penile squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) remains rare yet clinically aggressive, even with organ-sparing techniques and standardized inguinal lymph node dissection (ILND), survival is dictated mainly by post-treatment biology. Reliable outcome estimates are essential to refine risk stratification and guide adjuvant therapy. This study assessed recurrence, metastasis and cancer-specific mortality (CSM) in a surgical cohort, correlating clinicopathologic features and surgical approach with disease-free (DFS) and overall survival (OS). METHODS: Retrospective single-center analysis (2013–2025) of histologically confirmed SCC. Variables included pathologic (pT/pN), lymphovascular/perineural invasion (LVI/PNI), margins, histology, surgery type, ILND, adjuvant therapy, recurrence, metastasis, and vital status. DFS and OS were analyzed by Kaplan–Meier and log-rank tests, predictors by multivariable Cox regression modeling recurrence as a time-dependent covariate. Fine–Gray analysis addressed competing CSM events, and inverse-probability weighting corrected selection bias. RESULTS: Organ-sparing surgery predominated, as ILND nearly universal, reflecting a paradigm of oncologic thoroughness with functional preservation. Recurrence occurred in one-third of cases, being the primary determinant of mortality. In adjusted Cox models, recurrence was the strongest predictor of DFS and OS (HR 4.87; 95% CI 2.81–8.42; p<0.001), persisting after weighting and imputation. Advanced T stage (HR 2.35; p=0.003), positive margins (HR 1.78; p=0.02), LVI (HR 2.14; p=0.008), and PNI (HR 1.96; p=0.01) intensified risk, denoting synergism between aggressiveness and microscopic persistence. Penectomy type lost independent significance (HR 0.91; p=0.64), confirming oncologic equivalence under negative margins and proper nodal control. Competing-risks modeling reaffirmed recurrence as the main driver of CSM (sub-HR 5.22; 95% CI 2.71–10.06; p<0.001), with strong discrimination (Harrell’s C=0.83) and calibration. CONCLUSIONS: Relapse is the pivotal determinant of prognosis in penile SCC, surpassing surgical extent and baseline pathology. With optimized margins and nodal control, organ-sparing surgery remains oncologically sound. Next frontier lies in recurrence prevention through risk-adapted adjuvant therapy, vigilant surveillance and early salvage.

title: IP13-10: Pure testicular seminomas that relapse with nonseminomatous elements: clinical patterns and management
parentSessionTitle: IP13: Penile & Testicular Cancer I
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: A subset of testicular seminomas, though initially pure seminoma and without alpha fetoprotein (AFP) elevation, will relapse with nonseminomatous germ cell tumor (NSGCT) elements. This phenomenon, marked by nonseminomatous histology or AFP elevation, is rare but potentially clinically significant, and herein we report on our management and outcomes. METHODS: We included male patients who had pure seminoma at diagnosis with no AFP elevation and who developed subsequent relapse with either histologically confirmed nonseminoma or elevated AFP (>15ng/mL) between 1980-2024. Patient characteristics, disease stage, therapy details, perioperative outcomes, and follow-up data were collected from medical records. RESULTS: Pure seminoma was histologically confirmed in 2116 patients undergoing orchiectomy across all stages. In patients who met our criteria relapse occurred in 305 patients (14%) of which 22 patients (1%) had nonseminomatous elements and/or AFP >15 ng/mL. At diagnosis, laterality of the tumor was equal and rete testis invasion was positive in 55%. Clinical stage was I in 41%, II in 45%, and III in 14% of patients. Table 1 presents details stratified by clinical stage. Active surveillance was performed in 36% of patients, while 64% received treatment after orchiectomy. Primary treatment entailed radiotherapy in 36% and chemotherapy in 64% of patients. Median time to follow-up was 8 years (IQR 5-12). Relapse-free survival was 1 year (IQR 0.6-1.6 years). Most common relapse site was retroperitoneal in 50% of patients. 73% of patients had elevated AFP at relapse, median peak level of AFP was 30 ng/mL (IQR 20-132). Retroperitoneal lymph node dissection (RPLND) was performed in 45% of patients of which 80% were post- chemotherapy. Nonseminomatous histology was found in 60% of RPLNDs and no RPLND specimen showed seminoma. CONCLUSIONS: In patients with pure seminoma who experience relapse, awareness of possible nonseminomatous elements is essential. At relapse, evaluating AFP levels and obtaining histological confirmation - particularly when clinical or radiological findings are atypical - is recommended. Although the presence of nonseminomatous components is rare, its recognition is critical, as management differs from that of seminoma relapse. | | | --- | | |

title: IP13-11: Primary Retroperitoneal Lymph Node Dissection for Clinical Stage II Seminoma: Comparative Analysis Against Established Paradigms Using the National Cancer Data Base
parentSessionTitle: IP13: Penile & Testicular Cancer I
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: While primary retroperitoneal lymph node dissection for clinical stage II seminoma can reduce chemotherapy and radiation burden, no comparative analyses of this approach currently exist. We utilized a national oncologic data registry to perform the first comparative analysis of outcomes after primary retroperitoneal lymph node dissection for stage II seminoma. METHODS: Using the National Cancer Data Base, we identified patients with stage II germ cell tumors between 2004 to 2022. Cox regression was used for survival analyses. Primary analysis examined overall survival for patients with stage II seminoma. Sensitivity analysis after energy-balancing weighting was performed. Secondary analyses were performed for overall survival in patients who underwent primary retroperitoneal lymph node dissection for stage II germ cell tumor generally and for salvage-chemotherapy-free survival after primary retroperitoneal lymph node dissection for stage II seminoma. RESULTS: Primary analysis included 4,661 patients (median follow-up 6.8 years, IQR 3.6-10.5yr). Overall survival did not differ by primary treatment (versus chemotherapy – HR1.34, 95% CI 0.93-1.93, p=0.12; versus radiation – 1.02, 0.65-1.59, p=0.95). Sensitivity analysis results were similar. Secondary analysis showed increased mortality with nonseminomatous germ cell tumor (HR2.63, 1.07-6.49, p=0.036) and increased salvage chemotherapy with cN2 (HR3.88, 1.87-8.03, p=0.00027) and cN3 (HR6.03, 2.1-17.3, p=0.00083) compared to cN1. CONCLUSIONS: Overall survival after primary retroperitoneal lymph node dissection for stage II seminoma appears comparable to alternatives and possibly improved in favor of seminoma compared to nonseminomatous germ cell tumor. Risk of needing salvage chemotherapy increases with clinical disease extent.

title: IP13-12: Primary Retroperitoneal Lymph Node Dissection (RPLND) for clinical stage IIA/IIB Seminoma – Updated Population-Based Results from Swedish and Norwegian Testicular Cancer Group (SWENOTECA)
parentSessionTitle: IP13: Penile & Testicular Cancer I
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Cure rates for metastatic testicular cancer are very high, but this comes at a cost for patients. While most achieve long-term remission, survivors face elevated risks of cardiovascular disease, secondary malignancies, and reduced life expectancy. To reduce the long-term morbidity associated with chemotherapy or radiotherapy for metastatic seminoma, primary RPLND has been explored as a treatment option for patients with low-volume disease. Several prospective and retrospective series have reported on the efficacy and safety of this approach, leading to recommendations in both the AUA and SWENOTECA guidelines. In May 2024, SWENOTECA published the results of the first prospective population-based cohort of 62 metastatic patients treated with primary RPLND. Herein we present data for overall 135 patients treated with primary RPLND for presumed low-volume metastatic seminoma. METHODS: This is a population-based prospective cohort of 135 patients with presumed metastatic seminoma clinical stage (CS) IIA/IIB with a maximum of two suspected malignant lymph nodes with a maximum diameter of 3 cm. Patients were operated with primary RPLND from 2019 to 2025 at five tertiary hospitals in Sweden and Norway. RESULTS: Median age at RPLND was 44 years (IQR: 36-51). Median time of follow-up was 25 months (IQR: 12-39). Overall, 79 patients (59%) were included after relapse in former CS I, of whom 24 (19%) had received prior adjuvant chemotherapy. At time of RPLND, 97 patients (72%) had CS IIA, and 38 patients (28%) had CS IIB. In total, 98% had a prior FDG-PET, of whom 95% had a positive result. Robot-assisted laparoscopic RPLND was performed in 106 patients (79%). 40% were right sided unilateral template, 58% left sided unilateral template, and 2% bilateral RPLND. Median operating time was 158 min (IQR: 116-218), median blood loss 50 ml (IQR:20-100) and intraoperative complications occurred in 4 patients (3%). Post-operative complications Clavien-Dindo ≥ III occurred in 6 patients (4.4%), chylous ascites requiring drainage was the most common event. Median hospital stay was 2 nights (IQR: 2-4). 89% reported preserved ejaculation after RPLND (data available in 101 patients). Metastatic seminoma was confirmed in 131 patients (97%), one patient had a teratoma (0.7%), one patient had a non-seminoma other than teratoma (0.7%), one patient had necrosis/fibrosis and one patient had a glandular infection (pN0 1.5%). Median lymph node yield was 11 (IQR: 7-16), with a median of 1 malignant node (IQR: 1-2), and median largest metastasis diameter 20 mm (IQR:15-25). 58 patients (43%) received post-RPLND adjuvant chemotherapy, most one cycle of BEP. Post-RPLND relapse occurred in 16 patients (12%), 5 of those were outfield. Median time to relapse was 12 months (IQR: 7-18). Progression free survival at 25 months was 90% (95% CI 0.82-0.94) and overall survival was 100%. CONCLUSIONS: This approach to treat selected patients with surgery instead of conventional chemotherapy or radiation, still appears safe and effective. The relapse rate after RPLND remains low. The FDG-PET is a useful tool for selecting seminoma patients for surgery, thereby avoiding higher rates of benign outcomes.

title: IP13-13: Outcomes of primary retroperitoneal lymph node dissection for clinical stage IIB testicular seminoma: A binational retrospective analysis
parentSessionTitle: IP13: Penile & Testicular Cancer I
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Retroperitoneal lymph node dissection (RPLND) has been established as a first-line treatment for seminoma with small volume retroperitoneal metastases, aiming to reduce long-term toxicity from chemotherapy and radiotherapy. However, its role in clinical stage IIB disease remains unclear. This study evaluates the outcomes of primary RPLND in stage IIB seminoma. METHODS: In this retrospective study, we included consecutive patients who underwent primary RPLND with curative intent for clinical stage IIB seminoma, defined as a retroperitoneal lymph node size of 2 to 5 cm on preoperative imaging, at two large referral centers in the United States and Germany between 2016 and 2025. Those with insufficient clinical data were excluded. Perioperative and oncological outcomes of the patients were assessed. RESULTS: Forty patients with a median age of 35 years were included. The median preoperative mass size was 2.5 cm (range 2 – 4.5). A midline abdominal approach was used for all surgeries. Median operative time and blood loss were 154 minutes and 100 ml, respectively. A median of 21 nodes was removed, and final pathology revealed pN0, pN1, pN2, pN3 in 2 (5%), 1 (2.5%), 32 (80%), and 5 (12.5%) cases, respectively (Table). Complications within 90 days were observed in seven patients (17.5%), six of which were grade III. None of the patients received adjuvant chemotherapy.
