With a median follow-up of 27 (IQR 17-39) months, 9 patients (22.5%) experienced recurrence (5 in-field and 4 outfield). Of these, five were pN2 and four pN3; six received chemotherapy and three underwent additional surgery. Median time to recurrence was 10 months. Kaplan-Meier analysis estimated 2-year recurrence-free and overall survival rates at 78% and 100%, respectively. Recurrence-free survival was significantly lower in patients with pN3 disease ( Figure). CONCLUSIONS: RPLND can be considered as a first-line treatment for stage IIB testicular seminoma, offering low morbidity and favorable intermediate-term oncological outcomes if performed in specialized centers by expert surgeons. Larger nodal disease is not suitable for surgical management due to the increased recurrence risk. | | | --- | | |

title: IP13-14: Post-chemotherapy retroperitoneal lymph node dissection for patients with metastatic pure seminoma
parentSessionTitle: IP13: Penile & Testicular Cancer I
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Post-chemotherapy retroperitoneal lymph node dissection (pcRPLND) for metastatic testicular seminoma is reserved for highly select cases and can be associated with significant morbidity. We report contemporary outcomes of pcRPLND in patients with metastatic pure seminoma with the goal of better defining patient selection for surgery and exploring gaps in diagnostic staging. METHODS: Patients who underwent pcRPLND after ≥1-line of chemotherapy for metastatic pure seminoma at our institution between 2000-2024 were included. Clinicopathologic, radiographic, perioperative, oncologic, and survival outcomes are reported. RESULTS: 52 patients underwent pcRPLND for metastatic pure seminoma during the study period. Most patients (67%) received ≥2 lines of chemotherapy prior to surgery. Eight patients (15%) harbored residual viable seminoma at pcRPLND, 38% and 6% following first-line and ≥2-lines of chemotherapy, respectively (Figure). None of the patients that received high-dose chemotherapy (TI-CE) had viable disease at surgery. Over a median follow up of 50-months, 5 (10%) patients relapsed after pcRPLND, all of whom had viable residual seminoma at pcRPLND. Of the 8 patients with residual seminoma at pcRPLND, 2 were cured with pcRPLND alone, 3 with pcRPLND plus additional chemotherapy, and 3 died from progressive disease. CONCLUSIONS: The risk of finding viable residual seminoma at pcRPLND varied based on prior chemotherapy received. These data underscore the importance of careful patient selection given the competing risks of morbidity associated with pcRPLND, the high likelihood of cure with high-dose chemotherapy, and the need for better diagnostics to guide surgical decision-making in this setting. | | | --- | | |

title: IP13-15: Robotic versus Open Post-Chemotherapy Retroperitoneal Lymph Node Dissection: A Propensity Score Matched Study Across Eleven Academic Medical Centers
parentSessionTitle: IP13: Penile & Testicular Cancer I
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Post-chemotherapy retroperitoneal lymph node dissection (PC-RPLND) is crucial in testicular cancer treatment, as one-third of patients have residual masses post-chemotherapy. While the open approach remains the gold standard, it is associated with higher morbidity. Minimally invasive approaches like robotic PC-RPLND aim to reduce morbidity, and increasingly, is being performed at academic centres due to the potential for lower blood loss, shorter length of stay, and accelerated recovery. Our objective was to compare perioperative and survival outcomes of patients undergoing robotic versus open post-chemotherapy retroperitoneal lymph node dissection (PC-RPLND) for testicular cancer. METHODS: Analyzing data from patients who underwent PC-RPLND at eleven academic centres between 1990-2023, we used propensity score matching (PSM) to create a 1:1 (open-RPLND: robotic-RPLND) matched cohort. The primary endpoint was time to relapse. Secondary endpoints included operative time, length of stay, estimated blood loss, and surgical complications. Relapse free survival rates were calculated using the Kaplan-Meier methodology, and log-rank tests to compare perioperative outcomes between robotic vs. open PC-RPLND. RESULTS: A total of 134 robotic cases were propensity score matched to 134 open cases. At a median follow-up of 2.2 years, estimated relapse-free survival at 3 years was similar between robotic and open PC-RPLND (92.8% vs. 88.5%, p=0.18). Relapse occurred in 5.2% (robotic) vs. 12.3% (open), with most relapses occurring within the first year . Robotic PC-RPLND was associated with lower blood loss, shorter operative time and hospital stay, and fewer complications (16.4% vs. 32.1%), including a 0% rate of ileus compared to 12.7% in the open group. Lymph node yield and rates of viable tumor were comparable between approaches. The main limitation of this study was its retrospective nature. CONCLUSIONS: This is the first multicenter study to compare open versus robotic PC-RPLND using a PSM system. With appropriate patient selection and surgical experience at academic centers specializing in testicular cancer care, robotic PC-RPLND offers low morbidity and improved perioperative outcomes while maintaining the same oncological outcomes, compared to the open approach.

title: IP13-16: Robotic-Assisted Retroperitoneal Lymph Node Dissection for Metastatic Testicular Malignancies – a 9-Year Comparative Analysis of the Outcomes and Learning Curve
parentSessionTitle: IP13: Penile & Testicular Cancer I
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Robotic-assisted retroperitoneal lymph node dissection (RA-RPLND) is an emerging minimally-invasive alternative for treating and staging metastatic testicular malignancies. Whilst open RPLND remains the standard-of-care, global uptake of RA-RPLND has expanded. We report peri-operative outcomes of RA-RPLNDs by a single, fellowship-trained uro-oncologist over 9 years, with a focus on learning curve trends. METHODS: A prospective database for RA-RPLNDs performed between August 2016-2025 was analysed. Patients with retroperitoneal metastatic testicular tumours undergoing primary or post-chemotherapy resections were included. All cases used a transperitoneal robotic-assisted approach. Patients were stratified into 4 sequential cohorts of 20 cases each. Cohort comparisons used Kruskal-Wallis with Dunn’s post-hoc test. Predictors of outcomes were evaluated with generalised linear models. RESULTS: Of 80 consecutive RA-RPLND patients; 33 (41%) underwent primary and 47 (59%) post-chemotherapy RA-RPLND. Median operative time (OT) was 180 minutes (IQR 150-210), estimated blood loss (EBL) was 100 ml (IQR 50-150) and median hospital length of stay (LOS) was 1 night (1-7). Six high-grade (33) Clavien-Dindo complications were observed, 2 each in cohorts 2-4. Cohort analyses showed significant differences for template performed (p=0.01), OT (p=0.001) and lymph node (LN) yield (p0.001), but no difference in EBL (p=0.074), LOS (p=0.076) or complications (p=0.59). OT increased in later cohorts, with subset analysis showing an increase of 40 and 50 minutes in cohort 2 and 4 respectively (p=0.012, p=0.002), reflecting progressive shift in complexity and paralleled by proportion of bilateral templates and LN yield. On multivariate regression, bilateral template dissection independently predicted OT (p0.001), longer LOS (p0.001), greater EBL (p0.001) and higher LN yield (p=0.026). Cohort 4 showed longer OT (p=0.026) and higher LN yield (p 0.027-0.001), with unchanged EBL and LOS. Integrating peri-operative variables identified complications and open conversion to be independently associated with longer LOS (p=0.039, p0.001), while concomitant procedures prolonged operative time (p=0.033). CONCLUSIONS: This is the largest reported single-surgeon series of RA-RPLND for metastatic testicular cancer. Outcomes were most affected by surgical template and intra-operative factors rather than case sequence. These findings support the feasibility and oncological safety of RA-RPLND in high-volume hands, while underscoring the importance of case selection and formal training in this heterogenous and technically demanding procedure.

title: IP13-17: Robotic Primary and Post-Chemotherapy Retroperitoneal Lymph Node Dissection for Testicular Cancer: Single Institution Experience
parentSessionTitle: IP13: Penile & Testicular Cancer I
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Robotic retroperitoneal lymph node dissection (RPLND) has emerged as a minimally invasive alternative to open surgery for testicular cancer, but outcomes in post-chemotherapy patients remain incompletely characterized. We report our institutional experience evaluating peri-operative and early oncologic outcomes of robotic RPLND in both pre- and post-chemotherapy settings. METHODS: We performed a retrospective review of all patients undergoing robotic RPLND for testis cancer between 2015 and 2025 at a single academic institution. Demographic, operative, and pathologic variables were analyzed. Perioperative outcomes were compared between primary RPLND and post-chemotherapy RPLND cohorts. RESULTS: A total of 51 patients underwent robotic RPLND, including 25 post-chemotherapy and 26 primary RPLND cases. Median operative time was 410 minutes (IQR 305–514) for post-chemotherapy and 309 minutes (IQR 240–433) for primary cases. Median estimated blood loss was 200 ml (IQR 100–300) and 125 ml (IQR 75–250), respectively. Clavien I–II complications occurred in 2 post-chemotherapy (8%) and 2 primary RPLND (8%) patients. Clavien III or greater complications did not occur in either group. Conversion to open occurred in 0 post-chemotherapy and 1 primary RPLND case. Median lymph node yield was 31 (IQR 25–55) for post-chemotherapy and 29 (IQR 21–44) for primary RPLNDs. No in-field recurrences were observed in either cohort. CONCLUSIONS: Robotic RPLND is feasible and safe in both primary and post-chemotherapy settings, achieving comparable node yields and low morbidity. Despite longer operative times in post-chemotherapy patients, overall outcomes and early oncologic control were favorable. These findings support the broader adoption of robotic RPLND in post-chemotherapy setting at experienced centers.

title: IP13-18: Beyond a Simple Procedure: Multicenter Evaluation of Surgical Practices in Radical Orchiectomy for Testicular Germ Cell Tumors
parentSessionTitle: IP13: Penile & Testicular Cancer I
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Radical orchiectomy (RO) is the cornerstone and curative first-line treatment for testicular germ cell tumors (TGCT). Although often considered a straightforward procedure, it plays a crucial role in diagnosis, staging, and oncologic outcomes. Yet, data on surgical technique, perioperative variables, and short-term outcomes remain limited and mostly from single-center studies. A clearer understanding of perioperative practice across institutions is needed to identify variability and improve surgical standards. This study aimed to analyze perioperative and surgical outcomes of patients undergoing RO. METHODS: Data from 305 patients who underwent RO for TGCT between 2020 and 2024 across six academic institutions were retrospectively analyzed. Preoperative variables included Eastern cooperative oncology group (ECOG) performance status, serum tumor markers, hormonal profile, scrotal ultrasound (US), body CT scan, and sperm cryopreservation status. Perioperative parameters such as operative time, testicular prosthesis implantation, and drain placement were also collected. Postoperative recovery and complications were assessed according to the Clavien–Dindo classification, and surgical margin status was reported in relation to pathological tumor (pT) stage. Descriptive statistics were applied. RESULTS: The median (IQR) age was 35 (29-43) years. Most patients had an ECOG performance status of 0 (96.7%), while 5 (1.6%) patients had a status of 1, 2 (0.7%) had 2, and 1 (0.3%) had 3. Preoperatively, all serum tumor markers (LDH, β-hCG and AFP) were assessed in 219 (71.8%) patients, while hormonal profiling (total testosterone, LH, FSH) was performed in 57 (18.7%) patients. Scrotal US was performed in 99.7% of case, while preoperative body CT scan in 83%. Sperm cryopreservation was utilized in 192 (63%) patients. The median operative time was 64 (46-86) minutes. A testicular prosthesis was implanted in 42% of cases, and a surgical drain was placed in 2.3%. Postoperative complications occurred in 7 (2.3%) patients, all Clavien–Dindo grade I. Overall complication rates did not differ between patients with and without drain placement (2.3%% vs 2.1%) or prosthesis implantation (0.8% vs. 3.5%), respectively. Operative time was significantly longer with prosthesis implantation (70 \[50-94\] vs 60 \[44-79\] minutes, p=0.04). Positive surgical margins were reported in 5 (2.6%) patients, corresponding to pT1 in 1.2% cases, pT2 in 0.9%, and pT3 in 40% (p=0.008). CONCLUSIONS: Preoperative patients work-up is usually comprising serum markers, US, and CT scan assessment, but frequently lacks hormonal screening and cryopreservation, although representing two relevant aspects in patients with TGCT. RO is usually associated with few postoperative complications. Margin positivity is relatively rare overall but appear to be more frequent in higher pathological stages.

title: IP13-19: Delayed orchiectomy and retroperitoneal lymph node dissection pathology after chemotherapy: Correlation and prognostic impact in advanced germ cell tumors
parentSessionTitle: IP13: Penile & Testicular Cancer I

speakers.organization: UT Health San Antonio Long School of Medicine

fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: In patients with advanced nonseminomatous germ cell tumors (NSGCT), orchiectomy (OE) is often delayed when urgent chemotherapy is required. The prognostic value of post-chemotherapy OE pathology versus retroperitoneal lymph node dissection (RPLND) findings remains uncertain. We examined the histopathologic concordance between OE and RPLND specimens and evaluated the prognostic value of each site in relation to relapse-free (RFS) and overall survival (OS). METHODS: Among 807 NSGCT patients treated between 2000 and 2025, 87 who underwent post-chemotherapy OE and/or RPLND were analyzed. Pathology was categorized as necrosis/fibrosis, teratoma, or viable GCT. Combined-pathology risk was defined by the most aggressive histology. RFS and OS were estimated by Kaplan-Meier at 24 and 60 months with log-rank testing. Univariable and multivariable Cox models included RPLND pathology, combined pathology risk, International Germ Cell Cancer Collaborative Group (IGCCCG) risk group, and clinical stage. Serum AFP and β-hCG levels (pre- and post-chemotherapy) were analyzed for associations with pathology and outcomes. RESULTS: Median age was 28.0 years; 83.9% had Stage III disease and 49.4% were IGCCCG poor risk. OE pathology showed no viable tumor in 57.5%, teratoma in 27.6%, and viable GCT in 13.8%; corresponding RPLND results were 35.6%, 39.1%, and 12.6%. Among 76 paired cases, 36.8% were discordant: viable GCT appeared only in OE in 4 patients and only in RPLND in 8, indicating either site may harbor residual malignancy. Pre-chemotherapy AFP/β-hCG elevation occurred in 89.1% of patients and correlated with higher clinical stage and more aggressive histology. Marker elevation persisted in 40% with viable GCT, 8.6% with teratoma, and 13.5% with necrosis., Patients with discordant pathology had twice the rate of persistent marker elevation (17.6% vs 8.7%). Discordance was not associated with OS (p=0.354) or RFS (p=0.433). RPLND pathology was the strongest prognostic factor: patients with viable tumor had 24- and 60-month OS of 77.8% and 51.9%, compared with 96.8% and 92.7% for teratoma and 100.0% and 89.4% for necrosis. In multivariable analysis, RPLND pathology independently predicted OS (HR 8.51, p=0.034) and RFS (HR 2.59, p=0.030), while combined-pathology risk and marker normalization were not significant. CONCLUSIONS: Pathologic discordance between post-chemotherapy OE and RPLND is common, but only RPLND pathology predicts survival. These findings emphasize the dominant prognostic value of RPLND pathology and the continued importance of performing both procedures for complete disease assessment and clearance.

title: IP13-20: The Role of Delayed Orchiectomy Following Chemotherapy for Metastatic Germ Cell Tumours
parentSessionTitle: IP13: Penile & Testicular Cancer I
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: In patients with testicular germ cell tumors (TGCT) presenting with high-volume or site-critical metastases, upfront chemotherapy is often initiated to expedite systemic control, while orchiectomy is deferred. However, limited data exist characterizing testicular pathology in this context or identifying predictors of residual disease. This study aims to describe our institutional experience with post-chemotherapy orchiectomy and to determine clinical and radiologic factors associated with the absence of residual disease. METHODS: We retrospectively reviewed all patients with metastatic TGCT who underwent post-chemotherapy orchiectomy at Princess Margaret Cancer Centre between 1992 – 2025. Clinical, radiologic, and pathologic features were compared between patients with benign versus viable testicular pathology. Kaplan–Meier analysis was used to estimate relapse-free and cancer-specific survival (RFS and CSS), and logistic regression was used to identify predictors of viable disease. RESULTS: A total of 82 patients underwent post-chemotherapy orchiectomy, with a median follow-up of 3.7 years. Teratoma was identified in 36 cases (44%), viable seminoma identified in only 2 patients (2.4%) - both within teratoma-containing specimens. At 5 years, RFS and CSS were 92.2% and 94.5% for patients with benign pathology, compared to 64.9% and 81.6% for those with viable disease (log-rank p<0.001 and p=0.066, respectively). Specific orchiectomy histology was not significantly associated with CSS (log-rank p=0.2).On univariate analysis, predictors of viable disease included younger age, palpable testicular mass, poor-risk IGCCCG classification, receipt of second-line chemotherapy, adverse post-chemotherapy ultrasound features (vascularity and/or coarse calcifications), and concurrent extragonadal surgery for post-chemotherapy residual masses. Viable testicular pathology was also associated with viable disease at retroperitoneal lymph node dissection. Notably, no viable disease was identified in patients with post-chemotherapy ultrasound demonstrating normal or “burnt-out” findings, or in those with residual testicular masses <1 cm. CONCLUSIONS: In selected patients with favorable clinical and radiographic features, the risk of viable TGCT following chemotherapy is low. These findings support the consideration of surveillance or partial orchiectomy in lieu of routine radical orchiectomy in selected patients where testicular preservation is desired. Prospective validation is warranted.

title: IP13-21: Circulating Tumor DNA Performance in Primary Retroperitoneal Lymph Node Dissection: A Stage-Based Analysis
parentSessionTitle: IP13: Penile & Testicular Cancer I
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Novel biomarkers appear to have use in the surveillance and treatment monitoring of testicular germ cell tumors (GCT). Recently, ctDNA has been demonstrated to detect GCT in both primary and post-chemotherapy retroperitoneal lymph node dissection (RPLND), however the association of ctDNA levels with tumor burden has not yet been determined. Herein, we sought to determine the utility of ctDNA for predicting GCT on P-RPLND by comparing patients’ RPLND histology with their pre-operative ctDNA status in those with clinical stage (CS) 1 and 2 disease. Furthermore, we determined the association between ctDNA levels and clinical stage at RPLND. METHODS: Patients undergoing primary (P-RPLND) from 2023 to 2025 had prospectively collected plasma ctDNA assay (SignateraTM, Natera Inc.) Patients were stratified by CS based on pre-operative CT imaging and serum tumor markers. The association between ctDNA positivity and P-RPLND histology was assessed. Test statistics were calculated for ctDNA to detect active cancer on RPLND. Additionally, the association between ctDNA levels and CS as a surrogate for disease burden was determined using linear regression analysis. RESULTS: 64 patients undergoing P-RPLND had pre-operative ctDNA collection with a median age of 37 (IQR:29-42). Plasma was collected on average, 8 days pre-operatively. 10 (16%) patients underwent P-RPLND for CS 1 and 54 (84%) for CS 2 disease. ctDNA was positive in 47 (73%) patients in the entire cohort. In the CS I group, 7 patients had a (-) ctDNA all of which had a negative P-RPLND. Of the 54 CS 2 patients, 44 (81%) had a (+) ctDNA. No false positives were found in this cohort. The SN, SP, PPV, and NPV in the CS 1 cohort were 100%, 78%, 33%, and 100% and in CS 2 were 88%, 100%, 100%, and 40%, respectively. Additionally, ctDNA level does not appear to correlate to disease volume at this juncture (r2=0, p=0.948). CONCLUSIONS: CtDNA may have use in predicting retroperitoneal histology on P-RPLND. In CS 1 disease a negative test appears to be correlated with an absence of disease. In CS 2 disease, no false positives were found. ctDNA appears to be a binary test for detecting disease in the retroperitoneum. | | | --- | | |

title: IP13-22: Performance of Circulating Tumor DNA as a Biomarker in Testicular Seminoma and Non-seminomatous Germ Cell Tumor
parentSessionTitle: IP13: Penile & Testicular Cancer I
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Serum tumor markers have been the cornerstone in the detection and surveillance of testicular germ cell tumors (GCT). However, the sensitivity of specificity of STM for detecting GCT is poor. Circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) has shown promise in the detection of GCT in both primary and post-chemotherapy retroperitoneal lymph node dissection (RPLND). Herein, we sought to determine the utility of ctDNA for predicting active GCT on P-RPLND by comparing patients’ RPLND histology with their pre-operative ctDNA status in those with seminoma and non-seminomatous germ cell tumor (NSGCT). METHODS: Patients undergoing primary (P-RPLND) from 2023 to 2025 had prospectively collected plasma ctDNA assay (SignateraTM, Natera Inc.) Patients were stratified to seminoma or NSGCT based on orchiectomy and serum tumor markers. The association between ctDNA positivity and P-RPLND histology was assessed. Sensitivity (SN), specificity (SP), and positive (PPV) and negative predictive values (NPV) were calculated for ctDNA to detect seminoma or NSGCT on RPLND. RESULTS: 64 patients undergoing P-RPLND had pre-operative ctDNA collection. Plasma was collected on average, 8 days pre-operatively. 27 (42%) patients underwent P-RPLND for seminoma and 37 (58%) for NSGCT. ctDNA was positive in 47 (73%) patients in the entire cohort. Of seminoma patients, 16 had CS 2A and 11 had CS 2B disease. 24 (89%) seminoma patients had a (+) ctDNA. All seminoma patients had GCT present on P-RPLND. Of NSGCT patients, 10 had CS 1, 21 had CS 2A and 6 had CS 2B disease. 23 (62%) NSGCT patients had a (+) ctDNA. 2 patients in the NSGCT cohort had (+) ctDNA and negative RPLND. Of these, 1 patient had a persistently elevated ctDNA post-operatively, and had a lung recurrence. The second patient had a continually rising ctDNA test with negative surveillance imaging at 9 months. The SN, SP, PPV, and NPV in the NSGCT cohort were 88%, 85%, 91%, and 79%, respectively for predicting GCT. For the seminoma cohort these were 89%, undefined, 100%, and 0%. The undefined SP and 0% NPV in the seminoma group were due to the lack of patients with negative RPLND. CONCLUSIONS: This is the first study evaluating performance of ctDNA in relation to RPLND histology, when stratified by seminoma or NSGCT. These findings suggest that ctDNA may be a useful tool in predicting retroperitoneal histology. Persistently positive ctDNA after RPLND may be indicative of disease outside of the retroperitoneum.

title: IP13-23: Tumor-Informed Circulating Tumor DNA for Relapse Detection in Clinical Stage I Testicular Cancer
parentSessionTitle: IP13: Penile & Testicular Cancer I
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Serum tumor markers (STM) are integral to testicular cancer management but lack sensitivity for early relapse detection. Circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) may enhance surveillance accuracy. To determine the role of ctDNA in the surveillance protocols, we evaluated its performance for the detection of relapse in patients with clinical stage (CS) I disease on surveillance. METHODS: We performed a retrospective review of patients with CS I testicular cancer from 2019 to 2025 who underwent ctDNA testing during surveillance. All tests were performed during surveillance, post-orchiectomy, and at 3 months intervals onwards. Sensitivity (SN), specificity (SP), positive (PPV), and negative predictive value (NPV) were calculated for ctDNA to detect relapse, which was defined as radiographic progression or STM elevation. The relative risk and 95% confidence interval (CI) of relapse in ctDNA-positive versus ctDNA-negative patients was calculated. RESULTS: We included a total of 59 patients with CS I testicular cancer, of whom 30 experienced relapse during surveillance. A total of 80 ctDNA assays were performed, comprising 26 positive and 54 negative results; 36 patients (61%) had nonseminomas, 22 (37%) had seminomas, and 1 (2%) had a Sertoli cell tumor in their orchiectomy specimen. Median follow-up was 11 months (interquartile range 4-20). Of the 26 ctDNA-positive results, 24 (92%) were true positives and 2 (8%) were false positives. One false-positive patient had a repeat ctDNA test 3 months later that returned negative and remained relapse-free after 9 months of follow-up. The other underwent retroperitoneal lymph node dissection, which revealed no positive nodes, and was followed for 1 month before being lost to follow-up. Of the 54 ctDNA-negative results, 50 (93%) were true negatives and 4 (7%) were false negatives. All false negatives were in retroperitoneal relapses and included two pure seminomas (1.7 cm and 3.3 cm), one 4.2 cm pure embryonal carcinoma, and one 4.8 cm pure teratoma. The results corresponded to a SN, SP, PPV, and NPV of 86%, 96%, 92%, and 93%, respectively. The relative risk of relapse in ctDNA-positive versus ctDNA-negative patients was 12.5 (95% CI, 4.8-32.2; p<0.01). CONCLUSIONS: Tumor-informed ctDNA demonstrated high PPV and good SN for detecting relapse in patients on surveillance for CS 1 testicular cancer. ctDNA positivity was strongly associated with disease relapse, supporting its potential role as an adjunct biomarker to traditional STM.

title: IP13-24: Prospective evaluation of the performance of MiR371 test under real-life conditions for the diagnosis of testicular germ cell cancer
parentSessionTitle: IP13: Penile & Testicular Cancer I
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Testicular germ cell tumour (GCT) has a cure rate exceeding 90% in clinical stages (CS) I -II and approximately 75% in CS III. Cornerstones of clinical management are surgery, imaging and measurement of the serum tumour markers such as alpha fetoprotein (AFP), beta-human chorionic gonadotropin (beta-HCG) and lactate dehydrogenase (LDH). However, clinical utility of these tumour markers is limited due to their low sensitivity. Recently, miRNA-371a-3p (M371) has has emerged as promising biomarker in the diagnosis of GCT by performing better than conventional markers. The aim of this study was to evaluate the diagnostic performance of M371-Test under real-life clinical conditions in comparison with the classical markers AFP, beta-HCG and LDH in patients with suspected GCT. Furthermore, the study aimed to identify a correlation between tumour size and preoperative value of M371. A control group of healthy individuals was also included to verify the reliability and specificity of the results. METHODS: 99 M371 tests were performed from March 2021 to October 2025 and were prospectively included in this study. Of these, 79 tests were conducted in patients with clinical suspicion of GCT (median age: 38 years). In the remaining 20 cases the test was performed in healthy patients, used as control group. Results of M371, AFP, beta -HCG, LDH of the patients with suspicion of GCT were compared with the histology. Results of Mi371, AFP, beta-HCG, LDH of control group were compared to assess their performance in a healthy population. A relative quantification (RQ) cut-off value of >5, according to the manufacturer’s instructions, was used to calculate sensitivity, specificity, and predictive values RESULTS: M371 showed a sensitivity of 91.8% and a specificity of 90.0%, outperforming AFP (20.4%/96.7%), LDH (40.8%/93.3%), and β-hCG (44.9%/100%) in terms of sensitivity. The positive predictive value (PPV) and negative predictive value (NPV) were 93.7% and 87.1%, respectively. When patients were stratified by histological subtype, miR-371 sensitivity was 89.6% for seminomas and 95.0% for non-seminomas; moreover, after excluding teratoma cases, sensitivity reached 100% in the non-seminomatous subgroup. Receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve analysis yielded an area under the curve (AUC) of 0.93 (95% CI 0.87–0.99; p<0.001). The optimal cut-off value, determined by the Youden index and anchored to the nearest observed value in the dataset, was 5.3, corresponding to a sensitivity of 89.8% and a specificity of 93.3%. Finally, correlation analysis between serum miR-371 concentrations and tumor diameter revealed a moderate positive association (Spearman’s ρ=0.57), indicating that higher miR-371 levels are associated with larger tumor size. CONCLUSIONS: The M371 test demonstrated good diagnostic performance under real-world clinical conditions. It maintained high sensitivity even in patients with small testicular tumors, supporting its potential role as a new standard biomarker for GCT diagnosis.

title: IP13-25: Evaluation of miRNA-371a-3p (miR371a) assay to predict final pathohistology in patients undergoing primary nerve-sparing retroperitoneal lymphadenectomy (nsRPLND) for stage IIA/B seminomas and non-seminomas (NSGCT)
parentSessionTitle: IP13: Penile & Testicular Cancer I
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: 20-30% of patients with marker negative clinical stage IIA/B seminomas and nonseminomas might harbor non-malignant histologies. MiR371a is thought to represent a new biomarker with diagnostic and predictive properties. It was the purpose of our study to evaluate the predictive accuracy of this new biomarker to identify the presence or absence of lymph node metastases in clinical stage IIA/B TGCT. METHODS: In a cohort of 91 consecutive patients with marker negative CS IIA/B TGCT (n=45 seminoma, n=46 nonseminoma) serum concentration of miR371 was assessed one day before nsRPLND. Positive or negative findings were correlated with lymph node pathology. Blood specimens were drawn on the day prior to surgery and processed according to the manufacturer’s protocol (mirdetect, Bremerhaven, Germany). In brief, cubital vein blood was placed on ice and processed within 30 minutes for extraction of miR371a. The Maxwell RSC with the Maxwell® RSC MiRNA Plasma and Serum Kits (Promega GmBH, Walldorf, Germany) was used here to extract and purify the miRNA. The extracted miR371a waas transcribed into cDNA using cDNA Solution, Reverse Transcriptase and RNase Inhibitor. Subsequently, this cDNA was amplified. Using qPCR (Real Time-quantitative Polymerase Chain Reaction), the miR371a was quantified using Roche Lightcycler 480 II (Roche Diagnostics, Rotkreuz, Switzerland). Using the Lightcycler software, the median Cp (CP=Crossing Points) of the triplicates is calculated and converted into a RQ value (RQ=Relative Frequency), which indicates whether the sample is positive or negative. RESULTS: Histology revealed metastatic GCT in 79/91 (87%) patients. miR371a was positive in 66/71 (93%) patients with metastases. miR371a negative lymph node metastases included teratoma in 2, embryonal carcinoma in 2 and seminoma in 1 patient. Histology revealed no malignancy in 12 patients and all patients showed negative miR371a findings. Sensitivity and specificity for the whole cohort were 95% and 100%, respectively; positive predictive value (PPV) was 91% and negative predictive value (NPV) was 78%. For the seminoma cohort, sensitivity and specificity were 98% and 100%, PPV and NPV were 100% and 98%. For nonseminomas, sensitivity and specificity were 90% and 100%, PPV and NPV were 100% and 50%. CONCLUSIONS: Based on the available data, miR371a represents a highly reliable personalized tumor marker to predict the presence of small volume retroperitoneal lymph node metastases in marker negative TGCT. miR371 has to greatest potential in seminomas were we use miR371 to stratify patients for RPLND versus active surveillace. For nonseminomas miR371 is useful for non-teratomatous tumors and it is not reliable for teratomas and malignant somatic transformation.

title: IP13-26: Dynamics of Circulating miR-371a-3p Levels Before and After BEP Chemotherapy in Patients with Metastatic Seminoma and Non-seminomatous Germ Cell Tumor
parentSessionTitle: IP13: Penile & Testicular Cancer I
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: MiR-371a-3p (miRNA-371) is a promising biomarker for germ cell tumors. Its expression in blood may provide a non-invasive method for monitoring disease activity and treatment response. The aim of this study was to analyze miRNA-371 levels before and after BEP chemotherapy (bleomycin, etoposide, cisplatin) in patients with metastatic seminoma and non-seminomatous germ cell tumor (NSGCT). METHODS: A retrospective analysis of miR-371a-3p expression was performed in patients who received systemic PEB chemotherapy between 2022 and 2025. miRNA expression levels were quantified from serum samples using reverse transcription quantitative polymerase chain reaction (RT-qPCR). Crossing point (Cp) values were determined for each sample and converted into relative quantification (RQ) values using the ΔΔCp method. The dynamics of miRNA-371 levels and their correlation with clinical response were evaluated. RQ levels <5 were considered negative, and >10 were considered positive. RESULTS: MiRNA-371 levels were significantly higher before chemotherapy than after treatment (median 138.6 vs 4.19; p=0.0010) in patients with seminoma. In 7 of 11 patients, the levels dropped to undetectable, and in two patients to the indeterminate range. Two patients showed persistently positive miRNA-371 levels after chemotherapy despite radiological regression; they developed early relapse. In patients with intermediate measurements during chemotherapy (e. g. 2 of 3 cycles), a statistical significant (p=0.0078) decrease was also observed, although most values remained positive (median 445.5 vs 11.71). In the NSGCT cohort, data were available from before treatment and the admission day of the third treatment cycle. miR-371a-3p levels declined significantly (n=9, p=0.0156) after two cycles of BEP. However, most patients remained positive. Pre-chemotherapy miRNA-371 levels correlated significantly with initial tumor size (Spearman r=0,8239, p=0.0001), while post-chemotherapy levels showed no correlation with residual tumor size (Spearman r=-0.01425, p=0.9645). CONCLUSIONS: MiRNA-371 levels decrease significantly after BEP chemotherapy in patients with seminoma and non-seminomatous germ cell tumor. Our findings support the role of miRNA-371 as a potential biomarker for monitoring disease activity and treatment response in germ cell tumors.

title: IP13-27: How reliable are serum tumor markers in the diagnosis of small testicular masses? A multicentric analysis from the Milan Testis Cancer Alliance
parentSessionTitle: IP13: Penile & Testicular Cancer I
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: The diagnostic value of serum tumor markers (STM) (i. e., AFP, hCG, LDH) in men with testicular germ cell cancer is well established in advanced disease, but their role in the assessment of small testicular masses remains uncertain. We aimed to i) explore the relationship between tumor size and both biochemical and ultrasound (US) markers; and, ii) develop a model for discriminating benign from malignant lesions. METHODS: We retrospectively analyzed 497 men who underwent surgery for testicular masses at six academic centers (2020–2024). Baseline characteristics, US features (vascularity, echogenicity, microcalcifications, dimensions), and preoperative STM were retrospectively collected. Descriptive statistics compared benign and malignant tumors at final pathology. Tumor size–marker relationships were modeled using natural spline regression by histology, and a regression tree identified key predictors of malignancy. RESULTS: Of 497, 66 (13%) patients had benign and 431 (87%) patients malignant lesions. Median tumor size was larger in malignant masses (26 \[16–42\] vs 14 \[7–20\] mm; p<0.001). Serum markers were higher in malignant cases: AFP 2.3 \[1.3–9.9\] vs 1.66 \[0.23–3.5\] ng/mL (p=0.0027), β-hCG 1.4 \[0.19–9\] vs 0.35 \[0.005–2.3\] IU/L (p=0.004), and LDH 187 \[148–262\] vs 134 \[0–184\] U/L (p<0.001). Malignant lesions were more often hypoechoic (90% vs 73%; p<0.001) and hyper-vascularized (58% vs 38%; p=0.001), but did not differ in terms of microcalcifications compared to benign lesions (16% vs 11%; p=0.3). Marker levels correlated weakly with lesion size, particularly in small lesions (<20 mm), where benign masses occasionally showed rising values. Malignant lesions exhibited consistent marker elevation only beyond this threshold (Figure). The regression tree achieved high diagnostic accuracy (AUC 0.9), identifying echogenicity and microcalcifications as key discriminants, while vascularity was not predictive of malignancy ( Figure). CONCLUSIONS: In small testicular masses, tumor markers alone are unreliable for predicting malignancy. A “gray zone” exists below 20 mm, where marker trends are inconsistent and benign lesions may mimic malignant profiles. Integrating ultrasound parameters provides improved diagnostic discrimination in this challenging setting.

title: IP13-28: Association of Area Deprivation Index with Testicular Cancer Diagnosis and Outcomes in a Contemporary North American Cohort
parentSessionTitle: IP13: Penile & Testicular Cancer I
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: While current testicular management has led to impressive 5-year survival rates in patients, the incidence continues to increase and its disproportionate effect on younger patients leads to several long-term effects. Socioeconomic status and race have often been correlated to cancer outcomes but the underlying cause of these disparities is complex and multifactorial making them challenging to understand. The Area of Deprivation Index(ADI) could offer a distinctive and valuable metric for measuring the impact of socioeconomic factors. Our study examined the impact of ADI on Testicular Cancer(TCa) diagnosis and outcomes in a contemporary North American population. METHODS: The Michigan Department of health and Human Services (MDHHS) database was used to obtain data regarding patients with testicular cancer between 2004-2019. ADI was assigned to each patient dependent upon their residential census-block group and ranked as a percentile of deprivation relative to the national level. We stratified the cohort into quartiles based on national ADI-values, where the fourth quartile(75-100) represented the most disadvantageous socio-economic status. The main outcomes were TCa stage at diagnosis, all-cause mortality, and cancer-specific mortality. RESULTS: We analyzed 2,848 patients (94% NHW) with median age of 34 years (IQR 27-43). Among those, 10.3%, 29.7%, 32.9%, and 27.1% were in the first, second, third and fourth ADI-quartile respectively. Patients in the fourth ADI-quartile were younger, less frequently NHW, and more frequently without insurance compared to those in the first. Patients were predominantly diagnosed as stage I and on MVA, the odds of stage II and stage III testicular cancer was noted to be higher for higher ADI. The 15-year survival estimates based on their ADI quartile was 97.9% for ADI 0-24, 93.0% for ADI 25-49, 91.5% for ADI 50-74, and 87.8% for ADI ≥75 (p<0.0001). On MVA, all quartiles were significantly different from quartile 1. The 15-year cancer-specific mortality incidence based on their ADI quartile was 0.4% for ADI 0-24, 2.1% for ADI 25-49, 1.6% for ADI 50-74, and 2.9% for ADI ≥75 (Gray’s test p-value 0.1234). ADI was not significantly associated with testicular cancer specific mortality. CONCLUSIONS: Our study is a one of the first studies to evaluate the association between neighborhood deprivation and TCa outcomes in a contemporary North American cohort. While all-cause mortality and stage at diagnosis appears to be impacted by ADI, testicular cancer-specific mortality does not. Current management may potentially be one of the factors mitigating some of the effect on cancer-specific mortality. However, a delay in diagnosis and potential treatment-associated morbidity compel us to better understand disparities affecting this subset of patients.

title: IP14-01: Perioperative antibiotic prophylaxis does not affect infection rates after transperineal prostate biopsy
parentSessionTitle: IP14: Infections/Inflammation/Cystic Disease of the Genitourinary Tract: Prostate & Genitalia
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Transperineal prostate biopsy (TPB) is a modality to adequately sample the prostate gland for cancer with low infection rates postoperatively. There is still debate as to whether perioperative antibiotics are required as infection prophylaxis with TPB. Further, while infection rates \[urinary tract infections (UTIs)\] are felt to be low, acute urinary retention (AUR) after TPB is a known complication. The purpose of this study was to compare perioperative antibiotics versus no antibiotics for patients undergoing TPB. Secondarily, this study aimed to assess rates of AUR after TPB and its relation to prostate size. METHODS: This was a multi-institutional retrospective analysis of all patients undergoing TPB for elevated prostate specific antigen (PSA) or as confirmatory biopsies on active surveillance between 2012-2025. Patients were divided into two groupings based on whether they received perioperative antibiotics (second or third-generation cephalosporin) versus no antibiotics. Post TPB infection was defined as at least one of the following: fever (≥ 38.3°C) with/without symptoms of UTI or positive urine culture (>105 colony forming units) within 5 days post biopsy. AUR was defined as an inability to urinate within 72 hours of TPB requiring catheter. Independent samples t-test and chi squared test were used to compare patients based on antibiotic prophylaxis, presence infection, and AUR. RESULTS: 904 patients were included in the analysis (771 antibiotics and 133 no antibiotics; Table 1a). Age at TPB was equivalent between groups (p>0.05). Mean PSA at TPB and PSA density were greater in the no antibiotic group (13.5 ng/mL and 0.24 ng/mL/cm3) versus antibiotic group (3.6 ng/mL and 0.07 ng/mL/cm3; p<0.01). A total of 18 (2.0%) UTIs were observed after TPB and no difference in rate of infection was observed based on use of antibiotics (p>0.05; Table 1b). 2/18 (11%) patients, both of which received antibiotics, experienced urosepsis requiring readmission. Patients who developed a UTI after TPB were older than those who did not (71.1 years versus 66.4 years; p<0.01). 44 (4.9%) patients went into AUR after TPB. Mean prostate volume on magnetic resonance imaging was significantly greater in patients who went into AUR (77.1 cc) than those who did not (52.4 cc; p<0.01; Table 1c). CONCLUSIONS: Use of perioperative antibiotics does not appear to influence UTI rate after TPB. Older age at TPB is associated with developing an infection after TPB. Larger prostate size is associated with risk of developing AUR after TPB. | | | --- | | |

title: IP14-02: Incidence and Risk Factors of Perioperative Infections Following Robot-Assisted Radical Prostatectomy: A Multicenter Retrospective Analysis
parentSessionTitle: IP14: Infections/Inflammation/Cystic Disease of the Genitourinary Tract: Prostate & Genitalia
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: To clarify the incidence and risk factors of surgical site, urinary tract, and remote infections following robot-assisted radical prostatectomy in Japan and to examine their association with prophylactic antibiotic regimens. METHODS: We retrospectively analyzed 6,600 robot-assisted radical prostatectomy procedures performed at 13 institutions between 2009 and 2021. Eligible cases included those who were administered prophylactic antibiotics recommended by the guidelines: cefazolin, ampicillin/sulbactam, or second-generation cephalosporins. The incidence of surgical site, urinary tract, and remote infections within 30 days postoperatively was compared by antibiotic type and administration duration (≤24 h vs. >24 h). Multivariate analyses identified independent risk factors. RESULTS: The incidence rates of surgical site, urinary tract, and remote infections were 1.2%, 1.4%, and 0.3%, respectively. Bowel injury, particularly deep and organ or space infections, was a surgical site infection risk factor. Second-generation cephalosporins were associated with a lower surgical site infection rate than that of cefazolin. Prolonged urethral catheterization (≥8 days) was a risk factor for urinary tract and remote infections. Urinary tract infection incidence was higher with ampicillin/sulbactam than with cefazolin (no duration difference). Remote infection incidence did not differ by antibiotic regimen. CONCLUSIONS: Perioperative infection incidence following robot-assisted radical prostatectomy was low. Bowel injury and prolonged urethral catheterization were surgical site infection and urinary tract and remote infections risk factors, respectively. Early urethral catheter removal may prevent infection. Prophylaxis with first- or second-generation cephalosporins within 24 h is recommended, and broad-spectrum antibiotics may be appropriate bowel injury-complicated cases.

title: IP14-03: Value of Urine Culture before Radical Prostatectomy
parentSessionTitle: IP14: Infections/Inflammation/Cystic Disease of the Genitourinary Tract: Prostate & Genitalia
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Post-operative urinary tract infections (UTIs) are a notable complication of radical prostatectomy, contributing to prolonged hospital stays, increased healthcare costs, and diminished patient quality of life. Despite international guideline recommendations of European Association of Urology regarding the use of pre-operative urine cultures and antibiotic prophylaxis (AP) before radical prostatectomy, the role of pre-operative urine cultures in mitigating UTI risk remains uncertain. METHODS: This multi-center prospective cohort study analyzed data from six French urology departments. Patients who underwent radical prostatectomy between January 2019 and June 2023, with variable inclusion periods across centers, were included if pre-operative urine cultures were performed. Patients were stratified into subgroups based on the occurrence of post-operative UTIs. Uni-variable and multi-variable logistic regressions, as well as receiver-operating characteristic (ROC) curve analysis, were used. RESULTS: A total of 467 patients were analyzed, among whom post-operative UTIs developed in 30 patients. Among peri-operative factors, only the ASA (American Society of Anesthesiologists) score (p=0.014) and the duration of post-operative catheterization (p=0.001) were significantly associated with UTI occurrence in uni-variable analyses. Multi-variable logistic regression confirmed both factors as independent predictors of post-operative infections, with a model area under the ROC curve for catheterization duration of 0.789. A seven-day threshold for catheterization duration was identified as the optimal cutoff for predicting infection risk. Notably, neither pre-operative urine bacterial cultures nor AP reduced the incidence of post-operative UTIs. CONCLUSIONS: This study demonstrates that pre-operative urine cultures and prophylactic antibiotic agents do not mitigate UTI risk following radical prostatectomy, underscoring the need for optimized infection prevention tactics. The findings challenge the clinical utility of routine pre-operative urine cultures and highlight the critical roles of ASA score and post-operative catheterization duration in predicting infections.

title: IP14-04: Epididymo-orchitis a “Rare” Complication After Laser Enucleation of the Prostate: A Prostate Enucleation Collaborative Initiative
parentSessionTitle: IP14: Infections/Inflammation/Cystic Disease of the Genitourinary Tract: Prostate & Genitalia
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Infectious events after Holmium laser enucleation of the prostate (HoLEP) are recognized, however epididymo-orchitis is rarely reported as a discrete endpoint despite clear clinical impact. Most series aggregate scrotal infections under “soft-tissue” complications, leaving procedure-specific rates and risk profiles undefined. This study aimed to characterize the incidence of epididymo-orchitis after HoLEP and the corresponding impact on unplanned healthcare utilization. METHODS: Using the TriNetX Research Network, we conducted a retrospective cohort study of adults undergoing HoLEP between 2015 and 2024 with at least one outpatient encounter prior to the index procedure and documentation of continued follow-up beyond the defined 1-year observation period. First time epididymo-orchitis occurring within 1 year after HoLEP were analyzed using two-proportion z-tests (Wald method), Kaplan-Meier estimation, and Cox proportional hazards modeling. Baseline confounders were balanced using 1:1 propensity score matching (greedy nearest-neighbor algorithm; caliper=0.1 SD). RESULTS: In a cohort of 10,357 patients who underwent HoLEP between 2015 and 2024, incident epididymo-orchitis occurred in 146 individuals (1.4%), with a median time to diagnosis of 62 days (95% CI 54-81). Patients with a prior urinary tract infection had a higher adjusted incidence compared to men without a history of urinary tract infection (2.12% vs 1.10%; weighted absolute risk difference 1.02%, 95% CI 0.48-1.56%). Previous antibiotic resistant infection (HR 2.57, 95% CI 1.18-5.60) ≥14 days before the index procedure, was also independently associated with increased hazard. Among affected patients, most cases were successfully managed in the outpatient setting; however, 38% required an unplanned emergency department evaluation and 11% were admitted for inpatient care or observation. CONCLUSIONS: Epididymo-orchitis after HoLEP carries meaningful morbidity, frequently prompting emergency evaluation or hospital admission. A history of urinary tract or antibiotic-resistant infection identifies a subset of patients at higher risk, suggesting opportunities for targeted perioperative prophylaxis and tailored follow-up strategies. Further prospective research is indicated to validate these findings and determine whether enhanced perioperative infection control can mitigate risk.

title: IP14-06: Infection Risk Associated with Sodium-Glucose Cotransporter 2 Inhibitors in Patients with Chronic Kidney Disease: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
parentSessionTitle: IP14: Infections/Inflammation/Cystic Disease of the Genitourinary Tract: Prostate & Genitalia
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Recent researches established that Sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitors (SGLT2 inhibitors) exhibit cardiovascular and renal protective effect in heart failure and chronic kidney disease (CKD) population regardless of their DM status. However, the associated adverse events remain a pronounced concern, particularly urinary tract infections (UTIs) and genital infections (GIs). While CKD patients were at higher infection potential due to impaired immunity or present genitourinary tract anomalies, it is imperative to investigate the infection risk associated with SGLT2 inhibitors used in CKD populations. METHODS: We conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials (RCTs) enrolling patients with chronic kidney disease who received SGLT2 inhibitors or placebo/standard care. PubMed, Embase, and Cochrane databases were searched up to July 2025. Eligible trials reported incidence of urinary tract infections (UTIs) and/or Genital infections (GIs) as safety outcomes. The study followed the PRISMA 2020 guidelines, and the selection process was summarized in a PRISMA flow diagram. Pooled odds ratios (ORs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were calculated using ‘fixed- and random-effects’ models. Subgroup analyses were conducted for individual SGLT2 inhibitors in UTI category. RESULTS: Eighteen RCTs involving 30,308 participants were included. For genital infections, 381 events occurred among 16,023 patients receiving SGLT2i compared with 100 events among 14,440 controls, yielding a significantly increased risk with SGLT2i (OR 2.95, 95% CI 2.36–3.68; p0.001; I2=0%), favoring the control group. In contrast, for urinary tract infections, 1,620 events occurred among 15,868 patients receiving SGLT2i versus 1,301 among 14,440 controls, with no significant difference between groups (OR 1.07, 95% CI 0.95–1.21; p=0.27; I2=29.7%). CONCLUSIONS: In our study, SGLT2 inhibitors are associated with significant increased risk of genital infections rather than UTIs in CKD patients. The increased UTI risk observed with canagliflozin warrants further evaluation. These findings support careful monitoring of infection-related adverse events in CKD patients initiating SGLT2 inhibitors while recognizing the substantial cardio-renal benefits.

title: IP14-07: High Prevalence of Ureaplasma in Gonorrhea-Negative Male Patients: 40-Year Retrospective Analysis Supporting Routine Dual Testing
parentSessionTitle: IP14: Infections/Inflammation/Cystic Disease of the Genitourinary Tract: Prostate & Genitalia
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Ureaplasma urealyticum (UU) causes 3-11% of non-gonococcal urethritis (NGU). For symptomatic urethritis, it is recommended to test for and treat the more common pathogens (such as Chlamydia trachomatis, Neisseria gonorrhoeae (GC), and Mycoplasma genitalium) rather than routinely include Ureaplasma testing. We aimed to quantify the prevalence of UU in men tested for GC over four decades, hypothesizing that a meaningful proportion of GC-negative men harbor UU, warranting broader dual-testing protocols. METHODS: A retrospective chart review of all male patients (n=83,489) tested for GC by point-of-care, Nucleic Acid Amplification Test, or culture at a tertiary health care center in Detroit, Michigan from January 1st, 1985, to October 9th, 2025. We identified all men who presented with symptoms and tested for GC alone and simultaneous GC and UU and then evaluated the positive rates in each group. RESULTS: Of 83,489 males tested for GC, 80,662 (96.6%) were negative and 6,441 (7.7%) were positive. Among GC-negative patients, only 492 (0.6%) underwent simultaneous UU testing, with 79 (16.1%) testing positive for UU and 430 testing negative (see (https://www.auajournals.org/doi/abs/10.1097/01.JU.0001191352.93132.27.07#F1)). Among the 6,441 GC-positive patients, only 22 (0.3%) were simultaneously tested for UU, and 3 (13.6%) were positive. CONCLUSIONS: In this 40-year retrospective analysis, a notable prevalence of UU (16.1%) was identified among the subset of GC-negative males who underwent simultaneous testing. Despite this, only 0.6% of GC-negative and 0.3% of GC-positive patients were tested for UU, underscoring a substantial diagnostic gap. These findings suggest that selective dual testing in men with persistent or recurrent urethritis could improve diagnostic accuracy, guide targeted therapy, and reduce unnecessary empiric antibiotic use.

title: IP14-08: Evaluating the Role of the 9-Valent HPV Vaccine in Preventing Recurrence of Genital Warts
parentSessionTitle: IP14: Infections/Inflammation/Cystic Disease of the Genitourinary Tract: Prostate & Genitalia

speakers.organization: Rambam Health Care Campus, Haifa, Israel

fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Human papillomavirus (HPV) is the most common sexually transmitted infection worldwide. Although the 9-valent vaccine (Gardasil 9) prevents primary infection, its role in secondary prevention after condyloma acuminatum is uncertain. We evaluated whether post-treatment HPV vaccination lowers recurrence risk and identified predictors of recurrence among men treated with carbon dioxide (CO2) laser ablation. METHODS: We retrospectively reviewed men ≥17 years treated with CO2 laser ablation for genital condyloma at a tertiary center (June 2016–June 2025). The primary outcome was recurrence after documented clearance. Logistic and mixed-effects regression models tested associations between post-treatment vaccination and recurrence, adjusting for demographic and clinical factors. RESULTS: Among 560 patients (722 sessions), recurrence occurred in 28.4%. Those with recurrence were younger (32 ± 10 vs 37 ± 13 years; p<0.001) and more likely to need ≥2 sessions (18.6% vs 11.6%; p=0.02). Post-recurrence vaccination showed no significant association with reduced risk (aOR 0.49; 95% CI 0.14–1.69; p=0.26). Independent predictors were younger age (aOR 0.96 per year; p<0.001) and ≥2 sessions (aOR 2.44; p=0.003). Table 1. Baseline Characteristics by Future Recurrence Status. Table 2. Mixed-Effects Logistic Regression: Effect of Post-Recurrence HPV Vaccination on Future Recurrence. CONCLUSIONS: Post-treatment HPV vaccination did not reduce recurrence of genital condyloma. Younger age and multiple treatment sessions independently predicted recurrence, reinforcing vaccination’s role primarily in primary prevention. | | | --- | | | | | | --- | | |

title: IP14-09: Hidden Molecular Burden of Sexually Transmitted Pathogens: An Imperative for Urologists in Oncologic Screening and Prevention
parentSessionTitle: IP14: Infections/Inflammation/Cystic Disease of the Genitourinary Tract: Prostate & Genitalia

speakers.organization: Hospital Regional de Alta Especialidad de Ixtapaluca (UNAM)

fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: A dangerous, outdated paradigm persists in urology: equating the absence of symptoms with no risk for Sexually Transmitted Infections (STIs) in men. This approach, often prioritizing BPH, creates a diagnostic blind spot that conceals a large pathogen reservoir. Our objective was to dismantle this assumption using high-sensitivity molecular biology. We aimed to illuminate the true prevalence of the molecular infectious burden (HPV and bacterial pathogens) in this "asymptomatic" population and to quantify coinfection as a sentinel for active, unrecognized high-risk behaviors. METHODS: A descriptive, cross-sectional study was conducted on 102 male patients (age range: 23-84 years; mean: 56.17) from a general urology clinic. After obtaining informed consent, a standardized questionnaire on sexual risk behavior was administered, and a urethral swab sample was collected. Molecular analysis was performed using a multiplex PCR panel for the detection and genotyping of Human Papillomavirus (HPV) and the specific identification of three key bacterial pathogens: Chlamydia trachomatis, Mycoplasma hominis, and Ureaplasma spp. RESULTS: Molecular analysis revealed an overall infectious burden in 27.45% (1 in 4 men) of the cohort. The bacterial load was the most prominent, with a prevalence of 11.76% for Mycoplasma hominis (n=12) and 11.76% for Ureaplasma spp. (n=12). Chlamydia trachomatis was detected in 3.92% (n=4) of cases. HPV prevalence was 7.84% (n=8), with the identification of both high-risk (including HPV 51) and low-risk (HPV 6) genotypes. The pattern of coinfection proved to be the most clinically impactful finding: 100% of HPV-positive patients (both oncogenic and low-risk) were simultaneously harboring multiple bacterial pathogens. Notably, carriers of high-risk HPV were consistently positive for both M. hominis and Ureaplasma spp., establishing a synergistic, high-risk infectious profile. Consistent with the underlying risk, 100% of the patients with a positive molecular test result reported null or inconsistent condom use. CONCLUSIONS: The urology clinic is a silent risk epicenter that demands the immediate abandonment of symptom-based diagnosis. The high prevalence (27.45%) and the pattern of coinfection of oncogenic HPV with bacteria serve as a potent biological alarm, suggesting pro-inflammatory synergy that can enhance viral persistence and potentially accelerate anogenital carcinogenesis. This redefines the Urologist's role. Therefore, the implementation of molecular screening is a public health and oncologic imperative that must be embraced by modern urology, positioning the specialist on the front lines of prevention.

title: IP14-10: Sex-Based Epidemiologic Differences in Lichen Sclerosus: A Multicenter TriNetX Cohort Study (2018–2024)
parentSessionTitle: IP14: Infections/Inflammation/Cystic Disease of the Genitourinary Tract: Prostate & Genitalia
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Lichen sclerosus (LS) is a chronic inflammatory dermatosis with distinct male and female manifestations. Autoimmune, atopic, infectious, and mechanical factors contribute to sex-specific LS risk, but quantification of fixed versus modifiable risk factors and protective effects, like HPV vaccination, require further definition between sexes. This study quantified the incidence and association of these factors with LS development after adjusting for sex. METHODS: A retrospective, cohort study was conducted using the TriNetX Research Network (2018–2024). Adults ≥18 years without prior LS were followed for incident LS (ICD-10: L90.0, N90.4, N48.0). Multivariable Cox regression adjusted for sex, age, and autoimmune, atopic, metabolic, psychiatric, and viral covariates identified independent predictors. A 1:1 propensity score-matched comparison evaluated adjusted hazard difference by sex (balance <0.1). Significance defined as two-sided p<0.05. RESULTS: Among 1,118,878 adults (466,434 men; 652,444 women), LS incidence was higher in women (1.14%) than men (0.08%). Male sex was protective (HR 0.07, 95% CI 0.06–0.08, p<0.001). Each year of age increased hazard by 2.9% (HR 1.03). Significant predictors included obesity (1.09), autoimmune and atopic conditions: vitiligo (2.18), alopecia areata (1.76), autoimmune thyroiditis (1.62), psoriasis (1.57), Crohn’s disease (1.28), atopic dermatitis (1.26), asthma (1.17), and allergic rhinitis (1.14), viral infections: HSV (1.49), HPV (1.44), psychiatric disorders: depressive episode (1.18) and anxiety (1.11). Quadrivalent HPV vaccination was protective (0.52). Tobacco use (0.66) likely reflected detection bias. Type 1 and 2 diabetes were not independently significant after adjusting for obesity ( Table 1). After matching (455,923 per sex), female hazard remained significantly >10× higher (0.068). CONCLUSIONS: Across 1.1 million adults, LS risk was driven by autoimmune, atopic, viral, and psychiatric comorbidities, with female hazard remaining markedly higher after adjustment. Autoimmune and atopic diseases conferred the strongest risk, whereas HPV vaccination was protective. These findings underscore biologically distinct yet overlapping autoimmune–viral pathways and support coordinated, sex-specific interdisciplinary care to optimize disease prevention, management, reconstructive planning, and long-term outcomes. | | | --- | | |

title: IP14-11: Who’s at Risk? Autoimmune and Metabolic Predictors of Lichen Sclerosus in Epic Cosmos
parentSessionTitle: IP14: Infections/Inflammation/Cystic Disease of the Genitourinary Tract: Prostate & Genitalia
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Lichen sclerosus (LS) is a chronic inflammatory dermatosis associated with both autoimmune and metabolic dysregulation. Population based studies estimate an annual incidence of 50–80 cases per 100,000 person-years and a prevalence of only 0.1–0.3% in the general population. Leveraging the Epic Cosmos electronic health record network, which aggregates data from over 300 million patients nationwide, this study sought to quantify the 2- and 5-year risk of developing LS across major autoimmune and metabolic comorbidities. By comparing large scale, disease specific incidence estimates with established population baselines, we provide a contemporary, real world assessment of LS risk and its relationship to systemic immune and metabolic pathways. METHODS: Retrospective cohort of adults ≥18 years in Epic Cosmos (2017–2025). Inclusion required multiple clinical encounters and ≥1 year of follow-up. Autoimmune (psoriasis, type 1 DM, RA, MS, SLE, celiac, vitiligo) and metabolic (type 2 DM, obesity, HTN, dyslipidemia) cohorts were defined by ICD-10 codes. Diagnosis of LS by ICD-10 code within 2 and 5 years was the primary outcome. Cumulative incidence and adjusted odds ratios (OR, 95% CI) were calculated. Our IRB deemed the study exempt. RESULTS: Among 1,654,627 patients, 56,265 autoimmune and 447,881 metabolic patients developed LS within 2 years; by 5 years, 68,010 and 582,993 cases, respectively. LS prevalence within these cohorts reached 0.53% for autoimmune and 0.35% for metabolic, several fold higher than the reported 0.1–0.3% general population rate. Autoimmune conditions were associated with nearly threefold higher odds of LS at 2 years (OR=2.90, 95% CI 2.87–2.92, p<0.0001) and remained significantly elevated at 5 years (OR=1.51, 95% CI 1.49–1.52, p<0.0001), indicating an early and sustained autoimmune-linked risk pattern. CONCLUSIONS: Patients with autoimmune diseases exhibit substantially greater LS risk compared with those with metabolic disorders. While both groups show progressive incidence over time, autoimmune conditions demonstrate a disproportionate early rise, supporting immune mediated pathogenesis and emphasizing the need for targeted dermatologic screening in autoimmune populations.

title: IP14-12: Understanding the Clinical Presentation of Patients with Urogenital Tuberculosis in a Sub-Saharan Tertiary Care Setting
parentSessionTitle: IP14: Infections/Inflammation/Cystic Disease of the Genitourinary Tract: Prostate & Genitalia
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Tuberculosis remains the second leading infectious killer worldwide. Extrapulmonary tuberculosis represents 15%-40% of all cases, with urogenital tuberculosis (UGTB) as the second most common form. UG-TB can cause severe urologic complications - including obstructive uropathy, renal failure, and infertility - due to inflammation and scarring. This study describes the presentation of UG-TB at a tertiary hospital in a low- and middle-income country (LMIC), aiming to raise clinical suspicion among providers. METHODS: We conducted a retrospective, cross-sectional study of patients diagnosed with UG-TB at a semi-private, tertiary referral hospital with a 160-bed capacity in Kigali, Rwanda between 2015 and 2023. We collated patient logs from the hospital’s inpatient and laboratory's tuberculosis registry to identify all cases of UG-TB. RESULTS: Thirty-two patients were diagnosed and treated for UG-TB. Nearly all were male (96.9%), Rwandan nationals (90.6%), and younger than 55 years old (90.6%). Most had no known medical comorbidities (87.5%) and none were HIV positive. The majority (75%) presented with a scrotal mass, typically a unilateral epididymal nodule (83%); and the remaining presented with upper urinary tract and/or bladder TB. Nearly half (41%) of the patients required surgical intervention for their disease. Three patients required nephrectomy, one underwent bladder augmentation with bilateral ureteroneocystostomy, and one required unilateral nephroureterectomy with contralateral ileal ureter. CONCLUSIONS: UG-TB imposes a high surgical burden in otherwise young, healthy men. Expanding subspecialty training in complex urinary reconstruction is essential to equip urologists to manage these challenging cases. | | | --- | | | | | | --- | | |

title: IP14-13: Pathways of Pain: Incidence of Varicocele, Orchialgia, and Prostatitis in Males with Pelvic Floor Dysfunction
parentSessionTitle: IP14: Infections/Inflammation/Cystic Disease of the Genitourinary Tract: Prostate & Genitalia
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: The pelvic floor is a crucial but often overlooked determinant of male urologic health. Pelvic floor dysfunction (PFD) may manifest as chronic pelvic pain, voiding issues, and sexual dysfunction. However, its broader relationship to other genitourinary pain syndromes remains poorly characterized. While varicocele, orchialgia, and prostatitis are traditionally viewed as distinct pain conditions, they may share common pathophysiologic mechanisms. This study leverages a large, multi-institutional dataset to explore the incidence of these conditions among males with and without PFD, offering new insights into mechanisms of male pelvic pain. METHODS: Data were derived from the TriNetX Research Network, which aggregates de-identified electronic health records from participating health systems. Data from 2005-2025 were analyzed. Male patients currently aged ≥ 18 years old were classified as having PFD if they received a diagnosis of either pelvic/perineal pain (ICD-10 R10.2) or segmental/somatic dysfunction of the pelvic region (ICD-10 M99.05). Controls were defined as those who used healthcare services and did not receive either diagnosis. Using the TriNetX analytic platform, incidence proportions and rates (cases/person-day) were calculated for outcomes of interest. Analyses were stratified by age and race. RESULTS: This study included 798,868 patients with and 24,309,831 without PFD. Among those with PFD, the incidence proportions were 2.2% for varicocele (0.000005 cases/person-day), 8.2% for orchialgia (0.000019), and 6.6% for prostatitis (0.000015). In patients without PFD, corresponding proportions were 0.53%, 1.2%, and 0.91%, respectively. Incidence proportions were highest among PFD patients aged 10-14 and 20-24 for varicocele, 0-14 for orchialgia, and 50-59 for prostatitis. For patients without PFD, similar patterns were observed by age but with lower proportions. By race, varicocele was proportionally more common among Black and White males, orchialgia among American Indian/Alaska Native males, and prostatitis among White and Asian males. CONCLUSIONS: Males with clinical indicators of pelvic floor dysfunction appear to have higher burden of varicocele, orchialgia, and prostatitis compared to those without PFD. These findings suggest that pelvic floor pathophysiology may play a broader role in the pathogenesis of male urologic pain syndromes than previously recognized. Longitudinal studies are needed to clarify temporal and mechanistic relationships to develop targeted interventions that reduce the burden of chronic pelvic pain.

title: IP14-14: From Scrotal Pain to Serotonin Pathways: Duloxetine in Chronic Orchialgia
parentSessionTitle: IP14: Infections/Inflammation/Cystic Disease of the Genitourinary Tract: Prostate & Genitalia

speakers.organization: Penn State Milton S. Hershey Medical Center

fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Chronic orchialgia is persistent scrotal pain lasting at least 3 months and impairing the patient’s quality of life. There is no standard algorithm for treatment. Neuropathic pain medications often have side effects. The SNRI Duloxetine (Cymbalta) has been well studied and utilized off label by anesthesiologists to treat chronic neuropathic pain. This study evaluates the effectiveness of Duloxetine for chronic orchialgia. METHODS: A retrospective cohort study that analyzed 30 patients (>18yrs) diagnosed with chronic orchialgia between 2016 to present. Ten patients were excluded from final analysis due to loss of follow up. Data collected included patient demographics, Cymbalta prescription, duration of therapy and reported outcomes with side effects. Descriptive statistics were used to summarize baseline characteristics and treatment responses. The Wilcoxon rank-sum test was applied to compare pre- and post- prescription pain scores, assessing the significance of Cymbalta’s effect. RESULTS: For the 20 patients taking duloxetine, the mean pain score pre-treatment was 7.3 ± 2.5 on a pain scale form 0-10, which decreased to 3.6 ± 2.7 with treatment (p=0.0004). Mean pain reduction was 3.7 points (95% CI 2.44-4.96) indicating a clinically meaningful improvement. The effect size calculated using Cohen’s d, was 1.37, indicating a large treatment effect. Among the 19 patients with available side effects data, 11(58%) reported experiencing side effects. Patients who did not report side effects had a higher average of pain reduction (4.8 ± 2.4) compared to those who did not (2.7 ± 2.8) p=0.083, though not statistically significant. The reported side effects include constipation, hypertension and overall fatigue. Upon prescription of duloxetine, every patient was given a black box warning of increased risk of suicidal thoughts as issued by FDA. However, to our knowledge no patient quit because of increased thoughts of suicide and self-harm. CONCLUSIONS: In this cohort of patients with chronic orchialgia, treatment with Duloxetine resulted in a statistically and clinically significant reduction in pain scores with mild side effects reported. These findings warrant a prospective clinical trial.

title: IP14-15: Physico-enzymatic approach for chronic prostatitis management: long-term results of ESWT combined with bovhyaluronidase azoximer
parentSessionTitle: IP14: Infections/Inflammation/Cystic Disease of the Genitourinary Tract: Prostate & Genitalia
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Modern medicine faces the pressing challenge of treating chronic prostatitis (CP) and chronic pelvic pain syndrome (CPPS) due to the lack of treatment standards and their detrimental impact on quality of life. The aim of the study was to evaluate the long-term effect of the combined use of extracorporeal shock wave therapy (ESWT) and bovhyaluronidase azoximer (BA) in the comprehensive treatment of patients with CP II and CPPS IIIA–IIIB. METHODS: This open-label, randomized, placebo-uncontrolled study included 116 patients (mean age 45.5±9.5 years, disease duration 20.8±7.7 months) with CP and CPPS. According to the NIDDK/NIH classification, bacterial CP (II) was verified in 37 cases (32%), inflammatory CPPS IIIA in 39 cases (33.6%), and non-inflammatory CPPS IIIB in 40 cases (34.4%). Three groups were identified: Group 1 with CP II (n=37) - ESWT, "3-As" therapy; Group 2 with CPPS IIIA-IIIB (n=38) - ESWT monotherapy; Group 3 with CPPS IIIA-IIIB (n=41) - ESWT, BA. ESWT (Dornier Aries) sessions of 2,000 to 4,000 shocks were administered to the perineum twice weekly for a course of 12 procedures. At weeks 0, 7, 10, 18, 30, and 54, the following were assessed: NIH-CPSI, IPSS, IIEF-5, VAS, uroflowmetry (UFM) data, TRUS with elastography, Doppler ultrasonography, and laboratory tests. RESULTS: All patients completed the full course of treatment without adverse effects. At week 7, a more significant improvement was observed in Group 1 for NIH-CPSI, IPSS, VAS, and UFM (p<0.05). From weeks 10–54, a positive effect was noted in all groups, with a more consistent and significant effect in Group 3, which saw a reduction in the size of fibrotic zones and the number of calcinates, an increase in normal elastic zones, and improved blood flow (p<0.05). Between-group analysis confirmed the superiority of Groups 1 and 3 over Group 2 (p<0.05), with no significant differences between Groups 1 and 3 for NIH-CPSI, IPSS, or VAS (p>0.05). Patients with non-inflammatory CP/CPPS (IIIB) also showed an improvement in erectile function according to IIEF-5 (p<0.05). CONCLUSIONS: The presented treatment methods for CP and CPPS demonstrate safety. Effectiveness in eliminating clinical symptoms and improving the morpho-functional parameters of the pancreas. In long-term follow-up, ESWT and the drug BA demonstrate high efficacy in lysing fibrotic areas and pancreatic calcifications, and relieving symptoms of CP/CPPS.

title: IP14-16: Clinical Characteristics and Outcomes of Men with Chronic Pelvic Pain and Genitourinary Pain: A Single-Specialist Retrospective Review
parentSessionTitle: IP14: Infections/Inflammation/Cystic Disease of the Genitourinary Tract: Prostate & Genitalia

speakers.organization: Corewell Health William Beaumont University Hospital

fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Chronic pelvic pain syndrome/chronic prostatitis (CPPS/CP) is a heterogeneous disease process affecting 2-6% of men and severely impacting quality of life. AUA Guidelines on the Diagnosis and Management of Male CPPS recommend a multimodal treatment strategy, including medical therapy, psychological treatment, neuromodulation, and pelvic floor physical therapy (PFPT). As a major referral center for CPPS, we sought to review the presenting symptoms, prior evaluation and treatments from outside providers, our evaluation and management strategies, and clinical outcomes. METHODS: A retrospective review of male patients with ICD codes related to pelvic pain evaluated by a single subspecialty-trained urologist at our institution between February 2023 and July 2025 was done. Demographic data, presenting and associated symptoms, initial and most recent visual analog scale (VAS) pain scores, and prior interventions were collected. Interventions initiated after consultation with the male pelvic pain specialist were also recorded. RESULTS: 158 men were included (mean age 46.9 years, range 20-89; mean follow-up 301 days). 26 did not return after the initial visit. Urine cultures were obtained in 27.8%, of which 11.3% were positive. Mean initial 10-point VAS pain score was 3.4 (range 0-9), improving to a mean of 2.5 at most recent follow-up. Common associated symptoms included overactive bladder (45.5%), incomplete emptying (22.2%), and dysuria (12.7%); 5.7% of patients had Hunner’s lesions. Pain was most often diffuse (51.4%), followed by penile (14.6%) and rectal (12.0%). Bike riding/perineal compression (22.2%) and intercourse/masturbation (15.8%) were the most identified pain triggers, though 39.8% of patients could not identify their pain trigger. Prior to specialist consultation, 52.5% had undergone PFPT and 23.4% had received local anesthetic blocks. Most common treatments offered by the urologist were PFPT with therapists trained in intrarectal myofascial release (44.3%), local anesthetic/steroid blocks (pudendal, penile, spermatic cord, levator trigger point injections) (41.8%), and low intensity shockwave therapy (47.5%). Neuromodulation was performed in 8.2% of patients. CONCLUSIONS: Men with CPPS present with heterogeneous symptoms, frequently without clear pain triggers, and demonstrate low rates of urinary tract infection. Many patients have already pursued pelvic floor physical therapy or procedural interventions before further specialist evaluation. Modest improvements in pain scores over follow-up highlight the need for individualized, multimodal management strategies and further study of optimized treatment pathways.

title: IP14-17: Clues to Pain Relief: Treatment and Symptom Patterns in Men with Chronic Pelvic Pain
