parentSessionTitle: IP14: Infections/Inflammation/Cystic Disease of the Genitourinary Tract: Prostate & Genitalia

speakers.organization: Corewell Health William Beaumont University Hospital

fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Chronic pelvic pain syndrome/chronic prostatitis (CPPS/CP) is a complex syndrome affecting 2-6% of men and severely impacting quality of life. A multimodal treatment strategy is recommended by the AUA Guidelines. As a major referral center for CPPS, we examined differences between patients that had improvement in their pain scores compared to those who did not. METHODS: We conducted a retrospective review of male pelvic pain patients evaluated by a single subspecialty-trained urologist at our institution between February 2023 and July 2025. We included patients that had a baseline and follow up visual analog scale (VAS) pain score. Demographic data, presenting and associated symptoms, initial and most recent VAS pain scores, and prior interventions were collected. Interventions initiated after consultation with the male pelvic pain specialist were also recorded. Patients were stratified into two groups based on change in VAS scores: those with improvement and those without improvement or worsening scores. RESULTS: 103 patients had baseline and recent VAS scores with a mean follow-up of 311 days. 65 (63.1%) demonstrated improvement in VAS scores (mean improvement 3.1 points; follow-up 315 days), while 38 (36.9%) had stable or worsened pain (mean decline 1.2 points; follow-up 305 days). Patients who improved were slightly younger (mean age 44.4 vs. 47 years). Although not statistically significant, responders tended to report more overactive bladder symptoms (47.7% vs. 44.7%, p=0.77) and dysuria (13.8% vs. 7.9%, p=0.36), but less frequently reported incomplete emptying (18.5% vs. 23.7%, p=0.52). Rates of new pelvic floor physical therapy with intrarectal myofascial release were similar between groups; however, patients that improved more often received a peripheral nerve block (69.2% vs 44.7%, p=0.01) and neuromodulation (12.3% vs 7.9%, p=0.48). Analgesic and antispasmodic medication use was generally comparable, although responders more often received agents targeting obstructive voiding symptoms (15.4% vs. 2.7%, p=0.04). CONCLUSIONS: Younger age and differences in baseline urinary symptoms may distinguish men with CPPS who experienced pain improvement. Responders more often received peripheral nerve blocks, neuromodulation, and medications for obstructive voiding symptoms. These findings suggest that patient age, symptom profile, and treatment selection may influence outcomes and highlight the need for further investigation into tailored management strategies.

title: IP14-19: IgG4-related prostatitis: Proposal for its diagnostic criteria
parentSessionTitle: IP14: Infections/Inflammation/Cystic Disease of the Genitourinary Tract: Prostate & Genitalia
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: IgG4-related disease (IgG4-RD) is an immune-mediated fibro-inflammatory disorder that can affect multiple organs, characterized by elevated serum IgG4 levels and mass formation in various organs with infiltration of dense IgG4-positive plasma cells. Corticosteroid (CS) therapy is generally effective, but relapse is not uncommon. While any organs can be involved, IgG4-related prostatitis (IgG4-RP) has been scantly reported and lacks standardized diagnostic criteria. The utility of FDG-PET and Diffusion-weighted Whole-body Imaging with Background body signal suppression (DWIBS) has been reported in assessing organs involved by IgG4-RD. We experienced 2 IgG4-RP cases where IgG4-RD was pathologically confirmed by prostate biopsy. We aimed to propose diagnostic criteria for IgG4-RP and evaluate its incidence using DWIBS findings in male patients with histologically confirmed IgG4-RD. METHODS: Histological criteria were proposed based on the 2 biopsy-proven cases and previous case reports. The study cohort included 30 male IgG4-RD patients who underwent DWIBS. Positive DWIBS findings were defined as high signal intensity on DWIBS + inflammatory changes on T2-weighted MRI. We assessed the incidence of positive DWIBS findings and relations of CS response with changes in DWIBS and serum IgG4 levels. LUTS were assessed in a subset of cases and was defined as IPSS ≥8. RESULTS: We propose histological criteria of IgG4-RP as follows: the presence of dense lymphoplasmacytic infiltration with >10 IgG4-positive plasma cells/HPF or an IgG4/IgG-positive cell ratio of >40%. Among 14 patients underwent DWIBS before CS, DWIBS was positive in 9 (64%) including the 2 biopsy-proven cases. Of 6 patients re-evaluated after CS, 5 (83%) showed DWIBS improvement along with serum IgG4 decline. LUTS were found in 3 of 4 IPSS-assessed, DWIBS-positive patients before CS; post-CS IPSS was assessed in a biopsy-proven IgG4-RP case where IPSS normalized along with DWIBS and serum IgG4 levels. CONCLUSIONS: We propose the diagnostic criteria for IgG4-RP: histologically, the presence of dense lymphoplasmacytic infiltration with >10 IgG4-positive plasma cells/HPF or an IgG4/IgG-positive cell ratio of >40%, and clinically, positive findings on DWIBS or FDG-PET as well as elevated serum IgG4 levels. DWIBS evaluation suggests prostatitis in the majority of male IgG4-RD patients.

title: IP14-20: Comparison of Next Generation Sequencing DNA versus Traditional Cultures in Penile Implant Revision Cases: “What am I missing using only cultures?”
parentSessionTitle: IP14: Infections/Inflammation/Cystic Disease of the Genitourinary Tract: Prostate & Genitalia
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Traditional cultures are used to diagnose penile prosthesis (PP) infections and guide antibiotic therapy. However, false negative results are common, due to biased growth media, non-cultivable organisms, antibiotic usage, or insufficient sample volumes. Next generation sequencing (NGS) circumvents these issues by sequencing DNA directly from the samples. NGS allows for more sensitive and comprehensive identification of microorganisms, which in turn can guide antimicrobial treatment and surgical decision-making. Our goal is to evaluate the performance of NGS-based diagnostics compared to traditional culture in detecting bacteria on infected PPs. Our hypothesis is that NGS will be more sensitive and identify more isolates than traditional cultures. METHODS: 322 PPs removed for any reason from 2015 to July 2025 were included in the study. During revision surgery, two swab specimens were collected from the pump space if an inflatable PP / corporal space if rod: 1) sent for traditional culture testing at the institutional laboratory, and 2) for NGS testing (MicroGenDx, Lubbock, TX, USA), including targeted 16s rRNA and ITS gene sequencing. Positivity rates, numbers of species, and organism profiles per test were compared. RESULTS: NGS had a significantly higher rate of positive detections (n=111, 34.47%) compared to culture results (n=40, 12.42%, p<0.001). NGS identified significantly more bacterial species than culture (NGS mean=1.35 (2.55), Culture mean=0.30 (0.65), p<0.001). NGS found 3 fungal species and 55 bacterial species in comparison to the 1 fungal species and 16 bacterial species identified by traditional culture ( (https://www.auajournals.org/doi/abs/10.1097/01.JU.0001191352.93132.27.20#F1)). Unique species found by NGS included many fastidious organisms likely to be missed by culture including various anaerobes, Mycoplasma, and Ureaplasma. CONCLUSIONS: NGS offers a more sensitive and comprehensive characterization of the organisms contributing to PP microbiome, which may be a useful aid in diagnosis and treatment.

title: IP14-21: Harnessing Artificial Intelligence to Predict Post-Operative Infection after Inflatable Penile Prosthesis Implantation: A Machine Learning Prediction Model
parentSessionTitle: IP14: Infections/Inflammation/Cystic Disease of the Genitourinary Tract: Prostate & Genitalia

speakers.organization: Department of Urology, University of California, Irvine

fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Post-operative infection following inflatable penile prosthesis (IPP) surgery remains one of the most serious complications despite advances in antiseptic techniques. Current infection-risk assessment relies on surgeon experience rather than objective tools. We developed and validated a machine learning–based model using a unified complication taxonomy to enable preoperative infection risk stratification. METHODS: A total of 5,815 multicenter IPP cases (primary, revision, and infection-salvage) were analyzed. Unstructured operative entries were standardized into a 38-feature taxonomy encompassing demographics, comorbidities, surgical variables, prosthesis type, and intraoperative details. Among these, 117 cases (2%) were complication-positive for post-operative infection. We compared 80 model configurations (10 classifiers × 4 resampling strategies × 2 data splits). Model performance was evaluated using macro-averaged precision, recall, F1 score, and precision–recall area under the curve (PR-AUC). Feature interpretability was assessed with SHAP (Shapley Additive Explanations). RESULTS: Gradient Boosting with Random Undersampling (RUS) achieved the best standard-split performance (Precision=0.52, Recall=0.75, F1=0.46, PR-AUC=0.10). Logistic Regression without resampling performed best on temporal validation (Precision=0.52, Recall=0.63, F1=0.51, PR-AUC=0.06). SHAP analysis ( Fig 1) identified diabetes, coronary/peripheral vascular disease, and history of prior IPP infection as the strongest positive predictors of infection, with maximum SHAP contributions of +0.21, +0.67, and +0.83, respectively. Additional risk factors included intra-operative complications and older age. Protective associations were observed for AMS LGX prosthesis use and combined peri-operative antifungal + vancomycin prophylaxis. CONCLUSIONS: A gradient-boosting model integrating pre- and intra-operative variables achieved 75% sensitivity for post-operative infection prediction, supporting its role as a preoperative screening tool. SHAP interpretability highlights patient comorbidities and infection history as dominant drivers of infection risk, while combination antifungal-antibiotic prophylaxis may confer measurable protection. External validation is underway to optimize model calibration and clinical deployment.

title: IP14-22: UROPRIME (UROlogical Prosthetic Infection Model Evaluation): Development of a European Multicenter Nomogram Predicting Perioperative Infectious Risk in Urological Prosthetic Surgery
parentSessionTitle: IP14: Infections/Inflammation/Cystic Disease of the Genitourinary Tract: Prostate & Genitalia
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Postoperative prosthesis infection is a severe complication. Accurate, early risk stratification is essential to guide preventive strategies. We aimed to develop and externally validate a clinical nomogram to predict the 90-day risk of postoperative prosthesis infection in a large European cohort. METHODS: We conducted a multicenter retrospective study of patients undergoing urogenital prosthetic surgery. The cohort was randomly divided into a training (2/3, n=541) and test (1/3, n=271) dataset. The primary outcome was 90-day postoperative infection. A stepwise logistic regression model was developed on the training set to best combination of predictors. The final model was displayed as a nomogram. Model performance was evaluated for accuracy (C-index) and calibration plot plots). Clinical usefulness was determined using Decision Curve Analysis (DCA) on the validation dataset test. RESULTS: Of the 812 patients, 40 (4.9%) experienced an infection. The final model included Age at Surgery (OR 1.03, 95% CI: 0.99–1.08; p=0.124), Obesity (OR 2.28, 95% CI: 0.88–5.53; (p=0.075), Time of Surgery (OR 1.01, 95% CI: 1.00–1.02; p=0.001), and n° of days of prophylaxis antibiotics (OR 0.88, 95% CI: 0.74–1.04; p=0.145). In the internal validation, the model demonstrated good discrimination with a C-index of 0.72 and excellent calibration. In the split validation, the model retained acceptable discrimination with a C- Index of 0.69. The split calibration plot showed good agreement between predicted and observed probabilities. Decision curve analysis confirmed that using the nomogram provided a greater net benefit than the “treat all” or “treat none” strategies across a wide range of clinically relevant risk thresholds (approx. 2.5% to 10%). Based on Youden test a nomogram cut-off of 6% was identified showing a sensitivity, specificity, PPV and NPV of 63, 76.5, 12,3 and 97.5% respectively. CONCLUSIONS: We have developed and externally validated a simple nomogram that provides good predictive accuracy for 90-day postoperative prosthesis infection. This tool can assist clinicians in identifying high-risk patients who may benefit from targeted preventive measures.

title: IP14-23: Cystoscopy and risk of urinary tract infection. A nationwide 5-year cohort study
parentSessionTitle: IP14: Infections/Inflammation/Cystic Disease of the Genitourinary Tract: Prostate & Genitalia

speakers.organization: Odense University Hospital and University of Southern Denmark

fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: The aim of this study was to examine the 7-day risk of urinary tract infection (UTI) following cystoscopy in an outpatient clinic. METHODS: This nationwide population-based cohort study included all adult patients (age ≥18 years), who underwent a cystoscopy in an outpatient setting in Denmark in the period 2018-2023. We identified the patients through the Danish National Patient Registry (DNPR) using procedure codes KUKC0O2 or KKCD02. We defined UTI as a hospital diagnosis recorded in DNPR and/or redemption of at least one prescription for urinary tract infection-specific antibiotics (sulfamethizole, trimethoprim, pivmecillinam or nitrofurantoin) (ATC codes J01EB02, J01EA, J01CA08, and J01XE01) within one week after cystoscopy. From DNPR we obtained information on patients’ comorbidities registered before date of cystoscopy including by using Charlson Comorbidity index. We characterized the patients at date of cystoscopy including the prevalence of UTI within 5 years before date of cystoscopy and followed the individuals within the first week after the procedure. Among patients without UTI at the index date, we computed the 7-day risk of UTI overall and stratified by age, sex and underlying comorbidities. RESULTS: We included 294,075 patients who underwent cystoscopy in an outpatient setting in the period 2018-2023. Of these, 70% were men and 75% were 50 years or older (See table 1). A total of 49,855 (17%) had a UTI registered within 5 years before cystoscopy based on hospital diagnoses and redeemed prescriptions and 38% had no registered comorbidity according to the Charlson comorbidity Index. Within 7 days after cystoscopy, 2.6% (95% CI, 2.55–2.67) experienced an UTI (Table 2). Individuals aged 18-39 years had the highest risk, 4.19% (95% CI, 3.91–4.48) CONCLUSIONS: We conclude, based on this robust 5-year national study in a time when there is a large overuse of antibiotics, that it is NOT necessary to use antibiotics during outpatient cystoscopies except in selected patients e. g. such as patients with heart valve surgery or immunosuppressed patients.

title: IP14-24: AI-Based CT Analysis of Myosteatosis Predicts Mortality in Fournier Gangrene
parentSessionTitle: IP14: Infections/Inflammation/Cystic Disease of the Genitourinary Tract: Prostate & Genitalia
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Fournier’s gangrene (FG) is a fatal necrotizing infection with high mortality. Existing indices such as the Fournier Gangrene Severity Index (FGSI) rely on static parameters and may not reflect baseline metabolic status. Myosteatosis, or fat infiltration within skeletal muscle, is linked to poor outcomes in cancer and critical illness. This study evaluated the prognostic significance of myosteatosis in FG using artificial intelligence (AI)-based computed tomography (CT) analysis. METHODS: A retrospective review was conducted of 40 patients with Fournier’s gangrene treated between 2012 and 2022. Preoperative L3-level CT scans were analyzed using AI software (ClariSarco, ClariPi, Seoul, Korea) to quantify skeletal muscle quality. Parameters including normal attenuation muscle area (NAMA) were automatically extracted to assess myosteatosis, which was defined by sex-specific NAMA/TAMA cutoffs. Clinical characteristics, FGSI, septic shock, and mortality were compared, and predictors of mortality were evaluated by multivariate logistic regression. RESULTS: Among 40 patients, 22 (55 percent) had myosteatosis. These patients exhibited higher rates of septic shock (45.5 percent vs 11.1 percent, p<0.05) and mortality (31.8 percent vs 5.6 percent, p<0.05) than those without myosteatosis. Survivors had higher NAMA (79.1 ± 31.5 vs 46.2 ± 22.3, p<0.05) and lower myosteatosis percentage (37.9 ± 16.8 percent vs 56.5 ± 15.2 percent, p<0.05). Multivariate analysis revealed that myosteatosis percentage (odds ratio 1.11, 95 percent confidence interval 1.01–1.23, p=0.03), FGSI >9 (odds ratio 62.9, p=0.026), and cardiovascular disease (odds ratio 53.5, p=0.018) were independent predictors of mortality. CONCLUSIONS: AI-based CT analysis provides an objective and reproducible assessment of muscle quality in FG. Myosteatosis independently predicted septic shock and mortality, outperforming traditional measures such as BMI and FGSI. Incorporating AI-derived myosteatosis evaluation into clinical workflows may enable early risk stratification and individualized treatment planning for high-risk FG patients.

title: IP14-25: Autonomic Overdrive Unmasked: Peripheral Cold Hypersensitivity Reveals a Neurovascular Pathway to Premature Ejaculation
parentSessionTitle: IP14: Infections/Inflammation/Cystic Disease of the Genitourinary Tract: Prostate & Genitalia
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Cold hypersensitivity in the hands and feet (CHHF) reflects sympathetic overactivity and endothelial dysfunction affecting peripheral blood flow. Although associated with erectile dysfunction, its role in premature ejaculation (PE)—a disorder characterized by autonomic hyperexcitability—remains unclear. This study aims to investigate the independent association between CHHF and PE in men with preserved erectile function, isolating autonomic influences on ejaculatory control. METHODS: An anonymous web-based survey conducted in December 2022 enrolled 1,008 sexually active Taiwanese men aged 20–40 years. Those with erectile dysfunction (IIEF-5 ≤ 21) or phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitor use were excluded. CHHF was defined by persistent cold sensations in both hands and feet lasting ≥6 months. PE was identified by Premature Ejaculation Diagnostic Tool (PEDT) scores ≥9. Multivariate logistic regression adjusted for age, smoking, insomnia, and exercise to assess CHHF-PE association. RESULTS: Among participants (mean age 31.6 ± 5.2), 22.5% reported CHHF. Compared to non-CHHF men, CHHF-positive men had higher smoking prevalence (21.6% vs. 14.5%; p=0.018) and insomnia rates (13.2% vs. 7.0%; p=0.009). PE prevalence was significantly greater in CHHF men (25.1% vs. 18.3%; p=0.029). CHHF independently predicted PE with adjusted odds ratio 1.64 (95% CI 1.00–2.69; p=0.048). Item-level PEDT analysis revealed “ejaculation occurs too early” as the dominant symptom driving this link (odds ratio 2.03; p=0.011), implicating accelerated ejaculatory reflex over psychological distress. CONCLUSIONS: Peripheral cold hypersensitivity independently associates with premature ejaculation despite normal erectile function, unveiling a shared autonomic-vascular pathway. CHHF serves as an easily reportable sensory biomarker of systemic dysautonomia impacting male sexual health. This “cold–rapid” connection reframes PE within an autonomic-vascular continuum, highlighting the potential of interventions targeting microcirculatory and autonomic balance—such as aerobic exercise, stress reduction, and biofeedback—to complement pharmacotherapy. | | | --- | | |

title: IP14-26: Post-vasectomy pain syndrome and vasectomy complications: real-life data from a single tertiary referral center
parentSessionTitle: IP14: Infections/Inflammation/Cystic Disease of the Genitourinary Tract: Prostate & Genitalia
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Vasectomy is an increasingly utilized method of permanent male contraception. No-scalpel vasectomy (NSV) is the preferred technique due to its favorable safety profile and low complication rates. However, complications such as infection, hematoma, and chronic post-vasectomy pain syndrome (PVPS) can occur. The true incidence and risk factors for PVPS remain uncertain. This study aims to evaluate the rates of PVPS and other complications following vasectomy, as well as to identify associated risk factors. METHODS: This retrospective study evaluated 1,774 sexually active men undergoing vasectomy between 2016 and 2024 at a single tertiary-referral center. Baseline data, including age, number of children, and BMI, were collected preoperatively. Postoperative follow-up assessed complications, need for repeat surgery, and results of post-vasectomy semen analysis (PVSA) performed three months after the procedure. Statistical analysis utilized nonparametric tests and multivariate logistic regression to identify independent risk factors for complications (significance: p<0.05). RESULTS: Patients had a median age of 42 years (IQR 7.0), median BMI 26.95 (IQR 4.96), and median follow-up of 101 months (IQR 97–104). Most (90%) completed PVSA; 94.9% achieved azoospermia at first analysis, with 2% requiring re-vasectomy, and 0.2% undergoing vasovasostomy or TESE for regret. Postoperative recovery was uneventful in 97.3% of cases; infection and hematoma rates were 1.5% and 1.1%, respectively. PVPS occurred in 0.7% (n=14); most were managed with NSAIDs, a minority (n=3) required escalated treatment, including one surgical re-intervention. Multivariate analysis identified postoperative complications (p<0.001) and higher BMI (p=0.012) as independent risk factors for PVPS; age was not significant. CONCLUSIONS: No-scalpel vasectomy offers high efficacy and safety for male sterilization, with rare complications and a low PVPS incidence. Postoperative complications and elevated BMI independently increase PVPS risk and may merit consideration during preoperative counseling and risk stratification.

title: IP14-27: Early Follow-up of Decompressive Epididymectomy: Safety and Outcome Profiles
parentSessionTitle: IP14: Infections/Inflammation/Cystic Disease of the Genitourinary Tract: Prostate & Genitalia

speakers.organization: University of Florida, Department of Urology

fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Epididymectomy is an underutilized, yet effective intervention for scrotal content pain localized to the epididymis. Referral to a surgeon experienced in scrotal surgery is often valuable given possible injury to the testicle or gonadal vasculature which reside close to the epididymis. At our tertiary referral center, epididymectomy is offered to men with pinpoint, reproduceable, epididymal tenderness who present for scrotal content pain refractory to NSAIDs and conservative management. We describe a novel surgical approach which involves opening of the epididymal sheath and disarticulating the epididymis off the underlying posterior epididymal fascia which is kept in-situ overlying the testis and gonadal vasculature, and its early safety and outcome profiles. METHODS: Patients were assessed for chronic scrotal content pain who underwent decompression epididymectomy at a tertiary referral center from July, 2022 to October, 2025. Pain had to be present for greater than 30 days, reproducible on exam, and localized to epididymis. Men without post-operative follow up were excluded. Patients were assessed for laterality, prior surgeries, origin of pain, post-operative pain assessment and 90-day complications. Chi-square analysis was used for sub-group analysis. RESULTS: Fifty-four men underwent decompression epididymectomy. Forty-five men were included in the final cohort. Mean time to initial follow up was 3.9 weeks. Scrotal content pain improved in 74.1% (n=40) men, resolved in 26.2% (n=12), unchanged in 7.4% (n=4) and worsened in 2.2% (n=1) of men. Post-operative pain response improved when stratified by patients undergoing epididymectomy only, without concomitant scrotal surgery ( Table 1). Pain improvement was not associated with prior penoscrotal surgery (p-0.67), bilateral nature (p-0.47) or chronic narcotic pain medication (p-0.21). Surgical site inflammation (7%), scrotal hematoma (4%) and superficial wound dehiscence (2%) were noted 90 days post-operatively. Pain response did not corelate with prior genitourinary or scrotal surgical history. CONCLUSIONS: Our case series demonstrates that decompression epididymectomy is a safe and effective approach to epididymal resection for scrotal content pain. Our approach may help minimize potential complications and risk to the gonadal vessels, while optimizing pain relief. | | | --- | | |

title: IP14-28: Varicocelectomy with Peri-Vasal Denervation is a Safe Intervention in Setting of Idiopathic Orchalgia
parentSessionTitle: IP14: Infections/Inflammation/Cystic Disease of the Genitourinary Tract: Prostate & Genitalia
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Subinguinal microscopic varicocelectomy is a well-established treatment for men with varicoceles and chronic orchalgia. Peri-vasal veins are typically preserved to protect fertility and avert testicular atrophy. Incorporation of peri-vasal denervation (PVD) with varicocelectomy may be an appropriate surgical option for patients with varicoceles and orchalgia that does not align with typical varicocele symptoms. This study aimed to evaluate whether combining standard varicocelectomy with PVD is a safe operative intervention for men with varicocles and idiopathic orchalgia. METHODS: A retrospective review was conducted of men undergoing subinguinal microscopic varicocelectomy for the primary indication of orchalgia between July 2017 and December 2024 at our institution. Patient demographics, varicocele characteristics, surgical findings, and pre- and post-intervention pain severity scores (scale of 1–10) were collected. Inclusion required a palpable varicocele and ≥ 3 months of orchalgia, including typical varicocele pain and atypical symptoms more consistent with idiopathic orchalgia. Men desiring future fertility were excluded. PVD was performed only when the deferential artery was identified. RESULTS: We evaluated 91 patients who underwent varicocelectomy for the primary indication of orchalgia, with 21 patients undergoing PVD at time of varicocelectomy. Mean post-operative follow-up time of 4.73 months. No independent factors including varicocele grade or laterality, patient BMI, or comorbidities were associated with severity of pre-operative pain. Mean pre-operative pain severity was 6.7 (SD 2.7) and mean post-operative pain severity was 2.5 (SD 2.8). Pain improved in 19 (90.5%) patients, including resolution of pain in 9 (42.9%) patients. Two (9.5%) patients saw no change or worsening pain. No post-operative complications at the level of Clavien-Dindo Grade II or above were observed. CONCLUSIONS: Incorporation of PVD with varicocelectomy is a safe, viable intervention for men with varicoceles and orchalgia when the deferential artery is identified. Consideration of this surgical approach is appropriate for men with idiopathic orchalgia, with atypical symptom patterns suggestive of a neuropathic component. Further investigations of varicocelectomy with PVD are warranted to refine patient selection and compare outcomes with standard varicocelectomy. | | | --- | | |

title: IP14-29: Comparative analysis of minimal-incision modified fenestration technique and standard hydrocelectomy: reduced bleeding and healthcare utilization
parentSessionTitle: IP14: Infections/Inflammation/Cystic Disease of the Genitourinary Tract: Prostate & Genitalia
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Hydrocelectomy is typically a low-risk operation, but minimally invasive approaches may offer added benefits for patients and providers. The minimal-incision modified fenestration technique (MIMFeT), performed in-office under local anesthesia, may reduce complications and healthcare utilization. We compared postoperative outcomes of MIMFeT with standard hydrocelectomy. METHODS: We retrospectively reviewed patients who underwent hydrocelectomy at our institution from January 2018 to July 2024. Technique selection was based on surgeon preference. Primary outcomes were 30-day postoperative complications (bleeding, infection, reoperation). Secondary outcomes included unplanned patient contacts within 90 days and hydrocele recurrence within 1 year. Fisher’s exact test was used for categorical comparisons. RESULTS: Among 311 patients (130 MIMFeT; 181 standard), recurrence outcomes were available for 300. Overall 30-day complication rates were lower with MIMFeT (6.2%) versus standard (12.7%), though not statistically significant (OR 0.45, 95% CI 0.17–1.09; p=0.083). Rates of infection and reoperation were comparable. Notably, bleeding occurred in 6.1% of standard cases but in none of the MIMFeT cases (OR 0, 95% CI 0–0.53; p=0.003). MIMFeT patients also had fewer unplanned postoperative contacts (43.8% vs 58.6%; OR 0.55, 95% CI 0.34–0.89; p=0.011). One-year recurrence did not differ significantly between groups ( (https://www.auajournals.org/doi/abs/10.1097/01.JU.0001191352.93132.27.29#F1)). CONCLUSIONS: MIMFeT demonstrated comparable safety and recurrence rates to standard hydrocelectomy while eliminating bleeding events and reducing postoperative healthcare utilization. These findings suggest MIMFeT may be particularly advantageous for patients at elevated bleeding risk and offer a practical, office-based alternative for those seeking to minimize perioperative morbidity and follow-up needs.

title: IP14-30: The Utility of Autologous Tunica Vaginalis Graft Repair on Varying Testicular Pathologies
parentSessionTitle: IP14: Infections/Inflammation/Cystic Disease of the Genitourinary Tract: Prostate & Genitalia
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: The use of tunica vaginalis grafts has been incompletely described in the current literature. This surgical method could have potential benefits in patients with varying testicular pathologies. This includes testicular compartment syndrome due to torsion or epididymo-orchitis and for patients with large defects after testicular rupture. Our aim was to demonstrate the versatility and applicability of tension free autologous tunica vaginalis graft repair (aTVGR). METHODS: We conducted a retrospective case series of two surgeons. 68 patients underwent scrotal exploration between April 2017 and February 2021 for various indications. 11 patients received a TVGR and were included in this case series. Patient demographics, clinical history and indications were collected retrospectively. Written consent was obtained for the use of intraoperative images. All patients had post-operative follow-up at 2 and 6 weeks with a repeat ultrasound. RESULTS: 11 patients underwent TVGR. 6/11 (55%) for ruptured testicular tunica albuginea following blunt trauma, 3/11 (18%) epididymo-orchitis induced testicular compartment syndrome with post-operative ultrasound confirming good flow. 2/11 (27%) were re-do scrotal explorations for tension ischemia following primary repair of ruptured testicle with post-operative ultrasound confirming good flow. There were no post-operative complications at 2 or 6 weeks. CONCLUSIONS: TVGR should be considered in traumatic testicular rupture with extensive tunica albuginea defect or if tension-free primary closure cannot be achieved. TVGR is a safe and viable management solution for the treatment of testicular compartment syndrome of varying aetiology. Future prospective comparative studies with long term follow-up would help guide management.

title: IP15-01: EasyVoid: A Novel Portable Uroflowmeter for Home-Based, Container-Free Urinary Flow Testing on Any Toilet
parentSessionTitle: IP15: Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia: Epidemiology, Evaluation & Medical Non-surgical Therapy
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Conventional uroflowmetry requires patients to void into collection funnels or devices within clinics, often altering their natural voiding behavior and limiting access. Existing sound- or sensor-based systems attempt home use but face challenges of acoustic variability, calibration drift, and toilet incompatibility. We developed EasyVoid, a novel portable uroflowmeter that enables accurate, home-based, container-free urinary flow testing on any toilet, leveraging the Coandă effect to capture real-time flow without microphones, pressure sensors, or urine collection. METHODS: EasyVoid incorporates a passive novel helical rotor that converts urinary stream momentum into rotational velocity through the Coandă effect ( Fig. A). A Hall effect sensor detects rotor spin, transmitting data wirelessly for signal processing. Flow rate is calculated via a polynomial calibration model integrating noise filtering, Hilbert transform, and phase unwrapping ( Fig. B). The system was evaluated using simulated voiding across five standard flow patterns (bell-shaped, bell-with-tail, plateau, intermittent, and low-volume) and compared with a clinical uroflowmeter (MMS Flowmaster). Four key parameters—Qmax, Qave, voided volume, and voiding time—were analyzed. Six board-certified urologists also performed a single-blind review of 90 randomized flow curves to assess diagnostic concordance between EasyVoid and standard uroflowmetry. RESULTS: Across 45 simulated voids, EasyVoid demonstrated strong agreement with standard uroflowmetry: Qmax (R2=0.81), Qave (R2=0.89), voided volume (R2=0.73), and voiding time (R2=0.99) ( Fig. C). In the reader validation task, diagnostic interpretations between EasyVoid and standard uroflowmetry achieved 91% concordance (κ=0.84) ( Fig. D), consistent with expert-level inter-rater reliability. CONCLUSIONS: EasyVoid enables accurate, naturalistic uroflowmetry at home or in any restroom—without urine collection, calibration, or specialized hardware. Its low-cost, passive design supports longitudinal LUTS monitoring and postoperative follow-up in real-world settings. This technology represents a clinically ready step toward democratizing access to objective urinary flow assessment beyond hospital walls. Patent pending: PCT/US2025/034459.

title: IP15-02: Nocturnal Bladder Capacity Index Assessment To Improve Nocturia Management In Patients With Lower Urinary Tract Symptoms Related To Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia
parentSessionTitle: IP15: Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia: Epidemiology, Evaluation & Medical Non-surgical Therapy
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Nocturia is a prevalent and disruptive symptom in men with BPH. The Nocturnal Bladder Capacity Index (NBCI) is a diagnostic toolthat helps differentiate between nocturia subtypes, such as nocturnal polyuria (NP) and reduced nocturnal bladder capacity (NBC),guiding targeted treatments. This study compares the clinical outcomes of NBCI-guided management versus non-stratified standardtreatment approaches in men with BPH-associated nocturia. METHODS: This prospective study included men between 45 and 65 years old with significant nocturia (≥3 voids/night) and LUTS related toBPH. Participants were divided into the NBCI guided and non NBCI groups. The NBCI-guided group underwent differential diagnosisbased on NBCI values. Patients with NBCI >1.3, indicating reduced NBC, were treated with tamsulosin (0.4 mg/day) and solifenacin(5 mg/day). Patients with NBCI ≤1.3 underwent frequency-volume charts and nocturnal urine volume (NUV) assessment todetermine the presence of NP or other bladder dysfunctions. Patients with NP were treated with desmopressin (0.2 mg/day); thosewithout NP were treated according to their specific diagnosis. The non-NBCI group received treatment with tamsulosin (0.4 mg/day).Outcomes were assessed at 6 months, including nocturnal void frequency (NVF) and IPSS. RESULTS: A total of 150 men were included (75 in the NBCI-guided group and 75 in the non-NBCI group). The NBCI-guided group achieved a55% reduction in NVF (from 3.6 to 1.6, p<0.001), compared to a 30% reduction in the non-NBCI group (from 3.5 to 2.5, p<0.001).IPSS scores improved in the NBCI-guided group, decreasing from 22.6 to 13.7 (p<0.001). The non-NBCI group showed a smallerimprovement from 22.4 to 17.2 (p<0.09). In patients with NBCI≤1.3, 73% were diagnosed with NP and experienced a 58% reductionin NVF (from 3.5 to 1.5, p<0.001) with desmopressin (0.2 mg/day). The remaining 27% without NP achieved a 48% reduction in NVF(from 3.4 to 1.8, p<0.01) when treated according to the diagnosis. Patients with NBCI>1.3 treated with tamsulosin (0.4 mg/day) andsolifenacin (5 mg/day) showed a 41% reduction in NVF (from 3.8 to 2.2, p<0.01). CONCLUSIONS: The results demonstrate that NBCI-guided management is significantly more effective than non-stratified approaches in reducing NVF and improving IPSS. By distinguishing between NP and other bladder dysfunctions, NBCI-guided treatment enabled targeted interventions. Desmopressin was highly effective for NP. These findings highlight the clinical value of NBCI in optimizing treatmentfor nocturia and reducing symptom burden in men with BPH. NBCI-guided management outperformed non-stratified treatmentapproaches in reducing NVF, improving IPSS scores, and enhancing patient QoL. This study underscores the importance of NBCI as a diagnostic tool for tailored treatment in BPH-associated nocturia.

title: IP15-03: Perceptions of Ejaculation Among Patients Presenting to Urology Clinic for Lower Urinary Tract Symptoms
parentSessionTitle: IP15: Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia: Epidemiology, Evaluation & Medical Non-surgical Therapy
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Loss of ejaculatory function (EjF) is a risk for men undergoing treatment for benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH). A prior study assessing the perceived importance of EjF was performed at a state fair and included patients as young as 18 years of age. The objective of our study is to assess the perception of EjF among the population of men presenting to the urology clinic for BPH management. METHODS: A survey assessing EjF and perception was handed out to patients and their partners when they were seen for their consultation at our BPH clinic or in the pre-operative area for their BPH procedure. The questionnaire asked about baseline demographics and BPH medication use. Patients noted their current EjF and its importance to them and their partner through Likert scales (1 is strongly disagree, 5 is strongly agree). Responses were tallied and multiple linear regression was performed to determine factors that impacted ejaculation and their response to the statement: “Preserving ejaculation is more important than improving urination”. RESULTS: There were 203 surveys completed: 190 by the patients and 13 by their partners. The median age of patients and partners were 69 and 67, respectively. (https://www.auajournals.org/doi/abs/10.1097/01.JU.0001191356.52697.6d.03#F1) shows patient and partner responses in which they agreed or strongly agreed(scored 4 or 5 on the Likert scale) with the statements presented. 62% of patients agreed that EjF is important for pleasure but only 13% agreed that preservation of EjF is more important than improving urination. On multiple linear regression, alpha-blocker use was not associated with EjF. Increased age correlated with worsening EjF. Patients with a better EjF were more likely to agree that preserving EjF is more important than improving urination, as shown in (https://www.auajournals.org/doi/abs/10.1097/01.JU.0001191356.52697.6d.03#F2). CONCLUSIONS: Our study finds that ejaculation remains important at an older age, but when presented with the decision between treating BPH and preserving ejaculation: few patients or partners would favor ejaculation over urination.

title: IP15-04: The LURN SI-10 Questionnaire: A Valid and Clinically Meaningful Tool That Extends the IPSS in LUTS Assessment
parentSessionTitle: IP15: Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia: Epidemiology, Evaluation & Medical Non-surgical Therapy
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: To evaluate the psychometric performance and clinical utility of the Lower Urinary Tract Dysfunction Research Network Symptom Index-10 (LURN SI-10) in men with lower urinary tract symptoms (LUTS) and to explore its correlation with the International Prostate Symptom Score (IPSS). METHODS: A cross-sectional multicenter study was performed in 212 men with LUTS across four university hospitals. Participants completed both the IPSS and the LURN SI-10. Internal consistency was assessed using Cronbach’s alpha. Construct validity was analyzed by exploratory factor analysis (principal component extraction, Promax rotation). Convergent validity was evaluated by Spearman correlation between total scores. Discriminant validity was examined across IPSS severity strata and in patients with vs without urinary incontinence. ROC analysis determined optimal cut-off values, and multiple linear regression identified symptom domains independently associated with IPSS severity. RESULTS: Median total scores were 14 for IPSS and 9 for LURN SI-10. Internal consistency was high (α=0.85 and 0.82, respectively). Factor analysis confirmed two correlated components explaining 54% of variance (KMO=0.831; p<0.001). LURN SI-10 correlated strongly with IPSS (ρ=0.76, p<0.001). It discriminated across IPSS-defined severity groups (Welch F=84.85, p<0.001) and between patients with and without urinary incontinence (p<0.001). ROC analysis demonstrated excellent discrimination (AUC=0.86; 95% CI 0.81–0.91), with a cut-off ≥8 yielding 72% sensitivity and 87% specificity. Regression identified bladder pain (β=0.283, p<0.001), urgency incontinence (β=0.192, p=0.009), and post-micturition dribble (β=0.153, p=0.043) as independent predictors of higher IPSS scores. CONCLUSIONS: The LURN SI-10 demonstrated robust reliability and strong clinical concordance with the IPSS. By capturing additional domains such as incontinence, bladder pain, and post-micturition dribble, it provides a broader, patient-centered evaluation of LUTS that complements and extends the clinical scope of the IPSS.

title: IP15-05: From IPSS to LURN SI-10: Empiric Cutoffs Aligning Mild/Moderate/Severe BPH Symptoms Using 6,382 Same-Day Assessments
parentSessionTitle: IP15: Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia: Epidemiology, Evaluation & Medical Non-surgical Therapy

speakers.jobTitle: Vice Chief of Urology;Director of Urology Research;Clinical Associate Professor
speakers.organization: Endeavor Health; University of Chicago Pritzker School of Medicine

fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: The LURN SI-10 is a one-page questionnaire developed by the NIH Symptoms of Lower Urinary Tract Dysfunction Research Network that captures additional symptoms such as incontinence and pain not queried by the IPSS. For men with BPH, we sought to (1) quantify association between SI-10 and IPSS in a large real-world dataset and (2) evaluate SI-10 severity bands that correspond to IPSS mild, moderate, and severe categories to support clinical interpretation and future trial endpoints. METHODS: We performed a retrospective cohort study at a single integrated health system of adult men with a diagnosis of LUTS/BPH (N40.1) who completed both IPSS and SI-10 on the same calendar day. Pearson correlation quantified association between continuous IPSS and SI-10 scores. Differences in mean SI-10 scores across IPSS categories were tested using one-way ANOVA. Based on the observed SI-10 distributions within IPSS strata we derived candidate SI-10 ranges aligned with IPSS “mild,” “moderate,” and “severe.” RESULTS: Among 6,382 paired assessments, mean (SD) age was 71.8 (9.8) years, and mean (SD) IPSS and SI-10 scores were 11.2 (7.1) and 7.7 (4.5), respectively. Scores demonstrated strong correlation (r=0.77, 95% CI \[0.76-0.78\]). IPSS severity was mild, moderate, and severe in 36%, 50%, and 14%, respectively, with median (IQR) SI-10 scores of 4 (3, 6), 8 (6, 10), and 13 (10, 16), respectively (ANOVA p<0.001, Figure). Based on these empirical distributions, we propose preliminary SI-10 score ranges of 0–5 (mild), 6–9 (moderate), and ≥10 (severe) as thresholds mapping to the central tendency of each IPSS category in this real-world sample. CONCLUSIONS: In a large single-institution cohort of men with BPH, SI-10 demonstrated strong correlation with IPSS and showed stepwise increases across IPSS severity levels. The proposed SI-10 severity bands (0–5 mild, 6–9 moderate, ≥10 severe) offer an interpretable framework that preserves content advantages of SI-10 (continence and pain) while harmonizing with widely used IPSS categories. These real-world data provide an empirical foundation for clinical decision thresholds to be tested via rigorous prospective data collection in NCT05898932.

title: IP15-06: Prostate Transition Zone Stiffness Measured by Ultrasound Shear Wave Elastography Varies Across Clinical BPH/LUTS Phenotypes: A Feasibility Study
parentSessionTitle: IP15: Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia: Epidemiology, Evaluation & Medical Non-surgical Therapy
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Shear wave elastography (SWE) is a non-invasive method to characterize tissue stiffness. We hypothesize that elevated transition zone (TZ) stiffness alters prostatic urethra caliber during voiding altering flow dynamics, contributing to BPH/LUTS and the development of bladder outlet obstruction (BOO). Therefore, the purpose of this study was to demonstrate feasibility of prostate SWE in men without and with BPH/LUTS and BOO. METHODS: Transrectal prostate SWE was performed using a Siemens Sequoia ultrasound system with a modified 18H6 hockey stick probe. TZ stiffness (modulus of elasticity in kPa) was measured using 15 regions of interest on the midgland right and left periurethral TZ ( figure). Clinical data included age, International Prostate Symptom Score (IPSS), prostatic urethral length (PUL), uroflowmetry, and post-void residual (PVR). BOO was defined as peak flow 15 ml/s or PVR > 100 ml and bothersome LUTS (IPSS > 19). Participants were categorized as: 1) classic BPH (men > 50 years old with prostate mass > 40 g and BOO or bothersome LUTS), 2) normal (no BOO or LUTS), and 3) high risk (BOO or bothersome LUTS with prostate mass 40 g or age 50 years). The Kruskal-Wallis test was used to compare stiffness across phenotypes with post-hoc Mann-Whitney U tests for pairwise comparisons. Relationships between TZ stiffness and clinical parameters were assessed. RESULTS: In 15 men (median age: 48 years, range: 30–74), mean TZ stiffness (mean±SEM) differed significantly across phenotypes (p=0.02, figure). Classic BPH (n=4) demonstrated the lowest TZ stiffness (5.75±0.89 kPa), normal/reference (n=6) intermediate (15.96±4.77 kPa), and high-risk (n=5) the highest (29.09±4.35 kPa). Post-hoc analysis revealed significantly lower stiffness in classic BPH compared to high-risk patients (p=0.016). TZ stiffness correlated with phenotype severity when treated as an ordinal variable. Additionally, TZ stiffness showed a trend with IPSS severity, although not statistically significant. CONCLUSIONS: Transrectal prostate SWE reveals distinct stiffness patterns across clinical BPH/LUTS phenotypes. Higher stiffness in high-risk patients suggests tissue stiffness contributes to BOO, independent of prostate size.

title: IP15-07: Relationship Between Prostate MRI Morphology and Lower Urinary Tract Symptoms
parentSessionTitle: IP15: Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia: Epidemiology, Evaluation & Medical Non-surgical Therapy
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Increasing use of prostate MRI (pMRI) for prostate cancer detection offers a unique opportunity to evaluate prostate morphology including prostate volume (PV), intravesical prostatic protrusion (IPP), urethral angle, and bladder neck angle (BNA). Previous works have looked at prostate imaging and lower urinary tract symptoms due to benign prostatic hyperplasia (LUTS/BPH) but this has not been comprehensively evaluated in the MRI era. METHODS: Patients with a pMRI were eligible for inclusion. For this study they needed to have an American Urological Association Symptom Scores (AUASS) obtained within 6 months of their prostate MRI. PV, IPP, urethral angle, and BNA were measured by a single trained reviewer on pMRIs performed from 2015–2025. Multiple linear regression assessed associations between MRI variables and total AUASS and symptom subscores. Significance was defined as p<0.05. RESULTS: We analyzed 324 MRIs from 138 men. AUASS were taken an average of 29 days from pMRI (SD 74, range 180 days before to 177 days after). Mean AUASS was 9.8 ± 6.5 (Median 9, IQR 4.8-14, range 0-31) and mean PV was 69.3 ± 37.2 cc. Median IPP was 11.5 mm (IQR 8.4-16.4). IPP length was independently associated with higher AUASS (p<0.001; R2 ≈ 8.9%), while PV, urethral angle, and BNA were not independently associated with LUTS (p>0.05).When looking at LUTS subscores, IPP length also correlated with urgency (p=0.003), frequency (p=0.015), and weak stream (p=0.001). BNA was associated with frequency (p<0.001). No other MRI features predicted LUTS subscores. CONCLUSIONS: While PV, urethral angle, and BNA were not predictive of symptoms, IPP length demonstrated the strongest independent association with LUTS/BPH severity, particularly urgency, frequency, and weak stream. These findings reinforce IPP as a clinically relevant marker for LUTS burden and warrant routine reporting in men undergoing prostate MRI.

title: IP15-08: The microscopic structural changes of prostate reflected by the apparent diffusion coefficient value affect lower urinary tract function
parentSessionTitle: IP15: Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia: Epidemiology, Evaluation & Medical Non-surgical Therapy

speakers.organization: Fukushima Medical University Department Of Urology

fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: The prostate volume and morphological features of the prostate are well known to be associated with lower urinary tract symptoms (LUTS) in the male patients. However, whether microscopic structural changes of prostate contribute to LUTS and lower urinary tract dysfunction (LUTD) has not been established. On the other hand, recent attention has focused on the apparent diffusion coefficient (ADC) which is a non-invasive functional MRI technique that can assess changes in diffusion of water molecules due to microscopic structural changes. We considered that the ADC can provide the quantitative information about the microscopic structural changes of the prostate. The aim of this study was to evaluate the effect of microscopic structural changes of prostate on LUTS and LUTD by evaluating the association between ADC values and LUTS and lower urinary tract function. METHODS: Patients who underwent MRI before random transrectal ultrasonography–guided prostate biopsy and had a diagnosis of benign by the biopsy at our hospital between May 2019 and January 2022 were included in this study. Before the biopsy, uroflowmetry parameter, bladder voiding efficiency (BVE); (voided volume/total bladder capacity) × 100, International Prostate Symptom Score (IPSS) and overactive bladder symptom score (OABSS) were evaluated. The voiding and storage IPSS sub-score (IPSS-V and IPSS-S, respectively) were recorded separately. We measured mean ADC value at the base of the prostate by MRI. The relationship between the mean ADC value and the parameters evaluated before the biopsy was analyzed. All values were expressed as mean ± standard deviation. A linear regression analysis was used for continuous variables. P-values of <0.05 were considered to be statistically significant. RESULTS: A total of 111 patients (68.9 ± 6.3 years) entered the study. The mean ADC value at the base of prostate was 1,468 ± 190 mm2/sec. The mean ADC value was significantly positively correlated with IPSS-S (C. C=0.22, P=0.03) and OABSS (C. C=0.25, P=0.02). The mean ADC value was significantly negatively associated with BVE (C. C=-0.22, P=0.04). The IPSS-V, maximum flow rate and bladder capacity were not significantly associated with the mean ADC value. CONCLUSIONS: We demonstrated that high ADC value at the base of prostate caused storage symptoms and decreased the BVE. The microscopic structural changes of prostate reflected by high ADC value may affect lower urinary tract function through the different mechanism from the prostate volume and morphological features of prostate. The evaluating ADC value of prostate may provide individualized treatment options for patients.

title: IP15-09: PSA Kinetics Following Benign Prostate Biopsy: Temporal Patterns and Clinical Implications
parentSessionTitle: IP15: Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia: Epidemiology, Evaluation & Medical Non-surgical Therapy
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Transient elevations in prostate specific antigen (PSA) levels occur following prostate procedures such as prostate needle biopsy (PNB). After PNB, normalization of PSA back to baseline could be a function of prostatic inflammation, natural PSA progression, and PSA half-life kinetics. Understanding such timing has important implications for subsequent laboratory testing. Here, we evaluate the timeline of PSA normalization following PNB in men with benign prostate biopsy to guide best practice of retesting PSA following the procedure. METHODS: A retrospective cohort review of TriNetX research database using ICD10, LOINC, CPT codes from 2005-2025 was conducted. Males with a PSA value within 6 months before and 6 months following PNB were evaluated. Exclusion criteria included multiple PNB, lifetime diagnosis of prostate cancer (PCa) or lifetime treatment of PCa including radiation, surgical, androgen deprivation, or ablative therapy. Primary endpoint was return to baseline PSA following PNB, defined as PSA less than or equal to pre-PNB PSA. RESULTS: Of 751 patients who met criteria, 629 patients (83.8%) returned to pre-PNB baseline PSA in follow up. Median time to normalization was 161 days (95% CI 155-168). 61.4% of patients returned to pre-PNB baseline by 180 days and 74.2% by 1 year. Patients who normalized had less frequent PSA checks (mean 1.42 vs. 2.91, p<0.001) and higher pre-PNB PSA (6.5 vs. 5.38, p<0.001) but were not significantly different in age at biopsy, race, ethnicity, geographic region, 5-alpha reductase inhibitor therapy, or diagnosis of BPH. Higher baseline PSA showed faster normalization than lower PSA (HR 1.46, 95% CI 1.29–1.66). Of the patients without PSA resolution by 1 year, 37% ultimately normalized by end of recorded follow up. CONCLUSIONS: PSA trend demonstrates transient elevation immediately after PNB with a median normalization time of almost 6 months. A majority (74.2%) of patients return to baseline within 1 year following PNB. We recommend that PSA should not be rechecked before 3 months after PNB to maximize chance of clinical resolution of PSA and minimize potential for patient anxiety and frequent retesting.

title: IP15-10: Comprehensive identification of factors associated with worsening male lower urinary tract symptoms via meta-16S analysis using a large human gut microbiota database
parentSessionTitle: IP15: Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia: Epidemiology, Evaluation & Medical Non-surgical Therapy

speakers.organization: Fukushima Medical University School of Medicine

fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: The factors underlying the progression of male lower urinary tract symptoms (LUTS) remain unclear. Recent research has highlighted the role of various microbiomes, including those in the gut, urine, and oral cavity, in contributing to different diseases. Therefore, we sought to identify gut taxa associated with LUTS severity and prostate volume (Pvol), with emphasis on a malignancy-negative subcohort, and to explore lifestyle correlates. METHODS: Rectal swabs from 723 Japanese men undergoing prostate biopsy were profiled by 16S rRNA gene amplicon sequencing. Associations between genera and LUTS parameters-International Prostate Symptom Score (IPSS), Overactive Bladder Symptom Score (OABSS), and Pvol-were evaluated using Spearman’s correlation and nonparametric tests. Strong associations were highlighted using predefined thresholds (\|ρ\| ≥ 0.60, R2 ≥ 0.30, ≥5 non-zero samples). The association between lifestyle factors and identified genera were assessed via standardized questionnaires, and results were visualized with volcano plots. RESULTS: In the overall cohort, several genera were significantly correlated with LUTS parameters and Pvol. In the cancer-negative subcohort (n=262), Anaerofilum showed the strongest positive correlation with IPSS, while Lachnospiraceae showed negative correlations, suggesting a protective role. Bergeyella abundance was positively correlated with OABSS. For Pvol, Lachnospiraceae UCG-002, Eubacterium xylanophilum group, Asteroleplasma, and vadinBBE97 exhibited strong positive associations. Lifestyle analyses indicated that Anaerofilum abundance was positively associated with wine intake, overall alcohol consumption, fruit juices (melon/orange), and smoking. Bergeyella abundance was associated with recent cardiac infarction, urinary stone disease within one year, longer time spent fast walking, and birthplace variables (all FDR < 0.05). Lachnospiraceae showed no significant lifestyle associations after correction. CONCLUSIONS: This large-scale study identified specific gut microbial taxa associated with LUTS severity and Pvol in Japanese men, with consistent findings in a malignancy-negative subcohort. In addition, lifestyle factors might affect several specific taxa, which have the possibility to lead the protective strategy for male LUTS.

title: IP15-11: Tissue-Level Evidence of Microplastics in Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia
parentSessionTitle: IP15: Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia: Epidemiology, Evaluation & Medical Non-surgical Therapy
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Microplastics, defined as plastic particles smaller than 5 mm, have emerged as pervasive environmental contaminants. Recent evidence suggests their accumulation in urogenital tissues, raising concerns about potential clinical effects. Benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH), one of the most common urologic disorders, has not been extensively investigated in relation to microplastic exposure within the United States. The study aimed to characterize the chemical composition and spatial distribution of microplastics in BPH tissue samples obtained from a de-identified U. S.-based biorepository. METHODS: Prostate tissues from eight patients were analyzed using non-plastic equipment to prevent cross-contamination. Samples were digested following published protocol for corpus cavernosal tissue, incubating 5 ml of a solution (50 g KOH, 160 ml 13% NaOCl, 1 ml 10% Tween-20, 340 ml Milli-Q water) for 24 hours. Digested material was filtered through 0.8 µm gold-coated membrane filters to isolate microplastics. Particle composition was analyzed by Raman spectroscopy and morphology visualized by scanning electron microscopy. A reagent-only blank was included to control contamination. RESULTS: A total of 21 microplastic particles were identified in samples from 5 of 8 patients. Polystyrene was the predominant polymer, comprising 19 particles (90.5%), followed by single particles of polyacrylonitrile (4.8%) and polyvinyl chloride (4.8%). No contamination was detected in the reagent-only blanks. CONCLUSIONS: This pilot study provides the first U. S.-based evidence of microplastics in BPH tissue, identifying particle types not previously reported. These findings underscore the need for larger investigations to elucidate the sources and potential clinical implications of microplastic exposure.

title: IP15-12: Spatial transcriptomic reveals stromal heterogeneity and SRD5A2-independent metabolic niches underlying 5ARI resistance in BPH
parentSessionTitle: IP15: Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia: Epidemiology, Evaluation & Medical Non-surgical Therapy

speakers.jobTitle: Chief of Urologic Surgery / Beth Israel Deaconess Med Center
speakers.organization: Janet & William Dewolf Professor of Urology

fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: SRD5A2 is the therapeutic target of 5α-reductase inhibitors (5ARIs) widely used for benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH). However, its expression exhibits substantial inter-individual heterogeneity, with approximately 30% of patients showing low or absent SRD5A2 expression in prostatic tissues. This variability likely contributes to the heterogeneous clinical response to 5ARI therapy. Elucidating the molecular drivers of SRD5A2-deficient BPH is essential to understanding 5ARI treatment failure and identifying novel therapeutic targets. METHODS: Using tissue microarray technology, we performed Xenium spatial transcriptomic profiling on 142 prostatic tissue regions from 63 patients with benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH), generating spatial transcriptomic profiles across prostatic areas exhibiting variable SRD5A2 expression levels. RESULTS: We observed pronounced heterogeneity in SRD5A2 expression not only among patients but also across distinct regions within the same prostate. This intra-patient heterogeneity was more pronounced in men over 60 years (P=0.052). Spatial transcriptomic analysis identified two SRD5A2high expression fibroblast subtypes (Fib1 and Fib2) and one SRD5A2low subtype (Fib3) within the prostatic stroma. These fibroblasts, together with other stromal components, formed distinct spatially organized niches with divergent functional characteristics in SRD5A2-high and SRD5A2-low prostatic regions. The Fib1/2-dominant niches were SRD5A2-dependent, characterized by activation of androgen, WNT, and mTOR signaling pathways, and constituted the predominant stromal spatial architecture in SRD5A2-high areas. In contrast, Fib3-dominant niches were SRD5A2-independent, enriched for metabolic and EGFR–KRAS signaling pathways, and maintained these features regardless of SRD5A2 levels, constituting the dominant stromal spatial configuration in SRD5A2-low regions. Notably, patients with a BMI > 28 exhibited a trend toward a higher proportion of Fib3-dominant niches (P=0.09), supporting their metabolically driven nature. CONCLUSIONS: SRD5A2-high and SRD5A2-low regions exhibited distinct stromal composition and spatial organization. The SRD5A2-independent, metabolically driven Fib3-dominant niches may underlie 5ARI resistance and highlight metabolic and EGFR–KRAS pathways as potential therapeutic targets.

title: IP15-13: MMP7-Triggered Mitophagy via Regulating Parkin-Mediated Ubiquitination of VDAC1 Conferred Anoikis Resistance in the Epithelium of Hyperplastic Prostate
parentSessionTitle: IP15: Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia: Epidemiology, Evaluation & Medical Non-surgical Therapy

speakers.organization: Ningbo Medical Center Lihuili Hospital, Ningbo, China

fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH), prevalently disturbing aging men, is characterized by aberrant cell death of prostate cells. Anoikis, a particular branch of apoptosis, is triggered when cells are detached from the extracellular matrix, whereas those with anoikis resistance (AR) are susceptible to various pathological conditions including abnormal cell death and proliferation. However, whether AR plays a role in BPH is still scarcely understood. METHODS: Bulk RNA-sequencing (RNA-seq) data and single cell RNA‑seq data of prostate tissues from normal individuals and BPH patients were analyzed. Immunoprecipitation-mass spectrum (IP-MS) analysis was performed to identify the proteins interacted with Matrix metalloproteinase 7 (MMP7). In vitro approaches including diverse staining strategies, transmission electron microscopy, flow cytometry, mitochondrial cell stress assay, immunoblotting, co-IP and ChIP analysis together with in vivo experiments on testosterone propionate-induced BPH (TP-BPH) rats were employed to ascertain the underlying functional mechanisms. RESULTS: In this study, elevated AR level was observed in BPH tissues compared to normal prostates. Furthermore, MMP7 was identified as a critical regulator of AR in hyperplastic prostatic epithelium. Under anoikis-inducing conditions, MMP7 promoted mitophagy via the PINK1-Parkin pathway, alleviated mitochondrial stress damage, and enhances AR in BPH-1 cells. Mechanistically, MMP7 interacted with VDAC1 and bond specifically at lysine residues K109 and K110, thereby inhibiting VDAC1 oligomerization and increasing the accumulation of VDAC1 monomers, which served as additional binding sites for Parkin-mediated polyubiquitination. Moreover, clinical data revealed that MMP7 expression levels correlated significantly with International Prostate Symptom Score (IPSS) and nocturia frequency. Additionally, in vivo experiments demonstrated that inhibition of MMP7 suppressed mitophagy and markedly attenuated prostatic epithelial hyperplasia in BPH model rats. CONCLUSIONS: Collectively, our findings elucidated the functional significance of the MMP7-VDAC1 axis in BPH pathogenesis and highlighted its potential as a therapeutic target for the management of BPH.

title: IP15-14: Distinct SRD5A2-reduced Subtypes of Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia Exhibit p-AMPK/Rab9a/PLIN3-Mediated Lipophagic Compensation for Androgen Signaling Defects
parentSessionTitle: IP15: Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia: Epidemiology, Evaluation & Medical Non-surgical Therapy
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: 5-α-reductase inhibitors (5-ARIs) are among the standard pharmacologic therapies for benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH). However, patients with BPH subtypes characterized by reduced 5-α-reductase 2 (SRD5A2) expression often show poor responsiveness to 5-ARIs, and the underlying mechanisms remain unclear. This study aimed to elucidate the alterations in lipid droplet metabolism in SRD5A2-reduced BPH and identify key molecular events that may serve as potential therapeutic targets. METHODS: Testosterone and dihydrotestosterone (DHT) levels in BPH tissues were determined using high-performance liquid chromatography. SRD5A2, perilipin-3 (PLIN3), Rab9a, AMPK, phosphorylated AMPK (p-AMPK), and autophagy-related markers were assessed by immunohistochemistry (IHC), RT-qPCR, and Western blotting. Lipid droplets (LDs) distribution and morphology in BPH tissues and prostatic epithelial cells were evaluated by Oil Red O (ORO) staining and microscopy. Immunofluorescence staining (IF) was performed to examine the distribution of perilipin on LDs. Cell proliferation following DHT, oleic acid (OA), or chloroquine treatment was analyzed using the CCK-8 assay. RESULTS: IHC analysis of prostate tissues from 72 BPH patients revealed decreased (33%, 24/72) or nearly absent (14%, 10/72) SRD5A2 expression (experiment group) in a subset of cases. DHT were markedly reduced in experiment group. In these tissues, LDs were smaller but more numerous, indicating enhanced lipid turnover. Compared with control group, experiment group exhibited increased LC3 expression, decreased p62 levels, and elevated PLIN3 and AMPK phosphorylation. In vitro, androgen deprivation induced autophagy and AMPK phosphorylation in prostatic epithelial cells, while autophagy inhibition impaired LDs utilization and slowed or arrested cell proliferation. PLIN3 is the predominant perilipin responsible for regulating LDs metabolism in prostatic epithelial cells. PLIN3 expression was inversely correlated with DHT levels and shown to interact with Rab9a. CONCLUSIONS: Distinct BPH subtypes exist according to SRD5A2 expression. In SRD5A2-reduced BPH, activation of the p-AMPK/Rab9a/PLIN3 axis triggers lipophagy, compensating for impaired androgen receptor signaling to sustain epithelial cell proliferation and drive hyperplastic progression.

title: IP15-15: Revisit embryonic reawakening in BPH through Hayflick analysis of prostatic stromal cells
parentSessionTitle: IP15: Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia: Epidemiology, Evaluation & Medical Non-surgical Therapy

speakers.organization: Pittsburgh School of Medicine Urology Department

fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH) is a non-cancerous proliferation of epithelial and stromal cells primarily within the prostate’s transitional zone. While aging, androgens, and inflammation are recognized contributors, the potential role of embryonic reawakening and cellular senescence in BPH pathogenesis remains to be clarified. The increased stromal-to-epithelial ratio observed in BPH underscores the pivotal involvement of stromal cells in disease progression. Whether this imbalance arises from reactivation of developmental stromal–epithelial signaling (“embryonic reawakening”) or from the paracrine influence of senescent cells remains uncertain. We revisited the Hayflick principle by culturing patient-derived primary stromal cells from BPH and normal adjacent prostate (NAP) tissues to assess whether BPH stromal cells exhibit features of extended proliferative capacity, consistent with embryonic characteristics, or reduced proliferative capacity, reflecting a senescence phenotype. METHODS: Four cancer-free matched pairs of BPH and normal adjacent prostate (NAP) tissues were obtained from patients with low-volume prostate cancer and BPH under IRB approval. Minced tissues were digested with Dispase II for 2 h at 37 °C on a rocker, centrifuged, and resuspended in PDE medium. Cells were cultured in T75 flasks at 37 °C, 5% CO2 for 5 days, then supplemented with fresh medium to reach confluence. Then, the stromal cells were serially passaged in T25 Flasks using trypsin–EDTA until the Hayflick limit, with cell counts recorded throughout the experiment. For the first patient, only two repeat NAP and one BPH flasks were available, whereas for the remaining three patients, NAP and BPH triplicate flasks were established once sufficient cell numbers were obtained. Cell morphology and proliferation were monitored microscopically, and immunofluorescent staining was used to verify the stromal cell population, and -galactosidase staining was used to reconfirm senescence in flasks. RESULTS: BPH stromal cells reached the Hayflick limit much sooner than the NAP counterparts in three of the four paired samples. In the last paired sample, the BPH and NAP stromal cells reached the Hayflick limit after similar numbers of doublings. CONCLUSIONS: The lower proliferative capacity of BPH-derived stromal cells compared to their NAP counterparts challenges the notion that BPH stromal cells regain embryonic proliferative features. Our findings warrant further investigation into role of stromal cells senescence in BPH.

title: IP15-16: Prostate-Specific Plasma Proteomic Aging Clocks for Disease Prediction
parentSessionTitle: IP15: Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia: Epidemiology, Evaluation & Medical Non-surgical Therapy
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Aging proceeds heterogeneously across organs, and organ-specific plasma proteomic clocks have shown promise for predicting tissue-relevant disease risk. The prostate, a leading source of age-related morbidity in men, has not been characterized with this approach. METHODS: Using plasma proteomes from 20,346 male participants in the UK Biobank, we identified prostate-enriched proteins and trained two elastic-net–based prostate aging models: Model 1 calibrated to chronological age and Model 2 trained using mortality via Cox regression. We compared model performance for predicting prostate cancer, benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH), and all-cause mortality against a conventional global proteomic age and other organ-specific proteomic ages. We also examined associations between prostate age acceleration and modifiable environmental factors using multivariable linear regression. RESULTS: We report a prostate-specific plasma proteomic clock. Model 1 (chronological-age trained) outperformed Model 2 in discriminating prostate disease endpoints. The prostate-specific proteomic age exceeded a global proteomic age and other organ-specific ages in predicting prostate-related conditions. Prostate age acceleration correlated with several modifiable exposures. CONCLUSIONS: A prostate-focused plasma proteomic clock captures organ-relevant biological aging and improves prediction of prostate disease risk beyond existing proteomic aging measures. External validation and mechanistic studies are warranted.

title: IP15-17: Stem-like Prostate Remodeling in Obesity Mediates Resistance to 5a-Reductase Inhibition Therapy in BPH
parentSessionTitle: IP15: Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia: Epidemiology, Evaluation & Medical Non-surgical Therapy

speakers.jobTitle: Chief of Urologic Surgery / Beth Israel Deaconess Med Center
speakers.organization: Janet & William Dewolf Professor of Urology

fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Obesity and metabolic syndrome are significant risk factors for the development and progression of BPH. Although 5α-reductase inhibitors (5ARIs) are widely used to treat BPH, their effectiveness varies significantly, particularly in obese patients. The mechanisms by which obesity promotes prostate growth and modulates therapeutic responses remain poorly understood. METHODS: Prostate tissues from Srd5a2‑null and control mice fed regular‑fat or high‑fat diet (HFD) for 3 months underwent scRNA‑seq. Clinical human validation integrated Xenium spatial transcriptomics from institutional transurethral resection prostate specimens and bulk transcriptomics from the Medical Therapy of Prostatic Symptoms (MTOPS) trial, integrated with MTOPS longitudinal clinical data. RESULTS: In mice, HFD increased prostate weight and induced SRD5A2-independent epithelial remodeling with expansion of proximal urethral luminal epithelial cells. ScRNA-seq showed enrichment of proximal stem-like populations, reduced androgen signaling, and activation of WNT and NOTCH pathways via heightened stromal-epithelial crosstalk. Clinically, BMI gain, regardless of 5ARI use, correlated with transition zone growth, stronger activity of stem-cell signatures, and reduced SRD5A2, androgen signaling. Spatial profiling indicated that BMI gain expands stem-like epithelial populations and a NOTCH‑enriched periepithelial stromal niche surrounding epithelial compartments, supporting stemness. MTOPS patients with substantial BMI gain were less responsive to 5ARI, whereas weight control plus 5ARI therapy synergistically improved outcomes. CONCLUSIONS: BMI gain promotes proximal prostate enlargement through an SRD5A2-independent stem-like cell mediated pathway that blunts 5ARI efficacy. Combining pharmacotherapy with weight control yields superior efficacy and supports individualized management of BPH.

title: IP15-18: RETHINKING LONG-TERM MONITORING OF BENIGN PROSTATIC HYPERPLASIA: DOES SERIAL UROFLOWMETRY PREDICT CLINICAL PROGRESSION?
parentSessionTitle: IP15: Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia: Epidemiology, Evaluation & Medical Non-surgical Therapy
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Current guidelines recommend medical therapy for initial management of bothersome lower urinary tract symptoms (LUTS) due to benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH). Many patients elect to remain on medical therapy for years, with unknown long-term effects on bladder function. In this study, we utilize serial uroflowmetry to assess long-term changes in voiding parameters and the risk of progression to acute urinary retention (AUR) or outlet surgery in men with medically managed LUTS due to BPH. METHODS: We conducted a retrospective review of patients who presented to our institution from 2008-2015 with a diagnosis of BPH (ICD 10 code N40.1). Patients were included if they had at least three uroflowmetry studies performed, each at least one year apart. Uroflowmetry parameters evaluated included Qmax, post void residual (PVR), and voiding efficiency \[voided volume/(voided volume + PVR)\]. Patients with a history of prostate surgery, pelvic radiation, urethral stricture disease, and neurogenic bladder were excluded. Univariable and mixed effects logistic regression was utilized to determine the association between changes in uroflowmetry parameters, type of medical therapy, international prostate symptom score (IPSS), prostate size, PSA, patient comorbidities, and progression to AUR or outlet procedure. RESULTS: A total of 142 patients were included in the analysis. Median age at first uroflowmetry was 69.0 years (IQR: 64.0, 74.0) and median international prostate symptom score (IPSS) was 13 (IQR 9-19). At initial uroflowmetry, 55 men (38.7%) were on no medications and 43 men (30.3%) were on alpha blockers alone. There was no significant change in Qmax, voiding efficiency (VE), or post-void residual (PVR) over the seven-year study period. The use of alpha-blockers was associated with an increase in PVR (p=0.04). Changes in IPSS and uroflowmetry parameters were weakly correlated over time (all R values <0.3). A total of 21.8% of patients developed AUR and 25.4% underwent outlet surgery. Increasing PVR was associated with an increased risk of outlet surgery (p=0.04). Median time from first uroflowmetry to outlet surgery was 8.7 years (IQR 6.9-12.2). Changes PVR, Qmax, and VE were not predictive of AUR. CONCLUSIONS: Serial uroflowmetry parameters did not significantly change over time in men with medically managed BPH and were poorly associated with subjective measures of voiding. None of the uroflowmetry parameters evaluated were associated with progression to acute urinary retention and only increases in PVR were associated with progression to outlet surgery.

title: IP15-19: Association Between Glucagon-Like Peptide-1 Agonist Use and Escalation to Surgical Treatment for Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia: A Nationwide Claims Database Study
parentSessionTitle: IP15: Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia: Epidemiology, Evaluation & Medical Non-surgical Therapy

speakers.organization: Johns Hopkins University School of Medicine

fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH) is typically medically managed for many patients with alpha-blockers and/or 5-alpha reductase inhibitors (5-ARIs) prior to surgical intervention. Previous research has suggested reduced prostate cancer risk with Glucagon-Like Peptide-1 (GLP-1) agonist use, but little is known about their association with BPH and its progression. This study investigates the impact of GLP-1 agonist use on the incidence of BPH-related surgery. METHODS: Using the TriNetX national claims database, we identified BPH patients aged 40-75 on alpha-blockers alone, 5-ARIs alone, or combination therapy. Within each cohort, patients actively using GLP-1 agonists were compared to a control group with no GLP-1 exposure. The primary outcome was BPH surgery at 1, 3, and 5 years post-GLP-1 initiation. Patients with prior prostatectomy or BPH surgery were excluded. Propensity score matching (PSM) was utilized on demographics, type II diabetes mellitus, hypertensive disorders, hyperlipidemia, obesity, inflammatory diseases of the prostate, personal and family history of prostate neoplasm to address the association between GLP-1 use and progression to BPH surgery.
