RESULTS: Following PSM, the study arms included 17,232 (alpha-blocker), 807 (5-ARI), and 6,257 (combination therapy) patients per matched group (i. e., GLP-1 users and non-users), respectively. For patients with or without GLP-1, no statistically significant difference in rates of BPH surgery was observed in the alpha-blocker or combination therapy arms at any time point ( Table 1). However, the 5-ARI cohort demonstrated a significant reduction in BPH surgery risk at 3, and 5 years after initiating GLP-1 agonist use (p<0.05). CONCLUSIONS: The use of GLP-1 agonists is associated with a reduced risk of surgical intervention for BPH in patients treated with 5-ARIs alone, suggesting that GLP-1 agonists may augment the therapeutic effects of 5-ARIs on the prostate in patients with BPH or patients on 5-ARI and GLP-1 seek surgery at decreased rates. Further laboratory research should focus on GLP-1 receptor expression in the non-malignant prostate tissue and its potential therapeutic value. | | | --- | | |

title: IP15-20: Efficacy and safety of vibegron in men =75 years of age with symptoms of overactive bladder on pharmacotherapy for benign prostatic hyperplasia: a subgroup analysis of the COURAGE trial
parentSessionTitle: IP15: Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia: Epidemiology, Evaluation & Medical Non-surgical Therapy
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Vibegron is a selective β3-adrenergic receptor agonist approved by the US Food and Drug Administration for the treatment of overactive bladder (OAB) symptoms in adults and adult males on pharmacological therapy for benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH). We report efficacy and safety of vibegron from the COURAGE trial in the subgroup of men ≥75 y with persistent OAB symptoms on pharmacotherapy for BPH. METHODS: COURAGE (NCT03902080) was a phase 3, multicenter, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial that evaluated efficacy and safety of once-daily vibegron 75 mg vs placebo. Men ≥45 y with OAB and BPH receiving a stable dose of α-blocker ± 5α-reductase inhibitors were randomized 1:1 to vibegron or placebo for 24 weeks. This subanalysis assessed change from baseline in the mean number of daily micturitions, urgency episodes, and nightly nocturia episodes and adverse events (AEs) in patients ≥75 y and <75 y. RESULTS: Of the 1080 participants included in the COURAGE trial efficacy analyses, 192 were ≥75 y (92 received vibegron, 100 received placebo). Demographics and baseline clinical characteristics were generally similar between ≥75 y and <75 y subgroups; however, respectively, 96.4% and 85.7% were White, 75.0% and 63.7% had preexisting hypertension, 37.5% and 26% had urinary incontinence, and patients ≥75 y were more likely to have had prior therapies. Clinically significant reductions from baseline at week 12 and 24 were observed in average daily number of micturitions, urgency episodes, and nocturia episodes with vibegron vs placebo (Figure). These results were comparable to outcomes in men <75 y. For men ≥75 y, 52.1% of patients receiving vibegron had ≥1 treatment-emergent AE (TEAE), compared with 43.5% for men <75. The most common TEAEs in men ≥75 y receiving vibegron were hypertension (5.2%), hematuria (4.2%), and upper respiratory tract infection (4.2%). For men <75 y, these TEAEs were reported in 9.8%, 1.5%, and 1.3% of patients receiving vibegron, respectively. TEAEs were similar to placebo in both subgroups. CONCLUSIONS: Vibegron was associated with substantial improvements in clinical efficacy outcomes vs placebo and was safe and well tolerated in men ≥75 y with persistent OAB symptoms on pharmacotherapy for BPH, comparable to men <75 y.

title: IP15-21: The Association of Finasteride for Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia with Development of Male Breast Cancer in the United States: A Retrospective Cohort Study of TriNetX Database
parentSessionTitle: IP15: Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia: Epidemiology, Evaluation & Medical Non-surgical Therapy
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: 5-α reductase inhibitors (5AI: finasteride, dutasteride) inhibit the conversion of testosterone to dihydrotestosterone, reducing the overall androgenic stimulus to growth of the prostate and is used as medical therapy for benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH). 5AI class is associated with gynecomastia and erectile dysfunction(ED) as adverse events but it’s association with breast cancer in males (MBC) has been controversial. To address this, we conducted a retrospective cohort study comparing the association of 5AI for BPH with MBC, gynecomastia and ED in the United States (US). METHODS: We queried the U. S. collaborative network of TriNetX database. We included patients ≥ 18 years of age diagnosed with BPH. The exposure of interest was 5AI for BPH. We propensity score matched (PSM) for demographic features, comorbidities and breast cancer risk factors. Balance between the 5AI cohort and non-5AI cohort was assessed by standardized mean difference (SMD) <0.1. Outcomes of interest included diagnosis of MBC at 1-yesr, 2 years and beyond, gynecomastia and ED defined using ICD-10-CM diagnostic codes and procedural codes (ICD-10-PCS, CPT). Further to assess the differential risk associated with either finasteride or dutasteride, we conducted subgroup analysis for either medication. Outcomes were reported as risk ratio (RR) and 95% confidence intervals (CI). All statistical analysis were done using software built within TriNetX. RESULTS: 5-AI cohort and non-5AI cohort included: 637,804 and 2,426,442 patients, respectively before PSM and 273,403 patients each after PSM. Both cohorts were well balanced after PSM (SMD<0.1). Follow up of median 2.69 years and interquartile range (IQR) of 5.05 years in the 5AI cohort versus median 2.56 years (IQR: 4.98 years) in the non-5AI cohort. Patients in the 5AI cohort were not associated with a statistically significant increased risk of MBC (RR 1.07; 95%CI: 0.86-1.32). There was an increased risk of gynecomastia (RR 1.36, 95%CI: 1.28-1.44) and ED (RR 1.07, 95%CI: 1.05-1.09) associated with the use of 5AI. ( Table-1) CONCLUSIONS: In this multi-institutional retrospective cohort study, we did not find an increased risk of MBC associated with the use of 5AI for BPH. | | | --- | | |

title: IP15-22: Lenalidomide: an antifibrotic reduces outpatient visits related to Lower Urinary Tract Symptoms/Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia
parentSessionTitle: IP15: Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia: Epidemiology, Evaluation & Medical Non-surgical Therapy

speakers.jobTitle: Assistant Professor at Ohio State University

fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Medical treatment of lower urinary tract symptoms secondary to BPH (LUTS/BPH) primarily consists of alpha blocker therapy, 5-alpha reductase inhibitors, or combination therapy. Still, over 20% of men have clinical progression of LUTS/BPH despite being on maximum medical treatment. Animal and human pathologic studies supports the hypothesis that prostate fibrosis contributes to LUTS and is an untargeted mechanism. Lenalidomide, a thalidomide analogue is an anti-fibrotic and FDA-approved for the treatment of multiple myeloma (MM). Thus, our objective was to determine whether lenalidomide reduces the risk of LUTS/BPH-related outpatient visits compared to non-antifibrotic therapy. METHODS: We analyzed the Merative Marketscan database between 2016-2023 for men who were newly diagnosed with MM, had ≥ 6 months of continuous enrollment prior to first MM diagnosis, and a prescription for lenalidomide (experimental group) or cyclophosphamide (non-antifibrotic MM treatment, control group) within 30 days of MM diagnosis. Men with any oncologic diagnosis other than MM were excluded. Inverse probability weighting was applied to balance baseline characteristics (age, U. S. region, rurality, Medicare Advantage plan, Charlson index, baseline inpatient and ED visits, and Index year) between experimental and control groups, reducing potential confounding. Our primary outcome was time to first BPH-related outpatient visit up to 5 years. We performed Kaplan-Meier probability analyses and Cox regression to adjust for residual confounding. RESULTS: A total of 1,834 patients met the study criteria (1,665 experimental and 169 controls). On average patients were 64 years old, 43% resided in the U. S. South, and 36% had a Medicare Advantage plan. The hazard ratio for a LUTS/BPH-related outpatient visit for men treated with lenalidomide was 0.44 (95% CI: 0.40-0.48, p<.0001) compared to the control group ( (https://www.auajournals.org/doi/abs/10.1097/01.JU.0001191356.52697.6d.22#F1)). CONCLUSIONS: Men treated with lenalidomide had a significantly reduced risk of LUTS/BPH-related outpatient visits compared to those treated with cyclophosphamide. These results support exploring antifibrotics as a novel treatment for LUTS/BPH. Randomized trials are needed to explore these findings in a non-MM population.

title: IP15-23: Does Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia Affect the Risk of Repeat TURBT?
parentSessionTitle: IP15: Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia: Epidemiology, Evaluation & Medical Non-surgical Therapy

speakers.organization: University of Vermont Larner College of Medicine

fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Non-muscle invasive bladder cancer (NMIBC) is one of the most challenging urological cancers to treat. These patients need to be closely followed with periodic cystoscopy and imaging due to the highly recurrent nature of this disease. Independently, benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH) is a highly prevalent condition in aging men. Bladder outlet obstruction is associated with urinary stasis, poor bladder emptying, and increased chronic inflammation and mucosal irritation, all of which are potential contributors to carcinogenesis. This investigation aims to determine whether the diagnosis of BPH has an appreciable effect on the risk of requiring a repeat transurethral bladder tumor resection (TURBT). METHODS: We conducted a retrospective study using the TriNetX Diamond database. The cohorts included men with an initial diagnosis of NMIBC who underwent TURBT. The cohort was then separated into two groups: those diagnosed with BPH before undergoing their TURBT and those who were not. For men with BPH, we excluded patients who underwent BPH surgeries. The risk of requiring a repeat TURBT was determined for both groups to determine the risk difference between the groups. An absolute risk reduction between the cohorts was calculated with TriNetX’s statistical analysis. Statistical significance was defined as p<0.05. RESULTS: 7927 men with a mean age of 67.8 did not have BPH at the time of TURBT, and 7869 men with a mean age of 72.9 had BPH at the time of TURBT. The distribution of T1, Ta, and Tis for patients without BPH was 55.6%, 33.3%, and 11.1%, and for those with BPH was 50.0%, 37.5%, and 12.5%, respectively. For patients without BPH, there was a 35.7% risk for requiring a repeat TURBT within 1 year, 43.5% within 5 years. For patients with BPH, the risk of requiring a repeat TURBT was found to be 40.2% and 51.2% within 1 and 5 years, respectively. The risk difference between the cohorts for repeat TURBT within 1 and 5 years are -4.51% (95% CI: -3.00 - -6.02%) and -7.74% (95% CI: -6.12 \- -9.30%), respectively, showing a lower risk for the group without the BPH co-diagnosis (p<0.0001). CONCLUSIONS: This preliminary, large sample population investigation demonstrates that there may be a relationship between BPH that is not surgically treated and repeat TURBT given that we saw up to a 7.74% risk increase of a repeat TURBT in patients who had BPH at the time of their index TURBT. These findings raise interesting questions about the importance of treating BPH in patients with NMIBC and require further prospective validation.

title: IP15-24: INCIDENCE AND PREDICTORS OF THE COMPLICATIONS OF CATHETER-DEPENDENT BENIGN PROSTATIC HYPERPLASIA WAIT-TIMES: A MULTI-CENTRE RETROSPECTIVE STUDY
parentSessionTitle: IP15: Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia: Epidemiology, Evaluation & Medical Non-surgical Therapy
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Surgical wait times are a key quality indicator in healthcare. Recent literature has focused on reducing delays for oncological surgeries, while non-oncological surgeries have received little to no attention. Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia (BPH) affects nearly 80% of men by their eighties, often causing lower urinary tract symptoms (LUTS) and urinary retention, leading to reduced quality of life and financial burden. Treatment options for moderate-to-severe LUTS-BPH range from medical therapy to minimally invasive and invasive surgeries. This study aims to examine surgical wait times for BPH and identify predictors of complications related to catheter dependence. METHODS: A retrospective review was undertaken to identify catheter dependent BPH patients who underwent surgical treatment in the form of transurethral resection of prostate (TURP), Green Light Laser of prostate (GLLP), simple prostatectomy and Holmium laser enucleation of the prostate (HoLEP) from May 1, 2022 to May 1, 2024 in Western Canada. Collected data included patient characteristics (BMI, ASA classification, pre-operative anti-coagulation use, prior BPH surgery, pre-operative 5-alpha reductase inhibitor use, prostate volume), catheter dependent period until surgery and preoperative complications. RESULTS: Of 494 catheter-dependent patients, 332 (67.2%) underwent TURP, 85 (17.2%) GLLP, 19 (3.8%) simple prostatectomy, and 58 (11.8%) underwent HOLEP. Excluding patients with comorbidities delaying surgery, the mean time from catheter insertion to OR was 109 days (median: 85 days). Preoperative complications occurred in 281 patients (56.9%), including ER visits for UTI (63.3%), recurrent UTIs (19.2%), hematuria (40.2%), epididymitis (2.5%), catheter-related issues (40.2%), and hospital admissions for urosepsis or hematuria (13.9%). Binary regression on a subset of patients with complications identified catheter duration as the only significant predictor (OR=1.013, p<0.001), representing a 1.3% increase in the odds of complications per additional day with catheter. Mean time to complication in this group was 43 days (median: 30 days). CONCLUSIONS: More than half of the patients experienced complications associated with prolonged catheterization. Alarmingly 13.9% of patients required admission for catheter-related complications while waiting for bladder outlet surgery. These findings highlight the significant impact of delayed surgical intervention, emphasizing the need for targeted strategies to reduce wait times and enhance patient care.

title: IP15-25: Total sleep duration and rapid eye movement sleep following surgical intervention for benign prostatic hyperplasia: a comparative analysis using wearable device data
parentSessionTitle: IP15: Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia: Epidemiology, Evaluation & Medical Non-surgical Therapy
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH) is associated with nocturia, which can reduce sleep quality and contribute to fragmented sleep. Specifically, rapid eye movement (REM) sleep is a critical restorative sleep phase linked to cognitive function, mood regulation, and overall health. This study investigates whether surgical management with transurethral resection of the prostate (TURP) or holmium laser enucleation (HoLEP) influences total and REM sleep duration compared with patients experiencing nocturia from BPH on conservative management. METHODS: Data were obtained from the NIH All of Us Research Program Controlled Tier v8 database. Three cohorts were defined using standardized concept IDs: (1) conservative management (CM), (2) TURP, and (3) HoLEP. Fitbit Sleep Daily Summary data were analyzed to quantify nightly total sleep duration and REM sleep duration in minutes, with each sleep record representing one night of sleep. For each cohort, the average total sleep, average REM sleep, and standard deviation were calculate using Python. Group differences were tested using Welch’s t-tests. Statistical comparisons were made between surgical intervention vs. CM for both sleep metrics, and between TURP vs. HoLEP to assess procedure-specific differences. RESULTS: For total sleep duration, a total of 10,005 sleep records were identified for CM and 25,123 for surgical intervention. For total sleep duration, the record-level mean was 322.44 min (CM) and 346.56 min (surgical intervention), with surgical patients sleeping 24 minutes longer (p<0.001). When comparing procedure types, HoLEP patients (349.42 min) slept longer than TURP patients (329.78 min) (p<0.001). Table 1. REM sleep characteristics across treatment groups. Surgical intervention vs CM (p<0.001); TURP vs HoLEP (p<0.001). CONCLUSIONS: Surgical intervention for BPH was associated with significantly longer total sleep duration and REM sleep duration compared to CM, highlighting the positive impact of surgical intervention for patients with BPH. These results highlight the physiological connection between urological intervention and sleep physiology, suggesting that sleep quality is an important factor to consider when making decisions in BPH management. | | | --- | | |

title: IP15-26: Cost-Effectiveness of Surgical Options for Large Gland BPH depends on Patient Priorities: A Comparison of HoLEP, Aquablation, and Simple Prostatectomy
parentSessionTitle: IP15: Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia: Epidemiology, Evaluation & Medical Non-surgical Therapy
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: For patients requiring surgical intervention for BPH with a large gland (>80-150cc), guideline options include HoLEP and simple prostatectomy (SP). Robotic waterjet therapy (RWT) is also being increasingly utilized. These treatments vary in their costs and outcomes, as do individual patient priorities. In this study, we assessed cost effectiveness (CE) for these three BPH treatments for large glands, and the sensitivity to relative weighting of different outcomes. METHODS: Using a microsimulation model, a CEA was performed comparing HoLEP, SP, and RWT. Model probabilities were based on published values, and effectiveness was calculated using post-operative complication severity, sexual function, and urinary symptom scores (IPSS). The model was performed from a U. S. Medicare payer perspective, with quality-adjusted life years (QALYs) and incremental cost-effectiveness ratios (ICERs) used to assess cost-effectiveness at a willingness-to-pay threshold of $100,000/QALY. Univariate and probabilistic sensitivity analyses were performed. RESULTS: Over a patient’s lifetime, HoLEP and SP resulted in nearly identical effectiveness (12.25 vs. 12.26 QALYs), but HoLEP had a significantly lower lifetime BPH cost per patient ($8,361 vs. $19,012) and was therefore CE (SP ICER > $2,000,000). RWT was the least effective (12.19 QALYs) with intermediate cost ($11,969). The model was found to be sensitive to changes in multiple input parameters. Specifically, SP became more CE if the cost decreased significantly, whereas RWT was more CE if the utility value (effectiveness) assigned to post-operative ejaculatory dysfunction increased, the cost of RWT decreased, or the relative post-operative symptom improvement of HoLEP decreased ( Figure 1-2). CONCLUSIONS: At baseline assumptions, HoLEP is the most cost-effective surgical option for patients with a gland size 80-150cc. However, this was dependent upon procedure cost and patient priorities. Such findings highlight the benefit of HoLEP on a systems-level, while emphasizing the importance of surgical selection driven by individual patient priorities.

title: IP15-27: High Patient Adherence to Smartphone-Based Home Uroflowmetry: Real-World Evidence from a Large Commercial Database
parentSessionTitle: IP15: Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia: Epidemiology, Evaluation & Medical Non-surgical Therapy

speakers.jobTitle: Chief of Urology at Plainview and Syosset Hospital

fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Patient adherence to digital health monitoring is often cited as a barrier to adoption in chronic urological care. Smartphone-based home uroflowmetry provides non-invasive, high-frequency monitoring of lower urinary tract symptoms (LUTS) between clinic visits. This study evaluated real-world adherence and engagement patterns in a large voluntary cohort using physician-referred home uroflowmetry. METHODS: This retrospective analysis examined de-identified data from a commercial smartphone-based uroflowmetry service database (proudP, FDA Class II) comprising 3,332 male patients who enrolled between November 2020 and October 2025. Patients were referred by urologists from 33 US urology practices and paid directly for the self-directed monitoring service. Data were extracted from a HIPAA-compliant database; patients consented to research use of de-identified data per service terms. Practices included in this analysis had at least 3 active service users. Patients were predominantly monitored for BPH/LUTS, with additional voiding conditions including urethral stricture. Analysis included total tests, monthly monitoring frequency, and uroflow parameters (Qmax and VT). Correlation between baseline symptom severity and monitoring frequency was investigated. RESULTS: The cohort conducted 209,718 home uroflowmetry tests over the 5-year study period. Patients demonstrated sustained engagement with a median monitoring frequency of 5.0 days per month (mean: 7.5 days). Analysis showed 80.9% of patients tested on 2-15 days monthly, while only 7.6% tested on a single day. Median Q\_max was 14.2 ml/s (mean: 14.8 ml/s, SD: 5.9) and median VT was 29.6 seconds (mean: 37.0 s, SD: 26.3 s). The 25th percentile Qmax of 10.5 ml/s confirmed most patients had flow compromise consistent with mild-to-severe LUTS. Baseline symptom severity (Qmax) showed no significant correlation with monitoring frequency or daily measurement frequency (p>0.05). CONCLUSIONS: This large real-world study demonstrates sustained patient adherence to smartphone-based home uroflowmetry over a 5-year period across diverse urology practices, with consistent monitoring regardless of symptom severity. These findings provide evidence that digital LUTS monitoring can achieve meaningful patient engagement in routine urological practice and may facilitate more frequent assessment between clinic visits.

title: IP16-01: COMPARING URINARY URGENCY PATIENTS WITH AND WITHOUT PAIN — A LURN II STUDY
parentSessionTitle: IP16: Urodynamics/Lower Urinary Tract Dysfunction/Female Pelvic Medicine: Overactive Bladder
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Urinary urgency (the cardinal symptom of OAB) and pain are both subjective noxious sensations. Some OAB patients experience pain in addition to urinary urgency. 54% of adult women with OAB symptoms stated that their urge to urinate was associated with pain, pressure, or discomfort (Reynolds et al 2017). The objective of this study was to phenotype urinary urgency patients with pain, and to compare to urgency patients without pain. METHODS: Adults seeking treatment for bothersome urinary urgency, without or with urgency urinary incontinence, were enrolled in the LURN II Study. A sex-matched control group without urinary symptoms was also enrolled. Urgency was assessed using the LURN SI-29s? subscale. Urologic pain was assessed using the GUPI (genitourinary pain index) pain subscale and LURN SI-29 pain subscale. Widespread pain was defined as pain involving 3 or more body regions on a pain map. Urologic and widespread pain were compared urgency patients and controls. Patients with a diagnosis of IC/BPS were excluded. RESULTS: Urgency patients (n=742) were significantly more likely to report any urologic pain on GUPI (49% vs. 11%, p<0.01) and LURN SI-29 (56% vs. 23%, p<0.01) compared to controls without urgency (n=139). GUPI pain subscale scores were higher among urgency patients compared to controls (mean 4.3 vs. 0.7, p<0.01). LURN SI-29 pain subscale scores were also higher among urgency patients compared to controls (13.3. vs. 2.3, p<0.01). Urgency patients were also more likely to report widespread pain on the pain map than controls (32% vs. 14%, p<0.01). There were significant positive correlations between worsening LURN SI-29 pain scores and OAB-q scores, LURN SI-29 urgency subscale scores, and LURN SI-29 incontinence subscale scores (see Figure). \\* \[means p<0.05; number in figure=correlation coefficient\]. CONCLUSIONS: In care-seeking patients with urinary urgency, over half reported mild urologic pain and one-third reported widespread pain. There were positive correlations between their OAB and pain symptoms. These data support the concept that OAB patients may have heightened sensitivity to noxious stimulation and/or central sensitization. Studies are needed to examine if urgency patients with pain might represent a distinct phenotype.

title: IP16-02: COMPARING SYMPTOM PRESENTATION, TREATMENT PATTERNS, AND SYMPTOM TRAJECTORIES BETWEEN MEN AND WOMEN WITH URINARY URGENCY — A LURN II STUDY
parentSessionTitle: IP16: Urodynamics/Lower Urinary Tract Dysfunction/Female Pelvic Medicine: Overactive Bladder
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Overactive bladder (OAB) in men is poorly understood and under-studied. The co-occurrence of storage and voiding symptoms makes it challenging to recognize and manage. The objectives of this study were to compare the symptom presentation, treatment patterns, and symptom trajectories between men and women with urinary urgency, the cardinal symptom of OAB. METHODS: Adult men and women seeking treatment for bothersome urinary urgency, without or with urgency urinary incontinence, were enrolled in the LURN II Study. Patients with a clinical impression of bladder outlet obstruction or pain as a primary diagnosis were excluded. LUTS were assessed using the OAB-q and LURN SI-29 questionnaires at baseline, 3, 6, 9, and 12-month. Treatment data were queried during study visits. RESULTS: 272 men and 339 women with urinary urgency were enrolled. Men were older and reported less severe OAB-q symptoms and better HRQL at baseline compared to women. Men also had lower LURN SI-29 total scores, urgency scores, and incontinence scores compared to women. Conversely, men reported higher nocturia and voiding scores compared to women. In terms of treatment patterns, more men used BPH medications (61% alpha blockers, 19% 5-alpha reductase) than OAB medications (40% anticholinergics, 22% beta-agonists). It was uncommon for men to do pelvic floor muscle exercises (3.1%) or pelvic floor physical therapy (4.2%) to manage their urgency (see Table). Although men had less severe OAB symptoms at baseline, there was greater improvement in OAB symptoms and HRQL over time among women, such that there were no differences between them at follow-up (see Figure). CONCLUSIONS: At baseline, women reported more severe urgency, incontinence, and overall OAB burden, whereas men had higher nocturia and voiding scores. Despite these sex-specific differences, women experienced greater improvement in urgency and quality-of-life measures over time. At study end, there were no significant differences in OAB outcomes between men and women.

title: IP16-03: A prospective longitudinal study of urinary metabolites among women with and without overactive bladder
parentSessionTitle: IP16: Urodynamics/Lower Urinary Tract Dysfunction/Female Pelvic Medicine: Overactive Bladder
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: There has been little research evaluating the urinary metabolome and its relationship to overactive bladder (OAB). We aim to bridge this gap by evaluating the urinary metabolome in postmenopausal women with and without OAB. METHODS: This is a prospective observational study of postmenopausal women with clinical OAB, defined by LURN Symptom Index-10 responses, who were not managed with medications or recent procedures, and controls. LURN Symptom Index-29 (LURN-SI-29) and catheterized urine specimens were collected at baseline and 5-weeks. Untargeted metabolomics using reverse phase negative ionization (RP-neg) and ion pairing negative ionization (IP-neg) assays were performed at the University of Michigan Metabolomics Core. Peak intensity of metabolites was compared between groups and over time. RESULTS: Urine at baseline and 5 weeks was available for all cases (n=25) and controls (n=11). The mean age was similar between the OAB and control groups (65 vs 61 years, respectively). LURN-SI-29 scores discriminated between cases (x̄=25.7, IQR 21-31) vs controls (x̄=7.6, IQR 3.8).RP-neg assays found that 19 metabolites, primarily bile acids, had statistically significant higher peak intensity among cases vs controls. Examples include Taurohyocholic acid (p<0.001) and Tauroursodeoxycholic acid and Taurohyodeoxycholic acid (p=0.003, Figure 1a, 1b). The excitatory neurotransmitter Glutaric acid was also higher in urine of cases (p=0.003, Figure 1c). IP-neg found that 11 metabolites showed statistically significantly higher peak intensity among cases vs controls, several of these were amino acid or caffeine metabolites. Examples included Alanine (p=0.003), 1,7-Dimethyluric acid (p=0.005), and 1,3,7-Trimethyluric acid (p=0.010, Figures 2a-c). CONCLUSIONS: Post-menopausal women with OAB have distinct urine metabolites compared to controls. Specifically, we found higher peak intensity among urine bile acid levels, including primary, secondary and conjugated bile acids. These represent multiple steps in bile acid metabolism, suggesting these pathways as potential therapeutic targets.

title: IP16-04: Proteomic Analysis of Human Urothelium  Reveals Distinct Molecular Mechanisms  Underlying Overactive Bladder due to Bladder Outlet Obstruction
parentSessionTitle: IP16: Urodynamics/Lower Urinary Tract Dysfunction/Female Pelvic Medicine: Overactive Bladder
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Overactive bladder (OAB) in men with bladder outlet obstruction (BOO) due to benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH) represents a major therapeutic challenge, as symptoms often persist even after surgical relief of obstruction. The underlying molecular mechanisms, however, remain poorly defined. The aim of this study was to identify differentially expressed proteins in the urothelial tissues of patients with BOO-related OAB using a proteomic approach. METHODS: Bladder urothelial tissues were obtained via cold-cup biopsy during transurethral resection of the prostate from 11 male patients with BPH (6 OAB, 5 non-OAB). Patients with hematuria, neurogenic bladder, active urinary tract infection, urological malignancy, or prior pelvic radiation were excluded. Proteomic profiling was conducted using liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry (LC-MS/MS). Differential expression analysis utilized MaxQuant and Perseus software. Functional annotation and pathway enrichment were performed using Ingenuity Pathway Analysis and Gene Ontology tools. RESULTS: Proteomic analysis identified 1,510 proteins, of which 133 were differentially expressed proteins in patients with OAB compared with the non-OAB group. Dysregulated pathways included cytoskeletal remodeling, Rho GTPase signaling, serotonergic signaling, and immune responses. Structural proteins such as ACTA2, CFL2, MYLK, and PPP1R12B were markedly downregulated, whereas GNA13 and multiple inflammatory mediators were upregulated. Functional analysis confirmed the enrichment of neurotransmitter catabolic processes, immune responses, and impaired cell–cell contact, suggesting structural disorganization and aberrant epithelial signaling in the OAB group. CONCLUSIONS: BOO-related OAB exhibits distinct proteomic signatures characterized by cytoskeletal disorganization, aberrant neurotransmitter signaling, and chronic inflammatory responses. Downregulation of structural proteins alongside upregulation of inflammatory mediators suggests impaired mechanotransduction and barrier dysfunction in OAB pathophysiology. These findings provide novel molecular insights and identify potential therapeutic targets for biomarker discovery and precision medicine approaches in OAB management.

title: IP16-05: URINE IN INDIVIDUALS WITH OVERACTIVE BLADDER HARBORS GREATER ABUNDANCE OF CALCIUM- AND FAD-BINDING PEPTIDES RELATIVE TO HEALTHY CONTROLS
parentSessionTitle: IP16: Urodynamics/Lower Urinary Tract Dysfunction/Female Pelvic Medicine: Overactive Bladder
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Urinary peptide composition remains poorly understood both in the physiological state and in the overactive bladder state. We sought to investigate and compare the urinary peptidome of individuals with and without overactive bladder (OAB). We hypothesized that urine from individuals with OAB would harbor unique peptide signatures relative to those of healthy controls. METHODS: Adult female patients with and without overactive bladder were included. Urine specimens were prospectively obtained via midstream clean catch collection. Samples were analyzed for peptide composition following standard fractionation techniques and isolation from the peptide-rich supernatant. Data were analyzed by PEAKS Online V11 using all spectra to search against the human UniProtKB protein sequence databases in addition to Deep Novo peptide identification for peptide identification and quantitative values. RESULTS: 102 patients with OAB and 54 healthy controls were included. Peptide composition and concentration differed between OAB and control groups (p=0.001). Peptides associated with calcium binding and FAD binding were more abundant in OAB, and peptides associated with cAMP metabolism and mitochondrial translocation were more abundant in controls (false discovery rate corrected p-values <0.05 and log2 fold changes >2, Figure). Machine learning classifiers were generated and the greatest explainers in the models were a human mitochondrial ribosomal protein (more abundant in OAB) and extracellular superoxide dismutase (more abundant in healthy controls), a secreted antioxidant. CONCLUSIONS: This study demonstrates that the urinary peptidome differs between individuals with overactive bladder and healthy controls, revealing biologically plausible peptide signatures that may reflect underlying pathophysiology. Enrichment of peptides related to calcium and FAD binding in the OAB cohort suggests altered cellular signaling and oxidative pathways. The identification of mitochondrial ribosome- and extracellular superoxide dismutase-derived peptides as discriminators highlights potential mechanistic links between oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, and bladder overactivity. The findings establish urinary peptidomics as a promising noninvasive approach to uncover molecular correlates and candidate biomarkers of overactive bladder.

title: IP16-06: Serum Uric Acid Partially Mediates Nocturia-Associated Mortality: NHANES Analysis
parentSessionTitle: IP16: Urodynamics/Lower Urinary Tract Dysfunction/Female Pelvic Medicine: Overactive Bladder

speakers.organization: Hallym University Kangnam Sacred Heart Hospital

fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Nocturia is linked to increased mortality risk, potentially via metabolic pathways. This study evaluates serum uric acid (sUA) as a mediator in the nocturia-mortality association using nationally representative data. METHODS: We analyzed NHANES data (2005–2014) from 12,522 adults aged ≥40 years with complete nocturia, sUA, and follow-up data (median 107.3 months; mortality via National Death Index linkage). Nocturia was defined as ≥2 nighttime voids. sUA was categorized into quartiles (Q1–Q4) and modeled continuously. Cox proportional hazards regression assessed associations with all-cause and cardiovascular mortality, adjusting for age, sex, race/ethnicity, BMI, smoking, alcohol, sleep duration, hypertension, diabetes, and dyslipidemia. Hazard ratios (HR) with 95% confidence intervals (CI) were estimated. Restricted cubic spline (RCS) models evaluated nonlinear relationships. Mediation analysis quantified direct/indirect effects of nocturia via sUA using the regmedint package. RESULTS: Higher sUA quartiles were associated with older age, greater nocturia prevalence (41.3% in Q4 vs. 35.4% in Q1), and elevated mortality (all-cause: 24.3% vs. 12.9%; cardiovascular: 7.2% vs. 2.9%). In fully adjusted models, nocturia predicted all-cause (HR 1.984, 95% CI 1.803–2.182) and cardiovascular mortality (HR 1.915, 95% CI 1.617–2.267). RCS revealed J-shaped associations for sUA with both outcomes (p for nonlinearity <0.001). Mediation analysis showed partial mediation by sUA: for all-cause mortality, total indirect effect HR 1.031 (95% CI 1.018–1.044); direct effect HR 1.909 (95% CI 1.736–2.101). Similar patterns held for cardiovascular mortality. CONCLUSIONS: Nocturia independently predicts all-cause and cardiovascular mortality. sUA partially mediates this pathway, suggesting integrated management targeting hyperuricemia and metabolic risks to mitigate nocturia-associated mortality.

title: IP16-07: Skin Sympathetic Nerve Activity Reflects Sympathetic Overactivation in a Rat Model of Overactive Bladder Induced by Partial Bladder Outlet Obstruction
parentSessionTitle: IP16: Urodynamics/Lower Urinary Tract Dysfunction/Female Pelvic Medicine: Overactive Bladder
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Overactive bladder (OAB) has been increasingly linked to autonomic dysregulation. However, direct measurement of sympathetic drive in vivo remains technically challenging. This study aimed to validate whether skin sympathetic nerve activity (SKNA), recorded from body surface sites, accurately reflects the underlying sympathetic hyperactivity in a rat model of OAB induced by partial bladder outlet obstruction (pBOO). METHODS: Eight female Sprague–Dawley rats were included (Sham=4; pBOO=4). pBOO was induced by partial urethral ligation, while Sham rats underwent urethral exposure only. Sympathetic activity was simultaneously recorded at thoracic and abdominal skin and directly from the sympathetic ganglion inside a Faraday cage. Mean signal amplitude (µV) was quantified at each site. Between-group differences were analyzed using one-tailed Welch’s t-tests (pBOO > Sham), and effect sizes were calculated as Cohen’s d. A composite sympathetic index was computed by averaging z-scores across the three sites. Fisher’s method was used to integrate site-specific p-values. RESULTS: Compared with Sham, pBOO rats demonstrated classic OAB features, including increased voiding frequency, reduced voided volume, and higher bladder weight (all p<0.05) ( Fig. A). Sympathetic nerve activity was consistently elevated in pBOO rats across thoracic skin, abdominal skin, and ganglionic recordings ( Fig. B). Fisher’s combined analysis confirmed global sympathetic overactivation (p=0.045). The composite three-site index demonstrated significant sympathetic hyperactivation in the pBOO group (p=0.013) ( Fig. C). Importantly, even when restricted to the two skin electrodes only, the non-invasive composite index remained significantly elevated (p=0.027) ( Fig. D), confirming that skin SNA reliably reflects sympathetic drive. CONCLUSIONS: This animal study provides physiological validation that skin-derived sympathetic nerve activity faithfully mirrors autonomic hyperactivation in a rat model of overactive bladder. The strong concordance between skin and direct ganglionic recordings establishes SKNA as a reliable surrogate of sympathetic drive. These findings lay the experimental foundation for future translational development of surface SKNA as an objective biomarker to diagnose and monitor autonomic dysfunction in overactive bladder.

title: IP16-08: Regional White Matter Differences in Overactive Bladder Identified by Diffusion Tensor Imaging: Five Distinct Clusters Including Two Accessible to Brain Optical Technologies
parentSessionTitle: IP16: Urodynamics/Lower Urinary Tract Dysfunction/Female Pelvic Medicine: Overactive Bladder
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Recent MRI studies have identified overactive bladder (OAB) associated with alterations in brain white matter microstructure. Diffusion tensor imaging (DTI) quantifies these changes through fractional anisotropy (FA) reflecting white matter integrity and connectivity. This study aimed to a) identify regional FA differences between individuals with OAB and healthy controls (HC), and b) to determine whether DTI areas of interest were accessible to optical monitoring systems such as brain functional near-infrared spectroscopy specifications. METHODS: Participants were classified by ICIQ-OAB responses (HC ≤1 on all questions; OAB ≥2 on the “urgency” question). All participants were cognitively intact and completed a standardized hydration protocol. DTI data were processed using MRtrix3 and FSL pipelines, including denoising, eddy-current and motion correction, skull stripping, and registration to the Johns Hopkins University DTI atlas (ICBM-DTI-81 1 mm). Voxel-wise FA maps were analyzed within a mask combining white and deep gray matter (basal ganglia and thalamus) derived from the Harvard-Oxford subcortical atlas. Group differences and correlations between FA and ICIQ scores were evaluated using a general linear model (p<0.05, FDR q<0.05). Geography was mapped to subjects also underlying fNIRS with natural bladder filling protocols. RESULTS: Twenty-one females (6 HC, 15 OAB; ages 24–80) were included. Compared to HCs, OAB participants exhibited significantly reduced FA across multiple white matter tracts involved in sensory integration and urgency perception, including the corpus callosum (body and genu), internal and external capsules, and corona radiata. Five discrete clusters showed lower FA in OAB relative to controls, consistent with disrupted interhemispheric and thalamocortical communication. Notably, two of these clusters were in cortical regions within optical penetration depth and thus targetable by non-invasive brain imaging modalities such as fNIRS. CONCLUSIONS: OAB is associated with reduced white matter integrity across five specific brain regions, supporting the concept that bladder dysfunction involves central connectivity changes. Two of these regions are accessible using superficial optical technologies, establishing a foundation for future fNIRS-based optical correlations or biomarker studies.

title: IP16-09: A NON-INVASIVE APPROACH TO DETECTNG DETRUSOR OVERACTIVITY IN PATIENTS WITH OVERACTIVE BLADDER VIA BLADDER NEAR-INFRARED SPECTROSCOPY
parentSessionTitle: IP16: Urodynamics/Lower Urinary Tract Dysfunction/Female Pelvic Medicine: Overactive Bladder

speakers.organization: Virginia Commonwealth University School of Medicine

fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Detrusor overactivity (DO) is characterized by involuntary bladder contractions that may cause overactive bladder (OAB) symptoms, such as urination and incontinence. While Urodynamics (UDS) is the established gold standard test for diagnosis of DO, Near-infrared spectroscopy (NIRS) measures tissue hemodynamics non-invasively, offering a potential cost-effective imaging alternative to UDS. This study evaluates bladder NIRS as a potential non-invasive alternative for detecting DO in individuals with OAB. METHODS: OAB patients participated in simultaneous bladder NIRS and UDS studies. Peak and area-under-the-curve (AUC) values were calculated during DO events using detrusor pressure (pDet) and bladder NIRS (oxygenated hemoglobin (O2Hb)). NIRS segments during DO events were compared within subjects to control segments without DO (internal control), and externally to segments from participants without DO (external control). To account for data drift, a normalized AUC for NIRS data over the testing period was computed after motion artifact correction and subtraction of the area under a linear fit. RESULTS: Among 44 enrolled female OAB participants, four experienced demonstratable DO, producing a total of 39 DO events. During DO events, pDet peaks were significantly higher (51.8 ± 7.3 cm H2O) compared to internal (3.7 ± 0.5 cm H2O), and external control periods (5.4 ± 1.2 cm H2O) (p0.001). Likewise, NIRS O2Hb peaks were higher during DO events (p0.001). pDet AUC was 30,988 ± 7,318.2 (DO), 444.5 ± 86.7 (internal control), and 1,036.6 ± 352.9 (external control), with similar outcomes seen with NIRS O2Hb (p0.001). Normalized NIRS AUC was greater in patients with DO (0.56 ± 0.11) than in external controls (0.09 ± 0.01, p0.001). Using a threshold AUC value of 0.146, provides clear separation between urodynamic segments with and without DO, p0.05 ( (https://www.auajournals.org/doi/abs/10.1097/01.JU.0001191360.00345.d8.09#F1)). CONCLUSIONS: DO events were consistently associated with marked increases in both pDet and NIRS O2Hb values when compared to control segments. These findings support the potential use of bladder NIRS as a non-invasive tool for detecting DO in OAB patients.

title: IP16-10: ALTERATIONS IN BLADDER HEMODYNAMICS USING NEAR-INFRARED SPECTROSCOPY IN FEMALES WITH OVERACTIVE BLADDER AND NORMAL HEALTHY CONTROLS
parentSessionTitle: IP16: Urodynamics/Lower Urinary Tract Dysfunction/Female Pelvic Medicine: Overactive Bladder
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: A common condition, overactive bladder (OAB) is characterized by urinary urgency, frequency, and incontinence. While alterations in bladder hemodynamics are suspected to contribute to OAB pathophysiology, current diagnostic methods lack the ability to directly assess bladder hemodynamics. The objective of this study was to evaluate whether a noninvasive imaging modality, near-infrared spectroscopy (NIRS), could detect differences in bladder hemodynamic patterns between healthy females and those with OAB during bladder filling. METHODS: A total of 22 female participants (13 with OAB and 9 healthy controls) completed a natural filling protocol while a bladder-mounted NIRS device measured oxygenated hemoglobin (O2Hb) levels. Real-time bladder sensation of fullness was recorded using a previously published and validated “Sensation Meter”. Data were segmented into low and high sensation phases using “first desire to void” as the cutoff threshold. Comparisons were made between the last 10% and first 10% of the high sensation phase, defined as the difference in mean O2Hb (ΔO2Hb). Motion artifacts were corrected using a head-mounted inertial measurement unit (IMU) for detection, and then the data were processed using a custom MATLAB algorithm. RESULTS: Participants with OAB showed significantly lower ΔO2Hb levels during bladder filling compared to controls (−1.2 ± 0.8 vs. 0.7 ± 0.18, p0.05). The slopes of linear fit lines (ΔO2Hb/%time) were significantly higher in the normal control group compared to the OAB group (0.008 ± 0.002 vs. -0.016 ± 0.01, p=0.01. A ΔO2Hb threshold of 0.26 correctly identified OAB participants in 90% of participants, (https://www.auajournals.org/doi/abs/10.1097/01.JU.0001191360.00345.d8.10#F1). CONCLUSIONS: Our study demonstrates that bladder NIRS can non-invasively identify altered hemodynamics in females with OAB. These findings, particularly with threshold identification, highlight the potential of NIRS to serve as an objective diagnostic and stratification tool for OAB. Future studies are needed to validate its clinical utility.

title: IP16-11: PEOPLE WITH URGENCY HAVE DIFFERENT SENSATIONS TO URINATE: A LURN II STUDY
parentSessionTitle: IP16: Urodynamics/Lower Urinary Tract Dysfunction/Female Pelvic Medicine: Overactive Bladder
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: The sensation of the need to urinate (NTU) and the sensation of urinary urgency varies. Using the Symptoms of Lower Urinary Tract Dysfunction Research Network (LURN II) dataset, we aimed to identify the variety of bladder sensations to void, including the character, location and temporal description. We assessed if these vary based on symptom severity or if distinct sensations to void are interpreted by people with urinary urgency (URG) and urinary urgency incontinence (UUI). METHODS: Six LURN research sites enrolled men and women with bothersome URG or UUI as well as controls without symptoms. Bladder questionnaires were administered. Percentages of participants indicating specific sensations and locations were calculated by sex and patient type and, differences were tested with Chi-square tests. RESULTS: There were 819 symptomatic participants (218 URG and 466 UUI) and 135 controls. Of these 54% were female and the vast majority were white (82%). While most participants localized the sensation of NTU to the “bladder area” (74-90%), more people with URG or UUI localized sensation to the urethra (33-65% URG/UUI vs 9-26% Control, p≤0.001) or penis/scrotum/vagina compared to controls (39-58% URG/UUI vs 8-15% Control, p≤0.001). ( FIGURE) Both control and URG/UUI participants described the sensation of NTU as “pressure” (47-88%) or “fullness” (47-78%). Compared to controls, those with URG/UUI had larger proportions describing the sensation as “tingling” (20-42% vs 7-11%), “urgency” (88-94% vs 28-34%), “discomfort” (67-78% vs 14-20%) or “stinging” (6-11% vs 0-1%). CONCLUSIONS: The sensations and locations of the need to urinate is felt differently among controls versus people with URG and/or UUI. Higher proportions of people with URG report sensation of NTU as discomfort, stinging, pressure or fullness and localize this to areas beyond the bladder.

title: IP16-12: IS THERE A CENTRAL SENSITIZATION PHENOTYPE IN FEMALES WITH OVERACTIVE BLADDER?
parentSessionTitle: IP16: Urodynamics/Lower Urinary Tract Dysfunction/Female Pelvic Medicine: Overactive Bladder
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Overactive bladder (OAB) is challenging to treat due to its broad symptomatology and absent unifying pathophysiologic mechanism. Central sensitization (CS) may be an underlying mechanism affecting up to 48% of individuals with OAB. This study evaluated potential phenotypic characteristics associated with CS in OAB involving affect, pain, and co-occurring conditions. We hypothesized that CS would be elevated in OAB compared to controls and associated with increased psychosocial burden, co-morbidity, and urinary symptoms in OAB. METHODS: We recruited adult females with OAB (OABv3≥4) to complete validated symptom measures and a sensory sensitivity protocol, including quantitative sensory testing evaluating average pain threshold, tolerance, and temporal summation of pain (TSP) at 48 degrees C. TSP slopes were calculated using regression, compared between groups, and correlated with proposed phenotypic features within OAB. RESULTS: N=202 with OAB and N=27 controls were recruited, of whom 183 OAB and 23 controls completed TSP testing. 26 (12.6%) with OAB had positive TSP slopes, suggesting CS, versus 1 control (0.5%). There was no difference in pain threshold and tolerance levels, but significant differences in TSP slopes (p=.005, Table). Within the OAB group, there was no association between self-reported emotional distress, sensory sensitivity, increased pain comorbidity, or urinary symptoms based on TSP ( Table). CONCLUSIONS: Results are inconclusive regarding OAB-CS phenotypes. Individuals with OAB may have more difficulty habituating to pain stimuli. Results contradict prior OAB work, including our own, with both lower rates of CS and no association between TSP and putative phenotypic characteristics in OAB. Sample differences and study methodology may partially explain disparate findings between investigations. We highlight the importance of objective measures of bladder hypersensitivity in identifying CS in those with OAB. | | | --- | | |

title: IP16-13: Hidden Voiding Dysfunction in Refractory Female Overactive Bladder: Insights from Real-World Urodynamic Profiling
parentSessionTitle: IP16: Urodynamics/Lower Urinary Tract Dysfunction/Female Pelvic Medicine: Overactive Bladder
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Up to 20% of patients with overactive bladder (OAB) remain refractory to conventional therapy, representing a growing clinical challenge, particularly among elderly women. While recent reports question the clinical utility of urodynamic studies (UDS) in refractory OAB, the underlying bladder pathophysiology in these patients remains poorly defined. This study aimed to characterize the urodynamic features of women with refractory OAB to uncover potential mechanisms of treatment resistance. METHODS: Female patients with idiopathic OAB who failed to improve after ≥12 weeks of behavioral and pharmacological therapy and were referred for surgical consideration underwent standardized UDS. Those with known neurological disease were excluded. Storage and voiding phase parameters were analyzed to identify distinct urodynamic phenotypes. RESULTS: A total of 184 women (mean age, 65.7 years) were analyzed. The mean OAB symptom score was 7.8, and 85.3% reported urgency urinary incontinence. In the UDS, detrusor overactivity (DO) was identified in 71.2% of patients, whereas 19% demonstrated no abnormality in the storage phase, including urinary sensation. Notably, in voiding phase, 32.6% exhibited urodynamic evidence of detrusor underactivity (DU; maximum urinary flow rate \[Qmax\] 10 ml/s and detrusor pressure at Qmax \[PdetQmax\] 30 cmH2O), often voiding by abdominal straining. The coexistence of DO and DU was found in 23.3% of cases, with a higher mean age (75.1 years). Furthermore, one-fourth of patients showed poor voiding bladder efficiency (70%). CONCLUSIONS: Nearly one-third of women with refractory OAB exhibit detrusor underactivity, and coexistence of DO and DU is common among the elderly—findings that are often undetectable without UDS. These results highlight that in refractory female OAB, particularly in older patients, UDS remains an indispensable tool for uncovering hidden voiding dysfunction and guiding individualized therapeutic strategies.

title: IP16-14: Urodynamic correlates of anticholinergic burden: evidence for cholinergic saturation and detrusor overactivity supression
parentSessionTitle: IP16: Urodynamics/Lower Urinary Tract Dysfunction/Female Pelvic Medicine: Overactive Bladder

speakers.organization: Faculdade de Medicina da Universidade do Porto

fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Overactive bladder syndrome (OAB) is a prevalent and bothersome condition for which detrusor overactivity (DO) is a key urodynamic correlate. Anticholinergic drugs (AC) remain a cornerstone of treatment; however, many patients are exposed to other medications with anticholinergic properties, contributing to the overall anticholinergic burden (ABu). The Drug Burden Index (DBI) quantifies this cumulative exposure and has been associated with reduced response to OAB antimuscarinic therapy. Whether this observation reflects a true pathophysiological effect at the bladder level or identifies a distinct patient phenotype remains unclear. Elevated anticholinergic burden may suppress detrusor contractility through peripheral muscarinic blockade, while central or sensory pathways sustaining urgency remain unaffected. We aimed to investigate the relationship between DBI and urodynamic findings, exploring a potential mechanistic link between systemic anticholinergic load and detrusor overactivity. METHODS: We retrospectively reviewed all urodynamic studies performed at our tertiary center over a 7-month period (n=200). Children and patients with neurological disease, structural genitourinary malformations, or prior botulinum toxin injection within six months were excluded. Demographic and clinical data, including medication history, were collected from medical records. Anticholinergic burden was quantified using the Drug Burden Index (DBI). The primary outcome was the presence of detrusor overactivity (DO) on urodynamic testing. RESULTS: After exclusions, 134 non-neurogenic studies were analyzed. Median age was 64 years (IQR 19.5; 29–87), and 61% were female. Patients were taking a median of two medications (IQR 5; 0–15), with a median DBI of 0.5 (IQR 0.7; 0–3.6). Overall, 34% showed DO. The frequency of DO decreased with increasing DBI: 45% for DBI=0, 33% for DBI 0–1, and 10% for DBI≥1 (p=0.0037). Among patients reporting urgency (n=45), DO was observed in 87.5% with DBI=0 but only in 10% with DBI≥1 (p=0.0026). Logistic regression confirmed the inverse association between DBI and DO. In symptomatic patients, each unit increase in DBI reduced the odds of DO by 85% (OR 0.15, 95% CI 0.05–0.45, p=0.0007). The effect was strongest in urgency patients not treated with OABspecific medication, where each DBI unit decreased the likelihood of DO by 95% (OR 0.05, 95% CI 0.008–0.30, p=0.001) CONCLUSIONS: Higher ABu is strongly associated with the absence of DO, particularly in urgency patients not receiving OAB-specific therapy. Cumulative AC exposure may saturate muscarinic pathways, suppressing detrusor excitability despite persistent urgency. These findings provide mechanistic support for reduced antimuscarinic responsiveness in patients with high DBI and underscore the importance of considering ABu when interpreting urodynamic studies and tailoring OAB treatment.

title: IP16-15: A COMPARISON OF UROGYNECOLOGY AND RECONSTRUCTIVE PELVIC SURGERY (URPS) VS NON-URPS-INTERPRETED URODYNAMIC STUDIES (UDS): DIFFERENCES IN COMPLETENESS AND OUTCOMES
parentSessionTitle: IP16: Urodynamics/Lower Urinary Tract Dysfunction/Female Pelvic Medicine: Overactive Bladder
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Urodynamic studies (UDS) help provide valuable information that guides clinical practice, but testing is costly, time consuming, and not without risks. Our aim is to compare UDS studies interpreted by URPS-trained vs non-URPS-trained urologists for completeness and secondarily assess differences in objective outcomes. METHODS: Patients with CPT code of 52718 were queried between 2024-2025 at a single institution and divided into a URPS and non-URPS reading group. Assuming a 25% difference in our primary outcome between groups with an α of 0.05 and a power of 80%, 33 patients need to be included in each group. A random sample of 101 patients was ultimately assessed: 13 patients from 4 current URPS attendings and 5 patients from each of the 10 non-URPS attendings who performed the most UDS. Chi square and Fisher’s exact test were performed to compare completeness in documenting capacity, compliance, course sensation, cough stress test, detrusor overactivity, contractility, complete emptying, clinical obstruction, EMG findings, and flow curve shape, as well as differences in whether an intervention occurred after UDS. RESULTS: A total of 101 UDS (51 URPS and 50 non-URPS) were analyzed. UDS ordered by URPS-trained attendings were significantly more complete; URPS UDS document compliance, contractility, cough stress testing, PVR, and EMG findings significantly more (all p<0.01) compared to non-URPS UDS ( Table 1). URPS UDS were more frequently ordered based off AUA UDS guidelines (98% URPS vs 74% non-URPS, p<0.01), and were more likely to document a new diagnosis compared to non-URPS read studies (52.9% URPS vs 30% non-URPS, p=0.02). There were no statistically significant differences in whether an intervention occurred after UDS (88% URPS vs 76% non-URPS, p=0.1) or whether the intervention was indicated between these groups (98% URPS vs 91% non-URPS, p=0.36). CONCLUSIONS: URPS-read UDS reports were more complete and more commonly ordered based on UDS guidelines. Additionally, URPS-read studies were more likely to document a new diagnosis compared to non-URPS reports. The rate of guideline-indicated intervention that occurred after UDS between the two groups is similar. These data suggest URPS-read UDS are of higher quality and provide greater clinical value compared to non-URPS read studies. | | | --- | | |

title: IP16-16: What Level of Benefit Justifies Beta-3 Agonist Therapy for Overactive Bladder? Estimating the Patient-Perceived Treatment Threshold Using the Smallest Worthwhile Difference Approach
parentSessionTitle: IP16: Urodynamics/Lower Urinary Tract Dysfunction/Female Pelvic Medicine: Overactive Bladder
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: The smallest worthwhile difference (SWD) represents the minimal beneficial effect of an intervention that patients consider valuable when weighed against its burdens, including potential harms, costs, and inconveniences. We aimed to determine the SWD for overactive bladder (OAB) treatment with beta-3 agonists and to evaluate the impact of trust in physicians on the SWD. METHODS: We recruited participants with symptoms suggestive of OAB in February 2025 through a research crowdsourcing service. The SWD for beta-3 agonists was estimated as a patient-required improvement in response rate to lifestyle modifications after three months using a benefit-harm trade-off approach. Trust in physicians was measured using the five-item Wake Forest Physician Trust Scale. RESULTS: Of 630 respondents, 472 who had symptom-related distress but were medication-naïve were included. Of these, 261 (55%) did not consider beta-3 agonist treatment worthwhile even if it achieved a 100% response. For the 211 participants willing to consider beta-3 agonists, the median SWD was a 20% improvement in response rate, with a wide IQR (5 to 40) ( (https://www.auajournals.org/doi/abs/10.1097/01.JU.0001191360.00345.d8.16#F1)). Multivariable generalized linear model analysis showed that higher levels of trust in physicians were associated with smaller SWDs (mean difference per SD, -4.11; 95% CI, -7.00 to -1.22) ( Table 1). CONCLUSIONS: More than half of participants with symptoms suggestive of OAB and associated distress did not consider that beta-3 agonist treatment would be worthwhile given its burdens, even if there was a 100% response. Even among those willing to consider beta-3 agonists, the SWD varied substantially between individuals. Trust in physicians may influence SWD.

title: IP16-18: Beyond Glycemic Control: Concurrent GLP-1 Receptor Agonist Use Is Associated with Reduced Urinary Adverse Events Following OnabotulinumtoxinA Treatment in Non-Diabetic Adults with Overactive Bladder
parentSessionTitle: IP16: Urodynamics/Lower Urinary Tract Dysfunction/Female Pelvic Medicine: Overactive Bladder
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Overactive bladder (OAB) affects nearly 20% of adults and is strongly associated with obesity. OnabotulinumtoxinA (BTX-A) is an established treatment for refractory OAB but carries risks of urinary retention and urinary tract infection (UTI). Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1 RAs), such as semaglutide, have demonstrated metabolic and anti-inflammatory benefits beyond weight loss. We investigated whether concurrent GLP-1 RA use reduces urinary adverse events among non-diabetic OAB patients treated with BTX-A. METHODS: Using the TriNetX Research Network, we conducted a retrospective, propensity-matched cohort study of non-diabetic adults with OAB who received BTX-A alone or BTX-A plus a GLP-1 RA. Matching (1:1) adjusted for age, race, ethnicity, hypertension, and obesity/BMI. Primary outcomes included incidence of urinary retention, UTI, and new antispasmodic use following BTX-A. Kaplan–Meier survival analyses were performed for one-year event-free survival. RESULTS: After matching, 992 patients were included per group with comparable demographics. GLP-1 RA use was associated with significantly lower urinary retention (4.9% vs. 8.6%; risk difference 3.7%; p=0.0044) and UTI incidence (8.8% vs. 13.3%; risk difference 4.5%; p=0.0224). One-year retention-free (log-rank p=0.0064; HR 1.74) and UTI-free survival (log-rank p=0.0420; HR 1.48) were higher with combination therapy. No differences were observed in new antispasmodic initiation (10.3% vs. 11.8%; p=0.69). Increased antiemetic and laxative use reflected known gastrointestinal side effects of GLP-1 RAs. CONCLUSIONS: In this large, real-world analysis of non-diabetic OAB patients, concurrent GLP-1 RA therapy was associated with reduced risks of urinary retention and UTI following BTX-A treatment, independent of weight loss. These findings suggest potential anti-inflammatory or neuromodulatory effects of GLP-1 signaling on bladder function and warrant prospective studies to evaluate its role as an adjunctive therapy in OAB management.

title: IP16-19: Intradetrusor OnabotulinumtoxinA is Safe and Effective in Men with Overactive Bladder following Stress Urinary Incontinence Surgery
parentSessionTitle: IP16: Urodynamics/Lower Urinary Tract Dysfunction/Female Pelvic Medicine: Overactive Bladder

speakers.organization: David Geffen School of Medicine at UCLA

fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Men with stress urinary incontinence (SUI) treated with artificial urinary sphincter (AUS) or male sling (MS) may develop overactive bladder (OAB). Intradetrusor onabotulinumtoxinA (onabotA) is effective for refractory OAB, but safety and long-term outcomes in this population are poorly defined. This study evaluates safety, success, and persistence of onabotA therapy in men with and without prior AUS or MS. METHODS: We conducted a retrospective review of men with prior AUS or MS treated with intradetrusor onabotA for OAB at a single center from January 2018 to September 2025. Safety outcomes included new clean intermittent catheterization (CIC), elevated post-void residual (PVR ≥200cc), and escalation to advanced therapy. Persistence was assessed by total number of injections and by Kaplan-Meier analysis of time to discontinuation or escalation. Group comparisons were performed using Fisher’s exact and Mann-Whitney U tests. RESULTS: 126 men met inclusion criteria, 23 with prior SUI surgery (19 AUS, 7 MS, 3 both) and 103 without. Most with AUS/MS (19/23) had prior prostate surgery. No patient with AUS or MS required new CIC or experienced elevated PVR after onabotA compared to 6% and 19% of men without AUS or MS (p=0.591 and p=0.023, respectively). Therapy escalation occurred in 13% of men with AUS or MS and 15% of mean without. Mean number of injections was higher in the AUS/MS group (3.50 ± 2.48 vs 2.66 ± 2.29; p=0.059). Kaplan-Meier analysis showed similar 36-month continuation rates among men with AUS or MS and men without (70.9% vs 68.1%; log-rank p=0.970). CONCLUSIONS: Intradetrusor onabotA for OAB is well tolerated in men with prior AUS or MS. No post-AUS or MS patient required CIC or developed elevated PVR, highlighting a favorable safety profile. Success rates and persistence were comparable or higher than in men without SUI surgery. These findings support onabotA as a safe and effective treatment for refractory OAB in men with prior SUI surgery.

title: IP16-20: Initiation of de-novo medical therapy for overactive bladder after bladder outlet procedures
parentSessionTitle: IP16: Urodynamics/Lower Urinary Tract Dysfunction/Female Pelvic Medicine: Overactive Bladder
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Despite mechanical relief of bladder outlet obstruction from benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH), some men have persistent or de-novo storage symptoms necessitating pharmacologic therapy, resulting in patient dissatisfaction. Identifying clinical or procedural factors that may identify these men preoperatively could better inform shared decision making, especially as the BPH procedural portfolio continues to grow. We sought to report the rates and factors associated with overactive bladder (OAB) prescriptions following BPH surgery. METHODS: Using Michigan statewide claims data (2017–2023), we identified patients who had BPH surgery without OAB prescriptions (β3-agonist or anticholinergic) within 90 days preoperatively. Procedures included water vapor thermal therapy (WVTT), transurethral resection of the prostate (TURP), prostatic urethral lift (PUL), laser photovaporization (PVP), simple prostatectomy (SP), robotic waterjet therapy (RWJT), transurethral microwave thermotherapy (TUMT), and laser enucleation of the prostate (LEP). Medication initiation was defined as a prescription between 3 months and 12 months after surgery. Cox proportional hazards models, adjusted for demographic and clinical factors, were used to identify predictors of medication initiation. RESULTS: 11,926 patients underwent BPH surgery and were OAB medication naive. At 6 months, the initiation rates of OAB medications ranged from 3-8% and by 12 months, ranged from 5-12% ( (https://www.auajournals.org/doi/abs/10.1097/01.JU.0001191360.00345.d8.20#F1)). On multivariable analysis, predictors of OAB medication initiation included increasing patient comorbidity as measured by the Elixhauser score (HR 1.02, 95% CI 1.0-1.05). Compared to TURP, only PVP was associated with higher risk of medication initiation (HR 1.5, 95% CI 1.3-1.8). In contrast, preoperative catheterization was associated with a lower risk (HR 0.7, 95% CI 0.6-0.9). CONCLUSIONS: OAB medication initiation occurs in 5-12% of patients after BPH surgery and varies by procedure type. Compared to TURP, PVP demonstrated the highest rate of medication initiation, indicating a procedure-related risk for postoperative irritative symptoms. Patients who were catheter-dependent prior to surgery were at lower risk, likely reflecting that bladder outlet obstruction, rather than detrusor overactivity, was the predominant underlying pathology.

title: IP16-21: Incidence of and Time to Minimally Invasive Therapy among Patients with Idiopathic Overactive Bladder
parentSessionTitle: IP16: Urodynamics/Lower Urinary Tract Dysfunction/Female Pelvic Medicine: Overactive Bladder
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Overactive bladder (OAB) is a common condition affecting up to 43% of adults, yet adoption of minimally invasive therapies (MIT), including percutaneous tibial nerve stimulation (PTNS), botulinum toxin (BTX), and sacral neuromodulation (SNM), remains low. There is limited data describing whether physician practice models influence MIT uptake. This study compares rates and time to MIT in large, community-based practices within the Large Urology Group Practice Association (LUGPA) and at a single academic institution. METHODS: This retrospective study evaluated rate of progression to MIT and time to progression to MIT in two cohorts: 1) the claims of patients with an encounter for overactive bladder from 2020 to 2023 in 41 independent Large Urology Group Practice Association (LUGPA) practices and 2) the medical records of patients with an encounter for OAB between 2012 and 2021 from an academic tertiary care center, University of Michigan (UM). Descriptive statistics, Kaplan-Meier analyses, and Cox proportional hazards models assessed MIT adoption and predictors of progression. RESULTS: During the study period, 42,633 of 419,041 patients in the LUGPA cohort and 1,013 of 15,655 patients in the UM cohort progressed to MIT. In LUGPA, the MIT most often utilized was BTX (52%), followed by SNM (42%) and PTNS (17%). At UM, the MIT most often utilized was PTNS (46%), followed by BTX (34%) and SNM (20%). Kaplan-Meier analysis showed cumulative MIT uptake at 1, 2, and 3 years of 9.6%, 13.7%, and 17.3% in LUGPA, compared with 9.1%, 10.9%, and 12.8% in UM. Across both cohorts, MIT was more common among female and older patients. In LUGPA, Medicare insurance and smaller practice size (<50 providers) were associated with higher uptake, while in UM, commercially insured patients were more likely to undergo MIT. CONCLUSIONS: We found that progression to MIT was more common and more rapid in independently owned private urology practices compared to a single academic center. Practice model-specific factors, such as the presence of nurse navigators, may play a critical role in long-term uptake. Broader evaluation across academic centers is warranted to define best practices for optimizing patient access to MIT.

title: IP16-22: Comparative outcomes for minimally invasive therapies for idiopathic overactive bladder in older adults: A national study of Medicare beneficiaries
parentSessionTitle: IP16: Urodynamics/Lower Urinary Tract Dysfunction/Female Pelvic Medicine: Overactive Bladder
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: To compare 2-year treatment continuation outcomes among minimally invasive therapies \[onabotulinumtoxinA injections (BTX-A), sacral neuromodulation (SNM), and percutaneous\ tibial nerve stimulation (PTNS)\] for idiopathic overactive bladder (OAB) in older adults. METHODS: This is a retrospective cohort study of a 100% sample of fee-for-service Medicare beneficiaries who underwent minimally invasive therapy for idiopathic OAB from 2015-2020. Therapies were identified by Current Procedural Terminology (CPT) codes and included intravesical BTX-A, SNM, and PTNS. The primary outcome was continuation of therapy, which was defined as follows for each treatment: BTX-A: at least one repeat injection within 2 years; SNM: progression to implantable pulse generator (IPG) within 90 days of initial implant and no explant at 2 years; PTNS: completion of induction PTNS (11 treatments in 15 weeks) followed by at least 9 maintenance PTNS treatments within 2 years (definitions based on prior research from our group). Propensity score weighting and modified Poisson regression were used to compare outcomes between therapies. RESULTS: A total of 111,494 Medicare beneficiaries initiated a minimally invasive OAB therapy during the study period, and 34.5% (n=38,502) demonstrated continuation of therapy over 2 years. Rates of therapy continuation were as follows: BTX-A 58%, SNM 36.3%, PTNS 9.9%. On weighted regression analyses, beneficiaries undergoing BTX-A were 5.9 times more likely to continue treatment compared to PTNS (95% CI 5.71-6.10) and 1.63 times more likely to continue treatment compared to SNM (95% CI 1.60-1.65). Beneficiaries undergoing SNM were 3.63 times more likely to continue treatment compared to PTNS (95% CI 3.57-3.68). CONCLUSIONS: Older adults with idiopathic OAB undergoing minimally invasive therapy are most likely to continue BTX-A and least likely to continue PTNS over 2 years of follow-up. However, rates for continuation of any type of minimally invasive OAB therapy are low. Further research is needed to determine reasons for discontinuation of minimally invasive OAB therapy in older adults.

title: IP16-23: Real-world experience with implantable tibial nerve stimulation in patients with and without prior failed neuromodulation for overactive bladder
parentSessionTitle: IP16: Urodynamics/Lower Urinary Tract Dysfunction/Female Pelvic Medicine: Overactive Bladder

speakers.organization: University of Texas Southwestern Medical Center

fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: The BlueWind Revi system is an implantable tibial nerve stimulator for overactive bladder (OAB). This study reports institutional outcomes, focusing on patients with prior failed sacral neuromodulation (SNS) or percutaneous tibial nerve stimulation (PTNS). METHODS: A retrospective chart review was performed for all patients undergoing Revi implantation between May 2024 and April 2025. Outcomes were assessed at baseline, 3-month, and 6-month follow-up. Statistical comparisons were made between patients with and without prior neuromodulation. RESULTS: Twenty-one patients (median age 73, 71% female, 5% neurogenic) were included. Most had previously used anticholinergics (81%), beta-3 agonists (24%), PTNS (52%), and/or SNS (10%). All prior PTNS patients were responders. Comparing preoperative symptoms to first (median 3.5 months) and second (median 6.1 months) follow-up: Median daily voids decreased from 9 (IQR 7–12) to 6 (IQR 5–8) at first (p=0.002), and to 7 (IQR 5–9) at second (p=0.004). Median nocturia decreased from 2 (IQR 1–3) to 1 (IQR 0–2) at first (p=0.01) and remained at 1 (IQR 0–2) at second (p=0.02). Median UUI episodes/day dropped from 1 (IQR 0–1) to 0.5 (IQR 0–1) at first (p=0.03), and to 0.5 (IQR 0–1) at second (p=0.04). Median pads/day decreased from 1 (IQR 0–1) to 0.5 (IQR 0–1) at both follow-ups (p ≤ 0.05). Median UDI-6 improved from 45 (IQR 35–62) to 29 (IQR 25–33) at first (p=0.002), and to 27 (IQR 25–33) at second (p=0.003). ≥50% reduction in UUI was achieved by 69% at first and 70% at second follow-up (McNemar’s p<0.05). No serious device- or procedure-related adverse events occurred. Subgroup analysis (n=8 prior neuromodulation \[1 SNS, 7 PTNS\] vs. n=13 without) showed no significant differences in baseline or outcomes at either follow-up (all p>0.05; Table 1). CONCLUSIONS: In this small, real-world cohort, Revi implantation resulted in significant, durable improvements in OAB symptoms and quality of life, with similar efficacy in patients regardless of prior failed neuromodulation. | | | --- | | |

title: IP16-24: Exploring patient perspectives on sacral neuromodulation: a qualitative analysis of online discussions
parentSessionTitle: IP16: Urodynamics/Lower Urinary Tract Dysfunction/Female Pelvic Medicine: Overactive Bladder
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Sacral neuromodulation (SNM) is an established treatment for refractory overactive bladder and urinary incontinence, yet patient perceptions and understanding of this therapy remain underexplored. Online forums increasingly serve as major sources of peer-to-peer education and informal health advice. This study qualitatively analyzed patient discussions about SNM on Reddit to characterize shared experiences, identify misconceptions, and assess the educational value of online discourse. METHODS: A qualitative content analysis was conducted using public posts and comments from the subreddits r/OveractiveBladder and r/Incontinence. Entries containing the terms “sacral neuromodulation,” “InterStim,” “Axonics,” or “sacral nerve stimulation” were included. Two independent reviewers performed systematic, line-by-line coding, applying Braun and Clarke’s six-phase thematic analysis framework. Coding reliability was evaluated using Cohen’s kappa. Non-relevant posts were excluded. RESULTS: A total of 464 threads comprising 3,413 comments were analyzed. Five overarching themes emerged: (1) Expectations and Decision-Making, (2) Postoperative Experiences, (3) Device Function and Performance, (4) Emotional and Psychosocial Responses, and (5) System- and Industry-Related Concerns. Patients frequently expressed anxiety about candidacy, surgical risks, and long-term outcomes, often comparing SNM to other third-line therapies. Postoperative accounts ranged from life-changing improvement to persistent discomfort or loss of efficacy. Users discussed differences between InterStim and Axonics devices, battery life, MRI compatibility, and programming challenges. Emotional responses varied from hope and gratitude to frustration and distrust of medical providers. Cost, insurance coverage, and company support were additional recurrent issues. CONCLUSIONS: Reddit discussions about SNM reveal a complex landscape of patient expectations, lived experiences, and misconceptions. While many describe substantial benefits, others express uncertainty and disappointment, reflecting ongoing gaps in patient education and clinical communication. Social media analysis offers a valuable lens for understanding patient perspectives and improving educational outreach around advanced bladder therapies.

title: IP16-25: Occupational Voiding Restrictions Associated with Overactive Bladder Symptoms: Low Income Individuals Most Affected
parentSessionTitle: IP16: Urodynamics/Lower Urinary Tract Dysfunction/Female Pelvic Medicine: Overactive Bladder
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Prior studies suggest that overactive bladder (OAB) may be associated with certain occupations, such as healthcare, transportation, and education. They propose that these occupations limit natural voiding patterns and thereby lead to OAB.
