This study aims to determine the association between overactive bladder symptoms and occupational voiding restrictions and to identify healthcare disparities. METHODS: A cross-sectional survey of employed adults was conducted via ResearchMatch. Participants were asked about demographics, income level, OAB symptoms via OAB symptom score (OABSS) and occupational voiding restrictions via a novel survey. Differences in median reported occupational voiding restrictions was determined via Kruskal-Wallis H test and post-hoc Dunn test. Spearman’s Rank-Sum correlations were conducted to determine associations between OABSS and occupational voiding restrictions scale. RESULTS: Three hundred and forty one participants completed the survey with median age of 35-44 years old, predominantly female gender (76.0%), predominantly white ethnicity (87.1%), and median household income of $60-80K. As shown in (https://www.auajournals.org/doi/abs/10.1097/01.JU.0001191360.00345.d8.25#F1), low-income participants reported significantly higher occupational voiding restrictions than high-income participants (H(2)=6.52, p=0.038). As shown in Table 1, weak correlations were found between OABSS and occupational voiding restrictions (r=0.16, p<.01). When stratified by income, low income individuals had a moderate association between OABSS scores and distress caused by occupational voiding restrictions (r=0.40, p<.01). CONCLUSIONS: Occupational voiding restrictions are associated with OAB symptoms in a large sample of employed adults. Low-income individuals are most affected by occupational voiding restrictions and experience greater association between restrictions and distress. Physicians should advocate for healthy toileting behaviors at the workplace.

title: IP16-26: Understanding Primary Care Provider Urinary Incontinence Knowledge
parentSessionTitle: IP16: Urodynamics/Lower Urinary Tract Dysfunction/Female Pelvic Medicine: Overactive Bladder
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Urinary incontinence (UI) places a substantial social and economic burden on women, with its prevalence rising alongside an aging population. We are conducting a study to improve the quality of care for women with UI. As part of this effort, we assessed baseline knowledge of primary care providers (PCPs) regarding UI using a validated questionnaire. Here, we present the findings from our baseline assessment. METHODS: This is an ongoing a multi-site cluster randomized comparative effectiveness trial at three academic institutions: University of California of San Diego, University of California Los Angeles, Cedars-Sinai Medical Center, and University of Kansas. As part of the baseline assessment, participating PCPs complete the Pelvic Floor Awareness Knowledge Survey (PFAKS), a validated 31-item knowledge questionnaire with three domains: stress urinary incontinence (10 items), overactive bladder (10 items), and pelvic organ prolapse (11 items), with questions on condition pathophysiology, management, and quality of life. Responses from the PFAKS will undergo thorough analysis to evaluate PCPs’ knowledge levels across the three topics. RESULTS: Results from 158 UI knowledge questionnaires were reviewed. The average number of years in practice is 7.17 years. For 15 of the 20 questions related to OAB/UI, PCPs had the correct answer more than 60% of the time (See (https://www.auajournals.org/doi/abs/10.1097/01.JU.0001191360.00345.d8.26#F1)). More than a third (28.4%) of PCPs incorrectly indicated that medications could cure pure stress urinary incontinence (SUI), with the highest rate of incorrect responses. In addition, PCPs were given the option to indicate whether they did not know the answer to a question. The top two questions with the highest rate of uncertainty were understanding whether surgery could cure urinary incontinence and the relationship between overactive bladder and fluid intake. CONCLUSIONS: Although most PCPs have strong overall knowledge of UI pathophysiology, treatment, and quality of life, significant knowledge gaps remain. These data have informed our targeted education and custom clinical decision support tools to enhance PCPs’ UI knowledge as part of our ongoing UI quality improvement work.

title: IP16-27: Post-Micturition Dribbling: New Insights into the Role of Post-Void Residual Volume and After-Contractions — A Prospective Study
parentSessionTitle: IP16: Urodynamics/Lower Urinary Tract Dysfunction/Female Pelvic Medicine: Overactive Bladder
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Post-micturition dribbling (PMD) is defined as passive urinary leakage immediately following voiding. Despite its high prevalence among men, affecting up to 58%, and its significant impact on quality of life, research on its etiological and clinical aspects remains limited. Notably, PMD is not included in the International Prostate Symptom Score (IPSS) questionnaire. We aimed to search for clinical risk factors for PMD, perhaps providing clues about its possible etiology. METHODS: A prospective study was conducted with systematic data collection. Male patients aged 18 and above referred for urodynamic evaluation for any indication were asked to complete a structured form incorporating the IPSS and specific questions regarding PMD. Additional clinical parameters were recorded, including PSA levels, US data, age, comorbidities, medications, and prior surgeries. Data was collected from a total of 160 patients. Statistical analysis was performed to assess correlations between clinical variables and the presence of PMD ( Table 1). RESULTS: Univariate analysis revealed a statistically significant correlation between post-void residual (PVR) volume and PMD, as well as between after-contractions and PMD. Multivariate logistic regression ( (https://www.auajournals.org/doi/abs/10.1097/01.JU.0001191360.00345.d8.27#F1)) demonstrated a linear association between increasing PVR volume and PMD, with an odds ratio (OR) of 1.08 for every 10 ml increase in residual volume (95% CI: 1.03–1.14). The strongest association was observed in patients with PVR exceeding 85 ml (AUC=0.63). This correlation persisted after adjustment for additional clinical variables, including diabetes, prior surgeries, benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH), age, detrusor overactivity (DO), bladder outlet obstruction (BOO), and after-contractions. No significant correlation was found between PMD and the presence of BOO or DO on urodynamic testing. CONCLUSIONS: Elevated post-void residual volume and after-contractions are independent and significant risk factors for post-micturition dribbling. These findings suggest a pathophysiological link that warrants further investigation to elucidate the underlying mechanisms and to develop targeted diagnostic and therapeutic approaches. | | | --- | | |

title: IP16-28: COMPARATIVE ASSESSMENT OF TWO STANDARD OF CARE PAIN MANAGEMENT PROTOCOLS FOR INTRADETRUSOR ONABOTULINUMTOXINA INJECTIONS IN A DIVERSE URBAN PATIENT POPULATION
parentSessionTitle: IP16: Urodynamics/Lower Urinary Tract Dysfunction/Female Pelvic Medicine: Overactive Bladder
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Intravesical alkalinized lidocaine instillation prior to intradetrusor onabotulinumtoxinA (BTX-A) injection for refractory overactive bladder (OAB) may be undesirable to some patients due to prolonged appointment time and associated discomfort. This study evaluates the utility of oral phenazopyridine as a feasible alternative to intravesical instillation for periprocedural pain control. METHODS: This ongoing prospective, non-randomized study includes nonpregnant women aged ≥18 years undergoing BTX-A for idiopathic, refractory OAB. Patients received either oral phenazopyridine two hours pre-procedure or a 20-minute intravesical alkalinized lidocaine instillation for pain control. The primary outcome was post-procedure pain measured using a 100 mm visual analog scale (VAS). Secondary outcomes included overall satisfaction and preference for future pain control. Preliminary statistical analysis was performed by Mann-Whitney (Wilcoxon) tests with p<0.05 considered significant. RESULTS: Eighty-six patients were recruited; 60 received intravesical lidocaine and 26 received oral phenazopyridine. Participants represent a racially and socially diverse population; 51.4% percent self-identified as Hispanic and 32.4% as Black, and 51.1% live in areas where over 27.7% of women live below the poverty level. There were no differences in sample demographics between groups. Most patients (73.3%) had previously received BTX-A. Post-procedure pain scores and overall satisfaction were not significantly different between groups (p=0.212 and p=0.359, respectively). Among phenazopyridine recipients, 13/14 reported they would choose it again for future injections. CONCLUSIONS: Oral phenazopyridine represents a feasible alternative for periprocedural pain control prior to intravesical onabotulinumtoxinA injections when patients prefer a less invasive or quicker option. These findings highlight an important opportunity for shared decision-making and operational efficiency in the outpatient procedure setting. | | | --- | | |

title: IP16-29: Intradetrusor OnabotulinumtoxinA is Safe and Effective in Men with Overactive Bladder following Radical Prostatectomy or Outlet Surgery
parentSessionTitle: IP16: Urodynamics/Lower Urinary Tract Dysfunction/Female Pelvic Medicine: Overactive Bladder

speakers.organization: David Geffen School of Medicine at UCLA

fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: After radical prostatectomy (RP) or outlet surgery (OS), men often experience overactive bladder (OAB) and may be offered intradetrusor onabotulinumtoxinA (onabotA) for refractory symptoms. Efficacy and safety of onabotA are well established in the general population, but outcomes in men with surgically altered lower urinary tracts remain poorly characterized. This study evaluated safety and persistence of onabotA in men with and without prior RP or OS. METHODS: We conducted a retrospective review of men treated with intradetrusor onabotA for OAB at a single center from January 2018 to September 2025. Patients were categorized into 3 groups: (1) prior RP (n=33), (2) prior OS (TURP, HoLEP, TURBN, GreenLight, or Aquablation) (n=42), and (3) no prior OS or RP (n=51). Outcomes included new clean intermittent catheterization (CIC), elevated post-void residual (PVR ≥200cc), escalation of therapy (sacral neuromodulation or augmentation cystoplasty), and persistence of therapy by Kaplan-Meier analysis. Group comparisons were performed using Fisher’s exact and log-rank tests. RESULTS: Table 1 compares CIC, elevated PVR, and escalation rates in the 3 groups. Kaplan-Meier analysis demonstrated 36-month continuation rates of 85.8% for prior RP, 38.4% for prior OS, and 81.5% for no OS or RP. Pairwise comparisons showed lower persistence in the OS group compared to without (p=0.045) but no difference between prior RP and no OS or RP (p=1.000). CONCLUSIONS: Intradetrusor onabotA for OAB is safe and well tolerated in men with or without prior prostate surgery. Men with prior RP had no new catheterizations and lower rates of adverse outcomes compared with those without prior OS or RP, while also demonstrating long-term persistence. In contrast, patients with prior OS had comparable safety outcomes to patients with no prior OS or RP but exhibited reduced persistence. | | | --- | | |

title: IP17-01: Impact of Intravesical Prostatic Protrusion on Continence Outcomes Following Single-Port Transvesical Radical Prostatectomy
parentSessionTitle: IP17: Prostate Cancer: Localized: Surgical Therapy I
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: The effect of intravesical prostatic protrusion (IPP) on continence recovery after radical prostatectomy is not well established. Previous studies relied on intraoperative assessment and categorized IPP only as present or absent. We sought to evaluate IPP quantitatively on preoperative MRI using a validated grading system and to assess its impact on continence recovery following single-port transvesical radical prostatectomy (SP-TV RARP). METHODS: We retrospectively reviewed a prospectively maintained database of patients who underwent SP-TV RARP between November 2020 and August 2024. IPP was measured on mid-sagittal T2-weighted MRI as the perpendicular distance from the tip of the protruding prostatic tissue into the bladder to the bladder circumference at the prostate base. IPP was graded as: 0 (none), I (≤5 mm), II (>5–10 mm), or III (>10 mm). Continence, defined as <2 pads/day, was assessed immediately (≤1 week), and at 6 weeks, 3, 6, 9, and 12 months after Foley removal. Kaplan–Meier analysis and chi-square tests compared outcomes across IPP groups (Python 3.11, Python Software Foundation, Wilmington, DE). RESULTS: Of 208 eligible patients with complete MRI and continence data ( Table 1), immediate continence rates were 46.8%, 43.5%, 25.5%, and 25.0% in IPP 0, I, II, and III groups, respectively. There is no significant difference among IPP groups in BMI. Older age is associated only with IPP grade 3 compared to grade 0. Prostate volume is significantly larger in IPP grade 2 and 3 compared to grade 0, and larger in grade 3 compared to grade 1. Higher IPP grades were associated with lower immediate continence, though the difference approached but did not reach statistical significance (P=0.052). Patients with grade II–III IPP demonstrated delayed recovery, yet continence exceeded 95% in all groups by 9–12 months (p>0.05) ( (https://www.auajournals.org/doi/abs/10.1097/01.JU.0001191364.82577.9a.01#F2)). CONCLUSIONS: While IPP may create a wider bladder neck defect, it does not seem to adversely affect short or long-term continence outcomes of SP-TV RARP.

title: IP17-02: Optimizing PSA Follow-Up After Radical Prostatectomy: A Population-Based Analysis of Biochemical Recurrence Patterns
parentSessionTitle: IP17: Prostate Cancer: Localized: Surgical Therapy I
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: The oncological follow-up of patients with prostate cancer treated with radical prostatectomy (RP) is based on serial PSA measurements. However, the optimal duration and frequency of PSA testing during follow-up remain debated. In this context, we evaluated the incidence and patterns of biochemical recurrence (BCR) following RP. METHODS: This population-based study utilized data from the STHLM0 register. We included only patients undergoing RP between 2003 and 2023, resulting in a final cohort of 11,070 patients. All PSA values during their lifetime were available. We calculated the annual incidence of BCR (defined as PSA ≥0.2 ng/mL on two consecutive measurements) for patients grouped according to CAPRA risk categories. In addition, we plotted BCR incidence using the LOWESS smoothing function. The same analyses were performed for high-risk (HR) and low-risk (LR) BCR, defined according to EAU criteria. RESULTS: The median preoperative PSA was 7.3 (interquartile range \[IQR\]: 5.0–11.0). Overall, 2696 (30%) patients had pT3 disease, and 4328 (39%) and 985 (9%) patients had ISUP 3 and 4-5 at final pathology, respectively. According to CAPRA risk stratification, 4575 (41%), 5170 (47%), and 1325 (12%) patients were classified as low-, intermediate-, and high-risk, respectively. After a median follow-up of 85 months (IQR: 51–136) among patients without BCR, 2392 (22%) experienced recurrence. Among these, 1439 had HR-BCR. (https://www.auajournals.org/doi/abs/10.1097/01.JU.0001191364.82577.9a.02#F1) illustrates the annual incidence of BCR by year of follow-up. The incidence of BCR and HR-BCR was highest in the CAPRA high-risk group (≈13% in the first year), decreasing steadily during the first 5 years of follow-up before stabilizing thereafter (≈1%, Figure 1b). Similar patterns were observed among patients in the low- and intermediate-risk groups. Conversely, the incidence of LR-BCR remained relatively stable throughout follow-up ( Figure 1c); for example, LR-BCR incidence ranged from 3% to 2% among patients in the CAPRA high-risk group. CONCLUSIONS: Most BCR after RP occur within the first 5 years after treatment, particularly among high-risk patients. Similarly, the incidence of HR-BCR after 5 years of follow-up is very low. PSA follow-up schedules after RP should be guided by patient-specific risk factors. Given that most recurrences arise within 5 years after surgery, a de-intensified surveillance strategy may be appropriate beyond this period, especially for low-risk patients.

title: IP17-03: Integrating Preoperative PSMA-PET and MRI Findings to Predict Nodal Metastasis in Prostate Cancer Patients Undergoing Prostatectomy
parentSessionTitle: IP17: Prostate Cancer: Localized: Surgical Therapy I

speakers.organization: American University of Beirut Medical Center

fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: PSMA-PET scan and MRI are increasingly utilized in prostate cancer staging, particularly in differentiating between localized and metastatic disease and in predicting regional lymph node involvement. We aimed to evaluate the accuracy of PSMA-PET in predicting lymph node involvement among patients undergoing prostatectomy, and to assess other predictors of lymph node positivity. METHODS: Patients who underwent robotic-assisted radical prostatectomy at our center between 2018 and 2024, with available preoperative PSMA-PET and MRI scans were included. Patients with positive lymph nodes on pathology were compared to those without using t-tests for continuous variables and Chi-Square or Fisher’s Exact tests for categorical variables. The index prostate lesion was defined as the one with the highest PIRADS score (or largest size if equal) on MRI and the highest SUVmax on PSMA-PET. MRI was used to measure index lesion size. PSMA-PET sensitivity, specificity, PPV, and NPV for predicting nodal positivity were calculated. Univariate and multivariate logistic regression identified predictors of nodal metastasis. RESULTS: A total of 190 patients were included. 17 patients (8.9%) had positive lymph nodes on pathology, and 22 patients (11.6%) had positive lymph nodes on PSMA-PET scan, resulting in a sensitivity of 41.2%, specificity of 90.5%, PPV of 31.8% and NPV of 93.5%. Patients with positive lymph nodes on pathology had a higher probability of having PSA>10 ng/dL (p=0.01), higher SUVmax of index lesion (p=0.049), higher proportion of higher gleason grade group on biopsy (p=0.001), and a larger index lesion size on MRI (p=0.007). After adjusting for age, BMI, preoperative PSA and SUVmax of index lesion, we found that index lesion size was significantly associated with increased odds of having positive lymph nodes on pathology (OR 2.91, p=0.045). Alternatively, SUVmax of index lesion failed to show a statistically significant association after adjusting for age, BMI, preoperative PSA and index lesion size. CONCLUSIONS: PSMA-PET demonstrates high specificity but limited sensitivity for detecting lymph node metastasis, suggesting it should not be solely relied upon to omit lymph node dissection during prostatectomy. Index lesion size is a strong predictor of nodal positivity, while other PSMA-PET parameters such as index lesion SUVmax may also be associated, warranting further exploration in other cohorts. | | | --- | | |

title: IP17-04: Saline-Assisted Fascial Engorgement (SAFE) Nerve Preservation Guided by Micro-Ultrasound During Robotic Radical Prostatectomy: Interim Analysis of a Phase III Randomized Controlled Trial
parentSessionTitle: IP17: Prostate Cancer: Localized: Surgical Therapy I

speakers.organization: Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai.

fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Erectile dysfunction remains a major morbidity after radical prostatectomy. The Saline-Assisted Fascial Engorgement (SAFE) technique, first described by our group (BJU Int, 2023), uses real-time 29-MHz micro-ultrasound–guided low-pressure hydrodissection to achieve atraumatic fascial separation and enhance visualization of the neurovascular bundle. This randomized controlled trial (RCT) compared the functional and oncologic outcomes of SAFE and standard robotic-assisted radical prostatectomy (RARP). METHODS: In this single-center RCT, patients were randomized 1:1 using permuted blocks, stratified by age (<60 vs ≥60 years) and baseline SHIM score (<22 vs ≥22). Patients and outcome assessors remained blinded. The primary endpoint was 6-month erectile function recovery (SHIM ≥17). Secondary outcomes included SHIM/EHS (Erection Hardness Score) trajectories, urinary continence, and oncologic parameters. The primary endpoint was analyzed using a one-sided pooled z-test (α=0.15), and secondary outcomes were evaluated descriptively. This report presents the planned interim analysis. RESULTS: A total of 107 patients were included (SAFE=54, Control=53). At 6 months, erectile function recovery occurred in 51.9% of SAFE vs 43.4% of controls (Δ=8.5%, 95% CI –10 to 27; one-sided p=0.22). SAFE showed higher early recovery at 6 weeks (37.0% vs 20.8%; p=0.032) and a trend at 3 months (44.4% vs 37.7%; p=0.24). Linear mixed models demonstrated faster early SHIM and EHS improvement in the SAFE group (+2 SHIM, +0.5 EHS; p ≈ 0.04), converging by 6 months. Urinary continence and oncologic outcomes were similar (PSM 9.3% vs 11.3%; BCR 3.7% vs 5.7%; p>0.6). No technique-related complications occurred. CONCLUSIONS: Although the primary endpoint of 6-month erectile function recovery was not statistically significant, the SAFE technique achieved faster early recovery at 6 weeks, with no differences in complication rates or oncologic outcomes. These findings suggest that SAFE may enhance early neurovascular recovery without compromising safety or cancer control.

title: IP17-05: Erectile Function Outcomes After Menon Precision Prostatectomy: Analyzing Predictors of Functional Recovery and Evidence of Reproducibility of Outcomes
parentSessionTitle: IP17: Prostate Cancer: Localized: Surgical Therapy I

speakers.organization: Icahn School of Medicine At Mount Sinai

fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Menon Precision Prostatectomy (MPP) is a subtotal surgical treatment for localized prostate cancer (PCa) that involves preserving the unilateral capsule and seminal vesicle on the side opposite the dominant nodule. We sought to assess potency rates after MPP, identify predictors of potency recovery, and explore the reproducibility of outcomes. METHODS: MPP was offered to patients with intermediate-risk PCa who prioritized maintaining erectile function. Four surgeons performed MPP at three different centers with different surgical teams. Potency was defined as SHIM≥17 both preoperatively and postoperatively. The primary study measure was the potency rate at 12 months. Multivariable Cox regression was used to identify predictors of potency recovery. RESULTS: A total of 175 patients underwent MPP for intermediate-risk PCa. The median age and preoperative SHIM score were 61 years (IQR 56-66) and 22 (IQR 18-24.5) respectively, with 79% reporting SHIM≥17 prior to surgery. At 12 months, 90% of preoperatively potent patients regained erectile function. Cox regression analysis showed that age (>60 yr vs. ≤60 yr: HR=0.53) and preoperative potency status (Preoperative SHIM≥17 vs. SHIM<17: HR=8.3) were significant predictors of potency recovery. The type of nerve-sparing on the radical side did not influence postoperative recovery. There was no difference in potency recovery between surgeons. CONCLUSIONS: Nearly 90% of patients undergoing MPP recover erectile function by 12 months. While age and preoperative functional status are the primary determinants of postoperative function, nerve-sparing on the radical side does not impact erectile recovery. The technique was reproducible across multiple surgeons with varying levels of experience. Further studies are required to support these findings.

title: IP17-06: Omitting Pelvic Lymph Node Dissection in Prostate Cancer Patients with Negative PSMA-PET/CT: A Multicenter Study Challenging Current Nomogram Recommendations
parentSessionTitle: IP17: Prostate Cancer: Localized: Surgical Therapy I
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Pelvic lymph node dissection (PLND) remains controversial in prostate cancer (PCa) patients with nodes-negative preoperative PSMA-PET/CT imaging. This study aimed to evaluate the oncological outcomes of performing versus omitting PLND in PSMA-negative PCa patients with a high risk of lymph-node invasion, undergoing radical prostatectomy. METHODS: From an initial cohort of 1713 high (HR) and intermediate (IR) PCa patients, miN0M0 at preoperative PSMA-PET, we retrieved those with lymph node invasion (LNI) probability exceeding the threshold defined by the Briganti 2023 score. Patients were divided into PLND and no-PLND. Outcomes were PSA persistence, biochemical recurrence (BCR) and radiological recurrence (RR)-free survival (FS). Kaplan-Meier analysis was used for survival outcomes. Multivariable regression analyses were performed to identify preoperative and postoperative predictors of disease persistence or progression, adjusting for PLND status and covariates encompassed by the UCSF-CAPRA and postoperative S-CAPRA scoring systems. RESULTS: A total of 963 patients were included, comprising 208 without ePLND and 755 with ePLND. PLND was associated with increased 90-day postoperative complications (n=97,18.7% vs n=20, 10%), especially high-grade complications (n=54, 10.4% vs n=12,6% p=0.02). No significant differences were found between PLND (n=755) and no-PLND (n=208) in PSA persistence (11.6% vs 8.7%, p=0.23), BCR (19.7% vs 16.4%, p=0.29) and RR (8.4% vs 10.2%, p=0.41) rates after a median follow up of 25 months. Survival analyses showed that BCR-FS and RR-FS were comparable between groups (p>0.05). In the multivariable analyses avoiding PLND was not predictive of PSA persistence, BCR and RR. Limitations of the study include the retrospective design. CONCLUSIONS: PLND did not provide significant oncological benefit in PCa patients with a node-negative PSMA-PET/CT scan but a high risk of LNI. Avoiding PLND in this setting seems not to compromise short-to-medium term oncological outcomes but has a significant impact in reducing perioperative complications. | | | --- | | |

title: IP17-07: The RoboSling randomised controlled trial - continence outcomes with autologous vascularised bladder neck sling during robotic radical prostatectomy
parentSessionTitle: IP17: Prostate Cancer: Localized: Surgical Therapy I

speakers.organization: Urological Society of Australia and NZ & University of Toronto

fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: The morbidity of robot-assisted radical prostatectomy (RARP) is often secondary to functional complications i. e. post-prostatectomy incontinence and sexual dysfunction. The gold standard surgical treatment for PPI succeeds by strengthening the urethral-sphincter mechanism with a sling or an artificial sphincter. Intra-operative methods to do the same are a crucial knowledge gap in the RARP era. This study evaluates the use of a novel well-vascularised, autologous intra-operative sling to support the bladder neck and the urethra – the ‘RoboSling’. A retrospective cohort study evaluating this technique in our institution has demonstrated improved continence outcomes. METHODS: In this phase 3 study, adult men with localised prostate cancer who underwent RARP were randomised, and blinded, to RARP with RoboSling (intervention) or RARP alone (control) in a 1:1 fashion following a strict inclusion criteria. RARP and RoboSling techniques were standardised with only clinically indicated variations taking place to the prostatectomy portion. Sample size and power calculations (90% power, α=0.05) were based upon institutional continence data and pilot study results. The primary outcomes were early (3 month) and late (12 month) urinary incontinence measured via pad-free rate, mean pad number and 24-hour pad weight. Secondary endpoints included functional urinary parameters, peri-operative outcomes, oncological outcomes and patient reported outcomes. The trial was protocoled by the SLHD Human Research Ethics Committee (No. X16-0294&HREC/16/RPAH/377) and registered with the Australian New Zealand Clinical Trials Registry (ACTRN12618002058257). RESULTS: 123 patients were recruited between April 2019 and October 2024 (RoboSling: 62, Control: 61). There was no cross-over. 123 patients have reached 3-month follow-up, 12-month analysis is ongoing and will be completed in November 2025. At 6 weeks, of patients who did require continence pads, there were fewer mean number of pads in RoboSling arm (p=0.04) At 3 months, the complete pad-free rate was 42% in RoboSling and 41% in controls with no significant difference. There were no significant differences found with mean 24-hour pad weight or mean number of pads between the groups. There were no differences in secondary outcomes. CONCLUSIONS: The RoboSling at time of RARP was well tolerated with no adverse clinical or oncological outcomes. However, the RoboSling failed to demonstrate improvement in early continence compared to RARP alone. At 6 weeks, incontinent patients required fewer pads with RoboSling. Late continence outcomes are pending.

title: IP17-08: Evaluating Efficacy of Surgical Intervention Against Combination Radiation and Androgen Deprivation Therapy for men with Locally Advanced Prostate Cancer: An NCDB Analysis
parentSessionTitle: IP17: Prostate Cancer: Localized: Surgical Therapy I

speakers.organization: The George Washington School of Medicine and Health Sciences

fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Locally advanced prostate cancer (LAPCa), defined as cT3-4N0-1M0 prostate adenocarcinoma, remains a challenge in urologic oncology management. Although radiation therapy with androgen deprivation therapy (RT+ADT) is widely recommended as first-line treatment, radical prostatectomy (RP) +/- extended pelvic lymph node dissection has gained interest as an effective definitive treatment for this advanced disease. This study aims to compare overall survival (OS) between an RP-first approach and definitive RT+ADT in a large, contemporary cohort of patients with LAPCa. METHODS: A retrospective cohort study was conducted using the National Cancer Database (NCDB) for patients diagnosed from 2010 to 2022. We identified men with cT3-4N0-1M0 LAPCa who received either an RP-first strategy or definitive RT+ADT. After exclusions, 1:1 propensity score matching was performed to balance baseline characteristics and yielded n=4,271 patients in each treatment arm. The primary outcome was OS, analyzed using Kaplan-Meier curves and multivariable Cox proportional hazards models on the matched cohort, along with subgroup analyses. RESULTS: Definitive RT+ADT demonstrated superior OS compared with a surgery-first approach, with clear separation of Kaplan-Meier curves and an adjusted hazard ratio of 0.770. Subgroup analyses showed the survival benefit of RT+ADT was confined to node-negative patients (cN0 HR 0.748; p<0.001) and was concentrated in patients with Gleason Grade Group ≥ 4 (HR 0.726; p<0.001), with no significant advantage observed for node-positive or lower-grade subgroups, and the treatment effect was consistent across age (<70 and ≥70 years). In comparative Cox models using RP Alone as the reference, definitive RT+ADT had the best survival (HR 0.783; p<0.001), RP followed by postoperative radiation alone showed improved survival (HR 0.856; p=0.009), and patients who required RP with multimodal postop therapy (RP + postop RT + ADT) experienced the worst survival (HR 1.201; p=0.003). CONCLUSIONS: The survival advantage of RT+ADT over RP was strongest for N0, high-grade tumors and was consistent across age groups. Therefore, our findings support prioritizing RT+ADT for appropriate patients with cT3-4, N0, high Gleason grade disease and highlight the prognostic importance of nodal status, tumor grade, and comorbidity. However, how these results fare in the modern PSMA PET era remains to be seen.

title: IP17-09: Mortality after radical treatment of non-metastatic prostate cancer: A population-based cohort study
parentSessionTitle: IP17: Prostate Cancer: Localized: Surgical Therapy I
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: The comparative effectiveness of radical prostatectomy (RP) and radiotherapy (RT) for localized and locally advanced prostate cancer remains a topic of debate, particularly regarding prostate cancer–specific mortality (PCSM). We aimed to compare PCSM after RP and RT, stratified by biochemical recurrence-risk group, using long-term registry-based data. METHODS: We conducted a population-based cohort study including all men in Stockholm, Sweden, treated with curative intent for non-metastatic prostate cancer between July 2005 and December 2023, as identified through Swedish national registers. Flexible parametric survival models (Royston-Parmar) were used to estimate cumulative incidence and risk differences (RD), accounting for death from other causes as a competing risk. Models were adjusted for age, civil status, income, education, country of birth, year of treatment, healthcare utilization in the preceding year, Charlson comorbidity index, family history of prostate cancer, neoadjuvant hormonal therapy, prostate-specific antigen (PSA), Gleason grade, T-stage, and biochemical recurrence-risk group (low-, intermediate-, high-risk localized, and high-risk locally advanced) unless otherwise stratified. RESULTS: During the study, 17,794 men were treated radically for non-metastatic prostate cancer. Of them, 11,332 (63.7%) underwent RP, while 6,462 (36.3%) received RT. 3,597 (20.2%) men were < 60 years at time of treatment, 8.531 (47.9%) men aged 60-69, 5,320 (29.9%) men aged 70-79, and 346 (1.9%) were ≥80 years. Biochemical recurrence-risk distribution was 13.7% low-risk, 54.0% intermediate-risk, 16.5% high-risk localized, and 15.8% high-risk locally advanced disease. Over follow-up, 107 men (0.9%) died from prostate cancer after RP and 254 (3.9%) after RT. At 18-years, the cumulative incidence of PCSM was 1.8% (95% CI 1.4%, 2.4%) for RP and 4.7% (95% CI 3.8%, 6.0%) for RT, corresponding to an RD of 2.9% (95% CI 1.6%, 4.2%) favoring RP. Among men with low-risk disease, 9 deaths occurred during the follow-up (six among men treated with RP, and three after RT). At 18-years, the RD for PCSM favored RP with 2.1% (95% CI 0.4%, 3.7%) for intermediate-risk, 6.4% (95% CI 1.0%, 11.9%) for high-risk localized, and 11.6% (95% CI 4.8%, 18.3%) for high-risk locally advanced disease. CONCLUSIONS: Prostate cancer–specific mortality following radical treatment is low at 18-years. Comparing the radical treatment modality, RP was associated with a lower risk of PCSM compared with RT, improving with higher risk-group. While the non-randomized design limits causal interpretation, these results may inform shared decision-making alongside consideration of treatment-related adverse events.

title: IP17-10: Initial Outcomes Assessing Margin Status After Robot-Assisted Prostatectomy Using a Real-Time Digital Microscopy Device
parentSessionTitle: IP17: Prostate Cancer: Localized: Surgical Therapy I
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: In patients with prostate cancer undergoing robot-assisted radical prostatectomy (RARP), positive margins occur in approximately 11-38% of cases. Intraoperative frozen sections have been used for margin evaluation, but are limited to select regions, time-consuming, and resource-intensive. SamanTree Medical’s Histolog Scanner is a digital microscopy (DM) tool that enables rapid visualization and comprehensive margin assessment of much larger areas of the prostate directly in the operating room. This study evaluates the diagnostic accuracy of DM after RARP. METHODS: Specimens from RARPs performed from June 2025 to August 2025 were collected fresh, sent to pathology, and scanned in 5 quadrants (apex, left/right lateral, posterior, and base) using a DM unit. Each quadrant was recorded as being negative or suspicious for adenocarcinoma and compared to margin status on the final pathology report. Initially, five pathologists analyzed DM images. In a second evaluation, one pathologist who underwent advanced technical training reviewed all DM images independently. True negatives (TN) were defined as negative for adenocarcinoma on DM and positive for adenocarcinoma on final pathology. False negatives (FN) were negative on DM and positive on final pathology. True positives (TP) were positive on DM and positive on final pathology. False positives (FP) were positive on DM and negative on final pathology. Data from both phases were aggregated and diagnostic accuracy statistics were calculated. RESULTS: 31 RARPs were performed with 154 prostate locations analyzed for the presence of adenocarcinoma using DM. Results summarized in Tables 1 and 2. CONCLUSIONS: Our initial experience with DM demonstrates an excellent negative predictive value for ruling out positive margins after robot assisted radical prostatectomy (RARP). These results indicate that DM may be a useful tool for the efficient assessment of negative margin status during RARP. Future study should focus on optimizing the ability to accurately detect positive margins using DM and to investigate potential benefits in OR time and perioperative outcomes from its use. | | | --- | | | | | | --- | | |

title: IP17-11: Accuracy of Indocyanine Green Fluorescence in Detecting Lymph Node Metastases in High-Risk Prostate Cancer
parentSessionTitle: IP17: Prostate Cancer: Localized: Surgical Therapy I
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Prostate cancer is the most common solid malignancy in men worldwide. Although PSA screening and multiparametric MRI (mpMRI) enable early diagnosis and curative radical prostatectomy, accurately identifying nodal metastasis remains difficult. Extended pelvic lymphadenectomy (ePLND) is the staging gold standard but adds morbidity. Fluorescence-guided lymph node mapping with indocyanine green (ICG) offers a less invasive alternative. This study evaluated lesion-targeted ICG fluorescence (ICG-F), achieved by mpMRI–ultrasound fusion injection into the index lesion, to detect node metastasis. METHODS: This prospective, non-randomized study included 50 men with high-risk prostate cancer undergoing robotic prostatectomy. ICG was injected into the mpMRI-defined index lesion using fusion guidance, and fluorescence was visualized intraoperatively with the Firefly® system. All patients also underwent ePLND, and every lymph node was examined histologically. The primary endpoint was sensitivity for fluorescent node identification on a per-patient basis; secondary endpoints included specificity, positive and negative predictive values (PPV/NPV), and overall diagnostic accuracy. Statistical analyses were conducted in R using logistic regression, McNemar’s test, and the weighted kappa coefficient. RESULTS: The cohort’s mean age was 67 years (61–84) with BMI 25.4 kg/m2 (18.0–27.6). Median Charlson comorbidity index was 4.0 (3.0–5.0). Initial PSA averaged 20.52 ng/mL (9.6–23.2). Histology showed high-risk distribution: ISUP 4 in 48.2% and ISUP 5 in 30.4%. Most were ASA II (80%) and ECOG 0 (73.2%). Median Briganti score was 50% (21.2–72.0). Concordance between positive fluorescence and pathologic nodal metastasis occurred in 23 of 25 pN1 cases. Per-patient performance was: sensitivity 100% (95% CI 86–100), specificity 92% (74–99), PPV 93% (76–99), NPV 98% (85–100), and accuracy 96% (86–99). No adverse events related to ICG were observed. On lymph-node chain analysis, ICG-F showed sensitivity 0.66 and specificity 0.64 with NPV 0.93, outperforming mpMRI (sensitivity 0.04; specificity 0.99) and PET-PSMA (0.13;0.98, respectively). CONCLUSIONS: Lesion-targeted ICG-F achieved 96% accuracy for detecting nodal metastases in high-risk cases, outperforming PSMA PET/CT and mpMRI and providing real-time anatomic guidance. Given its high NPV, deferring completion ePLND after a positive fluorescence but negative intraoperative pathology seems safe in most patients, with ≈4% risk of missed nodal disease. The technique is safe and may support selective, anatomy-guided lymphadenectomy that lowers morbidity without compromising oncologic control.

title: IP17-12: Refining patient selection for salvage radical prostatectomy beyond EAU recommendations: development of a nomogram to estimate metastasis-free survival
parentSessionTitle: IP17: Prostate Cancer: Localized: Surgical Therapy I

speakers.organization: City of Health and Science, Molinette University Hospital, University of Turin

fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Salvage radical prostatectomy (sRP) represents a potentially curative treatment for locally recurrent prostate cancer (PCa), though it is associated with substantial morbidity. According to EAU recommendations, sRP should be reserved for patients in good condition and with favorable recurrence profiles, primarily defined by biochemical recurrence risk. Our objective was to construct a more precise predictive model for metastasis-free survival (MFS) to optimize candidate selection for sRP. METHODS: We retrospectively evaluated 1,265 men who underwent sRP between 2000 and 2021 across 14 high-volume centers. We excluded men with metastatic or castration-resistant disease, or with incomplete clinical data. Independent predictors of MFS were identified through multivariable Cox regression and used to generate a nomogram. The optimal threshold distinguishing low- and high-risk progression groups was established by maximizing the C-index for 10-year MFS. RESULTS: A total of 408 patients satisfied inclusion criteria. Preoperative PSA, clinical T stage, Gleason score, and time interval to sRP emerged as independent predictors of MFS (all p<0.05). Only 30% fulfilled EAU eligibility criteria (C-index 0.61; 10-year MFS for EAU-compliant men=84% \[95% CI: 76–93\]). Using a 75% 10-year MFS cut-off, our model stratified 60% of patients as high-risk and 40% as low-risk, enhancing discrimination (C-index 0.68). Kaplan–Meier analysis (p<0.001) demonstrated clear separation between high-risk (10y-MFS=51% \[95% CI: 42–63\]) and low-risk groups (10y-MFS=86% \[95% CI:\ 80–93\]), expanding the pool of potential surgical candidates by 33% (N=41). CONCLUSIONS: Conventional selection criteria may overlook patients suitable for curative surgery. Our Cox regression–based nomogram provides improved prognostic accuracy and supports individualized counselling, potentially extending access to local curative treatment. Further external validation and integration with novel imaging strategies are recommended.

title: IP17-13: Negative Preoperative PSMA PET Does Not Rule Out Nodal Metastasis Identification by Pelvic Lymphadenectomy
parentSessionTitle: IP17: Prostate Cancer: Localized: Surgical Therapy I
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: With the improved staging of prostate cancer afforded by prostate-specific membrane antigen positron emission tomography (PSMA-PET), the role of pelvic lymphadenectomy (PLND) at the time of prostatectomy has been called into question. We evaluated patients with negative preoperative PSMA-PET scans who underwent PLND to determine how often nodal metastasis was detected to inform whether PLND is still warranted in such patients. METHODS: We reviewed our prospective database of 1,231 prostatectomies between February 2023-October 2025 performed by a single surgeon (RA) and identified 501 patients who had undergone preoperative PSMA-PET scanning since it became available in our region. Of these patients, 478 had negative scans, and 23 had oligometastatic disease or suspicion of nodal metastasis on PSMA-PET and underwent prostatectomy but were excluded from analysis. All patients had identical PLND including external iliac, obturator and internal iliac nodes (Zones I-III). RESULTS: Among the 478 patients with negative preoperative PSMA-PET, 63% had Gleason 6 or 7 disease on biopsy and 37% had Gleason 8, 9 or 10. Mean PSA was 10.1 (0.2-122). A total of 38 patients (8%) with negative preoperative PSMA-PET had nodal metastasis identified on PLND with 1 to 3 nodes involved. Among these, 22 (58%) had Gleason 7 disease on biopsy with only 2 upgraded on final pathology (to Gleason 9). Mean preoperative PSA in this group was 14.2ng/mL with only 7 patients having a PSA greater than 20ng/mL. Sixteen patients had Gleason 7 on biopsy and PSA of 10ng/mL or less yet had nodal metastasis on PLND despite negative PSMA-PET. CONCLUSIONS: PSMA-PET failed to identify nodal metastasis in 8% of patients found to have involved nodes on PLND, which suggests that PLND is still warranted in these patients. Omission of PLND based on PSMA-PET would have understaged a significant number of patients, including many who did not have high-risk disease preoperatively.

title: IP17-14: Comparative Outcomes of Robotic Radical Prostatectomy Techniques: A Network Meta-Analysis of 5,641 Patients
parentSessionTitle: IP17: Prostate Cancer: Localized: Surgical Therapy I
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Single-port (SP) robotic-assisted radical prostatectomy (RARP) aims to minimize invasiveness while maintaining oncological and functional outcomes comparable to conventional multi-port (MP) surgery. This network meta-analysis compared perioperative, functional, and oncological results across five RARP techniques: transvesical single-port (TV-SP), extraperitoneal single-port (EXTRA-SP), intraperitoneal single-port (INTRA-SP), extraperitoneal multi-port (EXTRA-MP), and transperitoneal multi-port (TP-MP). METHODS: Nineteen comparative studies (n=5,641) were analyzed using random-effects network meta-analysis. Primary endpoints were 3-month continence, potency, and positive surgical margins (PSM). Secondary outcomes included estimated blood loss (EBL), catheter duration, length of stay (LOS), operative time, complications, nerve-sparing, and pelvic lymph node dissection (PLND) rates. Treatments were ranked using SUCRA probabilities. RESULTS: Functional outcomes: Early continence recovery favored EXTRA-SP (RR 1.80, p=0.003) and TV-SP (RR 1.67, p=0.01) over multi-port approaches. At 6 months, continence equalized. Potency was highest with EXTRA-SP (RR 1.15, p=0.007) and INTRA-SP (SUCRA 0.90), while MP approaches ranked lower but not significantly different. PSM rates were equivalent across all groups (p>0.05). Perioperative outcomes: SP approaches achieved significantly lower EBL (TV-SP –101 mL; EXTRA-SP –62 mL, p < 0.01), shorter LOS (EXTRA-SP –1.25 days; INTRA-SP –1.11 days, p < 0.01), and earlier catheter removal (TV-SP –4.3 days; INTRA-SP –2.8 days, p < 0.05). Operative time was modestly longer for SP (TV-SP +22 min; EXTRA-SP +11 min, p < 0.05). Complication rates and nerve-sparing frequency were comparable between SP and MP groups. PLND was performed less often in TV-SP (RR 0.34, p < 0.001) than in MP RARP. CONCLUSIONS: Across 19 studies, SP RARP provides equivalent oncological safety and superior early functional recovery compared with MP RARP. SP techniques—particularly TV-SP and EXTRA-SP—achieve faster continence and shorter hospitalization, while INTRA-SP yields the highest potency ranking. MP approaches remain advantageous when extended PLND is required. These data support SP RARP as a safe, effective, and recovery-enhancing alternative to traditional MP approaches in experienced hands.

title: IP17-15: Evaluating the Impact of Calculated Free Testosterone on Oncological Outcomes in Prostate Cancer Men Post Radical Prostatectomy
parentSessionTitle: IP17: Prostate Cancer: Localized: Surgical Therapy I

speakers.organization: University of California, Irvine Medical Center

fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Recent studies have shown that low testosterone levels have been associated with decreased libido, diminished energy, and increased mortality from cardiovascular disease and cancer. Calculated free testosterone (cFT), which reflects the biologically available portion of testosterone, is a more precise marker than total testosterone (TT) alone. This study evaluates the association between preoperative cFT and oncological outcomes, specifically biochemical recurrence (BCR), in men undergoing radical prostatectomy (RP). METHODS: Retrospective analysis of prospectively collected data of 1,299 men who underwent RP by a single surgeon between October 2005 and June 2025. Preoperative TT and sex hormone-binding globulin (SHBG) levels were collected, and cFT was calculated using the Vermeulen equation. Patients were stratified into cFT quartiles: Group 1 (≤4.65), Group 2 (4.66–6.01), Group 3 (6.02–7.56), and Group 4 (>7.56). Kaplan–Meier analysis was used to assess time to BCR, and multivariate regression identified independent predictors of recurrence. RESULTS: Baseline characteristics significantly differed across cFT quartiles for age, prostate weight, preoperative PSA, TT, SHBG, and Gleason Grade Group (all p<0.05). Men in the lowest cFT quartile (≤4.65) had higher rates of adverse pathology (pT3/4 disease 42.7%; p=0.0146), positive surgical margins (25.0%, p=0.0402), and BCR (36.0%; p<0.001) compared to higher quartiles. Kaplan-Meier analysis showed significantly worse BCR-free survival among men with lower cFT levels (p=0.0012). On multivariate analysis, independent predictors of BCR included age (OR 1.03, p=0.003), preoperative PSA (OR 1.14, p<0.001), BMI (OR 1.07, p<0.001), prostate weight (OR 0.99, p=0.008), and cFT (OR 0.88, p=0.003). CONCLUSIONS: Lower preoperative cFT was independently associated with increased risk of BCR after RP. These findings suggest that integrating cFT into preoperative risk stratification could enhance prediction of oncologic outcomes and support a more personalized postoperative management approach. | | | --- | | |

title: IP17-16: Impact of Primary Treatment Modalities on Survival in Ductal and Intraductal Prostate Carcinoma
parentSessionTitle: IP17: Prostate Cancer: Localized: Surgical Therapy I
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Ductal and Intraductal prostate carcinoma (DIPC) are rare, aggressive variants with limited disease-specific management guidelines. Based on risk stratification, treatment for localized DIPC varies between radical prostatectomy (RP), radiation ± androgen deprivation therapy (RT±ADT), and observation. A few studies in the literature evaluate survival outcomes across different treatment modalities. To evaluate this, we used the national cancer registry to compare survival outcomes between different treatment modalities in localized DIPC. METHODS: We identified patients diagnosed with localized DPC between 2004 and 2020. The analytical cohort included 3 groups: the RP cohort, comprising patients who underwent RP; the RT±ADT cohort, comprising patients who underwent RT±ADT; and the observation cohort, comprising patients under observation. We performed a Kaplan-Meier survival analysis to evaluate overall survival (OS). We also conducted a multivariate Cox proportional hazards model adjusting for age, race, NCCN risk classification, comorbidities, socioeconomic factors, and facility type to evaluate survival hazards. RESULTS: Among 2,650 patients with localized DIPC, 1,586 (59.8%), 785 (29.6%), and 279 (10.6%) underwent RP, RT±ADT, and observation, respectively. 2-year OS for RP, RT±ADT, and Observation was 98%, 94%, and 78% respectively (p<0.001). Similarly, 5-year OS was 92%, 81%, and 54% respectively (p<0.001). Multivariate Cox regression showed that RT±ADT was associated with increased mortality compared to RP (HR: 2.27; p<0.001). 2-year OS for patients with PSA ≤4ng/dL and >4ng/dL was 89.9% and 97.2%, respectively. Similarly, 5-year OS were 75.8% and 88.8%, respectively. Multivariate Cox regression showed that PSA ≤4 was associated with an increased risk of mortality compared with PSA >4 (HR: 1.27; p<0.05). CONCLUSIONS: In our study on localized DIPC, we observed that RP, with or without salvage therapy, had better OS than RT±ADT. The association of low PSA with worse prognosis could be due to dedifferentiation-driven aggressiveness. Therefore, based on risk stratification, a multimodal approach with RP as the initial treatment and RT±ADT could provide additional survival benefits.

title: IP17-17: Positive Surgical Margins Are Not Independently Associated with Biochemical Recurrence After Single Port Robot-Assisted Radical Prostatectomy: A Multi-Institutional Analysis from the Single Port Advanced Research Consortium (SPARC)
parentSessionTitle: IP17: Prostate Cancer: Localized: Surgical Therapy I
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: While prior studies have shown that positive surgical margins (PSMs) are not consistently associated with biochemical recurrence (BCR) after robot-assisted radical prostatectomy (RARP), evidence specific to the Single Port (SP) platform remains limited. In this study, we aimed to evaluate the relationship between PSMs and BCR following SP-RARP and to identify independent predictors of recurrence using data from the multi-institutional SP Advanced Research Consortium (SPARC). METHODS: A retrospective review was conducted using the prospectively maintained, IRB-approved database of the SPARC to identify all consecutive patients who underwent SP RARP across participating centers. Patients without postoperative PSA data or with less than 6 months of follow-up were excluded. BCR was defined according to the AUA guidelines. Kaplan–Meier analysis with log-rank testing and multivariable Cox regression were performed to evaluate predictors of BCR, including margin status. Grade Group, and pathologic stage. RESULTS: A total of 2,825 patients were identified across participating centers, of whom 1,473 met inclusion criteria for analysis. Among these, 396 (26.9%) had PSMs. Median follow-up was 27 months, during which 42 patients (2.9%) developed BCR. In multivariable Cox regression, PSM was not independently predictive of BCR (HR 1.24, 95% CI 0.74–2.08, p=0.42). Higher pathologic stage (pT3/4 vs pT2: HR 3.00 (95% CI 1.49–6.04), p=0.002) and higher Grade Group (GG 4–5 vs 1–3: HR 2.59 (95% CI 1.35–4.98), p=0.004) were independently associated with recurrence. The proportional hazards assumption was met (global p=0.269), and model robustness was confirmed with a site-level frailty analysis, which demonstrated similar findings. CONCLUSIONS: In this large multi-institutional analysis, PSMs were not independently associated with BCR following SP RARP. Pathologic stage and tumor grade were the primary determinants of recurrence. These findings suggest that margin status alone does not appear to confer additional prognostic significance beyond established pathologic factors. | | | --- | | |

Uric acid kidney stones — comprised of uric acid crystals and
precipitated by acidic urine — account for 10-15 % of all cases of
nephrolithiasis1. Multiple factors contribute to the development of uric
acid kidney stones, including hypovolemia, persistently low urine pH, and
hyperuricosuria, as well as comorbidities such as obesity, metabolic

IP18-21: Effect of Preoperative Silodosin on Outcomes
                                                               of Ureteroscopy for Ureterolithiasis: A Systematic
                                                               Review and Meta-Analysis
                                                               Godinho N.J.S; Colhado C.H., de Amorim L.G.C.R., Andrade M.A., Vilela M.A.D., Menezes, T.H.F., da Costa S.E.M., Lipkin M.,
                                                               Mazzuchi E.M.



                                      PURPOSE
To perform a systematic review and meta-analysis evaluating the efficacy and safety of
preoperative silodosin in improving ureteroscopy (URS) outcomes for ureterolithiasis.


                                      METHODS
PubMed, EMBASE and Cochrane Central were systematically searched for studies
comparing preoperative silodosin with placebo or ‘no preoperative silodosin’ in patients
undergoing URS for ureteral stones. Primary outcomes included ureteral wall injury,
analgesia use, fever, hematuria, stone-free rate (SFR), operative time, and complications.
Statistical analysis was performed using Review Manager 5.1.7. Study quality and risk of
bias         were           assessed            per          Cochrane              guidelines.
                                                                                                    Figure 1 - PRISMA flow diagram of study screening and selection.
                                       RESULTS
Nine studies, including eight randomized clinical trials, including 960 patients were
analyzed; 450 (46.8%) received silodosin. Compared to controls, silodosin significantly
reduced ureteral injuries (RR 0.30; 95% CI: 0.18–0.49; p < 0.00001) and operative time
(MD -17.72 minutes; 95% CI: -24.72 to -10.72; p < 0.00001). It also lowered analgesia
needs (RR 0.35; 95% CI: 0.16–0.75; p = 0.007), with trends toward reduced fever (RR

0.06). In studies with ≥10 days of preoperative use, silodosin significantly improved SFR
(RR 1.17; 95% CI: 1.10–1.26; p < 0.00001).

supporting its use to improve safety and efficiency of URS for ureterolithiasis.

title: IP19-23: Predicting Success of Non-Operative Management in Renal Trauma: Accuracy of CT-Based Grading Systems
parentSessionTitle: IP19: Reconstruction: External Genitalia and Urotrauma (including transgender surgery and traumatic fistula)
fulltext:
IP19-23: Predicting Success of Non-Operative Management in Renal
                                                     Trauma: Accuracy of CT-Based Grading Systems
                                                     Authors: Silva P., Severo L., Cunha J., Caceiro R., Lança M., Almeida R., Gouveia S., Campos
                                                     Pinheiro L.
                                                     ULS S José; Nova Medical School                                              Lisbon, Portugal



INTRODUCTION                                                                         RESULTS
Non-operative management (NOM) has become the preferred strategy for                 Study characteristics:
hemodynamically stable renal trauma, but outcome prediction remains uncertain,       • 11 studies (5 high-grade only; 3 all grades; 3 unspecified), total ≈ 3 500 patients.
especially in high-grade injuries. This systematic review evaluated the predictive   • 8 retrospective, 2 prospective, 1 multi-institutional.
accuracy of CT-based grading systems and radiologic parameters for determining       Non-operative success:
NOM success across renal trauma severities.                                          • High-grade injuries (III–V): 52–92 % success.
                                                                                     • All-grade cohorts: 80–92 % success.
                                                                                     • AAST/CT grade predictive in 4 of 6 studies (OR up to 7.36).
METHODS                                                                              Quantitative accuracy:
A semantic systematic search using Pubmed, Embase and Scopus. Eleven met             • AUC = 0.83–0.88; sensitivity 90.5 %, specificity 78 %.
inclusion criteria: human studies using CT-based grading (AAST or equivalent),       • Active bleeding or contrast extravasation consistently predicted NOM failure.
reporting NOM outcomes and predictive accuracy. Extracted variables included         • Hematoma diameter > 3 cm and parenchymal devascularization > 25 % strongly associated
injury grade, CT features, NOM success rate, and diagnostic metrics (AUC,              with adverse outcomes.
sensitivity, specificity, OR/RR).
                                                                                     Combined predictive models:
                                                                                     • Variables most frequently included: injury grade, hemodynamic stability, hematoma size, and
                                                                                       extravasation.
                                                                                     • Best model (Kim et al., 2021): AUC 0.88; intrarenal contrast extravasation OR 7.41.
                                                                                     Functional outcomes:
                                                                                     • Two studies linked > 25 % parenchymal devascularization to long-term renal function loss.
                                                                                     • Successful NOM preserved renal units in > 75 % of cases (van der Wilden et al., 2013).



                                                                                     CONCLUSIONS
                                                                                     CT-based grading provides moderately accurate prediction of NOM success (AUC ≈ 0.85), but
                                                                                     precision increases when specific CT parameters—such as hematoma size, active bleeding, and
                                                                                     devascularization—are integrated. AAST grade alone underestimates risk in complex injuries.
                                                                                     Standardization of CT reporting and inclusion of quantitative markers could enhance decision-
                                                                                     making and reduce unnecessary nephrectomies. Prospective validation of AI-assisted CT
                                                                                     nomograms should be prioritized to optimize trauma triage and renal preservation

                                                                   Godinho N.J.S., Onofre J.C.M., Colhado C.H., Vilela M.A.D., Menezes T.H.F., Rodrigues H.G., Donalisio R.S.




                                         PURPOSE
The management of benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH) has evolved with the introduction of less
invasive surgical therapies. However, optimal treatment selection remains unclear due to limited
data. This network meta-analysis ranks the efficacy of established and emerging surgical
interventions to guide evidence-based clinical decision-making.


                                         METHODS
PubMed, EMBASE, and the Cochrane Library from 2015 to 2025 were searched for randomized
controlled trials comparing surgical interventions for BPH. Outcomes included International
Prostate Symptom Score (IPSS), maximum urinary flow rate (Qmax), postvoid residual (PVR),
and quality of life (QoL). Bayesian network meta-analysis was performed. Surface under the
cumulative ranking curve (SUCRA) values were calculated to rank the surgical procedures.
                                                                                                        Figure 1 - PRISMA flow diagram of study screening and selection.
                                         RESULTS
Among 36 randomized controlled trials and 4,782 patients, 12-month follow-up results
demonstrated that no individual intervention significantly outperformed bTURP in symptom
control, peak urinary flow, hospital stay, complications, or medical retreatment. PUL was the only
individual technique significantly inferior to bTURP in bladder emptying (MD 67.47 mL; 95% CrI
11.02 to 125.79). However, PUL demonstrated superior ejaculatory function preservation (MD
4.99; 95% CrI 1.32 to 8.64), despite comparable ejaculation. Surgical retreatment rates were
significantly lower for HoLEP, bTURP, mTURP, and PAE compared to mTURP. When techniques
were grouped by therapeutic class, Stent/Implant/Endoluminal devices were significantly inferior
to Enucleation, Ablation, and Resection in urinary function efficacy outcomes. Despite superior
ejaculatory function for Stent/Implant devices versus Resection (MD 5.01; 95% CrI 1.33 to 8.65),
ejaculation bother was comparable between groups. Enucleation was the only class to show
significantly reduced surgical retreatment rates versus sham.

                                      CONCLUSION
No intervention was superior to bTURP in urinary efficacy. HoLEP demonstrated better long-term
durability with lower surgical retreatment rates, whereas Stent/Implant/Endoluminal approaches          Figure 2 - Postvoidal Resdual Volume: (A) Surface under the cumulative ranking curve

                                                          BPH Treatment: Final Five-Year Results of Optilume BPH in the EVEREST
                                                          Study
                                                          Steven Kaplan and the EVEREST Investigators



INTRODUCTION                                                                  RESULTS
Optilume BPH is a novel drug/device combination product that utilizes         Three subjects (3/80, 3.8%) pursued additional BPH therapy (2 medication, 1 surgery) and were discontinued from
mechanical dilation of the prostatic urethra to achieve an anterior           further follow-up. Significant improvement was maintained in symptom scores, with IPSS improving from 22.3 at
commissurotomy while delivering the drug paclitaxel to maintain long-term     baseline to 11.1 at 5 years. Quality of life metrics, including IPSS QoL and BPH-II, showed steady improvement from
urethral patency. The EVEREST-I study is a prospective, single arm,           baseline. Functional improvement was also maintained, with an average baseline Qmax of 10.9 mL/sec improving to
multicenter study evaluating functional improvement in urine flow and         17.8mL/sec at the 5-year follow-up.
improvement in lower urinary tract symptoms (LUTS) after treatment with
the Optilume BPH System.


METHODS
80 subjects were enrolled at 6 centers in Latin America. Fifty-three (53)
subjects completed 5-year follow-up. Symptom improvement was
measured utilizing the International Prostate Symptom Score (IPSS) and
BPH Impact Index (BPH-II), functional improvement measured by peak
urinary flow rate (Qmax) and post-void residual volume (PVR). Subjects
receiving alternative therapy for BPH such as re-initiating medication
therapy or surgical intervention were considered treatment failures and
discontinued from further follow-up.


CONCLUSION
Treatment with Optilume BPH resulted in significant symptomatic and
functional improvements that were sustained through long-term follow-up.
These improvements were maintained with very limited rates of re-
treatment, with only 1 surgical retreatment (1.3%) and 2 patients re-
initiating BPH medications (2.5%). Optilume BPH represents a compelling
and durable option for the minimally invasive treatment of LUTS
secondary to BPH.

title: IP27-02: Predicting Persistent SUI After Weight-Loss Surgery: A Clinical Risk Score
parentSessionTitle: IP27: Urodynamics/Lower Urinary Tract Dysfunction/Female Pelvic Medicine: Female Incontinence
fulltext:
IP27-02: Predicting Persistent SUI After
                                                             Weight-Loss Surgery: A Clinical Risk
                                                             Score
                                                             Authors
INTRODUCTION                                                     RESULTS
Stress urinary incontinence (SUI) affects roughly one in
three women, and obesity is an independent risk factor.
Although bariatric surgery frequently produces marked
weight loss and symptomatic improvement, a subset of
patients remain incontinent. The objective was to identify
preoperative predictors of persistent SUI at six months
following bariatric surgery and to derive a point-based
clinical riskscore. Secondary aim: assess patient-
reported urinary symptoms and quality of life.


METHODS
Prospective observational study of women who
underwent bariatric surgery between 2015 and 2019 at
Irmandade da Santa Casa de Misericórdia de São
Paulo, Brazil. Evaluations occurred preoperatively and
at six months. Primary outcome: presence of SUI on
standardized stress testing. Multivariable analysis
identified independent predictors that informed a
weighted point score.


RESULTS
                                                                                    CONCLUSIONS
                                                                                    Age >47.5 years, menopause and genital
                                                                                    prolapse independently predict persistent
                                                                                    SUI after bariatric surgery.

fulltext:
Interactive Poster IP29 · AUA Annual Meeting 2026

                                                                                            Learning Curve of Aquablation: Insights from the First 252
                                                                                            Consecutive Cases in a High-Volume European Centre
                                                                                            Rodrigues T¹, Guerra J¹, Vilas Boas V¹, Pardal H¹, Apolinário M¹, Calais F¹, Zorn KC², Gomes JM¹
                                                                                            ¹GUPURO | Hospital Cruz Vermelha, Lisbon, Portugal                ²BPH Canada Surgical Solution Center, Montreal, Canada




    Introduction                                                                                      Results
                                                                                                      Cohort 252 cases · Mean prostate volume 78 → 100 mL across Q1→Q4 · Efficiency r = –0.24, p = 0.002 · Overall complications 8.3 %
    Aquablation in BPO
    • Robotic, image-guided waterjet ablation — surgeon-independent
    resection with minimal thermal injury.
    • Standardised technology with growing real-world adoption across
    Europe.
    Knowledge gap
    • Real-world learning curve data remain limited.
    • Pivotal trials enrolled experienced operators — proficiency timing in
    adoption settings is unclear.
    Aim
    • Characterise the learning curve and safety profile of Aquablation in 252
    consecutive cases at a high-volume European centre.                                                                    Fig 1 Robotic & total operative time, 20-case moving average — stabilisation after ≈40–50 cases.            Fig 2 Efficiency (min / mL) improves over time despite increasing prostate volume.




    Methods                                                                                           Safety & Functional Outcomes — across quartiles
                                                                                                      No statistical difference across Q1–Q4 in complications, catheterisation, hospital stay or IPSS.
    Design
    • Single-centre, retrospective review of 252 consecutive cases
    (Nov 2022 – Mar 2024).

    Cohort partitioning
    • Cases ordered chronologically and divided into quartiles (Q1–
    Q4, n = 63 each).
    • 20-case moving averages used to visualise temporal trends.

    Outcomes assessed                                                                                 Conclusions
    ▸ Robotic resection time (primary)                                                                Short, safe learning curve.
    ▸ Total operative time                                                                            • Proficiency in robotic resection time achieved within 40–50 cases.
    ▸ Efficiency (min / mL prostate volume)                                                           • Total operative time stable from outset — workflow consistency, not compensatory delay.
    ▸ Complications (Clavien-Dindo)
                                                                                                      Efficiency improves with experience.
    ▸ Catheterisation duration & length of stay
                                                                                                      • Min/mL decreases significantly (r = –0.24, p = 0.002) despite a parallel rise in prostate volume from 78 → 100 mL.
    ▸ Functional outcomes — IPSS, IIEF-5
                                                                                                      Safety preserved throughout.
    Statistics                                                                                        • Overall complications 8.3 %; catheterisation, hospital stay and functional scores stable across Q1–Q4.

    • Descriptive comparison across quartiles; Spearman correlation
                                                                                                      Take-home
    for efficiency vs case order.                                                                     • Aquablation is a reproducible, scalable, trainable technique — relevant for accreditation pathways and broader European adoption .
    • Significance threshold p < 0.05.

                                                               1 Urology Division, Rabin Medical Center, Petah Tikva, 2 Faculty of Medicine, Tel-Aviv University, Tel-Aviv, Israel




                    Introduction                                                                               Results                                                                              Clinical Plan
 • The use of artificial intelligence (AI) in medicine is rapidly
   expanding.
 • Urodynamic study (UDS) interpretation is complex and
   highly dependent on expertise.
 • This study evaluated the reliability of ChatGPT-5 in UDS
   interpretation and its agreement with expert clinical
   recommendations.
                    Methods
• High-resolution images of urodynamic studies, retrospectively
  interpreted by three independent experts, were uploaded to
  the ChatGPT-5 platform.
• The model completed a structured interpretation form
  comprising 32 filling, voiding, and summary categories and
  proposed a treatment plan.
• Outputs were compared with expert interpretation, and a
  weighted reliability score was calculated for each case.
• The model was not trained between cases.

title: IP33-18: Nocturnal Bladder Capacity Index Assessment to Improve Nocturia Management in Patients with Lower Urinary TractSymptoms Related to Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia
parentSessionTitle: IP33: Urodynamics/Lower Urinary Tract Dysfunction/Female Pelvic Medicine: Non-neurogenic Voiding Dysfunction (excluding OAB)
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Nocturia is a prevalent and disruptive symptom in men with BPH. The Nocturnal Bladder Capacity Index (NBCI) is a diagnostic toolthat helps differentiate between nocturia subtypes, such as nocturnal polyuria (NP) and reduced nocturnal bladder capacity (NBC),guiding targeted treatments. This study compares the clinical outcomes of NBCI-guided management versus non-stratified standardtreatment approaches in men with BPH-associated nocturia. METHODS: This prospective study included men between 45 and 65 years old with significant nocturia (≥3 voids/night) and LUTS related toBPH. Participants were divided into the NBCI guided and non NBCI groups. The NBCI-guided group underwent differential diagnosisbased on NBCI values. Patients with NBCI >1.3, indicating reduced NBC, were treated with tamsulosin (0.4 mg/day) and solifenacin(5 mg/day). Patients with NBCI ≤1.3 underwent frequency-volume charts and nocturnal urine volume (NUV) assessment todetermine the presence of NP or other bladder dysfunctions. Patients with NP were treated with desmopressin (0.2 mg/day); thosewithout NP were treated according to their specific diagnosis. The non-NBCI group received treatment with tamsulosin (0.4 mg/day).Outcomes were assessed at 6 months, including nocturnal void frequency (NVF) and IPSS. RESULTS: A total of 150 men were included (75 in the NBCI-guided group and 75 in the non-NBCI group). The NBCI-guided group achieved a55% reduction in NVF (from 3.6 to 1.6, p<0.001), compared to a 30% reduction in the non-NBCI group (from 3.5 to 2.5, p<0.001).IPSS scores improved in the NBCI-guided group, decreasing from 22.6 to 13.7 (p<0.001). The non-NBCI group showed a smallerimprovement from 22.4 to 17.2 (p<0.09). In patients with NBCI≤1.3, 73% were diagnosed with NP and experienced a 58% reductionin NVF (from 3.5 to 1.5, p<0.001) with desmopressin (0.2 mg/day). The remaining 27% without NP achieved a 48% reduction in NVF(from 3.4 to 1.8, p<0.01) when treated according to the diagnosis. Patients with NBCI>1.3 treated with tamsulosin (0.4 mg/day) andsolifenacin (5 mg/day) showed a 41% reduction in NVF (from 3.8 to 2.2, p<0.01). CONCLUSIONS: The results demonstrate that NBCI-guided management is significantly more effective than non-stratified approaches in reducing NVF and improving IPSS. By distinguishing between NP and other bladder dysfunctions, NBCI-guided treatment enabled targeted interventions. Desmopressin was highly effective for NP. These findings highlight the clinical value of NBCI in optimizing treatmentfor nocturia and reducing symptom burden in men with BPH. NBCI-guided management outperformed non-stratified treatmentapproaches in reducing NVF, improving IPSS scores, and enhancing patient QoL. This study underscores the importance of NBCI as a diagnostic tool for tailored treatment in BPH-associated nocturia.
