However, the EC group had significantly more frequent subfascial revision procedures (p=0.005) and less frequent superficial stoma revision (p=0.02), but this was not significant on multivariate analysis. At the end of follow-up (median: 12 years \[7–21\]), 82% of patients remained continent (NB: 83%, EC: 75%). CONCLUSIONS: A short and straight abdominal segment of the CCUD appears to reduce complication rates, as recommended by the technique involving implantation into a detrusor flap. However, reservation of the native bladder may contribute to persistent overactivity. The study is limited by its low external validity and the heterogeneity of patient characteristics, which may reduce statistical power. Nevertheless, the results reflect a real-life experience with a complex and uncommon surgical procedure. Implantation of the conduit into the native bladder seems to be associated with better long-term continence outcomes and fewer subfascial revisions despite multiple confounding factors. Further studies are needed to refine surgical techniques and reduce complications.

title: PD01-14: Preclinical feasibility of continuous bladder volume monitoring using wearable near-infrared spectroscopy versus ultrasound in Yucatan minipigs
parentSessionTitle: PD01: Urodynamics/Lower Urinary Tract Dysfunction/Female Pelvic Medicine: Neurogenic Voiding Dysfunction
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Patients with neurogenic bladder lack reliable tools for continuous bladder volume monitoring, leading to overdistension and catheter-related complications. This study evaluated whether a wearable near-infrared spectroscopy (NIRS) patch estimates bladder volume as accurately as portable ultrasound. Secondary objectives were to assess reproducibility under varied attachment conditions and tissue safety in a Yucatan minipig model. METHODS: In an AAALAC-accredited facility, two female Yucatan minipigs underwent repeated, controlled bladder filling under general anesthesia. A wearable NIRS patch and a portable ultrasound scanner were tested at matched time points. Primary endpoints were Pearson correlation (r) with infused volume and mean absolute error (MAE), with 95% confidence intervals estimated by cluster bootstrap. Secondary endpoints included reproducibility across attachment pressure/position and histopathology. RESULTS: Across eight infusion cycles in the smaller and fifteen in the larger animal, NIRS tracked bladder volume closely (r=0.97–0.99) with MAE similar to ultrasound. In head-to-head testing: small animal—NIRS MAE 23.1±4.7 mL, r=0.98±0.01 vs ultrasound 32.5±12.2 mL, r=0.95±0.04; large animal—NIRS 31.1±9.7 mL, r=0.98±0.00 vs ultrasound 30.4±14.5 mL, r=0.99±0.01. Accuracy improved with firm fixation, while inferior displacement increased error. Histopathology confirmed no device-related inflammation or tissue injury. Limitations include small sample size, anesthesia, saline infusion, and species differences limiting extrapolation. CONCLUSIONS: A wearable NIRS patch provided ultrasound-comparable accuracy with continuous, noninvasive monitoring in animal models. The finding suggests that a wearable NIRS based monitoring could help people with neurogenic bladder empty at the right time and avoid overfilling or infections.

title: PD01-15: Smart, Reusable Catheter System for Longitudinal Urinary Monitoring at the Point of Care
parentSessionTitle: PD01: Urodynamics/Lower Urinary Tract Dysfunction/Female Pelvic Medicine: Neurogenic Voiding Dysfunction
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Driven by the needs of individuals with spinal cord injury (SCI) who rely on intermittent urinary catheterization, CathBuddy, Inc. developed the Aurie System—a reusable catheter platform with a cleaning and disinfection unit to ensure safe reusability. Building on this, we present a Smart Catheter integrating reusable pressure (P), temperature (T), and pH sensors for real-time urodynamic monitoring, with Near Field Communication (NFC) data transfer at the point of care. Longitudinal bladder P monitoring offers clinical-level insight into bladder dynamics, while monitoring urinary T and pH may support early detection of catheter-associated urinary tract infections. By combining multimodal sensing, wireless communication, and accessible technology, this Smart Catheter aims to enhance independence, reduce long-term healthcare costs, and support personalized, patient-centered care for individuals SCI patients. METHODS: Commercial P and T sensors were selected based on biocompatibility, low power, and compact packaging, and integrated into a 3D-printed catheter tip made with biocompatible elastomers. Custom potentiometric pH sensors were built using Pt/Ir and Ag wires, as the working (WE) and reference (RE) electrodes, respectively, forming an electrochemical cell. The WE surface was activated to create iridium oxide sites, and open circuit potentiometry (OCP) measured voltage shifts from hydronium ion activity. The pH sensors were calibrated using standard pH buffers, while integrated P and T sensors were validated in a customized bladder model against reference instruments. RESULTS: The customized testing setup successfully demonstrated integration and reliable data transmission from the P and T sensors. The potentiometric pH sensors exhibited near-Nernstian behavior across a physiologically relevant pH range (4.5–8.0), validating their suitability for urinary monitoring. Sensor robustness and reproducibility were demonstrated, and functionality was retained after multiple cleaning and disinfection cycles following Aurie’s standardized procedures. CONCLUSIONS: This work validates a multimodal Smart Catheter capable of measuring P, T, and pH with wireless data transfer. Sensors maintained stability, reproducibility, and responsiveness after repeated sterilization, confirming feasibility for reusable point-of-care urinary monitoring.

title: PD02-01: Is Hunner lesion-interstitial cystitis/bladder pain syndrome (HL-IC/BPS) a B cell-driven autoimmune disease? A comprehensive, population-based analysis of autoimmunity amongst a large cohort of HL-IC/BPS patients.
parentSessionTitle: PD02: Infections/Inflammation/Cystic Disease of the Genitourinary Tract: Interstitial Cystitis
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: We explored whether the observed propensity for widespread autoimmunity amongst interstitial cystitis/bladder pain syndrome (IC/BPS) patients might be driven by the Hunner lesion (HL) cohort and their propensity for B cell-driven autoimmune diseases (BCDAD), which would support a B cell-driven etiopathogenesis of this inflammatory phenotype. METHODS: We used administrative datasets from the Institute for Clinical Evaluative Sciences (ICES) to create a population-based cohort of female patients with HLs who were treated with fulguration in the province of Ontario, Canada over a 10-year period. Our control group were age-matched women undergoing surgery for stress urinary incontinence (SUI). We evaluated the relative rate (RR) of concomitant BCDADs and non-BCDADs amongst the HL cohort compared to controls. RESULTS: Our cohort includes n=953 cases of HL-IC/BPS compared with n=953 age-matched SUI controls. All BCDADs examined in this analysis were significantly more likely to be present in the HL cohort, including multiple sclerosis (MS), systemic lupus erythema (SLE), and rheumatoid arthritis (RA) (see Table 1). Some non-BCDADs examined – including Crohn’s, ankylosing spondylitis, and Still’s disease – were also significantly increased amongst the HL cohort. Several additional non-BCDADs showed no differences between the groups, including psoriasis, giant cell arteritis, and polymyalgia rheumatica. Important limitations include lack of a non-HL IC/BPS control group, and the RR reported for SLE may represent an overestimate, as this is a composite diagnostic code and includes other, albeit more rare rheumatologic diagnoses. CONCLUSIONS: Our population-based analysis of B cell-driven autoimmune diseases amongst a large cohort of Hunner lesion patients supports a B cell-driven autoimmune etiopathogenesis of this inflammatory phenotype of IC/BPS. | | | --- | | |

title: PD02-02: The first prospective cohort study comparing fulguration of biopsied Hunner lesions (HLs) to bladder biopsy and fulguration of non-HL interstitial cystitis/bladder pain syndrome
parentSessionTitle: PD02: Infections/Inflammation/Cystic Disease of the Genitourinary Tract: Interstitial Cystitis
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Several cohort studies comparing fulguration of Hunner lesions (HLs) with active control groups has led to it being recommended as an effective treatment option for HL-interstitial cystitis/bladder pain syndrome (IC/BPS) in several clinical guidelines. All such studies lacked a placebo control or a non-HL control group. We report for the first time, a HL fulguration trial, with a non-HL control group undergoing bladder biopsy and fulguration. METHODS: In this prospective cohort study, part of a larger investigation evaluating the immunologic microenvironment of the urothelium in HL-IC/BPS vs non HL-IC/BPS patients, patients underwent cold cup biopsy under general anesthetic; HL and biopsy site were fulgurated in the HL arm while non-HL subjects underwent biopsy site fulguration. Completed symptom questionnaires at baseline and at 3 months post-treatment were compared between the groups. RESULTS: 16 HL-IC/BPS and 15 non HL-IC/BPS patients were enrolled. Of these, complete baseline and 3-month Interstitial Cystitis Symptom Index (ICSI), Interstitial Cystitis Problem Index (ICPI) were collected from 15 HL-IC/BPS and 9 non HL-IC/BPS patients. Six patients from each cohort also had full Genitourinary Pain Index (GUPI) data for analysis. Baseline scores were not significantly different between groups. At three months follow-up, HL patients demonstrated a significantly greater improvement than non-HL: ICSI decrease of –5.9 (±5.3) vs –0.6 (±3.4) (p=0.009) and ICPI –6.9 (±5.5) vs –0.6 (±3.8) (p=0.009). The GUPI outcomes similarly showed greater improvement in the HL arm though this difference was not statistically significant (see Table 1). CONCLUSIONS: Our findings confirm fulguration is an effective treatment of HL-IC/BPS, for the first time comparing improvements in pain and urinary symptoms to a non-HL control group, who underwent limited ablation of their urothelium. These findings more broadly confirm the real existence of HLs as painful, focal inflammatory lesions within the bladder. | | | --- | | |

title: PD02-04: Urinary Proteins Stratify Severe and Non-severe Patient Phenotypes of Urologic Chronic Pelvic Pain Syndrome (UCPPS): A MAPP Research Network Study
parentSessionTitle: PD02: Infections/Inflammation/Cystic Disease of the Genitourinary Tract: Interstitial Cystitis
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: The pain and urological severity of urologic chronic pelvic pain syndrome (UCPPS) is currently determined by patient questionnaires. An objective and non-invasive molecular test that scales with urinary and/or pain severity would improve management of UCPPS. In this study, we quantify and validate the varying urinary proteome in the UCPPS subpopulation with severe symptom scores, as compared to non-severe subjects. METHODS: Quantitative urinary proteomic analysis of 81 UCPPS subjects was performed. Patients were stratified into “severe” (n=37) and “non-severe” (n=44) subpopulations based on summing pain and urinary severity scores which were derived from the GenitoUrinary Pain Index (GUPI) questionnaire. RESULTS: Utilizing quantitative urinary proteomics, a total of 118 proteins were significantly altered (p<0.05) between the severe and non-severe UCPPS subpopulations. Over 40% of all differentially expressed urinary proteins were regulated by one or more of TGFB1, KRAS, or TNF, implicating these as putative key regulators of UCPPS severity. We developed a model utilizing logistic regression and 4-fold cross validation to identify a panel of 5 proteins with a ROC AUC of 0.928 to predict severe and non-severe UCPPS subpopulations. A parallel analysis of the proteomics data using a decision tree analysis performed similarly. CONCLUSIONS: UCPPS patients with severe pain and urinary symptoms have differentiating quantitative proteomic changes in urine compared to UCPPS patients with less severe symptoms. These markers may be used as an objective measure of severity of UCPPS. These changes impact the activation status of proinflammatory signaling. A subset of these differentially regulated proteins can differentiate severe and non-severe UCPPS patients with high sensitivity and specificity. Informatic analysis of the quantitatively altered urinary proteome implicates specific upstream regulators that could be evaluated as therapeutic targets to minimize UCPPS symptoms.

title: PD02-05: Comprehensive Profiling of Urinary Extracellular Vesicle microRNAs Identifies Novel Diagnostic Biomarkers for IC/BPS
parentSessionTitle: PD02: Infections/Inflammation/Cystic Disease of the Genitourinary Tract: Interstitial Cystitis

speakers.organization: The Jikei University School of Medicine

fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Interstitial cystitis/bladder pain syndrome (IC/BPS) is characterized by chronic pelvic pain with urinary symptoms, yet diagnosis remains challenging due to reliance on subjective assessment and cystoscopic findings. A reliable, objective biomarker could standardize diagnosis and enable earlier intervention. Extracellular vesicle (EV)–associated microRNAs (miRNAs) are stable in biofluids and have shown promise as disease-specific biomarkers. We conducted comprehensive urinary EV miRNA profiling to identify novel diagnostic markers for IC/BPS. METHODS: We prospectively collected urine samples from 8 patients with Hunner-type IC (HIC), 2 with BPS, and 10 controls without lower urinary tract symptoms. HIC/BPS diagnoses followed the Japanese IC/BPS guideline and were confirmed cystoscopically. Urinary EVs were isolated using a nanowire-based device, and miRNA expression was analyzed with a 3D-Gene Human miRNA Oligo Chip covering 2,632 miRNAs. Quality control yielded 485 miRNAs for analysis. Leave-one-out cross-validation and ROC analysis identified candidate miRNAs with area under the curve (AUC) ≥0.85 and accuracy ≥0.85. Associations with clinical scores (O’Leary–Sant indices, VAS) were assessed via Pearson correlation. RESULTS: Principal component analysis and heatmaps showed distinct clustering of HIC, BPS, and controls ( Figure 1A,B ). Two urinary EV miRNAs—miR-375-5p and miR-6766-5p—met selection criteria, with AUCs of 0.89 and 0.86, and cross-validated accuracies of 0.90 and 0.85, respectively, for differentiating IC/BPS from controls. In HIC vs control analysis, miR-375-5p achieved AUC 0.86 (sensitivity 0.88, specificity 0.90) and miR-6766-5p AUC 0.86 (0.88, 0.80) ( Figure 1C ). No significant correlation was found between candidate miRNA expression and symptom or quality-of-life scores. BMI showed no association with miRNA levels. CONCLUSIONS: This first comprehensive urinary EV miRNA profiling in IC/BPS identified two novel candidates—miR-375-5p and miR-6766-5p—with high diagnostic accuracy. These biomarkers could offer a rapid, non-invasive, objective diagnostic tool for IC/BPS, reducing diagnostic variability and enabling earlier treatment. Validation in larger, multi-center cohorts is warranted.

title: PD02-06: Integration of single-cell and spatial transcriptomic analyses reveals pathogenic mechanisms in interstitial cystitis/bladder pain syndrome
parentSessionTitle: PD02: Infections/Inflammation/Cystic Disease of the Genitourinary Tract: Interstitial Cystitis

speakers.organization: Department of Urology, Samsung Medical Center, Sungkyunkwan University

fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Interstitial cystitis/bladder pain syndrome (IC/BPS) is a chronic inflammatory bladder disorder characterized by pelvic pain and urinary dysfunction that severely impairs quality of life. However, the underlying pathogenic mechanisms remain poorly understood. This study aimed to elucidate the cellular and molecular architecture of Hunner-type IC/BPS by integrating single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) and spatial transcriptomic analyses of patient bladder tissues. METHODS: Bladder tissues were surgically obtained from IC/BPS patients (n=8) and healthy controls (n=2). Single-cell transcriptomic profiling and spatial mapping were conducted to identify cell-type-specific alterations. Gene Set Enrichment Analysis (GSEA) used Hallmark gene sets from MSigDB, and Gene Ontology (GO) analysis was performed via the DAVID database. Cell clusters and subpopulations were annotated based on marker gene expression ( (https://www.auajournals.org/doi/abs/10.1097/01.JU.0001191260.74872.fd.06#F1)), and spatial gene expression patterns were integrated to examine immune–stromal interactions and smooth muscle remodeling ( (https://www.auajournals.org/doi/abs/10.1097/01.JU.0001191260.74872.fd.06#F6)). RESULTS: A total of 24 transcriptional clusters were identified, comprising 12 distinct cell types including epithelial, immune, and stromal populations ( (https://www.auajournals.org/doi/abs/10.1097/01.JU.0001191260.74872.fd.06#F1)). Compared with normal bladder tissue, Hunner lesions exhibited marked infiltration of Th17 cells ( (https://www.auajournals.org/doi/abs/10.1097/01.JU.0001191260.74872.fd.06#F2)) and enrichment of pro-inflammatory and autoimmune-related pathways ( (https://www.auajournals.org/doi/abs/10.1097/01.JU.0001191260.74872.fd.06#F3)), suggesting an activated autoimmune microenvironment. Among smooth muscle cell (SMC) subtypes, one IC-enriched cluster showed transcriptional signatures of a phenotypic shift from contractile to synthetic states ( (https://www.auajournals.org/doi/abs/10.1097/01.JU.0001191260.74872.fd.06#F4)). Pseudotime trajectory analysis revealed that a transition from contractile to synthetic phenotype in this subtype ( (https://www.auajournals.org/doi/abs/10.1097/01.JU.0001191260.74872.fd.06#F5)). Collectively, these findings delineate an immune–stromal crosstalk tha contributes to the chronic inflammatory and fibrotic features of IC/BPS. CONCLUSIONS: Integration of scRNA-seq and spatial transcriptomics provided a comprehensive single-cell map of the IC/BPS bladder microenvironment. Coordinated alterations in Th17 cells and SMCs suggest that autoimmune activation and aberrant muscle remodeling contribute towards pain and dysfunction in Hunner-type IC/BPS. These insights reveal key cellular targets for future immunomodulatory or anti-fibrotic therapies.

title: PD02-07: Molecular characterization of chronic inflammatory diseases of the urinary bladder based on next-generation RNA sequencing and digital image analysis
parentSessionTitle: PD02: Infections/Inflammation/Cystic Disease of the Genitourinary Tract: Interstitial Cystitis

speakers.organization: Urology, Shinshu University School of Medicine

fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: This study aimed to elucidate distinct cellular and immunological characteristics associated with chronic inflammatory conditions of the urinary bladder, including Hunner-type interstitial cystitis (HIC), bacillus Calmette–Guérin (BCG)-related cystitis, follicular cystitis (FC), and chronic bacterial cystitis (CBC), by next-generation RNA-sequencing and digital image analysis. METHODS: Mucosal bladder biopsies of HIC (n=21), BCG cystitis (n=13), FC (n=5), or CBC (n=3) were subjected to RNA sequencing and quantitative polymerase chain reaction for key genes involved in adaptive immune responses. Digital immunohistochemical quantification was performed to evaluate and compare the degree of urothelial denudation and the density of infiltrating T-lymphocytes, B-lymphocytes, mast cells, and plasma cells. RESULTS: HIC specimens exhibited a markedly distinct transcriptional profile ( (https://www.auajournals.org/doi/abs/10.1097/01.JU.0001191260.74872.fd.07#F1)), with 3,566 differentially expressed genes and enrichment of 116 biological processes particularly associated with microbial response and heightened autoimmunity with Th1/Th17 axis polarization. HIC samples showed significantly increased levels of mRNA expression for genes associated with Th1-immune responses (specifically, IL12A/B, IFNG, and TBX21). Histologically, the density of IL-17-positive cells, epithelial denudation, and plasma cell ratio were significantly higher in HIC bladders than other types of cystitis, while there was no difference in the densities of lymphoplasmacytic and mast cells, or in B cell ratio between the groups ( (https://www.auajournals.org/doi/abs/10.1097/01.JU.0001191260.74872.fd.07#F2)). CONCLUSIONS: HIC inflammation is characterized by increased plasma cell infiltration in the context of a Th1/17-polarized immune environment, coupled with epithelial denudation. These findings provide a platform for development of novel treatment strategies, and facilitate basic research into the pathophysiology of this enigmatic disease.

title: PD02-08: Corneal confocal microscopy as a diagnostic tool for detecting small fiber neuropathy in patients with chronic pelvic pain syndrome
parentSessionTitle: PD02: Infections/Inflammation/Cystic Disease of the Genitourinary Tract: Interstitial Cystitis
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Chronic pelvic pain syndrome (CPPS) is a challenging condition that has a major impact on the quality of life of both men and women. CPP is a multifactorial disorder where pain may originate in any of the urogynecological, gastrointestinal, pelvic musculoskeletal, or nervous systems and usually unknown etiology. Corneal confocal microscopy (CCM) is a novel technique allows for the quantification of small fibers located near the center of the cornea. CCM is noninvasive and fast, and might be a useful method to confirm small nerve fiber pathology. Our objective was to assess corneal small nerve fiber morphology in patients with CPPS and to determine the prevalence of Small fiber neuropathy (SFN) in patients with CPPS using CCM. METHODS: This was a cross-sectional observational study aimed at evaluating corneal small nerve fiber morphology in patients with CPPS and determining the prevalence of SFN in this population. The study included 27 patients with CPPS who were either unresponsive to initial treatment or had comorbid pain syndromes, along with 10 healthy controls. All participants completed standardized questionnaires assessing symptoms of CPPS, including a neuropathic pain questionnaire, to map clinical characteristics. Corneal imaging was performed using in vivo confocal microscopy (IVCM). Measurements of corneal nerve thickness and dendritic cell density were conducted by a single ophthalmologist blinded to the clinical diagnosis. Outcome Measures: Corneal stromal nerve thickness (quantified in micrometers). Dendritic cell density (cells per square millimeter). Prevalence of SFN based on IVCM findings. RESULTS: In patients with CPPS, the mean stromal nerve thickness was 4.8±1.0 micrometers, which was significantly lower than that of the control group (6.0±1.3 micrometers, p=0.01). Dendritic cell density was significantly higher in patients with CPPS: 10±2 vs. 3±1 in controls (p=0.01). 73% of patients with CPPS showed evidence of SFN as measured by CCM. Comorbid conditions such as chronic prostatitis, irritable bowel syndrome, fibromyalgia and others were frequently observed in patients with CPPS. CONCLUSIONS: Small fiber neuropathy plays an important role in the pathogenesis of chronic pelvic pain. Corneal confocal microscopy is a useful non-invasive method to diagnose SFN in patients with CPPS. The results emphasize the potential of CCM as a tool for early diagnosis and monitoring of SFN, as well as for studying the pathophysiological mechanisms of chronic pain. The lack of changes in the microscopic picture in the background of treatment indicates the need for further studies to identify possible pathogenetic links between SFN and CPPS.

title: PD02-09: Antler Stem Cell Exosomes Ameliorate Interstitial Cystitis via Mitochondrial Component Transfer to Reprogramming Macrophage Polarization
parentSessionTitle: PD02: Infections/Inflammation/Cystic Disease of the Genitourinary Tract: Interstitial Cystitis
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Interstitial cystitis (IC) is a chronic inflammatory bladder disease lacking effective treatments. Exosomes from antler stem cells (ASC-Exos), derived from regenerating deer antler tissue, exhibit immunomodulatory properties, but their mechanisms in IC remain unclear. METHODS: An IC rat model was established via intravesical LPS/protamine sulfate instillation and treated with ASC-Exos. Therapeutic efficacy was evaluated through pain threshold testing, urodynamics, histopathology, and immunofluorescence. Fluorescently labeled ASC-Exos were tracked in vivo. Single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) identified cellular targets and transcriptional changes. Mitochondrial transfer was assessed using MitoTracker labeling and confocal microscopy. Mitochondrial function was measured via mtDNA copy number, membrane potential, oxygen consumption rate, ATP production, and mitochondrial ROS. Macrophage polarization was evaluated by flow cytometry and immunofluorescence. Co-culture systems assessed ASC-Exos-treated macrophage effects on epithelial repair. Macrophage depletion confirmed their therapeutic necessity. RESULTS: ASC-Exos significantly ameliorated IC pathology, reducing inflammation, restoring barrier integrity, and alleviating pain and voiding dysfunction. Fluorescence tracking showed preferential ASC-Exos uptake by bladder macrophages. ScRNA-seq identified macrophages as predominant infiltrating immune cells with markedly downregulated oxidative phosphorylation genes and mitochondrial respiratory pathways in IC. ASC-Exos transferred mitochondrial components to macrophages, restoring mitochondrial function (increased mtDNA, membrane potential, oxygen consumption, ATP; decreased mitochondrial ROS). This mitochondrial rescue promoted M1-to-M2 macrophage polarization, reducing pro-inflammatory and increasing anti-inflammatory markers. ASC-Exos-treated macrophages enhanced epithelial cell migration, proliferation, and tight junction expression. Macrophage depletion abolished therapeutic effects. CONCLUSIONS: ASC-Exos alleviate IC by transferring mitochondrial components to dysfunctional macrophages, restoring metabolic homeostasis and reprogramming M1-to-M2 phenotype, thereby promoting epithelial repair. This establishes ASC-Exos as a novel mitochondrial transfer-based cell-free therapy for IC.

title: PD02-10: Therapeutic Efficacy of Capacitive-Resistive Monopolar Radiofrequency in Patients with Chronic Pelvic Pain Syndrome: A Randomized Controlled Trial
parentSessionTitle: PD02: Infections/Inflammation/Cystic Disease of the Genitourinary Tract: Interstitial Cystitis
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Capacitive-resistive monopolar radiofrequency (CRMRF) therapy at a frequency of 448 kHz is a non-invasive technology that delivers energy to tissues via specialized electrodes. It effectively alleviates pain through both thermal and non-thermal mechanisms. Non-thermal effects promote tissue regeneration by stimulating mesenchymal stem cell proliferation and exert anti-inflammatory actions, potentially via modulation of cytokine expression (e.g., MCP-1, IL-4). Thermal stimulation enhances blood flow, oxygen delivery, and metabolic clearance, thereby reducing ischemic pain . METHODS: A total of 150 patients (100 females, 50 males) diagnosed with myofascial pain syndrome, pudendal neuralgia, interstitial cystitis, chronic prostatitis, or endometriosis were enrolled. Participants completed standardized questionnaires including:Visual Analog Scale (VAS) for pain intensity (0–10) Sexual Quality of Life-Female Version (SQOL-F) or Male Version (SQOL-M) Pelvic Pain and Urgency/Frequency Symptom Scale (PUF) International Prostate Symptom Score (IPSS) – for male participantsPatients were randomly assigned to two groups:Intervention group : CRMRF therapy (8 sessions every 5–7 days) targeting the suprapubic and perineal regions using capacitive (10 min) and resistive (15 min) modes, combined with supervised physical therapy. Intensity was gradually increased from level 1 to 5 based on treatment progress. Control group: Supervised physical therapy only. RESULTS: In the intervention group, significant improvements were observed compared to the control group: Pain reduction : Mean VAS score decreased from 7.34±1.28 to 2.82±1.19 vs. 7.49±1.17 to 4.51±1.12 in the control group (p<0.05) Sexual Quality of Life : Significant improvement in SQOL scores indicating enhanced sexual satisfaction and overall well-being Symptom burden : Improvement in PUF and IPSS scores suggesting reduced urinary urgency/frequency and better functional outcomes. CONCLUSIONS: The addition of CRMRF therapy to standard physical therapy significantly improves pain relief, sexual function, and overall quality of life in patients with chronic pelvic pain syndromes. These findings support its integration into multidisciplinary management protocols aligned with current international urological congress standards for patient-centered care.

title: PD02-11: To Remove, Reconstruct, or Retain? Evaluating Surgical Management of the Native Bladder in Patients with Interstitial Cystitis/Bladder Pain Syndrome
parentSessionTitle: PD02: Infections/Inflammation/Cystic Disease of the Genitourinary Tract: Interstitial Cystitis
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Interstitial cystitis / bladder pain syndrome (IC/BPS) is a chronic, debilitating condition characterized by bladder pain and urinary urgency in the absence of infection or other identifiable causes. Although conservative management with lifestyle modification and pharmacotherapy provides relief for many patients, a subset remains refractory to these interventions. For these individuals, surgical options such as substitution cystoplasty or urinary diversion with or without cystectomy may be pursued. This study examines over three decades of surgical cases at Stanford Hospital to characterize patient demographics and quantify postoperative pain outcomes, aiming to identify patterns and differences in recovery across surgical approaches. METHODS: This single-institution, IRB-approved retrospective cohort study included patients with IC/BPS identified by CPT code who underwent substitution cystoplasty or urinary diversion at Stanford Hospital over the past 30 years. A REDCap database identified 58 patients, of whom 49 were confirmed to have a true diagnosis of IC/BPS upon direct chart review. These patients were categorized into three surgical treatment groups: (1) total cystectomy with urinary diversion, (2) supratrigonal cystectomy with substitution cystoplasty, and (3) urinary diversion without cystectomy. Excluded cases were used as a matched non-diseased cohort for comparative outcome analysis. De-identified clinical data were analyzed descriptively and through multivariable logistic regression using SPSS software. RESULTS: Of the 58 patients included in this study, the average age ranged from 54–60 years with comparable BMIs across study groups (26.6–30.7 kg/m). Baseline symptom severity did not differ significantly based on available chart data (ICSI 14.6–15.5, p=0.84; ICPI 10.7–13.7, p=0.80). Chronic overlapping pain conditions (COPs) were also comparable between groups (p=0.75). Postoperative pain improvement was reported across all surgical cohorts without statistically significant differences noted amongst the different types of surgical intervention (p=0.37). Most patients discontinued urologic IC/BPS pain medications postoperatively, though no difference was observed between treatment groups (p=0.63). Race, however, was found to be statistically different between treatment groups (p=0.011). CONCLUSIONS: The findings demonstrate that patient demographics, baseline symptom severity, and postoperative outcomes were largely comparable across surgical treatment groups for IC/BPS. While pain relief and medication discontinuation were commonly observed following surgery, no statistically significant differences were detected between the different surgical interventions. The only factor that differed significantly between groups was race, which may warrant further investigation to assess potential sociodemographic or access-to-care disparities, as well highlight a limitation in our homogenous study cohorts. Overall, these results suggest that each surgical approach yielded similar postoperative outcomes, supporting the interpretation that surgical selection may be tailored based on clinical presentation and patient preference rather than expected differences in efficacy.

title: PD02-12: Are There Urological Consequences to Medicinal Ketamine?  A Five-Year Multi-Institutional Analysis
parentSessionTitle: PD02: Infections/Inflammation/Cystic Disease of the Genitourinary Tract: Interstitial Cystitis
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Ketamine is an FDA-approved anesthetic and analgesic now used for treatment-resistant depression. Though medically indicated, it is also misused recreationally, where chronic exposure causes bladder inflammation, fibrosis, and upper tract injury. These findings raise concern for long-term urologic effects in therapeutic use. We evaluated the 3- and 5-year incidence of urinary diagnoses and procedures following medicinal ketamine exposure using a large, multi-institutional dataset. METHODS: A retrospective cohort study was performed using the TriNetX Research Network (2000–2020). Adults aged 18–50 years with substance use disorder diagnoses (ICD-10: F10–F19) were included. To isolate medicinal rather than recreational exposure, patients with F16 (hallucinogen-related disorders), which includes illicit ketamine, were excluded. Because TriNetX aggregates data from hospital-based populations, both cohorts consisted of individuals with substance-related conditions rather than healthy controls. Cohort A included those prescribed ketamine (RxNorm 6130) within one year before a substance use diagnosis; Cohort B comprised matched controls without ketamine exposure. Propensity-score matching (1:1) on 21 demographic and clinical covariates yielded 51,198 patients per arm. Incident urologic diagnoses and procedures were evaluated at 3 and 5 years using risk ratios (RR, 95% CI). RESULTS: After matching, 102,396 patients were included (mean age 34.7±8.3; 56% male). Medicinal ketamine users had higher risks of multiple urinary diagnoses and procedures at both 3 and 5 years. Greatest increases were seen for neurogenic bladder and urinary retention, while cystitis and voiding difficulty showed smaller but significant elevations. Effect sizes persisted, though slightly attenuated over time, suggesting sustained rather than progressive risk. Full estimates are shown in Tables 1 and 2. CONCLUSIONS: Within a hospital-based, substance-diagnosed population, exposure to medicinal ketamine was associated with modest but sustained elevations in bladder-related diagnostic and procedural coding over 3 to 5 years. Although causality cannot be inferred and dosing patterns were not available, these findings align with prior literature showing that urinary effects from ketamine appear related to cumulative exposure rather than isolated use. Considering that legitimate medical indications, such as chronic pain and treatment-resistant depression, may involve ongoing administration rather than single doses, continued evaluation of the long-term urologic safety profile of therapeutic ketamine is warranted. | | | --- | | | | | | --- | | |

title: PD02-13: Elevated Psychiatric Comorbidity and Polygenic Risk for Depression in Interstitial Cystitis/Bladder Pain Syndrome
parentSessionTitle: PD02: Infections/Inflammation/Cystic Disease of the Genitourinary Tract: Interstitial Cystitis
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Interstitial cystitis/bladder pain syndrome (IC/BPS) is a chronic pain condition with significant psychiatric comorbidity. However, systematic psychiatric evaluation of individuals with IC/BPS using gold-standard diagnostic interviews has not yet been performed. Therefore, we conducted the first study integrating Structured Clinical Interview for DSM-5 (SCID-5) assessments and genome-wide polygenic risk scoring (PRS) to evaluate whether psychiatric comorbidity in IC/BPS reflects psychosocial effects of chronic pain or shared genetic vulnerability. METHODS: Forty-three individuals with clinically confirmed IC/BPS completed the SCID-5 to establish DSM-5 psychiatric diagnoses. Two genotyped cohorts of individuals with clinically confirmed IC/BPS (IC1: n=88; IC2: n=76) were analyzed using the Illumina Global Screening Array and imputation to the 1000 Genomes reference. Polygenic risk scores (PRS) for depression and anxiety traits were computed using validated Polygenic Score Catalog models and compared to matched European-ancestry controls using Wilcoxon tests with false discovery rate (FDR) correction. RESULTS: Among 43 participants completing the SCID-5 (43% of those invited to participate), 55% met criteria for an anxiety disorder and 42.5% for a depressive disorder, with Panic Disorder (27.5%) and Major Depressive Disorder (20%) most prevalent; 15% reported suicidal ideation attributable to IC/BPS. PRS analysis revealed significantly higher genetic risk for ‘Recent feelings of depression’ (PGS001899; adjusted p=0.04) in IC1. Though significance did not survive correction for multiple testing for any other PRS, the direction of effect was consistent across cohorts with PRS distributions elevated for _Major depression_ (PGS000193; _IC1_), _Seen a psychiatrist for nerves, anxiety, tension or depression_ (PGS000141; _IC2_), and _Depression_ (PGS000145; _IC2_). CONCLUSIONS: IC/BPS is associated with significant psychiatric morbidity and genetic susceptibility to depression, indicating a shared biological pathway between affective regulation and pain perception. These findings support integrating psychiatric screening and cognitive behavioral therapy into IC/BPS management. Incorporating PRS into clinical risk assessment may enable precision stratification and improved outcomes in urologic care.

title: PD02-14: Paraurethral injection of hyaluronic acid for the treatment of recurrent postcoital cystitis.
parentSessionTitle: PD02: Infections/Inflammation/Cystic Disease of the Genitourinary Tract: Interstitial Cystitis
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Postcoital cystitis (PC) impacts patients' quality of life. Current treatment strategies, primarily antibiotic prophylaxis, are associated with increasing antimicrobial resistance and various side effects. Periurethral hyaluronic acid injections have emerged as an alternative treatment option for women. Our study examines the efficacy and cost-effectiveness of periurethral hyaluronic acid (HA) injections for reducing the frequency of PC episodes. To evaluate the effectiveness of periurethral injection of a bulking gel in reducing the frequency of postcoital cystitis episodes over a 12-month follow-up period compared to a control group. METHODS: The study included 318 women with postcoital cystitis and a positive O'Donnell-Hirschhorn test, treated between 2018 and 2025. The study group (n=268) received combination therapy (standard treatment and paraurethral injections of a hyaluronic acid-based filler). The control group (n=50) received antibiotic therapy alone. Paraurethral injections of gel (1–2 ml) were performed using fan-shaped movements from the 6 o'clock position. This technique created a "gel cushion" that elevated the external meatus and distal urethra, thereby limiting their mobility and preventing injury during sexual intercourse. Follow-up examinations were performed at 3, 6, and 12 months after the injection. RESULTS: In the combination therapy group, postcoital cystitis recurred for the first time after 12 months in only 47 patients (17.5%), as the gel biodegraded, requiring repeat filler injections. Quality of life (UDI 6 and PISQ-12 questionnaires) improved in 82.5% of patients (p<0.05). In the control group, postcoital cystitis recurred for the first time after 3 and 6 months in 47 patients (94%), requiring repeat antibiotic therapy. Quality of life improved in 3 patients (6%). No complications were observed. CONCLUSIONS: The results of this study will enable the widespread adoption of an effective, minimally invasive, and safe treatment method for postcoital cystitis associated with urethral dystopia. This will serve as an alternative to both long-term antibiotic therapy and invasive surgical interventions. This will improve treatment adherence and quality of life for millions of women.

title: PD02-15: Analysis of novel genetic factors contributing to LL-37 resistance in clinically isolated uropathogenic Escherichia coli
parentSessionTitle: PD02: Infections/Inflammation/Cystic Disease of the Genitourinary Tract: Interstitial Cystitis
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: The human cathelicidin, LL-37 is a broad-spectrum cationic antimicrobial peptide that defends the urinary tract against infection. Escherichia coli (UPEC) is the most common causative agent of UTI, and some strains have developed resistance towards LL-37, causing severe and recurrent infections. UPEC strains likely employ a diversity of mechanisms to resist LL-37 but few have been characterized. Recurrent UTI isolate EcPNK007 exhibits extreme resistance to LL-37 (MIC>32 μM), but this resistance is independent of previously identified mechanisms. The goal of this work was to determine the mechanistic basis for LL-37 resistance in rUTI UPEC to better understand how UPEC subverts host defenses. METHODS: A transposon mutant library of LL-37-resistant EcPNK007, a UPEC strain isolated from a postmenopausal woman with active rUTI, was constructed using the Himar1 mariner transposon system. Genomic DNA was isolated from the transposon library grown in LB and LB with 16 μM LL-37 and subject to Illumina sequencing to identify genes essential for LL-37 fitness in EcPNK007. Markerless gene deletions were performed using the Lambda Red system. SDS-EDTA growth inhibition assays were performed to assess outer membrane (OM) integrity. Broth microdilution LL-37 susceptibility testing was performed to quantify LL-37 minimum inhibitory/bactericidal concentrations (MIC/MBC) of single and double gene mutants to define epistatic relationships between genes required for LL-37 resistance. RESULTS: Tn-seq identified 69 genes required for growth in 16 μM LL-37. Top hits included genes encoding proteins involved in OM integrity (ybjX, nlpD), drug efflux (yqjA), and global gene regulation (phoPQ). Isogenic ΔphoP, ΔybjX, ΔyqjA, ΔnlpD, PNK007ΔphoPΔybjX, PNK007ΔphoPΔnlpD, and PNK007ΔphoPΔyqjA mutants demonstrated >3 log10 reduction in the presence of 16 μM LL-37. Mutant strains showed similar MIC/MBCs to LL-37 sensitive strains (<8 μM). Deletion mutants ΔphoP, ΔnlpD, ΔamiC, and ΔyqjA, showed significant SDS-EDTA sensitivity, highlighting their critical role in OM integrity. Finally, epistasis analysis of LL-37 resistance genes revealed that while ybjX and yqjA are regulated by phoP, amiC and nlpD are part of a different, yet to be defined, regulatory pathway in EcPNK007. CONCLUSIONS: Genes critical for rUTI UPEC fitness in LL-37 were identified and found to contribute to OM integrity, revealing enhancement of OM integrity as a critical LL-37 resistance mechanism. Epistasis analysis revealed multiple regulatory pathways are involved in rUTI UPEC LL-37 resistance and identified the contribution of both Pho-dependent and Pho-independent regulatory mechanisms to LL-37 fitness.

title: PD03-01: The MILES trial: Prospective randomized trial of safety and efficacy of minimally invasive versus standard laser enucleation of the prostate
parentSessionTitle: PD03: Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia: Surgical Therapy & New Technology II
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Endoscopic enucleation of the prostate (EEP) is standard treatment for benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH). A smaller resectoscope in minimally invasive laser enucleation (MiLEP) may reduce stress urinary incontinence (SUI) and urethral stricture compared with standard EEP. The aim of the study is to compare the efficacy and safety of MiLEP versus standard EEP. METHODS: This is an ongoing prospective randomized trial with IRB approval. Men with BPH (30–150 сс), severe LUTS (IPSS ≥20) and Qmax ≤15 ml/s are being randomized (1:1) to MiLEP (22 Ch) or standard EEP (26 Ch). Both arms use a thulium fiber laser with pulse modulation (FiberLase U-MAX; 2 J × 40 Hz). Enucleation is performed using the en bloc technique. SUI is defined as urine leakage requiring ≥1 pad/day. The primary endpoint is SUI after catheter removal; secondary endpoints are perioperative, functional outcomes and complication rate. RESULTS: 77 patients underwent MiLEP and 78 – standard EEP. Baseline characteristics were comparable, including age (p=0.34), prostate volume (p=0.52), IPSS (p=0.14), and Qmax (p=0.36). Operative time (p=0.26) as well as enucleation and morcellation durations did not differ (p=0.17 and 0.14); enucleation and morcellation efficiencies were comparable (p=0.4 and 0.06). Tissue weight was 34 \[25–42\] vs 35 \[27–42\] g (p=0.19). Median catheterization was 1 day (p=0.6) and length of stay 3 days (p=0.7) in both arms. Functional outcomes improved significantly in both groups, with no significant intergroup differences ( Table 1). Minor (Clavien–Dindo I–II) complications were comparable: 21.7% in MiLEP vs 28.0% in standard EEP (p=0.74). SUI after catheter removal was less frequent with MiLEP (6.5% vs 29.5%; p=0.04); at 3 months, continence was 100% after MiLEP vs 87.2% after standard EEP (p=0.23). Urethral stricture at 3 months was 1.3% vs 6.4% (p=0.06). Bladder neck contracture was 5.1% after standard EEP (p=0.15). CONCLUSIONS: MiLEP provides comparable perioperative and functional outcomes to standard EEP with a significant reduction in early SUI. Longer follow-up and expanded enrollment are required to prove the observed trends in urethral complications. | | | --- | | |

title: PD03-02: Multicenter 24-month outcomes of Rivermark FloStent™: the RAPID-II study
parentSessionTitle: PD03: Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia: Surgical Therapy & New Technology II
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: The Rivermark FloStent™ is a catheter-free device therapy for BPH that integrates with a standard flexible cystoscope for outpatient delivery. The RAPID-II clinical trial is an ongoing ethics-approved multi-center single-arm early feasibility intended to evaluate the safety and efficacy profile of the FloStent System. METHODS: The initial study cohort is fully enrolled and currently in the follow-up phase. Study implantations were performed in an outpatient setting at four centers in Australia, New Zealand, and Mexico. Various types of reusable (Olympus, Storz) and single-use (Ambu) cystoscopes were used for implantation. RESULTS: 55 subjects (age 64.5 ± 9.3 yr) with mean prostatic volume 47.9 ± 14.6 ml were implanted. Implantation success rate was 100%. No patient required a post-procedure catheter. Baseline IPSS score was 23.4 ± 4.7, and was reduced by 11.6 ± 7.3 and 9.9 ± 7.2 points at the 12-month and 24-month timepoints, respectively . Notably, a clinically significant IPSS reduction of 8.3 ± 7.1 was seen at the 2-week timepoint. QOL scores followed the favorable trend of IPSS scores, being reduced by 3.0 ± 1.4 and 2.6 ± 1.2 points at the 12-month and 24-month timepoints. At 12 months, Qmax increase was 2.1 ± 0.6 ml/sec and PVR reduction was 18.6 ± 18.9 ml. Measures of sexual function (IIEF-5 and MSHQ-EjD) remained stable throughout the follow-up period. Current device tolerability rate is 89.1% (number of patients who have the device removed due to symptomatic dissatisfaction, divided by the total number implanted). All device retrievals and exchanges have been performed with standard cystoscopic equipment, accessories, and techniques. The most common adverse events have been transient irritative LUTS. CONCLUSIONS: The Rivermark FloStent™ has demonstrated good clinical performance with rapid recovery and a durable treatment effect in a multi-center early feasibility study. Placement and retrieval with standard urological equipment has been demonstrated. Ongoing evaluation of clinical performance is underway, in the form of a randomized double-blinded sham-controlled pivotal clinical study.

title: PD03-03: Medical treatment of benign prostatic hyperplasia after bladder outlet procedures
parentSessionTitle: PD03: Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia: Surgical Therapy & New Technology II
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: One benefit of outlet procedures for benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH) is discontinuing medical therapy for obstructive lower urinary tract symptoms. However, medical therapy may be necessary again if there is significant regrowth of BPH tissue. We aimed to determine the rate of starting alpha blockers or 5-alpha reductase inhibitors (5ARi) after Laser enucleation of the prostate (LEP), Transurethral resection of the prostate (TURP), Photoselective vaporization of the prostate (PVP), Prostatic Urethral Lift (PUL), Transurethral water vapor thermal therapy (WVTT), and Robotic Waterjet Treatment (Aquablation). METHODS: The TriNetX Research Database was queried for men 35 years or older with the diagnosis of BPH (ICD 10: N40) without neurogenic bladder (ICD 10: N31) who underwent any of the following procedures between 2005 and 2025: LEP (CPT 52649), TURP (CPT 52601), PVP (CPT 52648), PUL (CPT 52441), WVTT (CPT 53854), or Aquablation (CPT 0421T). We investigated the initiation of alpha-blockers or 5-ARIs at least 3 months after the index outlet procedure. Primary outcomes were rate and time-to-first new alpha-blocker or 5-ARI between procedure groups. Kaplan Meier method with log-rank test was used to assess differences in time-to-first alpha-blocker prescription after index outlet procedure using LEP as a reference. RESULTS: At the index procedure, 14,269 underwent LEP, 50,644 TURP, 23,702 PVP, 7,372 PUL, 3,653 WVTT, and 4,897 Aquablation. The median time to new alpha-blocker therapy was not reached in the LEP group, 7.1 years in the TURP group, 7.9 years in the PVP group, 3.7 years in the PUL group, 3.4 years in the WVTT group, and not reached in the Aquablation group ( Figure). The 5-year probabilities of new alpha-blocker therapy in the LEP, TURP, PVP, PUL, WVTT and Aquablation groups were 28%, 43%, 40%, 58%, 57%, and 27% respectively ( Table). CONCLUSIONS: Patients who had LEP had a significantly lower rate of starting alpha-blockers after surgery compared to TURP, PVP, PUL, and WVTT. However, these rates were similar to Aquablation.

title: PD03-04: Downstream Effects: The Rate of Post-Procedural Urethral Stricture Rate After Aquablation® is Higher than Previously Reported
parentSessionTitle: PD03: Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia: Surgical Therapy & New Technology II
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Prior reports describe a 5% rate of urethral stricture (US) after Aquablation®, most commonly affecting the fossa navicularis. We observed US rates higher than previously described, and sought to further categorize presentation, surveillance, and management of these patients. METHODS: We retrospectively reviewed a prospectively maintained database of patients undergoing Aquablation® from February 2019 to September 2025. Patients were assessed at 6-weeks, 3-months, and annually thereafter. The primary outcome was US, which was diagnosed on office cystoscopy, performed for new-onset or worsening LUTS – and confirmed on fluoroscopic imaging. Secondary outcomes included time to US diagnosis, postoperative IPSS, and perioperative factors previously associated with US. Univariable analysis was used to compare stricture and non-stricture cohorts. RESULTS: Across 193 patients with median follow-up 9.6 months (range 1-78.6 months), the post-procedural US rate was 8.3% (16/193) with 68.8% (11/16), 12.5% (2/16), and 12.5% (2/16) affecting the fossa navicularis, penile urethra, and bulbar urethra, respectively. Mean stricture length was 2 cm (range 0.5-6.0 cm), and 69% of patients underwent substitution urethroplasty for definitive repair. No patients had a prior history of US or radiation. The median time from Aquablation® to stricture diagnosis was 3.5 months (range 1-20 months). Stricture patients had a greater 3-month post-operative IPSS (median 12.5, IQR 8 - 18.25) compared to the non-stricture cohort (median 7.0, IQR 4-12, p<0.01). Stricture patients had statistically significantly longer traction time (21.0 vs 19.0 hours, p<0.01) and indwelling catheter duration (3.5 vs 2.0 days, p<0.01) than non–stricture patients. CONCLUSIONS: In this cohort, 8.3% of Aquablation® patients developed US, higher than prior reports. US was associated with longer traction duration and indwelling catheter duration. With longer follow up, time to diagnosis ranged from 1-20 months, suggesting surveillance over time is necessary. IPSS may aid in surveillance for postoperative US, but a high index of suspicion remains necessary. Multi-institutional investigations are needed to validate the US rate following this increasingly popular bladder outlet procedure. | | | --- | | |

title: PD03-05: Perioperative and Trifecta Outcomes of Single Port Transvesical Robotic Simple Prostatectomy: A Report from the Single Port Advanced Research Consortium
parentSessionTitle: PD03: Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia: Surgical Therapy & New Technology II
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: To report the perioperative and functional outcomes of Single Port (SP) Transvesical Robotic Simple Prostatectomy (RASP). METHODS: A retrospective review was completed on the prospectively maintained, IRB-approved database of the SP Advanced Research Consortium (SPARC) to identify 503 patients who underwent SP-RASP. Only procedures performed with the Transvesical approach were included. Baseline clinicodemographic, perioperative, and postoperative variables were collected. Trifecta was defined as the absence of postoperative complications, urinary continence, and maximum urinary flow rate (Qmax) >12 ml/s at 3 months. RESULTS: A total of 492 patients were included, with a median age of 70.6 years (IQR 65 – 76), BMI of 27.4 kg/m2 (IQR 24.8 – 30.4), prostate volume of 124 ml (IQR 96 – 169), and 42.7% having a history of previous abdominal surgery. All procedures were completed successfully, with a median operative time of 178 minutes (IQR 144 – 220) and with a median estimated blood loss of 100 ml (IQR 50 – 150). Postoperatively, 96.5% did not require continuous bladder irrigation, 67.4% were discharged home the same day, and 85.7% experienced no postoperative complications. The median Foley catheter duration was 6 days (IQR 4 – 8). At 3 months, 92.5% were continent, with a median IPSS reduction of 78.3% (IQR 47.6 – 88.1) and Qmax improvements of 75.1% (IQR 35.7 – 327.9), corresponding to an overall trifecta rate of 82.4%. CONCLUSIONS: Transvesical SP-RASP is a safe and effective minimally invasive treatment option for large-gland benign prostatic hyperplasia, featuring high rates of outpatient surgery, low morbidity, minimal risk of transient urinary incontinence, and excellent early functional outcomes.

title: PD03-06: Real-World Outcomes of Aquablation for Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia: A Comparative Analysis of the International Collaborative Aquablation Research Urology Society (ICARUS) database, WATER and WATER-II Trials
parentSessionTitle: PD03: Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia: Surgical Therapy & New Technology II
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: The WATER and WATER-II clinical trials of Aquablation demonstrated effectiveness for treatment of lower urinary tract symptoms secondary to benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH) in men with prostate volumes (PV) 30-80 and 80-150 ml, respectively. In this study, we compare real-world Aquablation outcomes of men with similar PVs to results from WATER/WATER-II. METHODS: We retrospectively analyzed 1,946 consecutive men from the International Collaborative Aquablation Research Urology Society (ICARUS) database between 2018 and 2024 with PV≤150 ml who underwent Aquablation at one of four international centers. Baseline characteristics, functional outcomes and complications were compared to data from WATER/WATER-II using ANOVA and Kruskal-Wallis tests. RESULTS: From the ICARUS database, 1,069 men (PV≤80 ml) were compared to 116 men (WATER), and 877 men (PV 80-150 ml) were compared to 101 men (WATER-II). As expected, there were slight differences in baseline characteristic between cohorts. Quality of Life and International Prostate Symptom Scores (IPSS) were slightly higher at some timepoints in the real-world (E. g. IPSS at 3-months: ICARUS-I 9.9±6.9 vs. WATER 7.0±5.7, p<0.001). Anejaculation rates, Qmax flow rates, and post-void residuals at 3 months were consistent across cohorts. Transfusion rates were significantly lower in the real-world large prostate dataset (ICARUS-II 1.3% vs. WATER-II 5.9%, p=0.01). CONCLUSIONS: Real-world outcomes of Aquablation are broadly comparable to those observed in the pivotal WATER/WATER-II trials. These findings support its generalizability and sustained effectiveness beyond the rigorous selection criteria of WATER/WATER-II, validating its role as a viable treatment for BPH in routine clinical practice. | | | --- | | |

title: PD03-07: Reintervention rates and patterns of reoperation following surgical management of benign prostatic hyperplasia
parentSessionTitle: PD03: Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia: Surgical Therapy & New Technology II
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: There is currently a wide variety of surgical treatments available for benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH) that differ in invasiveness and durability. This study evaluates reintervention rates across frequently performed BPH procedures and identifies patterns of reoperative management for recurrent BPH. METHODS: A retrospective cohort study was conducted using TriNetX, a multi-institutional network of deidentified electronic health records (January 2010 – October 2025). Male patients undergoing initial BPH surgery and subsequent reoperation were identified via CPT codes for the following procedures: simple prostatectomy (open, laparoscopic/robotic), transurethral resection of prostate (TURP), laser enucleation of the prostate (LEP), laser prostate vaporization (PVP), robotic waterjet therapy (RWT), water vapor thermal therapy (WVTT), prostatic urethral lift (PUL), transurethral needle ablation (TUNA), transurethral microwave therapy (TUMT), and balloon commissurotomy. Reoperation rates were assessed at 1, 3, and 5 years. Among patients with ≥ 5-year follow-up, secondary procedures were identified to characterize the distribution of reoperations by index surgery. RESULTS: We evaluated 112,091 patients with 1-year, 81,554 with 3-year, and 52,426 with 5-year follow-up ( Table 1). Simple prostatectomy and LEP had the lowest reoperation rates (0.9–1.4% and 1.5-6.0%, respectively) while less invasive modalities demonstrated higher reoperation rates (WVTT \[5.3–14.8%\], PUL \[4.3–16.6%\], and TUNA \[5.8–21.0%\]). Among reoperations, TURP (61%), PVP (22%), and LEP (8%) were the most common for recurrent BPH in patients with a minimum of 5 year follow up ( (https://www.auajournals.org/doi/abs/10.1097/01.JU.0001191296.28297.ff.07#F1)). CONCLUSIONS: In this cohort, TURP was the most popular BPH surgery but had a relatively high reoperation rate. LEP, a less invasive alternative to simple prostatectomy, demonstrated comparable low retreatment risk. Less invasive modalities (WVTT, PUL, and TUNA) showed higher reoperation rates and often required more invasive secondary procedures. Optimal surgical management of BPH requires balancing durability, invasiveness, and patient-specific factors. | | | --- | | |

title: PD03-08: Comparative outcomes of holmium laser enucleation (HoLEP), prostatic urethral lift (UroLift), Rezum, and transurethral resection of the prostate (TURP): a systematic review of evidence from 2015 to 2025
parentSessionTitle: PD03: Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia: Surgical Therapy & New Technology II
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Transurethral resection of the prostate (TURP) has long been regarded as the surgical gold standard for men with lower urinary tract symptoms (LUTS) caused by benign prostatic obstruction (BPO). In the past decade, minimally invasive surgical therapies (MISTs) such as the prostatic urethral lift (UroLift) and Rezūm water vapor therapy, as well as holmium laser enucleation of the prostate (HoLEP), have emerged as alternatives with varying durability, recovery, and sexual function outcomes. Objective: To systematically compare efficacy, safety, and retreatment outcomes of HoLEP, UroLift, Rezūm, and TURP to determine whether TURP remains the current gold standard in the modern treatment landscape. METHODS: A systematic review was conducted according to PRISMA guidelines (PROSPERO-compliant methodology). Literature searches were performed in PubMed, Embase, and the Cochrane Library for studies published between January 2015 and June 2025. Eligible studies included randomized controlled trials (RCTs), prospective comparative series, and meta-analyses reporting International Prostate Symptom Score (IPSS), peak urinary flow rate (Qmax), sexual function outcomes, and retreatment rates with ≥3 years of follow-up. Risk of bias was evaluated using the Cochrane ROB-2 and ROBINS-I tools. RESULTS: A total of 42 studies (15 RCTs, 12 prospective cohorts, 10 systematic reviews, and 5 meta-analyses) met inclusion criteria. HoLEP demonstrated the largest mean IPSS reduction (−18 to −21 points, 65–75% improvement) and the lowest retreatment rate (~6% at 5 years). TURP achieved durable symptom relief (mean IPSS reduction 13–15 points) with pooled retreatment ~7–8% at 5 years. Rezūm produced moderate improvement (IPSS −12 to −14; 45–50% improvement) with 4–5% reoperation at 4 years and minimal new sexual dysfunction. UroLift provided rapid recovery and ejaculatory preservation but smaller symptomatic gain (IPSS −11; 35–40% improvement) and higher retreatment (~13% at 5 years). Across RCTs, HoLEP and TURP yielded statistically equivalent IPSS and Qmax improvements at 12–60 months, while HoLEP reduced bleeding, catheterization time, and hospital stay. CONCLUSIONS: HoLEP demonstrates equal or superior long-term efficacy compared to TURP with lower morbidity and retreatment, positioning it as the new surgical benchmark where laser expertise exists. Rezūm and UroLift offer valuable, patient-centered MIST options for men prioritizing recovery and sexual function preservation. Contemporary evidence supports a transition toward HoLEP as the durable, size-independent gold standard in the surgical management of BPO.

title: PD03-09: Durable Symptom Relief and Functional Preservation: Final 3-Year Results from the PINNACLE Trial of the Optilume® BPH Catheter System
parentSessionTitle: PD03: Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia: Surgical Therapy & New Technology II

speakers.organization: Icahn School  of Medicine at Mount Sinai

fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Optilume BPH is a novel minimally invasive surgical therapy (MIST) that combines mechanical dilation with the delivery of paclitaxel for the treatment of lower urinary tract symptoms (LUTS) secondary to BPH. Mechanical dilation with Optilume BPH achieves an anterior commissurotomy, while delivery of paclitaxel is intended to maintain luminal patency during healing. The PINNACLE study was a randomized, sham controlled study evaluating Optilume BPH against a sham procedure, with long-term follow-up limited to the active (Optilume BPH) treatment group. METHODS: 148 subjects were randomized in a 2:1 fashion (100 Optilume BPH, 48 sham) at 18 centers in the US and Canada. Subjects and evaluating personnel were blinded to the treatment received through 12-months, subjects randomized to receive treatment with Optilume BPH continued follow-up through 2 years. Symptom improvement was measured utilizing the International Prostate Symptom Score (IPSS), functional improvement measured by peak urinary flow rate (Qmax). Erectile and ejaculatory function were evaluated utilizing validated questionnaires. RESULTS: Sixty-nine subjects have completed the 3-year follow-up in the per-protocol set. A total of 6 subjects (6/100, 6%) pursued additional surgical management (PAE (1), TURP (2), laser ablation (2), prostatic urethral lift (PUL)(1)) through the 3-year timepoint. Improvement in IPSS was maintained through 3 years (23.4 vs 10.3; -12.9 improvement). Qmax improved from 8.9 ml/sec at baseline to 17.1 ml/sec through 3-year follow-up. Paired analysis showed minimal changes in IPSS and Qmax from 12 month to 3-year follow-up. There were no changes in perceived sexual or ejaculatory function. CONCLUSIONS: Treatment with Optilume BPH results in impressive and durable functional improvements in flow rate and symptomology. The peak flow rate nearly doubled from baseline and remained consistently above normal thresholds through 3 years, suggesting long term efficacy. Minimal surgical retreatment has occurred in the cohort of patients randomized to receive Optilume BPH as part of the pivotal randomized, sham controlled trial.

title: PD03-10: Clinical evaluation of AI-based software for diagnosing bladder outlet obstruction and detrusor underactivity in men with lower urinary tract symptoms
parentSessionTitle: PD03: Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia: Surgical Therapy & New Technology II

speakers.organization: Department of Urology, Samsung Medical Center, Sungkyunkwan University

fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Lower urinary tract symptoms (LUTS) in men are commonly caused by bladder outlet obstruction (BOO) or detrusor underactivity (DU). The pressure–flow study (PFS) is the typical diagnostic reference but is invasive and not always available. This study aimed to validate an artificial-intelligence-based software (Esther Prostex 1™) that predicts BOO and DU non-invasively using uroflowmetry, symptom scores, laboratory data, and ultrasound images. METHODS: A retrospective study was conducted in 456 men aged ≥40 years presenting with LUTS between January 2021 and July 2023. Inclusion criteria were Qmax < 15 ml/s, transrectal ultrasound (TRUS), uroflometry, IPSS data, and available PFS results. The AI model integrated multimodal inputs (IPSS, uroflowmetry, and laboratory tests) to classify BOO and DU, with PFS-based diagnosis as the reference. Primary outcome was evaluated by the area under the ROC curve (AUC), and secondary outcomes included sensitivity, specificity, and overall accuracy. RESULTS: The AI model achieved high diagnostic accuracy for both BOO and DU. For BOO, AUC was 0.8995 (95% CI 0.8589–0.9401, p<0.001) and for DU, AUC was 0.8747 (95% CI 0.8366–0.9129, p<0.001). Five-level AUC interpretive criteria indicates that AUC over 0.8 is considered "good". The ROC curves ( (https://www.auajournals.org/doi/abs/10.1097/01.JU.0001191296.28297.ff.10#F1)) demonstrated excellent diagnostic accuracy for both disease types, with the BOO curve positioned slightly higher, reflecting superior overall specificity. Sensitivity and specificity analysis ( (https://www.auajournals.org/doi/abs/10.1097/01.JU.0001191296.28297.ff.10#F2)) showed complementary strengths: BOO exhibited sensitivity 78.6% and specificity 87.6%, whereas DU showed sensitivity 92.3% and specificity 66.3%. This pattern indicates that the AI system accurately differentiates obstructive cases while maintaining high sensitivity for underactive bladder identification. Both models exceeded the predefined lower 95% CI superiority margins, confirming statistically robust and clinically reproducible performance across subgroups. CONCLUSIONS: Esther Prostex 1™ demonstrated clinically meaningful diagnostic capability for identifying BOO and DU using only non-invasive data. High AUC values (> 0.87) and complementary sensitivity/specificity profiles support its utility as a practical AI-driven alternative to PFS for evaluating male LUTS.

title: PD03-11: Efficacy and Safety of Mirabegron and Tamsulosin Combination Therapy Compared to Taumsulosin Monotherapy for Lower Urinary Tract Symptoms Due to Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia : Results of Multicenter, Randomized, Double-Blind, Phase III Clinical T
parentSessionTitle: PD03: Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia: Surgical Therapy & New Technology II
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: This study aimed to evaluate the efficacy and safety of mirabegron and tamsulosin combination therapy compared to tamsulosin monotherapy in benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH) patients with lower urinary tract symptoms (LUTS). METHODS: This phase 3, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled clinical trial evaluated the efficacy and safety of mirabegron/tamsulosin combination therapy versus tamsulosin monotherapy in men with LUTS. The trial, conducted across 25 centers from July 2021 to October 2023. Eligible participants were randomly assigned to either the combination or monotherapy group for 12 weeks. Primary efficacy endpoints included changes in total urinary frequency score (TUFS) and International Prostate Symptom Scores (IPSS), with secondary endpoints evaluating various urinary symptoms and changes in post void residual volume (PVR), maximum urinary flow rate (Qmax), and quality of life scores. Safety assessments included adverse events, PVR, Qmax, vital signs, electrocardiogram, and laboratory tests. RESULTS: A total of 795 participants were randomized to monotherapy (n=397) and combination therapy (n=398) groups. After 12 weeks, 342 in the monotherapy and 339 in the combination therapy group completed the study, with no significant baseline differences. The combination therapy group showed a greater improvement in TUFS (-11.28) and IPSS (-10.85) scores compared to monotherapy (-8.30 and -9.85, respectively) with significant differences (p<0.0001, p=0.0325). Combination therapy showed significant improvements in storage symptoms and voiding diary variables, including daytime frequency, urgency, and incontinence, compared to monotherapy. The incidence of treatment-emergent adverse events was similar between the groups (13.10% vs 16.58%, p=0.1943), with no serious drug-related adverse events, confirming an acceptable safety profile for combination therapy. CONCLUSIONS: Combination therapy with mirabegron and tamsulosin is more effective than monotherapy in improving LUTS in patients with BPH, particularly storage symptoms, with a comparable safety profile. A fixed-dose combination formulation in the future may further improve patient adherence and quality of life. | | | --- | | |

title: PD03-12: Beyond Operative Time: NASA-TLX Workload Scores Reveal Cognitive and Physical Demands Across the HoLEP Learning Curve
parentSessionTitle: PD03: Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia: Surgical Therapy & New Technology II
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Holmium laser enucleation of the prostate (HoLEP) has a steep learning curve which limits widespread adoption. Objective metrics to define surgical proficiency, efficiency, and perceived workload remain underexplored outside academic institutions. This study aimed to characterize the learning curve for HoLEP from a regional rural hospital. METHODS: A total of 103 patients underwent HoLEP for BPH between March 2024 and August 2025. Surgical cases were stratified into three sequential groups of 34, 34, and 35 cases, respectively, based on operative chronology. Operative characteristics were compared across groups: enucleation time, laser energy, fluid use, and enucleation speed (enucleation time/specimen weight). Perceived workload was assessed using NASA Task Load Index (NASA-TLX), to evaluate perceived workload across several domains (mental demand, physical demand, temporal demand, performance, effort, and frustration). Comparisons of outcome metrics were made for 90-day postoperative complications and urinary continence postoperatively. Univariable and multivariable multinomial logistic regression analyses were performed to examine associations between surgical characteristics and group classification. RESULTS: Progressive improvement was observed in operative time, enucleation time, laser energy, total fluid, enucleation speed, and NASA TLX, as seen in Table 1. No statistically significant associations were observed between group classification and 90-day postoperative complications or urinary continence outcomes at any follow-up interval. In multivariable multinomial logistic regression analysis, the NASA-TLX score (OR 0.84, 95%CI, 0.72-0.99, p=0.04) remained an independent predictor of higher learning curve classification. ( Table 2.) CONCLUSIONS: Progressive reductions in operative time, energy use, and perceived workload signify quantifiable improvement. The NASA-TLX score correlated independently with improvement in proficiency, outperforming traditional operative measures in defining the HoLEP learning curve. | | | --- | | | | | | --- | | |

title: PD03-13: Ejaculation-Sparing Thulium Laser Enucleation of the Prostate (ES-ThuLEP): A Feasible and Effective Alternative for BPH Treatment
parentSessionTitle: PD03: Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia: Surgical Therapy & New Technology II

speakers.organization: Fondazione Policlinico Universitario Campus Bio-Medico, Rome, Italy

fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH) is an age-related condition affecting approximately one-third of men over the age of 50, commonly leading to both storage and voiding lower urinary tract symptoms (LUTS). A major drawback of endoscopic treatments for BPH is the frequent occurrence of retrograde ejaculation. This study aims to assess the efficacy and feasibility of ejaculation-sparing thulium laser enucleation of the prostate (ES-ThuLEP) in managing LUTS due to BPH while preserving ejaculatory function. METHODS: Between June and September 2024, sexually active patients with BPH were enrolled and followed up at 3 and 6 months after surgery. Baseline data were collected, and two standardized questionnaires—the International Index of Erectile Function short form (IIEF-5) and the International Prostate Symptom Score (IPSS)—were administered. In addition, all patients underwent uroflowmetry and an assessment of post-void residual volume (PVR). The surgical technique involves two key steps aimed at improving ejaculatory outcomes: preservation of bladder neck muscle fibers from the 7 o’clock to the 5 o’clock position; preservation of the entire posterior urethral plate from the colliculus seminalis to the bladder neck. The main differences compared to the conventional technique are illustrated in (https://www.auajournals.org/doi/abs/10.1097/01.JU.0001191296.28297.ff.13#F1). RESULTS: A total of 30 patients were enrolled. Median age was 60 yrs (IQR, 55-70). Median prostate volume was 65 ml (IQR, 50-70 ml). No patient presented with a large middle lobe. A statistically significant improvement in IPSS score, maximum flow (Qmax), and post-void residual volume (PVR) was observed at both 3 and 6 months postoperatively (p<0.05), while no statistically significant differences were found in IIEF-5 scores before and after surgery. All patients maintained ejaculation at 6 months postoperatively. However, some degree of hypospermia was reported by 43.7% and 30.6% of patients at 3 and 6 months, respectively. CONCLUSIONS: The ES-ThuLEP technique demonstrated good functional outcomes while preserving ejaculation in all patients, suggesting that it may represent a feasible option for the surgical management of BPH in sexually active men. However, further studies with larger patient cohorts and longer follow-up are warranted to confirm these findings.

title: PD03-14: Durability of holmium laser enucleation of the prostate: A 10-year multi-institutional comparison using the Cosmos Database
parentSessionTitle: PD03: Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia: Surgical Therapy & New Technology II
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Holmium Laser Enucleation of the Prostate (HoLEP) is a size-independent, minimally invasive surgery for the treatment of benign prostatic hyperplasia which has gained significant popularity in the last decade. The durability of HoLEP lacks robust, long-term data. We aimed to examine durability and postoperative outcomes for HoLEP compared to other procedures. METHODS: We performed a retrospective, cross-sectional analysis using a multi-institutional electronic health record database (Epic Cosmos) from 2015 to 2025. We compared HoLEP to alternative prostate procedures (transurethral resection of prostate, prostatic urethral lift, photoselective vaporization, water vapor therapy, waterjet ablation, and microwave therapy) using CPT and ICD codes as well as de-identified data from Cosmos. Outcomes measured were durability (no subsequent prostate procedures), independence from medications (lack of filled prostate medication prescriptions following the procedure), immediate outcomes in the first 30 days, and early postoperative outcomes from 31 to 180 days. Categorical variables were compared using chi-squared tests, and all analyses were performed in R version 4.5.1. RESULTS: In total 60,352 patients underwent a HoLEP procedure while 506,959 patients underwent an alternative procedure. HoLEP showed superior surgical durability with 96.1% of patients remaining free of subsequent prostate procedures versus 88.5% in the non-HoLEP group (p<0.001). HoLEP demonstrated better independence from prostate medications with 65.6% of patients free of medications versus 41.8% (p<0.001) ( (https://www.auajournals.org/doi/abs/10.1097/01.JU.0001191296.28297.ff.14#F1)). Perioperative (0-30 days) and early postoperative (31-180 days) outcomes were similar between HoLEP and non-HoLEP procedures with statistically significant but modest absolute differences ( (https://www.auajournals.org/doi/abs/10.1097/01.JU.0001191296.28297.ff.14#F2)). CONCLUSIONS: When compared to alternative prostate procedures for urinary symptoms, HoLEP demonstrated superior durability and independence from prostate medications. Postoperative outcomes were similar between the two groups. Our findings suggest that HoLEP can serve as a definitive treatment for patients deciding between surgical options.

title: PD03-15: How to avoid complications during Robotic Waterjet ablation therapy (Aquablation) in BPH patients?
parentSessionTitle: PD03: Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia: Surgical Therapy & New Technology II
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Robotic Water-jet ablation has become an alternative to transurethral resection of the prostate to treat bladder outlet obstruction (BOO) in BPH patients. The significant advantages of this procedure are the ability to treat prostates of various sizes, reduced sexual side effects, and a shorter learning curve. However, some major complications such as higher post-procedural transfusion rates and recently reported 5% of post-procedure urethral stricture could not be brushed aside. We have aimed to identify predictive factors that could lead to serious complications during Aquablation to improve the durability and safety of the procedure. METHODS: We have reviewed the logs of all prospective patients who underwent Aquablation and presented with Clavien-Dindo (CD) Gr II-V complications.
