Deviations from the standard Aquablation protocol were recorded and analyzed about complications and their management. RESULTS: We have identified 87 (16.6%) out of 524 prospectively followed patients operated by a single surgeon between 2023- 2025. There were CD Gr II 66 (12.6%), Gr IIIa 12 (2.2%), and Gr IIIb 9 (1.7%) complications, respectively. None presented with Gr IV and V. False route passing of the hand piece of the Aquablation device was associated with urethral stricture and bladder neck undermining requiring longer indwelling catheter time in 47 (8.9%) patients, SPT in 5 (0.9%), and meatoplasty in the remaining 2 (0.3%) patients. Incorrect planning of the water jet alignment step at the bladder neck was associated with significant bleeding and a need for hemotransfusion, with a mean of 51+ 3.5 (SD) (blood PC). Incorrect nozzle position before placement of depth markers was associated with increased postoperative bleeding, but did not reach statistical significance. 6(1.1%) patients who required redo surgery due to failure of weaning the indwelling catheter underwent TUR-P of the apical tissue and voided spontaneously. Seventeen patients (3.2%) who required redosurgery 5.19 + 3.9 months due to de novo obstructive symptoms were diagnosed with cross-healing of the lateral distal prostatic lobes, obstructing the prostatic utricle. Two patients with severe postoperative hemorrhage were diagnosed with aberrant vessels of the prostatic artery and underwent successful PAE. CONCLUSIONS: Our data show that meticulous planning of the jet alignment at the bladder neck is crucial for avoiding significant bleeding. Verumontanum area preservation might lead to residual obstructive symptoms and the need for additional intervention. Patients with severe postoperative bleeding need PAE without delay.

title: PD04-01: Clinical Decision Support as a Nudge towards Improved Perioperative Care
parentSessionTitle: PD04: Health Services Research: Quality Improvement & Patient Safety I
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Clinical Decision Support (CDS) systems seek to “nudge” provider behavior toward an intended goal. CDS comes in several forms such as pop up alerts, dynamic order sets, and others. We implemented perioperative CDS tools with the hypothesis that these interventions would increase adherence to target perioperative care goals over time. This study aims to assess the utility of these tools over a multi-year period to influence provider behavior. METHODS: Our department incorporated three CDS tools within our electronic medical record (EMR), and retrospectively studied the target outcome before and after implementation of each: To reduce postoperative opioid prescriptions, all opioid orders were removed from the urology discharge order set. Data regarding postoperative opioid prescriptions were gathered from 12,820 surgical cases over 94 months. To improve the number of electronic consents created prior to the day of surgery (DOS) so families could review ahead of time, a close visit validation warning was added to check for a surgical order and recommend the electronic consent be created if it was not. Data regarding consent creation prior to DOS were gathered from 5,707 surgical cases over 24 months. To improve preoperative urine culture (prUC) rates, pop-up recommended orders were added on when targeted procedures are ordered. Data regarding prUC orders were gathered for 193 target surgical procedures over 12 months. We summarized each data set for individual cases by month and analyzed the data via Statistical Process Control (SPC) chart with a cut-point representing the date of CDS intervention. RESULTS: The average monthly rate of postoperative opioid prescriptions dropped from 59% to 11% after intervention 1 (p<.0001). The average monthly rate of surgical consent forms prior to DOS climbed from 16% to 49% after intervention 2 (p<.0001). The average monthly rate of targeted prUC rose from 21% to 46% after intervention 3 (p=0.0060). Interventions 1 and 2 showed no seasonality after time series analysis; no interrupted time series modeling was performed for intervention 3 due to relative paucity of data. CONCLUSIONS: Our data show statistically significant improvements in adherence to perioperative goals after implementation of three targeted CDS interventions. However, it is important to acknowledge that these changes did not occur in isolation from departmental effort and intention. In light of the relative simplicity and cost-effectiveness of implementing these changes, we believe leveraging the functionality of CDS is a valuable tool to foster consistency in perioperative care and nudge providers towards desired departmental goals.

title: PD04-02: Impact of nighttime centralization on referral efficiency and testicular salvage in pediatric acute scrotum: A regional experience from Japan
parentSessionTitle: PD04: Health Services Research: Quality Improvement & Patient Safety I
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Acute scrotum is a pediatric urological emergency that requires prompt diagnosis and timely surgical management to prevent testicular loss. However, in rural regions, timely care is often limited by the shortage of pediatric urologists and the absence of 24-hour surgical coverage. To address this problem, a nighttime centralization system was introduced in Yamanashi Prefecture, Japan, in October 2018. Under this policy, all pediatric patients presenting with suspected acute scrotum during nighttime hours (6:00 PM–8:00 AM) were directly referred to our hospital. This study aimed to evaluate whether this regional centralization improved referral efficiency and clinical outcomes for pediatric acute scrotum. METHODS: We retrospectively analyzed electronic medical records of pediatric patients diagnosed with acute scrotum at the University of Yamanashi Hospital between January 2003 and December 2024. Patients were divided into two groups: before centralization (2003–September 2018) and after centralization (October 2018–2024). Cases lacking documented onset or consultation time, or those exceeding 24 hours (1,440 minutes) from symptom onset to consultation, were excluded. Annual case numbers, surgical rates, and testicular salvage rates were compared between the two groups. RESULTS: A total of 215 cases were identified. After October 2018, the number of nighttime consultations increased from 32 to 58, and surgical cases rose from 11 (26%) to 25 (43%). The testicular salvage rate improved from 71% to 88%. The median time from symptom onset to consultation decreased from 323 minutes (IQR 181–507) before centralization to 269 minutes (IQR 165–404) after implementation (p=0.0865). Among surgically treated patients, the median onset-to-surgery interval was significantly shorter in salvaged testes (258 \[170–455\] min) than in orchiectomy cases (434 \[281–1120\] min, p=0.032). CONCLUSIONS: Nighttime centralization improved the timeliness of care for pediatric acute scrotum, leading to increased surgical intervention and higher testicular salvage rates. Although the reduction in onset-to-consultation time did not reach statistical significance, the findings suggest that centralization effectively eliminated referral delays and enhanced regional coordination in pediatric urological emergencies.

title: PD04-03: EHR-Integrated Clinical Decision Support for Primary Care Provider Engagement for Urinary Incontinence
parentSessionTitle: PD04: Health Services Research: Quality Improvement & Patient Safety I
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Urinary incontinence (UI) affects nearly half of adult women, yet only ~20% receive guideline-concordant care. Embedding clinical decision support (CDS) tools into electronic health records (EHRs) may improve UI detection and management in primary care. The INTUIT trial evaluates whether a bundled CDS intervention enhances provider engagement and promotes evidence-based UI care. METHODS: Optimizing Primary Care Tools for Incontinence Management (OPTIMA) is a multi-site, cluster-randomized controlled trial across 60 primary care offices within four health systems. Providers were randomized to usual care vs. a bundled intervention including academic detailing and EHR-integrated CDS tools (order sets, note templates, and referral pathways). All providers received an interruptive Best Practice Advisory (BPA) when a patient with UI symptoms checked in; the intervention arm’s BPA linked to the order set. BPA engagement was defined as opening the order set (intervention) or selecting “Will address UI” (control). A chart review of 100 intervention encounters assessed CDS usage. Multivariable logistic regression examined predictors of BPA engagement and tool use. RESULTS: Between April 2023 and January 2025, the BPA fired 430 times (Table 1). Engagement was higher in the intervention arm (67.8% vs. 33.0%, p<0.001; (https://www.auajournals.org/doi/abs/10.1097/01.JU.0001191300.98315.e9.03#F1)). Engagement declined with repeat alerts but was positively associated with being in the intervention arm (OR 4.1, 95% CI 2.6–7.8) and provider (vs. assistant) encounters (OR 4.2, 95% CI 2.5–8.1). CDS tools were used in 20% of reviewed charts, and BPA engagement strongly predicted tool use (OR 12.0, 95% CI 1.5–94.4;Table 2). CONCLUSIONS: Bundled CDS interventions significantly increased provider engagement with EHR alerts for UI. Early interaction with interruptive alerts appears critical for sustained tool adoption, underscoring the role of thoughtful design and workflow alignment in CDS effectiveness.

title: PD04-04: Consensus is possible: utilization of a modified Delphi analysis to standardize postoperative orders and expectations in a multi-site pediatric urology practice
parentSessionTitle: PD04: Health Services Research: Quality Improvement & Patient Safety I
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Inconsistencies in postoperative management and low-quality discharge instructions are associated with negative clinical outcomes and avoidable frustration for patients and families. Developing high quality instructions for pediatric urology practices is challenging given the wide range of procedure types and patient ages/development. This study aimed to use modified Delphi methodology to standardize post-operative instructions in a group of pediatric urologists and facilitate creation of a single postoperative discharge order set implementable across a large children’s health system. METHODS: Seven pediatric urologists and a transitional urologist in a single practice who perform surgeries at four locations were queried via REDCap survey using a two-round modified Delphi process between June 2024 and May 2025. Questions covered activity and travel restrictions, diet, bathing, swimming, dressings/wound care, medications, catheter management, and follow up for categories of pediatric urologic procedures including endoscopic, meatal, groin/scrotal, penile, kidney, ureteral reimplant, and lower tract reconstruction. Consensus was established for areas with ≥80% agreement. Outcomes of questioning were used to create a common post-operative discharge order set for ambulatory and inpatient surgery with branching logic based on procedure type, age, and— for areas without consensus— surgeon. RESULTS: After the first round, there was consensus in 21 of 106 (19.8%) areas queried. After the second round, consensus was reached for all activity restrictions, travel, diet, bathing/wound care, swimming, medications, catheter management, and routine follow up for all procedure categories. Consensus was not achieved for postoperative dressings (particularly those for penile surgery), and surgeon-specific dressing types were included in the order set. The order set was implemented successfully across all four locations, easing workflow for surgeons, surgical trainees, postoperative care unit staff, surgery schedulers providing anticipatory guidance regarding postoperative management, and clinic nurses fielding post-operative calls. CONCLUSIONS: Pediatric urologists have varied and individual preferences regarding postoperative instructions. A modified Delphi analysis brought these to light, yet consensus was achievable for most aspects of postoperative care, simplifying teaching for recovery and clinic nurses. Delphi process results may be implemented via order sets to standardize postoperative care, communication, and expectations across large health systems.

title: PD04-05: Multi-Disciplinary Trial of Void Algorithm Reduces Catheter-Associated Urinary Tract Infections: Long-Term Outcomes on a Surgical Unit
parentSessionTitle: PD04: Health Services Research: Quality Improvement & Patient Safety I
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Prolonged indwelling urethral catheter use predisposes patients to catheter-associated urinary tract infections (CAUTIs), an avoidable morbidity and healthcare expenditure. As such, efforts to minimize CAUTIs remain a priority for patients, providers, and hospital administration. We therefore sought to assess the long-term impact of a multi-disciplinary trial of void (TOV) algorithm on CAUTI rates and indwelling urethral catheter use on a surgical Step-Down Unit. METHODS: From April 2021 to March 2024, we performed an interrupted time series on a 36-bed surgical Step-Down Unit in a large urban academic medical center – with the TOV algorithm as the intervention ( Figure 1A). Our cohort included patients treated with intra-abdominal, thoracic, vascular, urologic, and gynecologic surgeries. The primary outcome was mean CAUTI rates 1.5 years before and after algorithm implementation. Secondary outcomes included mean rate of indwelling catheter use and mean total patient days before and after algorithm implementation. Given the low incidence of CAUTIs, our unit of analysis was a fiscal quarter. Univariable analysis was performed using Student's t-test. We compared outcomes on a surgical Step-Down Unit where the algorithm was implemented to a 34-bed surgical floor unit – where the algorithm was not implemented – to serve as a natural control. RESULTS: Over 12 fiscal quarters, there were 4124 indwelling urethral catheter days and 10 CAUTIs on the surgical Step-Down Unit. Average CAUTIs decreased from 1.3 per quarter to 0.3 (p=0.03, Figure 1B). Average indwelling urethral catheter days appeared to decrease after implementation of the TOV algorithm though this finding was not statistically significant (384.7 vs. 302.7, p=0.09). There was no difference in mean total patient days before and after algorithm implementation (2942.0 vs. 2991.0, p=0.27). During the same study period, the surgical floor unit experienced a decrease in catheter use (502.3 vs. 377.2, p<0.01) though CAUTI rates did not change (0.7 vs 0.2, p=0.09). CONCLUSIONS: Long-term implementation of a multi-disciplinary TOV algorithm to standardize catheter care is effective and appears to reduce CAUTIs without affecting patient care volume. Further investigations should assess what aspects of quality initiatives allow for sustained improvements to achieve superior patient care and hospital metrics.

title: PD04-06: From Problem to Practice: Learning from a Catheter Self-Irrigation Program to Reduce Preventable Emergency Department Visits
parentSessionTitle: PD04: Health Services Research: Quality Improvement & Patient Safety I
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: In prior work, we identified foley catheter malfunction as a major cause of preventable emergency department (ED) visits in postoperative urologic patients. Based on this, we implemented a program of catheter self-irrigation for patients who underwent surgery for benign prostatic hyperplasia. We aim to assess this program’s effectiveness. METHODS: Using the Institute for Healthcare Improvement’s Model for Improvement as a framework, we conducted 7 Plan-Do-Study-Act (PDSA) learning cycles, starting June 2024. Process measures included: 1) intervention reach, defined as the proportion of patients who were discharged with catheters who received teaching, and 2) quality of teaching. Outcome measure was change in preventable ED visits, defined as a visit where patient was discharged home from the ED without imaging or urologic consultation. Statistical process control charts were used to measure changes over time. RESULTS: We conducted 7 PDSA cycles ( (https://www.auajournals.org/doi/abs/10.1097/01.JU.0001191300.98315.e9.06#F1)). A P chart illustrates how each PDSA cycle increased our intervention reach ( Figure 2A). By increasing the reliability of our intervention through creation of a default order set in the electronic medical record and integration of automatic patient education materials in cycle 6, intervention reach increased to 94%. 18% (15/83) of patients performed self-irrigation at home, and 60% of those (9/15) avoided an ED visit ( Figure 2B). Of the remaining 6, all represented appropriate escalations in care. Patients rated the teaching as valuable (median score 8/10) and reported confidence in performing self-irrigation (median score 8/10). CONCLUSIONS: Patient self-irrigation of catheter at home is a feasible alternative to the emergency department for catheter malfunction, and decreases preventable ED visits.

title: PD04-07: Enhancing Prostate Cancer Care with Educational Videos: A Quality Improvement Initiative
parentSessionTitle: PD04: Health Services Research: Quality Improvement & Patient Safety I
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Prostate biopsy pathology reports are often too complex for patients to interpret despite their role in diagnosis and treatment decisions. We developed an instructional video to improve patient understanding of the biopsy report. We then evaluated the video's impact on patient anxiety, satisfaction, and comprehension. METHODS: On the day of biopsy, we presented 11 prostate cancer patients with a mock pathology report standardized for a patient (Mickey Mouse). Subsequently, we evaluated their understanding of the report as well as their anxiety, satisfaction, and comprehension (Scores 1–4). Approximately a week later, patients received their actual biopsy report, along with a supplemental educational video explaining it. Re-using the prior survey, we re-evaluated patient’s understanding of their report, anxiety, and satisfaction. We analyzed changes in these measured outcomes using Fisher’s Exact test and the Mann-Whitney U test. Educational Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=c2e1VhhaUWc. RESULTS: Eleven patients completed the baseline survey, with a 45% response rate to the follow-up survey. Before presenting the educational video, only 55% of participants accurately identified “Mickey Mouse’s” cancer status and Gleason score. After watching the educational video and receiving their biopsy reports, 100% of patients accurately identified their cancer status and Gleason score. Furthermore, patient satisfaction scores significantly increased ( Figure A). There was a modest increase in understanding of next steps of care following review of the video. No change in anxiety levels pre-and-post video education was observed. CONCLUSIONS: Pathology reports are difficult to interpret. Providing patients with report specific explanatory videos improved comprehension, and satisfaction. Given the low cost and ease of implementation, video educational videos may play a role in prostate cancer care.

title: PD04-08: At-home And Mail-in Semen Analysis: A Critical Review Of Scientific Validation, Regulatory Oversight, And Marketing Claims
parentSessionTitle: PD04: Health Services Research: Quality Improvement & Patient Safety I

speakers.organization: University of Florida College of Medicine

fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: At-home and mail-in semen analysis (SA) platforms are expanding rapidly, marketed as convenient and private tools for fertility screening and post-vasectomy testing. However, many use clinical terminology without the regulatory or scientific backing required for diagnostic use. We aimed to critically evaluate major SA companies to determine their clinical purpose, regulatory status, validation evidence, and marketing accuracy. METHODS: A structured review was performed of 10 companies actively marketing SA services in the U. S. (Reprosource, Fellow Health, PVSA, Legacy, Trak, Yo, SpermCheck, CryoChoice, MaleFromHome, and Sapyen). Data sources included PubMed, FDA filings, and company documentation (January–April 2025). Each platform was assessed across four domains: (1) clinical purpose (diagnostic vs wellness), (2) regulatory oversight (CLIA \[New\ York State\], CAP, or FDA approval), (3) published analytical or usability validation, and (4) public-facing marketing claims. RESULTS: All mail-in fertility tests failed to meet NYS Department of Health standards and only Fellow Health had a NYS approved PVSA test, representing the current regulatory gold standard. Only Fellow Health and Reprosource demonstrated both CLIA certification and peer-reviewed validation for delayed mail-in analysis. Most other platforms, notably MaleFromHome, Legacy, and Sapyen, were marketed as diagnostic tools but lacked peer-reviewed validation or displayed legal-facing disclaimers citing wellness purposes in their Terms and Conditions. Consumer at-home tests (Trak, Yo, SpermCheck) showed good usability data yet remained qualitative or semi-quantitative, with labeling that risks consumer misinterpretation. Most companies lacked transparency regarding algorithmic adjustments involved in SA reporting. Marketing language frequently overstated diagnostic equivalency without disclosure of laboratory limitations. CONCLUSIONS: Few mail-in or at-home SA platforms meet criteria for true diagnostic-grade testing. High-Complexity, validated mail-in systems can safely expand access, whereas unverified at-home or “wellness” products may mislead consumers and providers. Greater regulatory transparency, peer-reviewed validation, and clinician integration are needed to ensure evidence-based adoption of these emerging reproductive technologies. | | | --- | | |

title: PD04-09: Diagnostic Accuracy of Prostate MRI Reads from Non-Academic Versus Academic Centers: Impact on Detection of Clinically Significant Prostate Cancer and Avoidance of Unnecessary Biopsies
parentSessionTitle: PD04: Health Services Research: Quality Improvement & Patient Safety I
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Multiparametric MRI (mpMRI) is integral to prostate cancer diagnosis but remains reader-dependent. Interpretation variability between non-academic and academic centers may affect detection of clinically significant prostate cancer (csPCa) and lead to unnecessary biopsies. This study evaluated patients whose non-academic MRI showed a suspicious lesion that was deemed negative on academic re-read, comparing diagnostic accuracy and clinical impact between interpretations. METHODS: We prospectively analyzed 44 patients referred for mpMRI re-evaluation after non-academic imaging demonstrated one or more suspicious lesions not confirmed on academic re-read. Outside MRIs were performed using 3T scanners and interpreted per PI-RADS v2.1. Academic re-reads were performed by experienced genitourinary radiologists. All patients underwent MRI-targeted biopsies based on outside reads plus concurrent 12-core systematic biopsies. Pathology was categorized as benign, Grade Group (GG) 1, or GG≥2 (csPCa). Diagnostic performance and biopsy outcomes were compared. RESULTS: Median PSA was 5.7 ng/mL and prostate volume 60 g. Outside MRIs reported lesions as PI-RADS 3 (36%), 4 (52%), and 5 (11%). Overall cancer detection was 38.6%, and csPCa 16%. Targeted biopsies of non-academic MRI lesions yielded benign/GG1 results in 41/44 (94%) and csPCa in 3/44 (6.8%). Only one case (2%) represented csPCa detected solely within the MRI target. Academic re-reads classified all lesions as non-suspicious, which would have safely avoided biopsy in 36/44 (82%) cases. In 12 patients, the outside MRI was the only biopsy indication; of these, 3/12 (25%) had csPCa (two from systematic cores, one from target). Relying on academic reads would have missed 3/44 (6%), all detected by systematic sampling. CONCLUSIONS: Academic prostate MRI re-reads markedly improve diagnostic specificity and reduce unnecessary biopsies with minimal risk of missed csPCa. Centralized review by expert radiologists optimizes accuracy, decreases procedural morbidity, and enhances efficiency in prostate cancer diagnostic pathways.

title: PD04-10: Cancer Surgery Outcomes after Implementation of a Global Budget Model in Rural Hospitals
parentSessionTitle: PD04: Health Services Research: Quality Improvement & Patient Safety I
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Rural hospitals face increasing financial strain, threatening the sustainability of essential surgical services. The Pennsylvania Rural Health Model (PARHM), initiated in 2019, represents the first U. S. global budget program designed specifically for rural hospitals. The model aims to stabilize hospital finances and promote population health; however, its impact on the quality of complex surgical care remains uncertain. This study evaluated the association between PARHM implementation and short-term outcomes following inpatient cancer surgery among rural residents. METHODS: Analysis used a stacked difference-in-differences design leveraging the staggered implementation of PARHM across rural hospitals. Linked Pennsylvania Health Care Cost Containment Council (PHC4) discharge data and Pennsylvania Cancer Registry (PCR) records from 2016–2023 identified 17,048 patients residing in hospital service areas (HSAs) with a PARHM-participating hospital who underwent inpatient surgery for one of 11 cancers. Primary outcomes were 30- and 90-day mortality, readmission, and composite measures. Models applied HSA-level propensity score weights, adjusted for patient and area covariates, and clustered standard errors by HSA. RESULTS: Among 17,048 cancer surgery admissions, 3,537 occurred in PARHM HSAs and 13,511 in non-PARHM HSAs. In adjusted analyses, PARHM implementation was not associated with statistically significant changes in short-term surgical outcomes. The estimated effect on 90-day mortality was +1.1 percentage points (pp) (95% CI, −1.8 to 3.9; p=0.46) and on 90-day readmission was −1.6 pp (95% CI, −5.8 to 2.7; p=0.47). Findings for 30-day mortality, readmission, and composite outcomes were similarly nonsignificant. Cohort- and cancer site–specific analyses identified isolated significant estimates without consistent directional patterns. CONCLUSIONS: Implementation of PARHM was not associated with changes in short-term postoperative outcomes among rural residents undergoing cancer surgery. These results suggest that Pennsylvania’s global budget model did not measurably influence surgical oncology outcomes during the demonstration period. | | | --- | | |

title: PD04-11: Unplanned Healthcare Utilization after Benign Prostate Intervention in Michigan
parentSessionTitle: PD04: Health Services Research: Quality Improvement & Patient Safety I
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Randomized controlled trials have demonstrated the safety and efficacy of therapies for benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH). These common procedures are performed in a wide variety of patient populations and perioperative contexts in routine clinical practice. However, real-world data on perioperative outcomes are limited. Therefore, we sought to understand the incidence and predictors of emergency department (ED) visits after BPH procedures in a contemporary, real-world cohort. METHODS: Using Michigan statewide claims data, patients who underwent a BPH procedure between 2015 and 2023 were identified. Procedures included: water vapor thermal therapy (WVTT), transurethral resection of prostate (TURP), prostatic urethral lift (PUL), transurethral microwave thermotherapy (TUMT), laser photovaporization (PVP), simple prostatectomy (SP), robotic waterjet therapy (RWJT) and laser enucleation of prostate (LEP). ED visit rates were assessed within 30 days of index procedure and categorized by the primary ICD-9/10 diagnosis code. Multivariable logistic regression models were used to identify predictors of 30-day ED visits. RESULTS: A total of 55,693 procedures were identified. ED visit rates ranged from 10% to 17% by procedure ( (https://www.auajournals.org/doi/abs/10.1097/01.JU.0001191300.98315.e9.11#F1)) with an overall rate of 13.3%. The most common urologic reasons for ED visits were: urinary retention (39%), hematuria (29%), UTI/infection (21%), and catheter-related complications (17%). Patients experiencing an ED visit were older and more comorbid. On multivariable analysis, predictors of ED visits included: higher age (OR 1.01, 1.00-1.02), preoperative catheter use (OR 1.47, 1.29-1.67), and preoperative anticoagulation (OR 1.38, 1.22-1.55). Compared to TURP, patients undergoing RWJT had a higher risk of ED visits (OR 1.56, 1.12-2.17) and LEP a lower risk (OR 0.63, 0.51-0.78). CONCLUSIONS: Emergency department visits are common after BPH intervention particularly amongst older patients who are on anti-coagulation and are catheter dependent preoperatively. The most common causes of ED visits included hematuria, urinary retention, UTI and catheter-related complications. Further, the risk of unplanned ED visits differs by procedure with RWJT being the highest and LEP the lowest. Future work should develop strategies to reduce these visits.

title: PD04-12: Both over-prescription and under-prescription of opioids after inpatient urologic surgery increases odds of postsurgical opioid refills
parentSessionTitle: PD04: Health Services Research: Quality Improvement & Patient Safety I
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: To assess the impact of mismatched (over-prescription and under-prescription) discharge opioid prescriptions on opioid refills up to 90 days after inpatient urologic surgery. METHODS: A retrospective single institutional cohort study examined 7,381 adult opioid-naïve and non-opioid-naïve patients discharged after inpatient urologic surgery between 2017 and 2024. Each patient’s daily dose of discharge opioid prescription was compared to their last inpatient daily opioid consumption before discharge. Discharge opioid prescriptions were categorized as matched, over-, and under-prescribed, defined as prescribed daily dose within 7.5 oral morphine equivalents \[OME\], ≥7.5 OME above, and ≤7.5 OME below of inpatient daily dose, respectively. Fisher’s test and multiple logistic regression analyses were used. RESULTS: 38.3% of patients were discharged with matched opioid prescriptions while 38.0% were over-prescribed and 23.7% were under-prescribed. Compared to the patients with matched prescriptions, patients with either over-prescription or under-prescription had higher opioid refill rates at 1-30, 31-60, and 61-90 days ( (https://www.auajournals.org/doi/abs/10.1097/01.JU.0001191300.98315.e9.12#F1)). Multiple logistic regression analyses revealed that when controlling for opioid-naïve status, type of surgical procedure, and other factors such as age, gender, and length of stay, opioid over-prescription independently increased the odds of refills at 1–30, 31-60, and 61–90 days after discharge by 85%, 49%, and 85%, respectively, while opioid under-prescription increased odds refills at 1–30 and 61–90 days by 47% and 33%, respectively ( (https://www.auajournals.org/doi/abs/10.1097/01.JU.0001191300.98315.e9.12#F2)). In contrast, the total dose of opioid prescriptions had minimal contribution to opioid refills. CONCLUSIONS: Both over-prescribing and under-prescribing of opioids, rather than the total dose of opioid prescriptions, independently contribute to increased odds of refills. Patient-centered, individualized discharge opioid dosing based on inpatient consumption may reduce prescription mismatch, enhance opioid stewardship and improve postoperative outcomes.

title: PD04-14: Spinal Anesthesia in Urology for Responsive Pediatric Anesthesia and Satisfaction in Surgery (SURPASS): A Novel Pediatric Spinal Anesthetic Program
parentSessionTitle: PD04: Health Services Research: Quality Improvement & Patient Safety I
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Children less than 12 months of age are at the greatest risk for complications associated with general anesthesia including hypoxia, hypotension, and cardiac arrest. Additionally, significant debate surrounds the lasting effects of general anesthesia on pediatric neurocognitive development. Spinal anesthesia (SA) offers an alternative that circumvents many risks associated with general anesthesia. We present our pilot program establishing an awake spinal anesthesia program for pediatric urologic procedures. METHODS: Initial implementation included distribution of educational materials regarding risks and benefits of spinal anesthesia to families in urology clinic. In parallel, the anesthesia department completed hands-on training with providers on performance of both tactile and ultrasound guided SA techniques. Operating room implementation began in August 2024. Pediatric urology patients were eligible for SA if they were 24 months or younger, planned for open outpatient procedure of 90 minutes or less, and had American Society of Anesthesiologists (ASA) status 1-3. Laparoscopic cases were excluded. The final anesthetic type was determined jointly by the anesthesiologist, surgeon, and patient’s guardian on the day of surgery. RESULTS: To date, 161 procedures have been attempted under SA. 141 procedures (87.58%) were successful, and 20 (12.42%) were converted to general anesthesia. Reasons for conversion included failed motor block resulting in partial anesthetic effects in 17 patients (85.00%), bronchospasm in 2 patients (10.00%), and vasovagal response in 1 patient (5.00%). The most common procedures successfully performed under SA were circumcision (58.87%), circumcision revision (23.40%), and penile torsion repair (23.40%). The median age for successful SA was 6 months (IQR: 4.00-8.00). The youngest patient was 1 month and the oldest was 20 months. The median weight of all patients was 7.90 kg (IQR: 6.94-9.10), with successful spinals weighing a median of 7.91 kg (IQR: 6.94-9.10) and converted patients weighing a median of 7.84 kg (IQR: 7.02-8.95). There was no statistically significant difference between the weight or age of successful spinals versus those that were converted to general anesthesia. CONCLUSIONS: Many pediatric urologic procedures performed on infants can be safely completed under spinal anesthesia. Beginning a successful and sustainable SA program requires a multidisciplinary approach. We hope to continue expanding this program to additional surgical specialties and procedures.

title: PD04-15: I’ve Had a Couple of Situations Where They’ve Talked Suicide…”:  A Qualitative Study to Improve Behavioral Health Support for Patients Undergoing Cystectomy
parentSessionTitle: PD04: Health Services Research: Quality Improvement & Patient Safety I
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Despite increasing recognition of the psychological burden of bladder cancer and cystectomy, behavioral health services are inconsistently implemented in uro-oncology. This study explored provider-perceived barriers to integrating behavioral health care throughout the perioperative cancer pathway and identified opportunities for system-level improvement and workflow-based solutions. METHODS: Four semi-structured focus groups were conducted with nurse navigators (two groups; n=7), ostomy nurses (n=4), and advanced-practice providers (total n=3). Guided discussions explored perceptions of patient distress, workflow barriers, and opportunities to integrate behavioral health services into routine care. Sessions were transcribed verbatim and analyzed in NVivo using the Sort & Sift, Think & Shift method. A hybrid deductive–inductive codebook guided analysis, and thematic summaries were developed through iterative synthesis and team consensus. RESULTS: Participants described multiple, interrelated barriers to addressing mental health needs in uro-oncology. Providers acknowledged the emotional toll of cystectomy but cited limited training and uncertainty about recognizing or responding to patient distress. Mental health was often addressed informally and outside of structured workflows, resulting in inconsistent screening and delayed referrals. Communication gaps across inpatient, outpatient, and behavioral health teams further fragmented care, with unclear referral ownership and poor coordination between oncology, primary care, and behavioral health services. Although behavioral health and other supportive care resources were available, their lack of standardization and visibility rendered them difficult to access. Providers emphasized that limited workforce capacity, competing demands, and the absence of clearly defined roles compounded these gaps, ultimately hindering consistent delivery of behavioral health care for cystectomy patients. CONCLUSIONS: Providers identified multilevel barriers—spanning knowledge, communication, and resource limitations—that impede integration of behavioral health services into uro-oncology care. Embedding structured psychosocial screening and designated behavioral health partnerships within the uro-oncology workflow may enhance patient outcomes and improve continuity of care. | | | --- | | |

title: PD05-01: Socioeconomic Deprivation and Male Fertility: Decreasing Prosperity Associated with Lower Semen Parameters in a Nationwide Cohort
parentSessionTitle: PD05: Infertility: Epidemiology & Evaluation I

speakers.organization: University of Florida College of Medicine

fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Socioeconomic disadvantage has been associated with disparities in nutrition, environment, and access to reproductive care, yet its relationship to semen quality has not been well quantified at a national level. We sought to evaluate the association between neighborhood socioeconomic deprivation, measured by the Area Deprivation Index (ADI), and semen quality parameters across adult men in the United States. METHODS: We conducted a population-based epidemiological study of adult men who ordered a mail-in semen analysis through Fellow Health between September 2020 and October 2024. Census tract code-level data enabled linkage to the ADI, a census-based metric of socioeconomic deprivation, and categorized by deciles (Q1=least deprived, Q10=most deprived). Demographic covariates included age, region, reason for ordering, and urbanization. Mean sperm concentration (million cells/mL), and total motile count (TMC, millions) were compared across ADI deciles using ANOVA tests. RESULTS: The total cohort included 29,071 adult men, with a mean age of 34.7 years. Men in the least prosperous decile (Q10) were younger, more likely to reside in the South or rural areas, and predominately ordered tests after trying to conceive for >1 year. Men in the most prosperous decile (Q1) were older, resided in the West or urban areas, and primarily ordered tests because they were planning to conceive in ≥1 year, (all p<0.001). Mean TMC across deciles (Q1-Q10) declined significantly ( (https://www.auajournals.org/doi/abs/10.1097/01.JU.0001191332.93827.7c.01#F1)). Increasing (decreasing prosperity) ADI was significantly associated with lower TMC (p<0.001). Concentration demonstrated a similar pattern, decreasing significantly from Q1 to Q10 ( (https://www.auajournals.org/doi/abs/10.1097/01.JU.0001191332.93827.7c.01#F2), p<0.001). CONCLUSIONS: Across a nationwide cohort, increasing socioeconomic deprivation was associated with significantly lower sperm concentration and TMC. This study supports a strong association between neighborhood disadvantage and male reproductive potential, emphasizing the role of social determinants in male fertility and the value of mail-in testing as a tool for population-level surveillance.

title: PD05-02: Reversal or Retrieval? Cost-Effectiveness of Vasectomy Reversal vs IVF/ICSI Under Employer Fertility Benefit Caps
parentSessionTitle: PD05: Infertility: Epidemiology & Evaluation I
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Many employers now offer capped fertility benefits, creating a practical choice for post-vasectomy couples: microsurgical vasectomy reversal or direct testicular sperm extraction (TESA) with IVF/ICSI. We developed an age-stratified decision model to compare pregnancy outcomes, total costs, and coverage thresholds for couples pursuing natural conception after reversal versus direct surgical sperm retrieval with ART. METHODS: A Monte Carlo microsimulation of 100,000 couples was conducted using parameters from AUA/ASRM guidelines and contemporary cohort studies. Female partner age distribution was modeled as 70% <40 years and 30% ≥40 years. Natural conception rates following VR were set at 58% for partners <40 and 14% for those ≥40. ICSI per-cycle pregnancy rates were 45% (<40) and 11% (≥40), allowing up to three cycles. Procedure costs included vasectomy reversal ($3,500–$17,000), testicular sperm retrieval ($1,000–$10,000), and ICSI ($14,500 per cycle). Employer fertility benefit caps of $30,000 and $40,000 were applied to estimate out-of-pocket and employer-paid costs. The primary outcome was successful pregnancy, with cost per additional pregnancy (ICER) as the secondary outcome. RESULTS: Overall, vasectomy reversal achieved higher pregnancy rates (75.8% vs 67.3%) and lower mean total costs ($32,114 vs $34,648) than TESA/ICSI, demonstrating cost dominance (ICER=–$29,601 per additional pregnancy). Among couples with female partners <40 years, reversal yielded pregnancy rates of 91.7% versus 83.2% for ART, with mean costs of $25,414 and $31,098, respectively (ICER=–$66,223; reversal dominant). For partners ≥40 years, reversal achieved 38.2% versus 29.7% pregnancy rates at mean costs of $47,960 and $43,043 (ICER=$58,816; marginal advantage for ART). Under employer fertility caps, 50% of reversal and 35% of ART couples achieved pregnancy within a $30k benefit, increasing to 61% and 55%, respectively, with a $40k cap. CONCLUSIONS: Vasectomy reversal is the most cost-effective first-line strategy for post-vasectomy couples, particularly when the female partner < 40 years. While ART approaches achieve comparable or slightly superior efficiency in older partners, the majority of couples under 40 can achieve pregnancy within typical $30,000–$40,000 employer fertility benefits, supporting routine consideration of reversal as the preferred initial approach.

title: PD05-03: Alcohol Use and Semen Quality in a North American Preconception Cohort (PRESTO)
parentSessionTitle: PD05: Infertility: Epidemiology & Evaluation I
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Men planning pregnancy often ask whether alcohol impairs semen quality, yet evidence at low-to-moderate intakes is inconsistent. We studied a large preconception cohort with repeated semen samples to estimate the association of baseline alcohol intake with standard semen parameters. METHODS: We analyzed men in Pregnancy Study Online (PRESTO) who provided ≥1 semen sample. Alcohol intake at enrollment was categorized as 0, 0.1-6.9, 7.0-13.9, and ≥14 drinks/week. Semen outcomes were volume, concentration, motility, total count, and total motile count (TMC); “low semen quality” was defined as volume ≤1.5 ml, concentration <16 million/mL, total count <39 million/ejaculate, motility <42%, or TMC <21 million. Missing data were addressed with multiple imputation. We fit generalized linear models to estimate adjusted percent differences and 95% confidence intervals and log-binomial regression with generalized estimating equations to estimate adjusted risk ratios (RRs) for low semen quality by alcohol intake. RESULTS: We analyzed data from 929 men (mean ± SD age was 32 ± 5 years) who provided 1,669 semen samples. The distribution of alcohol intake was 0 (22.1%), 0.1-6.9 (49.6%), 7.0-13.9 (19.2%), and ≥14 drinks/week (9.2%). In models using binary semen quality endpoints, ≥14 vs 0 drinks/week produced RRs of 0.67 (95% CI: 0.26-1.73) for low volume, 0.90 (0.52-1.56) for low concentration, 1.10 (0.56-2.16) for low total count, 1.19 (0.79-1.77) for low motility, and 1.40 (0.75-2.62) for low TMC. Among men 25 years, volume was higher at 0.1-6.9 (+12.9%, 95% CI: 2.6-23.2) and ≥14 (+15.3%, 0.7-29.9) drinks/week versus 0, and 7.0-13.9 vs 0 drinks/week was associated with higher risk of low motility (RR 2.23, 1.12-4.46); among men 30-34 years, ≥14 vs 0 drinks/week showed a moderately elevated but imprecisely estimated risk of low motility (RR 1.65, 0.98-2.77), while estimates in ≥35 years were near null. Among men with BMI 25-29.9 kg/m2, ≥14 vs 0 drinks/week suggested higher risks of low motility (RR 1.77, 0.94-3.34) and low TMC (RR 3.27, 1.22-8.80); RRs in other BMI subgroups were imprecise. CONCLUSIONS: Associations between baseline alcohol intake and semen volume, concentration, total count, motility, and TMC were generally modest, with isolated age- and BMI-specific elevations and no consistent dose-response pattern.

title: PD05-05: Sleep Disorders and Long-Term Risk of Male Infertility and Endocrine Dysfunction: A National Retrospective Cohort Study
parentSessionTitle: PD05: Infertility: Epidemiology & Evaluation I
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Sleep disruption has been implicated in impaired male reproductive health, but large-scale studies evaluating clinically diagnosed sleep disorders and infertility outcomes are limited. We investigated the long-term association between sleep disorders and male reproductive and endocrine dysfunction using a national database. METHODS: We conducted a retrospective cohort study using TriNetX, identifying men aged 18–50 with and without documented sleep disorders from 2005 to 2020. Exclusion criteria removed known causes of infertility, including genetic, endocrine, infectious, neoplastic, and medication-related factors. Propensity score matching was performed 1:1 across more than 60 covariates, including demographic, metabolic, psychiatric, and reproductive variables. Outcomes included infertility diagnoses, testicular hypofunction, fertility-related encounters, and pharmacologic treatment. Risk ratios (RRs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were calculated at 1-, 2-, 3-, 5-, and 10-year follow-up. Subgroups were stratified by age, body mass index (BMI), and disorder subtype (insomnia vs sleep apnea). RESULTS: The matched cohort included 117,154 men (58,577 per group). Sleep disorders were associated with a higher risk of the composite outcome across all follow-ups (1-year RR 1.40, 95% CI 1.26–1.56; 10-year RR 1.35, 95% CI 1.25–1.47). Testicular hypofunction emerged earliest and remained consistent (RR 1.55–1.60). Infertility treatment was also elevated (1-year RR 1.89, 95% CI 1.27–2.82; 10-year RR 1.65, 95% CI 1.34–2.02). Minimal signal was seen in men 18–25, with progressively stronger associations in ages 26–50, especially for infertility treatment (RR ~1.98 at 10 years in ages 36–45). Obese men showed the greatest risk. Sleep apnea conferred immediate and sustained elevations, while insomnia effects were modest and delayed. The composite findings are illustrated in the forest plot ( (https://www.auajournals.org/doi/abs/10.1097/01.JU.0001191332.93827.7c.05#F1)). CONCLUSIONS: Clinically diagnosed sleep disorders, particularly sleep apnea, are associated with increased long-term risk of male reproductive and endocrine dysfunction. Testicular hypofunction may represent an early indicator. These findings support the incorporation of sleep assessment into fertility evaluations and highlight the need for prospective studies to investigate whether treating sleep disorders can mitigate the risk.

title: PD05-06: Real world results of post-vasectomy semen analysis: a large national sample of over 100,000 men
parentSessionTitle: PD05: Infertility: Epidemiology & Evaluation I
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Mail-in testing has improved access and compliance with post-vasectomy semen analysis (PVSA). We aimed to characterize PVSA testing results among individuals undergoing multiple mail-in tests in a large nationwide cohort. METHODS: We evaluated the results of mail-in PVSA tests performed between 2020-2024 at Fellow Health by prospectively following men from the time of vasectomy to the time of PVSA sample submission within one year of their vasectomy. For individuals with sperm detected after vasectomy, additional tests were provided until azoospermia was achieved. For each individual, time to the first test was determined for the following categories: 0 sperm (azoospermia), 1-100k sperm, 100k-1M sperm and 1M or greater sperm. Due to the mail-in nature of the test, motility was not reported. RESULTS: Our cohort consisted of 103,592 individuals who underwent 117,826 PVSA tests. The majority (88.8%) underwent one PVSA test, 9.1% underwent two tests, and 2.1% underwent three or more tests. Incorporating all tests, 94.2% achieved azoospermia after vasectomy in our cohort. At 8 weeks post-vasectomy, 80% of men were azoospermic, and at 16 weeks, 87% were azoospermic; the percentage of men who achieved PVSA sperm clearance continued to increase until reaching a plateau at 42 weeks ( (https://www.auajournals.org/doi/abs/10.1097/01.JU.0001191332.93827.7c.06#F1)). At 6 months (26 weeks) 2% of men had at least 100k sperm detected, although motility could not be assessed due to the mail-in nature of the testing. CONCLUSIONS: Most individuals achieve PVSA sperm clearance 8-16 weeks post-vasectomy as recommended by American Urological Association guidelines. There was considerable variation in time to azoospermia with a small number of individuals achieving PVSA sperm clearance prior to 8 weeks and an increase in azoospermia rates observed until 42 weeks post-vasectomy. Detection of at least 100k sperm at and after 6 months post-vasectomy suggests a real world 2% rate of unsuccessful vasectomy in our cohort.

title: PD05-07: Second semen analysis after first assessment: Challenging the current American Urological Association guidelines using a trial emulation design study
parentSessionTitle: PD05: Infertility: Epidemiology & Evaluation I
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: The question of whether a single semen analysis suffices when initial parameters meet or exceed WHO reference thresholds remains contentious in the evaluation of male infertility. Current recommendations from AUA do not advise routine repetition of semen analysis when the first assessment demonstrates normozoospermia according to WHO criteria. We aimed to assess whether infertile men whose initial semen parameters meet or exceed the WHO reference thresholds should undergo a second semen analysis. METHODS: Data from 2070 infertile men were analyzed. All patients underwent at least one semen analysis, evaluated according to WHO 2021 criteria. Two groups were defined: i) normal, when all parameters meet or exceed reference thresholds; and, ii) abnormal, when at least one parameter was belowreference limits. We implemented a Synthpop-based trial simulation comprising 1000 iterations to evaluate two distinct scenarios: (i) universal testing of both groups, and (ii) adherence to current guidelines. This statistical analysis was used to estimate the diagnostic yield under both scenarios. RESULTS: Median (IQR) age was 37 (34-41) yrs and total motile sperm count (TMSC) 12 (1.5-46.9) mln. Men with abnormal semen analysis were older than those with normal semen analysis (37 \[34–41\] vs 36 \[32–40\] yrs, p=0.034), had higher BMI (25.2 \[23.4–27.4\] vs 24.7 \[22.8–26.6\], p=0.030), and higher rate of hypertension (9.2% vs 0.8%, p=0.003). Men with abnormal semen analysis also showed higher prevalence of chromosomal abnormalities (2% vs 0.8%, p=0.004), history of cryptorchidism (14.5% vs 1.7%, p<0.001) and reduced testicular volume (15 \[12-20\] vs 20 \[15-25\] Prader, p<0.001). To quantify the proportion of missed diagnoses, trial simulations estimated that adherence to guidelines recommendations would fail to identify 16.4% of semen abnormalities upon repeat analysis (95%CI 15.5–17.3%). Conversely, repeating the test when the initial semen analysis was altered resulted in a normal semen analysis in 2.5% (1.7-2.9%) of group 1 and 2.4% (1.8-3%) of group 2 ( (https://www.auajournals.org/doi/abs/10.1097/01.JU.0001191332.93827.7c.07#F1)). CONCLUSIONS: Re-testing only in case of abnormal semen analyses would result in missing approximately one in six cases of semen parameter deterioration on repeat analysis. These findings challenge existing recommendations and underscore the need to consider revised criteria for selected subgroups of infertile men.

title: PD05-08: Missed karyotype abnormalities and Y-chromosome microdeletions in male infertility: trial simulation challenges current European Association of Urology guidelines genetic testing thresholds
parentSessionTitle: PD05: Infertility: Epidemiology & Evaluation I
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Current EAU guidelines recommend karyotyping for infertile men with sperm concentrations <5 million/mL and Y-chromosome microdeletion testing for ≤1 million/mL, with consideration for testing between 1-5 million/mL. The proportion of genetic diagnoses missed under guideline-adherent versus universal screening remains unknown. We used synthpop-based trial simulation to quantify diagnostic yield loss, providing robust estimates with confidence intervals unattainable from observational data alone. METHODS: We analyzed 641 consecutive white-European infertile men who all underwent comprehensive genetic screening (karyotype and Y-microdeletion testing). We employed trial simulation across 1000 iterations to model three scenarios: (1) testing all; (2) inclusive guideline adherence (Y-microdeletions for <5 million/mL); and, (3) strict guideline adherence (Y-microdeletions only for ≤1 million/mL, karyotype for <5 million/mL). This statistical approach was used to estimate the diagnostic yield under each scenario with quantified uncertainty through confidence intervals. RESULTS: Median (IQR) age was 36 years (33–40) and sperm concentration 1.8 mln/mL (0.3–6.7). Overall, 53 men (8.3%) had genetic abnormalities: 22 (3.4%) Y-microdeletions and 35 (5.5%) karyotype defects. Detection varied by sperm concentration: 12.6% (NOA), 8.9% (≤1 mln/mL), 10.4% (1–5 mln/mL), and 3.7% (≥5 mln/mL). Men with abnormalities had lower sperm concentration (1.0 vs 1.8 mln/mL, p=0.012) and smaller testicular volume (12 vs 12 ml, p=0.003). Trial simulation (1000 iterations) estimated strict guidelines would miss 20.6% of cases (95% CI 7.5–35.8%), while inclusive guidelines reduced missed diagnoses to 7.2% (95% CI 3.8–18.8%). CONCLUSIONS: Strict application of current guidelines (Y-microdeletions only for ≤1 million/mL, karyotype for <5 million/mL) would miss one in five genetic diagnoses. Expanding testing to <5 million/mL reduces this to one in fourteen. The current trial simulation methodology provides more robust estimates of missed diagnoses with quantified uncertainty. These findings challenge current threshold-based screening recommendations and suggest that revised cutoffs may be reconsidered.

title: PD05-09: Concentration matters: Prevalence of genetic disorders in oligozoospermic and azoospermic men
parentSessionTitle: PD05: Infertility: Epidemiology & Evaluation I

speakers.jobTitle: Assistant Professor. Faculty of Medicine. University of chile
speakers.organization: University of Chile / Shady Grove Fertility Chile

fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Genetic factors, including chromosomal abnormalities and Y-chromosome microdeletions, represent established causes of male infertility. Current International guidelines recommend genetic screening based on sperm concentration thresholds. EAU/ASRM guidelines recommend karyotype analysis for men with concentration below 5 million/mL and Y-chromosome microdeletion testing particularly in patients below 1 million/mL. However, comprehensive data comparing genetic abnormalities prevalence across distinct concentration ranges in systematically screened cohorts remain limited. Understanding real life genetic disorders prevalence, could help clinical decision-making, resource allocation and correct patient counselling. The objective of the study is to determine the prevalence of genetic abnormalities (karyotype alterations and Y-chromosome microdeletions) in men presenting with azoospermia and severe oligozoospermia METHODS: Retrospective cohort study, analyzing 245 infertile men with severe oligozoospermia (sperm concentration ≤ 5 mill/mL) and azoospermia with palpable vas deferens, consulting at a tertiary andrological unit, between 2018 and 2025. Patients were stratified by sperm concentration: Azoospermia, ≤ 2 mill/mL and 2-5 mill/mL. All patients underwent standard G banding karyotyping and multiplex polymerase chain reaction (PCR) based Y-chromosome microdeletion analysis targeting AZFa, AZFb and AZFc regions RESULTS: Among 245 patients, 18 presented genetic abnormalities (7.3%). Distribution by concentration revealed that in the azoospermic group (n=136), 15 patients presented genetic alterations (11.2%); of which 9 were Karyotype abnormalities (6.5%) including Klinefelter syndrome variants (47,XXY and mosaics, n=3), 47,XYY mosaicism (n=1), and balanced chromosomal translocations (n=4). In this group, 7 patients presentes Y-chromosome microdeletions (5.1%) including AZFc (n=4), multiple deletions (n=2), and AZFa (n=1)In the ≤2 million/mL group (n=70): 3 patients (4.3%) presented genetic alterations. Y-chromosome microdeletionswere found in 3 patients, including AZFc (n=2) and AZFb (n=1) regions. No karyotype abnormalities were detected. Lastly, in the 2-5 million/mL group(n=39), no patients presneted genetic abnormalities. Overall, patients presenting Y-chromosome microdeletions (n=10) slightly exceeded the number of patients with karyotype abnormalities (n=9), with one patient presenting both CONCLUSIONS: This study, of infertile men with seminal alterations, showed a concentration dependent gradient in genetic abnormalities prevalence. These findings validate current EAU/ASRM guidelines recommendations for genetic screening in azoospermia and severe oligozoospermia, while highlighting the diminishing diagnostic yield as sperm concentration increases. The absence of any genetic abnormalities in the 2-5 million/ml group could influence resource allocation within genetic testing protocols. Nevertheless, the 4.3% detection rate below 2 million/mL warrants extending systematic genetic evaluation in this patient group, particularly considering its implications for assisted reproductive technology planning and counselling

title: PD05-10: Comparative Effects of Finasteride and Dutasteride on Semen Parameters in Young Men with Androgenic Alopecia: A Randomized Controlled Study
parentSessionTitle: PD05: Infertility: Epidemiology & Evaluation I
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: To compare the impact of finasteride and dutasteride on semen parameters in young men treated for androgenic alopecia and to evaluate whether the duration of 5α-reductase inhibitor therapy affects sperm quality and hormonal profiles. METHODS: This single-center, randomized, controlled study enrolled 380 men aged 25–35 years who had been treated for androgenic alopecia with either finasteride 1 mg/day (n=190) or dutasteride 0.5 mg/day (n=190) for at least 3 months. Each drug group was further divided into five subgroups according to treatment duration: <6 months, 6–12 months, 13–18 months, 19–24 months, and >24 months. Serum total testosterone, FSH, and LH levels were measured, and semen analysis included semen volume, sperm concentration, total and progressive motility, morphology, vitality, and sperm DNA fragmentation. Statistical comparisons were performed using ANOVA and multivariate regression analyses, with p<0.05 considered significant. RESULTS: Semen volume, total motility, progressive motility, and vitality significantly decreased with longer treatment duration in both finasteride and dutasteride groups. DNA fragmentation index (DFI) increased progressively with treatment length. The decline in semen parameters was more pronounced among men taking dutasteride, particularly after 18 months of continuous therapy. No significant differences were observed in sperm concentration or morphology. Serum total testosterone remained stable across all groups, while FSH and LH showed mild, non-significant increases. CONCLUSIONS: Prolonged treatment with 5α-reductase inhibitors is associated with a time-dependent deterioration in semen quality, especially in sperm motility and DNA integrity. Dutasteride exerts a slightly greater suppressive effect than finasteride, likely due to its dual inhibition of type I and II 5α-reductase. Clinicians should exercise caution when prescribing these agents to young men who wish to maintain future fertility, and periodic semen monitoring is recommended during long-term therapy. | | | --- | | |

title: PD05-11: Cancer Risk Among Men with Azoospermia: A Multi-Institutional Analysis Using the Cosmos Database
parentSessionTitle: PD05: Infertility: Epidemiology & Evaluation I
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Infertility affects about 4 million American men. Azoospermia, the absence of spermatozoa in semen, occurs in ~1% of all men and 15% of infertile men. Research has suggested an association between male infertility and long-term health risks, including increased cancer incidence. However, the degree to which azoospermic men differ in cancer risk from other infertile men remains unclear. Prior work by Eisenberg et al. demonstrated that men with azoospermia had nearly a threefold increased risk of cancer compared to the general population. We evaluated whether men with azoospermia have an increased risk of developing cancer compared to infertile men with oligospermia or normal semen parameters. METHODS: We conducted a retrospective cohort study using the Epic Cosmos database, identifying men who underwent semen analysis between 2000 and 2025. We included men who had at least one reported sperm concentration value from a semen analysis. We excluded individuals who were non-male, younger than 18 or older than 70 years, had a history of cancer, testosterone or chemotherapy exposure, prior vasectomy or lacked sufficient follow-up activity. Men were categorized by sperm concentration as normal (>=15 mil/ml), oligospermic (<15 and > 0), or azoospermic (=0). The primary outcome was incident cancer diagnosis following semen analysis. Time-to-event analyses were performed using Kaplan-Meier survival estimates and Cox proportional hazards models. Hazard ratios (HRs) were reported before and after adjustment for age. RESULTS: A total of 56,880 men met inclusion criteria: 75% had normal semen parameters, 21% had oligospermia, and 5% azoospermia, with a median age of 34 years. Both oligospermic and azoospermic men exhibited higher rates of cancer compared with normospermic men. In unadjusted analyses, HRs for cancer were 1.58 (95% CI 1.37-1.80) for oligospermia, relative to normal, and 1.68 (1.32-2.13) for azoospermia (both p<0.001). After adjusting for age, the associations remained significant with HRs of 1.46 (1.27-1.67) for oligospermia and 1.39 (1.09-1.76) for azoospermia, relative to normal. CONCLUSIONS: Men with azoospermia and oligospermia had a significantly higher risk of developing cancer compared to those with normal semen parameters. However, cancer risk did not differ substantially between the two low-count groups, though this comparison was limited by the smaller size of the azoospermic cohort. Findings suggest impaired spermatogenesis may serve as a biomarker for future systemic disease. Further investigation is needed to explore the underlying mechanisms and evaluate whether enhanced cancer surveillance is warranted in this population.

title: PD05-12: Elevated Cardiometabolic and Mental Health Comorbidity Burden in Men with Infertility: Analysis from 7.2 Million Patients
parentSessionTitle: PD05: Infertility: Epidemiology & Evaluation I
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Emerging evidence suggests male infertility may serve as an early clinical indicator for broader, underlying health issues, including but not limited to cardiovascular, metabolic, and musculoskeletal disorders. Large-scale, real-world data analysis is needed to comprehensively characterize the disease burden and comorbidities in this patient population. METHODS: This retrospective cohort study used de-identified electronic health record data from several large healthcare platforms, encompassing over 16 million total patients using the Mayo Clinic Platform Discover. Two cohorts were created: Cohort A consisted of patients with a male infertility diagnosis by ICD code, and Cohort B consisted of patients defined by male sex alone. Primary outcomes measured included differences in demographics and the prevalence of comorbidities. Descriptive statistics, rate ratios (RR), chi-square tests, and p-values were used to compare cohorts. RESULTS: Cohort A consisted of 20,599 male patients compared to Cohort B which included 7.2 million male patients. Demographically, men in Cohort A presented at a significantly younger mean age (35.1 years) compared to men in Cohort B (39.6 years; Cohen's D=-0.25). Cohort A had significantly more patients identified as Asian (RR 1.5; p<0.001). Regarding systemic disease burden, men in Cohort A exhibited a substantially and statistically significant (all p<0.001) higher prevalence of multiple conditions, including obesity (RR 2.4), hyperlipidemia (RR 1.6), obstructive sleep apnea (RR 2.3), myocardial infarction (RR 1.2), essential hypertension (RR 1.2), liver disease (RR 1.6), and osteoporosis (RR 1.8). Type 2 diabetes mellitus (RR 1.0) and chronic kidney disease (RR 1.0) prevalence was similar. Cohort A also demonstrated an elevated mental health burden, with significantly higher prevalence of generalized anxiety disorder (RR 2.9), major depressive disorder (RR 2.9), alcohol use disorder (RR 2.2), and nicotine dependence (RR 2.1) (p<0.001 for all). CONCLUSIONS: This large-scale, real-world data analysis provides evidence that men diagnosed with infertility are captured at a younger age while simultaneously carrying a significantly greater burden of cardiometabolic, hepatic, musculoskeletal, and mental health comorbidities. These results validate the concept of male infertility as a risk stratification opportunity, underscoring need for comprehensive screening and integrated care to address systemic health risks in this population.

title: PD05-13: Poor Metabolic Health Associated with Lower Semen Quality and Higher IVF Rates: Analysis of 25,000 US Men
parentSessionTitle: PD05: Infertility: Epidemiology & Evaluation I

speakers.jobTitle: Director, Men's Health and Male Reproductive Medicine

fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: The link between male fertility and metabolic health (MH) remains uncertain. Our main objective was to assess this relationship. We hypothesized that men residing in US counties with poorer MH have reduced semen quality and a greater reliance on assisted reproductive technologies, such as in vitro fertilization (IVF). Previous studies in the US have been limited by single-site sampling and a lack of clinical data connected to semen analysis (SA). METHODS: We used data from Fellow Health mail-in SA, US Census (USC) and CDC PLACES. The PLACES dataset contains prevalence estimates for chronic diseases for all U. S. counties, such as diabetes (DM), obesity, hypertension (HTN), and high cholesterol (HC). Prevalence of health conditions (quintiles) across counties were geocoded by county to link health conditions with SA variables and USC. We explored the relationship between MH and semen quality (Total Motile Count, TMC), and need for IVF (TMC < 5 M) while adjusting for geographic region, age, socioeconomic status, and urbanization. RESULTS: Our cohort (n-25,622) was distributed across the US (Mid-W 21%; NE: 7%; S: 36%; W: 36%). Most patients were aged 30-39 (61%), lived in urban areas (50%), and were trying to conceive or planning to in the next year (86%). Men in counties with the highest prevalence of DM, obesity, HTN, and HC had lower TMC and were more likely to require IVF. ( (https://www.auajournals.org/doi/abs/10.1097/01.JU.0001191332.93827.7c.13#F1), p<0.001). Mean TMC in the least healthy quintile for each parameter was at least 20 M lower than in the healthiest group. After adjusting for confounders, the odds of needing IVF for the least healthy versus the healthiest quintile was significantly higher ( Table 1): DM (OR 1.42), Obesity (OR 1.28), HTN (OR 1.39), and HC (OR 1.27). CONCLUSIONS: These data reveal a strong association between increased prevalence of metabolic disorders and diminished sperm quality. Prevalence of DM, obesity, HTN, and HC were associated with a 27% - 42% higher odds of needing IVF, reinforcing the link between semen quality, overall men’s health, and the need for fertility care. Semen analyses are an important window into metabolic health and may play a key role as the contemporary men’s health “vital sign”.

title: PD05-14: Validation of an AI-Guided Sperm Identification System in Post-Vasectomy Patients Deemed Azoospermic by Conventional Semen Analysis
parentSessionTitle: PD05: Infertility: Epidemiology & Evaluation I
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: The Sperm Tracking and Recovery (STAR) system integrates artificial intelligence, high-speed imaging, and microfluidics to identify and isolate rare sperm in semen samples that have no sperm found with conventional analysis. To further validate its efficacy, STAR was used on a cohort of post-vasectomy patients whose samples were deemed azoospermic using conventional semen analysis. METHODS: Male patients who underwent vasectomy at a single institution between August 2024 and June 2025 provided on-site semen samples that were initially analyzed by an andrology-trained laboratory technician using 2021 World Health Organization criteria. Samples deemed azoospermic by conventional semen analysis were further analyzed by STAR. Patients who had sperm identified on their initial STAR analysis were invited to return for a repeat STAR. All samples were discarded after STAR analysis. Sperm motility was not assessed. RESULTS: Fourteen patients provided ejaculated samples at a median of 115 days post-vasectomy (range 24 to 165 days) wherein conventional semen analysis found no sperm. STAR identified sperm in 11 of 14 participants, with a median of 17 spermatozoa identified (range 1 to 1,000 sperm). Three of the 11 patients with sperm identified by STAR returned for a second collection, with sperm identified in two of three samples: one sample with 2 spermatozoa at 234 days and one with 9 spermatozoa at 339 days. CONCLUSIONS: The STAR system identified the presence of rare sperm in the majority of post-vasectomy samples in which no sperm were found using conventional semen analysis. Men deemed azoospermic by conventional semen analysis may benefit from more extensive sperm identification methods such as STAR. Continued prospective data collection will further validate the utility of this technology and may also enable more effective interrogation of surgically retrieved samples for the presence or absence of sperm.

title: PD05-15: From PI-RADS to Te-RADS: Testicular MRI biomarkers predicting sperm retrieval in non-obstructive azoospermia
parentSessionTitle: PD05: Infertility: Epidemiology & Evaluation I

speakers.organization: La Fe University and Polytechnic Hospital

fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Microsurgical testicular sperm extraction (microTESE) is the standard treatment for men with non-obstructive azoospermia (NOA),although sperm retrieval (SR) rates remain limited. No validated biomarkers currently predict the presence of testicular sperm. This study aimed to identify magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) parameters associated with successful SR, proposing a non-invasive predictive model for NOA patients. METHODS: NOA patients who underwent testicular MRI and microTESE between 2022 and 2024 were included. MRI-derived parameters oftesticular architecture were quantified, including magnetization transfer ratio (MTR), fat fraction (FF), apparent diffusion coefficient(ADC), diffusion coefficient (D), pseudo-diffusion coefficient (D\*), and perfusion fraction (f). Partial Least Squares–DiscriminantAnalysis (PLS-DA) was used for dimensionality reduction and identification of variables associated with SR. Data were normalized using the Centered Log-Ratio transformation. Diagnostic performance was evaluated by ROC analysis, including sensitivity, specificity, predictive values, and odds ratio (OR) RESULTS: Thirty-six NOA patients were analyzed; SR was positive in 38.9% (n=14) and negative in 61.1% (n=22). PLS-DA showed partial separation between SR-positive and SR-negative groups, with the first two components explaining 34.2% of total variance. HigherFF values were associated with negative SR. Logistic regression based on the first PLS-DA component achieved an AUC of 0.831 (p<0.001), with 85.7% sensitivity, 77.3% specificity, 89.5% negative predictive value, and 80.6% overall accuracy. A first-component value below −0.56759 strongly predicted successful SR (OR=20.4; 95% CI: 3.98–164.39; p<0.001). CONCLUSIONS: MRI-derived biomarkers effectively discriminated between successful and unsuccessful SR in NOA. The proposed model demonstrated high sensitivity and predictive accuracy, particularly for identifying patients unlikely to benefit from microTESE. MRI-based predictive modeling could enhance patient selection and reduce unnecessary invasive procedures.

title: PD06-01: Radical prostatectomy without prostate biopsy based on a noninvasive diagnostic strategy: a prospective singlecenter study
parentSessionTitle: PD06: Prostate Cancer: Detection & Screening I

speakers.organization: The First Affiliated Hospital of USTC

fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Prostate biopsy is the most common approach for diagnosing prostate cancer (PCa); however, it has inherent limitations, such as the invasive procedure, postoperative complications, and false negative results. We aimed to provide a noninvasive diagnostic strategy for patients with highly suspected PCa and to evaluate the feasibility of performing biopsy-spared radical prostatectomy. METHODS: This prospective study included a total of 86 patients between November 10, 2022, and October 1, 2025. All 86 patients underwent radical prostatectomy without prior prostate biopsy based on a noninvasive diagnostic strategy consisting of a diagnostic prediction model \[comprised of the prostate imaging-reporting and data system (PI-RADS)\ score and prostate-specific antigen density (PSAD)\] and the 18F-prostate-specific membrane antigen (PSMA)-1007 positron emission tomography (PET)/computed tomography (CT) examination. The primary endpoint was the positive predictive value (PPV) of clinically significant PCa\[the International Society of Urological Pathology (ISUP)\ grade ≥2, Gleason score ≥3 + 4\]. The secondary endpoints were a PPV of any-grade PCa (ISUP grade ≥ 1, Gleason score ≥3 + 3) and high-grade PCa (ISUP grade ≥3, Gleason score ≥4 + 3), and the false positive rate of the diagnostic strategy. RESULTS: Of the 401 screened patients with clinically suspected PCa, 86 patients fulfilled the criteria and consented to participate in this study. The median PSAD level was 0.52ng/mL2; 22 (25.6%) patients were identified as having a PI-RADS score of 4, and 64 (74.4%) patients with a PI-RADS score of 5. The median SUVmax of 18F-PSMA-1007 PET/CT was 19.7. For the 86 enrolled patients who received radical prostatectomy directly, the PPV of clinically significant PCa was 97.7% \[84/86\]. Only 2.3% \[2/86\] of patients were diagnosed with clinically insignificant PCa (ISUP grade=1, Gleason score=3 + 3). The PPV of any-grade PCa and high-grade PCa were 100% and 72.1% (62/86), respectively. No one had a false positive result. CONCLUSIONS: We proposed a noninvasive diagnostic strategy consisting sequentially of a diagnostic prediction model and the 18F-PSMA-1007 PET/CT examination for diagnosing PCa. Despite some limitations, our initial findings suggest the potential feasibility of radical prostatectomy without prior prostate biopsy.

title: PD06-02: A dual-threshold strategy for predicting high-risk prostate cancer in biopsy-free radical prostatectomy cohorts: a retrospective study based on Chinese multicenter clinical data
parentSessionTitle: PD06: Prostate Cancer: Detection & Screening I

speakers.organization: The First Affiliated Hospital of USTC

fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Our previous study has suggested that biopsy-free radical prostatectomy reduces burdens for selected prostate cancer (PCa) patients based on a noninvasive diagnostic strategy(Prostate Cancer Prostatic Dis.2025 Jun;28(2):496-502.). However, the absence of pre-operative pathology precludes high-risk PCa (HRPCa) identification, crucial for determining the need for pelvic lymph node dissection (PLND). In this study, we try to explore a new non-invasive method for predicting HRPCa before surgery. METHODS: This retrospective diagnostic study included a development cohort of 93 patients from USTC center, as well as two external validation cohorts: one cohort of 83 patients from XYH Hospital and another cohort of 117 patients from XJH Hospital. All enrolled patients met the USTC model value≥0.6 criteria (https://ustcprostatecancerprediction.shinyapps.io/dynnomapp/) and obtained definitive pathological results within 4 weeks after 18F-PSMA-1007 PET/CT examination. Patients were stratified as HRPCa (D'Amico criteria: tPSA>20 ng/mL, GS≥8, or ≥cT2c) or non-high-risk (NHR). Maximum standardized uptake value (SUVmax) and target-to-background ratios (TBRs) of PSMA-PET/CT were quantified. Diagnostic performance for HRPCa was evaluated using ROC analysis. Multivariate logistic regression analysis identified independent predictors. RESULTS: Of 93 patients from development cohort, 63 (67.7%) had HRPCa. SUVmax (AUC=0.807, optimal cut-off=20.9) and tPSA (AUC=0.777, optimal cut-off=15.09 ng/mL) were independent HRPCa predictors (p<0.05). Patients meeting both thresholds (SUVmax>20.9 and tPSA>15.09 ng/mL, n=31) demonstrated a 100% HRPCa positive predictive value (PPV) and specificity (31/31), significantly outperforming single parameters (p<0.001). Patients below both thresholds (n=29) had only 31.0% HRPCa. In two external validation cohorts, similar diagnostic performance was observed. CONCLUSIONS: A dual-threshold non-invasive strategy is established for predicting HRPCa in biopsy-free radical prostatectomy cohorts, which can be used to decide whether PLND is needed.

title: PD06-03: Safety and Feasibility of Transperineal Prostate Biopsy Without Antibiotic Prophylaxis: A Multicentric Retrospective Study
parentSessionTitle: PD06: Prostate Cancer: Detection & Screening I
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Transperineal prostate biopsy (TPBx) is increasingly adopted due to its favorable infectious risk profile. However, real-world data on its systematic use in a fully outpatient setting without antibiotic prophylaxis remain limited. This study aimed to evaluate the safety and feasibility of TPBx performed without prophylactic antibiotics in routine urological practice.
