METHODS: We retrospectively analyzed 423 consecutive patients who underwent TPBx across three Italian urology centers between 2018 and 2024. All procedures were performed in an outpatient setting under local perineal anesthesia with lidocaine, without sedation or prophylactic antibiotics; skin preparation consisted of povidone-iodine only. The primary endpoint was the rate of infectious complications within 30 days (fever, culture-confirmed urinary tract infection \[UTI\], and sepsis). Secondary outcomes included complication grading according to the Clavien-Dindo classification. RESULTS: A total of 423 patients (mean age 65.4 ± 8.3 years) were included. Median prostate volume was 50 g (IQR 40–60). The mean number of biopsy cores was 10.2 ± 2.1, and the mean procedural time was 14.7 ± 1.1 minutes. Infectious complications were uncommon: 12 patients (2.8%) developed fever and 2 (0.5%) had culture-confirmed UTI. No cases of sepsis were observed. Overall, 292 patients (69%) had no complications. Grade I events occurred in 105 patients (24.8%), including hematuria (13.4%), hemospermia (13.4%) and transient LUTS (0.2%). Urinary retention was observed in 1.2% of cases and resolved with short-term catheterization. Grade II complications were recorded in 12 patients (2.8%), all of whom required oral antibiotics for fever or UTI. No Grade ≥III complications occurred. No emergency visits or readmissions were required. CONCLUSIONS: In this multicenter cohort, TPBx performed without antibiotic prophylaxis showed a low rate of infectious and clinically significant complications, and was feasible in an outpatient setting. These findings support the potential role of selective, risk-based antibiotic use in TPBx. Further prospective studies are warranted to confirm safety outcomes and better define patient selection strategies for prophylaxis-free pathways.

title: PD06-04: Detection rate plateau in prostate biopsy: how many cores are enough? A retrospective analysis of two thousand biopsies
parentSessionTitle: PD06: Prostate Cancer: Detection & Screening I

speakers.organization: IRCCS Regina Elena National Cancer institute

fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: The optimal number of cores in prostate biopsy remains debated. Increasing sampling may improve cancer detection but also increases procedural time, patient discomfort, and complications. We aimed to evaluate whether detection rates (DR) continue to rise with the number of cores, and to identify a potential plateau beyond which additional samples provide negligible diagnostic benefit. METHODS: We retrospectively analyzed 2,089 consecutive prostate biopsies (2019-2024). Clinical, imaging, and pathological data were retrieved from an institutional database. DR were assessed for both overall prostate cancer (PCa) and clinically significant PCa (csPCa, ISUP 2–5). Analyses were restricted to cases with ≤25 cores. Crude DR were calculated by core number classes. Multivariable logistic regression models with restricted cubic splines (4 df) were used to estimate the adjusted probability of detection, adjusting for age, PSA density, PI-RADS score, previous biopsy, prostate volume, and biopsy approach (transperineal vs transrectal). A plateau was defined when the marginal gain per additional core was < 1% for ≥ 3 consecutive increments. RESULTS: Patients' characteristics are reported in Table 1. The crude DR for any PCa decreased from 97% (≤10 cores) to 52% (> 20 cores), reflecting a selection bias in highly suspicious cases ( Table 2, (https://www.auajournals.org/doi/abs/10.1097/01.JU.0001191336.68744.5b.04#F1)). After adjustment, the detection probability stabilised beyond 16–18 cores (≈ 70%). For csPCa, the adjusted probability plateaued at ≈ 17 cores, corresponding to a predicted detection probability of ≈ 70% ( (https://www.auajournals.org/doi/abs/10.1097/01.JU.0001191336.68744.5b.04#F2)). Beyond this threshold, additional cores increased detection by < 1% per core, indicating diminishing diagnostic returns. CONCLUSIONS: In prostate biopsy, both overall and clinically significant cancer DR a plateau around 17 cores. Sampling beyond this threshold provides minimal diagnostic gain while increasing procedural burden.

title: PD06-05: Association between heterogeneity of primary prostate cancer on PSMA PET/CT and oncological outcomes in localized cases: a whole-mount pathology-based retrospective study
parentSessionTitle: PD06: Prostate Cancer: Detection & Screening I
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: The heterogeneity of prostate-specific membrane antigen (PSMA) in the tumor has been implicated as a contributing factor in the limited efficacy of PSMA-targeted radioligand therapy for certain prostate cancer patients. Previous study has demonstrated that elevated PSMA heterogeneity correlates with circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) characteristics and abiraterone treatment responserates in metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer. However, the heterogeneity of PSMA in localized prostate cancer remains unexplored. This study aims to elucidate the spatial heterogeneity of PSMA uptake in localized prostate cancer and to examine its potential associations with adverse oncological outcomes and biochemical recurrence (BCR). METHODS: This retrospective analysis included 128 prostate cancer patients who underwent 68Ga-PSMA-11 PET/CT prior to radicalprostatectomy (RP). We used SUVmax-mean (derived by subtracting SUVmean from SUVmax within the index lesion) to quantify intra-tumor PSMA uptake heterogeneity, while SUVhetero (the variance of SUVmean across all PSMA-positive lesions) captured inter-tumor heterogeneity. Adverse oncological outcomes were evaluated across PSMA heterogeneity subgroups. Kaplan–Meier analysis with log-rank test was used to test the ability of heterogeneity parameters to determine the survival probability. RESULTS: After excluding 10 patients had none PSMA positive lesion on PET/CT, a total of 118 patients were included for analysis. Patients with higher SUVmax-mean had greater initial serum PSA level (p<0.001), however, similar relation was not observed in patients with higher SUVhetero (p=0.401). Higher ISUP grade at RP, higher pathological T stage, more Positive Surgical Margin and Seminal Vesicle Invasion were found in patients with higher SUVmax-mean (all p<0.05). Only the ratio of Positive Surgical Margin was found to be significantly different in patients with different SUVhetero (p=0.036). Kaplan–Meier analysis revealed that patients with higher SUVmax-mean had shorter Biochemical Recurrence-free (BCR-free) survival compared to those with lower SUVmax-mean (log-rank p=0.003). There is no significant difference in BCR-free survival between patients with higher and lower SUVhetero (log-rank p=0.400) CONCLUSIONS: Our findings suggest that heterogeneity in 68Ga-PSMA-11 PET/CT uptake is associated with adverse oncological outcomes and increased risk of BCR in patients with localized prostate cancer, highlighting the potential of PSMA heterogeneity as a predictive marker for disease progression in localized prostate cancer.

title: PD06-06: A Prospective Study on the Value of CK5/6 Rapid Immunohistochemistry in Rapid Frozen Section Diagnosis of Prostate Targeted Biopsy Specimen
parentSessionTitle: PD06: Prostate Cancer: Detection & Screening I
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Prostate biopsy remains the reference standard for preoperative diagnosis of prostate cancer (PCa). While recent studies have explored strategies for performing radical prostatectomy (RP) without prior biopsy, the issue of false positives results in imaging findings cannot be entirely avoided. The application of rapid frozen section (RFS) diagnosis to targeted biopsy specimens may reduce the number of biopsy cores required and potentially enable same-stage RP. This study investigated the feasibility of CK5/6 rapid immunohistochemistry (RIHC) as an adjunctive diagnostic tool and evaluated its accuracy and reliability. METHODS: This single-center prospective study enrolled 124 patients between October 2022 and September 2023. Eventually, clinical and pathological information from 116 patients was analyzed. For each patient, one biopsy core was obtained from both targeted and non-targeted regions for RFS diagnosis and CK5/6 RIHC testing. Two pathologists independently performed the diagnoses. The diagnostic accuracy of CK5/6 RIHC and its influencing factors were assessed using the remaining frozen tissue and conventional immunohistochemistry (IHC) as the reference standard. RESULTS: A total of 232 biopsy specimens from 116 patients were analyzed. Final pathological diagnosis confirmed PCa in 117 cases (50.4%). RFS alone identified 101 cases (43.5%) as PCa, 101 (43.5%) as benign, and 25 (10.8%) as indeterminate. Among CK5/6-negative cases by RIHC, all 115 (100%) were also negative on conventional IHC and were ultimately diagnosed as PCa. The concordance between RIHC and conventional IHC was excellent (Kappa=0.92, p<0.001). Junior pathologists diagnosed 102 cases (44.0%) as PCa, 95 (40.9%) as benign, and 35 (15.1%) as equivocal. With RIHC assistance, diagnostic certainty improved to 113 PCa cases (49.1%), 117 benign cases (50.4%), with only 1 (0.4%) remaining equivocal. Interobserver agreement between junior and senior pathologists significantly increased (Kappa=0.525, 95% CI 0.426-0.613 for RFS alone; Kappa=0.902, 95% CI 0.875-0.923 for RIHC) when incorporating RIHC (both p<0.001). Further multivariate logistic regression analysis revealed that tumor proportion in biopsy specimens may be an independent risk factor influencing diagnostic difficulty (likelihood of equivocal diagnosis) (p<0.001, 95% CI: 0.040 \[0.007–0.237\]). CONCLUSIONS: CK5/6 RIHC demonstrates clinical feasibility and high diagnostic accuracy in prostate targeted biopsy evaluation. Its incorporation significantly improves diagnostic confidence, particularly for less experienced pathologists. These findings support the potential of RIHC as a valuable adjunct to frozen section diagnosis. Further validation through multicenter studies with larger cohorts is warranted.

title: PD06-07: A prospective, paired-cohort, blinded, validation of the Ibex Prostate AI Pathology system compared to expert uro-pathology reporting of prostate biopsies: the Cancer Histology Artificial Intelligence Reliability Study (IP6-CHAIROS)
parentSessionTitle: PD06: Prostate Cancer: Detection & Screening I
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Artificial intelligence in assessment of digital prostate biopsy pathology has shown promise. We aimed to definitely assess the diagnostic accuracy of Ibex Prostate AI in a prospective paired-cohort blinded validation study. METHODS: Ibex Prostate AI pathology (index test) was compared to histopathology expert review (reference standard) with H&E pathology slides evaluated prospectively in consenting consecutive patients from 6 UK centres (8/Mar/2023-18/Mar/2025). Ibex Prostate AI pathology was evaluated within the pre-biopsy MRI pathway with those undergoing MRI-targeted and systematic biopsies eligible. The reference standard was determined using a first and second pathology review, and in cases of discrepancy, a third. The AI system was blind to all pathology reports. Patients, physicians and reporting pathologists were blind to the AI report. All pathologists were blinded to other pathology reports. The Ibex Prostate AI pre-specified algorithm thresholds in this study were set to give very high sensitivity with a view to potential use as a pre-screening tool for prostate biopsy. The primary endpoints were sensitivity and specificity for GG >/=2 at the patient level. These were compared against pre-specified thresholds of 94% and 75%, respectively, and success would be declared if both two-sided 95%CIs (Wilson's method) exceeded these. ClinicalTrials. gov NCT05228197. RESULTS: Of 712 eligible patients, 623 consented to participate. 26 subsequently withdrew consent. The analysis was based on 597. Median (IQR) age and PSA was 68.3 (61.50-74.10) and 7.40 (5.16-11.00). Any cancer was diagnosed in 425 (71.2%) and Grade Group >/=2 in 382 (64.0%).Primarily, sensitivity was 97.4% (372/382) (95%CI 95.2-98.6%) and specificity 89.8% (193/215) (95%CI 85.0-93.1). Success was declared according to pre-specified thresholds. Secondarily, positive and negative predictive values were 94.4% (91.7-96.3) and 95.1% (91.2-97.3). AUROC was 0.99 (0.978-0.993).For any cancer, Ibex Prostate AI had sensitivity 100.0 (99.1-100), specificity 69.2% (61.9-75.6), PPV 88.9% (85.8-91.4), NPV 100.0% (96.9-100.0) and AUROC 0.99 (0.987-0.997). CONCLUSIONS: Ibex Prostate AI has sufficiently high diagnostic accuracy in evaluating prostate biopsies for use in clinical practice. Ibex Prostate AI could also be used to triage cases suspicious of cancer for pathology review.

title: PD06-08: Comparison of prostate cancer yield per MRI target lesion for LATP versus TRUS prostate biopsy: new insights from the TRANSLATE randomised clinical trial
parentSessionTitle: PD06: Prostate Cancer: Detection & Screening I
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: The TRANSLATE UK-wide multi-centre randomised clinical trial (RCT) detected a 5.7% uplift in detection of Gleason grade group ≥2 (GGG≥2) prostate cancer (PCa) in previously biopsy naïve individuals randomised to local anaesthetic transperineal (LATP) versus transrectal (TRUS) ultrasound guided prostate biopsy. All 1126 randomised participants in TRANSLATE underwent pre-biopsy MRI. We now test the hypothesis that increased detection of GGG≥2 PCa observed for LATP versus TRUS biopsy in TRANSLATE is due to better sampling of anterior and apical target lesions of the prostate. METHODS: We interrogated the positive diagnostic biopsies present in the 326 of 443 randomised participants recruited from the largest TRANSLATE UK centre and diagnosed with PCa. MRI lesion location was defined with the following categories: anterior, mid and posterior in the sagittal plane; base, mid or apex in the transverse plane; lateral or crossing midline. We considered each MRI-visible PIRADsv2 3-5 lesion and compared these against targeted prostate biopsy results for LATP and TRUS. Pairwise comparisons were analysed in SPSS using the chi-squared test. RESULTS: A total of 168/326 (51.5%) patients received LATP and 158/326 (48.5%) received TRUS biopsy. Of these, 323/326 (99%) patients had at least one MRI-visible lesion, with 423 lesions reported in total. Of these 423 MRI-visible lesions, 353 were PIRADs 4/5, and 70 PIRADs 3. Regarding location, 55 were restricted to the anterior gland, 280 were only posterior; 92 were basal, 241 mid, and 90 apical; 310 were lateral, and 113 crossing midline. GGG≥2 PCa was detected in lesions with an anterior component in 34/41 (82.9%) for LATP versus 35/47 (74.5%) TRUS (OR 1.67, 95%CI 0.59-4.73, p=0.336), posterior lesions in 114/149 (76.5%) LATP versus 106/146 (72.6%) TRUS (OR 1.23, 95%CI 0.73-2.08, p=0.441). For lesions located solely anteriorly, GGG≥2 was detected in 20/24 (83.3%) LATP versus 21/31 (67.7%) TRUS (OR 2.38, 95%CI 0.64-8.84, p=0.188) and for solely posteriorly 98/126 (77.7%) LATP versus 88/127 (69.3%) TRUS (OR 1.55, 95% 0.88-2.73, p=0.126). For apical lesions we observed GGG≥2 in 38/46 (82.6%) in LATP versus 22/38 (57.9%) in TRUS (OR 3.46, 95%CI 1.27-9.37, p=0.013). For basal lesions it was 31/43 (72.1%) LATP versus 27/41 (65.8%) TRUS (OR 1.34, 95% 0.53-3.39, p=0.536) and for mid-gland it was 81/104 (77.9%) LATP versus 87/113 (76.9%) TRUS (OR 1.05, 95%CI 0.56-1.99, p=0.875) lesions. Overall, LATP demonstrated higher detection in every location, but only apical lesions reached statistical significance in this cohort. CONCLUSIONS: Initial analysis of single centre data from the TRANSLATE RCT indicate MRI-visible apical prostate lesions are better sampled by LATP versus TRUS biopsy, when considering detection of GGG≥2 PCa.

title: PD06-09: Diagnostic performance of prostate MRI-based artificial intelligence models in detecting cancer: a systematic review and meta-analysis
parentSessionTitle: PD06: Prostate Cancer: Detection & Screening I
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Artificial intelligence (AI) is actively being explored as a transformative technology in modern medicine, particularly in MRI-based prostate cancer (PCa) prediction. The growing number of models demonstrating technical feasibility prompts the need for a comprehensive evaluation of their performance, generalizability and clinical utility. METHODS: A systematic review and meta-analysis was performed in accordance with the Checklist for Artificial Intelligence in Medical Imaging (CLAIM-2024) and PRISMA-Diagnostic Test Accuracy (PRISMA-DTA) guidelines. A comprehensive literature search was conducted across PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, Scopus, and the Cochrane Library on February 28, 2025 to identify English-language studies published starting from January 1, 2017, on the development of MRI-based machine learning (ML) or deep learning (DL) models with independent testing cohorts for predicting PCa. RESULTS: After screening 5090 retrieved articles, 50 studies involving 8078 patients were included in the meta-analysis. Compared with the clinically evaluated Prostate Imaging-Reporting and Data System (PI-RADS v2.1) score (SUCRA=0.247), AI prediction models, particularly DL models (SUCRA=0.966), exhibited superior efficacy in predicting PCa at the patient level (AUROC=0.95, 95%CI: 0.93-0.97). Furthermore, these models demonstrated diagnostic performance comparable to that of senior radiologists. When used independently, AI models exhibit excellent specificity (mean: 0.698±0.16); when deployed as a clinical adjunct, AI models can significantly improve radiologists’ sensitivity in detecting csPCa (mean: 0.907±0.03) (Figure). CONCLUSIONS: AI models demonstrate high accuracy in PCa detection, offering significant advantages for both large-scale, standalone screening and clinician-assisted diagnosis of aggressive disease. To fully realize this potential, future efforts should focus on the development of deep learning-based models by integrating multi-modal omics technologies, followed by their rigorous validation in multi-center, large-scale real-world datasets. This will facilitate the establishment of standardized AI-assisted diagnostic workflows of "AI-first read, physician-verification", thereby mitigating current challenges of both ”over-reliance” and ”under-utilization”.

title: PD06-10: Detection Rate of Prostate Cancer Using Prostate-Specific Membrane Antigen/Ultrasound-Fusion Biopsy in Patients with Suspected Recurrence or Inconclusive/Negative Biopsies: A Single-Center Retrospective Study
parentSessionTitle: PD06: Prostate Cancer: Detection & Screening I
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Prostate-specific membrane antigen (PSMA)/ultrasound (US)-fusion biopsy may improve the detection of prostate cancer (PCa). This study evaluated its diagnostic performance, with the primary outcome being the PCa detection rate and the secondary outcome assessing the association between PSMA positron emission tomography (PET)–derived parameters and biopsy results. METHODS: We analyzed patients with suspected recurrent PCa or prior inconclusive/negative biopsies who underwent PSMA PET/CT as standard-of-care imaging to guide PSMA/US-fusion biopsy at UCLA (April 2021–April 2025). Lesion contouring was performed using dedicated software (ProFuse), and real-time fusion biopsy (Artemis) was conducted by an expert urologist. Detection rates were evaluated at the patient and lesion levels. SUVmax differences between PCa and non-PCa lesions and lesion-level detection across PRIMARY scores were retrospectively analyzed. Subgroup analyses compared detection rates by clinical background (post-non-surgical treatment vs. treatment-naïve). RESULTS: Sixty-two patients with 89 lesions were analyzed. Median PSA was 8.3 ng/dL (IQR, 4.2–13.8), and 36 (58%) were post-non-surgical treatment, most commonly cryoablation (36%). Twenty-six patients were treatment-naïve, and 13 were under active surveillance. Median Gleason grade found on biopsy was 3 (IQR, 2–3). Median SUVmax of target lesions was 6.35 (IQR, 5.33–8.41). Detection rates were 66% (41/62) at the patient level and 58% (52/89) at the lesion level. PCa lesions showed higher SUVmax (8.03 vs. 5.93; p<0.001) and higher PRIMARY scores, with detection increasing from 14% (score 2) to 80% (score 5) (p=0.0072, Cochran–Armitage trend test). Subgroup analysis suggested slightly lower detection in post-treatment lesions compared to treatment-naïve status (patient 64% vs. 69%, p=0.78; lesion 55% vs. 63%, p=0.52). CONCLUSIONS: PSMA/US-fusion biopsy shows favorable diagnostic performance and clinical utility in identifying PCa lesions in a more challenging subset of patients. Considering PSMA PET parameters and patient background may help optimize lesion targeting.

title: PD06-11: Predicting Gleason Grade Group at Radical Prostatectomy: A Machine Learning Approach for Prostate Cancer Risk Stratification
parentSessionTitle: PD06: Prostate Cancer: Detection & Screening I

speakers.organization: Massachusetts General Hospital, Harvard Medical School

fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Prostate biopsy remains associated with significant rates of prostate cancer grade misclassification which can adversely impact risk stratification (RS) and clinical management. To address this limitation, we aimed to develop machine learning (ML) models to predict prostate cancer grade group (GG) at radical prostatectomy (RP). METHODS: Patients who underwent RP were identified in our institutional TRUS fusion prostate biopsy database (2014-2021). We defined a 3-class ordinal outcome measure: GG1, GG2-3, or GG4-5 on RP. The cohort was split into training and test sets (75/25%). Feature selection among the available demographic, clinical, imaging and pathology variables, was performed using the importance scores obtained from an ordinal LightGBM model. Seven ML models were trained and optimized using 5-fold cross-validation. Model performance was evaluated on the test set and compared with permutation tests against biopsy GG and NCCN Risk Group, where low, intermediate, and high risk predicted GG1, GG2-3, and GG4-5, respectively. Performance was assessed with the quadratic weighted kappa (QWK), mean absolute error (MAE), accuracy and macro F1 score. RESULTS: A total of 535 patients were identified, of which 82 (15.3%) had GG1, 368 (68.7%) GG2-3, and 85 (15.8%) GG4-5 prostate cancer at RP. The biopsy misclassification rate was 25.4% (136/535), with 15% (80) upgrading and 10.4% (56) downgrading at RP. Important predictive features included age, highest biopsy GG, primary biopsy target GG and maximum positive core length, PSA density, and a weighted score calculated as the sum of the number of biopsy regions per GG, each multiplied by its GG value. The best performance was achieved by the ExtraTrees and AdaBoost models adapted for ordinal outcomes with a QWK of 0.738 (95% CI: 0.619 - 0.832) and 0.734 (95% CI: 0.613 - 0.836), respectively. Both models significantly outperformed NCCN Risk Group (QWK=0.637 (0.483 \- 0.753), p=0.02, 0.026) and biopsy GG (QWK=0.632 (0.467 - 0.754), p=0.01, 0.037) (Figure). CONCLUSIONS: Our models demonstrated strong overall predictive ability outperforming biopsy GG and NCCN Risk Group in predicting prostate cancer GG at RP. These findings highlight the potential of ML models as future risk calculators to enhance RS and improve guidance of prostate cancer management.

title: PD06-12: Machine Learning-Based Radiomics for Precision Diagnosis in Repeat Prostate Biopsies
parentSessionTitle: PD06: Prostate Cancer: Detection & Screening I
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: A significant clinical challenge in current prostate cancer diagnosis is the risk of false-negative results from the initial biopsy. Following a negative initial biopsy, there is a lack of standardized assessment protocols for active surveillance strategies or for determining the necessity of a repeat biopsy. Furthermore, there is limited research on ML models that predict missed diagnoses based on MR imaging and biopsy pathology data. This study aims to address the need for precision diagnostics by developing a machine learning model that integrates radiomics features to provide early warning of missed diagnoses, predict high-risk regions, and guide the decision for repeat biopsies. METHODS: This study employed a single-center design. We enrolled patients with a PI-RADS score of ≤3, treated at Jiangsu Provincial People's Hospital between 2019 and 2023, who had complete clinical data (including mp-MRI images and biopsy/radical prostatectomy pathology results). Patients who underwent repeat biopsies were specifically included. Collected data encompassed clinical information, laboratory test reports, prior medical records, imaging, and pathology data, including age, PSA levels, medical history, prostate volume, PI-RADS score (v2.0), and biopsy/radical prostatectomy pathology findings. All enrolled patients underwent mp-MRI examination prior to biopsy. The images were independently reviewed by two experienced radiologists who assigned PI-RADS scores. Radiomic features were then extracted from the manually delineated lesions on mp-MRI images. Patients were randomly allocated to the model's training set and internal validation set. A machine learning model was developed by integrating the extracted radiomic features with clinical data. Feature selection was performed to identify the most predictive features. The dataset was randomly split into training and testing sets in a 6:4 ratio. The model's diagnostic performance was evaluated on the test set, reporting the Area Under the Curve and the Youden index. Finally, the model's efficacy was validated using imaging data from the repeat biopsy cohort. RESULTS: The study enrolled 894 patients with PI-RADS scores ≤ 3 and complete clinical data, including 89 who underwent repeat biopsies. The machine learning model demonstrated robust performance in predicting prostate cancer diagnosis. In the validation set, it achieved an AUC of 0.922 (95% CI: 0.809-1.000), a sensitivity of 0.792, and a specificity of 1.000.; these results were confirmed in the test set with an AUC of 0.875 (95% CI: 0.850-0.950), a sensitivity of 0.858, and a specificity of 0.804 For diagnosing clinically significant prostate cancer (csPCa), the model also showed high accuracy, with an AUC of 0.978 (95% CI: 0.975-0.981), sensitivity of 0.958, and specificity of 0.750 in the validation set, and an AUC of 0.877 (95% CI: 0.837-0.918), sensitivity of 0.813, and specificity of 0.814 in the test set. CONCLUSIONS: The machine learning model utilizing radiomics data from patients with PI-RADS scores ≤3 demonstrated superior performance in predicting repeat biopsy outcomes compared to traditional radiomics prediction models.

title: PD06-13: Imaging-derived radiomic features as predictive markers of Gleason score assessment in prostate cancer.
parentSessionTitle: PD06: Prostate Cancer: Detection & Screening I
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Prostate cancer (PCa) comprises one-third of new male cancers. While MP-MRI offers non-invasive tumor characterization, visual assessment shows limited concordance with pathology. Computational texture analysis from medical imaging offers extraction of quantitative information beyond human perception. This study sought to determine if MRI feature extraction could distinguish histological grade groups. METHODS: We analyzed 244 patients with PCa who underwent prostatectomy. T2WI and ADC maps were acquired; T2WI were z-score normalized using patient-specific prostate masks. Digitized whole slide images (n=732) were Gleason annotated (G3, G4, and G5), and non-linearly aligned to the T2WI. Mean MRI intensities and 107 radiomic features were extracted per grade and normal tissue. Kruskal-Wallis with post-hoc Dunn’s tests assessed inter-grade differences. Pearson correlations with FDR p<0.001, evaluated histology-MRI relationships. RESULTS: Kruskal-Wallis analyses revealed 104 (T2WI) and 106 (ADC) features significantly differing across Gleason grades (FDR< 0.001). Additionally, 102 and 104 features, respectively, significantly correlated with Gleason scores (T2WI/ADC median \|ρ\|=0.54, 0.57; both max ρ=0.80) ( Fig 1). Notably, T2WI intensity showed no correlation with Gleason grade, whereas ADC was negatively correlated (ρ=-0.28, Fig 2). CONCLUSIONS: This study demonstrates that quantitative radiomic features extracted from MP-MRI correlate with Gleason patterns. Texture features captured biologically relevant tissue characteristics beyond visual assessment. The inverse ADC-Gleason relationship, coupled with non-significant T2WI intensity correlations, highlights the complementary value MP-MRI in characterizing PCa aggressiveness. These findings suggest radiomics can be used a non-invasive tool for predicting histopathological grade and improve prostate cancer assessment.

title: PD06-14: The influence of Germline Pathogenic Variants in DNA Repair Genes on a cohort of patients who underwent curativesurgery for Prostate Cancer
parentSessionTitle: PD06: Prostate Cancer: Detection & Screening I
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Family history represents a significant risk factor for prostate cancer (PCa), emphasizing its genetic basis. Early identification ofgermline pathogenic variants (PVs) in DNA repair genes (DRGs) is crucial for timely PCa diagnosis, prognosis, and for informing at-risk relatives. Conversely, the presence of variants of uncertain significance (VUS) has been associated with worse clinicaloutcomes. This study aimed to assess how the presence of germline PVs and VUS affect clinical and pathological outcomes in amonocentric cohort of patients who underwent robot-assisted laparoscopic prostatectomy (RALP) for PCa. METHODS: This prospective study, supported by AIRC - Fondazione AIRC per la Ricerca sul Cancro (registered and emended with the numberID-IG-25027-V1.3), was conducted at a tertiary referral center in collaboration with the Departments of Oncology, Urology, Pathology,Radiology, and Medical Genetics. A total of 179 men aged 58–70 years who underwent RALP for localized PCa were screened forgermline PVs and VUS in DRGs prior to surgery. Patients were enrolled if they had an ISUP grade ≥3 at biopsy and/or a confirmedPCa diagnosis at ≤50 years of age. Individuals harboring a VUS or PVs were compared to those with negative genetic results. RESULTS: Of the 179 patients screened between 2021 and 2024, 162 shared the results of genetic testing. Median age at surgery did not differ between groups (65 years, IQR 59–70). Among them, 114 (69.9%) tested negative, while 39 (29.4%) and 9 (5%) carried a VUS orPVs in DRGs, respectively. The most frequent VUS involved ATM (22.2%), CHEK2 (15.6%), BRCA2 (13.3%), ATR (6.7%), NBN(6.7%), RAD51D (6.7%), and MSH6 (4.4%). The nine PVs identified were: BRCA2, PALB2 + NBN, PALB2 + BRCA2, BRCA1PALB2, CHEK2 + PMS2, CHEK2, and ATM. A family history of cancer was reported in 50% of VUS/PV carriers compared to 34.6%of non-carriers. High-grade PCa (ISUP > 3) was found in 46.3% of carriers versus 38.0% of non-carriers. A pathological stage ≥pT3a occurred in 53.6% of carriers versus 45.1% of non-carriers, while nodal involvement (pN1) was more frequent among carriers(21.4% vs 12.6%). Biochemical recurrence (BCR) occurred in 36.8% of carriers versus 30.4% of non-carriers. CONCLUSIONS: This study provides valuable insight into the role of germline VUS, by the first, and PVs in DRGs among PCa patients, suggestingthat such variants may confer a less favorable disease course. Although differences did not reach statistical significance, carrierstended to present with higher-grade and more advanced disease at final pathology. Genetic screening for PCa may therefore aid notonly in early detection among high-risk individuals but also in guiding clinical management and follow-up strategies.

title: PD06-15: Discovery of a Recurrent Frameshift Ashkenazi Jewish Founder Mutation (F722fs) in the PARPi-Sensitive MMS22L Gene Associated with Increasing Risk of Prostate Cancer
parentSessionTitle: PD06: Prostate Cancer: Detection & Screening I
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Most established prostate cancer (PCa) susceptibility genes (e. g., BRCA2) are involved in DNA repair with a subset involved in PARP inhibitor (PARPi). We systematically tested association of newly reported 65 genes in these pathways with PCa risk. METHODS: Ancestry-specific association between loss-of-function (LoF) germline variants in these genes and PCa risk was first tested between PCa patients from Johns Hopkins University (Hopkins) and population controls from the Genome Aggregation Database (gnomAD). Results were confirmed in additional three PCa patient cohorts and UK Biobank (UKB). RESULTS: Among men of Ashkenazi Jewish ancestry (ASJ), the carrier rate of LoF mutations in MMS22L was significantly higher in 469 Hopkins cases than 5,573 gnomAD controls. The association was confirmed in the UKB. In the combined analysis of all cohorts, the carrier rate of F722fs, an ASJ founder mutation, was 1.5% in cases vs 0.31% in controls, Odds Ratio (OR)=4.9 (95% confidence interval: 2.1-10.6), PFisher=1.44E-04. Furthermore, carriers had a significantly higher proportion of aggressive disease (83%) than non-carriers (27%), OR=12.3 (2.2-132.5), PFirth=0.003. Another founder mutation in non-Finnish European (NFE), c.340+1G>A, was also significantly associated with PCa risk in the UKB; OR=7.7 (2.6-21.0), PFirth=5.10E-04. Somatic DNA analysis and response to therapeutic PARPi need to be characterized. CONCLUSIONS: We provide suggestive evidence that MMS22L is a novel major PCa susceptibility gene. Its carrier rate and effect size are similar to that of BRCA2. If validated, it can be used for risk stratification of PCa risk and aggressiveness.

title: V01-01: Robotic Parastomal Hernia Repair of Ileal Conduit: Keyhole Technique with Novel Mesh Collar Modification
parentSessionTitle: V01: Upper Tract Reconstruction I
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Parastomal hernia repair has low success rates in the literature. Recurrence rates range from <20% for Sugarbaker technique to >30% for keyhole technique. However, these data may not apply to urinary conduits as there are few urinary conduits in these series. We are concerned that the Sugarbaker technique could cause renal obstruction in urinary conduits. Concerns with the existing keyhole technique include the risk of sliding hernia and the risk of the permanent mesh triangle flaps eroding into the conduit. We sought to modify the keyhole technique to address these shortcomings. METHODS: We have developed a mesh collar that is absorbable on both the inner and outer face. We demonstrate how we create this collar and secure it to the keyhole mesh. We then demonstrate the technique for robotic implantation. We review our success in all patients undergoing this procedure (with our without a collar) in the last 18 months. Success was defined as no recurrence on cross-sectional imaging. RESULTS: Among 7 patients undergoing robotic parastomal hernia repair of a urinary stoma with a keyhole technique, 6 were in ileal conduits and one in a Mitrofanoff. We performed the keyhole without a stomal collar in 4 (including the one Mitrofanoff) and with a stomal collar in 3. Success rates by cross sectional imaging are 100% but follow-up is limited to 6 months. There were no complications. CONCLUSIONS: Robotic parastomal hernia repair of urinary stomas is a minimally invasive option that helps minimize further injury to the fascia. A keyhole repair is feasible and safe. The addition of a mesh collar may help reduce recurrence rates. The innovative double-sided feature of the collar may help reduce the risk of erosion into native bowel and the conduit.

title: V01-02: Single-Port Robotic Ureteroenteric Stricture Repair
parentSessionTitle: V01: Upper Tract Reconstruction I
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Ureteroenteric strictures (UES) are a significant complication following urinary diversion and often require surgical reconstruction. This video aims to illustrate ureteroenteric stricture repair using the single-port (SP) robotic platform and to demonstrate non-transecting techniques—specifically side-to-side anastomosis and Y-V plasty—that preserve ureteral vascularity. METHODS: Representative cases were performed using the SP robotic platform via a transperitoneal approach. Key operative steps included stricture exposure, flap creation, and anastomosis under near-infrared fluorescence guidance. Non-transecting techniques were applied for short or moderate strictures with preserved ureteral mobility, while complex cases were managed with bowel flaps. Outcomes were evaluated for perioperative parameters, complications, and stricture-free rates. RESULTS: Twenty-eight SP robotic UES repairs were performed. Median operative time was 189 minutes and median blood loss 20 mL. The median stricture length was 2 cm (range 1–10). Median hospital stay was one day, with five day-case surgeries. Minor complications occurred in 21.7% and major in 13%. At a median 23-month follow-up, the overall success rate was 96.4%. CONCLUSIONS: Single-port robotic ureteroenteric stricture repair using non-transecting and selective flap techniques is safe, precise, and effective. The SP platform facilitates minimally invasive reconstruction with high success and low morbidity. | | | --- | | |

title: V01-03: Robotic ureterocalicostomy for complex proximal ureteral strictures: surgical experience and technical considerations
parentSessionTitle: V01: Upper Tract Reconstruction I
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: This video is to demonstrate the surgical technique and clinical outcomes of robotic ureterocalicostomy (UC) for complex proximal ureteral strictures in our institution, particularly in patients with congenital anomalies and a history of prior urinary tract reconstruction. METHODS: Between January 2024 and February 2025, four patients underwent UC in our institution. The procedure involved mobilization of the distal ureter and lower pole of the kidney, carefully avoiding the collecting system and renal vessels. A fan-shaped proximal ureter was prepared for anastomosis, followed by opening of the dependent lower calyx and mucosa-to-mucosa anastomosis with 4-0 barbed sutures. In one patient with congenital megaureter and a history of ureteroneocystostomy, a combined side-to-side ureteroneocystostomy was performed to address distal ureteral stricture. The video showcases the technical subtleties, such as hemostatic control and preservation of the renal vasculature. RESULTS: All patients had a history of prior upper urinary tract reconstruction. Three had congenital anomalies, including renal malrotation with horseshoe kidney, congenital ureteropelvic junction obstruction, and congenital megaureter. The remaining patient, although without anomalies, had undergone multiple prior interventions for ipsilateral ureteral calculi. The mean operative time was 160.25±24.22 minutes, with a median estimated blood loss of 30 mL (range 20–30). During a median follow-up of 16 months (range 8–22), all patients achieved clinical success, and no Clavien–Dindo grade ≥II complications occurred. Representative cases demonstrated patent anastomoses, unobstructed drainage, and favorable functional outcomes on follow-up imaging. CONCLUSIONS: Preliminary clinical results indicates that robotic ureterocalicostomy is a safe, effective, and feasible reconstructive option for managing complex upper urinary tract obstructions. It provides new treatment methods and approaches for patients with congenital malformations or previous failed repairs in clinical practice. However, large-sample, and long-term studies are still needed.

title: V01-04: Single Port Robotic Total Urinary Tract Reconstruction After Pelvic Crush Injury
parentSessionTitle: V01: Upper Tract Reconstruction I
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: This video details a total urinary tract reconstruction of a patient following pelvic crush injury using the da Vinci Single Port Robot System. The objective of this video is to demonstrate that the SP system enables concurrent ureteral reimplantation and posterior urethroplasty. METHODS: Surgical video detailing SP robotic repair. The patient was then monitored for several months with post operative imaging to evaluate for successful repair. RESULTS: The patient had an uneventful postoperative course. Following discharge, he has been observed for several months without evidence of recurrence. The patient had no post operative hydronephrosis and is voiding spontaneously successfully. CONCLUSIONS: The SP robotic system enabled concurrent bilateral ureteral repair and posterior urethroplasty allowing for a successful reconstruction. SP can be a useful tool when treating a patient after trauma to provide access to complex and difficult to reach areas.

title: V01-05: Single-Port Robotic-Assisted Transvaginal Retroperitoneal Ureteral Reimplantation: Early Experience
parentSessionTitle: V01: Upper Tract Reconstruction I
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Single-port robotic-assisted transvaginal retroperitoneal ureteral reimplantation represents a novel, minimally invasive technique for managing distal ureteral strictures in female patients. This approach provides direct retroperitoneal access without entering the peritoneal cavity, potentially reducing morbidity and expediting recovery. METHODS: Between January 2024 and September 2025, the transvaginal approach was attempted in six female patients undergoing robotic ureteral reimplantation. The retroperitoneal space was entered through an anterolateral vaginal fornix incision using a small SP access port. The ureter was dissected along the external iliac and superior vesical vessels and reimplanted into the bladder using a refluxing technique. RESULTS: The mean age was 48 years (range 42–62), and five patients had a history of prior abdominal surgery. In three patients with prior surgery and iatrogenic ureteral injury, conversions to the robotic low anterior approach was necessary—two due to dense scarring at the ureteral stump preventing safe dissection, and one due to a higher-than-anticipated ureteral injury necessitating a transperitoneal ileal ureter. No intraoperative complications occurred; one converted case required blood transfusion. The mean operative time for the transvaginal cases was 195 minutes and all were discharged within 24 hours. At a mean follow-up of 6.5 months (1–19), all patients were hardware-free, symptom-free, and had no obstruction on imaging. No sexual dysfunction or major complications were observed. CONCLUSIONS: Single-port robotic-assisted transvaginal retroperitoneal ureteral reimplantation is a feasible and safe technique for distal ureteral reconstruction, offering minimal invasiveness and rapid recovery with excellent short-term outcomes. Surgeons offering this technique should be facile with alternative approaches, as previous surgery with iatrogenic ureteral injury can lead do dense fibrosis and distortion of the anatomy, necessitating conversion.

title: V01-06: Robotic Right to Left Transureteroureterostomy with a Left Ureteral Reimplant in Bilateral Ureteral Stricture Disease
parentSessionTitle: V01: Upper Tract Reconstruction I
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Reconstructive urologic surgery is typically the gold standard for definitive management of complex bilateral ureteral strictures. In this video, we present a case of a robotic right to left transureteroureterostomy with a left ureteral reimplant in a patient with stage IV endometriosis who subsequently developed bilateral ureteral strictures. METHODS: Patient was placed in supine position. Robotic ports were placed in a standard fashion. The peritoneum was divided at the level of the right iliac vessels to expose the retroperitoneal space. The right hydronephrotic ureter was identified and transected at the level of the strictured segment. Then, the proximal landing point on the left ureter was identified. A tunnel was created under the sigmoid colon to pass the right ureter to the proximal mid left ureter. The distal most aspect of the left ureter was identified for the neocystotomy and the anterior peritoneum was incised to expose the bladder. A left posterior dome cystotomy was made and the left ureter was reimplanted into the bladder. A ureterotomy was made in the left ureter and an end to side ureteral anastomosis was made between the right and left ureter to form the transureteroureterostomy. A ureteral stent was placed and both a peritoneal flap and omental tissue were placed over the distal suture lines. A drain was placed and the robot was undocked. RESULTS: Total operative time was 316 minutes. Estimated blood loss was minimal. The patient was discharged on post operative day (POD) 3. The foley was removed on POD7. Patient’s post operative course was complicated by two hospital admissions for urinary tract infections. The patient’s stent and left nephrostomy tube were removed at 5 weeks after confirmatory retrograde pyelogram demonstrated a well healed and patent ureteral anastomosis. The right nephrostomy tube was removed after 7 weeks. CONCLUSIONS: This video features key components of robotic bilateral ureteral reconstruction. Our approach demonstrated that it is feasible to perform robotic concomitant distal and proximal ureteral reconstruction without compromising vascularity and without the need for more complex ureteral reconstruction methods, which can be associated with higher morbidity.

title: V01-07: Robotic Appendiceal Onlay Flap for Salvage Ureteroplasty After Failed Buccal Mucosa Graft
parentSessionTitle: V01: Upper Tract Reconstruction I
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: § A 65-year-old female presented with severe right hydronephrosis, recurrent right ureteral stones secondary to a proximal ureteral stricture and was therefore taken to the operating room for a Single-Port right ureteroplasty with buccal mucosal graft and omental wrap. However, she represented three more times with right flank pain, hydronephrosis, and more stones. Retrograde pyelogram at the time of a ureteroscopy for stone surgery revealed a UPJ obstruction proximal to the buccal graft site. She underwent laser endopyelotomy and ballon dilation. She recovered well initially but then returned once more with the same symptoms. She had a nephrostomy tube placed and then diagnostic testing with antegrade nephrostogram, retrograde pyelogram and cystogram. There was evidence on these imaging studies of a distal ureteral stricture. She was booked for a robotic right ureteral reimplant with psoas hitch. However, once she was in the OR and her distal ureter was dissected, it appeared normal. Ureteroscopy was performed at this time which confirmed the suspicion that the distal ureter was indeed patent. In fact, the flexible ureteroscope was able to traverse the entire ureter. However, proximally at the site of the buccal mucosal graft and omental wrap, there was tortuosity and kinking of the patent ureter. METHODS: Though the ureter was patent and the ureteroscope could easily navigate and ascend to the renal pelvis, we suspected that these kinks were the cause for her functional obstruction. We excised the omentum that was wrapped around the right ureter. We also mobilized the lower pole and lateral aspect of the kidney. We then incised the ureter and detubularized it for roughly 7 cm, essentially the entire proximal ureter. We identified the appendix and isolated its origin off the cecum. A robotic 8 mm staple load to ligate off the appendix from the cecum with care to preserve the ileocecal artery. The appendix was aligned over the detubularized portion of the ureter and identified which orientation would be proper (in this case the distal tip was placed most cephalad). We then detubularized the appendix. We sewed the appendix onto the detubularized portion of ureter using 4-0 Vicryl suture in multiple locations to anchor it in place and then using 3-O STRATAFIX in a running fashion to perform the anastomosis. We performed ureteroscopy once more to confirm the ureter was straight, without stricture, without kinking, and the repair was watertight. We placed an 8 French by 24 cm double-J stent over a wire, left a 15 Blake drainand closed in standard fashion. RESULTS: The patient was discharged on POD2 after she passed trial of void and JP was removed. She was discharged with the nephrostomy to drainage as she was having right flank pain, although the opening pressure was low. After 2 weeks, antegrade nephrostogram confirmed patency with the stent and nephrostomy tube was removed. The stent was removed after 6 weeks. Two months out from surgery, patient is doing well without any flank pain, hydronephrosis, AKI, UTIs, or stones. CONCLUSIONS: Appendiceal onlay flap is a good salvage option for long right ureteral reconstruction.

title: V01-08: Technical Considerations for Robotic Cystectomy with Intracorporeal Urinary Diversion in Congenital Intestinal Malrotation
parentSessionTitle: V01: Upper Tract Reconstruction I
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Congenital intestinal malrotation is a rare anatomical abnormality that affects up to 1:500 live births who ultimately have symptomatic malrotation. Malrotation results from abnormal rotation of the gut during embryogenesis. During normal development, the gastrointestinal tract rotates 270 degrees as it migrates into its final position in the abdomen. Congenital intestinal malrotation results when the full rotation is not completed. As a result, the mesentery is narrowed, and the surgeons should expect the large intestine to be on the patient’s left and the small bowel on the right ( (https://www.auajournals.org/doi/abs/10.1097/01.JU.0001191264.83903.71.08#F1)). Our objective was to describe technical considerations when approaching intracorporeal diversion in a patient with congenital intestinal malrotation. METHODS: The patient was a 77 yo male with HGT1 bladder cancer who had failed and exhausted multiple therapies including BCG induction x2, gemcitabine/docetaxel induction x1, pembrolizumab, and nadofaragene firadenovec. He consented to undergo robotic radical cystectomy with intracorporeal urinary diversion. RESULTS: The operative time was 6 hrs 38 mins with an estimated blood loss of 100 ccs. Postoperatively, the patient developed an ileus on postoperative day 4, which resolved with an NGT and TPN. He was discharged home on postoperative day 14. His final pathology was pTisN0 with negative surgical margins. CONCLUSIONS: Congenital intestinal malrotation should not preclude patients from receiving an intracorporeal ileal conduit diversion. The primary consideration is staying oriented and recognizing that the intestinal anatomy will be atypical. In cases of incomplete malrotation the large intestine is positioned predominantly on the left, the ileocecal junction lies near the midline, and the small intestine occupies the right side of the abdomen. Most importantly, the conduit should be rotated in a counterclockwise direction rather than clockwise, to prevent ischemic complications.

title: V01-09: Single port robotic Non-transecting Pyeloplasty in Renal Transplant
parentSessionTitle: V01: Upper Tract Reconstruction I
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Ureteral obstruction occurs in 2-10% of renal transplant patients, with ureteric ischemia accounting for around 90% of cases. Management of Ureteropelvic junction obstruction (UPJO) in transplant recipients presents unique challenges due to altered anatomy, compromised vascular supply, and the need to preserve graft function. Single-port robotic surgery offers enhanced visualization and precision while minimizing surgical trauma. Non-transecting techniques may reduce ischemic injury in transplanted kidneys with already compromised blood supply. METHODS: Patient Presentation: A 69-year-old female with a complex medical history including diabetes mellitus, hypertension, hyperlipidemia, treated hepatitis C virus infection, and end-stage renal disease underwent deceased donor renal transplantation in June 2022\. The immediate post-transplant period was complicated, requiring surgical re-exploration and revision. One year post-transplant (June 2023), the patient developed hydronephrosis of the transplanted kidney requiring percutaneous nephrostomy tube (PCNT) placement for urinary drainage and preservation of graft function. Surgical Technique: A single incision was placed to access the transplanted kidney in the iliac fossa. The ureteropelvic junction was carefully dissected and exposed with meticulous preservation of periureteral tissues to maintain vascular supply. A non-transecting technique was employed, utilizing a longitudinal incision through the stenotic segment following the Heineke-Mikulicz principle. The spatulated anastomosis was performed with running absorbable suture, and a double-J ureteral stent was placed for internal drainage. RESULTS: The patient tolerated the procedure well without intraoperative complications. The postoperative recovery was excellent, with the patient being discharged home within 24 hours of surgery. The patient has remained free of urinary tract infections since the procedure. Renal function has been preserved with serum creatinine remaining stable and similar to her pre-obstruction baseline values throughout the follow-up period. Resolution of hydronephrosis was achieved, and the patient has maintained good graft function. CONCLUSIONS: Single-port robotic non-transecting pyeloplasty is a safe, effective option for UPJO in renal transplant recipients, achieving successful reconstruction with preserved function and minimal morbidity.

title: V01-11: Bilateral Ureteral Stricture: Total Ureteral Replacement with Cecal Appendix – Video-Assisted Technique Description
parentSessionTitle: V01: Upper Tract Reconstruction I
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Extensive ureteral strictures represent a major therapeutic challenge in pediatric urology. In selected cases where conventional reconstructive techniques prove insufficient, the use of the cecal appendix as a ureteral substitute constitutes a viable—though uncommon—alternative in the pediatric population. The objective of this video is to describe the key technical aspects of ureteral replacement using the cecal appendix in a pediatric patient with severe right ureteral stricture secondary to BK virus infection. METHODS: We performed a Video showing step by step of a combined approach in a complicated patient. RESULTS: A 15-year-old male with a history of acute myeloid leukemia in remission and unrelated bone marrow transplantation developed BK virus infection, resulting in bilateral ureteral stenosis, renal insufficiency, and pelvicalyceal dilatation. He underwent multiple endourological procedures and an initial surgery consisting of left-to-right transureteroureterostomy with right vesicoureteral reimplantation (Psoas Hitch technique). Due to progressive hydronephrosis and functional deterioration, retrograde pyelography confirmed recurrence of right ureteral stenosis, prompting the decision to perform ureteral replacement using the cecal appendix. The procedure began in the Valdivia–Galdakao position with a transabdominal laparoscopic approach aimed at identifying the right ureter and the cecal appendix, optimizing access and allowing for a targeted open approach. Through a minimal incision, conventional open dissection was completed, identifying the previously exposed structures. The stenotic right ureter was resected, the appendix was divided with closure of the cecal stump, and a term-to-term anastomosis was constructed—proximally to the right renal pelvis and distally to the bladder. Simultaneously, the left transureteroureterostomy was reconstructed by anastomosing it to the appendiceal graft using 5-0 PDS sutures. Bilateral 5 Fr double-J stents, Foley and suprapubic catheters, and an abdominal drain were placed. The postoperative course was uneventful; bladder catheters were removed on postoperative day 5 and the drain on day 7. CONCLUSIONS: The cecal appendix represents a valuable option for ureteral replacement in patients with long or complex strictures where other reconstructive techniques have failed. Its successful application requires careful preoperative planning and advanced reconstructive urology expertise. This case highlights the feasibility and usefulness of this technique in highly complex clinical scenarios.

title: V01-12: Robotic assisted laparoscopic retroperitoneal non-transecting ureteroneocystostomy with onlay buccal mucosal ureteroplasty
parentSessionTitle: V01: Upper Tract Reconstruction I

speakers.organization: Division of Urology, Department of Surgery, Faculty of Medicine Siriraj Hospital, Mahidol University

fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Ureteric stricture is one of the most common complications after stone surgery. The more episodes of stone interventions a patient undergoes, the greater risk of accumulated ureteric injury. When multiple strictures are encountered, it a near impossible to perform a single reconstructive surgery with reliable outcomes. This suffers our patients, and may lead to loss follow-up, subsequently, infectious complications and progressive renal function loss. This recording demonstrates robotic-assisted, laparoscopic retroperitoneal non-transecting ureteroneocystostomy with onlay buccal mucosal ureteroplasty. Utilizing advantages of robotic surgery, precise dissection and port versatility to perform a two-field ureteric stricture correction using a single set of cannula placements. METHODS: A 72-year-old male recurrent stone former underwent multiple open and endourologic stone surgeries. He later developed multi-segmental ureteric strictures. Repeated endoscopic procedures results a failure. He was subsequently referred to Siriraj Hospital for definitive reconstruction. RESULTS: The operation a success. The robotic surgical system enabled a minimally invasive retroperitoneal approach, allowing meticulous ureteric dissection while preserving its blood supply. A side-to-side, non-transecting ureteroneocystostomy and a buccal graft upper ureteroplasty were performed simultaneously. Console time was 1 hour and 30 minutes for ureteroneocystostomy and 1 hour and 10 minutes for buccal graft ureteroplasty. There were no major postoperative complications, and estimated blood loss was 50 milliliters. Postoperative opioid use was minimal. The Foley catheter was retained for 5 days, and the patient was discharged on postoperative day 6. 1-month postoperative ultrasound showed no residual hydronephrosis, and a 3-month postoperative ureteroscopy revealed patent anastomoses and a viable buccal mucosal graft. The DJ stent was removed just before ureteroscopy. CONCLUSIONS: Robotic-assisted laparoscopic retrperitoneal non-transecting ureteroplasty is a viable surgical option for patients with multiple ureteric strictures. It allows same-incision, simultaneous, multi-segmental ureteric reconstruction with high precision in perfusion preservation. Retroperitoneal approach minimizes bowel-related complications and shortens recovery time. The use of buccal graft provides a tension-free anastomosis and may ultimately reduce patient suffering from repeated corrective surgeries in the future.

title: V02-01: Clinical efficacy of the Automatic Tissue Recognition Function in a Super-pulsed Thulium Fiber Laser: A Multicenter Lithotripsy Study
parentSessionTitle: V02: Urolithiasis/Endourology

speakers.organization: Urology Center of the Central Clinical Hospital of Civil Aviation

fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Laser lithotripsy is the "gold standard" for urolithiasis treatment; however, risks of iatrogenic mucosal injury remain due to stone migration, calculus fracture, or poor endoscopic visibility. Thermal damage is particularly undesirable for ureteral stone treatment. These risks are exacerbated when inexperienced operators perform procedures. Automatic tissue recognition technologies integrated into laser systems and controlling on/off-target radiation have the potential to improve the safety of the procedure. The aim of this multicenter prospective study was to evaluate the efficacy and safety of the automatic tissue recognition feature (Tissue Sensor, TS) in a new-generation Super-pulsed thulium fiber laser (SP TFL) for lithotripsy of kidney and ureteral stones. METHODS: This multicenter prospective study, approved by the Ethics Committee, included 70 patients with 101 stones (22 ureteral, 48 renal). Lithotripsy was performed using a SP TFL Urolase+ Premium (VPG Laserone, Russia) with TS function. The duration of the procedure, laser time, pedal on time, energy parameters, ablation efficiency, and effectiveness were assessed. Safety was assessed using the Traxer-Sierra scale (thermal damage assessment) and the Clavien-Dindo classification (complications). The impact of TS on the effectiveness and safety of the procedure was recorded using a standardized surgeon questionnaire. RESULTS: The efficiency coefficient of TS (laser time/pedal on time) was 54% for the ureter and 69% for the kidney, demonstrating active intervention of the system to prevent off-target radiation. The incidence of thermal injuries was minimal: in the ureter group, no injuries were observed in 64% of cases (n=14), and grade 1 injuries were recorded in 36% (n=8). In the kidney group, grade 1 injuries were noted in 52% (n=25), grade 2 injuries in 10% (n=5), and no injuries in 38% (n=18) of cases. Complications (Clavien-Dindo ≥ IIIa) were absent. The stone-free rate was 100% for the ureter and 97% for the kidney. Most surgeons (73% for the ureter and 56% for the kidney) noted that TS does not significantly affect the duration of the operation. CONCLUSIONS: The automatic tissue recognition feature Tissue Sensor in the SP TFL significantly improves the safety of lithotripsy by reducing the incidence and severity of thermal mucosal injuries. The system effectively prevents off-target laser radiation in complex anatomical conditions without significantly affecting surgical duration or ablation efficacy. This technology is particularly valuable for ensuring the safety of procedures performed by surgeons of varying experience levels.
