Thermal damage is particularly undesirable for ureteral stone treatment. These risks are exacerbated when inexperienced operators perform procedures. Automatic tissue recognition technologies integrated into laser systems and controlling on/off-target radiation have the potential to improve the safety of the procedure. The aim of this multicenter prospective study was to evaluate the efficacy and safety of the automatic tissue recognition feature (Tissue Sensor, TS) in a new-generation Super-pulsed thulium fiber laser (SP TFL) for lithotripsy of kidney and ureteral stones. METHODS: This multicenter prospective study, approved by the Ethics Committee, included 70 patients with 101 stones (22 ureteral, 48 renal). Lithotripsy was performed using a SP TFL Urolase+ Premium (VPG Laserone, Russia) with TS function. The duration of the procedure, laser time, pedal on time, energy parameters, ablation efficiency, and effectiveness were assessed. Safety was assessed using the Traxer-Sierra scale (thermal damage assessment) and the Clavien-Dindo classification (complications). The impact of TS on the effectiveness and safety of the procedure was recorded using a standardized surgeon questionnaire. RESULTS: The efficiency coefficient of TS (laser time/pedal on time) was 54% for the ureter and 69% for the kidney, demonstrating active intervention of the system to prevent off-target radiation. The incidence of thermal injuries was minimal: in the ureter group, no injuries were observed in 64% of cases (n=14), and grade 1 injuries were recorded in 36% (n=8). In the kidney group, grade 1 injuries were noted in 52% (n=25), grade 2 injuries in 10% (n=5), and no injuries in 38% (n=18) of cases. Complications (Clavien-Dindo ≥ IIIa) were absent. The stone-free rate was 100% for the ureter and 97% for the kidney. Most surgeons (73% for the ureter and 56% for the kidney) noted that TS does not significantly affect the duration of the operation. CONCLUSIONS: The automatic tissue recognition feature Tissue Sensor in the SP TFL significantly improves the safety of lithotripsy by reducing the incidence and severity of thermal mucosal injuries. The system effectively prevents off-target laser radiation in complex anatomical conditions without significantly affecting surgical duration or ablation efficacy. This technology is particularly valuable for ensuring the safety of procedures performed by surgeons of varying experience levels.

title: V02-02: All-in-One Stone Management: Complete Endourological Procedure Using Only a Steerable Suctioning Ureteroscope
parentSessionTitle: V02: Urolithiasis/Endourology
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Definitive treatment of large renal calculi traditionally involves the use of percutaneous nephrolithotomy (PCNL). However, this procedure carries significant risks, especially for patients with extensive comorbidities who may not be surgical candidates for PCNL. The new direct in scope suction (DISS) technology offers an opportunity to manage these large stone burdens in a less invasive way. The objective of this video presentation is to demonstrate the use of a DISS device as an “all-in-one” approach for cystoscopy, stent removal, renal access, stone fragmentation, and aspiration. METHODS: Definitive management of a 2.62 cm left renal stone for an 82 year old male patient was performed using the CVAC Aspiration System (Calyxo, Inc., Pleasanton, CA). The device was used to complete each procedural step, including cystoscopy, bilateral stent removal, ureteral and renal access, laser lithotripsy, and aspiration of stone fragments. The case was successfully completed without the use of a cystoscope, stent grasper, guidewire, ureteral access sheath, and ureteral stent. Only the floppy-tip introducer sheath was required to cannulate the ureteral orifice and advance into the kidney. This was replicated in four other cases. RESULTS: A total of 5 patients underwent the All-in-One Stone Management with the sole use of the DISS ureteroscope and nitinol basket. The average Charlson comorbidity index was 5.8 +/- 1.3 and average stone burden was 28 +/- 13 mm. 80% of patients were pre-stented and 80% of patients were left stent-free after the procedure. All surgeries were completed without intraoperative complications. Appropriate fluid irrigation and suction was maintained throughout the procedures without the use of ureteral access sheaths. CONCLUSIONS: In high-risk patients with large stone burdens who are poor candidates for PCNL, DISS systems offer an appropriate alternative treatment. We present the novel use of this system without the aid of cystoscopes, guidewires, or ureteral access sheaths showcasing the feasibility of this All-in-One stone management method. With this approach, patients can have a high likelihood to be left without a stent, significantly improving quality of life, and minimizing overall medical waste. | | | --- | | |

title: V02-03: Retro-mini-percutaneous nephrolithotomy: description of the technique, case series, and advantages of retroperitoneoscopic assistance in the treatment of patients with retro-renal organs
parentSessionTitle: V02: Urolithiasis/Endourology
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: European guidelines recommend percutaneous nephrolithotomy (PCNL) as the first-line treatment for kidney stones >2 cm. However, injury to surrounding organs remains a possible complication, with colonic injury occurring in 0.3–1% of cases. A retro-renal colon, present in 0.6% of the population, represents the main risk factor. Treating patients with large stones and retro-renally located organs close to the puncture pathway remains a challenge. Techniques such as ultrasound- or laparoscopic-assisted puncture have proven effective in reducing injury risk. Retroperitoneoscopy-assisted Mini-PCNL is a less described but potentially valuable alternative. This study aims to describe the technique and outcomes of Retro-mini-percutaneous nephrolithotomy (Retro-Mini-PCNL). METHODS: We report a 45-year-old patient with a horseshoe kidney and a 2 cm, 1500 UH left renal stone associated with a retro-renal colon. The patient was positioned laterally at 45°, ensuring optimal C-arm orientation. A ureteral occlusion catheter was placed for retrograde pyelography. Retroperitoneal access was achieved using a balloon trocar, followed by fluoroscopy-guided puncture using the 0/90° technique. Tract dilation was performed up to 18 Ch, allowing access with a 12 Ch nephroscope. Lithotripsy was achieved using a Ho:YAG laser, and fragments were retrieved with a basket. The collecting system was inspected with a 16 Ch flexible nephroscope. A 6 Ch × 26 cm double-J stent and a 12 Ch Foley nephrostomy were placed. Subsequent cases were performed in a 30° modified Galdakao position, achieving both retroperitoneal access and percutaneous puncture from a single side using a split-screen view, reducing trocars from three to two and enabling an ECIRS approach. RESULTS: We present the first European case series of Retro-Mini-PCNL, including four patients (three left-sided, one right-sided). Mean operative time was 3 h 54 min, and mean hospital stay was 5 days. One patient developed a Clavien-Dindo I complication (postoperative leukocytosis), and one a Clavien-Dindo IV (septic shock requiring ICU admission). The stone-free rate was 75% (3/4). CONCLUSIONS: Retroperitoneoscopy-assisted Mini-PCNL is a feasible and safe option for patients with retro-renal organs, providing direct visualization during puncture, reduced risk of visceral injury, and favorable clinical outcomes.

title: V02-04: Robotic-Assisted Mini-Percutaneous Nephrolithotomy with the MONARCH™ Platform, Urology
parentSessionTitle: V02: Urolithiasis/Endourology
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Percutaneous nephrolithotomy (PCNL) is the standard of care for treating large renal stones. The MONARCH™ Platform, Urology (Johnson & Johnson) is a novel FDA-cleared flexible robotic platform that combines robotic-assisted flexible ureteroscopy (URS) and mini-percutaneous nephrolithotomy (PCNL) with electromagnetically guided percutaneous access. METHODS: This is a 61-year-old male who presented with 2 cm lower pole stone and multiple interpolar stones for a total stone burden of 3.5 cm. The patient was taken to the operating room where a cystoscopy was performed and a ureteral access sheath placed. The robotic arms were positioned next to the patient and the ureteroscope advanced to the renal pelvis by using the handheld controller. An interpolar calyx was chosen for percutaneous access based on preoperative CT and intraoperative ureteroscopic evaluation. The electromagnetic guidance system was used to gain access into the intended calyx on the first attempt and a percutaneous sheath placed. The ureteroscope with a laser was used to fragment stones while a flexible percutaneous suction catheter removed stone fragments. The ureteroscope, laser, suction catheter as well as the fluidics system were controlled with a handheld controller. When the patient was deemed to be stone free by visual assessment of the collecting system the MONARCH™ system was undocked and a ureteral stent was placed. RESULTS: The operative time was 2 hours and 44 minutes. Imaging on POD1 showed no residual fragments and the patient was discharged from the hospital. The stent was removed one week later. The stone analysis showed calcium oxalate 82% and calcium phosphate 18%. The patient recovered without complications. CONCLUSIONS: Our initial experience suggests a future where MONARCH™ robot-assisted mini-PCNL may provide urologists with expanded capabilities for safe and effective treatment of select patients with nephrolithiasis.

title: V02-05: Simultaneous bilateral endoscopic surgery: Mini-percutaneous nephrolithotomy with pulsed Thulium YAG and flexible ureteroscope with Thulium laser fiber
parentSessionTitle: V02: Urolithiasis/Endourology
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Simultaneous bilateral endoscopic surgery (SBES) is a well-described and evolving technique for the treatment of bilateral renal stones in a single surgical session. The advantages of this approach include fewer hospital admissions, reduced need for anesthesia, and optimized use of surgical and hospital resources—while maintaining patient safety and achieving high stone-free rates with minimal complications. Several modalities of SBES exist, including simultaneous PCNL, simultaneous ureteroscopy, or a combination of both performed concurrently on each renal unit. The optimal choice of laser energy remains undefined, highlighting the need for further studies with newer laser technologies. METHODS: A 70-year-old female with a history of bilateral nephrolithiasis was diagnosed with bilateral renal stones. On the right side, stones were located in the lower calyceal group (LCG), with the largest measuring 14 mm and 1400 HU. On the left, stones were present in the middle and lower calyceal groups, measuring 7 mm and 14 mm, respectively, with 1190 HU. After an episode of obstructive pyelonephritis, bilateral double-J stents were placed. Under general anesthesia and in the Galdakao-modified supine Valdivia position, simultaneous 18 CH mini-PCNL was performed using a 0–90° puncture technique and balloon dilation to 18 CH with a high-pressure balloon. A 12 CH rigid nephroscope (“M” mini-perc set) was used. Lithotripsy of the right renal stones was performed using a pulsed Thulium:YAG laser. Subsequently, a flexible 18 CH cystoscope was used to access stones in other locations. On the left side, retrograde intrarenal surgery (RIRS) was performed using a 9.5 CH LithoVue flexible ureteroscope with Thulium Fiber Laser (TFL) in dusting mode. Bilateral double-J stents were left in place, and no nephrostomy tube was placed on the right. RESULTS: Operative time was 120 minutes, with no intraoperative or postoperative complications. The patient was discharged 16 hours after surgery. A follow-up CT scan revealed mild right-sided pelvicalyceal ectasia with narrowing at the ureteropelvic junction suggestive of ostium syndrome, but no significant residual stone fragments. CONCLUSIONS: SBES is a promising option for managing bilateral nephrolithiasis in a single session. However, careful patient selection remains critical for its successful implementation.

title: V02-06: Fluoroscopic-Free Ultrasound-Guided Percutaneous Nephrolithotomy: Surgical Technique
parentSessionTitle: V02: Urolithiasis/Endourology

speakers.organization: Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai

fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Historically, percutaneous nephrolithotomy (PCNL) has been performed with fluoroscopic guidance to establish access in the collecting system. However, use of intraoperative ultrasonography (US) has provided comparable outcomes while safely reducing radiation exposure and minimizing costs associated with fluoroscopy. Here, we present our technique for fluoroscopic-free US-guided PCNL. METHODS: The patient is a 45-year-old-female with an obstructing 1.5 centimeter proximal ureteral stone with moderate hydronephrosis. Once general anesthesia is established, the patient is placed in the supine flank-free position. First, complete sonographic assessment of the kidney is performed; Doppler mode is used to identify areas of increased vascularity to avoid when obtaining access. Under US guidance, an 18-gauge needle is inserted into the collecting system, and the needle’s depth of advancement is noted. A sensor wire is advanced into the collecting system and once confirmed sonographically, the needle is removed. All instruments are marked to the appropriate depth of advancement. The percutaneous tract is established through serial dilation with a 10Fr fascial dilator, followed by balloon dilation, and finally a 24Fr sheath – at each step, proper placement and depth of advancement is confirmed both sonographically and via markings made on the instruments. PCNL is then performed and all stone fragments are removed. Upon completion, a double-J stent is placed and stent position is confirmed endoscopically. RESULTS: Patient was discharged home on postoperative day 0 and stent was removed on postoperative day 9. She suffered no postoperative complications. Stone analysis showed stone composition of 90% calcium oxalate dihydrate, 5% calcium oxalate monohydrate, and 5% calcium phosphate. Between August-October 2025, 53 patients underwent fluoroscopic-free US-guided PCNL at our institution, of which 77% (n=41) were ambulatory and 57% (n=30) were totally tubeless. The median operative time was 59.2 minutes and no intra-operative complications were noted. 11% (n=6) of patients visited the ER postoperatively, and 7% (n=4) required readmission. CONCLUSIONS: Fluoroscopic-free US-guided PCNL is a feasible and effective technique for the surgical management of stone disease.

title: V02-07: Miniaturizing ureteroscopy: Novel use of an 8/10Fr ureteral dilator as a ureteral access sheath with a 6.3Fr single-use flexible ureteroscope
parentSessionTitle: V02: Urolithiasis/Endourology
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: The ureteral access sheath (UAS) is one of the most commonly employed tools during retrograde intrarenal surgery (RIRS). Flexible ureteroscope sizes have dictated UAS size, thus their relatively large size often raises concerns of ureteral wall ischemia and need for post-procedure stent placement. In some cases, insertion of the UAS is not possible or may cause ureteral injuries leading to case cancellations. The new 6.3Fr single-use flexible ureteroscopes offer new opportunities to miniaturize RIRS. The goal of this video is to demonstrate the feasibility of using an 8/10Fr ureteral dilator as a UAS with a 6.3Fr flexible ureteroscope in RIRS. METHODS: Definitive management of a right 11 mm renal stone for a 76 year old male patient was performed using the 6.3Fr single-use flexible ureteroscope (HugeMed, Inc., Shenzen, China). The ureteroscope is first used to place a sensor wire followed by passage of a standard 8/10Fr ureteral dilator. The wire and 8Fr dilator are then removed allowing easy passage of the 6.3Fr ureteroscope. The ureteral stone is fragmented in standard fashion and the renal stone is extracted through the 10Fr sheath without difficulty utilizing gravity irrigation. The case was successfully completed without the need for a post-procedure ureteral stent. This was replicated in five other cases. RESULTS: A total of 6 patients underwent the 8/10Fr UAS with a 6.3Fr flexible ureteroscope. Patients tended to be younger with an average age of 46.2 +/- 23.6 years and an average stone burden of 10.5 +/- 5.8 mm. All patients were not pre-stented and did not require stent placement at the conclusion of the procedure. All surgeries were completed without intraoperative complications with an average operative time of 31.2 +/- 8.3 minutes. CONCLUSIONS: We present the novel use of an 8/10Fr ureteral dilator as a UAS in conjunction with a 6.3Fr single-use flexible ureteroscope. This approach affords the benefits of a UAS while minimizing the trauma to the ureter that traditionally-sized UAS may cause and maintaining the 0.75 ureteroscope to sheath ratio described in the literature. Furthermore, this atraumatic approach reduces the need for post-procedure ureteral stent placement. Miniaturizing RIRS appears to be of special benefit for younger patients, patients with a history of ureteral stricture formation, or first-time stone formers who may have narrow ureters to begin with. | | | --- | | |

title: V02-08: The Fast and the Frictionless: Capabilities of a 6.3Fr Single-Use Digital Flexible Ureteroscope
parentSessionTitle: V02: Urolithiasis/Endourology
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: The advent of flexible ureteroscopy (URS) has transformed endourology, enabling safe and effective management of renal stones and upper tract urothelial carcinoma. However, traditional reusable ureteroscopes remain limited by progressive image degradation, instrument weight, and difficulty accessing narrow ureters due to scope diameter. The introduction of a thin single-use digital ureteroscope may potentially broaden clinical applications of URS. In this teaching video, we demonstrate the unique capabilities of a 6.3Fr flexible ureteroscope using real-world surgical scenarios. METHODS: Five representative clinical cases were collected to illustrate the range of performance of a 6.3Fr ureteroscope (HugeMed, China). All cases were performed by one of two surgeons at a tertiary academic center. Surgical footage was recorded and edited for educational presentation. Demonstrated applications included: wireless ureteric access and stent omission; upper tract tumor ablation; sheathless antegrade URS; office-based awake URS for oncologic surveillance; and endoscopic-guided percutaneous access for complex stone disease. Technical parameters such as operative feasibility, visual clarity, surgeon scope handling, were narratively reported. RESULTS: Across all five cases, the 6.3Fr ureteroscope demonstrated excellent image quality, maneuverability, and clinical versatility. 1. Stent omission for stones: surgical access was achieved without a guidewire or need for postoperative stent, with atraumatic passage under direct vision; 2. Tumor ablation: providing clear visualization and continuous irrigation through the 3.6Fr working channel; 3. Sheathless antegrade ureteroscopy for impacted ureteral stone: over a working wire without tract dilation or need for access sheath, allowing better two-handed control for fragmentation; 4. In-office awake URS: completed without general anesthesia, with the patient reporting minimal discomfort (pain score rated 0 - 1/10); and, 5. Endoscopic-guided percutaneous access: the slim profile allowed direct-vision puncture and tract dilation in the setting of a complete staghorn and tight space. No intraoperative complications occurred across all cases. CONCLUSIONS: The 6.3Fr single-use digital flexible ureteroscope demonstrates excellent visualization, ergonomics, and access capability across a wide spectrum of endourologic applications. Future work will clarify additional indications and technical limitations of these smaller diameter instruments, enabling more tailored, goal-directed surgical management.

title: V02-09: Tips and Techniques for Maximizing Efficiency with Flexible and Navigable Suction (FANS) Ureteral Access Sheaths
parentSessionTitle: V02: Urolithiasis/Endourology
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Flexible and Navigable Suction (FANS) ureteral access sheaths represent a significant advancement in retrograde intrarenal surgery (RIRS) by combining access and suction in a single device. The ClearPetra sheath is the first FANS system approved by the U. S. FDA (February 2024) and has been shown to have improved outcomes when compared to RIRS without suction and mini-percutaneous nephrolithotomy (PCNL). This video demonstrates tips and technical maneuvers to maximize efficiency and safety when using the ClearPetra access sheath. METHODS: Through a series of example videos, we showcase advanced techniques that may improve surgeon efficiency while utilizing a ClearPetra sheath. We detail indications for use, sheath anatomy, appropriate setup, and stepwise surgical maneuvers. RESULTS: Key technical insights are demonstrated throughout this video. Proper setup and selection of an appropriately sized sheath are essential for the safe and effective use of the ClearPetra system. Lasering stones located distal to the sheath enables passive suction of fine fragments and stone dust. Intra-sheath lasering is a safe and effective technique for dislodging and removing stones trapped within the sheath itself. For stone debris embedded in blood clots or located in challenging anatomical locations, gentle manipulation of the sheath against the calyces and renal pelvis, referred to as the “raking” maneuver, facilitates clearance. In cases where the sheath cannot access all calyces, simultaneous irrigation via the ureteroscope and aspiration through the ClearPetra helps mobilize and evacuate residual fragments. When used synergistically, these techniques significantly enhance the sheath’s overall utility and procedural efficiency. CONCLUSIONS: The ClearPetra FANS ureteral access sheath integrates suction and flexibility to improve visualization, efficiency, and stone clearance during ureteroscopy. Achieving optimal outcomes requires a thorough understanding of sheath anatomy, careful selection of sheath size, and proficiency in suction modulation techniques. These practical insights may help urologists safely adopt and fully leverage the advantages of FANS technology in retrograde stone surgery.

title: V02-10: Robotic retrograde intrarenal surgery using flexible and navigable suction ureteral access sheath (Robotic FANS-RIRS): Initial feasibility assessment with Zamenix robotic flexible ureteroscopy platform in a porcine model
parentSessionTitle: V02: Urolithiasis/Endourology
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: This study aims to evaluate the initial feasibility of robotic retrograde intrarenal surgery using a flexible and navigable suction ureteral access sheath (Robotic FANS-RIRS), with the Zamenix robotic flexible ureteroscopy platform. In this video, various robotic surgical techniques were assessed in a porcine model. METHODS: The Zamenix robotic system enables a single surgeon to control a ureteral access sheath (UAS), ureteroscope, and surgical tools (laser or basket) from a console. We enhanced the robot's capabilities by incorporating the flexible and navigable suction ureteral access sheath (FANS) and multiple control modes for both the FANS and ureteroscope. The following instruments were used: 7.5 Fr (HU30S), 9.5 Fr URS (Lithovue), 11/13 Fr FANS (ZSR), and a thulium fiber laser (EMS). We tested the accessibility to renal calyces, stone dusting, and the retrieval of stone fragments using active suction. An assistant controlled the vent slider on the FANS suction port during retrieval procedures. Ureteral injury was also assessed after the procedures. A total of eight artificial stones were used in this trial, distributed across three renal units in three pigs. RESULTS: Basic manipulation of the FANS and ureteroscope was successful, allowing access to all renal calyces. During the stone dusting procedure, stones were effectively trapped and pulverized while maintaining a stable position. A total of 26 active-suction extraction trials were performed, resulting in the removal of 35 stone fragments. All fragments were successfully extracted, with an average pull-out time of 37.3 seconds. One Grade I ureteral injury was observed postoperatively, likely related to initial ureteral dilation during FANS insertion. Insufficient suction pressure due to air leakage at the robot–FANS connector was identified as the primary factor limiting extraction efficiency. CONCLUSIONS: Robotic FANS-RIRS using the Zamenix robotic flexible ureteroscopy platform demonstrated technical feasibility in a porcine model, with all procedures successfully completed and no major safety issues identified. Further studies are needed to validate the efficacy of the system for clinical application.

title: V02-11: FAST-PCNL (Fluoroscopy free, Ambulatory, Supine, and Totally Tubeless Percutaneous Nephrolithotomy)
parentSessionTitle: V02: Urolithiasis/Endourology
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Percutaneous nephrolithotomy (PCNL) has evolved from a complex inpatient operation into a streamlined, minimally invasive procedure through steady progress in imaging, access, and instrumentation. The FAST-PCNL technique incorporates these modern refinements: ultrasound-guided access, supine positioning, a totally tubeless approach, and an ambulatory workflow into one cohesive system. The goal of this technique is to minimize radiation exposure, reduce operative time and hospital dependence, and simplify recovery, while maintaining the safety and stone-free outcomes of standard PCNL. METHODS: Between August and October 2025, 21 patients underwent FAST-PCNL. Procedures were performed entirely under ultrasound guidance in the modified supine position using endoscopic combined intrarenal surgery (ECIRS). After stone clearance was confirmed through dual antegrade and retrograde visualization, the tract was sealed with a hemostatic agent without nephrostomy or ureteral stent placement. All patients were monitored in PACU (Post Anesthesia Care Unit) and Phase 2 recovery before same-day discharge. Primary endpoints included intraoperative safety, operative time, and 30-day complications. RESULTS: There were no intraoperative complications and the mean operative time 54 minutes. All patients were discharged on the day of surgery with a mean total stay of 3 hours 50 minutes post-procedure. During the 30-day follow-up of 11 patients, one emergency visit and one hospital readmission were recorded. No secondary interventions were required. CONCLUSIONS: FAST-PCNL demonstrates that a radiation-free, supine, totally tubeless PCNL can be safely completed within a six-hour ambulatory window. By combining ultrasound guidance, ECIRS precision, and tubeless closure, this technique minimizes radiation exposure, hospital resource utilization, and postoperative morbidity while maintaining safety and efficiency in appropriately selected patients.

title: V02-12: Flexible and Navigable Suction Ureteral Access Sheath (FANS): Tips and Tricks on Effective Usage
parentSessionTitle: V02: Urolithiasis/Endourology
fulltext: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Flexible and navigable Suction Ureteral Access Sheaths (FANS) are a recent development in ureteral access sheaths that incorporate a suction mechanism along with a flexible tip allowing for more effective stone removal during flexible ureteroscopy (URS). In this video, we will describe the components of FANS and tips and tricks on how to effectively utilize a novel technique with FANS for treatment of renal and ureteral stones. METHODS: The FANS has several unique features. First, the flexible distal segment allows for full deflection into hard-to-reach calyces. The pressure vent has holes that allow for adjustment of aspiration pressure. The watertight rubber seal ensures air tightness and prevents leakage of irrigation fluid. The oblique side branch connects to a stone collection canister and vacuum suction that allows for aspiration of stone fragments. The canister has an on/off valve that allows for manual control of the suction pressure. RESULTS: For treatment of proximal ureteral stones using FANS, we recommend dusting at 0.3J and 60Hz while keeping the ventilation holes partially uncovered. We intermittently occlude the holes with our fingers to manually control the suction pressure. For treatment of renal stones, we recommend dusting at 0.3J and 120Hz with holmium pulse modulation for softer stones and fragmenting at 1-2J and 10-20Hz for harder stones. When extracting stone fragments after lasering, we recommend covering the ventilation holes completely with the tubing to allow for maximal suction. Keep the suction set between 150-200 mm Hg and irrigation pressure between 200 to 300 mm Hg. In general, try to use the shortest sheath length that can reach the calyces. Positioning the patient in slight reverse Trendelenburg can also aid in more efficient stone extraction. FANS can be very effective for small stones, which can be aspirated around the scope. Withdraw the scope only for larger stones which cannot be suctioned around the scope. This technique helps avoid the need for routine basketing. Intermittently switch the suction on and off to allow for effective suction while preserving good irrigation flow and visualization. If the stone fragments are too large or stuck inside the sheath, gently lasering while inside the sheath can assist with better suction and more efficient stone extraction. When withdrawing the scope, the tip of the scope should be deflected up or down to enhance the Venturi effect. CONCLUSIONS: FANS are the future of ureteroscopy and has several benefits including limiting intrarenal pressure while improving stone clearance rates and operative efficiency.
